free.upm-2019-gs1-1:
Gandhara schoolGreco-BactrianKushanasIndo-Hellenistic art

Gandhara art flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent (the Peshawar valley, Taxila, Swat and eastern Afghanistan) from about the first century BCE to the fifth century CE, reaching its peak under the Kushanas. The region lay on the Silk Road, where India met Bactria, Iran and Central Asia. Gandhara gave Buddhism some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form, expressing Indian themes in a Greco-Bactrian (Hellenistic) style for patrons from Central Asia.

1. Historical background

  • Greek legacy: Alexander's campaign (327–325 BCE), the Greco-Bactrian kingdom and the Indo-Greek kings such as Menander (Milinda) brought Hellenistic coins, cities and craftsmen to the north-west.
  • Central Asian rulers: the Shakas (Scythians), the Indo-Parthians (Gondophares at Taxila) and the Kushanas (from the Yuezhi of Central Asia) followed. Kanishka ruled from Purushapura (Peshawar) and patronised Buddhism.
  • Trade and contact: Silk Road commerce linked Gandhara with China, Central Asia and the Roman world, so Roman as well as Greek models reached its workshops.

2. Greco-Bactrian (Hellenistic) elements

  • Apollo-like Buddha: an oval face, straight nose, almond eyes and wavy hair gathered into a bun over the ushnisha recall the Greek god Apollo.
  • Drapery: a heavy, toga-like robe covers both shoulders and falls in thick, rhythmic folds, as in Greco-Roman statues.
  • Realism: careful modelling of muscles and anatomy; the Fasting Siddhartha from Sikri (Lahore Museum) shows every rib and vein.
  • Greek gods and motifs: Vajrapani appears as Herakles, and Hariti resembles the Greek Tyche; Atlas figures, garland-bearing cupids, acanthus leaves, Corinthian capitals, vine scrolls and Dionysian drinking scenes decorate stupas; one relief even shows the Trojan horse.

3. Central Asian elements

  • Costume of the steppe: donors and kings wear Scythian–Kushana dress, namely tunics, trousers, belts, cloaks and heavy boots.
  • Princely Bodhisattvas: Bodhisattvas are shown as Kushana nobles with turbans, moustaches and heavy jewellery; some Buddhas also have moustaches.
  • Iranian and Kushana royal symbols: the halo and the flaming shoulders seen on Kushana coins appear on Buddhas from Kapisa (Shotorak, Paitava).
  • Coins as a bridge: Kanishka's coins show a standing Buddha with the legend BODDO in Greek script, a Central Asian ruler honouring an Indian teacher in a Greek alphabet.

4. The Indian core

  • The themes, namely the life of the Buddha and the Jatakas, and the iconography (ushnisha, urna, long earlobes, mudras) remained Indian. Grey-blue schist, and later stucco, were the main materials; Mathura, under the same Kushanas, developed an indigenous style in red sandstone.

Gandhara was a true synthesis: a Hellenistic form with an Indian soul, made for Central Asian patrons. Through Bamiyan and the Silk Road it shaped Buddhist art in Central Asia, China and beyond, a symbol of India's cultural exchange with the world.
free.upm-2019-gs1-2:
Revolt of 1857Civil rebellionsTribal uprisingsSepoy mutinies

In the century between Plassey (1757) and 1857, British expansion provoked a long chain of resistance: civil rebellions of dispossessed rulers, zamindars and poligars; peasant and religious movements; tribal uprisings; and sepoy mutinies. The Revolt of 1857, which began at Meerut on 10 May 1857, gathered these scattered grievances into one great upheaval. It was their culmination, though it also went beyond them in scale and aim.

1. A century of local rebellions

  • Civil rebellions: the Poligar wars of the Tamil country (1799–1801), Velu Thampi's revolt in Travancore (1808–09), the Paika rebellion of Odisha (1817) and Kittur Chennamma's resistance (1824) were led by chiefs who had lost land and power.
  • Peasant and religious movements: the Sanyasi–Fakir rebellion in Bengal, the Faraizi movement of Haji Shariatullah and Dudu Miyan, the Wahabi movement and the Moplah outbreaks in Malabar mixed religious revival with anger against revenue, zamindars and moneylenders.
  • Tribal uprisings: the Kol (1831–32), Bhil and Khond risings and the Santhal hul (1855–56) of Sidhu and Kanhu resisted land alienation and outsiders (dikus).
  • Sepoy mutinies: Vellore (1806), over new dress rules seen as a threat to caste and religion, and Barrackpore (1824), over service in Burma, showed early discontent in the Company's army.

2. Why 1857 was their culmination

  • The same grievances, accumulated: heavy land revenue and evictions, ruined artisans, the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur), the annexation of Awadh (1856) and fear of religious interference had built up for decades.
  • The same social groups: dispossessed rulers (Nana Saheb, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal), zamindars (Kunwar Singh) and peasants joined the sepoys, who were largely peasants in uniform from Awadh.
  • The same form: like earlier risings, 1857 was led by traditional elites and sought to restore an older order, symbolised by the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar.
  • Traditions of defiance: earlier risings had exposed British vulnerability, and the Santhal hul had been crushed only in 1856.

3. How 1857 went beyond them

  • Scale and unity: sepoys and civilians rose together across Delhi, Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bundelkhand, Bihar and central India, and Hindus and Muslims fought side by side.
  • A political aim: proclaiming Bahadur Shah emperor of Hindustan challenged Company rule itself, not just a local grievance.
  • Old limitations persisted: much of the south, Bengal and Punjab stayed quiet, many princes and the educated middle class stayed loyal, and there was no unified plan.

The Revolt of 1857 was thus both the climax of traditional resistance and a turning point: it ended Company rule (Government of India Act, 1858) and left a memory of united struggle on which modern nationalism later built.
free.upm-2019-gs1-3:
Indian RenaissanceRationalismCultural prideNational consciousness

The nineteenth-century Indian Renaissance was an intellectual and cultural awakening, beginning in Bengal with Raja Ram Mohan Roy, that applied reason and humanism to religion and society and rediscovered India's past. Though largely socio-religious, it produced the ideas, institutions and self-confidence from which a shared national identity grew, leading to the political associations of the 1870s and the Indian National Congress (1885).

1. Rediscovery of the past and cultural pride

  • Orientalist scholarship: the Asiatic Society (1784, William Jones), translations of Sanskrit texts and James Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi (1837) revealed a great civilisation, including the age of Ashoka.
  • Reform through tradition: Ram Mohan Roy drew on the Upanishads; Dayanand Saraswati's Arya Samaj (1875) called for a return to the Vedas; Vivekananda's address at Chicago (1893) proclaimed India's spiritual message to the world.
  • Answer to colonial contempt: this pride countered the "civilising mission" and gave educated Indians confidence in their own heritage.

2. Reason, reform and a more equal society

  • Social reform: campaigns against sati (abolished 1829), for widow remarriage (Act of 1856, through Vidyasagar) and for women's education built the idea of equal individuals, the basis of a modern nation.
  • Challenge to caste: Jyotiba Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and Narayana Guru in Kerala questioned caste hierarchy, widening the idea of who belonged to the nation.
  • Modern education: Sayyid Ahmad Khan's Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875) brought modern learning to Muslims.

3. Language, literature and the press

  • Vernacular literature: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandamath (1882), with the song Vande Mataram, and writers in Hindi, Marathi and Tamil turned the motherland into an object of devotion.
  • Newspapers: the Amrita Bazar Patrika (1868), The Hindu (1878) and Kesari (1881) created an all-India reading public that debated colonial policy.
  • Cultural nationalism: the Hindu Mela (1867) promoted swadeshi goods and national feeling.

4. From cultural to political identity

  • Rights and economics: Ram Mohan Roy protested the press regulation of 1823; later, Dadabhai Naoroji and M.G. Ranade showed how colonial rule drained India's wealth.
  • Associations: the British Indian Association (1851), Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), Indian Association (1876) and Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) prepared the ground for the Congress.

5. Limitations

  • Narrow base: the Renaissance was mostly urban, upper-caste and English-educated.
  • Divided identities: religious revivalism, as in cow-protection and shuddhi campaigns, and the separate path of Aligarh also strengthened community identities that later fed communal politics.

The Indian Renaissance thus supplied the intellectual foundation of nationalism: reason, pride in the past and a shared public sphere. Its limits show why later leaders had to build a broader, inclusive nationalism.
free.upm-2019-gs1-4:
Coral bleachingZooxanthellaeOcean acidificationMarine heatwaves

Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny polyps that live in symbiosis with algae called zooxanthellae, which feed them and give them colour. Reefs cover a tiny fraction of the sea floor but support about a quarter of marine species. Because corals live close to their upper heat limit in warm, clear, shallow seas, global warming threatens them severely: the fourth global bleaching event (2023–25), confirmed by NOAA in April 2024, was the most widespread on record.

1. Warmer seas and bleaching

  • Mechanism: when water stays about 1°C above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, corals expel their zooxanthellae and turn white; if the stress continues, they starve and die.
  • Mass events: global bleaching events struck in 1998, 2010 and 2014–17; the fourth, from early 2023 to about mid-2025, exposed about 84% of the world's reef area to bleaching-level heat stress, with mass bleaching in at least 83 countries and territories (NOAA Coral Reef Watch).
  • Examples: the Great Barrier Reef suffered mass bleaching in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. In India, a CMFRI survey found severe bleaching of hard corals across the Lakshadweep islands after marine heatwaves from late October 2023, and reefs of the Gulf of Mannar and the Andamans have bleached in earlier warm years such as 1998 and 2010.

2. Ocean acidification

  • The ocean absorbs about a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions, forming carbonic acid. This lowers the carbonate ions that corals need to build their limestone skeletons, slowing growth and weakening reef structures so that they erode faster.

3. Other climate stresses

  • Sea-level rise: stressed, slow-growing reefs may not keep pace, so they lose light and atolls lose their natural barrier.
  • Stronger cyclones: intense storms break branching corals and bury reefs under sediment.
  • Disease and run-off: heat-stressed corals are more prone to disease, and heavy rain brings sediment and fresh water onto reefs.

4. Impact on the coral life system

  • Biodiversity loss: fish, molluscs and crustaceans lose food and shelter, and dead reefs turn into algae-dominated rubble.
  • Livelihoods and coasts: reef fisheries and tourism (the Maldives, Lakshadweep, the Andamans) decline, and coasts lose a wave barrier.
  • Bleak projections: the IPCC Special Report on 1.5°C (2018) projected a 70–90% decline of warm-water reefs at 1.5°C and over 99% at 2°C. The Global Tipping Points Report (October 2025) warned that warm-water reefs are already passing their thermal tipping point, estimated at about 1.2°C of warming (range 1–1.5°C).

5. Way forward

  • Deep emission cuts under the Paris Agreement, protected areas such as the Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park and Biosphere Reserve, legal protection of corals under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, coral restoration, and reducing local stress from pollution, sand mining and overfishing.

Coral reefs are the early warning system of climate change; saving them needs both global mitigation and local reef resilience.
free.upm-2019-gs1-5:
MangrovesCoastal squeezeBio-shieldBlue carbon

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees and shrubs of tropical and subtropical tidal coasts, adapted to saline, waterlogged mud through breathing roots (pneumatophores), stilt roots and vivipary. India has 4,992 sq km of mangroves (ISFR 2023), the largest stretch in the Sundarbans. Worldwide, they are under severe pressure: IUCN's first global Red List of Ecosystems assessment of mangroves (May 2024) found half of the mangrove ecosystems assessed at risk of collapse.

1. Causes of depletion

  • Aquaculture and agriculture: conversion of mangroves into shrimp and fish ponds, rice fields and salt pans is the leading cause in South and Southeast Asia, including India's east coast.
  • Urban and industrial expansion: land reclamation for housing, ports, roads and industries, as around Mumbai, removes mangroves directly.
  • Less fresh water and silt: dams and diversions upstream reduce the freshwater flow and sediment that mangroves need, raising salinity, as in the Indus delta.
  • Pollution and over-harvesting: oil spills, sewage and plastics choke breathing roots, while cutting for fuelwood, fodder and timber thins the forests.
  • Climate change: rising seas squeeze mangroves against embankments and seawalls (coastal squeeze), and severe cyclones such as Amphan (2020) damage them; IUCN found climate change threatens a third of the mangrove ecosystems it assessed.

2. Importance in coastal ecology

  • Bio-shield: dense roots and trunks absorb wave energy and storm surges. A study of the 1999 Odisha super cyclone (Das and Vincent, 2009) found fewer deaths in villages behind wider mangrove belts.
  • Erosion control and land building: roots trap sediment, stabilise shorelines and help deltas grow.
  • Nursery and food web: fallen leaves become detritus, the base of the coastal food chain, and sheltered creeks serve as breeding and nursery grounds for fish, prawns and crabs that support fisheries.
  • Filters: mangroves trap sediment and absorb nutrients and pollutants, protecting seagrass beds and coral reefs offshore.
  • Blue carbon: their waterlogged soils store carbon for centuries, often much more per hectare than land forests, making them important carbon sinks.
  • Biodiversity: the Sundarbans tiger, the saltwater crocodiles of Bhitarkanika and the fishing cat of Coringa depend on them.

3. Conservation efforts

  • Law and planning: the CRZ Notification, 2019 treats mangroves as ecologically sensitive areas; Bhitarkanika and Coringa are protected.
  • Restoration: MISHTI (2023) promotes mangrove plantation on India's coasts, and India is a member of the Mangrove Alliance for Climate (launched at COP27, 2022).
  • Community management: the M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation's joint mangrove management, with fishbone canals at Pichavaram, shows how local people can restore degraded mangroves.

Mangroves are a low-cost, nature-based solution to coastal hazards and climate change; halting conversion and involving coastal communities are vital for coastal resilience.
free.upm-2019-gs1-6:
Resource-based manufacturingLabour-intensive clustersValue additionEmployment

Regional resource-based manufacturing means setting up processing industries close to a region's own resources, namely farm produce, milk, forests, fish, minerals and traditional crafts, so that value is added where the resource is produced. India needs such jobs: nearly half of its workforce is still in agriculture (PLFS), much of it underemployed. With the right support, this strategy can generate large-scale, local and labour-intensive employment.

1. How it promotes employment

  • Labour-intensive industries: food processing, textiles, leather, bamboo, handicrafts and coir absorb low- and semi-skilled workers, many of them women.
  • Jobs near home: units in rural areas and small towns absorb surplus farm labour and reduce distress migration to big cities.
  • Linkages and multipliers: suppliers of raw materials, transport, packaging, storage and marketing all gain, so each processing unit creates indirect jobs.
  • Better incomes for producers: value addition and less wastage raise the incomes of farmers, fishers, forest dwellers and artisans; Amul's dairy cooperatives in Gujarat are the classic example.
  • Exports and clusters: Tiruppur knitwear, Moradabad brassware, Firozabad glass, Bhadohi carpets and Kerala coir show how regional clusters create jobs on a large scale.

2. Policy support

  • One District One Product (ODOP), begun in Uttar Pradesh (2018) and now national, promotes one product per district.
  • PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME, 2020) supports small food units, and the PLI scheme supports large food processors.
  • PM MITRA textile parks (seven parks), SFURTI clusters for traditional industries and Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (2018) for minor forest produce add common facilities and market links.

3. Limitations

  • Capital-intensive mineral industries: steel, aluminium and cement create few jobs per rupee invested and often displace tribal people; mineral-rich Jharkhand and Odisha remain poor (the "resource curse").
  • Infrastructure gaps: poor roads, unreliable power, a lack of cold chains and weak market access limit small units.
  • Small scale and low productivity: most units are micro and informal, short of credit, skills and technology, and face cheap imports.
  • Environmental costs: tanneries, mining and some food units pollute rivers and land unless regulated.

4. What will make it work

  • Skilling linked to clusters, credit for MSMEs, farmer producer organisations, logistics under PM Gati Shakti, GI tags and branding, and strict environmental safeguards.

Yes, regional resource-based manufacturing can promote employment and balanced regional development, especially in agro, forest, marine and craft sectors. Its success depends on infrastructure, skills and markets, so that it complements the drive for inclusive industrialisation.
free.upm-2019-gs1-7:
Agro-processingLocalisation factorsGreen Revolution beltMarket access

Agro-based food processing turns crops, milk and fruit into flour, rice, sugar, dairy products, edible oil, snacks and juices. North-West India, namely Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, has become one of India's main hubs because of the Green Revolution surplus, assured irrigation and nearness to the vast market of the National Capital Region. Its location follows Alfred Weber's logic that industries using bulky, perishable or weight-losing raw materials locate close to their source.

1. Raw-material factors

  • Grain surplus: wheat and rice, including basmati, feed flour, rice and biscuit mills; the GI-registered basmati area covers Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Sugarcane: cane must be crushed soon after harvest, so sugar mills, khandsari and jaggery units cluster in western UP (Muzaffarnagar, Meerut, Shamli).
  • Milk: Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan have high per-capita milk availability, supporting cooperative dairies (Verka, Vita, Saras) and private dairies; Nestlé set up its first Indian factory at Moga, Punjab, in 1961 around local milk collection.
  • Horticulture and oilseeds: kinnow around Abohar–Fazilka, potatoes in the Jalandhar belt, Rajasthan's mustard for oil mills, guar for guar gum, and bajra and moth for snacks such as Bikaneri bhujia (GI).

2. Physical and infrastructure factors

  • Irrigation: the Bhakra–Nangal system, the Indira Gandhi Canal and tube wells assure two crops a year and a steady supply.
  • Procurement and storage: dense regulated mandis, procurement by FCI and State agencies, and large warehouses ensure reliable bulk supply.
  • Transport: a dense road and rail network, and the Western and Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridors, link the region to NCR and to the western ports for exports such as basmati.
  • Power and finance: good rural electrification and bank networks support mills and cold storage.

3. Market and human factors

  • Huge market: the NCR's large, affluent and growing urban population demands packaged and ready-to-eat foods.
  • Entrepreneurship and capital: Green Revolution savings, Punjabi and Marwari business networks, and cooperatives built a base of agro-entrepreneurs.
  • Policy support: food parks, PMFME and ODOP, and State agro-industries corporations encourage investment.
  • Labour: migrant workers from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar provide a large labour force.

4. Constraints

  • The share of produce processed is still low; the rice–wheat cycle drains groundwater (Punjab extracts about 156% of its extractable groundwater, CGWB 2025); and crop-residue burning, small holdings and a weak cold chain limit diversification.

North-West India's agro-processing rests on raw material, irrigation, infrastructure and markets together. Diversifying into fruits, vegetables, dairy and paddy-straw-based units would raise farm incomes while easing the region's water stress.
free.upm-2019-gs1-8:
Cultural continuityUnity in diversitySyncretismAdaptive tradition

India is one of the world's oldest continuous civilisations. Unlike ancient Egypt or Mesopotamia, whose religions and scripts died out, India still chants Vedic hymns, retells the epics, practises yoga and celebrates festivals rooted in antiquity. This continuity comes from a society that absorbs rather than rejects new influences, holds its diversity together through shared practices, and adapts tradition to modern life instead of breaking with it.

1. Tolerance, assimilation and syncretism

  • Absorbing newcomers: Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas, Turks, Mughals, Parsis, Jews and Syrian Christians all found a place, each adding to a composite culture.
  • Synthesis: the Bhakti and Sufi movements, Hindustani music, Indo-Islamic architecture and the Ganga–Jamuni tehzeeb blended traditions.
  • Pluralism of belief: the Rig Vedic idea that truth is one though the wise call it by many names allowed many paths to coexist.

2. Social institutions as carriers

  • Family and kinship: life-cycle rituals (samskaras), elders and joint-family values pass customs, language and food habits to each generation.
  • Community and caste: jatis preserved crafts, customs and dialects over centuries, though they also preserved inequality.
  • Oral and guru–shishya traditions: Vedic chanting, gharanas of music and dance, and folk theatre transmit knowledge person to person; Vedic chanting, Ramlila and Kutiyattam are on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

3. Religion, festivals and sacred geography

  • Festivals tied to nature: harvest festivals such as Pongal, Baisakhi, Onam and Bihu link culture to the agricultural year.
  • Pilgrimage networks: the Kumbh Mela (UNESCO intangible heritage, 2017), the char dham and the jyotirlingas knit distant regions into one cultural space.
  • Great and little traditions: the Sanskritic great tradition and local folk traditions constantly borrow from each other, as McKim Marriott showed in his study of Kishan Garhi (universalisation and parochialisation).

4. Adaptability to change

  • Change without rupture: M.N. Srinivas's Sanskritisation and Westernisation, and Yogendra Singh's Modernization of Indian Tradition (1973), show tradition adapting rather than disappearing.
  • Compartmentalisation: Milton Singer found industrial leaders in Madras who were modern at work and traditional at home.
  • New media: television, the internet and the diaspora spread festivals, music and epics; the International Day of Yoga (since 2015) and Garba's UNESCO listing (2023) carry them worldwide.

5. Constitutional and state support

  • Article 29 protects the distinct language, script and culture of any section of citizens, and Article 51A(f) makes it a fundamental duty to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture; the Ministry of Culture and its academies support the arts.

India's uniqueness lies in unity in diversity and the ability to modernise without losing its roots. Globalisation and consumerism are new tests, but India's long record of adaptive resilience suggests that its culture will be renewed rather than replaced.
free.upm-2019-gs1-9:
Women's empowermentTotal fertility rateReproductive rightsICPD 1994

India's total fertility rate (TFR) has fallen to 1.9 (SRS 2024), below the replacement level of 2.1, but it still ranges from 2.9 in Bihar to 1.2 in Delhi, and a young age structure will keep the population growing for some decades. The International Conference on Population and Development (Cairo, 1994) shifted population policy from targets to rights, holding that women's empowerment, through education, health, work and choice, is the most lasting way to lower fertility.

1. How empowerment lowers fertility

  • Education: NFHS-5 shows a TFR of about 2.8 for women with no schooling against about 1.8 for those with 12 or more years of schooling; educated women marry later, know about contraception and invest more in fewer children.
  • Later marriage: 23.3% of women aged 20–24 were married before 18 (NFHS-5); delaying marriage delays the first birth and shortens the reproductive span (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006).
  • Work and income: paid work raises the opportunity cost of frequent childbearing and gives women a say at home; female labour force participation is only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Decision-making: women who control resources can act on their own fertility preferences; the unmet need for family planning was 9.4% (NFHS-5).
  • Child survival: educated, healthy mothers have healthier children, so families no longer need extra births as insurance against child deaths.

2. Evidence

  • Kerala and Tamil Nadu: high female literacy, good health care and women's autonomy brought fertility down early, at modest income levels.
  • Bangladesh: girls' schooling, women's work in the garment sector, and NGO and family-planning outreach cut fertility sharply despite poverty.
  • High-fertility States: Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have lower female literacy, earlier marriage and less female autonomy.

3. Why empowerment alone is not enough

  • Services: contraceptive access and choice matter; Mission Parivar Vikas (2016) widens choices in high-fertility districts.
  • Men's role: female sterilisation (37.9% of married women) far outweighs male sterilisation (0.3%), and about 35% of men see contraception as a woman's business (NFHS-5).
  • Development and norms: poverty, old-age insecurity, son preference and religious and cultural norms also shape family size.
  • No coercion: the forced sterilisations of the Emergency (1975–77) set family planning back for years; India adopted a target-free approach in 1996.

4. Way forward

  • Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, ending child marriage, women's self-help groups under DAY-NRLM, maternal and child health care, and male involvement in family planning.

Empowering women is the most humane and lasting key to population stabilisation, but it must be combined with health services, men's responsibility and development; India's challenge now shifts from controlling numbers to building human capital.
free.upm-2019-gs1-10:
Indian secularismPrincipled distanceEssential religious practicesConstitutional morality

Secularism was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and held to be a basic feature of the Constitution in S.R. Bommai (1994). Indian secularism is not a wall of separation but principled distance (Rajeev Bhargava): equal respect for all faiths, with the State free to reform practices that violate rights (Article 25(2)(b)). Since Indian culture is deeply interwoven with religion, applying secularism to cultural practices creates several challenges.

1. Judges deciding what is "essential"

  • The test: since Shirur Mutt (1954), only essential religious practices get the protection of Article 25; critics say this makes judges theologians.
  • Contested rulings: Ismail Faruqui (1994) held that a mosque is not essential to Islam for namaz; the hijab ban in Karnataka classrooms was upheld by the High Court (2022) but produced a split verdict in the Supreme Court (October 2022).
  • Constitutional morality versus faith: in the Sabarimala case (2018) the majority struck down the bar on women aged 10–50, while Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent warned courts against interfering in deep matters of faith; wider questions were referred to a larger bench in 2019.

2. Reform versus tradition

  • Gender justice: instant triple talaq was struck down (Shayara Bano, 2017) and the Bombay High Court opened the Haji Ali dargah's sanctum to women (2016); reformers welcomed these rulings, while some saw them as State intrusion.
  • Animal welfare and environment: the 2014 ban on jallikattu provoked mass protests in 2017 and a new Tamil Nadu law, which a Constitution Bench upheld in May 2023; limits on firecrackers (green crackers, Arjun Gopal, 2018), idol immersion and loudspeakers are seen by some as targeting festivals.
  • Personal laws: the Uniform Civil Code debate (Article 44) pits equality against community customs; Uttarakhand's UCC (in force from January 2025) exempts Scheduled Tribes.

3. Political contest over the word

  • Charges of selectivity: the reversal of the Shah Bano judgment (1986 Act) led to allegations of minority appeasement, while minorities complain of pressure on their food, dress and conversions.
  • Religion in public life: ground-breaking pujas, lamp-lighting, school prayers and yoga are seen as culture by some and religion by others; a challenge to the Sanskrit morning prayer in Kendriya Vidyalayas was referred to a Constitution Bench (2019).

4. Deeper social challenges

  • Loss of shared practices: when identities harden, syncretic traditions, such as Hindus visiting dargahs or Muslims performing in Ramlilas, weaken.
  • Tradition as backward: a narrow, Western-style reading of secularism can treat all tradition as superstition, alienating believers.

The way forward is a contextual secularism: courts should protect individual rights with restraint, reform should come through dialogue within communities, and citizens should honour their duty to value India's composite culture (Article 51A(f)).
free.upm-2019-gs1-11:
Gandhian phaseMass nationalismPlural voicesSocial justice

The Gandhian phase (1917–47), from Champaran to independence, turned the national movement into a mass struggle through satyagraha, non-cooperation and civil disobedience. Yet it was never a single voice. Socialists, revolutionaries, Dalit and non-Brahmin leaders, women, peasants, workers, tribals, the Khudai Khidmatgars and the people of the princely states brought their own demands and methods. Their dialogue, and at times disagreement, with Gandhi widened the movement's social base and enriched its goals.

1. Left and radical voices

  • Socialists: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pushed the Congress to adopt Purna Swaraj (Lahore, 1929); the Karachi resolution (1931) on fundamental rights and an economic programme, and the Congress Socialist Party (1934) of Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev and Ram Manohar Lohia, added economic justice to freedom.
  • Revolutionaries: the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) of Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad, and Surya Sen's Chittagong armoury raid (1930), inspired youth by their sacrifice and spread socialist ideas.
  • Bose and the INA: the Forward Bloc (1939) and the Indian National Army; the INA trials (1945–46) united the country across communities.

2. Voices of social justice

  • B.R. Ambedkar: the Mahad satyagraha (1927), the Kalaram temple entry movement (1930) and the Poona Pact (1932) put the rights of the depressed classes at the centre of national politics; Gandhi responded with the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932).
  • South India: the Vaikom satyagraha (1924–25) and the Guruvayur satyagraha (1931–32) fought untouchability; Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (1925) challenged caste and Brahminical dominance.

3. Women

  • Leadership: Sarojini Naidu presided over the Kanpur Congress (1925), and Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay was prominent in the salt satyagraha.
  • Mass participation: thousands of women picketed liquor and foreign-cloth shops during civil disobedience; in Quit India, Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank and Usha Mehta ran the underground Congress Radio.

4. Regional, tribal and community voices

  • North-West Frontier: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars (1929), the "Red Shirts", made non-violence a creed among the Pathans.
  • Tribals: Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa rebellion (1922–24) and Rani Gaidinliu's movement in the Naga hills joined tribal grievances to the anti-colonial struggle.
  • Peasants and workers: Kheda (1918) and Bardoli (1928, Vallabhbhai Patel) showed the power of peasant satyagraha; the AITUC (1920) and the All India Kisan Sabha (1936) organised labour and peasants, and the Faizpur Congress (1936) adopted an agrarian programme.
  • Princely states and Muslims: the All India States People's Conference (1927) and Praja Mandals carried the struggle into the states; Maulana Azad and the Khilafat leaders brought Muslims into the Non-Cooperation Movement.

5. How these voices enriched the movement

  • They broadened its base beyond the urban middle class, and added social and economic justice to political freedom. Their demands later shaped the Constitution: Article 17 abolished untouchability, fundamental rights echoed Karachi, and zamindari was abolished.

Gandhi provided the mass framework, but the movement was a plural coalition; its debates and diversity made Indian nationalism democratic, inclusive and forward-looking.
free.upm-2019-gs1-12:
Transfer of powerDivide and ruleCripps MissionPartition

By the 1940s independence had become a question of when, not whether: the Second World War weakened Britain, and the Quit India Movement (1942), the INA trials and the naval mutiny (1946) showed that British rule could not last. Yet the British imperial power, through its wartime offers, vetoes and timing, made the transfer of power far more complicated: it strengthened the Muslim League's veto, left the princely states adrift and finally partitioned India in haste.

1. Wartime politics (1939–42)

  • War without consent: Viceroy Linlithgow declared India a party to the war in September 1939 without consulting Indian leaders; the Congress ministries resigned, and the League celebrated a "Day of Deliverance".
  • August Offer (1940): promised dominion status as the goal, but assured minorities that no constitution would be adopted without their consent, in effect a veto for the League.
  • Cripps Mission (1942): offered dominion status after the war and a constituent assembly, but allowed provinces to stay out of the Union, the first official acceptance of the possibility of Pakistan; it gave no real power at once.
  • Repression: Quit India was crushed and Congress leaders jailed, while the League expanded freely.

2. Encouraging the communal veto (1945–46)

  • Simla Conference (1945): Wavell let his plan collapse when Jinnah insisted that the League alone nominate all Muslim members, accepting the League's veto.
  • Cabinet Mission (1946): it rejected a sovereign Pakistan but proposed a weak Centre and groups of provinces, leaving unclear whether grouping was compulsory; each side read it differently, and the League's Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) unleashed the Calcutta killings.
  • Interim Government: the League joined it in October 1946 without accepting the long-term plan, and obstructed from within.

3. Haste and abdication (1947)

  • Attlee's deadline: the statement of 20 February 1947 fixed June 1948 for withdrawal and hinted that power might pass to more than one authority, encouraging a scramble for territory.
  • Mountbatten's acceleration: the 3 June Plan conceded partition and advanced the date to 15 August 1947, leaving barely ten weeks to divide armies, assets and services.
  • Radcliffe Line: drawn in about five weeks by a man new to India, and announced only on 17 August, it left millions uncertain of their country; mass migration and killings followed.
  • Princely states: the Indian Independence Act, 1947 ended paramountcy, leaving over 560 states free to choose; Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir became flashpoints.

4. Deeper roots and balance

  • Divide and rule: separate electorates (1909), the Communal Award (1932) and treating the League as the sole Muslim spokesman, despite its weak showing in 1937, built the communal deadlock.
  • Indian factors too: Congress–League mistrust, the failure of coalitions after 1937 and rising communal violence also played a part.

Britain's priority was a quick, face-saving exit that protected its interests, not an orderly transfer of power. The price, partition, mass violence and the Kashmir dispute, shows how imperial policy shaped the birth of two nations.
free.upm-2019-gs1-13:
Popular sovereigntyRights of ManConstitutionalismNationalism

The American Revolution (1775–83) and the French Revolution (1789) were the twin Atlantic revolutions that replaced the divine right of kings with popular sovereignty. Inspired by Enlightenment thinkers such as Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau, they produced the Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), the US Constitution (1787) and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (August 1789), documents that still shape the modern democratic state.

1. Political foundations

  • Government by consent: the American Declaration held that governments derive their powers from the consent of the governed; France abolished its monarchy and became a republic in 1792.
  • Written constitutions: the US Constitution (1787) is the oldest written national constitution still in force; it introduced federalism, a separation of powers based on Montesquieu, and checks and balances; judicial review followed in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
  • Representative democracy: elected legislatures and the idea of citizens rather than subjects spread; France's National Convention (1792) was elected on universal male suffrage.

2. Rights and equality

  • Bill of Rights (1791): freedom of speech, religion, press and assembly and due process became enforceable limits on government.
  • Rights of Man (1789): liberty, equality before law, property and resistance to oppression; liberty, equality and fraternity became the watchword of modern politics.
  • End of feudal privilege: on 4 August 1789 France abolished feudal dues and the privileges of the clergy and nobility, and slavery in French colonies was abolished in 1794 (restored by Napoleon in 1802).
  • Secular state: the First Amendment barred Congress from establishing a religion, and revolutionary France confiscated church lands.

3. Nationalism and the nation-state

  • The nation as sovereign: the French made the nation, not the king, the source of authority; the levée en masse (1793), the tricolour and the Marseillaise built a national army and identity.
  • Spread by Napoleon: the Napoleonic Code (1804) carried legal equality and property rights across Europe, and resistance to Napoleon awakened nationalism in Germany, Italy and Spain.
  • Anti-colonial example: the United States was the first colony in the Americas to win independence; Haiti (1804) and the Latin American revolutions under Bolívar followed.

4. Economic and social modernity

  • Abolition of guilds and internal customs, protection of property and free enterprise helped the rise of the middle class; France introduced the metric system and a rational administration of departments.

5. Limitations

  • Women were excluded; Olympe de Gouges answered with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791). Slavery survived in the US, and the Terror (1793–94) showed how revolutions can devour liberty.

These revolutions laid the foundations of the modern world: constitutional government, rights, nationalism and secularism. India's Constitution reflects both, with liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble and fundamental rights with judicial review, as does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948).
free.upm-2019-gs1-14:
Water stressFalkenmark indicatorGroundwater depletionRegional variation

Water stress occurs when the demand for fresh water exceeds the available supply, or when poor quality restricts its use. By the Falkenmark indicator, a country with less than 1,700 m³ of renewable water per person a year is water-stressed, below 1,000 m³ water-scarce and below 500 m³ absolutely scarce. India's per-capita availability fell from 1,545 m³ (2011) to 1,486 m³ (2021), so the country as a whole is water-stressed, but the stress varies sharply by region.

1. How water stress differs regionally

  • Overall: India has about 18% of the world's people but 4% of its freshwater, and NITI Aayog's Composite Water Management Index (2018) found about 60 crore people facing high to extreme water stress. The CGWB's 2025 assessment put national groundwater extraction at about 61% of the extractable resource, but in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan extraction exceeds recharge, while the eastern and north-eastern States still have unused potential.

2. Why it differs: physical factors

  • Rainfall: annual rain exceeds 200 cm on the west coast and in the North-East but is under 50 cm in western Rajasthan and Ladakh; most of it falls in June–September, so storage decides availability.
  • Aquifers: the thick alluvium of the Indo-Gangetic plain stores vast groundwater, while the basalt and granite of the peninsula hold little, so wells there fail in dry years.
  • Rivers: snow-fed Himalayan rivers are perennial, while peninsular rivers are seasonal; the Brahmaputra basin has a surplus, whereas the Cauvery, Pennar and Sabarmati basins are stressed.
  • Rain-shadow: the leeward side of the Western Ghats receives little rain and frequent droughts.

3. Why it differs: human factors

  • Cropping patterns: water-hungry paddy in Punjab and sugarcane in Maharashtra's dry districts mine groundwater; agriculture uses about 80% of the water withdrawn.
  • Policies: free or flat-rate farm power and the lack of metering encourage over-pumping.
  • Urbanisation: cities have built over their lakes and floodplains; Chennai's reservoirs ran dry in 2019.
  • Pollution: sewage and industrial effluents make river water, as in the Yamuna, unusable.
  • Climate change: erratic monsoons, heat waves and glacier retreat add uncertainty.

4. Measures

  • Jal Jeevan Mission, Atal Bhujal Yojana (community groundwater management in seven States), Jal Shakti Abhiyan's "Catch the Rain", Mission Amrit Sarovar, micro-irrigation under Per Drop More Crop, crop diversification and reuse of treated wastewater.

India's water stress is regionally differentiated, so solutions must be too: basin-level planning, aquifer mapping and region-specific crops and pricing, turning a quantity crisis into one of water governance.
free.upm-2019-gs1-15:
Mountain ecosystemsCarrying capacityEco-restorationSustainable tourism

Mountain ecosystems such as the Himalaya and the Western Ghats are water towers, biodiversity hotspots and homes of distinct cultures, but their steep slopes, young rocks and seismic activity make them fragile. Roads, hydropower projects, tunnels, unplanned towns and mass tourism have exceeded their carrying capacity, as the Kedarnath disaster (2013), the Chamoli flood (2021), the Joshimath subsidence (2023) and the Wayanad landslides (2024) show. Restoring them needs ecological, regulatory and community action together.

1. The damage done

  • Infrastructure: road widening, blasting and tunnelling destabilise slopes; muck is dumped into rivers; hydropower projects alter rivers, and the 2021 Chamoli flood washed away the Rishiganga project and badly damaged the Tapovan–Vishnugad project.
  • Tourism: crowds and vehicles choke hill stations such as Shimla, Manali and Mussoorie, plastic litters trekking routes, and hotels crowd riverbanks and slopes.
  • Forests: deforestation and pine plantations reduce water retention and fuel fires.
  • Climate stress: warming accelerates glacier retreat and raises the risk of glacial-lake outbursts, such as Sikkim's South Lhonak lake (October 2023).

2. Ecological restoration

  • Native forests: replant broad-leaved native species such as oak instead of fire-prone pine; treat the catchments of dams.
  • Slope bio-engineering: stabilise slopes with grasses, shrubs, retaining structures and proper drainage, and dispose of muck scientifically.
  • Springshed management: Sikkim's Dhara Vikas programme recharges drying springs through trenches and ponds in their recharge zones.
  • Glaciers and wetlands: protect high-altitude lakes and meadows; the UN declared 2025 the International Year of Glaciers' Preservation.

3. Regulating development

  • Carrying-capacity studies: set limits on buildings, vehicles and visitors for each town and valley; the NGT has capped vehicles going to the Rohtang Pass.
  • Cumulative impact assessment: assess cascades of dams and roads together, not project by project; after 2013, an expert body under Ravi Chopra examined the role of hydropower projects in the disaster.
  • Eco-sensitive zones: follow zoning such as the Doon Valley notification (1989) and the Gadgil (2011) and Kasturirangan (2013) reports on the Western Ghats; enforce building codes and ban construction on unstable slopes and floodplains.
  • National programmes: the National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem under the NAPCC (2008) and SECURE Himalaya (UNDP–GEF) link conservation with livelihoods.

4. Sustainable tourism

  • Community-based eco-tourism: homestays in Ladakh, Spiti and Sikkim keep income local and footprints small.
  • Pricing and limits: Bhutan's high-value, low-volume tourism policy, with a Sustainable Development Fee on tourists, shows how fees and caps can protect fragile areas.
  • Waste and transport: plastic bans, carry-back rules on treks, waste fees and electric shuttles reduce pollution.

5. People at the centre

  • Uttarakhand's Van Panchayats and the legacy of Chipko (1973) show that local communities protect forests best; forest rights, women's groups and payment for ecosystem services can reward conservation.

Mountains cannot be developed like the plains. Ecology-sensitive planning, respect for carrying capacity and community stewardship can turn mountain development into sustainable mountain development.
free.upm-2019-gs1-16:
Urban mass transportAgglomeration economiesTransit-oriented developmentInclusive growth

About 70% of India's population growth up to 2036 is projected to occur in urban areas (Technical Group on Population Projections, 2020). Urban mass transport, namely buses, metro, suburban rail and regional rapid transit, moves large numbers efficiently at a low cost per passenger. India's metro network, including the Delhi–Meerut Namo Bharat corridor, has grown to about 1,095 km in 26 cities (PIB, March 2026), the world's third largest. Efficient and affordable transit turns crowded cities into productive agglomeration economies.

1. Economic productivity

  • Bigger labour markets: fast, cheap transit lets workers reach more jobs and firms reach more workers, improving job matching; Mumbai's suburban railway makes a metropolis of millions function as one market.
  • Time and fuel savings: congestion wastes working hours and imported fuel; mass transit reduces both and lowers logistics costs by freeing roads for freight.
  • Investment and land value: transit-oriented development raises land values near stations; the Metro Rail Policy, 2017 promotes value-capture financing and comprehensive mobility plans.
  • New growth centres: the Namo Bharat regional rail on the Delhi–Meerut corridor (operational in stages from October 2023) links satellite towns to the core, spreading growth and easing housing pressure.

2. Inclusion and human capital

  • Affordability: informal and low-wage workers depend on buses and suburban trains; high fares or long commutes exclude them from city jobs.
  • Women's work: safe, cheap transport raises women's mobility and workforce participation; Delhi (2019), Tamil Nadu, Karnataka's Shakti scheme (2023) and Telangana offer free bus travel to women.
  • Access to services: students and patients reach schools, colleges and hospitals, building human capital.

3. Sustainability and health

  • Cleaner air and lower emissions: each bus or metro train replaces many private vehicles; PM-eBus Sewa and PM E-DRIVE support electric buses.
  • Safer roads and energy security: fewer private vehicles mean fewer crashes and lower oil imports.

4. Challenges

  • Too few buses and poor last-mile connectivity; fragmented agencies, with few cities having working Unified Metropolitan Transport Authorities; metro ridership often below projections; high capital cost and debt; fare affordability; and the rapid growth of private vehicles.

5. Way forward

  • Integrated planning: comprehensive mobility plans, transport authorities, bus priority lanes and integrated ticketing through the National Common Mobility Card (2019).
  • People first: feeder services, safe walking and cycling, and dense, mixed-use development around stations.

Efficient and affordable mass transport is economic infrastructure, not a welfare cost: it widens labour markets, includes women and the poor and cuts pollution, making India's urbanisation a driver of rapid and inclusive growth.
free.upm-2019-gs1-17:
Ocean currentsWater massesUpwellingThermohaline circulation

Ocean currents are large, continuous movements of seawater in a definite direction, driven by planetary winds, the Coriolis force and differences in density. Water masses are large bodies of water with a distinctive temperature–salinity signature, acquired at the surface in a source region, which then sink and spread at their own density level, as Antarctic Bottom Water does. Currents act mainly on the surface and coasts; water masses shape the deep ocean.

1. Currents and marine life

  • Upwelling: cold currents along the western coasts of continents (Humboldt off Peru, Benguela, California, Canary) accompany upwelling of nutrient-rich water, supporting rich fisheries such as Peru's anchoveta; El Niño weakens this upwelling and caused the anchoveta collapse of 1972–73.
  • Meeting of currents: where the Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current (Grand Banks of Newfoundland) and the Kuroshio meets the Oyashio (off Japan), mixing produces plankton and great fishing grounds.
  • Range of corals: warm currents let reefs grow far from the equator, as in Bermuda (Gulf Stream) and along the East Australian Current; cold western coasts have few reefs.
  • Dispersal and migration: currents carry larvae, turtles and eels; European eel larvae drift from the Sargasso Sea to Europe on the Gulf Stream.
  • Indian example: monsoon upwelling off the south-west coast supports Kerala's oil sardine and mackerel catch.

2. Currents and the coastal environment

  • Climate: the warm North Atlantic Drift keeps Norway's coast ice-free and western Europe mild, while cold currents create coastal deserts such as the Atacama (Humboldt) and the Namib (Benguela) and frequent fogs.
  • Coastlines: longshore currents move sand along beaches; ports and breakwaters that block them cause erosion downdrift.
  • Pollution: currents spread oil spills, and ocean gyres trap plastic, as in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

3. Water masses and marine life

  • Ventilation of the deep: cold, oxygen-rich water that sinks in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica carries oxygen to deep-sea life; poorly ventilated water combined with high productivity creates oxygen-minimum zones, as in the Arabian Sea.
  • Stratification: the Bay of Bengal's fresh, low-salinity surface layer, fed by great rivers, limits vertical mixing, lowering productivity compared with the Arabian Sea, and keeps the surface warm, helping cyclones intensify.
  • Nutrients: deep water masses accumulate nutrients over centuries and return them to the surface through upwelling.

4. Water masses and the coastal environment

  • Heat transport: the conveyor moves heat towards the poles; the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report says the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is very likely to weaken this century, which could alter European winters, monsoons and sea levels along coasts.
  • Salty outflows: the warm, salty Mediterranean and Red Sea waters spread at intermediate depths, influencing the Atlantic and the Arabian Sea.

Currents mainly shape surface productivity and coastal climate, while water masses govern the deep ocean's chemistry and long-term climate; understanding both is vital for fisheries, coastal planning and climate forecasting.
free.upm-2019-gs1-18:
Mini IndiaInternal migrationCosmopolitanismComposite culture

Migration for work, trade, administration, education and refuge has scattered communities across India; about 37% of Indians were migrants by place of last residence (Census 2011). The result is a network of cultural pockets: neighbourhoods where one region's language, food and festivals flourish far from home, and cosmopolitan towns where people from every State live together. Each is a small India and a living example of unity in diversity.

1. Regional pockets in metropolitan cities

  • Delhi: Chittaranjan Park, settled by families displaced from East Pakistan, is a Bengali enclave famous for its Durga Puja; Punjabi refugee colonies such as Lajpat Nagar grew after 1947.
  • Mumbai: Matunga has a strong Tamil and south Indian community; Gujarati and Marwari traders, Parsis, and migrants from Bihar and eastern UP (who celebrate Chhath at Juhu beach) shape the city.
  • Kolkata: Marwari traders of Burrabazar, the Chinese of Tangra, and Armenian and Anglo-Indian communities.
  • Bengaluru and Hyderabad: IT jobs have drawn people from every State.

2. Historical pockets

  • Saurashtrians of Madurai: silk weavers who migrated from Gujarat centuries ago still speak the Sourashtra language.
  • Marathas in the south and centre: Maratha rule left Marathi-speaking communities in Thanjavur, Indore, Gwalior and Vadodara.
  • Pilgrim centres: Varanasi has a Bengali Tola and ghats built by rulers from many regions.

3. Mini Indias: cosmopolitan towns

  • Steel and PSU townships: Bhilai, Rourkela, Bokaro and Jamshedpur drew engineers and workers from every region; their schools, clubs and festivals mix languages and cuisines.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands: settlers from Bengal, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and the Chotanagpur region have earned the islands the name "mini India", with Hindi as the link language.
  • National institutions: cantonments, central universities, IITs, Kendriya Vidyalayas and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, with their student-migration scheme, mix young Indians from all regions.

4. Refugee and minority pockets

  • Refugees: Tibetan settlements in Dharamshala (McLeod Ganj) and Bylakuppe; Sindhis at Ulhasnagar; Kashmiri Pandits in Jammu and Delhi after 1990.
  • Old minorities: the Jews of Kochi (Paradesi Synagogue, 1568), the Parsis of Mumbai and Gujarat, and the Siddis of African origin in Gujarat and Karnataka.

5. Significance and limits

  • Integration: such pockets spread festivals (Durga Puja in Delhi, Chhath in Mumbai, Ganesh Chaturthi across India), cuisines and languages; Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat (2015) and the Kashi Tamil Sangamam (2022) build on these links.
  • Limits: some pockets become ghettos, and sons-of-the-soil movements have targeted migrants, as in attacks on north Indian migrants in Mumbai (2008); laws reserving private jobs for locals, such as Haryana's (struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2023; the State has appealed), raise similar tensions.

Yes, India has cultural pockets of small India across the nation. They show that Indian identity is layered, regional and national at once; nurturing them through inclusive cities and respect for migrants strengthens national integration.
free.upm-2019-gs1-19:
Gender inequalityTime povertyPublic spacePolitical representation

Since independence, Indian women have gained constitutional equality (Articles 14, 15(3) and 39(d)), protective laws and many firsts, yet some challenges persist across time, from one generation to the next, and across spaces: the home, the workplace, the street, the internet and the legislature. India ranked 131st of 145 in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2026, a sign that progress has been slow and uneven.

1. Challenges that persist over time

  • Son preference: the sex ratio at birth is 918 girls per 1,000 boys (SRS 2024), despite the PCPNDT Act, 1994.
  • Early marriage and dowry: 23.3% of women aged 20–24 were married before 18 (NFHS-5), and dowry persists more than six decades after the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
  • Violence: about 29% of ever-married women aged 18–49 have experienced physical or sexual violence by their husbands (NFHS-5).
  • Time poverty: women spend about 289 minutes a day on unpaid domestic work against 88 minutes for men (Time Use Survey 2024), leaving less time for paid work, study and rest.

2. The home and the economy

  • Low participation: female labour force participation is only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24), concentrated in farm and informal work, with pay gaps and few women in senior positions.
  • Assets: land and housing remain mostly in men's names, although the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 and Vineeta Sharma (2020) gave daughters equal coparcenary rights.
  • Mobility: many women still need permission to travel alone, limiting education and work.

3. Public and digital spaces

  • Safety in public: the Nirbhaya case (2012) led to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, and the rape and murder of a trainee doctor at Kolkata's R.G. Kar hospital (August 2024) again exposed the risks women face even at work.
  • Workplace harassment: the POSH Act, 2013 is weakly enforced, and many internal committees are missing or inactive.
  • Digital divide and abuse: only 54% of women have a mobile phone that they themselves use (NFHS-5), and online harassment and deepfakes drive many women off the internet.
  • Religious spaces: restrictions on entry, as in the Sabarimala and Haji Ali disputes, show cultural limits on women's space.

4. Political space and regional variation

  • Representation: women are only about 14% of the Lok Sabha, and 9% of MLAs (ADR, March 2026); the 106th Amendment (2023) reserving a third of seats awaits delimitation. Reservation in panchayats has brought lakhs of women into local government, though proxy rule by husbands persists.
  • Regional and social gaps: sex ratios, literacy and mobility differ sharply between southern and north-eastern States and parts of the north; Dalit, tribal and rural women face multiple disadvantages.

Women's challenges have changed form but not disappeared. Laws must be matched by shared care work, safe public and digital spaces and real political power, so that women-led development and gender justice become a lived reality.
free.upm-2019-gs1-20:
GlobalisationGlocalisationCultural homogenisationHybrid identity

Globalisation, which accelerated in India after the 1991 reforms and again with cheap smartphones and data, spreads global brands, media, languages and lifestyles. Critics fear cultural homogenisation, what George Ritzer called "McDonaldization", and the erosion of local languages, crafts and customs. Yet Indian experience also shows glocalisation: global forms adapting to local tastes, and local identities reviving and even going global. The picture is mixed.

1. Signs of erosion of local identity

  • Languages: English is seen as the language of opportunity, and many children grow up weaker in their mother tongue; UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger (2009) listed 197 Indian languages as vulnerable, endangered or already extinct.
  • Food and dress: fast food, packaged snacks and fast fashion are replacing local cuisines, millets and handloom in daily life.
  • Crafts and livelihoods: cheap mass-produced goods and imports undercut weavers, potters and toy-makers.
  • Festivals and lifestyle: Valentine's Day, Halloween and online sale days grow, while local festivals become commercialised; nuclear families and individualism weaken community ties.
  • Built environment: malls and glass towers replace vernacular architecture and local markets.

2. Why local identity is not simply being lost

  • Glocalisation: global firms adapt to India; McDonald's sells the McAloo Tikki and avoids beef, and streaming platforms invest heavily in regional-language content.
  • Revival and pride: regional cinema has gone global ("Naatu Naatu" from the Telugu film RRR won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2023); yoga (International Day of Yoga since 2015) and millets (International Year of Millets, 2023) are local traditions turned global.
  • Recognition: GI tags (Darjeeling tea was the first, in 2004) and UNESCO's listing of Kolkata's Durga Puja (2021) and Garba (2023) protect and promote local culture.
  • Diaspora: Indians abroad celebrate Diwali, Onam and Durga Puja, carrying local identity into the global space.
  • Assertion: globalisation often provokes stronger local identities, through language movements, regional pride and campaigns for local products.

3. Hybrid, layered identities

  • People increasingly hold multiple identities: local, national and global at once. A young professional in Bengaluru may celebrate Ugadi and Christmas, speak Kannada at home and English at work, and enjoy both film music and K-pop.
  • Fusion music, Indo-western clothing and regional cuisines in global cities show creative mixing rather than simple loss.

4. Way forward

  • Language: NEP 2020 favours teaching in the mother tongue or regional language at least up to Class 5, and Bhashini (2022) brings Indian languages to the internet.
  • Livelihoods: Vocal for Local, One District One Product and GI branding support local crafts.
  • Heritage: conservation of monuments, documentation of oral traditions and community museums.

We are not so much losing local identity as renegotiating it. Globalisation threatens some languages, crafts and customs, but it also offers tools to revive them; India's challenge is to think globally while staying rooted locally.
free.upm-2019-gs2-1:
Separation of powersChecks and balancesArticle 50Basic structure

Separation of powers, theorised by Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), assigns law-making, execution and adjudication to separate organs so that no organ becomes tyrannical. The US Constitution applies it rigidly. India's Constitution does not: its parliamentary system fuses the executive with the legislature, and apart from Article 50 (separation of the judiciary from the executive) there is no explicit clause. It relies instead on a functional separation policed by checks and balances.

1. Why India does not follow strict separation

  • Fused executive and legislature: ministers must be members of Parliament (Article 75(5)) and are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)); the President is himself a part of Parliament (Article 79).
  • Executive law-making: the President and Governors issue ordinances (Articles 123 and 213), and much law is made through delegated legislation.
  • Judicial functions of the legislature: Parliament impeaches the President (Article 61), removes judges (Article 124(4)) and punishes breaches of privilege (Article 105).
  • Quasi-legislative role of courts: the Supreme Court frames its own rules (Article 145) and has issued guidelines where laws were silent, as in Vishaka (1997).
  • Judicial recognition: in Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) the Court held that India has not adopted the doctrine in its absolute rigidity, though the functions of the organs are sufficiently differentiated.

2. The core that is protected

  • Basic structure: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) counted separation of powers among the basic features; in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) the Court struck down Article 329A(4), by which Parliament had in effect decided an election dispute, a judicial function.
  • Mutual non-interference: legislatures cannot discuss a judge's conduct in the discharge of duties (Articles 121 and 211), and courts cannot question legislative proceedings for procedural irregularity (Articles 122 and 212).
  • Independent judiciary: security of tenure and salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund insulate judges from the other organs.

3. Checks and balances at work

  • Courts on the executive: in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) repeated re-promulgation of ordinances was held a fraud on the Constitution.
  • Parliament on the courts: after Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the First Amendment added Article 15(4) to permit special provisions for backward classes.
  • President on the Cabinet: the President may return the Cabinet's advice for reconsideration once (Article 74(1)) and return a Bill other than a Money Bill (Article 111).
  • Courts restraining themselves: in its opinion on the Presidential Reference (20 November 2025), the Supreme Court held that it cannot fix timelines for assent to Bills or deem assent, leaving room only for a limited direction in cases of prolonged inaction.

India therefore follows a separation of functions, not of persons: the organs overlap, but none may usurp another's core function. The balance rests on constitutional morality, with each organ exercising restraint and answering to the others.
free.upm-2019-gs2-2:
Article 323ACentral Administrative TribunalL. Chandra KumarJudicial independence

The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was set up on 1 November 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, made under Article 323A, which the 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice. It was meant to relieve High Courts of service litigation by giving central government employees a quick, specialised forum. Four decades on, it functions much like a court: it tests rules against the Constitution, enforces orders through contempt and is held to standards of judicial independence.

1. Original design: a forum for service grievances

  • Jurisdiction (Section 14): recruitment and service matters of persons appointed to Union civil services and posts, members of the all-India services, and employees of bodies notified by the Union.
  • Simple procedure: it is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure but by natural justice (Section 22); an application lies only after departmental remedies are exhausted (Section 20) and within a year (Section 21).
  • Mixed benches: judicial and administrative members bring together legal and service expertise.
  • Exclusive forum: Article 323A(2)(d) and Section 28 excluded all courts except the Supreme Court, and S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) accepted the tribunal as an effective substitute for the High Court.

2. How it now works as an independent judicial authority

  • Court-like powers: it can punish for contempt of itself like a High Court (Section 17), summon witnesses, call for documents and review its own decisions.
  • Constitutional adjudication: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that tribunals may test the validity of statutes and rules, except their parent Act, so the CAT strikes down service rules and promotion or seniority policies that violate Articles 14 and 16.
  • Binding the Union: its orders on transfers, penalties, pay and pensions bind ministries, and non-compliance invites contempt.
  • Independence standards: in R. Gandhi (2010) and the later Madras Bar Association cases, the Supreme Court required tribunals that replace courts to enjoy court-like independence in appointments and tenure; the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 created a National Tribunals Commission to oversee tribunal appointments and performance.

3. Limits on its independence and finality

  • Not the last word: after Chandra Kumar its decisions are open to a Division Bench of the High Court under Articles 226 and 227, which adds a tier and delays finality.
  • Executive control: the Department of Personnel and Training, a frequent litigant before the CAT, also handles its administration, budget and staff.
  • Vacancies and pendency: unfilled posts of members and short tenures slow disposal.
  • Narrow remit: it cannot hear challenges to its own parent Act, and many autonomous bodies remain outside its jurisdiction.

The statement is largely true: the CAT has grown from a grievance forum into a specialised court for service law. Timely appointments, administrative and financial autonomy and an effective National Tribunals Commission would secure its independence, while High Court review keeps it accountable.
free.upm-2019-gs2-3:
Pressure groupsFarmers' movementsSamyukt Kisan MorchaMinimum Support Price

Farmers' organisations are pressure groups: they seek to influence policy on prices, credit, power, land and trade without themselves seeking to govern. They range from the All India Kisan Sabha (1936) to the new farmers' movements of the 1980s, such as Sharad Joshi's Shetkari Sanghatana and Mahendra Singh Tikait's Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU), and the Samyukt Kisan Morcha (SKM), which led the 2020–21 protests against the three farm laws.

1. Methods used to influence policy-makers

  • Mass mobilisation: rallies, dharnas and rail and road blockades, from the BKU's mass sit-in at Delhi's Boat Club (1988) to the SKM's sit-in at Delhi's borders from November 2020 to December 2021.
  • Lobbying and negotiation: memoranda, meetings with ministers and officials, and seats on official bodies; farm unions held 11 rounds of talks with the Union government in 2020–21.
  • Electoral pressure: farmer leaders build parties or swing votes, from Charan Singh's Lok Dal to regional outfits such as Raju Shetti's Swabhimani Paksha.
  • Litigation: petitions led the Supreme Court to stay the farm laws in January 2021 and appoint an expert committee.
  • Ideas and media: campaigns for MSP at "C2 plus 50%", drawn from the Swaminathan Commission (2006), backed by social media and diaspora support; the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh lobbies from within its ideological network.
  • Transnational links: the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha joined La Via Campesina and campaigned against WTO rules and seed multinationals in the 1990s.

2. How effective are these methods?

  • Strong veto power: the Farm Laws Repeal Act, 2021 followed the Prime Minister's announcement of 19 November 2021, and the ordinance amending the land acquisition law of 2013 lapsed in 2015 after opposition from farmer groups and parties.
  • Agenda-setting: MSP, debt and input costs stay central to politics; a committee on MSP and crop diversification was set up in July 2022.
  • State-level gains: governments have announced loan waivers and better cane prices after agitations, and the 2018 Kisan Long March won assurances on forest-land rights.

3. Limits of their influence

  • Positive demands rarely met: a legal guarantee of MSP, sought again in protests at the Punjab–Haryana border in 2024–25, has not been granted.
  • Unequal voice: organisations are strongest among surplus-producing farmers of Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, while small and marginal farmers (86% of holdings, Agriculture Census 2015-16), tenants, women and landless labourers are weakly represented.
  • Fragmentation: divisions of crop, region, caste and ideology weaken bargaining, and coalitions such as the SKM later saw breakaway groups.
  • Costs of agitation: long blockades, violent incidents such as the one at the Red Fort on 26 January 2021, and public inconvenience can erode sympathy, and pressure often protects the paddy–wheat cycle despite its ecological cost.

Farmers' organisations are most effective as a veto force against policies seen as imposed, and least effective in securing positive reform. Regular consultation, pre-legislative dialogue and collective bargaining through Farmer Producer Organisations (10,000 FPO scheme, 2020) could turn protest into partnership.
free.upm-2019-gs2-4:
Seventh ScheduleFederal supremacyHarmonious constructionPith and substance

Article 246 divides legislative power through the Seventh Schedule into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Because no list can be drawn perfectly, entries overlap, and courts must decide whose law prevails. From these disputes two principles have emerged: federal supremacy, under which Union law prevails in a genuine conflict, and harmonious construction, under which entries are read together so that both legislatures' powers survive. Supporting doctrines such as pith and substance make the system work.

1. Principle of federal supremacy

  • Text of Article 246: Parliament's power over the Union List operates "notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3)", while the States' power over the State List is "subject to clauses (1) and (2)"; in an irreconcilable overlap the Union List therefore prevails.
  • Concurrent List (Article 254): a State law repugnant to a Union law is void to the extent of repugnancy, unless reserved for and assented to by the President (Article 254(2)); even then Parliament may later override it.
  • Tests of repugnancy: M. Karunanidhi (1979) asks whether there is a direct conflict, whether Parliament intended an exhaustive code, and whether both laws occupy the same field.
  • Application: in Adhiyaman (1995) a State law on standards of technical education yielded to the AICTE Act, made under Entry 66 of the Union List.
  • A last resort: courts apply it only when the entries cannot be reconciled.

2. Principle of harmonious construction

  • Meaning: entries are read together so that each has effect; a general entry yields to a specific one, and no entry is read so widely that another becomes useless.
  • Origin: in the C.P. and Berar Motor Spirit case (1939), the Federal Court reconciled the Centre's excise duty, a tax on manufacture, with the provinces' tax on the sale of goods.
  • Specific over general: in Calcutta Gas (1962) the specific State entry on gas and gas-works was held to cover the gas industry, so the State law stood despite the Union's power over industries.
  • Recent use: the Supreme Court has read the lists together in several major disputes (table).

3. Supporting doctrines

  • Pith and substance: a law is classified by its true nature, and incidental effects on another list do not invalidate it; Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee (Privy Council, 1947) upheld a Bengal money-lending law that touched promissory notes, and F.N. Balsara (1951) upheld Bombay's prohibition law though it affected imports.
  • Colourable legislation: a legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, 1953).

4. Significance

  • Unity: federal supremacy keeps national law uniform on defence, currency and standards.
  • Autonomy: harmonious construction protects the States' sphere; federalism is a basic feature (S.R. Bommai, 1994), and the 2024 judgments upheld State powers where the text allowed.

Together the two principles give India a federation with a centralising tilt but a cooperative spirit: the Union prevails when it must, but courts first try to give both levels room, the essence of cooperative federalism.
free.upm-2019-gs2-5:
LaïcitéPrincipled distanceEqual respectMinority rights

France's laïcité rests on the 1905 law on the separation of the Churches and the State and on its Constitution's description of France as "an indivisible, secular, democratic and social Republic". It keeps religion out of public institutions and treats faith as a private matter. India's secularism, a basic feature (S.R. Bommai, 1994), follows what Rajeev Bhargava calls principled distance: equal respect for all faiths, with State intervention only to protect rights and promote reform.

1. What France can learn

  • Accommodation, not exclusion: India lets citizens wear turbans, headscarves or crosses in public life and in most schools and workplaces. French bans on headscarves and face coverings have alienated many Muslims, and the UN Human Rights Committee (2018) found that the face-veil ban violated the rights of two women.
  • Equal respect rather than indifference: Indian secularism treats religious diversity as a public good; festivals of many faiths are public holidays, signalling that every faith belongs.
  • Group rights within common citizenship: Articles 29–30 protect minorities' languages, cultures and institutions, allowing integration without assimilation. France's 2021 law reinforcing respect for the principles of the Republic, often called the anti-separatism law, is seen by critics as treating Muslims with suspicion.
  • Judicial balancing over blanket bans: Indian courts weigh freedom of religion against public order, morality, health and equality, using tests such as the essential religious practices doctrine (Shirur Mutt, 1954), case by case.
  • A tradition of tolerance: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII urged respect for other sects, and Akbar's sulh-i-kul (peace with all) anticipated equal respect.

2. Limits of the Indian model

  • Gaps in practice: communal violence, hate speech and the split verdict in the Karnataka hijab case (2022) show that accommodation is contested in India too.
  • Different histories: laïcité grew out of a struggle against the Catholic Church's power over the State; Indian secularism grew out of deep religiosity and diversity, so neither model can simply be transplanted.
  • What India can learn from France: a firm commitment to equal citizenship, consistent State neutrality in public institutions and gender equality within communities.

3. Assessment

  • Contextual secularism: Bhargava argues that India's model, which can both keep distance and intervene, suits deeply diverse societies better than a single rule of exclusion.
  • Shared goal: both models aim at freedom of conscience and equal citizenship; they differ in how far the State may accommodate religion in public life.

France could borrow India's contextual, accommodative secularism, with equal respect, minority rights and judicial balancing, to integrate its Muslim citizens, while India must live up to its own ideal through constitutional morality in everyday governance.
free.upm-2019-gs2-6:
Inclusive growthHuman developmentJobless growthRegional disparities

India has been one of the world's fastest-growing large economies since 1991, yet its human development lags: in the UNDP's Human Development Report 2025 its HDI was 0.685, rank 130 of 193, and inequality cut the value by 30.7% (IHDI 0.475). Growth has reduced poverty, but it has not been balanced across regions, sectors and groups, or inclusive enough to reach people through good jobs, health and education.

1. Pattern of growth

  • Job-poor growth: growth has been led by services and capital-intensive industry; nearly half of all workers remain in agriculture, and about 90% work informally, without social security.
  • Weak manufacturing: the labour-absorbing route taken by East Asia has not taken off, so rural workers move into construction and petty services rather than factories.
  • Gender gap: female labour force participation of only 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24), unpaid care work and safety concerns waste women's potential.

2. Under-investment in human capabilities
