  • Health: government health spending was 1.43% of GDP in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts), below the National Health Policy 2017 goal of 2.5%, and households paid 43.4% of health expenditure out of pocket.
  • Nutrition: 29.3% of children under five were still stunted in NFHS-6 (2023-24), and NFHS-5 found 57% of women anaemic.
  • Learning: enrolment is near-universal, but ASER 2024 found only 23.4% of Class 3 children in rural government schools able to read a Class 2 text.

3. Unequal distribution of gains

  • Regional: southern and western States have pulled ahead, while Bihar and Jharkhand have the highest shares of multidimensionally poor people (NITI Aayog, 2023).
  • Rural–urban: average urban consumption was about 70% higher than rural in 2023-24 (₹6,996 against ₹4,122 a person a month, HCES).
  • Wealth: the richest 1% hold over 40% of national wealth (World Inequality Lab, 2024).
  • Social groups: Scheduled Tribes remain the most multidimensionally poor group, and SCs and minorities lag in assets, education and representation.

4. Governance and delivery

  • Weak local government: panchayats and municipalities lack funds, functions and functionaries.
  • Leaky delivery: targeting errors, absentee staff and authentication failures keep benefits from the poorest.
  • Fiscal priorities: subsidies and interest payments crowd out health and education spending in many States.

Progress is real: multidimensional poverty fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23) (NITI Aayog), and the World Bank estimates extreme poverty at 5.3% in 2022-23. To make development balanced and inclusive, India needs labour-intensive manufacturing, higher public spending on health and education, more women at work, empowered local governments and faster growth in lagging States, so that growth becomes people-centred.
free.upm-2019-gs2-7:
Calorie paradoxEngel's lawNon-food essentialsNutrition security

India's poverty has fallen sharply: the World Bank estimates that extreme poverty dropped from 27.1% (2011-12) to 5.3% (2022-23), and multidimensional poverty fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23). Hunger has fallen far more slowly: 29.3% of children under five were still stunted in NFHS-6 (2023-24). Angus Deaton and Jean Drèze (2009) noted this divergence: per-capita calorie intake fell even as real spending rose. One explanation is that rising costs of non-food essentials squeeze the food budgets of the poor.

1. Evidence of the divergence

  • Falling food share: household consumption surveys show the share of food in spending falling from 52.9% (rural) and 42.62% (urban) in 2011-12 to 46.38% and 39.17% in 2022-23, with a slight rise to 47.04% and 39.68% in 2023-24 (MoSPI; the 2011-12 survey used a different method).
  • Cereals squeezed: the share of cereals in rural spending fell from 10.69% to 4.89% between 2011-12 and 2022-23, partly because grain is now free.
  • Persistent undernutrition: stunting fell from 38.4% (NFHS-4) to 35.5% (NFHS-5) and 29.3% (NFHS-6), still very high, while NFHS-5 found 57% of women and 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months anaemic.
  • Diet quality: beverages and processed food are now the largest food item (HCES 2023-24).

2. How non-food essentials squeeze the food budget

  • Health: out-of-pocket spending rose from 39.4% of total health expenditure in 2021-22 to 43.4% in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts); one illness can push a family into debt and cut its food spending.
  • Transport and rent: conveyance is now a leading non-food item (7.59% of rural and 8.46% of urban spending in 2023-24), and rent takes 6.58% of urban budgets, reflecting long commutes to work and costly urban housing.
  • New necessities: the shares of toilet articles, consumer services and durable goods rose between 2011-12 and 2022-23, competing with food.
  • Weak public provision: where public hospitals, buses and housing are inadequate, the poor must buy these services privately.

3. How far does the statement hold?

  • Valid in part: government health spending fell from a pandemic-era 1.84% of GDP (2021-22) to 1.43% (2022-23), and costly private services do push households to trade food for other essentials.
  • But social spending has not simply shrunk: about 81 crore people receive free grain under PMGKAY, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers hospital costs, and out-of-pocket spending fell from 62.6% of health expenditure (2014-15) to 43.4% (2022-23).
  • Engel's law: food's share normally falls as incomes rise; Deaton and Drèze also linked lower calorie intake to less strenuous work and better health.
  • Malnutrition is multi-causal: sanitation, women's education, care practices and dietary diversity matter as much as the size of the food budget.

The answer is a shift from food security to nutrition security: pulses, millets and eggs through the PDS and PM POSHAN, public health spending of 2.5% of GDP, and affordable transport and housing, so that rising incomes become better diets.
free.upm-2019-gs2-8:
ICT projectsProcess re-engineeringCapacity buildingDigital inclusion

ICT-based projects, from Karnataka's Bhoomi land records and Kerala's Akshaya centres to Passport Seva, GST Network and CoWIN, have shown how technology can cut delays, discretion and leakages. Yet many projects stall after the pilot stage or fail to change how citizens are served. The Second ARC (11th Report, 2008) stressed that e-governance is about reforming governance, not merely computerising it. Implementation suffers on a few vital factors.

1. Vital factors where implementation suffers

  • Process: old paper procedures are put online without re-engineering, so delays simply move from files to servers.
  • People and capacity: governments have few in-house technology experts; frequent transfers of project champions and resistance from staff stall change.
  • Infrastructure and access: gaps in rural connectivity, power and devices; only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5).
  • Interoperability: departments build separate databases without common standards, so citizens submit the same documents again and again, and vendors lock systems in.
  • Procurement and funding: lowest-cost bids, under-budgeted operation and maintenance, and pilots that end when funds stop.
  • Security and trust: weak cyber hygiene and privacy concerns deter both departments and users.
  • Citizen interface: English-first portals, complex forms and online-only grievance redress exclude many; biometric failures denied rations in Jharkhand (2017).

2. Measures for effective implementation

  • Re-engineer first: simplify processes before automating, in line with e-Kranti's principle of "transformation, not translation" (2015).
  • Design with users: mobile-first services in Indian languages (Bhashini, 2022), assisted access through Common Service Centres and offline fallbacks.
  • Build capacity: Mission Karmayogi (2020) for officials, dedicated project teams and continuity of leadership.
  • Manage change: a senior champion, incentives and training for staff, and early, visible gains for citizens help a new system win acceptance.
  • Common architecture: the India Enterprise Architecture (IndEA, 2018), open standards and APIs, and reusable digital public infrastructure such as Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker.
  • Smarter procurement: outcome-based contracts, transparent buying through GeM and budgets for operation and maintenance.
  • Security and privacy by design: CERT-In audits and compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its Rules (2025).
  • Feedback and accountability: outcome dashboards, PRAGATI-style reviews (2015), social audit and CPGRAMS, with a human fallback for grievances.

Technology is the easy part; people, processes and trust decide success. Following the Second ARC's SMART ideal (simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent), with ownership by departments and attention to the last user, will turn ICT projects into lasting improvements in service.
free.upm-2019-gs2-9:
Special Strategic and Global PartnershipIndo-PacificEconomic securityQuad

India and Japan, Asia's two largest democracies, raised their ties to a Special Strategic and Global Partnership in 2014. Shared values, complementary economies (Japanese capital and technology, Indian markets and talent) and a common interest in a free and open Indo-Pacific underpin it. The 15th Annual Summit (Tokyo, August 2025) adopted a Joint Vision for the Next Decade, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's visit to New Delhi for the 16th Annual Summit (July 2026) added an economic security framework: the partnership is already becoming strategic and global.

1. Strategic and security pillar

  • Defence ties: the 2+2 dialogue, the logistics agreement (ACSA) and exercises with all three services, such as JIMEX (navy), Dharma Guardian (army) and Veer Guardian (air force, 2023).
  • Security cooperation: an updated Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation (2025); in July 2026 the two agreed in principle to jointly develop the UNICORN antenna system for Indian Navy warships.
  • Indo-Pacific: both are Quad members with the US and Australia, the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative (2021) links them with Australia, and Japan's Free and Open Indo-Pacific vision is being linked with India's MAHASAGAR.
  • Nuclear trust: the 2016 civil nuclear agreement was Japan's first with a country outside the NPT.

2. Economic and technological pillar

  • Investment: after a five-year target of ¥5 trillion (from 2022), the 2025 summit set a target of ¥10 trillion of private Japanese investment over a decade.
  • Infrastructure: Japan, India's largest bilateral development partner, has financed the Delhi Metro, the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor and the Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail, for which it has offered its E10 series Shinkansen in the early 2030s.
  • Economic security: the 2025 Economic Security Initiative and the 2026 declaration prioritise semiconductors, critical minerals, ICT and AI, clean energy and pharmaceuticals.
  • People and science: an Action Plan for exchanges of more than 500,000 people over five years, including 50,000 skilled Indians going to Japan, and the ISRO–JAXA lunar mission LUPEX.

3. Significance for Asia and the world

  • Balance in Asia: two democracies offering quality infrastructure and transparent finance, including joint work in Africa under a 2025 initiative.
  • Rules-based order: freedom of navigation, peaceful settlement of disputes and maritime security in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
  • Global governance: partners in the G4 for UN Security Council reform and in clean-energy cooperation through the Joint Crediting Mechanism (2025).

4. Constraints

  • Thin economic base: progress towards the ¥10 trillion goal has been slow.
  • Political churn: frequent changes of Japanese prime ministers raise questions of continuity, though annual summits cushion them.

The statement is apt: India–Japan ties have matured from aid to a strategic partnership spanning security, technology and supply chains. Turning targets into investment, co-production and trade will make it an anchor of stability in the Indo-Pacific.
free.upm-2019-gs2-10:
UNESCOUS withdrawalPoliticisationFunding crisis

UNESCO (1945, Paris) promotes peace through education, science, culture and communication, and administers the World Heritage Convention (1972). As a one-country-one-vote body that depends on assessed and voluntary contributions, it is exposed to both money and politics. The headline captures this double crisis: the United States, a founding member and once its largest funder, stopped paying in 2011 and has walked out twice since 2017, accusing it of anti-Israel bias.

1. "Too little cash"

  • The 2011 shock: after UNESCO admitted Palestine in 2011, US laws barring funds to UN agencies that admit Palestine as a full member cut off US contributions, about 22% of its budget, forcing deep programme cuts; in 2013 the US lost its vote in the General Conference for non-payment.
  • Earmarked funds: voluntary donor money lets donors set priorities; private-sector contributions were only about 8% of the budget in 2024.
  • The new exit: in July 2025 the US announced that it would leave on 31 December 2026; its share had fallen to about 8% of the budget, and Director-General Audrey Azoulay said UNESCO had prepared by diversifying its funding, while European donors, pressed to spend on defence, are reluctant to fill gaps.

2. "Too much politics"

  • Cold War: the US left in 1984, citing mismanagement and politicisation (including the debate on a New World Information and Communication Order), and returned in 2003.
  • Israel–Palestine: a 2016 resolution on occupied East Jerusalem and the listing of Hebron's Old City as a Palestinian World Heritage site in danger (2017) angered Israel and the US, and both announced their exit in 2017.
  • Heritage disputes: listings such as Preah Vihear (2008, Cambodia–Thailand) and Japan's Meiji industrial sites (2015, opposed by South Korea) became diplomatic battles.
  • Ideological charges: the 2025 announcement accused UNESCO of advancing "divisive social and cultural causes" and linked anti-Israel rhetoric to Palestine's membership. Nicaragua also left in 2025 after a press-freedom award to an opposition newspaper.

3. Assessing the US accusation

  • Supporting view: one-sided texts on Jerusalem and Hebron turned a technical body into a forum for the Arab–Israeli dispute.
  • Counter-view: Azoulay said the US reasons contradict UNESCO's Holocaust-education work in 85 countries and its fight against antisemitism; leaving also cedes US influence over heritage, education and AI ethics to other powers.
  • Not quite fighting for life: UNESCO survived 19 years without the US (1984–2003), it has diversified its funding, and Khaled El-Enany, the first Director-General from an Arab state, took office in November 2025.

4. Way forward

  • Reform: a wider donor base, more assessed and fewer earmarked funds, consensus on contested heritage and a focus on core mandates such as foundational learning and AI ethics (2021 Recommendation).
  • India's stake: with 45 World Heritage Sites (Sarnath became the 45th in July 2026) and as host of the 2024 World Heritage Committee, India can help keep UNESCO technical and inclusive.

UNESCO's crisis shows how multilateralism suffers when funding becomes leverage; it needs diversified, depoliticised funding and a mandate that all members share.
free.upm-2019-gs2-11:
Articles 102 and 191RPA 1951, Sections 8–11Lily ThomasStay of conviction

Articles 102 and 191 disqualify MPs and MLAs who hold an office of profit, are of unsound mind, undischarged insolvents or non-citizens, or defect under the Tenth Schedule, and let Parliament add grounds by law. Parliament did so in Part II of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Sections 8–11). Since Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4), which shielded sitting legislators who appealed within three months, a legislator is disqualified from the date of conviction.

1. Grounds of disqualification under the RPA

  • Conviction, not charges: only a conviction disqualifies; the Law Commission's 244th Report (2014) proposed disqualification on the framing of charges for serious offences, but this was not enacted.
  • Automatic effect: disqualification follows a conviction by operation of law, and the House secretariat notifies the vacancy.
  • Corrupt practices: under Section 8A the case goes to the President within three months of the order taking effect, and the President acts on the Election Commission's opinion.

2. Remedies available

  • Appeal and stay of conviction: an appellate court may stay the conviction itself, not merely the sentence; in Lok Prahari v. Election Commission of India (2018) the Supreme Court held that the disqualification then ceases to operate from the date of the stay. In 2023 two Lok Sabha members regained their seats after higher courts stayed or suspended their convictions.
  • Acquittal: if the conviction is set aside on appeal, the disqualification goes with it.
  • Election Commission (Section 11): for reasons recorded, it may remove or reduce the period of any disqualification except one under Section 8A; in 2019 it cut Sikkim Chief Minister P.S. Tamang's disqualification to one year and one month.
  • President's decision (Article 103): a question whether a sitting member has become disqualified under Article 102(1) is decided by the President, who must act on the EC's opinion; the member can put his case before the Commission.
  • Courts: an election petition (Section 100) decides whether a candidate was disqualified on the date of election, with an appeal to the Supreme Court (Section 116A); writs under Articles 32 and 226 lie against unlawful action, and Speakers' Tenth Schedule decisions are open to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).

3. Concerns

  • Delays: long appeals let convicted persons remain eligible after a stay, and trials of legislators are slow despite special courts.
  • Discretion: Section 11 orders are rare but give the Commission a wide, unstructured power.
  • Disclosure: Public Interest Foundation (2018) and Rambabu Singh Thakur (2020) require candidates and parties to publicise criminal antecedents and the reasons for fielding such candidates.

After Lily Thomas the law makes disqualification swift, while appeals, stays and the EC's power preserve due process. Speedy trials of cases against legislators and transparent use of Section 11 would advance decriminalisation of politics without unfairness.
free.upm-2019-gs2-12:
Article 368Basic structureMinerva MillsLimited amending power

Article 368 lets Parliament amend "by way of addition, variation or repeal" any provision of the Constitution, by a special majority and, for federal provisions, with ratification by half the States. The statement echoes Minerva Mills (1980): because the Constitution conferred a limited amending power, Parliament cannot use it to enlarge that power into an absolute one, and the limitation is itself a basic feature. Since Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Parliament may amend any provision but cannot destroy the basic structure.

1. The struggle over the amending power

  • Golak Nath (1967): amendments are "law" under Article 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights.
  • 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament excluded amendments from Article 13 (Article 13(4)), described its power as constituent and made the President's assent obligatory.
  • Kesavananda Bharati: the Court upheld the 24th Amendment but held that the power to amend does not include the power to destroy the Constitution's identity.

2. Attempts to expand the power and the Court's response

  • Ousting courts over elections: the 39th Amendment (1975) placed the Prime Minister's election beyond judicial scrutiny; the Court struck down the clause as violating free and fair elections and the rule of law.
  • Declaring the power unlimited: the 42nd Amendment inserted Article 368(4), barring any challenge to amendments in court, and 368(5), removing all limits on Parliament's constituent power. Minerva Mills struck down both: judicial review and limited amending power are basic features, and the holder of a limited power cannot make it unlimited. It also struck down the extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles, restoring their balance with Fundamental Rights.
  • Shielding laws through the Ninth Schedule: Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007) held that laws added after 24 April 1973 are open to review if they damage the basic structure.
  • Judicial appointments: the 99th Amendment (NJAC) was struck down in 2015 for undermining judicial independence.

3. Can Parliament destroy the basic structure?

  • No, by any route: an amendment that damages the basic structure is void whatever the majority, and because limited amending power is itself basic, Parliament cannot amend Article 368 to remove the limit.
  • What is protected: supremacy of the Constitution, democracy and free and fair elections, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review and judicial independence, the rule of law, and harmony between Parts III and IV.
  • Wide power remains: more than a hundred amendments stand; Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the EWS quota, and Dr Balram Singh (2024) upheld the words "socialist" and "secular" added to the Preamble in 1976.
  • Legitimacy debate: critics call the doctrine judicial supremacy without a textual basis; defenders point to the Emergency, and Bangladesh's Supreme Court adopted the doctrine in 1989.

The statement reflects settled law: Parliament's amending power is constituent but not sovereign. The basic structure doctrine keeps the Constitution adaptable yet anchored, and preserves constitutional supremacy over passing majorities.
free.upm-2019-gs2-13:
Article 243DProxy representationWomen's political empowermentPatriarchy

The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) reserved at least one-third of seats and chairpersons' posts in panchayats (Article 243D) and one-third of municipal seats (Article 243T) for women. Bihar raised the quota to 50% in 2006; 21 States and two UTs now reserve half, and women hold nearly half of all panchayat seats. Yet the patriarchal character of Indian politics, in which men control parties, tickets and decisions, has changed only slowly: presence has grown faster than power.

1. Where the impact has been limited

  • Proxy rule: husbands or male relatives often exercise power ("sarpanch-pati"). A Ministry of Panchayati Raj panel chaired by Sushil Kumar, set up in September 2023 after a Supreme Court order, reported in February 2025 and urged exemplary penalties for proxies.
  • Rotation: reserved seats rotate every term, so women rarely build a second term or a political career.
  • Weak devolution: panchayats have few funds, functions and functionaries, so even assertive women have little to wield.
  • Blocked upward mobility: women are only about 14% of the 18th Lok Sabha; parties rarely field women in winnable seats, and reservation in legislatures under the 106th Amendment (2023) awaits a post-Census delimitation.
  • Social barriers: purdah, care burdens, lower literacy among older women, harassment and caste hierarchies weigh most on Dalit and Adivasi women leaders.

2. Where reservation has made a difference

  • Changed priorities: a study of panchayats in Birbhum (West Bengal) and Udaipur (Rajasthan) (Chattopadhyay and Duflo, 2004) found that women pradhans invested more in drinking water, a priority of women voters.
  • Less bias, higher aspirations: research in West Bengal found that exposure to women leaders reduced voters' bias against them and raised parents' aspirations for their daughters (Beaman and others, 2009 and 2012).
  • A leadership pool: lakhs of elected women, many linked to self-help groups such as Kerala's Kudumbashree, have gained experience of public office.
  • Foundation for wider reform: the panchayat experience strengthened the case for the 106th Amendment.

3. Way forward

  • Capacity and support: training under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan, federations of women panchayat heads and gender resource centres, as the 2025 panel suggested.
  • Accountability: public swearing-in of women heads in Gram Sabhas, helplines and action against proxies.
  • Continuity and power: longer reservation of a seat before rotation, and real funds and functions for panchayats.
  • Parties: internal quotas for women in candidate lists, so that local leaders can rise.

The statement is largely valid: reservation has secured descriptive representation faster than it has dismantled patriarchy. But changing priorities and attitudes show a slow, generational shift towards substantive empowerment.
free.upm-2019-gs2-14:
Article 76Chief legal adviserArticle 88Officer of the Constitution

The Attorney General (AG) for India is a constitutional office created by Article 76. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge, who holds office during the pleasure of the President and receives the remuneration the President determines. R. Venkataramani took office as AG on 1 October 2022 and was reappointed for two years from 1 October 2025. The AG is the Union's chief legal adviser and principal advocate, and also an officer of the Constitution.

1. Chief legal adviser

  • Constitutional duty (Article 76(2)): to advise the Government of India on legal matters and to perform other duties of a legal character that the President refers or assigns.
  • Route of advice: ministries refer questions through the Department of Legal Affairs; his opinion does not bind the government.
  • Constitutional questions: he represents the Union in Presidential References under Article 143, such as the 2025 Reference on assent to State Bills.
  • Statutory role: his consent, or the Solicitor General's, is needed before a private person moves the Supreme Court for criminal contempt (Contempt of Courts Act, 1971).

2. The government's lawyer

  • In court: under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987, he appears for the Union in all Supreme Court cases in which it is concerned, and in any High Court when required.
  • Right of audience (Article 76(3)): in all courts in the territory of India.
  • Team: he is assisted by the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General, whose posts are not constitutional.
  • Voice in constitutional cases: civil courts must give him notice before deciding a substantial question of constitutional interpretation that concerns the Union (Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXVII-A).

3. More than a government lawyer

  • Parliament (Article 88): he may speak and take part in the proceedings of either House, joint sittings and any committee of which he is named a member, but cannot vote; he enjoys the privileges of an MP (Article 105(4)).
  • Officer of the court: his duty is to the Constitution and the court, not merely to the government; Attorney General Niren De's argument in ADM Jabalpur (1976) that detenus had no remedy during the Emergency shows what is at stake.
  • Not a civil servant: he is not a member of the Cabinet and may take private briefs, but not against the Government of India; he needs permission to defend accused persons or accept company directorships.

4. Issues

  • No security of tenure: the pleasure doctrine, and the convention of resigning when the government changes, can blur the line between independent advice and loyalty.
  • Dual loyalty: he must defend government policy while assisting the court impartially; as the government is the largest litigant (National Litigation Policy, 2010), candid advice before decisions saves public money.

The description is accurate but incomplete: the AG is the government's chief adviser and advocate, and also a constitutional officer whose integrity strengthens the rule of law. A fixed tenure and a published code of conduct would reinforce that role.
free.upm-2019-gs2-15:
Anti-defection lawParty whipExecutive dominanceQuality of deliberation

In the Westminster model the individual MP legislates, deliberates on policy and holds the executive to account. In India, the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule, 1985), the executive's control of the House's agenda and frequent disruptions have reduced most MPs to votes cast on the party whip. PRS data for the 17th Lok Sabha (2019–24) show the result: only 274 sittings, just 16% of Bills referred to committees, and 35% of Bills passed with less than an hour of debate.

1. Why the individual MP's role has declined

  • The whip on every vote: defying the whip on any motion, even an ordinary Bill, invites disqualification, so MPs cannot vote by conscience or constituency interest; Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld the law.
  • Executive control of time: government business takes precedence; only 14 private members' Bills have ever become law, the last in 1970.
  • Fewer sittings: the Lok Sabha sits far less than in the 1950s, below the minimum of 120 days a year suggested by the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002).
  • Bypassing Parliament: ordinances, wide delegated legislation and the Money Bill route, as for the Aadhaar Act, 2016, reduce scrutiny.
  • Incentives and capacity: constituency service and patronage reward MPs more than law-making, and MPs have little research support.

2. Impact on the quality of debates and their outcome

  • Hasty laws: the three farm laws of 2020 were passed without committee scrutiny and repealed in 2021 after prolonged protests.
  • Litigation and repeated corrections: the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 re-enacted provisions the Supreme Court had struck down, and the Court struck them down again in 2025.
  • Weak financial scrutiny: most demands for grants are guillotined, so the budget is barely debated.
  • Ritual debates: speeches follow party lines, amendments moved by individual MPs rarely succeed, and disruptions consume Question Hour.
  • Weaker accountability: less questioning of ministers strengthens executive dominance and lowers public trust in Parliament.

3. Not a uniform decline

  • Committees: departmentally related standing committees (1993) still allow detailed, bipartisan scrutiny behind closed doors, where the whip does not apply.
  • Private initiative: the Rajya Sabha passed Tiruchi Siva's private member's Bill on the rights of transgender persons in 2015, and Zero Hour lets MPs raise local issues.

4. Way forward

  • Narrower whip: confine disqualification to voluntarily giving up party membership and to confidence and no-confidence votes, as the Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) proposed.
  • Mandatory scrutiny: refer all major Bills to committees and follow the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014).
  • Time and support: a minimum number of sittings and research staff for every MP.

Restoring the individual MP's voice is essential for deliberative democracy: Parliament should be the place where laws are tested, not merely passed.
free.upm-2019-gs2-16:
Neo-liberal planningMulti-level planningSubsidiarityDistrict Planning Committee

Since the 1991 reforms, Indian planning has moved from a centralised, state-led model to a neo-liberal paradigm: markets and private investment drive growth, the State acts as facilitator and regulator, and plans are indicative. The Planning Commission gave way to NITI Aayog (2015), and the Twelfth Plan (2012–17) was the last. In this setting, multi-level planning, which links village, block, district, State and national plans, is expected to cut costs and remove blockages by taking each decision at the right level (subsidiarity).

1. How multi-level planning makes operations cost-effective

  • Local information: Gram Sabhas and ward committees know local needs, so assets match demand and fewer lie unused.
  • Convergence: district plans pool funds from many schemes and avoid duplication; the Aspirational Districts (2018) and Blocks (2023) programmes use local data and rankings.
  • Ownership and accountability: plans approved in Gram Sabhas and checked by social audits reduce leakages and maintenance costs.
  • A leaner Centre: with States and local bodies handling delivery, the Union concentrates on macro policy, regulation and infrastructure, while private partners finance and run projects such as urban services.
  • Integrated infrastructure planning: the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (2021) puts ministries' projects on one GIS platform to avoid clashes and delays.

2. Evidence from practice

  • Earlier groundwork: the Dantwala Working Group on block-level planning (1978) and the Hanumantha Rao Working Group on district planning (1984) laid the base.
  • Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996): devolving about 35–40% of plan funds to local bodies improved local services.
  • Gram Panchayat Development Plans (since 2015): strengthened by the People's Plan Campaign (2018); e-GramSwaraj (2020) tracks plans and spending online.

3. Why blockages persist

  • Hollow devolution: few States have transferred the funds, functions and functionaries for the 29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule and 18 in the Twelfth, and many District Planning Committees exist only on paper.
  • Top-down schemes: centrally sponsored schemes with uniform norms and tied funds leave little room for local choice.
  • Capacity gaps: few planners, and weak data and accounts, at block and panchayat levels.
  • Contradictions of the neo-liberal model: special purpose vehicles and parastatals often bypass elected local bodies, a criticism made of the Smart Cities Mission; market-led growth widens regional gaps that local plans alone cannot close.
  • Elite capture: dominant groups can steer local plans to their own benefit.

Multi-level planning fits a market economy in which the State steers and local bodies deliver, but its promise depends on fiscal decentralisation (the 16th Finance Commission's ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies), activity mapping as urged by the Second ARC, and planning capacity, so that subsidiarity becomes practice.
free.upm-2019-gs2-17:
PartnershipConvergenceCooperative federalismWhole-of-society approach

Development is now seen as the joint task of the State, market and civil society: governments bring scale, funds and legitimacy; businesses bring capital, technology and management; NGOs, cooperatives and self-help groups bring trust and last-mile reach. SDG 17, on partnerships for the goals, recognises this. In India, partnership runs across ministries (convergence), between the Union and the States (cooperative federalism) and across public, private and community sectors.

1. Partnership in India's development process

  • Public–private: the Delhi and Mumbai airports were modernised under PPPs, and the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016) revived highway building by sharing risk between the government and developers.
  • Government–community: about 10 crore women are in self-help groups under DAY-NRLM; Kerala's Kudumbashree (1998) works with panchayats; NABARD's SHG–bank linkage (1992) brought formal credit to the poor.
  • Cooperatives: Amul and Operation Flood (1970) made India a dairy giant; a Ministry of Cooperation was created in 2021.
  • Corporate responsibility: under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, 27,188 companies spent about ₹34,909 crore on CSR in 2023-24.
  • Government–civil society: NGOs run school-meal kitchens and health outreach, and NITI Aayog's NGO-DARPAN portal links NGOs with ministries.
  • Multi-agency campaigns: Pulse Polio, with the WHO, UNICEF and Rotary, helped India be certified polio-free in 2014.

2. Collaboration and team spirit within government

  • Cooperative federalism: the GST Council (2016) takes joint Union–State decisions, and NITI Aayog's Governing Council brings Chief Ministers together.
  • Convergence: the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) brings departments, foundations and companies together; Poshan Abhiyaan links health, women and child development, and sanitation.
  • Breaking silos: PM Gati Shakti (2021) puts infrastructure ministries on one planning platform.

3. Where partnership falls short

  • PPP stress: aggressive bidding and stalled projects led the Kelkar Committee (2015) to call for better risk-sharing and dispute resolution.
  • Shrinking civic space: stricter FCRA amendments (2020) reduced foreign funding for many NGOs.
  • Silos and turf: departments guard their schemes, and Centre–State friction over funding and GST compensation strains cooperative federalism.
  • Unequal reach: CSR funds concentrate in industrialised States and in a few sectors, leaving poorer regions underfunded.

4. Assessment

  • A visible shift: India's development has moved from state-led delivery towards a whole-of-society effort, as Swachh Bharat's community campaign and COVID-19 vaccine production and delivery showed.
  • Partnership needs equality: collaboration works when partners share decisions, not only tasks.

Stable contracts, respect for civil society's autonomy and institutionalised Centre–State dialogue would turn partnership from a slogan into a habit of collaborative governance.
free.upm-2019-gs2-18:
Participatory governancePolicy cycleSocial auditAwareness of entitlements

Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections, such as SCs and STs, women, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities and informal workers, often underperform not for lack of funds but because the intended beneficiaries remain passive recipients. Many do not know their entitlements, and they are rarely consulted at any stage of the policy cycle: agenda-setting, design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation. The Gram Sabha (Article 243A), the RTI Act (2005) and social audits were meant to change this.

1. How lack of awareness weakens schemes

  • Low take-up: eligible people do not apply for pensions, scholarships or insurance claims, and welfare boards for construction workers hold unspent cess funds because many workers are not registered.
  • Middlemen: touts exploit ignorance, charging fees for free services or diverting benefits.
  • Exclusion: documentation demands and authentication failures shut out those least able to complain, as with ration denials in Jharkhand (2017).
  • Rights unclaimed: large numbers of forest-rights claims have been rejected, often for want of documents or awareness of the Gram Sabha's powers.
  • Silent grievances: without knowledge of redress channels, failures go unreported and uncorrected.

2. Absence of involvement at each stage

  • Top-down design: uniform schemes, often in non-tribal languages, treat tribal people as beneficiaries rather than decision-makers.
  • Nominal participation: Gram Sabhas meet irregularly and are often dominated by local elites, while women and Dalits speak less.

3. Evidence that participation works

  • Social audit: the MKSS's public hearings in Rajasthan in the 1990s fed the movement for the RTI Act and pioneered social audits, made mandatory under MGNREGA and retained under the VB-G RAM G Act, which replaced it from 1 July 2026; Meghalaya's 2017 Act was the first State law to extend social audit across services.
  • Food security: Section 28 of the National Food Security Act, 2013 provides for social audits, and vigilance committees watch ration shops.
  • Water: under the Jal Jeevan Mission, village water and sanitation committees, at least half of whose members are women, plan and maintain supply.
  • Women's collectives: Kudumbashree and SHG federations help members claim entitlements and monitor services.

4. A balanced view

  • Not only awareness: poor design, delayed funds, staff shortages, corruption and the digital divide also cause failure, and participation cannot substitute for administrative capacity.
  • Participation can be captured: without safeguards, local elites dominate committees and audits.

Effective welfare needs citizens as partners: information campaigns in local languages, active Gram and Mahila Sabhas, independent social audit units and responsive grievance redress, so that schemes are shaped by those they serve, which is jan bhagidari in practice.
free.upm-2019-gs2-19:
Non-AlignmentGlobal SouthStrategic autonomyMulti-alignment

After independence India became a leading voice of colonised and developing nations: a sponsor of the Bandung Conference (1955), a founder of the Non-Aligned Movement (1961) and the Group of 77 (1964), and a champion of a New International Economic Order. Since 1991, as a rising power with strategic partnerships and an eye on a permanent Security Council seat, India has practised multi-alignment. Critics say this has cost it moral leadership; others see the role recast rather than lost.

1. The basis of the old image

  • Anti-colonialism and anti-racism: India raised racial discrimination in South Africa at the UN in 1946, cut trade ties with that government and backed liberation movements in Asia and Africa.
  • Non-alignment: refusal to join Cold War blocs and the Panchsheel principles (1954) offered new States a third path.
  • Economic justice: India hosted the second UNCTAD conference (New Delhi, 1968) and pressed for fairer trade and aid.
  • Solidarity: it recognised the PLO (1974) and the State of Palestine (1988), and trained officials from developing countries under ITEC (1964).

2. Why critics say the image has faded

  • Closer to the West: India became a US Major Defence Partner (2016), signed a 10-year defence framework with the US (2025) and joined the Quad and I2U2 with Israel and the UAE.
  • Joining exclusive clubs: the NSG waiver (2008) and entry into the MTCR (2016), the Wassenaar Arrangement (2017) and the Australia Group (2018) suggest seeking a seat at the high table rather than changing it.
  • Cautious votes: India abstained on UN resolutions on Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022) and on the October 2023 General Assembly call for a humanitarian truce in Gaza, though it voted for a ceasefire in December 2023.
  • Interest-based economics: it left the RCEP talks (2019) and has signed trade agreements with the EFTA States (2024) and the UK (2025); some neighbours see it as a dominant power rather than a champion of the weak.

3. Why the role is recast, not lost

  • Voice of the Global South: India has convened Voice of the Global South Summits since January 2023, and the African Union became a permanent member of the G20 under India's presidency (New Delhi, September 2023).
  • Development and relief partner: Vaccine Maitri (2021), about US$4 billion of support to Sri Lanka in its 2022 crisis, Operation Dost (2023), Operation Brahma (2025), and UPI technology for partners such as Namibia.
  • Southern causes in global forums: climate equity, food security at the WTO, the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019); as BRICS chair it hosted the 18th summit in New Delhi (September 2026), which took up unilateral tariffs and WTO reform.

The statement is only partly true. India's diplomacy has shifted from ideology to interest, and it no longer leads a protest bloc, but its ties with both the West and Russia let it speak for the developing world as a bridge within the system. Its credibility depends on consistent principles and on delivering for partners, above all in its neighbourhood.
free.upm-2019-gs2-20:
Strategic autonomyComprehensive Global Strategic PartnershipHyphenationTrade frictions

India and the United States, the world's largest democracies, describe their ties as a Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership (2020). Yet friction recurs because Washington tends to fit India into its own global priorities, once containing the Soviet Union, then non-proliferation, now competition with China and transactional trade, while India seeks recognition as an independent great power with strategic autonomy. The gap between US expectations of an aligned partner and India's national self-esteem explains much of the friction.

1. Historical frictions

  • Cold War alignments: the US made Pakistan an ally through a mutual defence agreement and SEATO (1954), and in 1971 sent the USS Enterprise into the Bay of Bengal during the Bangladesh war.
  • Non-proliferation: the US-led regime treated India as a non-nuclear State; fuel for Tarapur was stopped after the US Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act (1978), and sanctions followed the 1998 tests.
  • Hyphenation: policy often bracketed India with Pakistan instead of treating it as a major power in its own right.

2. When the US accommodated India's ambitions

  • Nuclear recognition: the civil nuclear deal (2005–08) and the NSG waiver (2008) de-hyphenated India from Pakistan and accepted it as a responsible nuclear power.
  • Defence partnership: Major Defence Partner (2016); the foundational agreements LEMOA, COMCASA and BECA (2016–20); GE F414 engines to be co-produced with HAL (2023 MoU); a 10-year framework for the defence partnership signed in Kuala Lumpur (October 2025).
  • Indo-Pacific role: US Pacific Command was renamed Indo-Pacific Command (2018), and Quad leaders have met since 2021.
  • Technology: iCET (2023) became TRUST (2025).

3. Contemporary frictions

  • Trade: the US withdrew India's GSP benefits in 2019. US tariffs on most Indian goods rose to 50% in August 2025, including a 25% Russian-oil penalty. The penalty was removed in February 2026, with a framework for an interim trade deal, and the reciprocal tariffs lapsed after a US Supreme Court ruling; but a new 10% duty has covered about half of India's exports since July 2026, and the deal was unsigned in October 2026.
  • Strategic autonomy: the threat of CAATSA sanctions (2017) over the S-400 purchase, pressure over Russian oil, and the expiry of the US waiver for Chabahar in April 2026.
  • Pakistan again: US claims to have brokered the May 2025 India–Pakistan ceasefire, which India says was agreed bilaterally, and warmer US ties with Pakistan's military leadership touched India's insistence on bilateralism.
  • People: a US$100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions (September 2025) hit Indian professionals.
  • Values: US reports criticising religious freedom in India are rejected by New Delhi as biased.

The statement holds: friction comes less from clashing interests than from mismatched expectations, since Washington seeks an aligned partner and India a partnership of equals. Shared interests in a balanced Indo-Pacific and in technology keep ties resilient; respect for strategic autonomy and a balanced trade deal would let the partnership match India's ambitions.
free.upm-2019-gs3-1:
Goods and Services Tax101st AmendmentSubsumed taxesRevenue buoyancy

The Goods and Services Tax (GST), introduced on 1 July 2017 under the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016, is a destination-based tax on the supply of goods and services. The Union (CGST) and the States (SGST) levy it concurrently, with IGST on inter-State supplies (Article 269A). It subsumed 17 Central and State taxes and 13 cesses, replacing cascading "tax on tax" with input tax credit along the chain.

1. Indirect taxes subsumed in GST

  • Union taxes (8): central excise duty; additional excise duties on goods of special importance; additional excise duties on textiles; excise under the Medicinal and Toilet Preparations Act; additional customs duty (CVD); special additional duty of customs (SAD); service tax; and central surcharges and cesses on supplies.
  • State taxes (9): VAT or sales tax; central sales tax; purchase tax; luxury tax; entry tax in all forms; entertainment tax (except that levied by local bodies); taxes on advertisements; taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling; and State surcharges and cesses on supplies.
  • Kept outside: basic customs duty, alcohol for human consumption, five petroleum products (until the GST Council recommends otherwise), stamp duty and electricity duty; tobacco also bears central excise.

2. Revenue implications: the gains

  • Wider base, better compliance: invoice-matched credit, e-way bills (2018) and e-invoicing for large firms (2020) leave a digital trail that curbs evasion.
  • Buoyant collections: gross GST revenue excluding the compensation cess grew about 8.3% to over ₹22 lakh crore in 2025-26 (official data, April 2026), though less once the shrinking cess is counted.
  • Gains for consuming States: revenue follows consumption, helping populous consuming States.
  • Efficiency dividend: lower costs without cascading or check posts widen the base.

3. Revenue implications: the strains

  • Below revenue neutrality: the Arvind Subramanian committee (2015) suggested a revenue-neutral rate of about 15–15.5%, but rate cuts after 2017 kept the effective rate lower.
  • Compensation and the pandemic: States were guaranteed 14% annual growth over their 2015-16 revenue for five years (July 2017–June 2022). The COVID-19 shortfall was met by back-to-back loans of ₹1.1 lakh crore (2020-21) and ₹1.59 lakh crore (2021-22), repaid by extending the compensation cess.
  • Loss of fiscal autonomy: States cannot set rates alone, and the Union's one-third vote in the Council works as a veto.
  • Leakages: fake invoices, fraudulent credit claims and delayed refunds to exporters.
  • GST 2.0 (22 September 2025): two main slabs of 5% and 18%, plus 40% for luxury and sin goods, cut rates on many goods; the compensation cess, removed from most goods, ended on 1 February 2026, replaced by a higher central excise duty on tobacco and a new cess on pan masala.

GST has moved from teething troubles to a buoyant revenue base. Stable rates, quicker refunds, the dispute-settlement mechanism of Article 279A(11) and, in time, petroleum within GST would make it a truly "good and simple tax" for both levels of government.
free.upm-2019-gs3-2:
GDP growthFlexible inflation targetingJobs and investmentMacroeconomic stability

When this question was set in 2019, inflation was low but growth was slowing. By 2026 India had both: real GDP grew 7.7% in 2025-26 (new series, base 2022-23) and 7.8% in April–June 2026, while CPI inflation was 4.8% in August 2026, within the RBI's 4% ±2% band. Growth and price stability are necessary for a healthy economy, but not sufficient; jobs, investment, debt and resilience matter too. The view is therefore only partly valid.

1. Why the view has merit

  • Steady growth: under the new series, growth was 7.2% in 2023-24, 7.1% in 2024-25 and 7.7% in 2025-26 (provisional).
  • Anchored prices: flexible inflation targeting (RBI Act amended in 2016) has kept inflation lower and more stable than in 2009–13; the RBI cut the repo rate by 125 basis points in 2025 and raised it to 5.50% in October 2026 as inflation picked up.
  • Fiscal consolidation: the Union's fiscal deficit fell from 4.8% of GDP (2024-25) to 4.4% (2025-26 RE) and 4.3% (2026-27 BE), alongside capital spending of ₹12.22 lakh crore.
  • Healthier banks: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and the 4R strategy cut banks' gross NPAs from 11.2% (March 2018) to about 2.3% (March 2025), reviving credit.
  • External buffers: record remittances of about US$135 billion (2024-25) cushion the current account.

2. Why growth and low inflation are not enough

  • Jobs: unemployment was 5.0% in September 2026 (PLFS, current weekly status), but about 46% of workers remain in agriculture (PLFS 2023-24), about 90% are informal, and women's labour force participation was only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Food-price volatility: headline averages hide spikes; food inflation touched nearly 11% in October 2024, hurting poor households whose budgets are food-heavy.
  • Debt and interest: central debt is 55.6% of GDP (2026-27 BE), above the target of 50±1% by March 2031, and interest takes about a quarter of Union spending, crowding out health and education.
  • Private investment and manufacturing: public capex has done the heavy lifting, while manufacturing remains about 17% of GVA.
  • Distribution and risk: the post-COVID recovery was K-shaped, favouring formal firms and the better-off; dependence on imported crude (over 85%) and climate shocks to farming threaten stability.

3. What "good shape" requires

  • Employment-rich growth: labour-intensive manufacturing, MSME credit, skills and formal jobs for women.
  • Human capital: better learning and health outcomes to raise productivity.
  • Fiscal space and resilience: tax buoyancy, better quality of spending, energy transition and climate-proof agriculture.

India's macroeconomic fundamentals are sound, so the view is right about stability but incomplete. An economy is in good shape only when growth creates decent jobs and rising incomes for most citizens, not merely good headline numbers.
free.upm-2019-gs3-3:
Integrated Farming SystemResource recyclingSoil healthSustainable intensification

An Integrated Farming System (IFS) combines interdependent enterprises, such as crops, dairy, poultry, fishery, goatery, horticulture, agroforestry, beekeeping and mushrooms, on one holding so that the waste of one becomes the input of another. ICAR's Indian Institute of Farming Systems Research, Modipuram (Meerut) leads research on it. With 86% of holdings small and marginal (Agriculture Census 2015-16), and with soil, water and incomes strained after the Green Revolution, IFS offers a way to sustain production, not merely raise it.

1. How IFS sustains agricultural production

  • Soil health: dung, crop residues, pond silt and vermicompost return organic matter to the soil, reversing the decline caused by continuous cereal monocropping and heavy chemical use.
  • Nutrient and energy recycling: residues feed animals, manure runs a biogas plant and the slurry fertilises fields and fish ponds, cutting purchased fertiliser, feed and fuel.
  • Water use: a farm pond harvests rainwater for fish and life-saving irrigation, while trees and fodder on bunds reduce runoff and erosion.
  • More output per hectare: the same land and family labour yield several products through the year.
  • Natural pest control: diversity breaks pest cycles; ducks in rice–fish–duck systems eat weeds and insects.

2. Benefits for farmers and resilience

  • Risk spreading: if the monsoon fails or crop prices crash, milk, eggs and fish still earn, which matters most to rainfed farmers.
  • Steady income and work: daily and weekly income from livestock, and year-round work for family labour, especially women.
  • Nutrition: milk, eggs, fish, fruit and vegetables diversify the family diet.
  • Climate resilience: diverse systems recover faster from droughts and floods, and agroforestry stores carbon.

3. How far: the limits

  • A complement, not a substitute: IFS sustains output on small farms but cannot by itself raise national grain output as high-yielding seeds and irrigation did.
  • Capital and skills: animals, ponds and sheds need upfront investment, and farmers must manage several enterprises at once.
  • Services and markets: veterinary care, quality feed and fingerlings, and markets for many small lots are often lacking.
  • Location-specific design: a model that works in wet lowlands may fail in arid areas, so zone-specific, research-backed models are needed.

4. Support available

  • The Rainfed Area Development component of the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, RKVY, the National Livestock Mission, PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020), demonstrations by Krishi Vigyan Kendras and FPOs for marketing promote IFS.

IFS is highly helpful in sustaining production on small farms because it protects soil, water and incomes, though it complements rather than replaces irrigation and better seeds. Scaling it with credit, extension and markets is a practical path to sustainable intensification.
free.upm-2019-gs3-4:
Watershed developmentRainfed agricultureRidge-to-valley approachWDC-PMKSY

About half of India's net sown area is rainfed, and ISRO's Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (2021) found about 97.85 million hectares, nearly 30% of the country, degraded. In such water-stressed areas the watershed approach treats the whole area draining to a common point, from ridge to valley, to conserve soil and water. The National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas (NWDPRA, 1990-91) applied it to farm land; its successors, the IWMP (2009-10) and WDC-PMKSY (from 2015-16), carry it forward.

1. How the project works

  • Area treatment: contour trenches, bunds and plantations on the ridge; gully plugs, check dams, percolation tanks and farm ponds along drainage lines.
  • Production systems: improved seeds, dryland horticulture, fodder and crop demonstrations on treated land.
  • Livelihoods: support for landless and asset-less households through livestock and micro-enterprises.
  • People's participation: watershed committees and user groups plan the works, contribute to their cost and maintain them.

2. Impact on agricultural production

  • More water for crops: recharged wells and farm ponds give protective irrigation during dry spells, saving the kharif crop and often allowing a rabi crop.
  • Higher cropping intensity and yields: evaluation studies report more area under a second crop, better yields and fewer crop failures in treated watersheds.
  • Soil conservation: less erosion keeps fertile topsoil and improves the moisture-holding capacity of fields.
  • Diversification: assured water and fodder support horticulture, dairy and small ruminants, raising farm incomes.
  • Success stories: Ralegan Siddhi and Hiware Bazar in drought-prone Ahmednagar (Maharashtra) and Sukhomajri (Haryana) turned water-scarce villages into surplus producers through community watershed work.

3. Limitations

  • Uneven gains: landowners with wells near drainage lines gain most; the landless and tail-end farmers gain less.
  • Groundwater rebound: recharged water is often pumped out for water-intensive crops such as sugarcane, wiping out the gains.
  • Sustainability: structures decay after a project ends if user groups weaken; short project periods limit impact.

4. WDC-PMKSY 2.0

  • Approved in December 2021 for 2021–26 with a central outlay of ₹8,134 crore, it targets 49.5 lakh ha, all sanctioned to the States; it raised unit costs to ₹22,000 per ha in the plains and ₹28,000 in difficult areas, added springshed rejuvenation for hilly areas, and monitors works through geo-tagging on ISRO's Bhuvan portal.

Watershed development has made water-stressed areas more productive and drought-resilient wherever communities owned it. Linking it with groundwater regulation, suitable crop choice and micro-irrigation under "Per Drop More Crop" can turn these gains into lasting water security.
free.upm-2019-gs3-5:
Water engineeringGreen RevolutionEngineers' DayEvergreen Revolution

India's journey from famine and drought to food self-sufficiency owes much to two scientists. Sir M. Visvesvaraya (1861–1962), engineer and Diwan of Mysore (1912–18), harnessed rivers through dams, gates and irrigation systems; his birthday, 15 September, is observed as Engineers' Day, and he received the Bharat Ratna in 1955. Dr M.S. Swaminathan (1925–2023), the scientific leader of India's Green Revolution, was the first World Food Prize laureate (1987) and was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 2024.

1. Visvesvaraya and water engineering

  • Automatic sluice gates: he designed and patented automatic flood gates, first installed at the Khadakvasla reservoir near Pune (1903), which raised storage without raising the dam; they were later used at the Tigra dam (Gwalior) and Krishnaraja Sagar.
  • Block system of irrigation: devised for the Deccan canals, it rotated water among blocks of land, spreading scarce water fairly and preventing waterlogging.
  • Krishnaraja Sagar dam: begun on the Kaveri near Mysore in 1911 under his leadership, it irrigates large areas of Mandya and supported power and industry.
  • Flood control: after the Musi flood of 1908 he planned Hyderabad's flood protection, including the Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar reservoirs; he also advised on protecting Visakhapatnam port from sea erosion.
  • Planning vision: his "Planned Economy for India" (1934), the Bhadravati iron works and the University of Mysore (1916) linked engineering to industrialisation.

2. Swaminathan and agricultural science

  • Green Revolution: he led the testing and adaptation of Norman Borlaug's dwarf wheat from the mid-1960s; with Minister C. Subramaniam's support, wheat output more than doubled between 1965-66 and 1971-72, reducing dependence on food imports.
  • Institution building: as Director-General of ICAR (1972–79) and of the International Rice Research Institute (1982–88) he strengthened research and extension, and he founded the M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation, Chennai (1988).
  • Evergreen Revolution: he warned against soil and water degradation from intensive farming and called for lasting productivity without ecological harm, through biovillages, mangrove conservation and village knowledge centres.
  • Farmers' welfare: the National Commission on Farmers (2004–06), which he chaired, recommended an MSP at least 50% above the weighted average cost of production (widely read as the comprehensive cost, C2), wider credit and insurance, and a regulated market within about 5 km of every farmer.
  • Nutrition security: he championed biofortification, millets and women farmers, shifting the goal from food to nutrition security.

Visvesvaraya gave India the water and Swaminathan the seeds for food security. Today's challenges, falling water tables and climate change, call for combining their legacies: efficient water engineering and an Evergreen Revolution.
free.upm-2019-gs3-6:
Bharatiya Antariksh StationGaganyaanHuman spaceflightMicrogravity research

India plans its own space station, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), as the next step after Gaganyaan, its first human spaceflight programme. In September 2024 the Union Cabinet approved the first module, BAS-01, by expanding the Gaganyaan programme, whose outlay was revised to ₹20,193 crore. As of 2026, BAS-01 is targeted for 2028 and a five-module station for 2035, a step towards an Indian landing on the Moon by 2040.

1. The plan

  • Configuration: five modules: BAS-01, a Core-Docking Module with several berthing ports, a Science Research Module, a Laboratory Module and a Common Working Module with crew quarters and airlocks.
  • Size and orbit: about 52 tonnes in an orbit of 400–450 km at an inclination of 51.6°, normally for three to four astronauts and up to six on short visits.
  • BAS-01: a module of about 10 tonnes (a full-scale 3.8 m × 8 m model was unveiled on National Space Day, August 2025) with an indigenous Environmental Control and Life Support System, the Bharat Docking System and Bharat Berthing Mechanism, and viewports. It is to fly on the LVM3; later modules on the Next Generation Launch Vehicle.
  • Operations: crew stays of three to six months once the station is complete.

2. Benefits for India's space programme

  • Long-duration human spaceflight: a permanent outpost lets India master life support, radiation protection, crew health and resupply, which a three-day Gaganyaan flight cannot.
  • Microgravity science: experiments in medicine, biology, protein crystals, materials and fluid physics, and space biotechnology for food and health.
  • Technology spin-offs: water recycling, closed-loop life support, robotics and advanced materials benefit industry on Earth.
  • Stepping stone to the Moon: docking, assembly in orbit and crewed operations support Chandrayaan-4's sample return (2028) and a crewed lunar landing by 2040.
  • Strategic autonomy: the ISS is due to retire around 2030 and China already runs Tiangong; a national station ensures India's own access to orbit.
  • Space economy and diplomacy: opportunities for private firms through IN-SPACe, space tourism, and research slots for partner countries.

3. Challenges

  • Heavy lift and reliability: assembling a 52-tonne station needs the NGLV and a high launch rate, after PSLV failures in May 2025 and January 2026.
  • Cost and timelines: human-rated systems, spacesuits and resupply are costly, and Gaganyaan itself has slipped.
  • Space debris: a crowded low Earth orbit raises collision risk.

The BAS would turn India from a visitor to orbit into a resident. Meeting the 2028 and 2035 milestones, with private industry and global partners, can make it the base of a self-reliant human spaceflight ecosystem.
free.upm-2019-gs3-7:
Coastal sand miningPlacer mineralsShoreline erosionCRZ Notification 2019

India's coastline, re-measured in 2025 at 11,098.81 km, holds beach and offshore sand used for construction and placer minerals such as ilmenite, rutile, zircon, garnet, sillimanite and monazite (a source of thorium). Whether mining is legal or illegal, removing sand faster than waves and rivers replace it upsets the coast's sediment budget. The result is erosion, ecological loss and hardship for coastal communities.

1. Environmental impacts

  • Erosion and shoreline retreat: sand taken from beaches and the nearshore is not replaced, so beaches shrink and the sea advances; about a third of India's coast (33.6%) was already eroding (NCCR).
  • Loss of natural defences: dunes and wide beaches absorb storm surges; mined coasts are more exposed to cyclones and tsunamis.
  • Saltwater intrusion: lowered beaches and mining pits let seawater reach wells and fields.
  • Habitat damage: turtle-nesting beaches, mangroves, estuaries and seabed life are destroyed; offshore dredging raises turbidity that smothers fish breeding grounds.
  • Radiation and dust: unregulated handling of monazite-bearing sand raises radiation and dust hazards.

2. Socio-economic impacts

  • Fishing communities: they lose landing beaches, homes and fishing grounds, while profits go elsewhere.
  • Revenue loss and crime: illegal mining creates sand mafias, evades royalty and corrupts officials.
  • Legal mining also harms: licensed mining by public sector units still alters sediment flows; legality decides who profits, not how the coast erodes.

3. Specific examples

  • Tamil Nadu: the CBI case shows how nearly two decades of illegal extraction of atomic and other minerals escaped regulation.
  • Kerala: at Alappad, residents blame mining for loss of land to the sea; off Kollam, fishers fear for fishing grounds and livelihoods.

4. Regulation and way forward

  • Rules: the CRZ Notification, 2019 prohibits sand mining in coastal zones except for rare minerals not available elsewhere; in 2019 the Centre stopped private mining of beach-sand minerals; the Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines (2016) and Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines (2020) require replenishment studies, GPS tracking and drone surveillance.
  • Offshore mining: the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2023 opened blocks to auction; cumulative impact assessment and consultation with fishers are essential.
  • Alternatives: manufactured sand (M-sand) from crushed rock and recycled construction waste.

Coastal sand is a natural buffer, not just a raw material. Mining guided by sediment-budget studies, strict enforcement and community oversight can protect both the coast and those who live on it.
free.upm-2019-gs3-8:
VulnerabilityExposure, sensitivity and capacityPressure and Release modelDisaster risk

Vulnerability is "the conditions determined by physical, social, economic and environmental factors or processes which increase the susceptibility of an individual, a community, assets or systems to the impacts of hazards" (UNDRR). A hazard becomes a disaster only when it meets vulnerable people: Risk = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability ÷ Capacity. The Odisha super cyclone of 1999 killed about 10,000 people, while Phailin (2013) and Fani (2019) killed far fewer, because vulnerability had been reduced.

1. How vulnerability can be characterised

  • Three components: exposure (people and assets in harm's way), sensitivity (how badly they are affected) and adaptive or coping capacity (ability to resist and recover), as used by the IPCC.
  • From root causes to unsafe conditions: the Pressure and Release model (Blaikie and others, 1994) traces vulnerability from root causes such as poverty and unequal power, through dynamic pressures such as rapid urbanisation and deforestation, to unsafe conditions such as fragile houses on floodplains.
  • Scale and time: it differs between individuals, households, communities and regions, and changes with seasons and years; a migrant in a city slum and a farmer in a drought-prone district face different risks.
  • Measurement and mapping: indicators of housing, income, literacy, health and access to services are combined into indices and maps, such as BMTPC's Vulnerability Atlas of India and MoES's coastal vulnerability maps.
  • Differential impact: women, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities and marginalised communities are often hit hardest.

2. Types of vulnerability

  • Physical: weak buildings, lifelines and settlements in hazard-prone locations.
  • Social: disadvantage due to gender, age, disability, caste, illiteracy or isolation, which limits access to warnings and relief.
  • Economic: poverty, informal jobs and lack of savings, credit or insurance, so a single shock pushes families into debt.
  • Environmental: degraded ecosystems that no longer buffer hazards, such as lost mangroves, deforested slopes and filled wetlands.
  • Institutional and political: weak planning, enforcement, warning systems and accountability.

3. Reducing vulnerability

  • Safer places and buildings: risk-informed land use, building codes and retrofitting of schools and hospitals.
  • Stronger households: social protection, crop insurance, savings and diversified livelihoods.
  • Nature and warning: protecting mangroves and wetlands, and early warning that reaches the last mile, under the NDMP and the Sendai Framework (2015–2030).

Vulnerability is socially produced and therefore reducible. Characterising it through exposure, sensitivity and capacity lets planners target the people most at risk, shifting disaster management from relief to risk reduction.
free.upm-2019-gs3-9:
Over-ground workersTerror ecosystemUAPA bansCounter-terror strategy

Over-ground workers (OGWs) are supporters of militant groups who do not carry arms openly but supply logistics, shelter, intelligence, money and propaganda while living as ordinary citizens. They form the terror ecosystem without which armed militants cannot survive. The Centre declared Jamaat-e-Islami, Jammu and Kashmir an unlawful association under the UAPA in February 2019, citing its links with militant groups, and extended the ban by five years in February 2024 (upheld by a UAPA tribunal later that year), drawing attention to such support networks.

1. Role of OGWs in insurgency-affected areas

  • Logistics and shelter: food, safe houses, transport, guides for infiltrators and movement of arms; attackers who strike tourists or security forces depend on such local help to approach targets and escape.
  • Intelligence and reconnaissance: tracking security forces and identifying soft targets, as in the targeted killings of minorities and migrant workers in Kashmir in 2021–22.
  • Finance: raising money through hawala, front organisations, donations, extortion and the drug trade.
  • Recruitment and radicalisation: spotting and grooming youth, spreading propaganda online and, in the past, mobilising stone-pelting crowds.
  • "Hybrid" militants: some carry out a single attack with a pistol or grenade and slip back into normal life, which makes them hard to detect.
  • Other theatres: in the North-East, networks collect extortion "taxes" for insurgent groups; Maoists, too, depended on village and urban supporters.

2. Why OGWs are hard to tackle

  • Indistinguishable from civilians: no uniform or weapon, so evidence is hard to gather.
  • Coercion and sympathy: some help out of fear, others out of ideology or kinship.
  • Digital networks: encrypted apps and social media replace physical meetings.
  • Risk of alienation: heavy-handed action can push communities towards militants.

3. Measures to neutralise their influence

  • Intelligence-led policing: mapping networks through the Multi-Agency Centre, NATGRID and CCTNS, and tracking money and online activity.
  • Legal and financial action: cases under the UAPA and the J&K Public Safety Act, 1978; NIA and ED terror-funding cases; attachment of property used for terrorism; and dismissal of government employees with terror links under Article 311(2)(c).
  • Banning fronts: UAPA bans on Jamaat-e-Islami J&K and the JKLF (both 2019, extended in 2024) are meant to cut off funds and institutions that the government links to militancy.
  • Winning hearts: civic action such as Operation Sadbhavana (1998), jobs, sports and counselling for youth, and surrender-and-rehabilitation policies.
  • Due process: fair, speedy trials and judicial oversight keep public trust, while prolonged detention without trial breeds resentment.

Militancy survives on its support base. Neutralising OGWs through intelligence, law and development, while respecting rights, is the key to dismantling the terror ecosystem for good.
free.upm-2019-gs3-10:
CyberdomePublic–private partnershipCyber intelligenceCybercrime prevention

Cyberdome is the technological research and development centre of the Kerala Police, inaugurated in February 2016 in Thiruvananthapuram as a public–private initiative against cybercrime. It brings police officers together with volunteer professionals from the IT industry, academia and research bodies. Such models matter: India recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024, up 17.9% over 2023, about 73% of them involving fraud (NCRB, Crime in India 2024).

1. What the Cyberdome project is

  • Partnership model: a small police team works with volunteer experts (about 500 professionals were to volunteer at its launch) and with government departments, research groups and private firms.
  • Functions: cyber forensics, cyber intelligence, cyber security and a social media lab; Kerala Police has also set up a darknet lab and trained officers as darknet analysts.
  • Research links: an agreement with NIT Calicut (2024) supports research, staff training, cyber forensics and data analytics.
  • A model for others: a team from Dubai visited to study its working.

2. How it can help control internet crimes in India

  • From reaction to prevention: continuous monitoring can spot phishing sites, fake apps, drug sales on the dark web and child sexual abuse material before victims complain.
  • Filling the skill gap: volunteer and academic experts bring skills in forensics, malware analysis and cryptocurrency tracing that most police forces lack, at low cost.
  • Faster investigation: quick analysis of devices, IP addresses and transactions helps freeze stolen money before it disappears.
  • Public awareness: alerts on new frauds such as fake "digital arrests" (no such procedure exists in law), loan-app harassment and investment scams.
  • Protecting systems: testing government websites and critical systems for weaknesses and responding to incidents with CERT-In.

3. Fitting into the national framework

  • Coordination: State centres like Cyberdome can feed the MHA's Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), whose helpline 1930 and fraud-reporting system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026.
  • Replication: every State needs similar centres of excellence, since policing is a State subject.

4. Concerns

  • Privacy: monitoring must respect the right to privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
  • Practical limits: vetting of volunteers, confidentiality of evidence, cross-border jurisdiction and steady funding.

Cyberdome shows that collaborative policing with industry and academia can keep pace with fast-changing crime. Scaling such centres nationwide, linked to I4C and bound by privacy safeguards, can make India's cyberspace safe and trusted.
free.upm-2019-gs3-11:
Inclusive growthSustainable developmentIntergenerational equityJust transition

Inclusive growth is growth that is broad-based: it creates opportunities for, and shares benefits with, the poor, women, disadvantaged groups and lagging regions. India's Eleventh Plan (2007–12) sought "faster and more inclusive growth", and the Twelfth Plan (2012–17) added "sustainable", recognising that growth which degrades nature cannot stay inclusive for long. The 2030 Agenda (2015), with its promise to "leave no one behind", joins the two. The statement is largely valid, though trade-offs remain.

1. Why inclusiveness and sustainability go together

  • The poor depend most on nature: forest dwellers, fishers, pastoralists and rainfed farmers lose their livelihoods first when forests, fish stocks, soil and groundwater decline.
  • Climate and pollution hit the poor hardest: heat waves, floods and droughts destroy the assets of those without savings or insurance, and polluted air and water burden those who cannot move away.
  • Intergenerational equity: the Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs, which is inclusion across time.
  • Durable growth needs both: unequal growth breeds social conflict, and resource-depleting growth breeds ecological crises; either can derail growth itself.

2. How India's strategy combines them

  • Poverty reduction: NITI Aayog estimates that 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23, helped by housing, sanitation, clean cooking fuel, electricity and financial inclusion.
  • Clean energy for all: about 55% of India's 554.5 GW installed power capacity was non-fossil in August 2026; PM-KUSUM solar pumps and rooftop solar let farmers and households earn from, or save on, power.
  • Green livelihoods: water-conservation works under rural employment schemes, natural farming and community forest rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Low-carbon pathway: Mission LiFE (2022), net zero by 2070 and updated climate targets for 2035.

3. Tensions that remain

  • Coal and jobs: only 29.2% of electricity came from non-fossil sources in 2025-26, and coal districts in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha depend on mining jobs, so the shift needs a just transition.
  • Uneven growth: women's labour force participation is only about 42%, and many green jobs need skills the poor lack.
  • Development vs ecology: mines, dams and highways serve national growth but can displace tribal communities and fragment forests.
  • Costs of the transition: clean technologies and stricter norms can raise costs for small firms and consumers unless supported.

Inclusiveness and sustainability are two sides of one coin: growth that excludes is not sustainable, and growth that degrades is not inclusive. Green jobs, a just energy transition and community rights over resources can make India's growth both fair and lasting.
free.upm-2019-gs3-12:
Public expenditure managementFRBM Act, 2003Committed expenditureOutcome budgeting

Public expenditure management (PEM) is the system of planning, allocating, releasing, controlling and evaluating government spending. It has three aims: aggregate fiscal discipline, allocation to priorities and value for money. After the 1991 crisis, liberalisation reduced the State's direct role in production but not its spending pressures, while tariff cuts and later GST narrowed its revenue levers. Budget-making has therefore become an exercise in managing expenditure within the FRBM Act, 2003.

1. Why expenditure management is a challenge

  • Committed expenditure: interest alone is budgeted at ₹14.04 lakh crore in 2026-27, about 26% of total spending of ₹53.47 lakh crore; salaries, pensions and subsidies leave little room for new priorities.
  • Fiscal rules vs needs: FRBM targets were relaxed after the 2008 crisis and in the pandemic, and central debt (55.6% of GDP, 2026-27 BE) is still above the target of 50±1% by March 2031.
  • Subsidies and leakages: food, fertiliser and fuel subsidies are hard to cut, and poorly targeted transfers leaked.
  • Hidden spending: off-budget loans from the National Small Savings Fund to the Food Corporation of India understated the deficit until the food subsidy came fully on budget in 2021-22.
  • Quality and execution: a revenue-heavy mix, the "March rush", unspent funds parked with agencies, and outputs rather than outcomes.
