  • Federal complexity: many Centrally Sponsored Schemes need matching State shares, and cesses outside the divisible pool strain Centre–State relations.

2. Reforms in budget-making since liberalisation

  • Fiscal rules: the FRBM Act, 2003 was amended in 2018 on the N.K. Singh Committee's advice to make debt the main anchor; the Union now targets debt of 50±1% of GDP by March 2031.
  • Budget restructuring (2017-18): the Plan/non-Plan distinction was abolished, the Railway Budget was merged into the Union Budget, and presentation moved to 1 February so that funds are available from 1 April.
  • Outcome focus: the Outcome Budget and Gender Budget (since 2005-06) and output–outcome monitoring by NITI Aayog.
  • Expenditure reviews: the Expenditure Management Commission (Bimal Jalan, 2014) and the regrouping of Centrally Sponsored Schemes into core and optional schemes (2016).
  • Digital control: the Public Financial Management System (PFMS), tighter releases to States through single nodal agency accounts, the Government e-Marketplace (2016) and Direct Benefit Transfer, which has moved over ₹52 lakh crore with estimated savings of over ₹5 lakh crore (August 2026).

3. Way forward

  • Medium-term view: a credible medium-term expenditure framework with regular spending reviews.
  • Transparency and scrutiny: accrual accounting, disclosure of contingent liabilities and an independent fiscal council.
  • Better mix: a gradual shift from subsidies to public goods such as health, education and infrastructure.

In the post-liberalisation era the challenge is not merely to spend less but to spend better. Rule-based discipline, outcome budgeting and digital tracking can make every rupee count, so that the Budget serves growth, equity and the quality of expenditure.
free.upm-2019-gs3-13:
Public Distribution SystemNFSA 2013One Nation One Ration CardEnd-to-end computerisation

India's food grain distribution has evolved from wartime rationing into a rights-based safety net. Under the Public Distribution System (PDS), the Food Corporation of India (1965) procures and moves grain, and the States identify beneficiaries and distribute it through fair price shops. The National Food Security Act, 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population, and about 81 crore people receive free grain under PMGKAY, extended for five years from January 2024.

1. Reforms in targeting and entitlements

  • Sharper targeting: the Revamped PDS (1992) for remote areas, the Targeted PDS (1997) for the poor and the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (2000) for the poorest.
  • Legal right (NFSA, 2013): 5 kg of grain per person per month (35 kg per Antyodaya household), the eldest woman as head of household on the ration card, and District Grievance Redressal Officers (Section 15).
  • Free grain: PMGKAY began as pandemic relief in 2020; since 2023 NFSA grain itself has been free.
  • Cleaner rolls: 99.2% of beneficiaries are Aadhaar-seeded, and 41.41 lakh ineligible cards were deleted in 2025 alone.

2. Technology reforms

  • End-to-end computerisation: digitised ration cards, online allocation, computerised supply chains and ePoS machines in almost all fair price shops; 98.75% of grain is distributed with digital authentication (Rajya Sabha, March 2026).
  • One Nation One Ration Card (2019): portability lets migrant workers draw grain at any fair price shop in the country, supported by the Integrated Management of PDS and the Mera Ration app.
  • Transparency: online stock records, tracked trucks, SMS alerts and helplines.

3. Procurement, storage and delivery

  • Decentralised procurement (1997-98): States procure and distribute locally, cutting transport costs and spreading procurement to more States.
  • Better storage: steel silos under public–private partnership and the grain storage plan in the cooperative sector (2023) reduce reliance on open storage.
  • Cash transfers: DBT for the food subsidy was piloted in Chandigarh and Puducherry in 2015, where markets work well.
  • Nutrition: fortified rice is supplied through the PDS, and millets can be distributed under the NFSA.

4. Accountability

  • Community oversight: social audits (Section 28), vigilance committees (Section 29) and State Food Commissions; Chhattisgarh's community-run shops showed how reform cuts leakage, which the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) had put at about 46%.

The PDS has moved from leakage-prone rationing to a technology-enabled, rights-based system. Updating coverage beyond Census 2011 data, diversifying the food basket and strengthening community audits can make it a true nutrition safety net.
free.upm-2019-gs3-14:
Food processingPost-harvest lossesPM Kisan SAMPADAPLISFPI and PMFME

India is the largest producer of milk and pulses and the second-largest of fruits and vegetables, yet only a small share of its perishables is processed and post-harvest losses are worth about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS, 2022). The food processing sector, a sunrise industry linking farm and factory, faces challenges of supply, infrastructure, finance, scale and standards. Government policy addresses each through infrastructure schemes, investment incentives and support for micro units.

1. Challenges of the sector

  • Fragmented supply: small, scattered farms make a steady, uniform supply of raw material difficult.
  • Infrastructure gaps: weak cold chains, pack-houses, power and testing labs raise costs and wastage.
  • Informality and finance: most units are tiny and unregistered, with poor access to credit, technology and branding.
  • Standards: meeting FSSAI and export standards is costly for small firms.
  • Skills and markets: shortage of trained workers, few Indian food brands abroad.

2. The policy response

  • Infrastructure – PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (2017): an umbrella for mega food parks, integrated cold chains, agro-processing clusters, food testing labs and backward and forward linkages; Operation Greens (2018) for tomato, onion and potato, later widened to other perishables.
  • Micro units – PMFME (2020, ₹10,000 crore): a 35% credit-linked subsidy of up to ₹10 lakh, seed capital for SHG members and common facilities under One District One Product.
  • Scale and exports – PLISFPI (₹10,900 crore, 2021-22 to 2026-27): incentives for ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat foods, processed fruits and vegetables, marine products, mozzarella cheese and millet-based products, and support for branding Indian foods abroad.
  • Investment and credit: 100% FDI under the automatic route in food processing; 100% FDI (government route) in retail trade, including e-commerce, of food made in India; a ₹2,000 crore Food Processing Fund with NABARD; priority-sector lending; and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020) for post-harvest units.
  • Standards, skills and markets: FSSAI under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; NIFTEM institutes and a sector skill council; FPOs for aggregation; and World Food India expos to attract investors and buyers.

3. Assessment

  • Gains: new capacity in cold chains and processing, formalisation of micro enterprises, and a push for Indian brands and millet products.
  • Gaps: cold-chain coverage, credit for micro units and the share of perishables processed still lag far behind potential.
  • Next steps: FPO-owned processing, cluster-based common facilities, quality labs near producing areas and stable trade policy for processed exports.

The policy mix tackles the sector's bottlenecks from farm to fork. Sustained execution, with FPO-led supply chains and quality standards, can make India the food basket of the world while raising farm incomes and rural jobs.
free.upm-2019-gs3-15:
Traditional knowledgeBiopiracyTKDLDisclosure of origin

India's traditional knowledge (TK) of medicine, in Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa Rigpa and Yoga, has been recorded for centuries. Because it is in the public domain, it can be misappropriated through patents on minor variations, a practice called biopiracy. A US patent on turmeric for healing wounds (1995, revoked in 1997 after CSIR's challenge) and a European patent on a neem-based fungicide (1994, revoked in 2000) exposed the threat. India now relies on defensive protection, domestic law and global diplomacy.

1. Defensive protection through TKDL

  • What it is: the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), set up in 2001 by CSIR and the Ministry of Ayush, converts formulations from classical texts into a searchable database in five languages: English, French, German, Japanese and Spanish.
  • How it works: patent offices such as the European Patent Office use it as prior art, and India files evidence against wrongful applications.
  • Defensive, not proprietary: TKDL gives India no patent; it stops others from getting one.

2. Safeguards in Indian law

  • Patents Act, 1970 (as amended): Section 3(p) says that TK, or an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditional components, is not an invention; applicants must disclose the source and origin of biological material, and a patent can be opposed for non-disclosure or for being anticipated by knowledge, oral or written, of local or indigenous communities (Section 25).
  • Biological Diversity Act, 2002: IP based on Indian biological resources or associated knowledge needs the National Biodiversity Authority's approval, with benefit-sharing; People's Biodiversity Registers document local knowledge. The 2023 amendment eased compliance for Ayush practitioners but kept NBA approval for such IP.
  • Benefit-sharing model: the Kani tribe of Kerala received a share of licence fees for "Jeevani", a drug developed by the Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute from their knowledge of the arogyapacha plant.

3. International efforts

  • Disclosure of origin: India has long demanded that patent applicants disclose the origin of genetic resources and TK and show prior informed consent and benefit-sharing, in line with the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Nagoya Protocol (2010).
  • WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (24 May 2024): makes such disclosure mandatory; India pushed for it but had not ratified it, and with only four parties by mid-2026 it was not yet in force.
  • Global standing: the WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine at Jamnagar (2022) supports evidence and standards.

4. Gaps

  • Oral knowledge: tribal and folk knowledge outside classical texts is poorly documented, and TKDL covers mainly codified systems.
  • Enforcement: monitoring patent filings worldwide is costly, and benefit-sharing with communities remains weak.

India has moved from fighting individual cases to a systemic defence of its heritage. Documenting oral knowledge with communities, ratifying the WIPO treaty and enforcing benefit-sharing can protect traditional medicine while letting it serve global health.
free.upm-2019-gs3-16:
Agricultural biotechnologyGenome editingBt cottonBioE3 Policy

Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or their molecules to make useful products. In agriculture it ranges from tissue culture and biofertilisers to marker-assisted breeding, genetic modification (GM) and genome editing. India approved Bt cotton in 2002 and released the world's first genome-edited rice varieties in May 2025, and its BioE3 Policy (August 2024) lists climate-resilient agriculture among its priorities. Used well, these tools can raise farmers' incomes, cut costs and reduce risk.

1. Higher yields and lower costs

  • Pest-resistant crops: Bt cotton, India's only commercial GM crop, cut insecticide sprays against bollworms and raised yields in its early years, though pink bollworm has since become resistant.
  • Genome-edited rice: DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) gives about 19% more yield and matures 15–20 days earlier, saving water; Pusa DST Rice 1 yields 9.7–30.4% more on saline and alkaline soils.
  • Hybrids: GM mustard DMH-11, cleared by the GEAC for environmental release in 2022, could raise oilseed output and cut edible-oil imports, but release is on hold after a split Supreme Court verdict (July 2024).

2. Resilience to climate and disease

  • Stress-tolerant varieties: marker-assisted breeding produced flood-tolerant Swarna-Sub1 rice; 109 high-yielding, climate-resilient and biofortified varieties were released in August 2024.
  • Healthy planting material: tissue-cultured banana, potato and sugarcane give uniform, disease-free crops.
  • Early diagnosis: quick kits detect plant and animal diseases before they spread.

3. Cheaper, greener inputs

  • Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azolla–Anabaena and mycorrhiza fix nitrogen or mobilise phosphorus, cutting fertiliser bills and improving soil.
  • Biopesticides: Bt formulations, Trichoderma and other biocontrol agents protect crops with fewer residues, opening premium markets.

4. Livestock, fisheries and value addition

  • Animal biotechnology: sex-sorted semen and embryo transfer under the Rashtriya Gokul Mission raise milk output, and vaccines such as the indigenous lumpy skin disease vaccine (2022) prevent losses.
  • Fisheries: Jayanti rohu, genetically improved by selective breeding, grows faster.
  • Nutrition and bio-industry: biofortified crops such as zinc-rich wheat and iron-rich pearl millet improve diets, and bio-based industries can pay farmers for crop residues.

5. Concerns to address

  • Cost and control: seed prices, patents and royalties can burden small farmers.
  • Biosafety and trust: transparent regulation by the GEAC, labelling, and the 2022 exemption of SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome editing from GM rules need public confidence.

Biotechnology can raise farmers' living standards by making farming more productive, less risky and less costly. Public research, affordable seeds, sound biosafety rules and extension through KVKs and FPOs will decide whether its benefits reach small farmers.
free.upm-2019-gs3-17:
Carrying capacitySustainable developmentAssimilative capacityRegional planning

Carrying capacity is the maximum population of a species that an environment can support indefinitely with its food, water, habitat and other resources, without being degraded; in ecology it is the ceiling "K" of the logistic growth curve. For human societies it is the level of population, consumption, construction and waste an area can sustain without irreversible damage. It depends on supportive capacity (resources) and assimilative capacity (the ability to absorb wastes). Respecting it is the core of sustainable development.

1. The concept

  • Limits and overshoot: when demand exceeds carrying capacity, resources are depleted and the system can collapse, as when farming draws groundwater faster than it is recharged.
  • Dimensions: ecological (land, water, biodiversity), physical (space, slope stability), infrastructural (roads, water supply, sewage) and social (crowding that residents and visitors accept).
  • Not fixed: technology, consumption and management can raise or lower it, so it must be reassessed periodically.

2. Why it is vital for planning sustainable development of a region

  • Fragile mountains: in Ashok Kumar Raghav v. Union of India (2023), the Centre told the Supreme Court that each of the 13 Himalayan States and UTs should assess its carrying capacity, reviewed by an expert committee headed by the Director of the G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, under guidelines first sent to them in January 2020.
  • Water budgeting: planning crops, industries and cities within the safe yield of aquifers and rivers prevents depletion and conflict.
  • Tourism management: limits on visitors, vehicles and hotels protect hill stations, beaches and protected areas, and spread tourists across seasons.
  • Pollution control: industries must be sited within the assimilative capacity of an airshed or river, an idea India applied as early as the Doon Valley notification (1989), which restricted polluting industries and mining.
  • Disaster risk reduction: building beyond carrying capacity on unstable slopes and floodplains magnifies landslides and urban floods.
  • Ecologically sensitive areas: the Gadgil (2011) and Kasturirangan (2013) reports on the Western Ghats proposed zoning by ecological sensitivity.

3. Challenges

  • Measurement: carrying capacity is hard to reduce to a single number, and data on slopes, aquifers and waste loads are patchy.
  • Pressure and enforcement: tourism and real-estate interests push for growth, and master plans are weakly enforced.

Carrying capacity turns the idea of sustainability into measurable limits. Making carrying-capacity studies mandatory for regional, tourism and urban plans, especially in the Himalaya and the Western Ghats, is vital for development that lasts.
free.upm-2019-gs3-18:
Disaster preparednessLandslide hazard zonationRisk-informed land useNLRMS 2019

Preparedness, knowing the risk and acting before a hazard strikes, is the first step of disaster management. For landslides, its foundation is landslide hazard zonation (LHZ) mapping: dividing an area into zones from very low to very high hazard according to the factors that cause slope failure. About 0.42 million sq km of India is landslide-prone; the Geological Survey of India is the nodal agency, and the NDMA's National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019) makes hazard mapping a core component.

1. What hazard zonation mapping involves

  • Landslide inventory: past landslides mapped from field surveys and satellite images, as in ISRO's Landslide Atlas of India (2023).
  • Causative factors: slope angle, rock type and structure, soil, land use and vegetation, drainage, rainfall and seismicity, weighted and combined in a GIS.
  • Scales: regional susceptibility maps at 1:50,000 under the GSI's national mapping for district plans, and larger-scale maps for towns, roads and project sites; the BIS code IS 14496 (Part 2) guides macro-zonation.
  • From hazard to risk: overlaying the zones on people, buildings and roads gives risk maps for planning.

2. How it helps disaster mitigation

  • Land-use planning: keeps new settlements, schools and hospitals out of high-hazard zones and guides building bye-laws and zoning regulations for hill areas.
  • Safer infrastructure: helps align highways, railways, tunnels and hydropower projects away from unstable slopes, or design protection where they cannot be avoided.
  • Targeted engineering: drainage, retaining walls, rock bolting, nets and bioengineering are concentrated on mapped hotspots, saving money.
  • Early warning: high-hazard slopes can be instrumented, and rainfall thresholds for each zone can trigger alerts and evacuation.
  • Preparedness and response: evacuation routes, shelters and pre-positioned rescue teams are planned around the map, and communities learn the warning signs.
  • Recovery: after events such as the Joshimath subsidence (2023) and the Wayanad landslides (30 July 2024), maps guide where to rebuild and whom to relocate.

3. Limitations

  • Scale and updating: many maps are too coarse for village-level decisions and must be updated as extreme rain becomes more frequent.
  • Enforcement: maps are often ignored in building approvals and road construction, and are not always shared with communities in local languages.

Hazard zonation turns landslide science into land-use decisions. Embedding the maps in master plans and building permits, backed by early warning and community preparedness, can shift India's hill regions from relief to risk reduction.
free.upm-2019-gs3-19:
UAPA, 1967NIA (Amendment) Act, 2019Designation of individualsCivil liberties

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, India's main anti-terror law since POTA was repealed in 2004, and the National Investigation Agency (NIA) Act, 2008, passed after 26/11, were both amended in 2019, the year of the Pulwama attack. The changes widened the State's powers against terrorists and their networks, but human rights organisations argue that they weaken due process and civil liberties.

1. Key changes in 2019

  • First designations: Masood Azhar, Hafiz Saeed, Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi and Dawood Ibrahim were declared terrorists in September 2019.
  • Treaty coverage: the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism (2005) was added to the UAPA's schedule.

2. The changes in the prevailing security environment

  • Leaders, not just outfits: banned groups re-emerged under new names while their leaders stayed free; designating individuals targets the person.
  • Wider threats: cross-border attacks (Pulwama, 2019; Pahalgam, 2025), online radicalisation, cyber-terrorism, narco-terror and counterfeit currency need one specialised agency with a wider remit, including attacks on Indians abroad.
  • Capacity and speed: letting inspectors investigate eases the shortage of senior officers, and designated courts can speed trials.
  • Global standards: stronger laws support India's FATF commitments; its 2024 evaluation placed India in "regular follow-up", the best category.

3. Scope and reasons for opposition by human rights organisations

  • Vague definitions: "terrorist act" and "unlawful activity" cover acts "likely to threaten" unity or security, which critics say can reach dissent and protest.
  • Designation without hearing: a person is branded a terrorist by executive notification, with only a government-appointed review committee and no prior judicial scrutiny, which critics say offends Article 21.
  • Bail almost impossible: Section 43D(5) bars bail if the accusation appears prima facie true, and in NIA v. Watali (2019) the Supreme Court told courts not to weigh evidence at that stage; detention before a charge-sheet can extend to 180 days.
  • Process as punishment: few of those arrested are convicted, while trials take years; the death in custody of 84-year-old Stan Swamy (2021), accused in the Bhima Koregaon case, became a symbol.
  • Federalism: police is a State subject, yet the NIA can take over cases and seize property without State consent; Chhattisgarh challenged the NIA Act in the Supreme Court (2020).

4. Balancing security and liberty

  • Judicial checks: in Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb (2021) the Supreme Court allowed bail after prolonged detention under Article 21, and in Prabir Purkayastha (2024) it held that the grounds of arrest must be given in writing.
  • Safeguards: narrower definitions, judicial review of designations, time-bound trials and compensation for wrongful prosecution, which the Law Commission's 277th Report (2018) recommended.

The 2019 amendments respond to a real and evolving threat of networked, transnational terrorism. Their legitimacy depends on careful use, judicial oversight and speedy trials, so that the fight against terror strengthens rather than erodes the rule of law.
free.upm-2019-gs3-20:
India–Myanmar borderFree Movement RegimeAssam RiflesAct East

India shares a 1,643 km border with Myanmar along Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram, guarded by the Assam Rifles (under the Home Ministry administratively and the Army operationally). Hilly, forested terrain, tribes with kin on both sides and a Free Movement Regime (FMR) make it porous, and Myanmar's civil war since the February 2021 coup has multiplied threats well beyond the cross-border movement of insurgents.

1. Challenges emanating across the border

  • Insurgent sanctuaries: holdout groups such as ULFA(I) and some NSCN factions operate from camps in Myanmar, beyond the reach of Indian forces.
  • Drug trafficking: heroin and methamphetamine tablets from the Golden Triangle enter through Manipur and Mizoram; armed groups tax the trade, and illicit poppy is grown in some hill areas.
  • Arms smuggling: weapons flow to insurgents and ethnic militias, feeding the violence in Manipur since May 2023.
  • Refugees: thousands of refugees from Myanmar crossed into Mizoram and Manipur after the coup, and fleeing Myanmar soldiers took shelter in Mizoram (2023–24), raising humanitarian duties and demographic anxieties.
  • Other smuggling and trafficking: gold, wildlife and arecanut smuggling, and trafficking of Indians into cyber-scam compounds in South-East Asia.
  • Weak authority across the border: much of the Myanmar side is held by ethnic armed groups, not the central government; China's influence adds a strategic dimension.

2. Challenges in policing the border itself

  • Terrain and command: dense forest and steep hills limit patrolling, and the dual control of the Assam Rifles complicates command.
  • Fencing gap: although fencing of the whole border was approved in 2024, only about 44 km had been fenced by March 2026 (about 55 km in Manipur by September 2026, according to the State's Home Minister).
  • Local opposition: Naga and Mizo communities with kin across the border oppose fencing and curbs on movement.

3. Steps to counter the challenges

  • Fencing and technology: the Cabinet Committee on Security approved ₹31,000 crore (2024) to fence the whole border; sensors, drones and integrated border management can cover gaps until the fence is complete.
  • Regulated movement: the FMR was cut from 16 km to 10 km, with border passes (December 2024), to record cross-border movement.
  • Intelligence and operations: coordinated action with Myanmar's army, as in Operation Sunrise (2019), more Assam Rifles posts and a unified command.
  • Drugs: NCB-led crackdowns, destruction of poppy fields, alternative crops and de-addiction under the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2020).
  • Border communities: the Vibrant Villages Programme Phase II (₹6,839 crore to 2028-29) for villages along the land borders, and peace accords.
  • Diplomacy and connectivity: engagement with all stakeholders in Myanmar; completion of the Kaladan project and the Trilateral Highway.

Securing the Myanmar border needs hard security (fencing, technology, unified command) together with soft measures that respect cross-border kinship and develop border villages. A stable Myanmar, encouraged through patient diplomacy, is the long-term key to a secure North-East.
free.upm-2019-gs4-1a:
Nolan principlesPublic trustIntegrityAccountability

Public office is a public trust: power and public resources are held on behalf of citizens, never for personal gain. The UK's Committee on Standards in Public Life, chaired by Lord Nolan, set out in 1995 seven principles that apply to everyone holding public office, the Nolan principles. In India, the Second ARC's fourth report, Ethics in Governance (2007), and the values added to the All India Services (Conduct) Rules in 2014 rest on the same ideas.

1. The basic principles of public life

  • Wide application: the principles apply to elected representatives, civil servants and members of public bodies, and to private bodies when they deliver public services.
  • Beyond legality: they ask for conduct above the minimum that law demands; an act may be legal and still fail the test of selflessness or openness.
  • Indian echo: the 2014 amendment to the AIS (Conduct) Rules asks officers to uphold integrity, impartiality, accountability, transparency and responsiveness to the public, particularly the weaker sections.

2. Integrity, illustrated

  • Meaning: consistency between private values and public conduct, and freedom from improper influence.
  • Example: Satyendra Dubey, an engineer working as a project director with the National Highways Authority of India, reported corruption in the Golden Quadrilateral project to the Prime Minister's Office and was murdered in Gaya in November 2003. His sacrifice led to the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004) to protect whistle-blowers.
  • Lesson: integrity may demand personal risk, so institutions must protect those who show it.

3. Accountability, illustrated

  • Meaning: accepting responsibility for the results of one's office, not only for one's personal acts.
  • Example: Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned as Railway Minister in 1956, accepting moral responsibility for a rail accident at Ariyalur (then in Madras State), though he was not personally at fault.
  • Institutional form: the RTI Act (2005), CAG audits, parliamentary committees and social audits make accountability routine rather than exceptional.

4. Objectivity, illustrated

  • Meaning: decisions based on merit and evidence, applying the same rules to all.
  • Example: T.N. Seshan, as Chief Election Commissioner (1990–96), enforced the Model Code of Conduct firmly and even-handedly against candidates of every party, restoring public faith in elections.
  • Institutional form: merit-based recruitment through the UPSC, an independent constitutional body, keeps appointments free of patronage.

These principles turn public office into a public trust. Codifying them in a short code of ethics, as the Second ARC recommended, and practising them daily would strengthen citizens' trust in governance.
free.upm-2019-gs4-1b:
Public servantPublic dutyNeutralityCitizen-centric service

A public servant is a person who holds an office or performs a duty on behalf of the State, exercising public authority and paid from public funds for it. In law the term is wide: Section 2(28) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Section 21 IPC) lists categories of public servants, and Section 2(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 goes further, covering anyone who performs a public duty, whatever the title of the post.

1. Meaning of the term

  • Legal sense: it covers civil servants, judges, police and armed forces officers, employees of local bodies and public-sector undertakings, and anyone authorised to perform a public duty.
  • Legislators included: the Supreme Court held a Chief Minister to be a public servant (M. Karunanidhi, 1979) and MPs to be public servants under the PC Act (P.V. Narasimha Rao, 1998); since Sita Soren (2024), legislators cannot claim parliamentary immunity for taking bribes.
  • Civil servant vs public servant: civil servants, governed by Articles 309–311, are a subset; every civil servant is a public servant, but not every public servant is a civil servant.
  • Ethical sense: the word "servant" signals that power is held in trust for the people; the citizen is the master, not a supplicant.

2. Expected role of a public servant

  • Guardian of the Constitution: upholding fundamental rights and the rule of law, and refusing illegal orders, so that governance follows the Constitution rather than personal or partisan will.
  • Neutral and continuous: governments change, but a non-partisan service implements every elected government's lawful policies faithfully and preserves institutional memory.
  • Welfare of the weak: Article 46 directs special care for the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections; the public servant is often their only link to the State.
  • Responsive and courteous: citizens' charters, Right to Services Acts and grievance portals such as CPGRAMS expect time-bound, polite service.
  • Problem-solver: Armstrong Pame, an IAS officer, built about 100 km of road in Manipur's Tamenglong district (2012) largely through public contributions, showing initiative within the law.

3. Values that make the role possible

  • Integrity and impartiality: the 2014 amendment to the AIS (Conduct) Rules lists integrity, impartiality, accountability, transparency and responsiveness, particularly to the weaker sections.
  • Empathy and dedication: compassion for the poor and diligence in crises separate service from mere compliance.
  • Accountability: to law, superiors, courts, audit and, above all, citizens.

The public servant is a trustee of public power. Moving from rule-based to role-based working, as Mission Karmayogi (2020) seeks, makes the service truly citizen-centric.
free.upm-2019-gs4-2a:
Public fundsUnder-utilisationMis-utilisationOutcome-based budgeting

Public money is raised from taxpayers or borrowed against the future, so every rupee carries a duty of stewardship. Schemes often suffer two opposite failures: under-utilisation, where allocated funds lie unspent or arrive too late to be used, and mis-utilisation, where funds are spent but diverted, wasted or stolen. Both turn budget outlays into weak outcomes and slow progress towards development goals such as the SDGs.

1. Reasons for under-utilisation

  • Poor planning and late release: schemes are announced before projects are ready, and funds pass from the Union to State treasuries to implementing agencies with delays, arriving late in the year.
  • Procedural bottlenecks: land acquisition, forest and environmental clearances, tendering and pending utilisation certificates hold up spending.
  • Weak local capacity: panchayats and municipalities often lack engineers, accountants and planners, and vacancies slow line departments.
  • Fear of vigilance: officers who fear later questioning avoid decisions and let funds lapse.
  • Idle dedicated funds: the Supreme Court (2018) found that only about Rs 9,500 crore of over Rs 37,400 crore of construction workers' welfare cess had been used, and the Nirbhaya Fund has repeatedly been reported as under-used.

2. Reasons for mis-utilisation

  • Corruption and leakages: inflated estimates, collusive tenders, ghost beneficiaries and fake muster rolls; the fodder scam in undivided Bihar, exposed in 1996, involved fraudulent withdrawals from treasuries.
  • Diversion: funds meant for one purpose spent on another or on inadmissible items, a recurring finding in CAG audits.
  • March rush: hurried spending to avoid lapse produces poor-quality assets; the General Financial Rules treat a rush of expenditure in the closing months of the year as a breach of financial propriety.
  • Visibility over need and weak monitoring: projects are chosen for visibility, and success is measured by money spent rather than results achieved.

3. Implications

  • Development deficits: unbuilt schools, health centres and roads hurt the poor most, as they depend most on public services.
  • Fiscal cost: the government pays interest on borrowing while money lies idle, and delays raise project costs.
  • Erosion of trust: visible waste and scams weaken tax morale and faith in institutions.
  • Ethical cost: honest officers lose heart, the corrupt are emboldened, and the stewardship owed to taxpayers and future generations is betrayed.

4. A critical view and the way forward

  • Not all unspent money is waste: savings from efficient procurement, or from dropping poor projects, are prudence; the problem is planning failure, not thrift.
  • Reforms under way: the Public Financial Management System (PFMS), Direct Benefit Transfer, GeM e-procurement and, for centrally sponsored schemes, the Single Nodal Agency system (2021) and its just-in-time variant SNA-SPARSH reduce idle balances and leakages.
  • What more is needed: capacity building for local bodies, outcome budgets that are actually reviewed, social audits, and timely follow-up of CAG reports by legislative committees.

Public funds are a public trust. Moving from outlays to outcomes, with planning, transparency and accountability at every stage, is the surest way to turn money into development.
free.upm-2019-gs4-2b:
CorruptionDereliction of dutyDevotion to dutyAccountability

Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Bribery is its most visible form, but a public servant who draws a salary and does not do the job also abuses a public trust. The CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964 (Rule 3) require every government servant to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty. I largely agree with the view, with one important qualification about intent.

1. Why non-performance is a form of corruption

  • Breach of trust: salary is paid for service; absence, shirking or deliberate delay takes public money without delivering, a quiet misappropriation of time and resources.
  • Private gain in another form: the gain may be leisure, a private practice or business, or simply avoided effort. A nationally representative survey published in 2005 (Kremer, Muralidharan and others) found about a quarter of teachers in government primary schools absent on a typical day.
  • Breeds bribery: deliberate delay creates the demand for "speed money"; the file moves only when someone pays.
  • Denial of rights: a doctor absent from a health centre or a police officer who refuses to register a complaint denies citizens their entitlements.
  • Recognised in law: Section 198 of the BNS (formerly Section 166 IPC) punishes a public servant who knowingly disobeys the law intending to cause injury, and Right to Services Acts, beginning with Madhya Pradesh (2010), fine officials for unjustified delay.

2. Why the view needs qualification

  • Intent matters: corruption in the legal sense, under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, involves dishonesty; non-performance caused by vacancies, lack of funds or training, or overwork is a systemic failure, not corruption.
  • Fear-driven inaction: honest officers sometimes avoid decisions for fear of later prosecution; the remedy is protection for bona fide decisions, not punishment.
  • Over-stretching the term: labelling every lapse as corruption dilutes the fight against serious graft and invites arbitrary action against officers.

3. Addressing non-performance

  • Accountability for outcomes: service standards in citizens' charters and Right to Services Acts, and outcome-based appraisal through the APAR.
  • Review and exit: periodic review and premature retirement in the public interest under FR 56(j) for officers whose performance or integrity is doubtful.
  • Technology: biometric attendance, e-office file tracking and grievance portals such as CPGRAMS make delay visible and traceable.
  • Motivation: capacity building under Mission Karmayogi (2020), recognition such as the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration, and leaders who set an example.

Wilful non-performance is a silent corruption: it takes the salary while denying the service. Distinguishing it from systemic incapacity, and combining accountability with support, is the way to restore the public servant's devotion to duty.
free.upm-2019-gs4-3a:
Constitutional moralityRule of lawSpirit of the ConstitutionFundamental Duties

Constitutional morality means adherence to the core values of the Constitution (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity and the rule of law) and respect for its institutions and processes, not merely obedience to its literal text. The term comes from the historian George Grote; Dr B.R. Ambedkar used it in the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948, stressing that it does not come naturally and has to be consciously cultivated.

1. What constitutional morality means

  • Spirit over letter: a functionary may act within formal powers yet against the Constitution's spirit, for example by using discretion to favour one party; constitutional morality forbids this.
  • Constitutional means: ends must be pursued through constitutional methods; in his last speech to the Assembly (25 November 1949), Ambedkar urged Indians to give up unconstitutional methods once constitutional ones were available.
  • Counter-majoritarian protection: it protects individuals and minorities against popular or social morality.
  • Judicial use: in Manoj Narula (2014) the Supreme Court said it means bowing to the norms of the Constitution and not acting arbitrarily; in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) it held that constitutional morality must prevail over social morality; in NCT of Delhi (2018) it asked constitutional functionaries to work in harmony.

2. How one upholds constitutional morality

  • As a citizen: Article 51A(a) asks every citizen to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions; protest through constitutional means, not violence, and respect the rights of those one disagrees with.
  • As a civil servant: apply laws impartially, protect the vulnerable against majoritarian pressure and record reasons for decisions; for instance, protecting couples who marry by choice, as directed in Shakti Vahini (2018) against honour crimes.
  • As an institution: Parliament should deliberate rather than rush legislation, and constitutional functionaries should use discretion with restraint and reasons.
  • As a judge: apply the doctrine with restraint, anchored in specific Articles and the basic structure; Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent in Sabarimala (2018) cautioned that it must also respect pluralism and religious freedom.
  • As a society: civic education, the Preamble in schools and a culture of debate make constitutional values a habit.

3. A caution

  • Vagueness: an undefined standard can let unelected judges or officials substitute their own preferences, so it must rest on the text, structure and history of the Constitution.

Constitutional morality turns a written Constitution into a living constitutional culture. Upheld by citizens and officials alike, it keeps power accountable and rights secure.
free.upm-2019-gs4-3b:
ConscienceMoral dilemmaWhistle-blowingMoral courage

Conscience is the inner moral sense that judges one's own actions as right or wrong. A crisis of conscience arises when this inner voice clashes with an external demand, such as an order, a law, loyalty to an organisation or self-interest, and a person cannot honour both. Arjuna's anguish at Kurukshetra, at the opening of the Bhagavad Gita, is the classic example. In public life it is common because officials carry role obligations that may conflict with personal values.

1. What a crisis of conscience involves

  • Conflict of duties: obedience to superiors versus duty to the public, loyalty to colleagues versus truth, or the letter of the law versus justice.
  • High personal stakes: the right choice may cost one's career, safety or relationships, which is why it is a crisis and not a simple choice.
  • Moral distress: guilt, anxiety and sleeplessness when one acts, or is pressed to act, against conviction.
  • A serious moral issue: it concerns fundamental questions of right and wrong, not mere differences of opinion or taste.

2. How it manifests in the public domain

  • Constructive forms: written dissent, complaints through proper channels such as the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004), and principled resignation keep conscience within the rule of law.
  • Whistle-blowing at great cost: Satyendra Dubey and S. Manjunath, who sealed a petrol pump selling adulterated fuel, were murdered after acting on conscience, showing why institutional protection matters.
  • Destructive forms: fear-driven silence, rationalisation that everyone does it, cynicism and burnout, or unauthorised leaks that may harm national security or individuals' privacy.
  • Across professions: doctors pressed to certify falsely, journalists asked to suppress news, and police pressured to shield the powerful all face such crises.
  • Global lesson: the Nuremberg Principles (1950) hold that acting on superior orders does not relieve a person of responsibility if a moral choice was in fact possible.

3. Resolving it ethically

  • An informed conscience: conscience must be tested against facts, law and constitutional values; an untested conscience can be mere prejudice.
  • Institutional channels first: seek written orders, record dissent and use grievance and vigilance mechanisms; the Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) asked officers to record oral instructions.
  • Support systems: mentors, peer counselling and whistle-blower protection help officers act rightly without being destroyed.

A crisis of conscience is a test of moral courage. Handled through informed judgement and lawful channels, it strengthens personal integrity and the institutions a public servant serves.
free.upm-2019-gs4-4a:
Citizens' CharterCitizen-centric administrationAccountabilitySevottam

A Citizens' Charter is a public document in which an organisation states the services it provides, the standards and timelines citizens can expect, how to seek redress, and what it expects of citizens in return. The movement began in the United Kingdom in 1991 under Prime Minister John Major, to make public services answerable to their users. India adopted it after the Conference of Chief Ministers (1997), with the DARPG as the nodal agency.

1. Basic principles of the movement

  • Service First (1998): the UK relaunched the programme with nine principles, adding consultation and involvement of users, fair treatment of all, putting things right when they go wrong, innovation and working with other providers.
  • Core idea: citizens are owners and users of public services, not supplicants; the charter makes the organisation's promises public and measurable.
  • Indian adaptation: charters were adopted by Union ministries, States, railways, banks, hospitals and municipal bodies.

2. Importance

  • Accountability: published standards give a yardstick against which performance can be judged and officials held answerable.
  • Transparency and anti-corruption: clearly stated procedures, fees and timelines reduce discretion and the scope for speed money.
  • Citizen empowerment: people know their entitlements and remedies; charters paved the way for Right to Services Acts, beginning with Madhya Pradesh (2010), which made timely delivery an enforceable right.
  • Service culture: it shifts administration from a "ruler" to a "servant" mindset, encouraging courtesy, feedback and continuous improvement.
  • Participation and trust: consultation in drafting charters, and citizen report cards pioneered by Bengaluru's Public Affairs Centre, involve citizens in judging services.
  • Feedback for reform: measured standards and complaints show where services fail, guiding better use of staff and money, as the Sevottam model's link between charters and grievance redress intended.

3. Limitations and the way forward

  • Gaps: many charters were drafted top-down, copied a standard format, were rarely updated, were little known to citizens (often available only in English or online) and lacked legal backing; the Citizens' Right to Grievance Redress Bill, 2011 lapsed in 2014.
  • Second ARC, 12th Report (2009): "Citizen Centric Administration" recommended specific, consultative, office-level charters with a seven-step model and effective redress.
  • Reforms: statutory backing with compensation for failure, digital tracking and escalation through CPGRAMS and State portals, and linking charter compliance to performance appraisal.

The Citizens' Charter embodies citizen-centric governance. Its promise will be fully realised when it moves from declaration to entitlement: backed by law, owned by staff and monitored by citizens.
free.upm-2019-gs4-4b:
Official Secrets Act, 1923RTI Act, 2005Section 22Public interest override

The Official Secrets Act (OSA), 1923, a colonial law, punishes spying (Section 3) and the wrongful communication of secret official information (Section 5). The Right to Information Act, 2005 makes disclosure the rule and secrecy the exception. In my view, the claim that the OSA obstructs RTI is partly true: in law the RTI Act prevails, but in practice the OSA's vague scope sustains a culture of secrecy.

1. Why the OSA is seen as an obstacle

  • Vague and sweeping: Section 5 covers any secret official code, document or information without defining "secret", so officials treat almost everything as confidential.
  • Culture of secrecy: classification markings are applied liberally, and information officers, unsure of the line, refuse requests citing confidentiality.
  • Chilling effect: the threat of prosecution deters officials, whistle-blowers and journalists from disclosing wrongdoing.
  • Overlapping exemptions: the RTI Act's own Section 8(1)(a) (sovereignty, security, strategic interests) and Section 24 (intelligence and security organisations, except for allegations of corruption and human-rights violations) mirror the OSA's concerns, making refusals easy to justify.

2. Why the view is only partly correct

  • Legal supremacy of RTI: Section 22 gives the RTI Act effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in the OSA, and Section 8(2) allows disclosure even of information protected by the OSA when public interest outweighs the harm.
  • Judicial support: in the Rafale review (Yashwant Sinha v CBI, 10 April 2019), the Supreme Court rejected the government's objection that documents published in the media were secret and privileged; Justice K.M. Joseph's concurring opinion stressed that Sections 8(2), 22 and 24 of the RTI Act override the OSA. The review itself was dismissed in November 2019.
  • Legitimate secrecy: defence, intelligence and diplomacy need some secrecy, as the RTI Act itself accepts; the OSA errs in breadth, not purpose.
  • Other obstacles matter more: vacancies and pendency in Information Commissions and poor record-keeping block access more often than the OSA.
  • A newer restriction: Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, 2023 (in force since November 2025) replaced Section 8(1)(j) with a blanket exemption for personal information, dropping its public-interest test; in February 2026 the Supreme Court declined to stay it and referred the challenges to a larger Bench (pending as of October 2026).

3. Way forward

  • Reform the OSA: the Second ARC's first report (2006) recommended repealing the OSA and placing provisions on official secrets in a chapter of the National Security Act.
  • Narrow classification: define secrets precisely, review classification periodically and declassify on schedule.
  • Strengthen RTI institutions: timely appointments to Information Commissions, proactive disclosure under Section 4, and digitised records.
  • Change mindsets: train officials that openness is the default and secrecy the reasoned exception.

The OSA is less a legal bar than a mindset barrier. Aligning it with the RTI Act, so that secrecy protects national security but never hides corruption or inefficiency, would reconcile security with transparency.
free.upm-2019-gs4-5a:
ProbityIntegrityConflict of interestEthics infrastructure

Probity means uprightness: adherence to the highest standards of honesty and integrity, going beyond mere legal compliance. Probity in governance requires that public office, money and information be used only for public purposes, that decisions be fair and transparent, and that officials avoid even the appearance of impropriety. The Second ARC's fourth report, Ethics in Governance (2007), and the UK's Nolan principles (1995) treat it as the foundation of good governance.

1. My understanding of probity

  • Integrity and honesty: no misuse of office for personal, family or political gain; truthfulness in records and reports.
  • Impartiality: the same rules for all, without fear or favour.
  • Accountability and transparency: reasons recorded, decisions open to audit, RTI and review.
  • Managing conflicts of interest: declaring interests and stepping aside from decisions where one's interest is involved.
  • Prudent use of resources: public money spent with the care one would take with one's own, and more.

2. Measures for ensuring probity

  • Codes of ethics, not only conduct rules: the Second ARC recommended a short code of ethics for civil servants and ministers, stating the values expected, beyond the list of prohibitions in conduct rules.
  • Strong anti-corruption law: the 2018 amendment to the PC Act made bribe-giving an offence and redefined criminal misconduct; its Section 17A, which requires prior approval before inquiring into decisions taken in official functions, drew a split verdict from a two-judge Bench of the Supreme Court in January 2026 (Centre for Public Interest Litigation v Union of India), and its validity awaits a larger Bench (as of October 2026).
  • Independent watchdogs: a well-staffed Lokpal and Lokayuktas with investigative autonomy, and time-bound decisions on sanction for prosecution.
  • Transparency through technology: e-procurement, GeM, DBT, e-office and faceless assessment reduce discretion and face-to-face contact; proactive disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act opens decisions to scrutiny.
  • Conflict-of-interest management: annual declarations of assets and interests, recusal, cooling-off periods before post-retirement commercial employment, and integrity pacts in large procurements, as promoted by the CVC.
  • Protection for whistle-blowers: the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004) operates, but the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 has still not been brought into force (as of 2026).
  • Values through training and leadership: case-based ethics training under Mission Karmayogi and leaders who model probity, so that integrity is rewarded rather than isolated.

Probity cannot be achieved by laws alone. External checks deter wrongdoing, but internalised integrity sustains it. Together, they build the public trust on which legitimate governance rests.
free.upm-2019-gs4-5b:
Emotional intelligenceSelf-regulationEmpathyEthical use of emotions

Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions and those of others. The idea was formulated by psychologists Peter Salovey and John Mayer (1990) and popularised by Daniel Goleman's book Emotional Intelligence (1995). The statement captures its essence: emotions are not enemies to be suppressed but energy and information to be harnessed. I agree, with the qualification that EI also concerns others' emotions and must serve ethical ends.

1. How EI makes emotions work for us

  • Anger channelled: anger at injustice, once regulated, becomes resolve to fix the system rather than an outburst that harms people.
  • Fear as information: anxiety before a cyclone or an election signals risk and prompts preparation instead of paralysis.
  • Stress managed: EI prevents burnout and sustains performance in long disaster operations or difficult postings.
  • Emotions aid reasoning: the neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, in Descartes' Error (1994), showed that patients with damage to brain areas that process emotion struggle to make even simple decisions.

2. Why I agree with the view

  • Administration: a police officer who stays calm before an angry crowd can de-escalate, while one who loses control may provoke violence.
  • Leadership: Nelson Mandela, after 27 years in prison, chose reconciliation over revenge and helped unite South Africa as its President (1994–99), turning personal pain into national purpose.
  • Better decisions: awareness of one's own biases and moods prevents impulsive or prejudiced decisions, and empathy keeps the weakest in view.
  • Teamwork: leaders who manage their emotions build trust and morale, essential in crises.

3. Qualifications

  • Not only about oneself: EI also means reading and responding to others' emotions; making emotions work only "for you" can become self-serving.
  • Its dark side: emotional skills can be used to manipulate, as demagogues and fraudsters show; EI must be guided by values and integrity.
  • Working with, not suppressing: making emotions work means acknowledging them; suppressed emotions resurface as stress or cynicism.
  • Not a cure-all: EI cannot substitute for knowledge, fair rules or adequate resources.

4. Developing EI in public servants

  • Behavioural competencies under Mission Karmayogi, mindfulness and yoga, 360-degree feedback, mentoring and reflective practice build EI over time.

Emotional intelligence turns emotions from masters into servants. Combined with ethics, it makes a public servant both effective and humane.
free.upm-2019-gs4-6a:
Self-examinationKnow thyselfReflective practiceMoral autonomy

Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) said this at his trial in Athens, as recorded in Plato's Apology, when he refused to give up philosophical questioning even to save his life. To him, a life lived by habit, custom or others' opinions, without asking what is good and why we act as we do, is not a fully human life. The value at its heart is self-examination, the basis of moral autonomy.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Know thyself: examine one's beliefs, motives, prejudices and actions honestly, the Delphic maxim that guided Socrates.
  • Questioning the unquestioned: practices such as untouchability and dowry persisted for centuries because people did not examine them.
  • Continuous growth: reflection turns experience into learning and mistakes into improvement.
  • Living by one's own reasons: not blind obedience to authority, crowds or social media trends.
  • Examination leading to action: reflection should produce responsibility and change, not endless doubt.

2. Examples from public life

  • Ashoka: after the Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE), he reflected on the suffering it caused; his Rock Edict XIII records his remorse, and he turned from conquest by war to dhamma.
  • Gandhi: his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth, is a record of constant self-scrutiny; he publicly admitted errors of judgement and suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura (1922).
  • Institutions: commissions of inquiry, after-action reviews of disasters and CAG audits are a form of examination at the level of institutions.
  • A warning: Hannah Arendt's account of the trial of Adolf Eichmann (1963) showed how thoughtless obedience lets ordinary officials take part in great wrongs.

3. Relevance for a civil servant

  • Reflective practice: reviewing one's decisions regularly for bias, fairness and impact, and keeping records of reasons.
  • Guarding against routine: mechanically following precedent can perpetuate injustice; asking "why" and "for whom" keeps administration humane.
  • Feedback: APAR self-appraisal, 360-degree feedback and citizen feedback are tools for an examined career.
  • Integrity check: asking whether one would be comfortable if a decision were made public, before taking it.
  • Personal life: balance, health and relationships also need examination; a burnt-out officer cannot serve well.

The examined life is a morally awake life. For a civil servant, habitual reflection guards against both corruption and mechanical governance, and keeps the citizen at the centre.
free.upm-2019-gs4-6b:
Power of thoughtAttitude formationSelf-disciplineCharacter

The quotation, attributed to M.K. Gandhi, holds that our thoughts are the seeds of our character: what we think repeatedly shapes our attitudes, words and deeds, and finally who we become. It echoes the Upanishadic idea that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation, and modern psychology's finding that beliefs shape behaviour. The value at its heart is self-mastery through discipline of the mind.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Thought precedes action: every deed begins as a thought; repeated thoughts harden into attitudes and habits.
  • Responsibility for one's inner life: we cannot always control circumstances, but we can choose our response to them.
  • Two kinds of cycles: thoughts of hatred and greed breed violence and corruption; thoughts of compassion and duty breed service.
  • Self-belief shapes achievement: a person who believes in their ability persists through difficulty.
  • A caveat: thought must be matched by effort and by enabling conditions; thinking alone does not remove poverty or discrimination.

2. Examples from public life

  • Gandhi himself: thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg in South Africa (1893), he chose to resist injustice non-violently rather than retreat or seek revenge; that resolve grew into satyagraha and shaped his whole life.
  • Arunima Sinha: after losing a leg when she was pushed from a moving train (2011), her determination carried her to the summit of Mount Everest in 2013, the first woman amputee to do so.
  • A negative example: online radicalisation shows how hateful ideas, repeated and reinforced, turn ordinary people towards violence.
  • Attitude and its components: social psychology describes attitudes as having cognitive (thought), affective (feeling) and behavioural parts; changing thought is often the first step in changing behaviour.

3. Relevance for a civil servant

  • Attitude to citizens: an officer who thinks of citizens as a burden behaves rudely; one who sees them as the purpose of the job serves with empathy.
  • Integrity begins in the mind: small rationalisations, such as "just this once", grow into habitual corruption; guarding thoughts guards conduct.
  • Solutions, not constraints: Armstrong Pame's road in Manipur (2012), built largely with public contributions, began with refusing to think that nothing could be done.
  • Cultivating the mind: reflection, reading, meditation or yoga, good company and value-based training under Mission Karmayogi help discipline thought.

Thought is the architect of character. A public servant who disciplines the mind with constitutional values and compassion will act rightly even when no one is watching, which is the essence of integrity.
free.upm-2019-gs4-6c:
RighteousnessCharacterHarmonyPeace

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (1931–2015), scientist and India's 11th President (2002–07), often spoke to young people about character. The quotation traces a chain of virtue from the individual to the world, beginning with righteousness in the heart. Its message is that world peace begins with personal ethics. A similar chain, from rectifying the heart to peace under heaven, appears in the Confucian classic The Great Learning.

1. What each link means to me

  • Righteousness in the heart: honesty, compassion and a sense of right and wrong in one's inner life; intentions matter, not only outward actions.
  • Beauty in character: inner goodness shows in conduct, such as truthfulness, humility and self-control; this beauty is moral, not physical.
  • Harmony in the home: persons of character treat family members with respect and fairness, rejecting domestic violence, dowry and discrimination against daughters; the family then passes good values to children.
  • Order in the nation: citizens raised in such homes obey the law, pay taxes and refuse corruption; order that comes from inner discipline is stronger than order imposed by force.
  • Peace in the world: nations that are just at home act responsibly abroad; India's G20 theme (2023), "One Earth, One Family, One Future", drew on the idea of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.

2. Examples from public life

  • Kalam himself: his simplicity, integrity and accessibility, especially to students, earned him the title of the "People's President".
  • Gandhi: he joined personal discipline with public struggle; non-violence practised in his own life became a national movement and inspired Martin Luther King Jr and Nelson Mandela.
  • The reverse chain: corruption, communal hatred and domestic abuse begin as failures of the heart and spread outwards into disorder; laws treat the symptoms, character treats the cause.

3. Relevance today and for a civil servant

  • Value education: the National Education Policy, 2020 stresses ethical and constitutional values, recognising that character is built early, in homes and schools.
  • Integrity in office: an officer of character creates harmony in the office, fairness in decisions and trust among citizens; personal integrity is the first condition of good administration.
  • Leading by example: in a district or department, the head's conduct sets the tone for subordinates.
  • A balanced view: individual virtue is necessary but not sufficient; just institutions, the rule of law and equitable development are also needed for national order and world peace.

Kalam's chain shows that transformation from within is the foundation of national order and global peace. For a civil servant, character building is the starting point of good governance.
free.upm-2019-gs4-7:
Disaster responseDuty of careLeadershipEmotional intelligence

As head of rescue operations after a severe natural calamity, I face the anger of people who have lost homes, food and water, an assault that has severely injured a team member, and a plea from some members to call off the operations. The case sets the duty to rescue against the duty of care owed to my team, and tests leadership under pressure.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: thousands of affected people, especially children, the elderly, the sick, pregnant women and persons with disabilities; my team and the injured member; the district administration and police; volunteers and NGOs; the government and the media.
  • Issues: the right to life and relief versus rescuers' safety; understandable anger versus violence against public servants, an offence under Section 132 of the BNS and, as obstruction, under Section 51 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005; fair distribution of scarce relief; team morale; and public trust in the state.

2. My response

  • Immediate steps: evacuate and treat the injured member; move the team briefly to a safe staging point; inform the District Magistrate and seek police support, more NDRF or SDRF teams and, where roads are cut, armed forces' helicopters for airlifts and air-drops.
  • Engage the community: meet panchayat members, elders, religious leaders and women's groups; acknowledge their suffering, explain the delay (rain, damaged routes) and share a clear plan and timeline; set up an information and grievance desk.
  • Make locals partners: involve local youth and volunteers in rescue and distribution; in the Kerala floods of 2018, local fishermen rescued thousands with their boats.
  • Deliver visibly and fairly: drinking water, food, medical camps and shelters, with priority to the most vulnerable and public distribution lists to prevent grabbing.
  • Restore access: work with road, power and telecom agencies to reopen routes, using boats and helicopters meanwhile.
  • Care for the team: lead from the front, rotate shifts, provide protective gear, insurance and counselling; record the assault and let the police act against the assailants through due process, without collective punishment.

Why this course: it fulfils the duty to save lives, the role obligation of a rescue leader and courage tempered by care. Calling off would punish thousands for the acts of a few, while reckless continuation would sacrifice my team.

3. Qualities required

  • Composure under provocation matters most: a leader who panics or retaliates turns a crisis into a conflict.
  • Moral courage means neither abandoning the people nor exposing the team to needless risk.

In disasters, the state must be seen as a source of help, not withdrawal. Compassionate firmness, protecting the team while continuing to serve the people, is the essence of public service in a crisis.
free.upm-2019-gs4-8:
Bona fide decisionsPolicy paralysisMens reaAccountability

The case concerns honest civil servants prosecuted, and sometimes imprisoned, for bona fide decisions that later had adverse consequences. Accountability for corruption must be strict, but treating an honest error of judgement as a crime confuses mistake with misconduct. The challenge is to protect the honest without shielding the dishonest, balancing accountability with the freedom to decide.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: honest officers and their families; the political executive; investigating and vigilance agencies; courts; citizens and investors who depend on timely decisions.
  • Issues: justice to the officer (no crime without a guilty mind, or mens rea); accountability for public money; the morale and moral fibre of the service; and the public interest in decisive governance.

2. How the trend affects the civil services

  • Risk aversion and policy paralysis: officers avoid decisions, refer files upwards or to committees and seek repeated legal opinions, so projects, procurement and investment stall.
  • Demoralisation and talent loss: capable officers avoid sensitive posts such as procurement, land and mining, or seek early exit.
  • Rule-bound, not outcome-oriented, administration: innovation and reasonable risk-taking, which good governance needs, are discouraged.
  • Perverse incentives: if honesty offers no protection, the incentive to remain honest weakens, and the corrupt can hide among the cautious.
  • Breakdown of trust: officers insist on written orders for everything, and relations with the political executive become defensive.

3. Measures to protect honest officers

  • A clear legal test of guilt: the 2018 amendment to the Prevention of Corruption Act redefined criminal misconduct (Section 13) as fraudulent misappropriation or intentional illicit enrichment, dropping the old clause (Section 13(1)(d)(iii)) under which obtaining a pecuniary advantage for anyone without public interest could be a crime even without a bribe.
  • Screening before a probe: Section 17A (2018) requires prior approval before inquiry into decisions taken in official functions. In January 2026 a two-judge Bench of the Supreme Court split on its validity, one judge striking it down and the other upholding it with approval tied to a Lokpal or Lokayukta recommendation; a larger Bench is yet to decide (as of October 2026). In October 2026 the Court held that it does not cover a demand for a bribe, which is not an official function (Tejaram v State of Rajasthan). Screening by an independent body rather than the government itself would best balance protection and accountability.
  • Time-bound sanction for prosecution: since 2018, Section 19 asks the sanctioning authority to endeavour to decide within three months, extendable by one month where legal consultation is needed; the decision should rest on a reasoned assessment of whether there was dishonest intent.
  • Administrative safeguards: clear delegation and guidelines, recorded reasons, collective decisions on complex matters, and vigilance practice that separates procedural lapses (departmental action) from corrupt intent (criminal action).
  • Support and culture: legal assistance for acts done in good faith, speedy trials, no media trials, appraisal that credits reasonable risk-taking, and decision-making training under Mission Karmayogi.

Why this course: it respects mens rea and fairness to the officer, keeps equality before law by refusing blanket immunity, and serves the public interest in honest, decisive governance.

A civil service that fears its own decisions cannot serve citizens. Distinguishing honest error from dishonest intent protects both integrity and initiative.
free.upm-2019-gs4-9:
Sexual harassmentPOSH Act, 2013Hush moneyDignity at work

A woman employee complained of sexual harassment by a high-performing marketing executive. The company ignored her, and after she filed an FIR it offered her a hefty sum to withdraw both complaints and to declare in writing that he was not involved. The case sets profit and reputation against dignity, justice and truth, and tests the integrity of the company and of the woman herself.

1. Stakeholders

  • The complainant; the accused executive; the many other women employees; the management and owners; the Internal Committee; the police and courts; customers, investors and society.

2. Ethical issues

  • Violation of dignity and safety: sexual harassment violates Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21, as the Supreme Court held in Vishaka (1997), and is an offence under Section 75 of the BNS.
  • Institutional indifference: ignoring a formal complaint breaches the employer's duties under the POSH Act, 2013, which requires an Internal Committee to complete its inquiry within 90 days and penalises non-compliant employers.
  • Profit over principle: earlier reports about the executive were ignored because he raised sales, a failure of corporate governance and of the duty of care.
  • Buying silence: the offer is hush money; the POSH Act bars monetary settlement as the basis of conciliation (Section 10), and asking her to sign a false statement asks her to lie and obstructs justice.
  • Power imbalance: an employee negotiating alone with her employer is under pressure, so her "consent" would not be truly free.
  • Wider harm: silence endangers other women and corrodes the workplace culture.

3. Options available to the woman employee

4. The course I would advise, and why

  • Refuse the offer firmly: make a dated note of who made the offer and its terms, and inform the investigating officer of the attempt to induce withdrawal.
  • Use the POSH Act: file a written complaint with the Internal Committee (within three months of the incident, extendable by three months) and seek interim relief under Section 12, such as transfer of the respondent or herself, or leave of up to three months.
  • Escalate if ignored: a firm of this size must have an Internal Committee (the District Officer's Local Committee hears complaints only from workplaces with fewer than ten workers or against the employer himself); if there is none, or it does not act, she can file a court complaint against the employer, punishable with a fine of up to Rs 50,000 (Sections 26 and 27), alert the District Officer, and use the SHe-Box portal or the State or National Commission for Women.
  • Seek support: free legal aid through the District Legal Services Authority (women are entitled under Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987), counselling, and support from family, colleagues and NGOs.
  • Lawful compensation: the Internal Committee can recommend compensation for mental trauma, medical expenses and lost career opportunities, payable by the harasser (Section 15), a legitimate remedy unlike hush money.

Why: it upholds truth and her dignity, protects other women, keeps her within the law, and gives her a lawful route to redress. Accepting the money would turn justice into a commodity and leave the workplace unsafe.

A safe workplace is a right, not a favour. Companies must treat POSH compliance as a core part of corporate ethics rather than a threat to reputation.
free.upm-2019-gs4-10:
Politicisation of bureaucracyNeutralityMeritRule of law

In a parliamentary democracy, the political executive sets policy and answers to the legislature, while the permanent executive gives impartial advice and implements lawful policy faithfully, whichever party governs. Politicisation of bureaucracy occurs when this boundary breaks down: officers are rewarded or punished for loyalty rather than merit, and ministers intervene in routine matters such as transfers. Sardar Patel defended the All India Services in the Constituent Assembly (October 1949) precisely so that officers could advise without fear.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: citizens, especially the weaker sections; honest officers; ministers and legislators; institutions such as the police, investigating agencies and the Election Commission; investors; democracy itself.
  • Issues: neutrality versus loyalty; merit versus patronage; responsiveness versus servility; rule of law versus personal rule; and the corrosive effect of materialism and acquisitiveness on both executives.

2. Consequences of the politicisation of bureaucracy

  • Loss of frank advice: a bureaucracy loyal to persons rather than to the Constitution turns into "yes-men", and policy errors go uncorrected.
  • Frequent transfers: short tenures stop officers from completing projects or understanding their districts; in T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court directed minimum tenure, Civil Services Boards to recommend transfers and postings, and the recording of oral instructions.
  • Partisan policing: in Prakash Singh (2006), the Court ordered police reforms, including State Security Commissions, fixed tenure for key officers and Police Establishment Boards, to insulate the police; compliance remains uneven.
  • Nexus and corruption: the Vohra Committee (1993) reported a nexus of criminals, politicians and officials; politicisation deepens it, as officers seek lucrative postings and post-retirement rewards.
  • Demoralised talent: upright officers are sidelined, others turn opportunist, and the merit principle of recruitment is undermined in practice.
  • Erosion of public trust: benefits flow to supporters, investigations lose credibility, and citizens come to see the State as partisan.
  • Waste and discontinuity: projects are tied to political cycles and abandoned when governments change, wasting public money.
  • A necessary distinction: ministers are entitled to set priorities and demand results; the harm begins when loyalty to persons or parties replaces loyalty to law and merit.

3. Options for reform

  • Preferred course: Civil Services Boards and minimum tenure under the AIS (Cadre) Rules as amended in 2014; written orders; a code of ethics for ministers and civil servants, as the Second ARC recommended; independent Police Establishment Boards; and value-based training. Officers too must refuse illegal orders and record dissent.
  • Why: it respects the elected government's right to set policy while protecting the impartial execution that citizens are entitled to.

Political direction is legitimate; political capture is not. A neutral yet responsive bureaucracy, answerable to the Constitution above any party, is the foundation of constitutional governance.
free.upm-2019-gs4-11:
Narcotics menaceNarco-terrorPolitician–police nexusDemand reduction

A frontier district is gripped by narcotics: poppy cultivation is spreading, drug money is being laundered, arms are smuggled and schools have nearly stopped working. Local politicians and some senior police officers reportedly shield the drug mafia. As the woman Superintendent of Police sent to restore normalcy, I must dismantle a criminal economy while handling possible insider collusion in a sensitive border area.

1. Stakeholders

  • Young people and addicts and their families; children out of school; poppy farmers; honest police personnel; local politicians and officials; traffickers and cross-border networks; border guarding forces; schools, NGOs and religious bodies; the State and the nation.

2. Dimensions of the crisis

3. Options

  • Enforcement-only crackdown: quick visible results, but it hits small peddlers and farmers, invites backlash and leaves demand and patrons untouched.
  • Welfare-only approach: wins goodwill but lets traffickers and their protectors carry on.
  • Avoid confronting the nexus: keeps me safe and the posting smooth, but betrays my duty.
  • Integrated approach (preferred): go after the network and its patrons on evidence, while reducing demand and giving farmers and youth alternatives.

4. Measures to deal with the crisis

  • Clean my own house first: a core team vetted for integrity, rotation of staff in sensitive posts and an internal vigilance cell; act against police personnel on evidence, and report allegations against senior officers and politicians in writing to the DGP and the vigilance authorities rather than leaking unverified claims.
  • Target the network, not just users: intelligence-led action against suppliers and kingpins under the NDPS Act, 1985, including forfeiture of drug-derived property and preventive detention under the PIT-NDPS Act, 1988; follow the money with the Enforcement Directorate under the PMLA.
  • Coordination: use the NCORD mechanism with the Narcotics Control Bureau, the State anti-narcotics task force, border forces, customs and excise; joint checkpoints against arms smuggling, and the NIA where terror links emerge.
