  • Poppy cultivation: map fields with satellite imagery and drones, destroy illicit crops through due process, and work with the agriculture department on alternative crops and livelihoods so that farmers are not pushed into destitution.
  • Demand reduction: de-addiction and rehabilitation under the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2020) and the MANAS helpline 1933; addicts charged with consumption or small-quantity offences who volunteer for treatment can get immunity under Section 64A of the NDPS Act, so they are treated as patients.
  • Restore education: reopen schools with security, run enrolment drives and anti-drug clubs, and provide counselling.
  • Community policing: village vigilance committees, sports for youth, religious leaders and women's groups; Manipur's Meira Paibis have long campaigned against drugs and alcohol.

Why this course: it combines firmness with compassion, follows due process, and treats causes as well as symptoms. Firm, fair leadership earns respect regardless of gender, and women's networks are powerful allies.

The narcotics menace is a crisis of security, health and governance at once. A whole-of-society approach, led by an officer of integrity, can restore the rule of law.
free.upm-2019-gs4-12:
Ethics infrastructureIntegrity riskEthical competenceMission Karmayogi

The case asks how to build an ethics infrastructure for the civil services: not only laws and anti-corruption agencies that punish wrongdoing after it happens, but institutions that anticipate threats to integrity, build officers' ethical competence, and embed integrity in everyday administrative processes. India has many pieces, from conduct rules and the CVC to the Lokpal and RTI, but internalising ethics remains the gap.

1. Stakeholders, issues and approach

  • Stakeholders: civil servants; the political executive; citizens and businesses who deal with government; oversight bodies (CVC, Lokpal, CAG, Information Commissions); training institutions.
  • Ethical issue: compliance-based integrity (rules and punishment) catches wrongdoing afterwards, while values-based integrity prevents it; relying on either alone fails.
  • Options: more punishment alone deters but breeds fear and paralysis; training alone builds values but lacks teeth; a combination of prevention, competence and enforcement (preferred) addresses all three issues.

2. Anticipating threats to ethical standards and integrity

  • Integrity risk mapping: each ministry should identify sensitive functions such as procurement, licensing, land, tax and recruitment, review them periodically and rotate officers from them, as CVC guidelines require for sensitive posts.
  • Data analytics: use PFMS, GeM and tax data to flag unusual patterns, such as repeated single bids, split contracts or assets out of line with income.
  • Conflict-of-interest management: annual declarations of assets and interests, recusal registers, cooling-off periods before post-retirement commercial jobs, and clear rules on gifts and lobbying.
  • New risks: guidelines on algorithmic decisions, data protection under the DPDP Act, 2023, and officers' conduct on social media.

3. Strengthening the ethical competence of civil servants

  • Recruitment: the ethics paper (GS IV) in the Civil Services Main Examination since 2013, and verification of character and antecedents.
  • Training: Mission Karmayogi (2020), with the Capacity Building Commission and the iGOT Karmayogi platform, should include case-based ethics modules, simulations of dilemmas and refreshers at every promotion.
  • Guidance: a short code of ethics, as the Second ARC's fourth report (2007) recommended, and an ethics counsellor in each department for confidential advice on dilemmas.
  • Leadership: senior officers who model integrity, and assessment of ethical leadership in empanelment.

4. Administrative processes that promote ethical values

  • Less discretion: e-office, faceless assessment, GeM e-procurement and Direct Benefit Transfer reduce face-to-face contact and opportunities for rent-seeking.
  • Transparency and participation: proactive disclosure under the RTI Act, social audits, citizens' charters and Right to Services laws.
  • Accountability with protection: an effective Lokpal and CVC; whistle-blower channels under the PIDPI Resolution and operationalisation of the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014; safeguards for bona fide decisions.
  • Incentives: integrity in the APAR, recognition through the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration, and premature retirement under FR 56(j) where integrity is doubtful; integrity pacts with independent external monitors in large contracts.

Why this combination: threats are anticipated before they materialise, officers are equipped to resolve dilemmas, and processes make the ethical choice the easy choice.

Integrity grows when rules, competence and culture reinforce one another. Such an ethics infrastructure turns integrity from an individual virtue into an institutional habit.
free.upm-2020-gs1-1:
Rock-cut architectureChaitya and viharaDonative inscriptionsAjanta murals

Rock-cut architecture means monuments carved out of living rock rather than built. In India it spans about a thousand years, from the Mauryan Barabar caves (3rd century BCE) to the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora (8th century CE). As early timber buildings have perished, these caves, with their sculptures, paintings and inscriptions, are a prime source for Indian art and for early India's religion, polity, economy and society.

1. A record of artistic evolution

  • From wood to stone: the doorway of the Lomas Rishi cave at Barabar copies the curved front of a thatched hut, and the chaitya halls at Bhaja and Karle imitate wooden beams and ribs, preserving a timber tradition that has otherwise vanished.
  • Mauryan polish: the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves in Bihar, given to the Ajivika sect by Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha, have mirror-like polished walls.
  • Buddhist chaityas and viharas: Bhaja, Karle, Nasik, Kanheri and early Ajanta (2nd century BCE–2nd century CE) show the prayer hall and monastery maturing; Karle's is the largest rock-cut chaitya.
  • Classical climax: the later Ajanta caves (5th century CE), Elephanta (6th century), the Pallava rathas at Mamallapuram (7th century) and Ellora, where 34 Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves stand side by side.

2. A source for political history

  • Royal records: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri (Odisha, c. 1st century BCE) records his campaigns year by year; Gautami Balashri's inscription at Nasik lists the victories of her son Gautamiputra Satakarni over the Shakas.
  • Dating dynasties: Varahadeva's inscription in Ajanta Cave 16 dates the later caves to the Vakataka king Harishena; Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh) inscriptions belong to Chandragupta II's reign.
  • Royal ideology: the Varaha panel at Udayagiri, Vishnu rescuing the Earth, is often read as an image of Gupta kingship; queen Naganika's Naneghat inscription records Satavahana Vedic sacrifices.

3. A source for economy and society

  • Trade and guilds: the caves cluster on Western Ghats routes linking ports such as Sopara and Kalyan with the Deccan; donor inscriptions at Karle, Nasik, Junnar and Kanheri name merchants, artisans, guilds (shreni) and Yavanas (foreigners).
  • Early banking: Ushavadata's Nasik inscription records deposits with weavers' guilds at Govardhana whose interest fed the monks.
  • Daily life: Ajanta's murals show palaces, dress, jewellery, music and ships alongside the Jataka stories.

4. A source for religious history

  • Hinayana to Mahayana: early chaityas centre on a plain stupa; later ones at Ajanta (Caves 19 and 26) carve the Buddha on it, marking the shift from symbol to image worship.
  • Puranic Hinduism and Jainism: Elephanta's three-headed Maheshmurti, Ellora's Ravana shaking Kailasa and the Jain caves of Ellora and Udayagiri–Khandagiri show new cults and their coexistence.

Few caves are precisely dated and donative inscriptions record merit rather than events, so they must be read with texts, coins and excavations. Still, they are history carved in stone, and conserving them (Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta are UNESCO sites) protects a primary archive of early India.
free.upm-2020-gs1-2:
Pala dynastyMahaviharasVajrayanaBuddhism in Tibet

The Pala dynasty, founded by Gopala around 750 CE when he was chosen king to end anarchy (matsyanyaya) in Bengal, ruled Bengal and Bihar for about four centuries. While Buddhism was fading elsewhere in India, the Palas were its last great royal patrons. Their mahaviharas made eastern India the intellectual centre of the Buddhist world, Vajrayana took mature form there, and teachers of the Pala age carried Buddhism to Tibet and beyond.

1. Royal patronage and the great monasteries

  • Vikramashila: founded by Dharmapala (late 8th century) near Bhagalpur in Bihar, it became the leading centre of tantric studies.
  • Somapura Mahavihara: Dharmapala's vast monastery at Paharpur (now in Bangladesh), one of the largest south of the Himalayas and a UNESCO site.
  • Odantapuri and Jagaddala: Odantapuri (Bihar Sharif) rose in the early Pala period; Ramapala founded Jagaddala in north Bengal in the late 11th century.
  • Nalanda revived: Devapala granted five villages to support a monastery built at Nalanda by the Sailendra king Balaputradeva of Suvarnadvipa (Sumatra), as the Nalanda copper plate records.

2. Doctrinal creativity: the Vajrayana phase

  • Vajrayana (Tantric Buddhism): liberation through mantras, mandalas, mudras, rituals and the guidance of a guru; female deities such as Tara gained importance.
  • Siddhas and literature: Mahasiddhas such as Saraha, Tilopa and Naropa composed mystical songs; the Charyapadas are among the earliest specimens of Bengali, Assamese and Odia.
  • Philosophy: Shantarakshita and his disciple Kamalashila of Nalanda combined Yogachara and Madhyamaka thought.

3. Spread beyond India

  • Tibet: Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava helped found Samye, Tibet's first monastery, in the late 8th century under King Trisong Detsen; Atisha Dipankara Srijnana of Vikramashila reached Tibet in 1042 and revived its monastic discipline, inspiring the Kadam school.
  • Two-way links: Atisha had studied under Dharmakirti of Suvarnadvipa (Sumatra); Pala manuscripts and bronzes reached Nepal, Tibet, Myanmar and Indonesia.

4. Art and manuscripts

  • Pala school of sculpture: images of the Buddha, Tara, Avalokiteshvara and Hindu deities in black stone and bronze, as in the Kurkihar and Nalanda hoards; Taranatha names Dhiman and his son Bitpalo as master artists.
  • Illustrated manuscripts: palm-leaf manuscripts of the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita, with small paintings, are among the earliest surviving Indian miniatures.

5. Why this phase matters most, and how it ended

  • Final creative climax: Buddhism spread most widely within India under the Mauryas and Kushanas, but the Pala age was its last intellectual flowering and its bridge to Tibet.
  • Vulnerability: dependence on great monasteries and royal patrons, and tantric Buddhism's closeness to Hindu tantra, narrowed its popular base; after the Senas replaced the Palas, Turkish raids under Bakhtiyar Khalji (c. 1200) sacked Nalanda, Odantapuri and Vikramashila, and monks fled to Tibet and Nepal.

The Pala period thus turned Buddhism from a declining Indian faith into a pan-Asian tradition. Its scholarship, art and Vajrayana practice live on in Tibetan and Himalayan Buddhism, and in the revived Nalanda University (2014).
free.upm-2020-gs1-3:
Lord Curzon (1899–1905)Partition of BengalSwadeshi movementCommunal politics

Lord Curzon, Viceroy from 1899 to 1905, was an able but arrogant imperialist who equated good government with efficiency and believed Indians unfit for self-rule; in private letters he hoped to help the Congress to a peaceful end. His reforms modernised parts of the administration, but his centralising, anti-nationalist measures, above all the Partition of Bengal (1905), produced the opposite of what he intended: a militant, mass-based national movement.

1. Administrative and economic measures

  • Famine and irrigation: after the famine of 1899–1900, a Famine Commission (1900) and an Irrigation Commission (1901) recommended better relief and more canals.
  • Agrarian measures: the Punjab Land Alienation Act (1900) restricted the transfer of land from peasants to moneylenders, and the Co-operative Credit Societies Act (1904) began the co-operative movement.
  • Institutions and heritage: the Police Commission (1902), the Railway Board (1905), an agricultural research institute at Pusa (Bihar), and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904) with a revived Archaeological Survey under John Marshall.

2. Measures that alienated educated Indians

  • Calcutta Corporation Act (1899): cut elected members, seen as an attack on local self-government.
  • Indian Universities Act (1904): following the Raleigh Commission (1902), it tightened official control over universities, seen as a curb on the educated class.
  • Official Secrets (Amendment) Act (1904): extended official secrets to civil matters and restricted the press.

3. Partition of Bengal (1905)

  • Stated reason: Bengal (with Bihar and Orissa) was too large to govern; a new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, with its capital at Dacca, came into being on 16 October 1905.
  • Real aim: to weaken Bengal, the nerve centre of nationalism, by dividing Bengalis by territory and religion: the new province had a Muslim majority, and Bengali speakers became a minority in the western province.
  • Reaction: the boycott resolution at Calcutta Town Hall (7 August 1905), a day of mourning on 16 October, and Tagore's call to tie rakhis as a symbol of unity.

4. Long-term implications for the national movement

  • First mass movement: Swadeshi and Boycott brought national education, swadeshi enterprises and mass meetings, methods Gandhi later used; in 1906 the Calcutta Congress under Dadabhai Naoroji adopted swaraj as its goal.
  • Rise of the Extremists and the Surat split (1907): Lal-Bal-Pal and Aurobindo Ghosh pressed for passive resistance, and the Moderates' petitions lost appeal.
  • Revolutionary nationalism: the Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar groups in Bengal, the Muzaffarpur bombing and the Alipore conspiracy case (1908).
  • Communal politics: the All-India Muslim League was founded at Dacca (December 1906), and separate electorates under the Morley–Minto Reforms (1909) institutionalised a divide that culminated in 1947.
  • Lesson of victory: its annulment in 1911 (with the capital moved to Delhi) showed that sustained agitation could force the Raj to retreat.

Curzon thus became an unintended unifier of Indian nationalism: efficiency without sympathy turned constitutional politics into mass nationalism, while his divisive methods left a communal legacy that outlived the Raj.
free.upm-2020-gs1-4:
Ring of FireSubduction zonesTrenches and island arcsMegathrust earthquakes

The Circum-Pacific Zone, popularly called the Ring of Fire, is a horseshoe-shaped belt about 40,000 km long around the Pacific Ocean, running from the southern Andes through North America, the Aleutians, Kamchatka, Japan and the Philippines to New Zealand. It is the world's most active zone of plate convergence: about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes and about 90% of its earthquakes occur along it.

1. Tectonic setting

  • Subduction all round the Pacific: dense oceanic plates sink beneath their neighbours: the Nazca under South America, the Juan de Fuca under North America, the Pacific beneath the Aleutians, Kamchatka and Japan, and the Pacific beneath the Philippine Sea plate at the Mariana Trench.
  • A shrinking ocean: the Pacific basin is slowly shrinking while the Atlantic widens.
  • Transform segments: in places the plates slide past each other, as along the San Andreas Fault in California and the Alpine Fault in New Zealand.

2. Relief features

  • Deep trenches: the deepest parts of the oceans lie here: the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep, nearly 11 km), and the Tonga, Kermadec, Kuril–Kamchatka, Japan and Peru–Chile trenches.
  • Island arcs: where ocean meets ocean, curved chains of volcanic islands form: the Aleutians, Kurils, Japan and the Marianas.
  • Continental arcs and fold mountains: where ocean meets continent, the Andes and the Cascades rise parallel to the trench.
  • Back-arc basins: stretching behind some arcs opened marginal seas such as the Sea of Japan.

3. Volcanism

  • Explosive volcanoes: water released from the sinking slab lowers the melting point of the mantle above it, producing viscous, gas-rich magma and steep composite cones such as Mount Fuji, Cotopaxi and Mount St Helens (1980).
  • Global effects: Pinatubo (Philippines, 1991) cooled global temperatures by about half a degree Celsius the next year; Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai (2022) set off a tsunami.
  • Mudflows: the lahar from Nevado del Ruiz (Colombia, 1985) buried the town of Armero, killing over 20,000 people.

4. Seismicity

  • Benioff zone: earthquake foci deepen along the sinking slab, from shallow near the trench to about 700 km under the arc.
  • Megathrust earthquakes: the locked plate boundary produces the largest quakes: Chile (1960, magnitude 9.5, the largest recorded), Alaska (1964), Tohoku in Japan (2011), whose tsunami caused the Fukushima nuclear accident, and Kamchatka (magnitude 8.8, July 2025).
  • Tsunami hazard: hence the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center in Hawaii.

5. Resources

  • Minerals and energy: subduction-related magma and fluids concentrate metals, so Chile and Peru are among the world's leading copper producers; New Zealand, Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia tap geothermal heat, and fertile volcanic soils support dense populations, as in Java.

The Circum-Pacific Zone is thus the most dynamic part of the Earth's crust, where landforms, hazards and mineral wealth all arise from subduction; for the countries around it, living with the Ring of Fire means investing in early warning and resilient buildings.
free.upm-2020-gs1-5:
DesertificationLand degradationHuman driversLand degradation neutrality

The UNCCD (1994) defines desertification as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities. Yet the underlying process, the loss of soil, vegetation, water and productivity, is driven mainly by human misuse of land and by climate change, which operate everywhere. A UNCCD report (December 2024) found that 77.6% of the Earth's land became drier in the three decades to 2020 than in the previous thirty years. Desertification thus has no fixed climatic boundary.

1. Why the process crosses climatic boundaries

  • Universal human drivers: deforestation, overgrazing, faulty irrigation, mining, monocropping and urban sprawl degrade land in wet and dry regions alike.
  • Water erosion, not only wind: ISRO's Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (2021) found water erosion, not wind, the leading process of land degradation in India, in wetter hills as well as drylands.
  • Shifting aridity: drylands now cover more than 40% of the Earth's land (excluding Antarctica), and the 2024 report warns that continued warming would extend drying to most of Europe, parts of the western USA, Brazil, eastern Asia and central Africa.
  • Too much water: over-irrigation raises the water table and leaves salts behind.

2. Indian examples across climatic zones

  • Scale: 97.85 million ha (29.7% of India) was degraded in 2018-19, up from 94.53 million ha in 2003-05 (ISRO atlas).
  • Arid and semi-arid: dune encroachment and overgrazing in the Thar; gully erosion in the Chambal ravines.
  • Humid: the Sohra (Cherrapunji) plateau in Meghalaya, among the wettest places on Earth, has thin, eroded soils and bare grasslands after deforestation, and is often described as a wet desert; mining and shortened jhum cycles degrade hill slopes elsewhere in the North-East.
  • Irrigated plains: waterlogging and salinity affect parts of Punjab, Haryana and the Indira Gandhi Canal command area.
  • Cold desert: overgrazing and frost action degrade the fragile soils of Ladakh and Spiti.

3. Global examples

  • Sahel (semi-arid): the droughts of the 1970s and 1980s combined with overgrazing and fuelwood cutting.
  • Aral Sea basin: Soviet-era irrigation diversions dried the sea, leaving a salty seabed that feeds dust storms.
  • Iceland (cool and humid): after settlement, the clearing of birch woods and sheep grazing left vast eroded, barren areas.
  • Madagascar's highlands (humid tropics): forest loss and burning have produced deep gullies (lavakas) and red, silt-laden rivers.

4. Way forward

  • Land degradation neutrality (SDG 15.3): India aims to restore 26 million ha of degraded land by 2030.
  • Solutions for every zone: watershed development, agroforestry, rotational grazing, efficient irrigation with drainage and mine reclamation, backed by the Green India Mission and the Aravalli Green Wall Project.

Desertification is better understood as land degradation anywhere, shaped by how people use land. Treating it as a problem of deserts alone would miss the eroding hills of the North-East and the salted fields of Punjab, so sustainable land management must cover every climatic zone.
free.upm-2020-gs1-6:
Himalayan glaciersPeak waterGlacial lake outburst floodsWater security

The Himalaya, often called the Third Pole, holds the largest store of ice outside the polar regions, and its glaciers and snow feed the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. ICIMOD's 2023 assessment found that glaciers of the Hindu Kush Himalaya disappeared 65% faster in the 2010s than in the previous decade and could lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100 even if warming is held to 1.5–2°C. This will change when, where and how much water India gets.

1. Short term: more water and more hazards

  • Higher melt flows: faster melting first raises summer river flows; ICIMOD expects flows in the region's 12 river basins to peak around mid-century (peak water) and then decline.
  • Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs): about 200 glacial lakes in the region are considered dangerous. The South Lhonak lake outburst in Sikkim (October 2023) destroyed the Teesta-III dam at Chungthang, and the rock-and-ice avalanche at Chamoli (February 2021) wrecked the Rishiganga and Tapovan hydro projects.
  • Sediment: more debris and silt reach reservoirs such as Bhakra and Tehri.

2. Long term: less water when it matters most

  • Lean-season flows: melt water sustains rivers in the dry pre-monsoon months, when irrigation and drinking-water demand peaks; shrinking glaciers will reduce these flows.
  • The Indus is most exposed: it depends far more on snow and glacier melt than the monsoon-fed Ganga and Brahmaputra, so Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and the canal systems of Punjab and Haryana face the greatest risk.
  • Groundwater: lower river flows mean less recharge in the Indo-Gangetic plain, where Punjab already extracts 156% of its annually extractable groundwater (CGWB 2025).
  • Mountain communities: Ladakhi farmers already build artificial glaciers (ice stupas) to store winter water for spring sowing.

3. Impacts on users of water

  • Agriculture and food security: the canal-irrigated Indo-Gangetic plain, India's food bowl, depends on these rivers in the rabi and summer seasons.
  • Hydropower: most of India's hydropower potential lies in the Himalaya; variable flows, silt and GLOFs threaten run-of-river projects.
  • Cities and pollution: Delhi and other plains cities draw on Himalayan rivers, and lower lean flows concentrate pollution in the Ganga and Yamuna.
  • Deltas and navigation: less fresh water lets salinity advance in the Sundarbans and reduces depth on National Waterway-1.
  • Transboundary stress: India shares these rivers with Pakistan, China, Nepal and Bangladesh; the Indus Waters Treaty has been in abeyance since April 2025.

4. Way forward

  • Science and warning: glacier and glacial-lake monitoring under the National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, NDMA's GLOF guidelines (2020), early-warning systems and GLOF-safe dam design.
  • Storing and saving water: spring-shed revival, small storages, aquifer recharge, micro-irrigation, crop diversification and basin-level data sharing with neighbours.

Himalayan glacier loss is a slow-onset threat: a deceptive surplus today and scarcity tomorrow. India's water security depends on adapting now, by storing monsoon water, using it efficiently and preparing for glacial hazards.
free.upm-2020-gs1-7:
Weight-losing industryCoastal steel plantsElectric arc furnacesMarket orientation

Iron and steel is a classic weight-losing industry: several tonnes of iron ore, coking coal and limestone produce one tonne of steel. In Alfred Weber's least-cost theory such industries locate near raw materials, which is why India's early plants (Jamshedpur, set up by the Tata Iron and Steel Company in 1907, and later Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur and Bokaro) grew in and around the mineral-rich Chhota Nagpur plateau. Today much new capacity is port- and market-based. India is now the world's second-largest crude steel producer.

1. Why raw materials pull less than before

  • Imported coking coal: India's coal is mostly high-ash and non-coking, so integrated plants import much of their coking coal by sea; a port site avoids hauling it hundreds of kilometres inland.
  • Cheaper bulk transport: large ships carry ore and coal cheaply over long distances, and ore increasingly moves as pellets.
  • New technology: electric arc and induction furnaces melt scrap and sponge iron (DRI) instead of smelting ore in blast furnaces, so they need power and scrap rather than coking coal.
  • Markets and exports: demand is concentrated in construction, automobile and engineering hubs of western and southern India, and exports need ports.
  • Liberalisation: after 1991 private investors chose sites by logistics and markets rather than by planned regional dispersal.

2. Coastal (port-based) integrated plants

  • Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (RINL): India's first shore-based integrated steel plant, commissioned in 1992, uses iron ore from Bailadila in Chhattisgarh and imported coking coal through Visakhapatnam port.
  • JSW Dolvi (Maharashtra): on the Konkan coast near Mumbai, it receives coal and ore by sea and serves the Mumbai–Pune market.
  • AM/NS India, Hazira (Gujarat): a port-based plant with gas-based DRI, close to western India's industrial market.

3. Market- and scrap-based units

  • Mini steel plants: electric arc and induction furnace units cluster at Mandi Gobindgarh and Ludhiana (Punjab) and around Delhi, Raipur, Mumbai and Chennai, close to buyers of bars, rods and castings.
  • Scrap sources: ship-breaking at Alang (Gujarat) and urban scrap feed these units; the Steel Scrap Recycling Policy (2019) encourages this route.
  • Downstream finishing: rolling, galvanising and pipe mills locate near user industries such as the automobile clusters of Pune and Chennai.

4. Raw materials still matter

  • Mineral-belt plants: most integrated capacity remains near ore in Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (Kalinganagar, Angul, Rourkela, Bokaro, Bhilai, Nagarnar), and in Karnataka near Ballari (JSW Vijayanagar).
  • Mixed logic: many plants now combine local ore with imported coal, so a site reflects the total cost of moving all inputs and products, not the pull of a single raw material.

The location of Indian steel has thus moved from Weber's pure raw-material orientation to a mixed pattern shaped by ports, scrap and markets. As the National Steel Policy (2017) targets 300 million tonnes of capacity by 2030-31 and low-carbon steelmaking emerges, coastal and market-oriented sites with access to clean power will matter even more.
free.upm-2020-gs1-8:
Caste (jati)Multicultural societyDominant casteCaste census

Caste (jati), an endogamous, hereditary group ranked by notions of purity and pollution, has long been the key concept of Indian sociology, from G.S. Ghurye to M.N. Srinivas. Urbanisation, education, markets and the Constitution (Articles 15 and 17) have weakened its ritual and occupational basis, and India's multicultural society is also shaped by religion, language, region, tribe and class. Yet caste remains essential to understanding marriage, politics and inequality: it has changed its form rather than lost its relevance.

1. Where caste has weakened

  • Ritual hierarchy: untouchability is abolished (Article 17), and shared eating, transport and workplaces in cities have eroded purity–pollution rules.
  • Occupation: the jajmani system and hereditary occupations have declined; jobs in services and industry are filled on credentials.
  • Mobility: education and reservations have created a middle class among SCs, STs and OBCs, and class, profession and consumption increasingly define status.
  • Other identities: many social conflicts turn on religion, language or region, such as communal tensions or the linguistic reorganisation of States, rather than on caste.

2. Why caste remains relevant: illustrations

  • Marriage: only about 5% of Indian marriages are inter-caste (India Human Development Survey, NCAER), and a Pew Research Center survey (2019–20, published 2021) found that 64% of Indians consider it very important to stop women of their community from marrying into another caste.
  • Politics: caste blocs shape tickets and voting; dominant castes such as the Jats, Marathas and Patidars have agitated for reservations; Bihar's caste survey (2023), which put Extremely Backward and Backward Classes together at about 63% of the State's population, and the decision (April 2025) to enumerate caste in Census 2027, the first full caste count since 1931, put caste at the centre of policy.
  • Discrimination and violence: atrocities against Dalits, honour killings (on which the Supreme Court issued guidelines in Shakti Vahini, 2018) and manual scavenging despite the 2013 Act.
  • Beyond Hinduism: caste-like divisions exist among Muslims (the Pasmanda movement), Christians (Dalit Christians) and Sikhs (Mazhabi Sikhs), so caste cuts across India's religious pluralism.
  • Diaspora: caste travels with migrants; Seattle became the first US city to ban caste discrimination (2023).

3. Caste transformed in a multicultural society

  • Sanskritisation and Westernisation: Srinivas showed how lower castes claimed higher status by adopting upper-caste customs, while elites adopted Western ways.
  • From hierarchy to identity: caste associations act as interest groups, as the Rudolphs argued in The Modernity of Tradition (1967); caste is now a resource for mobilisation as much as a ritual rank.
  • Intersections: caste combines with class, gender and region; Dalit women face multiple disadvantages, and in Davinder Singh (2024) the Supreme Court allowed sub-classification of SCs so that benefits reach the most deprived.

Caste has thus not lost its relevance; it has been reinvented. Understanding India's multicultural society still requires a caste lens alongside religion, class and region, while the constitutional goal remains a society built on fraternity and equal dignity.
free.upm-2020-gs1-9:
COVID-19 shockNew poorK-shaped recoverySocial protection

The COVID-19 pandemic and the nationwide lockdown from 25 March 2020 caused India's first annual GDP contraction in four decades (2020-21). Using World Bank data, the Pew Research Center estimated that the number of poor (living on $2 a day or less) rose by about 75 million in 2020 and the middle class shrank by 32 million. Losses fell hardest on informal workers, migrants, women and children, while asset-holders recovered fast, a pattern called a K-shaped recovery.

1. How the pandemic deepened poverty

  • Lost livelihoods: most Indian workers are informal, without contracts or social security; daily-wage earners, street vendors and domestic workers lost incomes overnight, and urban unemployment surged in April–June 2020.
  • Migrant crisis: millions of migrant workers walked or travelled home after the lockdown, losing jobs and savings; special Shramik trains ran from 1 May 2020.
  • Debt and distress sales: households borrowed, pawned gold and cut food spending; many small enterprises closed.
  • Health shock: the second wave (April–May 2021) brought heavy out-of-pocket hospital spending.

2. How class inequalities widened

  • K-shaped recovery: large formal firms, digital businesses and stock markets rebounded quickly, while informal workers and small firms lagged.
  • Education divide: online classes excluded children without smartphones or data; only 33% of women against 57% of men had ever used the internet (NFHS-5), and ASER 2022 recorded a fall in basic reading levels compared with 2018.
  • Gender: women were about seven times as likely as men to lose work in the 2020 lockdown and far less likely to return (State of Working India 2021, Azim Premji University), and carried more care work.

3. Mitigation: why the damage was contained

  • Food security: the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (April 2020) gave free grain to about 80 crore people, and free foodgrains under the National Food Security Act have been extended for five years from January 2024.
  • Cash and work: ₹500 a month for three months to women Jan Dhan account holders, free LPG cylinders under Ujjwala, and an extra ₹40,000 crore for MGNREGA, a fallback for returning migrants.
  • Credit: the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme helped small firms survive.
  • Recovery: the World Bank (2025) estimates that extreme poverty (US$ 3 a day at 2021 prices) fell from 27.1% in 2011-12 to 5.3% in 2022-23, and NITI Aayog finds that 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23.

4. Assessment

  • Poverty: the pandemic caused a sharp but largely temporary rise, cushioned by safety nets and recovery.
  • Inequality: its deeper legacy lies in lost learning, depleted savings and the weak bargaining power of informal workers; research such as the World Inequality Lab's 2024 study shows income and wealth highly concentrated at the top.

COVID-19 thus accelerated existing inequalities more than it created new ones. Universal social protection for informal workers (e-Shram and the Code on Social Security), learning recovery and quality jobs can build inclusive resilience against the next shock.
free.upm-2020-gs1-10:
RegionalismCultural assertivenessSons of the soilCooperative federalism

Regionalism is a strong attachment to a region, defined by language, culture, ethnicity or economic interest, sometimes placed above national interest. Since India's regions are cultural units, regional movements usually speak the language of cultural assertiveness: pride in language, script, festivals and history. But many have been driven as much by economic deprivation, competition for jobs and political ambition. Culture is often the idiom of regionalism, not its only cause.

1. Yes: cultural assertiveness as a driver

  • Language and statehood: Potti Sriramulu's death after a fast (December 1952) led to Andhra State (1953) and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, based on the Fazl Ali Commission's report.
  • Dravidian identity: the anti-Hindi agitation of 1965 in Tamil Nadu led to the Official Languages (Amendment) Act, 1967, which allowed English to continue indefinitely; debates over the three-language formula continue.
  • Ethnic identity: the Assam movement (1979–85) against illegal migration ended in the Assam Accord (1985); demands for Gorkhaland and Bodoland rest on distinct ethnic and linguistic identities.
  • Cultural symbols: the Jallikattu protests (2017) led Tamil Nadu to amend the law, which the Supreme Court upheld in 2023.

2. No: other drivers of regionalism

  • Economic neglect: Telangana (2014) separated from Andhra Pradesh although both speak Telugu; grievances over water, jobs and funds, not culture, drove the movement.
  • Development deficit: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand (2000) were created to address tribal and hill-area backwardness; demands for Vidarbha and Bundelkhand rest on similar grievances.
  • Sons of the soil: competition for jobs fuelled the Shiv Sena's campaign against south Indian migrants in Bombay in the 1960s; Haryana's 2020 law reserving 75% of private jobs for locals was struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2023, and the State has appealed to the Supreme Court.
  • Resources and federal friction: inter-State river disputes (Cauvery, Krishna, Mahadayi) and quarrels over tax devolution and GST compensation set States against the Centre or each other.
  • Political mobilisation: regional parties use regional identity to win votes, and coalition politics gives them bargaining power.

3. Assessment

  • Mixed causation: cultural pride usually combines with economic grievance; Telangana shows that a shared culture does not prevent regionalism, and Jharkhand shows culture and deprivation working together.
  • Positive and negative: assertion of language and culture is legitimate in a diverse democracy and enriches national life; it becomes harmful when it turns against migrants or minorities.
  • Accommodation works: linguistic States, the Sixth Schedule, Article 371 and accords such as the Bodo Accord (2020) show that democratic accommodation defuses separatism.

Regionalism in India is better explained by culture plus deprivation plus politics than by cultural assertiveness alone. Balanced regional development, fair fiscal federalism and respect for linguistic diversity can keep regional identity compatible with national unity.
free.upm-2020-gs1-11:
Sacred architectureVastu and AgamasStupa symbolismIndo-Islamic synthesis

Indian monuments were conceived not merely as buildings but as philosophy in stone. Ideas about the cosmos, the divine, liberation (moksha or nirvana) and righteous kingship, set out in the Shilpa Shastras, Vastu treatises and Agamas, shaped the plan, form, decoration and use of stupas, temples, mosques, tombs and gurdwaras. Each tradition, from the Buddhist to the Sikh, left its imprint.

1. Buddhist and Jain thought

  • The stupa as a cosmic diagram: at Sanchi the dome (anda) evokes the cosmic mountain, the harmika the abode of the gods, and the triple umbrella (chhatra) is often read as the three jewels; circumambulation makes worship meditative.
  • From symbol to image: early reliefs at Bharhut and Sanchi showed the Buddha only through symbols (Bodhi tree, footprints, empty throne, wheel); Mahayana devotion produced images at Gandhara and Mathura, and the Gupta-period Sarnath Buddha embodies calm compassion.
  • Ashoka's Dhamma: pillars bearing edicts carried a moral message across the empire; the Sarnath Lion Capital, originally crowned by the wheel of law, became India's State Emblem (1950).
  • Jain renunciation: standing Tirthankaras in the kayotsarga posture and the colossal Gommateshwara at Shravanabelagola (10th century) express detachment and ahimsa.

2. The Hindu temple as a model of the cosmos

  • Vastu-purusha mandala: the temple plan is a sacred grid, a microcosm of the universe.
  • Journey to the sanctum: the passage from the mandapa to the small, dark garbhagriha (womb-house) mirrors the soul's inward path to moksha.
  • Mountain of the gods: the rising shikhara or vimana represents Mount Meru or Kailasa.
  • Cosmic time and order: Konark's Sun temple is a chariot of Surya with 24 wheels and seven horses; the Chola Nataraja shows Shiva's cosmic dance of creation and destruction.
  • The aims of life: carvings at Khajuraho and Konark depict dharma, artha, kama and moksha, the breadth of human life.

3. Islamic, Sufi and Sikh traditions

  • Aniconism: Islam's avoidance of images turned decoration to geometry, arabesque and calligraphy, as in the Qutb complex and the Taj Mahal.
  • Paradise on earth: the charbagh, a garden divided into four by water channels, recalls the Quranic gardens of paradise at Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal.
  • Synthesis: Akbar's ideal of sulh-i-kul is reflected in Fatehpur Sikri's blend of Persian and Indian elements; Sufi dargahs such as those at Ajmer and Nizamuddin welcome people of all faiths.
  • Sikh equality: the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar has four entrances, open to people of every caste and creed, and its langar embodies equality.

4. Tradition, kingship and society

  • Divine kingship: the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur (1010) proclaimed Chola power under divine sanction.
  • Sacred utility: stepwells such as Rani ki Vav at Patan, a UNESCO site, combine water conservation with devotion, their walls carved with Vishnu's avatars.

Indian monuments are thus material expressions of philosophy: of cosmos, devotion, renunciation and equality. Preserving them, along with the living traditions around them, keeps alive India's composite culture.
free.upm-2020-gs1-12:
Indo-Persian historiographyCourt chroniclesSulh-i-kulComposite culture

From the founding of the Delhi Sultanate (1206) to the decline of the Mughals, Persian was the language of the court, administration and high literature. Chronicles (tarikh), memoirs, poetry, Sufi discourses and translations form the main written sources for medieval India. They reflect the spirit of the age: ideas of kingship, the tension between orthodoxy and accommodation, and the rise of a composite Indo-Persian culture, though they also carry the biases of court authors.

1. Sultanate period: conquest, kingship and orthodoxy

  • Minhaj-us-Siraj's Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (c. 1260): a history of the early Sultans written for Nasiruddin Mahmud, reflecting the age of conquest and the Turkish nobility.
  • Ziauddin Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi and Fatawa-i-Jahandari: describe Alauddin Khalji's market control and Muhammad bin Tughlaq's projects, and argue that the ruler's state laws (zawabit) may supplement the sharia; his scorn for the low-born mirrors the court's aristocratic outlook.
  • Amir Khusrau (1253–1325): his Khazain-ul-Futuh celebrates Alauddin's conquests, and Nuh Sipihr praises India, its languages and learning; his devotion to Nizamuddin Auliya, and the Hindavi verse attributed to him, show cultural fusion.
  • Other chronicles: Isami's Futuh-us-Salatin, written at the Bahmani court, criticises Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
  • Sufi discourses: Amir Hasan Sijzi's Fawaid-ul-Fuad records the conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya, revealing the spiritual and social life of ordinary people.

2. Mughal period: imperial ideology and synthesis

  • Memoirs: the Baburnama (written in Chaghatai Turkish and translated into Persian under Akbar) and Gulbadan Begum's Humayun-nama, a rare woman's view of court and family life.
  • Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari: present kingship as divine light (farr-i-izadi) and Akbar's policy of sulh-i-kul (peace with all); the Ain records the mansab system, revenue (zabt), prices and provinces.
  • Badauni's Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh: an orthodox critique of Akbar's religious experiments, showing that the age had its debates.
  • Later works: the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri reveals Jahangir's interest in nature, painting and justice, and Lahori's Padshahnama celebrates Shah Jahan's splendour.
  • Translations: Akbar's translation bureau rendered the Mahabharata into Persian as the Razmnama; Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar, 1657) and compared Sufism and Vedanta in Majma-ul-Bahrain.

3. How they reflect the spirit of the age

  • Monarchy and court culture: history is written around the ruler, with patronage, titles and ceremony at the centre.
  • Religion and politics: the contrast between Barani's orthodoxy, Abul Fazl's universalism and Badauni's dissent mirrors real debates of the time.
  • Composite culture: Persian revenue records under Todar Mal, Indo-Persian poetry (sabk-i-hindi) and translations drew communities together.

4. Limitations

  • Court bias: flattery (Abul Fazl) or prejudice (Barani's scorn for the low-born) colours the narrative.
  • Silences: peasants, artisans, women and regions get little space, so these sources must be checked against Sanskrit and regional literature, Bhakti poetry, European travellers such as Bernier, inscriptions and archaeology.

Persian sources are thus a mirror of the age, of its ideals of kingship, its religious debates and its growing composite culture, provided they are read critically and alongside other evidence.
free.upm-2020-gs1-13:
Mass nationalismSocialist and communist ideasRevolutionary nationalismSocial base

The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) turned the Congress from a forum of the educated middle class into a mass organisation. In the 1920s and early 1930s the national movement developed several ideological strands: Gandhian mass action, Swarajist constitutionalism, socialism and communism, revolutionary nationalism, and social-justice movements of Dalits and non-Brahmins. Each brought new groups (peasants, workers, women, youth, tribals) into politics and widened its social base, though some strands also pulled in different directions.

1. Gandhian mass nationalism

  • Organisation: the Nagpur session (1920) reorganised the Congress into provincial committees on linguistic lines, with a four-anna membership fee that opened it to ordinary people.
  • Non-Cooperation and Khilafat (1920–22): brought peasants, artisans, students, women and Muslims into the struggle.
  • Constructive programme: khadi, Hindu–Muslim unity, removal of untouchability and national schools took nationalism to villages; Civil Disobedience (1930) drew women and tribal communities in large numbers.

2. Swarajists and the Left

  • Swarajists: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru's Swaraj Party (1923) contested the councils to obstruct them from within, keeping the movement alive after Chauri Chaura.
  • Workers and communists: the All India Trade Union Congress (1920, first president Lala Lajpat Rai); the Communist Party of India (founded at Tashkent in 1920, conference at Kanpur in 1925) spread Marxist ideas, publicised by the Kanpur (1924) and Meerut (1929) conspiracy cases.
  • Socialist youth: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose led youth leagues and the Independence for India League (1928); the Lahore Congress (1929) adopted Purna Swaraj, the Karachi resolution (1931) promised fundamental rights and economic reforms, and the Congress Socialist Party followed in 1934.

3. Revolutionary nationalism

  • HRA to HSRA: the Hindustan Republican Association (1924) carried out the Kakori train action (1925); reorganised as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) by Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad and others, it adopted socialism as its goal.
  • Bengal: Surya Sen's Chittagong armoury raid (1930) inspired young men and women.

4. Peasants, Dalits, non-Brahmins and others

  • Peasants: the Eka movement in Awadh (1921–22), the Moplah rebellion (1921), the Bardoli satyagraha (1928) led by Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • Caste reform: the Vaikom satyagraha (1924–25), Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (1925), and B.R. Ambedkar's Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) and Mahad satyagraha (1927).
  • Tribals and Sikhs: Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa rebellion (1922–24); the Akali movement won the Sikh Gurdwaras Act (1925).
  • Women and business: the All India Women's Conference (1927); Sarojini Naidu became Congress president (1925); Indian industrialists formed FICCI (1927).

5. Divergent strands

  • Communal and sectional pulls: the RSS was founded (1925), and Jinnah's Fourteen Points (1929) marked a widening Congress–League gap; Ambedkar and Gandhi clashed over separate electorates until the Poona Pact (1932).

The 1920s thus made nationalism a broad coalition of ideas and classes. This plurality built the mass base that won independence and shaped the Constitution's commitments to rights and social justice, though communal strands left a divisive legacy.
free.upm-2020-gs1-14:
Interlinking of riversNational Perspective PlanInter-basin transferEcological costs

India's water is unevenly spread in space and time: Himalayan rivers such as the Brahmaputra and Ganga carry huge monsoon surpluses, while much of peninsular and western India faces recurrent drought. The National Perspective Plan (1980) proposed the inter-basin transfer of surplus water to deficit basins, and the National Water Development Agency has identified 30 links (16 peninsular, 14 Himalayan). As of August 2026, only the Ken–Betwa link was under implementation.

1. The promise: a multi-purpose solution

  • Drought: the Ken–Betwa link (₹44,605 crore) is to irrigate about 11.88 lakh ha and supply drinking water to about 62 lakh people in drought-prone Bundelkhand, besides 103 MW of hydropower and 27 MW of solar power.
  • Floods: storing and diverting the monsoon peaks of the Kosi, Gandak and Ghaghra could ease floods in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
  • Navigation: link canals could extend inland waterways and connect with National Waterway-1 on the Ganga.
  • Other gains: hydropower, urban water supply, groundwater recharge and more food; the Supreme Court (2012) directed time-bound implementation through a special committee.

2. Progress so far

  • Ken–Betwa: the foundation stone was laid in December 2024; the Daudhan dam on the Ken will transfer water to the Betwa basin.
  • Parbati–Kalisindh–Chambal (modified), integrated with the Eastern Rajasthan Canal Project: Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have signed an agreement for implementation.
  • Setbacks: the Par–Tapi–Narmada and Damanganga–Pinjal links have completed DPRs but were removed from the priority list, and the inter-State Kosi–Mechi link was dropped because of its international dimension.
  • Smaller links: Gujarat's SAUNI scheme and Andhra Pradesh's Godavari–Krishna link through the Polavaram canal apply the idea at a smaller scale.

3. Critical examination: limits and costs

  • Ecology: the Ken–Betwa reservoir will submerge part of the Panna Tiger Reserve; lower flows to deltas raise salinity and threaten mangroves and fisheries.
  • Hydrology: basins classed as surplus may have little to spare in the lean season, and climate change makes monsoon flows less predictable; Himalayan flood peaks are so large that canals can divert only a small fraction.
  • Navigation: seasonal flows, siltation and gradients that need locks limit the viability of canal waterways.
  • Society and federalism: links displace tribal and rural communities; water is a State subject (Entry 17, List II), so riparian States must agree; Himalayan links involve Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh.
  • Cost and time: huge capital costs and long gestation risk stranded investment.

4. Way forward

  • Link by link: proceed only after full studies of environmental flows, costs, benefits and rehabilitation.
  • Complementary solutions: watershed development, rainwater harvesting, aquifer recharge (Atal Bhujal Yojana), micro-irrigation, crop diversification, floodplain zoning and flood forecasting.

Interlinking can be one tool, not a silver bullet: viable for selected, well-studied links, while India's droughts, floods and navigation needs call for integrated water-resources management.
free.upm-2020-gs1-15:
Urban floodingEncroached lakes and drainsSmart citiesSponge city

India's million-plus cities (53 in Census 2011) now flood almost every monsoon: Mumbai (2005), Chennai (2015), Hyderabad (2020), Bengaluru (2022) and Delhi (2023). Even tech hubs regarded as smart, such as Hyderabad and Pune (one of the first Smart Cities Mission cities), go under after a few hours of heavy rain. The NDMA treats urban flooding as a distinct disaster because its causes lie as much in planning failure as in rainfall.

1. Natural and climatic triggers

  • Intense, short spells of rain: a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture. In October 2020 a deep depression from the Bay of Bengal brought extremely heavy rain to Hyderabad (Ghatkesar recorded 324 mm), and at least 33 people died in the city.
  • Topography: Hyderabad's rocky, undulating terrain has a chain of lakes linked by streams (nalas); Pune lies at the confluence of the Mula and Mutha below the Khadakwasla dam, so heavy rain and reservoir releases can coincide.
  • Reservoir releases: in 2020 the Himayat Sagar gates were opened, sending the Musi over its banks.

2. Human and planning causes

  • Encroached lakes and nalas: in Hyderabad many lakes, their full-tank-level areas and the nalas linking them have been built over, so overflow has nowhere to go; in Pune, in late September 2019, an intense overnight downpour turned the Ambil Odha, a stream whose course had been narrowed and built over, into a deadly flash flood in the south of the city.
  • Concrete and hill-slope construction: impervious surfaces and building on hills increase and speed up runoff.
  • Inadequate, clogged drains: drains designed for low intensities (Mumbai's for about 25 mm an hour) are choked with silt and plastic.
  • Fragmented governance: municipal bodies, development authorities and irrigation departments share responsibility, and peri-urban growth outside city limits lacks drainage.
  • Narrow smartness: area-based projects and digital services got more attention than drainage.

3. Lasting remedial measures

  • Plan with hydrology: map natural drainage, notify and protect lake and stream buffers, and prepare ward-level flood-hazard maps, as the NDMA Guidelines on Management of Urban Flooding (2010) recommend; Telangana set up HYDRAA (2024) to protect lakes and public land from encroachment.
  • Blue-green infrastructure: restore lakes, wetlands and floodplains, and use permeable surfaces, rain gardens and mandatory rainwater harvesting, on the lines of China's sponge cities.
  • Better drains: design for higher rainfall intensity, separate storm water from sewage, desilt before the monsoon and manage solid waste.
  • Institutions and funds: the Urban Flood Risk Mitigation Programme gives ₹3,075.65 crore to seven large cities, including Hyderabad and Pune, and covers 11 more in a second phase; the Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 provides for Urban Disaster Management Authorities.
  • Warning and preparedness: IMD nowcasts, city flood-warning systems such as IFLOWS-Mumbai (2020), SACHET alerts, community drills and flood insurance.

Hyderabad and Pune show that a city cannot be smart if it ignores its natural drainage. Lasting resilience needs risk-sensitive planning that gives water room in the city.
free.upm-2020-gs1-16:
Solar potentialInsolationRegional variationGrid integration

India lies largely in the tropics and receives about 4–7 kWh of solar energy per square metre per day on roughly 300 sunny days; the National Institute of Solar Energy puts its potential at about 748 GWp. Installed solar capacity reached about 171 GW by 30 September 2026 (MNRE). Development is, however, highly uneven: by September 2026 Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra together had nearly 60% of it.

1. The potential

  • High insolation: strongest in the Thar Desert, Gujarat, the Deccan and the clear, cold skies of Ladakh; weaker in the cloudy, rainy North-East, Kerala and the Himalayan foothills.
  • Land: arid wastelands in Rajasthan (Bhadla) and the Rann of Kutch (the Khavda park, planned for 30 GW) can host very large parks.
  • Distributed solar: rooftops (PM Surya Ghar: over 50 lakh homes by August 2026), farm solar (about 25 lakh pumps under PM-KUSUM), canal tops and floating solar on reservoirs (Omkareshwar; PM Surya Sarovar Yojana, 2026).

2. Regional variations in development

  • North-western leaders: Rajasthan leads with about 45 GW and Gujarat is second with about 36 GW (September 2026), thanks to high insolation, cheap wasteland, early policies (Gujarat's solar policy of 2009 and its Charanka park) and transmission under the Green Energy Corridors.
  • Western and southern States: Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka (Pavagada) and Andhra Pradesh (Kurnool, Ananthapuram) combine good sunshine with industrial demand and supportive policies.
  • Laggards: Uttar Pradesh had under 6 GW in mid-2026 despite its size, and Bihar, West Bengal, Kerala and the North-East far less, because of dense population and costly land, haze or heavy cloud, weak finances of distribution companies and difficult terrain.
  • Ladakh: very high potential but remote; a transmission project to evacuate 13 GW of renewable power from Ladakh was approved in 2023.

3. Challenges behind the variation

  • Intermittency: solar works only by day; non-fossil sources gave only about 29% of electricity in 2025-26, and evening peaks still need coal or storage.
  • Transmission and land: power from desert parks must travel far, and land acquisition and grazing rights cause conflicts.
  • Wildlife: power lines in Rajasthan and Gujarat cross the habitat of the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard; in 2024 the Supreme Court balanced its protection with climate goals and recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change.
  • Supply chain: dependence on imported polysilicon and wafers, and a coming wave of panel waste.

4. Way forward

  • Storage and grids: battery and pumped storage, inter-regional transmission and better forecasting.
  • Spreading the gains: rooftop, agri-voltaic and floating solar for land-scarce eastern and northern States, with healthier DISCOMs.
  • Self-reliance: domestic manufacturing of cells and wafers, and panel recycling.

India's solar potential is vast and its progress rapid, but the regional imbalance reflects differences in sunshine, land, grids and policy. Distributed solar and storage can make the transition truly national on the way to 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.
free.upm-2020-gs1-17:
Forest coverCarbon sinkISFR 2023Mitigation and adaptation

Forests regulate climate by storing carbon, recycling water and moderating temperature. According to the India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023 forest cover is 21.76% of India's geographical area and forest and tree cover together 25.17%, still short of the 33% goal of the National Forest Policy, 1988. India's forest and tree cover holds a carbon stock of about 30.43 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent, its main natural carbon sink.

1. Status: extent

  • Distribution: Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh have the largest forest areas; the North-East has the highest share of its land under forest, while Punjab, Haryana and the north-western plains have very little.
  • Mangroves: 4,992 sq km, the largest share in the Sundarbans.
  • Trend: small net gains, mostly from plantations and trees outside forests.

2. Status: quality and pressures

  • Degradation: much of the cover is open forest (canopy density 10–40%), and several North-Eastern States have shown declines in successive reports owing to shifting cultivation, development and felling.
  • Definition debate: the Forest Survey of India counts any land over one hectare with canopy density above 10%, whatever its ownership, so plantations and orchards count as forest; critics say this masks the loss of natural forests.
  • Fires, invasives and diversion: recurring fires (as in Uttarakhand), invasive Lantana and diversion for mining and infrastructure; after the 2023 amendment of the forest law (now the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam), the Supreme Court (2024) kept the broad Godavarman (1996) definition of forest in force.

3. Impact on climate change: mitigation

  • Carbon sink: India has added about 2.29 billion tonnes of carbon sink since 2005, against its NDC target of an additional 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent by 2030: on track, but not there yet.
  • Blue carbon: mangroves store much carbon in their soils; MISHTI (2023) promotes coastal mangrove planting.
  • Emission risk: fires, degradation and conversion release stored carbon and weaken the sink.

4. Impact on adaptation, and the reverse effect

  • Natural buffers: the mangroves of the Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika reduce cyclone and storm-surge damage; Himalayan and Western Ghats forests regulate river flows and reduce floods and landslides.
  • Climate stress on forests: heat waves and droughts increase fires and tree deaths, species shift uphill in the Himalaya and pests spread, so forests are both a solution and a victim.

5. Way forward

  • Quality, not just cover: restore natural forests with native species under the Green India Mission (revised 2025 roadmap for the Aravallis, Western Ghats, Himalaya and mangroves) and CAMPA funds.
  • People's participation: community forest rights under the Forest Rights Act (2006), joint forest management, agroforestry and campaigns such as Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam (2024).

India's forests are stable in area but stressed in quality. Strengthening them is India's most cost-effective nature-based solution for both mitigation and adaptation, essential to its NDC and its net-zero 2070 goal.
free.upm-2020-gs1-18:
GlobalisationCultural homogenisationGlocalisationPluralism

Diversity is the co-existence of many languages, religions, castes, tribes and regional cultures; pluralism is the acceptance of these differences as legitimate and equal. Globalisation, accelerated in India by the 1991 reforms and the digital revolution, moves goods, capital, people, media and ideas across borders. It does homogenise some ways of life, but it also revives, hybridises and globalises Indian cultures. The threat is real but partial, and the bigger danger to pluralism lies elsewhere.

1. Yes: how globalisation threatens diversity

  • Uniform lifestyles: global brands, fast food, fashion and malls create a standard urban consumer culture, which sociologist George Ritzer called McDonaldisation.
  • Languages: English dominates higher education and jobs; UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger (2009) listed 197 Indian languages as vulnerable, endangered or already extinct, more than for any other country.
  • Crafts and local knowledge: cheap mass-produced goods displace handloom and handicraft livelihoods; tribal communities displaced by mining and projects lose their languages and traditional knowledge.
  • Identity backlash: rapid change breeds insecurity that fuels fundamentalism, moral policing and nativist politics, while social media spreads misinformation and polarisation.

2. No: how globalisation sustains diversity

  • Glocalisation: global firms adapt to Indian tastes (vegetarian menus, regional-language advertising), and Indian-language content drives internet growth.
  • A global stage for Indian culture: the UN's International Day of Yoga (since 2015), the International Year of Millets (2023) and the Oscar for the song "Naatu Naatu" (2023) carried Indian traditions worldwide.
  • New markets for crafts: Geographical Indication tags, e-commerce, ONDC and GeM connect artisans with buyers.
  • Technology for languages: Bhashini (2022) uses AI to translate across Indian languages.
  • Rights consciousness: global human-rights norms have strengthened the claims of women, minorities, Dalits and LGBTQ persons, as in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), widening pluralism.
  • Diaspora: Indians abroad carry festivals, cuisine and languages overseas and bring back new ideas.

3. Assessment

  • Hybridisation, not erasure: most Indians combine the global and the local, wearing jeans and celebrating local festivals, so culture adapts rather than disappears.
  • Unequal risk: large traditions thrive, but small tribal languages and crafts are genuinely vulnerable.
  • The real threat: polarisation and intolerance, which globalised media can amplify, threaten pluralism more than global consumer culture does; constitutional safeguards (Articles 29–30, the Eighth and Sixth Schedules) remain the anchor.

Globalisation thus both threatens and enriches India's diversity. With support for vulnerable languages and crafts and a firm commitment to constitutional pluralism, India can globalise without losing its many cultures.
free.upm-2020-gs1-19:
ObscurantismScientific temperSocial reformConstitutional morality

Customs and traditions are inherited ways of behaving that give a community identity, continuity and cohesion. Obscurantism is opposition to reason, inquiry and the spread of knowledge. When customs are treated as beyond question they can indeed suppress reason, but tradition also carries accumulated wisdom and its own reformist voices. The Constitution balances the two: Article 51A(h) makes it a duty to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform, while Article 25 protects faith.

1. Yes: when custom suppresses reason

  • Harmful practices: sati (abolished in 1829 after Raja Ram Mohan Roy's campaign), child marriage (23.3% of women aged 20–24 were married before 18, NFHS-5) and dowry deaths persisted because custom outweighed reason.
  • Superstition and exploitation: witch-hunting, mostly of poor or widowed women, still occurs in parts of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. The murder of the rationalist Narendra Dabholkar (2013) was followed by Maharashtra's anti-black-magic law (2013), and Karnataka passed a similar Act in 2017.
  • Caste and untouchability: the idea of purity and pollution sanctified inequality for centuries; manual scavenging continues despite the 2013 Act.
  • Gender restrictions: menstrual taboos, purdah and limits on women's mobility and inheritance; the Sabarimala case (2018) and the triple talaq case (Shayara Bano, 2017) saw courts test custom against constitutional rights.
  • Health: quackery and resistance to vaccination in some communities, as during the polio campaign.

2. No: tradition is not inherently opposed to reason

  • A rational heritage: Nyaya logic, Charvaka materialism, the Buddha's advice to test teachings by experience, Upanishadic inquiry and the science of Aryabhata, Charaka and Sushruta are themselves Indian traditions.
  • Reform from within: Bhakti saints such as Kabir and Basavanna attacked ritualism and caste; Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (the Widow Remarriage Act, 1856), Jyotirao Phule, Sree Narayana Guru and B.R. Ambedkar used reason, and often scripture, to reform custom.
  • Ecological wisdom: sacred groves, the Bishnois' protection of trees and blackbuck (the Khejarli sacrifice of 1730), stepwells and millet-based diets are sustainable practices rooted in tradition.
  • Social cohesion: festivals, community kitchens and family care for the elderly give support that modern institutions struggle to replace.
  • Modern obscurantism: fake news and pseudoscience spread through social media show that unreason is not confined to tradition.

3. Way forward

  • Education for scientific temper: NEP 2020's emphasis on critical thinking, and science communication in local languages.
  • Law and constitutional morality: laws against harmful practices, with courts applying constitutional rather than popular morality (Navtej Singh Johar, 2018).
  • Reform with communities: change led by community leaders, women's groups and local role models lasts longer than imposed change.

I agree only in part: customs become obscurantist when they are placed beyond question, not by their nature. India's task is to keep the wisdom of tradition while testing every custom against reason, dignity and equality, in the spirit of Article 51A(h).
free.upm-2020-gs1-20:
Digital educationDIKSHA and SWAYAMDigital divideNEP 2020

Digital technology now runs through India's education system, from content and teacher training to assessment and governance. COVID-19 school closures (2020–21) accelerated the shift, and the National Education Policy 2020 calls for technology in teaching, learning, assessment and administration, with a National Educational Technology Forum. Platforms such as DIKSHA, SWAYAM and PM eVIDYA reach learners from school to university, though access remains uneven: UDISE+ 2025-26 found internet in 67.4% of schools.

1. Access to learning content

  • DIKSHA (2017): the national platform for school education; QR codes printed in textbooks link to lessons and practice material in many Indian languages.
  • PM eVIDYA (May 2020): unified digital, TV and radio learning: DIKSHA as one nation, one digital platform; one TV channel per class, expanded from 12 to 200 channels in the 2022-23 Budget; radio and podcasts; and content for children with special needs, including sign language.
  • Higher education: SWAYAM offers free online courses from Class 9 to postgraduate level, and UGC rules allow up to 40% of a programme's credits through SWAYAM; SWAYAM Prabha DTH channels, the National Digital Library of India and Virtual Labs widen access.
  • Continuity in crisis: during school closures these platforms, along with lessons shared by States over WhatsApp and television, kept learning going.

2. Teachers and pedagogy

  • Training at scale: NISHTHA (2019) modules run online on DIKSHA, so lakhs of teachers can be trained at the same time.
  • Classroom technology: ICT labs and smart classrooms under Samagra Shiksha; the PRAGYATA guidelines (2020) set screen-time norms for online learning.
  • Indian languages and AI: translation tools such as Bhashini help create content in many languages.

3. Governance, assessment and records

  • Data-driven planning: UDISE+ collects school-level data, the Performance Grading Index ranks States, and Vidya Samiksha Kendras monitor attendance and learning in real time.
  • Portable records: the Academic Bank of Credits (2021), the APAAR ID (2023) and DigiLocker store credits and certificates, supporting multiple entry and exit.
  • Transparency: online admissions, the National Scholarship Portal and online teacher transfers reduce delays and discretion.

4. Limits: the digital divide

  • Infrastructure gaps: about a third of schools still lack internet and computers, though 95% have electricity (UDISE+ 2025-26).
  • Unequal access at home: only 33% of women against 57% of men had ever used the internet (NFHS-5); poor, rural and disabled children share devices or have none, and ASER 2022 recorded a fall in basic reading levels compared with 2018.
  • Quality: screen content cannot replace teachers; online courses have low completion rates, and many teachers lack digital skills.
  • Safety and privacy: cyberbullying, screen addiction and children's data; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) requires verifiable parental consent to process children's data.

Digital initiatives have made Indian education more accessible, flexible and data-driven, but technology complements rather than replaces teachers. Closing the digital divide through connectivity, devices, teacher training and safeguards will decide whether it narrows or widens educational inequality.
free.upm-2020-gs2-1:
Corrupt practicesSection 8AElection petitionPurity of elections

Under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA), corrupt practices (Section 123) such as bribery, undue influence and appeals on religion or caste can void an election. Yet unlike a conviction, which disqualifies automatically (Section 8), a finding of corrupt practice leads to disqualification only through a separate, multi-stage route under Section 8A, which the Election Commission of India (ECI) has long found slow and circuitous.

1. The present procedure

  • Finding by the court: an election petition is filed in the High Court within 45 days of the result (Section 81); the court names those guilty of corrupt practices (Section 99), and an appeal lies to the Supreme Court (Section 116A).
  • Reference to the President: the case must then be submitted to the President, within three months of the order taking effect, by an authority the Central Government specifies (Section 8A(1); the three-month limit was added by the 2009 amendment).
  • ECI's opinion binds: the President obtains the ECI's opinion and acts according to it (Section 8A(3)); the period of disqualification is decided case by case, up to six years from the date of the court's order.
  • Voting bar: the person is also barred from voting for the same period (Section 11A(2)); the petition for removal in Section 8A(2) now covers only disqualifications imposed before 1975.

2. Why simplification is needed

  • Delay defeats deterrence: petitions meant to be decided within six months (Section 86(7)) often outlast the House's term, so the guilty member serves most of it.
  • The Bal Thackeray case: the corrupt practices were committed in the 1987 Vile Parle by-election and upheld by the Supreme Court in December 1995, but the notification barring him from voting came only in July 1999, although the six-year period ran from December 1995.
  • An old complaint: the Law Commission's 244th Report (2014) records the ECI's 1998 concern over inordinate delays in these cases.
  • Unequal treatment: conviction disqualifies at once (Section 8; Lily Thomas, 2013 ended the shield for sitting members), and the ECI itself disqualifies for three years for not lodging expense accounts (Section 10A); a corrupt practice, which strikes at the purity of elections, takes the slowest route.

3. Arguments for caution

  • Natural justice and graded penalties: disqualification is a grave consequence and corrupt practices differ in gravity, so a hearing and the ECI's neutral opinion have value.
  • The real bottleneck is the slow trial of election petitions, not only the reference to the President.

4. Way forward

  • One decision: let the court fix the period while naming the guilty, after hearing the ECI, removing the separate reference.
  • Time-bound trials: dedicated election benches that keep to the six-month limit.
  • Clear norms: a minimum period for grave practices such as appeals to religion or caste (Abhiram Singh, 2017), and a deadline for the ECI's opinion.

The demand is justified: a penalty that arrives after the House's term has ended loses its force. One time-bound judicial process, with a fair hearing, would protect the purity of elections.
free.upm-2020-gs2-2:
RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019Information CommissionsSecurity of tenureInstitutional autonomy

The Right to Information Act, 2005 made the Central and State Information Commissions the final appellate authorities and gave them the security of constitutional bodies: a fixed five-year term (or up to age 65) and pay equal to that of the Election Commissioners. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 amended Sections 13 and 16 so that the Central Government now prescribes the term, salaries and service conditions of all Information Commissioners, Central and State, raising concern about their autonomy.

1. What the amendments changed

  • Tenure: the fixed five-year term was replaced by a term prescribed by the Centre; the RTI Rules, 2019 set it at three years.
  • Pay and status: salaries are no longer linked to the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners (or, for State commissioners, to the Election Commissioners and the Chief Secretary) but fixed by central rules.
  • State commissions: the Centre now prescribes the service conditions of commissioners appointed by State governments.
  • Personal information: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Section 44(3), in force since November 2025 with the DPDP Rules) replaced Section 8(1)(j) with a blanket exemption for personal information, dropping the clause's own public-interest override.

2. The Government's case

  • Different nature: the Election Commission is a constitutional body (Article 324), while Information Commissions are statutory, so equal status was called an anomaly.
  • Rule-making gap: the original Act gave no power to frame rules on service conditions; the amendment was presented as streamlining.
  • Core intact: the right to information, time limits, appeals, penalties on officials, selection by a committee headed by the Prime Minister and removal only after a Supreme Court inquiry all remain.

3. Impact on autonomy and independence

  • Executive control: a body that decides appeals against ministries now depends on the executive's rules for its term and pay, and these can be changed without Parliament.
  • Lower stature: parity with Election Commissioners signalled that commissioners could direct the most senior officials; ending it weakens their authority.
  • Federal concern: the Centre fixes conditions for State commissions selected by State committees.
  • Wider secrecy: a blanket personal-information exemption may be used to refuse information on officials' conduct, assets or appointments.
  • Existing weaknesses magnified: vacancies and long backlogs already slow appeals; in Anjali Bhardwaj (2019) the Supreme Court ordered timely and transparent appointments, yet the Central Information Commission returned to full strength only in December 2025.

4. Way forward

  • Statutory security: restore a fixed term and status in the Act itself, beyond the reach of rules.
  • Cooperative federalism: leave State commissions' conditions to State laws or decide them with States.
  • Functioning commissions: fill vacancies on time, publish selection criteria, and enforce proactive disclosure under Section 4.

The amendments do not take away the commissions' powers, but placing their tenure and pay in executive hands weakens the independence on which RTI depends. Restoring statutory security, and a public-interest test for personal information, would keep RTI the master key to good governance, as the Second ARC (2006) called it.
free.upm-2020-gs2-3:
Cooperative federalismCompetitive federalismConfrontationUnion of States

India is a "Union of States" (Article 1) with a strong Centre, which K.C. Wheare described as quasi-federal; yet federalism is part of the basic structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994). In practice the federation has been shaped by three forces: cooperation through shared institutions, competition among States for investment and performance, and confrontation over powers and resources. Their balance has shifted with coalition politics, GST and recent disputes.

1. Cooperation: the dominant structure

  • GST Council (Article 279A): the Union and States pooled their indirect-tax powers in 2017 and decide rates together; "GST 2.0" moved to two main slabs from September 2025.
  • Pandemic response: the Centre and the States ran the COVID-19 vaccination drive together through the CoWIN platform.
  • NITI Aayog (2015): its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers, and the Aspirational Districts (2018) and Blocks (2023) programmes are run jointly with States.
  • Fiscal transfers: the 16th Finance Commission kept the States' share at 41% for 2026–31, and 50-year interest-free loans support State capital spending.

2. Competition: a growing force

  • Rankings: the Business Reforms Action Plan rankings (DPIIT, since 2015) and NITI Aayog's SDG India Index push States to reform; States compete for investment through summits and industrial policies.
  • Rewards for performance: the 15th Finance Commission linked urban grants to property-tax reform, and the 16th added a contribution-to-GDP criterion (10% weight) to the devolution formula.
  • States as laboratories: Kerala's decentralisation and Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats (2019) are studied and copied by others.

3. Confrontation: rising in recent years

  • Governors: delays in assent led to State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (April 2025); the Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025) held that courts cannot fix timelines or deem assent.
