  • Central agencies: several States withdrew general consent to the CBI, and the BSF's jurisdiction was extended to 50 km from the border in Punjab, West Bengal and Assam (2021).
  • Legislation without consensus: the farm laws (2020) drew Assembly resolutions before their repeal in 2021; the GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023 restored the Lieutenant Governor's control over Delhi's services after a Constitution Bench ruling.
  • Fiscal disputes: Kerala's suit over borrowing limits was referred to a Constitution Bench (2024), and States object to cesses and surcharges that are not shared.

4. How far each has shaped the federation

  • Cooperation is structural: most Centre–State business runs through shared bodies, and even disputes are usually settled within them or in court.
  • Competition helps when fair: it spreads good practice, but States with weak capacity can fall further behind without equalising transfers.
  • Confrontation reflects political divergence: when different parties rule the Centre and the States, Governors and central agencies become flashpoints, and courts become the main arbiters.

Indian federalism is cooperative in design, competitive in development and, at times, confrontational in politics. Regular meetings of the Inter-State Council (Article 263), fair fiscal sharing and constitutional morality in using central powers can keep the balance tilted towards cooperative and competitive federalism.
free.upm-2020-gs2-4:
Common lawJudicial reviewParliamentary sovereigntyJudicial independence

India inherited the common law tradition from Britain: binding precedent, adversarial trials and an independent judiciary. But India has a written Constitution with judicial review and a basic structure doctrine, while the UK rests on parliamentary sovereignty. Reforms in both countries over the last two decades have brought their judicial practices closer in some respects and kept them far apart in others.

1. Points of convergence

  • A separate apex court: the UK's Constitutional Reform Act, 2005 moved the highest court out of the House of Lords into a separate Supreme Court (2009) and ended the Lord Chancellor's role as head of the judiciary, closer to India's separate Supreme Court (Article 124) and the separation of the judiciary from the executive (Article 50).
  • Review of executive power: the UK Supreme Court held that giving notice to leave the EU needed an Act of Parliament (Miller, 2017) and that the 2019 prorogation of Parliament was unlawful (Miller/Cherry, 2019), much as Indian courts review executive action.
  • Rights-based review: the Human Rights Act, 1998 lets UK courts test laws against the European Convention on Human Rights, a role similar to review under Part III in India.
  • Constitutional references: the UK Supreme Court answers devolution references, as on a Scottish independence referendum (2022), comparable to India's advisory jurisdiction (Article 143).
  • Openness and technology: both stream hearings live (India's Supreme Court for Constitution Bench cases since 2022) and expanded virtual hearings during COVID-19.

2. Points of divergence

  • Power over legislation: Indian courts can strike down laws and even constitutional amendments (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; NJAC case, 2015); UK courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament and can only make a declaration of incompatibility, leaving Parliament the final word.
  • Appointments: the UK uses an independent Judicial Appointments Commission (2006) with lay members; India's collegium remains judge-led after the NJAC was struck down.
  • Access to courts: India's public interest litigation, letter petitions and suo motu cases (S.P. Gupta, 1981) have no parallel in the UK's ordinary standing rules.
  • Contempt: the offence of scandalising the judiciary was abolished in England and Wales in 2013; India retains criminal contempt, used against Prashant Bhushan (2020).
  • Juries: the UK keeps juries for serious criminal trials; India phased them out after independence.

3. Why the paths differ

  • Written vs unwritten constitution: India's courts guard a supreme Constitution; UK courts serve a sovereign Parliament.
  • Social role: Indian courts expanded Article 21 and PIL to reach the poor where the State failed; the UK's welfare and tribunal systems handle many such claims.
  • Institutional history: the UK reformed by statute (2005), while India's reforms, such as the collegium, came largely through judgments.

The two systems converge in judicial independence, openness and closer review of the executive, but diverge on the courts' power over Parliament. India can learn from the UK's transparent appointments and restraint in contempt, while the UK's debates show the value of codified rights that India's courts already enforce.
free.upm-2020-gs2-5:
Speaker's neutralityWestminster conventionTenth ScheduleParliamentary business

In the UK, the Speaker of the House of Commons gives up party membership on election; at the next general election the main parties do not field candidates against the Speaker, who stands as the Speaker seeking re-election and is usually returned to the Chair. This is the idea of 'Once a Speaker, Always a Speaker'. In India the Speaker (Article 93) usually remains a party member, and the office's neutrality has been questioned, especially in deciding defection cases under the Tenth Schedule.

1. Why the practice is attractive for India

  • Trust in rulings: a Speaker without party ties would be trusted on defection petitions (Paragraph 6), Money Bill certification (Article 110(3)) and suspensions; the Aadhaar Bill certification (2016) and the suspension of 146 MPs of both Houses (December 2023) were criticised as partisan.
  • Delays in defection cases: in Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) the Supreme Court said petitions should normally be decided within three months and asked Parliament to consider an independent tribunal.
  • Continuity and expertise: a long-serving Speaker builds procedural mastery and institutional memory, as in Westminster.
  • Indian roots: N. Sanjiva Reddy resigned from his party on becoming Speaker in 1967, and Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule already lets a Speaker give up party membership without disqualification.

2. Why it is difficult to transplant

  • No reciprocal convention: in India's competitive politics parties rarely leave a seat uncontested, and the Speaker's own election in June 2024 was contested before being decided by voice vote.
  • Voters' choice: the Speaker's constituents lose a partisan representative and their choice at the polls.
  • Electoral risk: without the convention, a neutral Speaker could lose the seat, so neutrality is penalised.
  • Majority still chooses: the Speaker would still be elected by the ruling majority; on 11 March 2026 a resolution for the Speaker's removal under Article 94(c) was defeated by voice vote, a sign of strain on the consensus around the office.

3. Implications for parliamentary business

  • Positive: fewer allegations of bias would mean fewer protests in the House, more time for debate and greater respect for rulings on adjournments, suspensions and admission of notices.
  • Better scrutiny: a neutral Chair could refer more Bills to committees; only 16% of Bills were referred in the 17th Lok Sabha (PRS).
  • Opposition's place: neutrality would pair well with electing a Deputy Speaker promptly, a post left vacant throughout the 17th Lok Sabha (2019–24).
  • Risks: an entrenched Speaker could become unaccountable, and the government might find business harder to manage.
  • Limits: disruption has deeper causes, such as the lack of opposition days and political bargaining, which neutrality alone cannot cure.

The practice would impart objectivity to the Chair, but conventions grow from trust, not law alone. Combined with an independent tribunal for defection cases, an all-party agreement on the Speaker's seat would strengthen the robust functioning of Parliament.
free.upm-2020-gs2-6:
Social developmentMaternal healthGeriatric careLife-cycle approach

Social development depends on good health at both ends of the life cycle: maternal health shapes the next generation, while geriatric care decides whether longer lives are lived in dignity. India's maternal mortality ratio (MMR) has fallen to 87 per lakh live births (SRS, 2022–24), but the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 10.5% (2022) to 20.8% by 2050 (India Ageing Report 2023), so both fields need sound and adequately funded policies.

1. Why these fields matter for social development

  • Intergenerational gains: a healthy, well-nourished mother has healthier babies; infant mortality has fallen to 24 per 1,000 (SRS 2024) as institutional care improved.
  • Women's empowerment: safe motherhood, birth spacing and nutrition keep women in education and work.
  • From demographic to longevity dividend: healthy older people work, care for grandchildren and share experience instead of depending on others.
  • Protection from poverty: out-of-pocket spending was 43.4% of total health expenditure in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts), and chronic illness or a complicated delivery can push families into debt.

2. Maternal health care: progress and gaps

  • Progress: institutional deliveries reached about 89% of births (NFHS-5) with Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005), free care under JSSK (2011), monthly antenatal check-ups under PMSMA (2016), maternity benefit under PMMVY (2017) and quality standards for labour rooms under LaQshya (2017).
  • Gaps: about 57% of women aged 15–49 are anaemic (NFHS-5); MMR remains well above the SDG target of below 70 in several States, while Kerala and Andhra Pradesh are at 30 (2021–23); specialists are short in community health centres, and post-delivery care is weak.

3. Geriatric health care: needs and policies

  • Needs: non-communicable diseases, several illnesses at once, dementia, falls and disability; about 90% of workers are informal and lack pensions.
  • Policies: since October 2024 PM-JAY covers everyone aged 70 and above regardless of income (Ayushman Vay Vandana card); the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (2010) supports geriatric wards and clinics; the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 and the Elder Line (14567) protect rights.
  • Gaps: few geriatricians, scarce palliative and long-term care, and a care burden that falls mainly on women in families.

4. Way forward

  • More public spending: government health expenditure was only 1.43% of GDP in 2022-23 (NHA), against the National Health Policy 2017 goal of 2.5%.
  • Strong primary care: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs for antenatal check-ups and screening of older adults, with home visits by ASHAs.
  • Health workforce: trained midwives, gynaecologists and anaesthetists in rural hospitals, and geriatric and palliative-care training.
  • Financing old age: wider pensions, long-term care insurance and support for family caregivers.
  • Data: maternal death reviews and the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) to target policy.

Mothers and older people are the two ends of one life cycle. Investing in safe motherhood and healthy ageing, within universal health coverage, will turn India's demographic change into lasting social development.
free.upm-2020-gs2-7:
Institutional qualityCivil service reformAccountabilityDemocratic governance

Institutions are the formal and informal rules that shape how people and governments behave; where they are impartial and capable, contracts are enforced and public money well spent. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson for their studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity. The civil service, the permanent executive that turns laws into services, is the institution through which most citizens meet the State, so its reform strengthens both economic performance and democracy.

1. How institutional quality drives economic performance

  • Rule of law: predictable rules and impartial enforcement lower risk and attract investment.
  • Low corruption, efficient delivery: Direct Benefit Transfer and the Government e-Marketplace reduced leakages and made purchases visible.
  • State capacity: collecting taxes, building infrastructure and regulating markets need competent officials.
  • Trust: citizens pay taxes and follow rules when institutions are fair, lowering the cost of governing.

2. Weaknesses of India's civil service

  • Political interference: frequent transfers and short tenures; in T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) the Supreme Court called for fixed minimum tenure, Civil Services Boards and written instructions from political executives.
  • Generalists in specialist roles: complex sectors need domain expertise.
  • Weak performance management: appraisals are subjective, and good and poor performers are treated alike.
  • Rule-bound culture: fear of audit and vigilance makes officers risk-averse, and procedures matter more than outcomes.
  • Weak accountability to citizens: grievance redress and citizens' charters often exist only on paper.

3. Reforms for strengthening democracy

  • Neutrality and tenure: implement the T.S.R. Subramanian directions through statutory Civil Services Boards, so that officers can give frank advice and serve all governments impartially.
  • Skills and specialisation: assign officers to domains in mid-career (Hota Committee, 2004; Second ARC, 10th Report, 2008); continue lateral entry at senior levels, begun in 2018, through a transparent process that respects reservation rules, since an August 2024 advertisement was withdrawn over reservation concerns.
  • Capacity: Mission Karmayogi (2020) shifts training from rules to roles and competencies with continuous online learning.
  • Performance and integrity: outcome-based and 360-degree appraisals, premature retirement of proven non-performers with due process, and effective Lokpal and Lokayuktas.
  • Citizen-centric accountability: enforceable citizens' charters, social audits, proactive disclosure under the RTI Act and time-bound grievance redress through CPGRAMS.

4. Why this strengthens democracy

A neutral, competent and accountable civil service ensures that elected governments' policies are implemented fairly, that citizens are treated equally regardless of identity or influence, and that power is exercised according to law. This builds legitimacy, the foundation of democratic stability.

Strong institutions are a public good: reforming the civil service towards professionalism, neutrality and citizen-centric accountability will raise both economic performance and the quality of democracy.
free.upm-2020-gs2-8:
Fourth Industrial Revolutione-GovernanceDigital public infrastructureData governance

The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR), a term popularised by Klaus Schwab of the World Economic Forum in 2016, fuses digital, physical and biological technologies: artificial intelligence, the internet of things, big data, cloud computing, blockchain and drones. As citizens live and transact online, governments too have moved from files to platforms, and e-governance has become the normal way the State works rather than an add-on. India's Digital India (2015) programme and its digital public infrastructure (DPI) of Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker show this shift.

1. How the digital revolution made e-governance integral

  • Scale of connectivity: India has 111.4 crore internet subscribers (TRAI, June 2026), so services can reach citizens directly on their phones.
  • Payments and welfare: UPI has handled over 20 billion transactions a month since August 2025, and Direct Benefit Transfer sends benefits straight to bank accounts.
  • Paperless government: DigiLocker, e-Office, e-Courts and faceless income-tax assessment (2020) cut visits, discretion and delay.
  • Transparent purchasing: the Government e-Marketplace (GeM, 2016) makes public procurement visible and competitive.
  • Data-driven planning: the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (2021) uses geospatial data to coordinate infrastructure across ministries.

2. 4IR technologies in governance

  • Artificial intelligence: the IndiaAI Mission (2024, ₹10,371.92 crore) builds compute and datasets as public goods; Bhashini (2022) offers services in Indian languages.
  • Drones and geospatial tools: SVAMITVA (2020) maps rural homes and issues property cards; drones assess crops and disasters.
  • Telemedicine: eSanjeevani brings doctors to remote areas.

3. Challenges

  • Digital divide: gaps in connectivity, devices and skills between rural and urban areas, men and women, and young and old.
  • Exclusion by design: biometric and network failures have denied entitlements, as with ration denials in Jharkhand (2017) linked to Aadhaar seeding.
  • Privacy and surveillance: after Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right, the DPDP Act, 2023 and its Rules (2025) are being phased in, though critics worry about broad exemptions for the State.
  • Cyber security: the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi's servers (November 2022) exposed vulnerabilities.
  • Accountability of algorithms: automated decisions are rarely explained, and data quality and bias can harm the vulnerable.
  • Old processes in new form: the Second ARC (11th Report, 2008) warned that e-governance means re-engineering processes, not just computerising them.

4. Way forward

  • Inclusion: assisted access through Common Service Centres, offline fallbacks and services in Indian languages.
  • Trust: privacy by design, security audits with CERT-In and human review of automated decisions.
  • Capacity: digital skills for officials through Mission Karmayogi and in-house technology teams.

The 4IR has made e-governance inseparable from government itself. Technology is the means; citizen-centric, inclusive and accountable governance, the Second ARC's SMART ideal, must remain the end.
free.upm-2020-gs2-9:
Global health securityInternational Health RegulationsPHEICPandemic Agreement

The World Health Organization (WHO), the UN's specialised health agency (1948), is the custodian of the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), which oblige States to report outbreaks and allow the Director-General to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC). COVID-19 was the hardest test of this system: WHO declared a PHEIC on 30 January 2020 and called the outbreak a pandemic on 11 March 2020. WHO estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020–21 alone.

1. What WHO did well

  • Alert and guidance: it shared information on the new virus and issued technical guidance on testing, clinical care and infection control to all countries.
  • Research: the Solidarity Trial (2020) tested repurposed drugs across many countries and showed that some, such as hydroxychloroquine, did not reduce deaths.
  • Equity: the ACT-Accelerator and COVAX (April 2020), with Gavi and CEPI, sought vaccines, tests and treatments for poorer countries; an mRNA technology-transfer hub was set up in South Africa (2021).
  • Support to weak health systems: supplies, training and efforts to counter the flood of misinformation.

2. Where it fell short

  • Speed and deference: WHO was criticised for delaying the PHEIC and for praising China's transparency early on; the Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response (May 2021) found that the alert system was too slow and that February 2020 was lost.
  • Weak powers: the IHR cannot compel States to report or allow independent investigation, as the inconclusive inquiry into the virus's origins showed.
  • Mixed messages: guidance on masks and airborne transmission changed slowly.
  • Vaccine inequity: COVAX missed its target of two billion doses in 2021 as rich countries pre-booked supplies; India and South Africa had to seek a TRIPS waiver at the WTO (2020).
  • Funding and politics: dependence on voluntary, earmarked funds; the US announced withdrawal in 2020, reversed it in 2021, and left again, with effect from January 2026.

3. Reforms since the pandemic (as of 2026)

  • IHR amendments (adopted June 2024, in force since 19 September 2025): add a new pandemic-emergency alert level and stronger provisions on equity and coordination.
  • Pandemic Agreement (20 May 2025): covers prevention, One Health, technology transfer and sharing of products in a pandemic; it can open for signature only after the annex on pathogen access and benefit-sharing (PABS) is adopted; in May 2026 the World Health Assembly let negotiations continue, with the annex now expected by the May 2027 Assembly.
  • Financing: the Pandemic Fund hosted by the World Bank (2022) supports preparedness in poorer countries.

4. India's perspective

India chaired WHO's Executive Board (2020–21), supplied vaccines abroad under Vaccine Maitri, but disputed WHO's excess-death estimate for India (2022) on methodology.

WHO was indispensable but under-powered and under-funded. Global health security needs a stronger, adequately and flexibly funded WHO, binding but fair rules, and equity built into the response from the first day.
free.upm-2020-gs2-10:
Indian diasporaSoft powerPolitical representationKnowledge economy

India has the world's largest diaspora, about 1.8 crore Indian-born emigrants (UN, 2020). In the USA, the UK and the rest of Europe it is highly educated, prosperous and increasingly visible in public life: people of Indian origin have reached the US vice-presidency, 10 Downing Street and the presidency of the European Council, and lead some of the world's largest firms. The question is whether this role is decisive or merely influential.

1. Role in the economies of America and Europe

  • Technology and corporate leadership: Sundar Pichai (Alphabet) and Satya Nadella (Microsoft) head global firms, and Indian professionals receive the large majority of US H-1B visas for skilled workers.
  • Entrepreneurship and capital: Indian-origin founders and investors are prominent in Silicon Valley start-ups; in Europe, Lakshmi Mittal built ArcelorMittal into a global steel giant.
  • Health care and academia: Indian-origin doctors serve in large numbers in the US and in Britain's National Health Service, and many teach and research in Western universities.
  • Knowledge bridges: diaspora executives helped build India's IT services industry and the Global Capability Centres that serve Western firms, linking the two economies.

2. Role in politics

  • USA: Kamala Harris was Vice-President (2021–25); Nikki Haley served as Governor of South Carolina and as US ambassador to the UN, and Kash Patel became FBI Director in 2025; several Indian-Americans sit in Congress.
  • UK: Rishi Sunak was Prime Minister (2022–24), and Priti Patel and Suella Braverman held the post of Home Secretary.
  • Rest of Europe: Leo Varadkar was Ireland's Taoiseach (2017–20 and 2022–24), and António Costa was Portugal's Prime Minister and has been President of the European Council since December 2024.
  • Advocacy: Indian-American groups lobbied the US Congress for the India–US civil nuclear deal (2005–08), and legislators of Indian origin shape debates on trade, immigration and India.

3. Influential, but not decisive

  • Small numbers: Indian-origin people are a small minority of voters in every Western country and are spread across parties.
  • Host loyalty first: leaders of Indian origin serve their own nations and do not shape policy towards India; a steep US fee on new H-1B visa petitions (2025) shows the limits of diaspora influence.
  • Diversity and division: the diaspora is split by region, religion and politics; separatist activity among a small section in Canada led to a diplomatic crisis in 2023, and communal clashes in Leicester (2022) showed how tensions can travel.
  • Backlash: high visibility can provoke anti-immigrant sentiment.

The Indian diaspora is a significant and growing force, influential rather than decisive. India gains most when it engages the diaspora as a bridge, through OCI facilities, Pravasi Bharatiya Divas and research links, while respecting its loyalty to host nations and avoiding the export of domestic divisions.
free.upm-2020-gs2-11:
Quasi-federalUnity and integrityConcurrent ListCooperative federalism

The Constitution creates a federation with a strong Centre, which K.C. Wheare called quasi-federal. Partition, the integration of princely States and security threats led the framers to give the Union overriding powers to protect unity and integrity; Dr B.R. Ambedkar said it could work as unitary or federal as circumstances required. Three laws, the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the Farm Acts, 2020, show this centralising tendency at work.

1. Constitutional basis of centralisation

  • Structure and legislation: a "Union of States" (Article 1) whose boundaries Parliament can alter (Article 3); residuary powers with the Union (Article 248), Union law prevailing in Concurrent List conflicts (Article 254) and power to legislate on State subjects (Articles 249, 250).
  • Executive and emergencies: binding Union directions (Articles 256–257), Governors appointed by the President, emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) and the All-India Services (Article 312).

2. The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897

  • Origin: a colonial law passed to fight bubonic plague in Bombay, it lets States take special measures and the Centre inspect and detain ships and travellers at ports.
  • 2020 amendment: made violence against health-care workers a cognisable, non-bailable offence with uniform national penalties, and extended the Centre's inspection powers to buses, trains, aircraft and land ports.
  • Federal angle: public health is a State subject (State List, Entry 6), but preventing the spread of infectious diseases from one State to another is in the Concurrent List (Entry 29), which allows uniform national action.

3. The Disaster Management Act, 2005

  • Central command: the National Disaster Management Authority is chaired by the Prime Minister; its National Executive Committee can issue directions binding on States (Section 10(2)(l)), and the Act overrides other laws (Section 72).
  • COVID-19 lockdown (March 2020): a national lockdown was ordered under this Act, with nationwide rules on movement, containment zones and reopening.
  • Debate: a uniform response helped against a fast-spreading virus, but sudden central orders left little room for consultation and contributed to the migrant workers' crisis.

4. The Farm Acts, 2020

  • Content: three Acts allowed trade outside State-regulated mandis, provided for contract farming and amended the Essential Commodities Act.
  • Centralising use of the Concurrent List: agriculture (Entry 14) and markets (Entry 28) are State subjects, but the Centre relied on trade in foodstuffs (Concurrent List, Entry 33) to create one national market.
  • Federal pushback: several Assemblies passed resolutions against the laws, the Supreme Court stayed them in January 2021, and Parliament repealed them in 2021.

5. Assessment

Centralisation is justified when a threat crosses State borders, as epidemics and disasters do. But federalism is part of the basic structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994), so central powers must be used with consultation and for limited periods; the farm laws showed that durable reform needs States' consent.

The centralising tilt is a safeguard for unity, not a licence for uniformity. Prior consultation through the Inter-State Council (Article 263), as the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions urged, can reconcile a strong Centre with cooperative federalism.
free.upm-2020-gs2-12:
Separation of powersJudicial legislationPublic interest litigationArticle 142

The Constitution does not adopt a rigid separation of powers, but each organ has a core domain: Parliament makes laws, the executive implements them and the courts interpret them (Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955). Separation of powers is part of the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973). When courts issue binding guidelines on petitions filed as public interest litigation (PIL), they appear to legislate; yet most such petitions arise because the other organs have failed to protect rights.

1. Why judicial legislation is criticised

  • Democratic legitimacy: judges are not elected or answerable to voters; in Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2007) the Supreme Court itself warned courts against encroaching on the legislature and the executive.
  • Institutional competence: courts lack the data, expertise, consultation and budgets that policy needs, so guidelines may be hard to implement, as States' partial compliance with Prakash Singh (2006) on police reform shows.
  • Rigidity and uncertainty: guidelines lack legislative debate and cannot be revised easily when circumstances change.
  • Self-correction: after State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (April 2025) set timelines for assent, the Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025) held that courts cannot fix timelines or deem assent.

2. Why so many PILs seek guidelines: the justification

  • Legislative vacuum: Vishaka (1997) laid down rules on sexual harassment at work, which applied until the POSH Act, 2013; Common Cause (2018) allowed living wills, and the procedure was simplified in 2023.
  • Executive failure that violates rights: D.K. Basu (1997) on custodial violence, Lalita Kumari (2013) on registering FIRs, Arnesh Kumar (2014) against routine arrests, and Tehseen Poonawalla (2018) on mob lynching.
  • Constitutional mandate: Article 32 is itself a fundamental right; the Court's law binds all (Article 141), and Article 142 allows orders for complete justice.
  • Access for the voiceless: relaxed standing (S.P. Gupta, 1981) let the poor and prisoners reach the Court, as in Hussainara Khatoon (1979).
  • Stopgap, not substitute: most guidelines apply only until the legislature acts, and Parliament has often then enacted laws.

3. Striking a balance

  • Restraint: Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) laid down guidelines against frivolous "publicity interest litigation"; guidelines should be a last resort.
  • Dialogue, not dictation: courts can identify the violation and give the government time to act, keeping supervision through continuing mandamus (Vineet Narain, 1997).
  • Legislative responsibility: Parliament should legislate promptly on issues the courts flag, after committee scrutiny.

Judicial guidelines are not usurpation when they fill a constitutional vacuum to enforce fundamental rights; they become overreach when they replace legitimate policy choices. Separation of powers in India means checks and balances: judicial restraint, executive responsiveness and timely legislation together protect both rights and democracy.
free.upm-2020-gs2-13:
73rd and 74th Amendments3FsFunctionalityLocal self-government

The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave panchayats and municipalities constitutional status. Their formative phase focused on the 3Fs: devolving functions (29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule and 18 in the Twelfth), functionaries and funds. The test today is functionality: whether elected local bodies actually plan, deliver services and answer to citizens. The Panchayat Devolution Index shows devolution rising only from 39.9% (2013-14) to 43.9% (2021-22), and new challenges have emerged.

1. Institutional and political challenges

  • Delayed elections and supersession: local polls are postponed for years and bodies run by administrators, although Kishansing Tomar (2006) required timely elections; the Supreme Court had to order overdue polls in Suresh Mahajan (2022).
  • Proxy leadership: husbands or relatives of elected women often exercise power in their place, defeating the purpose of reservation.
  • Parallel bodies: State parastatals, development authorities, user committees and legislators' local area funds bypass elected councils.
  • Bureaucratic dominance: State-appointed officials hold executive power; a CAG compendium of audits in 18 States (2024) found that on average 17 of 18 urban functions were devolved by law but only 4 with full autonomy.

2. Financial challenges

  • Low own revenue: own sources make up only about 32% of urban local bodies' revenue, and resources fall 42% short of expenditure (CAG, 2024); panchayats depend almost wholly on grants.
  • Irregular State Finance Commissions: they are set up late and their reports often ignored, so transfers stay discretionary.
  • Tied funds: Finance Commission and scheme grants leave little untied money; the 16th Finance Commission recommended about ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies for 2026–31.
  • Lost tax base: octroi and entry taxes were subsumed in GST without a share for cities.

3. Capacity and accountability challenges

  • Staff shortages: 37% of sanctioned posts in urban local bodies are vacant (CAG); many panchayats lack full-time staff of their own.
  • Weak planning: Gram Panchayat Development Plans are often wish lists; District and Metropolitan Planning Committees (Articles 243ZD and 243ZE) are frequently weak or not formed.
  • Weak Gram Sabhas and ward committees: low attendance, especially of women and the poor, limits social audit and accountability.
  • New expectations: local bodies must now localise the SDGs across nine themes, handle climate risks, run digital systems such as e-GramSwaraj and deliver services under national missions.

4. Way forward

  • Real devolution: activity mapping of functions (Second ARC, 2007), with staff and funds following functions.
  • Own revenue: reformed property tax and user charges, a fixed share of State revenue and timely SFCs.
  • Capacity: a professional local cadre and training under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan.
  • Accountability: active Gram Sabhas, social audits and measurable local SDG targets.

Three decades on, the 3Fs are necessary but not sufficient. Functionality needs political will, fiscal autonomy, capacity and citizen participation, so that local bodies become a true third tier of self-government, as Kerala's experience since 1996 shows is possible.
free.upm-2020-gs2-14:
Council of StatesFederal chamberRevising chamberCommittee system

The Rajya Sabha (Article 80) has up to 250 members (245 at present, including 12 nominated) and is a permanent House, one-third of whose members retire every second year. Early critics dismissed it as a redundant spare. Over the past few decades, however, it has emerged as an effective revising chamber and a voice of federalism, often shaping, delaying or improving the laws the Lok Sabha passes.

1. Factors behind the transformation

  • Coalition and minority governments: since 1989, ruling parties or coalitions have often lacked a majority in the Rajya Sabha, so its assent had to be negotiated.
  • Rise of regional parties: members elected by State Assemblies made it a forum for State interests and smaller parties.
  • Committee system: eight of the 24 department-related standing committees (set up in 1993) work under the Rajya Sabha, and Select Committees examine important Bills.
  • Expertise: nominated members from literature, science, art and social service (Article 80(3)) and experienced legislators raise the quality of debate.
  • Visibility: televised proceedings (Sansad TV since 2021) brought its debates to the public.

2. Areas where the transformation is visible

  • Legislative scrutiny: it defeated the 64th Amendment Bill on panchayats (1989); the Prevention of Terrorism Bill, rejected by it, was passed only at a joint sitting (2002); the Lokpal Bill stalled in December 2011 and became law in 2013 after a Select Committee review; the GST Amendment Bill was passed in 2016 with the Rajya Sabha's amendments.
  • Federal role: only it can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State subject in the national interest (Article 249) or create new All-India Services (Article 312).
  • Emergency safeguard: when the Lok Sabha is dissolved, its approval keeps proclamations under Articles 352, 356 and 360 alive.
  • Deliberation and rights: in 2015 it passed a private member's Bill on transgender rights, a rare event that preceded the 2019 Act.
  • A check that governments try to avoid: the use of the Money Bill route for the Aadhaar Bill (2016) to bypass it shows its importance; in Rojer Mathew (2019) the question was referred to a larger Bench.

3. Continuing limitations

  • Weaker federal character: the domicile requirement was removed and open ballot introduced in 2003, upheld in Kuldip Nayar (2006).
  • Disruptions and suspensions reduce time for deliberation.
  • Lok Sabha primacy: it has no role in Money Bills beyond recommendations, and joint sittings favour the larger House.
  • Party discipline: the anti-defection law makes members follow party whips rather than State interests.

The Rajya Sabha has become a useful chamber of second thought that slows hasty legislation and gives States a voice. Restoring its federal character, protecting it from misuse of the Money Bill route and reducing disruption would strengthen India's bicameralism.
free.upm-2020-gs2-15:
Constitutional amendmentArticle 368National Commission for WomenGender justice

A commission can be created by executive resolution, by statute or by the Constitution itself. Constitutional status gives it permanence and higher stature, as with the National Commissions for Scheduled Castes (Article 338), Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A) and Backward Classes (Article 338B, inserted by the 102nd Amendment, 2018). The National Commission for Women (NCW), constituted on 31 January 1992 under the NCW Act, 1990, remains a statutory body, which raises the question of whether constitutional status would advance gender justice.

1. Steps to constitutionalise a Commission

  • Policy decision and consultation: the Union consults States, the existing commission and civil society, and drafts a Constitution Amendment Bill.
  • A new Article: it lays down the composition, appointment by the President by warrant under hand and seal, tenure, functions, civil-court powers in inquiries, reports to the President to be laid before Parliament, and a duty of the Union and States to consult the commission, on the model of Article 338.
  • Article 368 procedure: the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting; ratification by half the State legislatures is needed only if it touches the federal provisions listed in the proviso; the President must give assent.
  • Follow-up: the statutory Act is repealed or amended, as the NCBC Act, 1993 was when the NCBC became constitutional (2018), and rules on staff and service conditions are framed.

2. Would constitutional status help gender justice? Reasons for

  • Permanence and independence: the NCW could not be weakened or abolished by ordinary law, and appointment by the President would add stature.
  • Binding consultation: a constitutional duty on the Union and the States to consult it on policies affecting women, beyond the present Section 16 of the NCW Act, which binds only the Centre.
  • Accountability of governments: reports laid before Parliament and State legislatures with action-taken memoranda would force responses.
  • Coherence: it would sit alongside Articles 14, 15(3), 39(a) and (d), 42 and 243D and the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (2023).

3. Reasons for caution

  • Status is not power: the National Commissions for SCs and STs are constitutional, yet atrocities persist, because their recommendations remain advisory.
  • Appointments: without an independent selection committee, members would still be chosen by the Union government.
  • Root causes lie elsewhere: female labour force participation is only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24), and women won only 74 seats in the 2024 Lok Sabha election; these need economic, social and political change, not a new Article.
  • Enforcement gap: justice depends on police, courts, One Stop Centres and local bodies, which a commission cannot replace.

Constitutional status would make the NCW more permanent and visible, but it is necessary rather than sufficient. Real gender justice needs, alongside it, an independent selection process, adequate resources, follow-up on its findings and the social and economic empowerment of women.
free.upm-2020-gs2-16:
Multidimensional Poverty IndexIncidence and intensityGlobal MPI 2026Leave no one behind

An income poverty line says nothing about how many deprivations the poor face. The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), published since 2010 by the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI), captures both the incidence of poverty (H, the share of people who are poor) and its intensity (A, the average share of weighted deprivations the poor face); the MPI is H × A. The latest 2026 Global MPI (October 2026) covers 108 countries and 6.3 billion people.

1. Why incidence and intensity matter

  • Beyond income: a family above the income line may lack clean fuel, sanitation or schooling; India's MPI headcount (16.4%) is 11.1 points higher than its income poverty rate at US$3.00 a day (5.3%).
  • Depth of poverty: countries with the same headcount can differ in intensity, so reducing deprivations counts as progress even before people cross the line.
  • Targeting: the index shows which deprivations drive poverty; in India living standards contribute 39.7%, health 32.2% and education 28.2%.

2. Key findings of the 2026 Global MPI

  • Scale: 1.2 billion people (18.9%) are in acute multidimensional poverty, and the number has risen for the first time since the index began, partly because populations grew in countries without new surveys.
  • Children: 617 million children are poor, 51.5% of all poor people; almost one child in three is poor.
  • Rural and regional concentration: more than eight in ten poor people live in rural areas; sub-Saharan Africa has 616 million poor people (51.4% of its population) and South Asia 393 million.
  • Progress is possible: 33 of the 89 countries with trend data halved their MPI value in less than 15 years.

3. India in the report

  • Latest estimate: using NFHS-5 (2019–21), India's headcount is 16.4%, intensity 42.0% and MPI 0.069, about 23.8 crore poor at 2024 population; 18.7% are vulnerable to poverty and 4.2% in severe poverty.
  • Progress: incidence fell from 55.1% (2005–06) to 16.4% (2019–21); NITI Aayog's national MPI, with 12 indicators, estimates a fall from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23), with 24.82 crore people escaping poverty.
  • Data lag: the 2026 report still uses 2019–21 data; NFHS-6 (2023-24), whose fact sheets were released in May 2026, will update it.

4. Analysis

  • Intensity is high: India's poor are deprived in over two-fifths of weighted indicators, so housing, water, clean fuel, nutrition and schooling must converge on the same households.
  • Vulnerability: nearly one in five people is close to the cut-off and can slip back after a health or climate shock.
  • Limits: old survey data, and access rather than quality (such as learning) is measured.

The MPI confirms the statement: counting how many are poor and how poor they are gives a truer picture than income alone. Using both measures with timely surveys is essential to the SDG pledge to halve poverty in all its dimensions and leave no one behind.
free.upm-2020-gs2-17:
Self Help GroupsMicrofinanceWomen's empowermentFinancial inclusion

Microfinance offers small loans, savings and insurance to people without collateral; Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh won the Nobel Peace Prize (2006) for it. In India it took the form of Self Help Groups (SHGs): groups of 10–20 women who save regularly, lend among themselves and borrow from banks. Through NABARD's SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (1992) and the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana–National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), about 10 crore rural women are now members.

1. Asset creation

  • From savings to assets: regular thrift builds a group corpus, and loans finance livestock, sewing machines, small shops and land leases.
  • Enterprise promotion: the Lakhpati Didi initiative aims to raise 3 crore SHG members to a household income of at least ₹1 lakh a year, and Namo Drone Didi provides 15,000 drones to SHGs for farm services.
  • Collective assets: SHG federations and producer groups run processing units and marketing; Kudumbashree (Kerala, 1998) links such enterprises with local governments.

2. Income security

  • Escape from moneylenders: emergency loans at lower interest smooth consumption after illness or crop failure.
  • Diversified livelihoods: farm and non-farm activities spread risk; market access through Mahila e-Haat and GeM's 'Womaniya' initiative.
  • Social security: members are linked to bank accounts and insurance and pension schemes.
  • Resilience: during COVID-19, SHGs made masks and ran community kitchens, showing their capacity in a crisis.

3. Empowering women

  • Economic agency: bank accounts, a credit history and a say over household income.
  • Social change: greater mobility, confidence and collective action against domestic violence, alcoholism and dowry.
  • Leadership: SHG members enter panchayats and work as bank and business-correspondent agents in villages.

4. Evaluation: the limits of the "vaccine"

  • Small loans, low returns: many loans go into consumption or crowded, low-value activities that do not lift income much.
  • Over-indebtedness: multiple borrowing from microfinance lenders caused the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis (2010), which led to a State ordinance and the Malegam Committee (2011); RBI's 2022 framework caps repayments at 50% of household income for households earning up to ₹3 lakh a year.
  • Regional imbalance: SHG bank linkage has been strongest in the southern States and weaker in the poorest regions.
  • Patriarchy and exclusion: men may control the loans, and the poorest, landless and disabled women are often left out.
  • Weak markets and skills: without training, branding and value chains, enterprises stay small.

SHGs have proved an effective anti-poverty vaccine against moneylender debt and social exclusion, and a strong platform for women's agency. To deliver lasting asset creation and income security, they must move from credit to enterprise, with skills, markets, digital finance and responsible lending.
free.upm-2020-gs2-18:
NEP 2020SDG 4Equity and inclusionFoundational learning

Sustainable Development Goal 4 (2015) commits countries to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all by 2030. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which replaced the 1986 policy, explicitly aligns itself with this goal. It seeks to restructure education (a 5+3+3+4 school design, a four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate degree) and to reorient it from rote learning towards competencies, critical thinking and values.

1. Conformity with SDG 4

  • Universal access: 100% gross enrolment from pre-school to secondary by 2030 (SDG 4.1).
  • Early childhood: the foundational stage (ages 3–8) brings pre-school into the school system (SDG 4.2).
  • Foundational learning and literacy: NIPUN Bharat (2021) aims at foundational literacy and numeracy for every child by Class 3 (SDG 4.1), and the ULLAS adult literacy programme (2022–27) serves those aged 15 and above (SDG 4.6).
  • Skills and higher education: vocational education from Class 6 and 50% gross enrolment in higher education by 2035 (SDG 4.3–4.4).
  • Equity: special attention to socio-economically disadvantaged groups and a Gender-Inclusion Fund (SDG 4.5); teaching in the mother tongue at least till Class 5.
  • Teachers: a four-year integrated B.Ed. as the minimum qualification by 2030 (SDG 4.c).

2. Restructuring and reorientation under way

  • School reform: PM SHRI (2022) is upgrading over 14,500 schools as NEP exemplars; PARAKH is the national assessment centre; CBSE allows two Class 10 board examinations from 2026.
  • Higher education: multiple entry and exit, the Academic Bank of Credits and the Anusandhan National Research Foundation Act, 2023; the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025, to replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with one regulator, is before a Joint Parliamentary Committee.

3. Critical examination

  • Learning crisis: ASER 2024 found that only 23.4% of Class 3 children in rural government schools could read a Class 2 text, up from 16.3% in 2022 but still low.
  • Higher education gap: a gross enrolment ratio of 28.4% (AISHE 2021-22), against the 50% target.
  • Funding: NEP's goal of public spending on education of 6% of GDP remains far from met.
  • Federal friction: education is in the Concurrent List; some States see the three-language formula, common entrance tests, a single regulator and Samagra Shiksha funds linked to PM SHRI agreements as centralising.
  • Equity risks: the digital divide, costly coaching and private schooling, and teacher vacancies in poorer States could widen gaps.
  • Implementation: mother-tongue teaching needs textbooks and teachers in many languages, and vocational education needs industry links.

4. Way forward

  • Money and teachers: raise public spending steadily and fill vacancies with trained teachers.
  • Cooperative federalism: flexible funding and room for States to adapt the policy.
  • Measure learning, not just enrolment: regular, independent assessment of outcomes.

NEP 2020 is in conformity with SDG 4 in vision and design. Whether it truly restructures education will depend on funding, teachers and Centre–State cooperation that turn policy into learning outcomes for every child.
free.upm-2020-gs2-19:
QuadIndo-PacificEconomic securityStrategic autonomy

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) of India, the USA, Japan and Australia grew out of the core group that coordinated relief after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami; first proposed in 2007, it was revived in 2017, and leaders' summits began in 2021. It has never been a military alliance: there is no treaty, no mutual-defence clause and no joint command. In recent years its agenda has moved towards supply chains, critical minerals and technology, but that does not make it a trade bloc.

1. The security core

  • Maritime cooperation: the four navies exercise together in Malabar; the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA, 2022) gives partners near-real-time data on "dark" shipping, and the Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission was launched in 2024.
  • Not an alliance: unlike NATO, it has no collective-defence obligation; India in particular rejects bloc politics, while China says it opposes "exclusive groupings".
  • Wider security: counter-terrorism exercises, disaster relief and health security.

2. The economic turn

  • Critical minerals: the foreign ministers launched a Quad Critical Minerals Initiative in July 2025, and at their New Delhi meeting in May 2026 adopted a framework to mobilise up to US$20 billion for mining, processing and recycling, voicing concern at "economic coercion" through export controls.
  • Energy and infrastructure: an Indo-Pacific energy security initiative, a first port project in Fiji and undersea cables for Pacific island countries.
  • Technology and health: cooperation on critical and emerging technologies and the Quad Vaccine Partnership (2021).
  • Related frameworks: the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative of India, Japan and Australia (2021) and the US-led IPEF (2022), in which India joined the supply-chain, clean-economy and fair-economy pillars but stayed out of the trade pillar.

3. Why the Quad is not becoming a trade bloc

  • No common trade agreement: India has a CEPA with Japan (2011) and an ECTA with Australia (2022) but no trade agreement with the USA; India stayed out of RCEP, and the USA left the TPP.
  • Trade frictions inside the group: US tariffs on most Indian goods rose to 50% in August 2025, including a 25% Russian-oil penalty. The penalty was removed in February 2026, with a framework for an interim trade deal, and the reciprocal tariffs lapsed after a US Supreme Court ruling; but a new 10% duty has covered about half of India's exports since July 2026, and the deal was unsigned in October 2026.
  • Summit drift: no leaders' summit was held in 2025, when India was to host, and in May 2026 the timing of the next one was still undecided.
  • Different priorities: India protects agriculture and small industry, while the others seek deeper market access.

4. Assessment

The Quad is moving from a narrow maritime dialogue to an economic-security partnership: resilient supply chains, critical minerals, energy and technology, framed against China's economic coercion. This is not trade liberalisation, and its security core remains.

For India, a flexible, issue-based Quad suits strategic autonomy. Its value will depend on delivering public goods to the Indo-Pacific and on managing trade frictions among its own members.
free.upm-2020-gs2-20:
Strategic autonomyIndo-PacificDefence diversificationInteroperability

Russia (earlier the Soviet Union) has been India's main arms supplier for six decades, but its share of India's arms imports fell from 70% (2011–15) to 51% (2016–20) and 40% (2021–25) (SIPRI, March 2026), as India, the world's second-largest arms importer in 2021–25, turned to France, Israel and the USA. Since the US recognised India as a Major Defence Partner (2016), Indo-US deals have grown fast, and on 31 October 2025 the two countries signed a ten-year framework for their defence partnership.

1. Significance of Indo-US defence deals

  • Maritime domain awareness: P-8I patrol aircraft, MH-60R helicopters and MQ-9B drones (bought in 2024) watch the Indian Ocean and its chokepoints.
  • Interoperability: the foundational agreements LEMOA, COMCASA and BECA (2016–20) allow logistics support, secure communications and sharing of geospatial data; exercises such as Malabar build joint operating skills.
  • Technology and co-production: GE F414 engines are to be co-produced with HAL (2023 MoU); in November 2025 the US approved sales of Javelin anti-tank missiles and Excalibur precision shells worth about US$93 million.
  • Strategic framework: the ten-year framework signed in Kuala Lumpur gives direction to exercises, technology collaboration and industrial partnerships.

2. Continuing value of Indo-Russian deals

  • Legacy platforms: much of India's in-service equipment, such as Su-30MKI fighters and T-90 tanks, is Russian-origin and needs Russian spares and upgrades.
  • Strategic systems: the S-400 air-defence system (2018 deal for five squadrons; the fourth arrived in mid-2026 and the fifth was still awaited in October 2026), the BrahMos missile joint venture (1998) and AK-203 rifles made at Korwa, Amethi.
  • Licensed production and cost: Russia has long shared production technology, as with the Su-30MKI built by HAL.
  • Continental deterrence: Russian systems underpin defence along the land borders with China and Pakistan.

3. Stability in the Indo-Pacific

  • Balancing China at sea: US-linked capabilities let India monitor and secure sea lanes from the Malacca Strait to the Arabian Sea, supporting a free and open Indo-Pacific with Quad partners.
  • Net security provider: surveillance, disaster relief and information-sharing help smaller littoral States.
  • Russia's changing reliability: Russia's closeness to China and the strain of the Ukraine war limit its value against India's main Indo-Pacific challenge.
  • Risks of tilting too far: the threat of US sanctions under CAATSA (2017) over the S-400, and US sanctions in late 2025 that cut India's access to discounted Russian crude, show the cost of dependence on any one partner.

4. Way forward

  • Diversify and indigenise: co-development with many partners and the Atmanirbhar Bharat push to cut import dependence.
  • Joint production: insist on technology transfer and production in India in every major deal.
  • Balance: keep Russia engaged for spares and strategic stability while deepening maritime cooperation with the USA.

Indo-US deals matter more for maritime stability in the Indo-Pacific and for advanced technology; Indo-Russian deals still sustain India's legacy forces and continental deterrence. Using both while building self-reliance is the essence of India's strategic autonomy.
free.upm-2020-gs3-1:
Intra-generational equityInter-generational equityInclusive growthSustainable development

Equity has two time dimensions. Intra-generational equity is fairness among people alive today, across classes, castes, genders and regions; it is the core of inclusive growth, which the Eleventh Plan (2007-12) made its goal. Inter-generational equity is fairness between the present and future generations. The Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development as development that "meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs".

1. Intra-generational issues: the inclusive-growth lens

  • Unequal access to jobs: growth led by capital- and skill-intensive sectors leaves about 90% of workers informal, and women's labour force participation was only 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Social and regional gaps: SCs, STs and backward districts lag in assets, learning and health; the Aspirational Districts (2018) and Aspirational Blocks (2023) programmes target these gaps.
  • Basic services: government health spending was only 1.43% of GDP and out-of-pocket spending 43.4% of health expenditure (National Health Accounts 2022-23), so illness pushes families into poverty.
  • Environmental injustice today: the poor bear most of the pollution, displacement by mines and dams, and climate shocks; the District Mineral Foundations (2015) and the Forest Rights Act (2006) try to share benefits with affected communities.

2. Inter-generational issues: the sustainability lens

  • Depleting natural capital: about 11% of groundwater assessment units are over-exploited, and Punjab extracts 156% of its annual recharge (CGWB, 2025); soils, forests and fisheries are also being run down.
  • Climate debt: today's emissions impose costs on future generations, which is why India has pledged net zero by 2070 and 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.
  • Fiscal burden: high public debt and unfunded liabilities shift costs to future taxpayers; the FRBM Act, 2003 seeks to limit this.
  • Human capital: 35.5% of children under five were stunted (NFHS-5); undernourished children today mean a less productive workforce tomorrow.

3. How the two are linked

  • Trade-offs: free farm power and cheap coal help poor households now but deplete aquifers and the climate budget for the future.
  • Synergies: watershed works, rooftop solar, natural farming and green jobs raise incomes today while protecting resources.
  • Global equity: the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (Rio, 1992) links equity among nations to equity across time.
  • Better measurement: GDP ignores resource depletion; natural-capital accounts and the inequality-adjusted HDI show who gains and what is lost.

Inclusive growth without sustainability borrows from the future, and sustainability without inclusion is unjust today. Following the precautionary principle (Vellore, 1996) and the spirit of Mission LiFE, India must grow in ways that are fair to both.
free.upm-2020-gs3-2:
Potential GDPOutput gapTotal factor productivityStructural constraints

Potential GDP is the highest level of real output an economy can sustain over time when its labour, capital and technology are fully and efficiently used, without pushing up inflation. The difference between actual and potential output is the output gap: a positive gap signals overheating and inflation, a negative one signals idle capacity. The Economic Survey 2025-26 raised its estimate of India's potential growth from 6.5% to about 7%.

1. Determinants of potential GDP

Potential output follows a production function, Y = A × f(K, L):

  • Labour (L): the size of the working-age population, participation rates (especially of women), hours worked and the health of workers.
  • Capital (K): the rate of investment; India's gross fixed capital formation was 31.9% of GDP in 2025-26 (current prices, NSO, June 2026).
  • Human capital: education, skills and nutrition raise the quality of each worker.
  • Total factor productivity (A): technology, innovation, efficient allocation of resources, and institutions such as contract enforcement and the rule of law.
  • Enablers: infrastructure, energy, logistics, natural resources and macroeconomic stability.

2. Factors inhibiting India from realising its potential

Real GDP grew 7.7% in 2025-26 (NSO provisional estimates), close to the estimated potential; the challenge is to raise potential itself.

  • Under-used labour: women's labour force participation was only 41.7%, about 46% of workers remain in low-productivity agriculture (PLFS 2023-24), and about 90% are informal.
  • Skill and health gaps: poor learning outcomes, limited vocational training and child stunting of 35.5% (NFHS-5) lower future productivity.
  • Weak private investment and costly capital: the twin balance-sheet problem (bank gross NPAs peaked at 11.2% in March 2018) held back credit for years, and the Survey flags a high cost of capital.
  • Infrastructure and logistics: logistics costs of 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT), costly power and slow land acquisition raise costs.
  • Narrow industrial and research base: manufacturing is only about 17% of GVA, and R&D spending is just 0.84% of GDP (2023-24).
  • Regulatory and judicial frictions: compliance burdens and slow contract enforcement deter firms from growing; the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 began decriminalising minor offences.
  • Shocks: the COVID-19 contraction of 2020-21, global protectionism and climate extremes such as heat waves cut output and investment.

Closing these gaps can lift potential growth towards 8%, the pace needed for Viksit Bharat@2047. That requires second-generation reforms in land, labour, power, skills and the judiciary, not just demand stimulus.
free.upm-2020-gs3-3:
Agricultural marketingRural logisticsPost-harvest lossesAPMC regulation

Agricultural marketing covers everything between the farm gate and the consumer: assembly, grading, transport, storage and sale. It is a State subject (Entry 28, State List, "markets and fairs") and is regulated by each State's APMC Act. Weak transport and fragmented markets mean that post-harvest losses are worth about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS, 2022), while India's logistics costs are about 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT).

1. Constraints in transport

  • Poor last-mile connectivity: many villages still depend on narrow or seasonal roads, so produce moves by tractor-trolley or head-load to the nearest buyer; PMGSY (2000) has improved but not completed rural links.
  • Small lots, high unit costs: 86% of holdings are small and marginal (Agriculture Census 2015-16), so each farmer sends tiny quantities and pays more per quintal.
  • Few refrigerated vehicles: a shortage of reefer trucks and pack-houses means fruits, vegetables, milk and fish spoil in transit.
  • Modal imbalance: roads carry most produce over long distances; rail and air are under-used for perishables, and Kisan Rail and Krishi Udan (both 2020) have stayed small.
  • Poor packaging and handling: open trucks, gunny bags and repeated loading and unloading bruise produce and cause losses.

2. Constraints in marketing

  • Too few, distant markets: the National Commission on Farmers (Swaminathan) sought a regulated market within about 5 km of every farmer, but mandis are far apart, so many sell to village traders at low prices.
  • Intermediaries and mandi practices: commission agents, cartels of licensed traders, multiple fees and delayed payments cut the farmer's share of the consumer's rupee.
  • No grading, storage or credit: without assaying, warehouses and pledge loans, farmers sell immediately after harvest, when prices are lowest.
  • Fragmented regulation and policy shocks: separate State laws, multiple licences and limits on inter-State trade split the national market; sudden export bans and stock limits, as on wheat (2022) and onion (2023-24), disrupt prices.
  • Information gaps and weak collectives: farmers often lack price and demand information, and many FPOs lack capital and market links.

3. The way ahead

  • Integrated value chains: village-level aggregation, grading and pack-houses linked to rail, road and cold storage.
  • Market reform by States: unified licences, private markets and fewer fees so that e-NAM supports real inter-State trade.

Better roads, cold chains and competitive markets together can turn "One Nation, One Market" into a fair price for the farmer and lower prices for the consumer.
free.upm-2020-gs3-4:
Food processingValue additionFarmers' incomeBackward linkages

Food processing turns farm, dairy, fishery and livestock produce into higher-value, longer-lasting products, from cleaning and grading to ready-to-eat foods. India is the largest producer of milk and pulses and the second-largest of fruits and vegetables, yet only a small share of its perishables is processed, and post-harvest losses are worth about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS, 2022). The Committee on Doubling Farmers' Income (Ashok Dalwai) saw value addition as a key lever.

1. Opportunities

  • Raw-material base: varied agro-climates give year-round supplies of cereals, millets, fruits, vegetables, spices, milk and fish.
  • Changing demand: urbanisation, rising incomes, working women and quick-commerce apps raise demand for packaged, ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat foods.
  • Exports: marine products, rice, spices and mango pulp already sell abroad; branded Indian and millet-based foods can capture more value.
  • Policy support: 100% FDI under the automatic route in food processing; the PLI scheme for food processing (₹10,900 crore); PMFME (₹10,000 crore) with One District One Product; PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (2017).

2. Challenges

  • Supply side: small, scattered farms make steady, uniform supply difficult, and many varieties are unsuited to processing.
  • Infrastructure gaps: cold chains, reliable power, pack-houses and food-testing laboratories are inadequate, especially near farms.
  • Informality: most units are tiny and unregistered, with weak access to credit, technology and FSSAI compliance.
  • Costs and markets: costly packaging, high logistics costs and consumer preference for fresh food limit margins.

3. How processing can substantially raise farmers' incomes

  • Assured markets and better prices: contract farming and direct sourcing by processors give farmers forward contracts for processing-grade potato, tomato or maize.
  • Less waste, steadier prices: processing absorbs gluts; Operation Greens, launched for tomato, onion and potato (2018), was widened to other fruits and vegetables in 2020.
  • A larger share of the consumer's rupee: when farmers own the processing, through cooperatives as in the Amul model of Operation Flood (1970) or through FPOs, they capture the margin instead of middlemen.
  • Primary processing in villages: grading, drying, milling and packing by FPOs and SHGs under PMFME keep value addition and jobs in rural areas.
  • New income streams: by-products such as rice-bran oil, and sugarcane and maize used for ethanol blending, give farmers extra demand.

With cold chains, credit and quality standards in place, food processing can link farm and factory, raise farm incomes and make India the food basket of the world.
free.upm-2020-gs3-5:
NanotechnologyTargeted drug deliveryNanodiagnosticsNanotoxicity

Nanotechnology is the control of matter at 1–100 nanometres (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m). Richard Feynman foresaw it in 1959 and Norio Taniguchi coined the term in 1974. At this scale the surface-area-to-volume ratio is very high and quantum effects change colour, strength and conductivity, so particles behave differently from bulk material. India's Nano Mission (DST, May 2007) built research capacity in the field.

1. Understanding nanotechnology

  • Why size matters in medicine: nanoparticles are about the size of proteins and viruses (a virus is about 100 nm), so they can enter cells and interact with biological molecules in ways larger particles cannot.
  • Two routes: materials are made top-down, by carving bulk material, or bottom-up, by assembling atoms and molecules.
  • New properties: gold nanoparticles look red, silver nanoparticles kill microbes, and nanoparticles can cross cell membranes.
  • Key nanomaterials: liposomes and lipid nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, quantum dots, metal and polymer nanoparticles.

2. How it is helping the health sector

  • Targeted drug delivery: nanocarriers deliver anti-cancer drugs to tumour cells, which take them up through leaky blood vessels, so lower doses work with fewer side effects; liposomal amphotericin B is used against kala-azar and was used against "black fungus" during COVID-19.
  • Vaccines: lipid nanoparticles protect the fragile mRNA of COVID-19 vaccines and carry it into cells.
  • Faster, cheaper diagnosis: lateral-flow strips and nano-biosensors give point-of-care results for infections, glucose and cancer markers, useful in rural health centres.
  • Imaging and theranostics: quantum dots and magnetic nanoparticles show disease early, and some particles both detect and treat it (theranostics), a step towards personalised treatment.
  • New frontiers under research: nanoparticles designed to cross the blood–brain barrier for brain tumours, and nanocarriers that deliver gene-editing tools to specific cells.
  • Regenerative medicine and infection control: nano-structured scaffolds, implant coatings and silver-based dressings speed healing and cut hospital infections; nano-filters such as IIT Madras's AMRIT remove arsenic and iron from drinking water.

3. Concerns and India's response

  • Nanotoxicity: inhaled or injected nanoparticles can reach deep into organs; some long nanotubes behave like asbestos in animal studies.
  • Environment and equity: nano-silver can harm useful microbes, and costly nano-medicines risk a "nano-divide".
  • Regulation: India has no nano-specific law; DBT, ICMR and CDSCO issued Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals (2019).
  • Capacity: the Nano Mission funds institutes such as INST Mohali, shared facilities and training.

Nanotechnology is moving medicine towards precision medicine: earlier diagnosis and targeted, gentler treatment. Clear safety standards and affordable access will decide whether its benefits reach every citizen.
free.upm-2020-gs3-6:
Scientific temperGreen RevolutionBiotechnologyDigital agriculture

Science is no longer confined to laboratories: it shapes how we eat, heal, communicate, travel and govern. The Constitution recognises this by making it a fundamental duty to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry (Article 51A(h)). Agriculture shows its impact most clearly: science-based technologies since the Green Revolution lifted foodgrain output from about 50.8 million tonnes (1950-51) to over 350 million tonnes (2024-25).

1. How science is interwoven with our lives

  • Health: vaccines made India polio-free (certified 2014) and delivered over 220 crore COVID-19 doses; diagnostics, antibiotics and telemedicine (eSanjeevani) extend care to villages.
  • Communication and money: mobile phones, the internet (over 111 crore subscribers, TRAI, June 2026) and UPI have changed how people learn, work and pay.
  • Energy and mobility: electricity, solar panels, electric vehicles and satellite navigation (NavIC) run daily life.
  • Safety: weather satellites and cyclone warnings helped Odisha evacuate about a million people before Cyclone Phailin (2013), keeping deaths low.
  • Way of thinking: evidence-based choices about food, health and the environment, against superstition and misinformation.

2. Striking changes in agriculture triggered by science

  • Seeds and breeding: high-yielding dwarf wheat and rice varieties of the 1960s; Bt cotton (2002), still India's only commercially grown GM crop; and the world's first genome-edited rice varieties, DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1 (May 2025).
  • Precision inputs: Soil Health Cards (2015) for balanced fertiliser use, and IFFCO's liquid nano urea (2021) and nano DAP (2023).
  • Water and energy: drip irrigation (about 90% efficiency) and sprinklers under "Per Drop More Crop", and about 25 lakh solar pumps under PM-KUSUM.
  • Machines and drones: tractors, combine harvesters and Happy Seeders, and drones for spraying given to women's SHGs under Namo Drone Didi (2023).
  • Space and data: satellite-based crop estimates, agromet advisories on phones, e-NAM (2016) and the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) with AgriStack farmer IDs.
  • Allied sectors: artificial insemination and sex-sorted semen in dairying, and tissue-culture banana and farmed shrimp.

3. The other side

  • Ecological costs: groundwater depletion, soil degradation, pesticide residues and stubble burning in the rice–wheat belt.
  • Uneven spread: gains concentrated in irrigated regions and larger farms; rain-fed and small farmers lag in access.
  • New concerns: biosafety of GM crops, farmers' data privacy and the digital divide.

Science has turned India from a food-deficit country into a food-surplus one. The next task, in M.S. Swaminathan's words, is an Evergreen Revolution: productivity growth that protects soil, water and biodiversity and reaches every small farmer.
free.upm-2020-gs3-7:
Environment Impact AssessmentPost-facto clearancePublic consultationPrecautionary principle

Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) predicts the environmental and social effects of a project before it is approved. It was made mandatory by a 1994 notification under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and is now governed by the EIA Notification, 2006, with four stages (screening, scoping, public consultation, appraisal) and categories A (cleared by MoEFCC) and B1/B2 (cleared by State authorities). In March 2020 the MoEFCC published the draft EIA Notification, 2020 to replace it; it drew about 17 lakh public comments.

1. Key differences

  • Regularising violators: the draft let projects that had started or expanded without clearance apply for approval after paying a penalty, whereas 2006 requires clearance before work begins.
  • Less public participation: a shorter notice period, more projects in Category B2, and exemption of linear projects such as roads and pipelines in border areas within 100 km of the Line of Actual Control.
  • Easier expansion: an EIA only for expansions above 25% and a public hearing only above 50%.
  • Weaker monitoring: annual instead of six-monthly compliance reports, and no role for citizens in reporting violations.

2. The case made for the draft

  • Ease of doing business: faster, online, time-bound approvals and standard terms of reference.
  • Bringing violators into the net: regulating and penalising projects already running without clearance rather than leaving them outside the law.

3. Concerns raised

  • Against environmental jurisprudence: post-facto approval conflicts with the precautionary principle (Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996); the Supreme Court in Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020) disapproved of ex post facto clearances.
  • Weaker voice for affected people: tribal and rural communities need time, local-language documents and hearings; the Delhi High Court extended the deadline for comments in 2020.
  • Timing: the LG Polymers gas leak at Visakhapatnam (May 2020) highlighted weak compliance just as the draft proposed lighter monitoring.

4. Status as of 2026

The 2020 draft was never notified as a whole, and the 2006 Notification, amended from time to time, still applies. In Vanashakti (July 2026) a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that prior clearance is the rule, upheld only the one-time 2017 window for violators and quashed the 2021 office memorandum prospectively.

EIA must remain a preventive safeguard, not a formality. Faster clearances should come from better data, cumulative and strategic assessment and digital processes, while keeping prior clearance and meaningful public participation intact.
free.upm-2020-gs3-8:
Jal Shakti AbhiyanCatch the RainJan BhagidariWater security

India's per capita water availability fell from 1,545 cubic metres (2011) to 1,486 cubic metres (2021), below the 1,700 m³ mark of water stress, while rain falls on only a few monsoon days. To make water conservation a people's movement, the newly formed Ministry of Jal Shakti launched the Jal Shakti Abhiyan (JSA) in 2019 in 1,592 water-stressed blocks of 256 districts. Since 2021 it has run every year as "Catch the Rain".

1. JSA 2019: the first campaign

  • Target areas: water-stressed blocks identified from groundwater data, with central teams led by Additional and Joint Secretaries working alongside district administrations, in two phases (July–September, and October–November for retreating-monsoon States).
  • Five interventions: water conservation and rainwater harvesting, renovation of traditional water bodies, reuse and recharge of borewells, watershed development, and intensive afforestation.
  • Jan Andolan: gram panchayats, schools, self-help groups and citizens were mobilised to plan and build structures themselves.

2. "Catch the Rain" (since 2021)

  • Launch: by the Prime Minister on World Water Day, 22 March 2021, extended to all districts, rural and urban, with the slogan "Catch the rain, where it falls, when it falls".
  • Annual themes: each edition adds a focus, from drinking-water sources to women's leadership.
  • Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari: launched at Surat on 6 September 2024; its first phase reported over 27 lakh recharge structures against a target of 10 lakh, and the second (from 1 June 2025) over 1.5 crore against a target of one crore, under verification (PIB, July 2026).

3. Salient features

  • People's participation (Jan Bhagidari): community, CSR and cost-sharing (the "3Cs"); the 2024 theme put women at the centre.
  • Convergence, not a new budget: works are funded through VB-G RAM G (which replaced MGNREGA in July 2026), PMKSY's "Per Drop More Crop" and water-body repair, CAMPA, Finance Commission grants and State schemes.
  • Scientific planning: geo-tagging and inventory of water bodies, GIS-based district water conservation plans and a Jal Shakti Kendra in every district as a knowledge hub.
  • Focus on stress: priority to over-exploited and critical groundwater districts, with Mission Amrit Sarovar (2022, 75 ponds per district) and the Atal Bhujal Yojana complementing it.
  • Recognition: the National Water Awards and the Swachh Sujal Shakti Samman reward communities and women.

4. Gaps

  • Quality and upkeep: structures need verification and maintenance; numbers alone do not show recharge.
  • Demand side: free farm power and water-hungry crops keep extraction high.

The Jal Shakti Abhiyan has turned water conservation into a Jan Andolan. Linking recharge with demand management, crop diversification and community regulation will make water security lasting.
free.upm-2020-gs3-9:
Cyber crimeIT Act, 2000I4C and helpline 1930Cyber hygiene

Cyber crime is any offence in which a computer, phone or network is the target or the tool.
