With over 111 crore internet subscribers (TRAI, June 2026) and digital payments everywhere, India's exposure has grown fast: NCRB's Crime in India 2024 recorded 1,01,928 cyber crime cases, up 17.9% over 2023, about 73% with fraud as the motive. The main law is the Information Technology Act, 2000.

1. Types of cyber crimes

  • Against individuals: fraud, stalking, sextortion and identity theft, often targeting the elderly, women and first-time users.
  • Against organisations: ransomware, data breaches and business-email fraud hit hospitals, banks and power utilities.
  • Against the State: cyber espionage and attacks on critical information infrastructure, often linked to hostile states.

2. Why the menace is hard to fight

  • Borderless crime: many scams are run from compounds abroad, so evidence and offenders lie outside Indian jurisdiction.
  • Mule accounts and crypto: money is layered through rented bank accounts and crypto assets within minutes.
  • Low awareness and under-reporting: new users fall for urgent calls; victims often do not report.
  • Capacity gaps: too few trained cyber police, forensic labs and specialised prosecutors.

3. Measures in place

  • Law: the IT Act (Sections 66C, 66D, 66F, 69A), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (organised crime, including cyber crime, under Section 111), and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 with its Rules (2025).
  • Institutions: CERT-In (incident reporting within 6 hours), NCIIPC for critical infrastructure, and the MHA's I4C with the 1930 helpline and cybercrime.gov.in; its fraud-reporting system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026.
  • Telecom and judiciary: Sanchar Saathi and Chakshu block fraudulent SIMs and calls; in December 2025 the Supreme Court asked the CBI to investigate digital-arrest scams.

4. Measures still required

  • Capacity: a cyber police station and forensic lab in every district, and training for police, prosecutors and judges.
  • Real-time coordination: shared data among banks, telecom firms and police to shut mule accounts, with tools to detect deepfakes.
  • Strategy and cooperation: an updated national cyber security strategy, faster mutual legal assistance with countries hosting scam centres, and engagement with the new UN Convention against Cybercrime (2024).
  • Cyber hygiene: awareness campaigns, school curricula and "pause before you pay" habits.

Fighting cyber crime needs technology, law and awareness working together, so that India's digital growth rests on trust and safety.
free.upm-2020-gs3-10:
Border area managementLocal support baseHearts and mindsPerception management

Militants in border areas, as in Jammu and Kashmir and the North-East, survive on local support: shelter, guides, couriers, recruits and information. Porous borders with Pakistan, Myanmar and Bangladesh, difficult terrain and ethnic ties across the frontier make such support easier. Effective border area management therefore means separating militants from the people while winning their trust, the "hearts and minds" idea associated with General Gerald Templer in the Malayan Emergency (1950s).

1. Why locals sometimes support militants

  • Fear and coercion: villagers are threatened into giving food, shelter and silence.
  • Alienation: civilian casualties, high-handed searches and delayed justice breed anger.
  • Economic distress: unemployment, and income from smuggling and extortion networks.
  • Identity and propaganda: ethnic kinship across the border and radical messaging on social media.

2. Steps to deny local support

  • Protect the population: area domination and secure villages; Village Defence Guards (2022) in Jammu and Kashmir arm and train local volunteers.
  • Intelligence-led, precise operations: human intelligence from trusted communities, minimal collateral damage and strict standard operating procedures.
  • Choke cross-border logistics: smart fencing under the Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System, anti-tunnel and anti-drone systems (the BSF seized 272 drones on the Punjab border between January and November 2025), and the curtailment of the Free Movement Regime with Myanmar to 10 km (December 2024).
  • Cut the money: NIA terror-funding cases, action against hawala and fake currency, and attachment of property under the UAPA.
  • A way back: surrender-and-rehabilitation schemes and deradicalisation for misled youth.

3. Managing favourable perception among locals

  • Civic action: the Army's Operation Sadbhavana (since 1998) runs Goodwill Schools, medical camps and national integration tours; the Assam Rifles are known as the "Friends of the Hill People".
  • Development that people can see: roads, mobile towers, schools and livelihoods under the Border Area Development Programme and the Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP-I, 2023; VVP-II, 2025), which also stem out-migration.
  • Rights and accountability: quick, transparent inquiries into excesses, as demanded after the Oting killings in Nagaland (December 2021), and phased withdrawal of AFSPA from large parts of the North-East since 2022.
  • Voice and participation: panchayat and District Development Council elections (2020) and the 2024 Lok Sabha turnout in Jammu and Kashmir (58.46%), the highest in 35 years.
  • Strategic communication: prompt rebuttal of fake news, local-language outreach and engagement of elders, women, teachers and religious leaders.

A militant cut off from the people cannot last. Combining firm security with people-centric governance turns border communities into the first line of defence.
free.upm-2020-gs3-11:
Capital formationGross fixed capital formationConcession agreementRisk allocation

In economics, investment does not mean buying shares; it means adding to the economy's stock of productive capital, that is, capital formation. Its main part, gross fixed capital formation (GFCF), is spending on buildings, roads, machinery, equipment and intellectual property. India's GFCF was 31.9% of GDP in 2025-26 (current prices, NSO provisional estimates, June 2026). Public–private partnerships (PPPs) bring private capital into infrastructure through concession agreements.

1. Investment as capital formation

  • Components: gross capital formation = GFCF + change in stocks (inventories) + valuables; net capital formation deducts depreciation.
  • Financing: domestic savings of households, firms and government, plus foreign savings (the current account deficit and FDI), fund investment; in a closed economy savings equal investment.
  • Link to growth: in the Harrod–Domar model, growth equals the investment rate divided by the incremental capital–output ratio (ICOR), so both the volume and the efficiency of capital matter.
  • Public and private roles: public capital expenditure, budgeted at ₹12.22 lakh crore for 2026-27, builds infrastructure and crowds in private investment.
  • Quality: stalled projects, idle capacity and badly chosen assets add to spending but not to productive capacity.

2. Factors in designing a concession agreement

A concession agreement lets a public authority grant a private firm the right to finance, build or operate an asset for a fixed period and recover its investment through user charges or payments from the government. The Planning Commission's Model Concession Agreements and the Kelkar Committee (2015) set out the key design issues:

  • Clear scope and output standards: service levels, maintenance standards, penalties and an independent engineer to monitor them.
  • Optimal risk allocation: each risk should rest with the party best able to manage it; land acquisition and clearances with the public authority, construction with the private partner, and traffic risk shared or retained by the government, as under the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016).
  • Sound financial terms: a realistic concession period, a tariff and indexation formula, revenue sharing, viability gap funding (scheme of 2006) where projects are socially needed but not commercially viable, and termination payments that protect lenders.
  • Flexibility: clauses for change in law, force majeure and a framework for renegotiation, because rigid contracts and aggressive bids caused many PPP failures in the 2010s.
  • Dispute resolution and transparency: conciliation and arbitration with time limits, competitive bidding (Kelkar advised against Swiss challenge), and a fair hand-back of the asset; the Delhi Airport Metro Express dispute, decided by the Supreme Court only in 2024, shows the cost of long litigation.

A good concession agreement balances value for money for the public with fair returns for the investor. Clear risk sharing, independent regulation and quick dispute resolution can revive private investment and sustain India's capital formation.
free.upm-2020-gs3-12:
GST compensationCompensation cessBack-to-back loansFiscal federalism

The Goods and Services Tax, introduced on 1 July 2017 by the 101st Constitutional Amendment, made States give up most of their indirect taxes. Section 18 of that Amendment Act required Parliament to compensate States for revenue loss for five years. The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guaranteed each State 14% annual growth over its 2015-16 revenue, funded by a compensation cess on luxury and "sin" goods.

1. Rationale of the Act

  • Insurance for a grand bargain: GST is destination-based, so producing States such as Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu feared losses; assured compensation won their consent.
  • Assured revenue growth: protected revenue grew at 14% a year from the 2015-16 base, and the shortfall was paid every two months for five years (July 2017–June 2022).
  • Dedicated funding: a cess on pan masala, tobacco, aerated drinks, coal and motor cars was credited to a GST Compensation Fund in the Public Account.

2. Impact of COVID-19 on the compensation fund

  • Collapse in collections: the 2020 lockdown cut sales of cess-bearing goods such as cars and coal, while protected revenue kept rising at 14%.
  • A huge gap: the Centre put the 2020-21 shortfall at ₹2.35 lakh crore, attributing about ₹97,000 crore (later ₹1.1 lakh crore) to GST and the rest to the pandemic, an "act of God" in the Finance Minister's words (August 2020).
  • Borrowing instead of cess: the Centre borrowed and passed the money on as back-to-back loans of ₹1.1 lakh crore (2020-21) and ₹1.59 lakh crore (2021-22), repayable from the cess.
  • Longer cess: compensation ended on 30 June 2022, but the cess was extended to March 2026 to repay these loans.

3. New federal tensions

  • Legal obligation disputed: States such as Kerala, Punjab and West Bengal held the Centre bound to pay in full; the Centre, citing the Attorney General's opinion, said it need not meet the shortfall from the Consolidated Fund of India.
  • Trust deficit: the CAG reported that ₹47,272 crore of cess was retained in the Consolidated Fund in 2017-18 and 2018-19, contrary to the Act; payments were also delayed.
  • Fiscal squeeze: States bore most pandemic health and relief spending; their borrowing limit was raised to 5% of GSDP for 2020-21, partly tied to reforms.
  • Strains in the GST Council: the episode exposed the absence of the dispute-settlement mechanism envisaged in Article 279A(11); in Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held the Council's recommendations persuasive, not binding.
  • No extension: several States' demand to extend compensation beyond June 2022 was not accepted.

Status (2026): the compensation cess has ended; tobacco now bears a higher central excise duty and pan masala the Health Security se National Security Cess, which, like other cesses, is not shared with States.

GST remains India's boldest experiment in cooperative federalism. Predictable transfers, a working dispute-resolution mechanism and limits on unshared cesses can rebuild trust between the Centre and the States.
free.upm-2020-gs3-13:
Rice–wheat systemGreen RevolutionGroundwater depletionCrop diversification

The rice–wheat cropping system, rice in kharif followed by wheat in rabi, dominates the Indo-Gangetic Plains of Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Born of the Green Revolution (from 1966-67), it turned India from a "ship-to-mouth" importer of PL-480 wheat into a food-surplus country: foodgrain output rose from about 50.8 million tonnes (1950-51) to over 350 million tonnes (2024-25).

1. Factors behind its success

  • High-yielding varieties: semi-dwarf wheat from Norman Borlaug's programme in Mexico and rice such as IR8 (IRRI, 1966) responded strongly to water and fertiliser; M.S. Swaminathan led their adaptation in India.
  • Assured irrigation: canals from projects such as Bhakra-Nangal and, later, millions of tube wells with cheap or free power.
  • Assured prices and procurement: the Agricultural Prices Commission and the Food Corporation of India (both 1965) offered MSP and near-certain procurement of rice and wheat.
  • Inputs, credit and research: fertilisers, pesticides, cooperative credit, and agricultural universities such as Pantnagar (1960) and Punjab Agricultural University (1962).
  • Fit with the land: fertile alluvium, a clear two-season calendar, mechanisation and dense mandi networks.

2. How the system became a bane

  • Groundwater depletion: paddy is water-hungry, and Punjab extracts 156% of its annual recharge (CGWB, 2025).
  • Soil fatigue: urea-heavy fertiliser use, falling organic carbon, zinc deficiency and a hard subsurface layer have flattened yields.
  • Stubble burning: the short gap between paddy harvest and wheat sowing leads to burning of paddy straw, which adds to the winter smog over Delhi-NCR.
  • Monoculture risks: pulses, oilseeds and millets have been displaced, pests and weeds have built up (herbicide-resistant Phalaris minor in wheat), and genetic diversity has narrowed.
  • Pollution and emissions: nitrate and pesticide residues in water, and methane from flooded paddy.
  • Economic and nutritional distortion: large central stocks and procurement costs, imports of pulses and edible oils, and diets heavy in cereals.
  • Climate stress: terminal heat, as in March 2022, cuts wheat yields.

3. The way forward

  • Diversify the north-west: shift part of the paddy area to maize, pulses, oilseeds and horticulture with assured markets.
  • Shift production east: support eastern States, where water is plentiful, through Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India.

The rice–wheat system secured India's food; now it must be made sustainable. An Evergreen Revolution that values water, soil and nutrition can turn it from a bane back into a boon.
free.upm-2020-gs3-14:
Water storageIrrigation efficiencyGroundwater rechargeDemand management

India has about 18% of the world's population but only about 4% of its freshwater, and per capita availability fell from 1,545 m³ (2011) to 1,486 m³ (2021), below the 1,700 m³ mark of water stress. Most rain falls in a few monsoon months, so storage decides how much water is available in the dry season, while only about half the gross cropped area is irrigated. Judicious use means "more crop per drop".

1. Improving water storage

  • Complete and maintain big storage: finish pending projects (99 priority AIBP projects funded through NABARD's Long Term Irrigation Fund, 2016), desilt reservoirs and keep old dams safe under the Dam Safety Act, 2021 and DRIP.
  • Revive small and traditional storage: tanks, johads, ponds and step-wells, as in Mission Amrit Sarovar (2022, 75 ponds per district), Telangana's Mission Kakatiya (2015) and the johads revived by Tarun Bharat Sangh in Alwar.
  • Use aquifers as reservoirs: recharge pits, check dams and recharge shafts; the first phase of Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari reported over 27 lakh recharge structures.
  • Harvest rain in cities and homes: rooftop rainwater harvesting, mandatory in Tamil Nadu since 2003, and protection of urban lakes and wetlands.
  • Move surplus water: river-linking with environmental safeguards, beginning with the Ken–Betwa project (foundation stone, December 2024).

2. Making irrigation judicious

  • Micro-irrigation: drip (about 90% efficiency) and sprinklers (about 70–80%) under PMKSY's "Per Drop More Crop", backed by NABARD's ₹5,000 crore Micro Irrigation Fund (2018).
  • Modern canals: lining, piped and pressurised distribution, and command area development; the M-CADWM sub-scheme (2025) pilots piped irrigation run by water user societies so tail-enders get water.
  • Farmer participation: water users' associations, pioneered by Andhra Pradesh's Farmers' Management of Irrigation Systems Act, 1997.
  • Water-saving agronomy: direct-seeded rice, alternate wetting and drying, laser land levelling, mulching, and a shift to millets, pulses and oilseeds.
  • Right price signals: metering, volumetric charges, separate farm feeders (Gujarat's Jyotigram Yojana, 2003) and solar pumps under PM-KUSUM that let farmers sell surplus power instead of pumping more.

3. Governance and data

  • Groundwater regulation and budgeting: CGWA guidelines (2020), aquifer mapping (NAQUIM) and village water budgets under the Atal Bhujal Yojana.
  • Integrated institutions: the Mihir Shah Committee (2016) proposed a National Water Commission merging the CWC and the CGWB to manage surface and groundwater together.
  • Reuse: treated urban wastewater for irrigation, with real-time data for allocation.

India must move from building irrigation potential to managing water as a scarce resource: store more, lose less and grow crops suited to each region. That is the path to water security.
free.upm-2020-gs3-15:
COVID-19 pandemicDigital public infrastructureVaccine platformsGenomic surveillance

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, was declared a pandemic by the WHO on 11 March 2020 and remained a global health emergency until 2023. Lockdowns, overwhelmed hospitals and lost livelihoods followed worldwide. Yet technology, from molecular diagnostics and genome sequencing to new vaccine platforms and digital public infrastructure, helped countries test, trace, treat and vaccinate on an unprecedented scale.

1. Detection and surveillance

  • Diagnostics: RT-PCR detected the virus's RNA; rapid antigen strips and home kits gave quick results; chip-based Truenat machines, first built for TB, extended testing to district hospitals.
  • Genomic surveillance: INSACOG (December 2020), a consortium of laboratories, sequenced samples to track variants such as Delta, first identified in India.
  • Contact tracing and data: the Aarogya Setu app (April 2020) alerted contacts, and dashboards and epidemic models guided containment zones and hospital planning.

2. Treatment and care

  • Telemedicine: Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (March 2020) and eSanjeevani kept outpatient care going; eSanjeevani had crossed 50 crore consultations by October 2026.
  • Oxygen and devices: indigenous ventilators, PSA oxygen plants and Oxygen Express trains (2021) during the second wave.
  • New and repurposed drugs: trials identified dexamethasone as life-saving, and DRDO's 2-DG received emergency approval as an add-on therapy (2021).
  • Drones and robots: ICMR's i-Drone delivered vaccines to remote areas of the North-East (2021), and robots disinfected wards.

3. Vaccination

  • New platforms: mRNA vaccines (Pfizer–BioNTech, Moderna), whose science won Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman the Nobel Prize (2023); India added viral-vector Covishield, inactivated Covaxin, ZyCoV-D (the world's first human DNA vaccine, 2021), Corbevax and the nasal iNCOVACC.
  • Digital delivery: CoWIN (2021) handled registration, slot booking and certificates in DigiLocker for over 220 crore doses, and the eVIN network tracked vaccine stocks and cold-chain temperatures.
  • Global role: Vaccine Maitri supplied vaccines abroad, and CoWIN was offered to other countries as open-source software.

4. Keeping society running

  • Cash and food: Direct Benefit Transfers to Jan Dhan accounts and One Nation One Ration Card portability reached migrants and the poor.
  • Work and learning: online classes through PM eVIDYA and DIKSHA, and work from home on digital networks.

5. Limits and lessons

  • Digital divide: the Supreme Court flagged CoWIN's online-only registration in 2021, and privacy concerns surrounded tracing apps.
  • Infodemic and inequity: misinformation spread fast, and poorer countries got vaccines late.

COVID-19 showed that science and digital public goods can save millions of lives. Investing in genomic surveillance, vaccine platforms and health systems, and in the WHO Pandemic Agreement (2025), is the best pandemic preparedness.
free.upm-2020-gs3-16:
Solar energyPhotovoltaic effectEnergy securityNational Solar Mission

Solar power converts sunlight into electricity through photovoltaic (PV) cells or, in concentrated solar power, through heat. India receives about 4–7 kWh of solar energy per square metre a day on roughly 300 sunny days, a potential of about 748 GWp (National Institute of Solar Energy). Installed solar capacity reached about 171 GW by 30 September 2026 (MNRE), the largest part of India's renewable capacity.

1. Benefits over conventional generation

  • Clean power: solar plants emit no carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide or fly ash while operating, supporting India's targets of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.
  • Energy security: sunlight is a free, domestic resource, unlike imported coal, oil and gas whose prices swing with global events.
  • Low and stable cost: with no fuel bill, solar tariffs in auctions have fallen to among the cheapest sources of new power.
  • Modular and quick: projects range from a rooftop to a gigawatt-scale park and can be built in months, against years for a thermal plant.
  • Decentralised access and incomes: rooftops and solar pumps make households and farmers "prosumers", and off-grid systems reach remote villages; Modhera (Gujarat) became India's first round-the-clock solar village (2022).
  • Less water use: coal plants need large volumes of cooling water; solar panels need little.

2. Government initiatives

  • National Solar Mission (2010): one of the eight missions of the National Action Plan on Climate Change; its target of 20 GW by 2022 was raised to 100 GW in 2015.
  • Solar Parks scheme (2014): ready land and transmission for large parks such as Bhadla (Rajasthan) and Pavagada (Karnataka); the target was raised to 40 GW.
  • Farmers and homes: PM-KUSUM (2019) for solar pumps and farm plants (about 25 lakh pumps, 13.1 GW by March 2026), and PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024, ₹75,021 crore) for rooftop solar with up to 300 free units a month, which had reached over 50 lakh homes by August 2026.
  • Manufacturing: a ₹24,000 crore PLI scheme for high-efficiency modules, and the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers, extended to solar cells from 1 June 2026.
  • Grid and storage: Green Energy Corridors, viability gap funding for battery storage, and the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana (2026) for 5,000 MW of floating solar with storage.
  • Global leadership: the International Solar Alliance (India and France, 2015) and the Green Grids Initiative–One Sun One World One Grid (2021).

3. Challenges

  • Capacity is not generation: non-fossil sources gave only 29.2% of electricity in 2025-26, because solar works only by day.
  • Storage, land and supply chains: evening peaks need batteries or pumped storage; large parks need land; China dominates polysilicon and wafers.

Solar energy can give India clean, cheap and secure power. Scaling up storage, grids and domestic manufacturing will turn installed capacity into round-the-clock supply.
free.upm-2020-gs3-17:
National Clean Air ProgrammeNon-attainment citiesCity action plansAirshed management

Air pollution is among India's leading health risks, and many cities exceed the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009), which set an annual limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM10 and 40 µg/m³ for PM2.5. In January 2019 the MoEFCC launched the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), India's first national, time-bound strategy for clean air, covering 130 cities, mostly non-attainment cities that repeatedly fail the standards.

1. Goals and coverage

  • Targets: originally a 20–30% cut in particulate pollution by 2024 from 2017 levels; later revised to a reduction of up to 40% in PM10 by 2025-26, or meeting the national standard.
  • City-specific approach: each non-attainment city prepares a city action plan against its main sources: road and construction dust, vehicles, industry, waste and biomass burning.
  • Science base: source-apportionment and emission-inventory studies, with IITs and other institutions as knowledge partners.

2. Funding and convergence

  • Performance-linked grants: funds are tied to measured improvement in air quality; 82 smaller cities are funded by the MoEFCC and 48 million-plus cities and urban agglomerations through air-quality grants recommended by the Fifteenth Finance Commission; about ₹16,400 crore had been released from 2019-20 to 2025-26 (PIB, July 2026).
  • Convergence: works are aligned with Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban), AMRUT, the Smart Cities Mission, SATAT (compressed biogas), electric-mobility schemes and Nagar Van Yojana.

3. Institutions, monitoring and participation

  • Multi-level committees: at the national, State and city levels to plan, review and coordinate departments.
  • Monitoring: a wider network of manual and continuous monitoring stations, and the PRANA portal (Portal for Regulation of Air-pollution in Non-Attainment cities) to track progress.
  • Competition and awareness: Swachh Vayu Survekshan ranks cities each year; the National Air Quality Index (8 pollutants, 6 bands) informs citizens.
  • Complementary measures: BS-VI fuel norms (April 2020), Ujjwala LPG, and the Commission for Air Quality Management with GRAP for Delhi-NCR.

4. Results as of 2026

In 2025-26, the target year, 108 cities had lower PM10 levels than in 2017-18, but only 26 had cut PM10 by more than 40% and only 14 met the PM10 standard (PIB, July 2026).

5. Gaps

  • Wrong pollutant focus: targets are set for PM10 (largely dust), though PM2.5 does most harm to health.
  • City boundaries vs airsheds: pollution in the Indo-Gangetic Plain crosses city and State lines.
  • Weak enforcement: under-staffed pollution control boards, slow use of funds, no statutory backing, and the 2025 relaxation of sulphur-dioxide norms for many coal plants.

NCAP has created a framework, data and funding for clean air, but not yet clean air itself. Its next phase needs PM2.5 targets, airshed-level planning across States, stronger regulators and a focus on public health.
free.upm-2020-gs3-18:
Disaster risk reductionDisaster Management Act, 2005Sendai FrameworkEarly warning

For decades India's disaster management was reactive: Relief Codes, Relief Commissioners and calamity relief funds came into play only after a disaster struck. The Odisha super cyclone (1999), the Bhuj earthquake (2001) and the Indian Ocean tsunami (2004) changed this. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 shifted the focus to prevention, mitigation and preparedness, and since 2015 India has aligned its policies with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030).

1. Institutional and legal shift

  • Dedicated authorities: the NDMA (chaired by the Prime Minister), SDMAs (Chief Ministers), DDMAs (Collectors), the NDRF (raised 2006; 16 battalions) and the National Institute of Disaster Management.
  • Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025: the NDMA and SDMAs now prepare national and State plans; national and State disaster databases; Urban Disaster Management Authorities for State capitals and large cities; statutory status for the National Crisis Management Committee; and State Disaster Response Forces.
  • Plans and policy: the National Policy on Disaster Management (2009), India's first National Disaster Management Plan (2016, revised 2019), aligned with Sendai, and the Prime Minister's Ten-Point Agenda (2016).

2. Money for mitigation, not just relief

  • Mitigation funds: the Fifteenth Finance Commission created separate mitigation funds alongside response funds at the national and State levels.
  • Risk-reduction projects: cyclone shelters and early-warning systems under the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project, the Urban Flood Risk Management Programme, dam safety under the Dam Safety Act, 2021, and heat action plans, pioneered by Ahmedabad (2013).
  • Resilient infrastructure: the India-led Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019), and Disaster Risk Reduction made a G20 working group under India's presidency (2023).

3. Early warning and technology

  • Better forecasts: IMD's impact-based, colour-coded warnings, the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS (2007) and Mission Mausam (2024).
  • Last-mile alerts: SACHET, based on the Common Alerting Protocol, works in all 36 States and UTs, and cell-broadcast alerts were added in 2026.
  • Results: Odisha's warnings and community shelters helped evacuate about a million people before Cyclone Phailin (2013), sharply cutting deaths.

4. Communities and capacity

  • Aapda Mitra: trained community volunteers, scaled up from a pilot in 30 districts to 350 districts.
  • Drills and inclusion: mock drills, school safety, and NDMA guidelines on disability-inclusive risk reduction (2019).
  • International role: search-and-rescue missions such as Operation Dost (Türkiye, 2023) and Operation Brahma (Myanmar, 2025).

India has moved from relief to risk reduction, but urban floods, heat waves and landslides show the gaps that remain. Making every new road, school and house safer, the essence of risk-informed development, is the next step.
free.upm-2020-gs3-19:
Left Wing ExtremismRed CorridorTribal alienationSAMADHAN

Left Wing Extremism (LWE), or Naxalism, began with the Naxalbari uprising (1967) in West Bengal and was consolidated as the CPI (Maoist) in 2004. Its stronghold was the forested, mineral-rich and largely tribal Red Corridor of eastern and central-eastern India: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Bihar and West Bengal. As of 2026 its reach has shrunk sharply: seven districts were affected by February 2026, and on 30 March 2026 the Home Minister told the Lok Sabha that Naxalism had been "wiped out".

1. Determinants of LWE in eastern India

  • Land alienation: despite protective laws such as the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act (1908) and the Santhal Pargana Tenancy Act (1949), tribal land passed to outsiders; in Bihar, caste and agrarian conflict saw private landlord armies such as the Ranvir Sena.
  • Displacement by mines and industry: Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh hold much of India's coal and iron ore, but displacement without fair rehabilitation left local people with the costs and few benefits.
  • Forest rights and governance deficit: harassment over forest produce, weak implementation of PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006), and absent schools, health care, roads and banks; a Planning Commission expert group (2008) saw LWE as a development challenge.
  • Terrain: dense forests such as Saranda (Jharkhand) and Abujhmarh (Chhattisgarh) and inter-State tri-junctions gave safe havens.
  • Maoist organisation and extortion: cadres exploited these grievances and ran on levies from mining, tendu-leaf trade and contractors.

2. Strategy: Government of India

  • Policy framework: the National Policy and Action Plan (2015) and the SAMADHAN doctrine (2017): smart leadership, aggressive strategy, motivation, actionable intelligence, dashboards, harnessing technology, action plans for each theatre and no access to financing.
  • Funds and connectivity: Security Related Expenditure and Special Central Assistance schemes, roads and mobile towers in affected districts, and the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018).
  • Coordination: CAPF deployment, including CoBRA units, joint inter-State operations, and NIA and ED action against Maoist funding.

3. Strategy: civil administration

  • Rights first: forest-rights titles, PESA and gram sabha consent (Niyamgiri, 2013), and fair compensation under the LARR Act, 2013.
  • Saturating services: 1,804 bank branches and 635 post offices in affected areas over 12 years, Eklavya schools, ITIs, PM-JANMAN and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan.
  • Responsive officials: filled vacancies, officers who stay in remote postings, and surrender-and-rehabilitation policies.

4. Strategy: security forces

  • State police in the lead: specialised forces modelled on Andhra Pradesh's Greyhounds and Chhattisgarh's District Reserve Guard, supported by CAPFs.
  • Clear, hold, build: fortified police stations and forward camps that let roads and services follow.
  • Restraint and trust: respect for human rights, local recruitment and civic action, so that operations win, not alienate, villagers.

The near-elimination of armed Maoism shows that security plus development works. Lasting peace now depends on good governance in tribal areas, so that the grievances that fed LWE do not return.
free.upm-2020-gs3-20:
Transborder crimesLine of ControlPorous bordersBorder guarding forces

India has a 15,106.7 km land border with seven countries. Three of them pose the sharpest internal security challenges: Bangladesh (4,096.7 km, India's longest border), Pakistan (3,323 km, running into the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir) and Myanmar (1,643 km). Riverine, forested and mountainous terrain, ethnic ties across the border and hostile actors make these borders conduits for transborder crimes.

1. Myanmar border

  • Insurgent sanctuaries: groups from the North-East have used camps across the border, and holdout factions still operate from there.
  • Drugs and arms: heroin and methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle enter through Manipur and Mizoram, and arms from Myanmar's civil conflict reach militant groups.
  • Refugees and ethnic conflict: the 2021 coup pushed refugees into Mizoram and Manipur, and cross-border ties have fed tensions in Manipur since May 2023.
  • Response: the Free Movement Regime was cut from 16 km to 10 km, with border passes (December 2024), and the Cabinet Committee on Security approved ₹31,000 crore to fence the whole border (2024); yet only about 44 km had been fenced by March 2026 (about 55 km in Manipur by September 2026).

2. Bangladesh border

  • Illegal migration and trafficking: riverine and char lands ease illegal entry and trafficking of women and children.
  • Smuggling: cattle, fake Indian currency notes (especially in the Malda belt), cough-syrup drugs, gold and arms.
  • Extremism: networks such as the Jamaat-ul-Mujahideen Bangladesh, exposed by the Burdwan blast (2014).

3. Pakistan border and the LoC

  • Cross-border terrorism: infiltration across the LoC and the Jammu frontier, cross-border tunnels and ceasefire violations; the Pahalgam attack (22 April 2025) led to Operation Sindoor.
  • Narco-terror: drones drop heroin and weapons in Punjab; the BSF seized 272 drones between January and November 2025.
  • Other crimes: smuggling across the Rajasthan and Gujarat frontier and the Sir Creek area, and fake currency.

4. Role of security forces

  • One border, one force: after the Kargil Review Committee, the Group of Ministers (2001) assigned one force to each border to fix accountability; the SSB guards Nepal and Bhutan, and the ITBP the China frontier.
  • Guarding and technology: fencing, floodlighting, border outposts and the Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System (as in BOLD-QIT at Dhubri, 2019), with anti-drone and anti-tunnel measures.
  • Counter-insurgency: the Army and Assam Rifles conduct operations in Jammu and Kashmir and the North-East, while CAPFs and State police act inland.
  • Investigation and intelligence: the NIA (terror and fake currency), NCB (drugs), DRI (smuggling), ED (hawala) and intelligence agencies.
  • Cooperation and outreach: BSF–BGB talks under the Coordinated Border Management Plan (2011), and civic action, BADP and the Vibrant Villages Programme-II (2025) in border villages.

India's borders need integrated border management: smart technology, coordination among forces and agencies, cooperation with neighbours and prosperous border communities that act as the nation's eyes and ears.
free.upm-2020-gs4-1a:
Comprehensive National PowerHuman capitalSoft powerSocial harmony

Comprehensive National Power (CNP), a concept developed by Chinese strategists, measures a nation's total strength: not only its economy, armed forces and technology, but also intangibles such as the quality of its people, the appeal of its culture and the cohesion of its society. These intangibles rest on ethics and values. Honesty, discipline, compassion and tolerance turn a population into human capital, culture and policy into soft power (Joseph Nye's term), and diversity into social harmony.

1. Human capital: values make people productive

  • Work ethic and integrity: punctuality, diligence and honesty raise productivity and reduce the cost of supervision; trust between employers, workers and the state lowers the cost of every transaction.
  • Ethics of care in health and education: treating schooling (Article 21A) and public health (Article 47) as moral duties, not mere expenditure, builds a healthy and skilled workforce; Kerala's record in literacy and health shows the payoff.
  • Gender justice: equal opportunity for women brings half the nation's talent into the economy; female labour force participation of about 42% (PLFS 2023-24) shows how much is still lost.
  • Value-based learning: NEP 2020 places ethical and constitutional values in the curriculum, and Mission Karmayogi (2020) builds both competence and integrity in the civil service.

2. Soft power: credibility comes from values

  • Culture: yoga (the UN General Assembly declared the International Day of Yoga in 2014), the Buddha's message and Gandhian non-violence (2 October is the UN's International Day of Non-Violence) win admiration abroad.
  • Political values: a working democracy, pluralism and peaceful transfers of power make India's voice credible in the Global South.
  • Policies with a moral core: Vaccine Maitri (2021), Operation Dost after the Türkiye–Syria earthquake (2023) and the G20 presidency's theme of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (One Earth, One Family, One Future), during which the African Union became a permanent G20 member (2023), show power used for others.
  • Consistency: soft power evaporates when words and deeds diverge; keeping promises is its real currency.

3. Social harmony: values hold a diverse nation together

  • Fraternity: the Preamble's promise of fraternity and the duty to promote harmony (Article 51A(e)) turn diversity into strength rather than a fault line.
  • Tolerance and constitutional morality: respect for others' faith, language and customs prevents conflicts that drain security budgets and scare investors.
  • Social capital: trust and civic cooperation multiply the state's capacity, as when Kerala's fishermen rescued thousands of people during the 2018 floods.
  • Justice for the weak: fair treatment of weaker sections (Article 46) prevents alienation and extremism, which are the costliest threats to national power.

Tangible power can be bought or built quickly, but its intangible core grows only from values. A nation whose people are honest and capable, whose conduct abroad is principled and whose society is united possesses the most durable form of national power.
free.upm-2020-gs4-1b:
Holistic educationNEP 2020Critical thinkingSocial transformation

An injunction is a command: a list of dos and don'ts imposed from above and memorised for examinations. The statement holds that true education is the opposite, a pervasive process that develops the whole person (intellect, character, body and emotions) and, through such individuals, transforms society. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, approved on 29 July 2020 on the basis of the Kasturirangan Committee's draft, replaced the 1986 policy and largely shares this vision of holistic and multidisciplinary education.

1. All-round development of the individual

  • Strong foundations: the 5+3+3+4 structure brings pre-school (ages 3–6) into the system, and NIPUN Bharat (2021) aims at foundational literacy and numeracy for every child by Class 3.
  • Understanding over rote: experiential and inquiry-based learning, a curriculum reduced to its core essentials, and board examinations that test core competencies rather than memory.
  • No hard separations: between arts and sciences, curricular and extra-curricular activities, or academic and vocational streams; vocational exposure with internships begins in the middle stage.
  • Character and confidence: ethics, constitutional values, sports and arts, and teaching in the mother tongue wherever possible, at least till Class 5 (preferably till Class 8); a 360-degree holistic progress card replaces a marks-only report.

2. A tool of social transformation

  • Equity: special attention to Socio-Economically Disadvantaged Groups, a Gender-Inclusion Fund and Special Education Zones for disadvantaged regions.
  • Wider access: a target of 50% gross enrolment in higher education by 2035, multiple entry and exit points, and an Academic Bank of Credits.
  • Knowledge society: the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF Act, 2023) for research, and respect for Indian languages and knowledge systems.
  • Dignity of labour: the aim that at least half of all learners have vocational exposure by 2025 links learning with livelihoods.

3. Where practice still falls short (as of 2026)

  • Learning crisis: ASER 2024 found that only 23.4% of Class 3 children in rural government schools could read a Class 2 text, so the foundations remain weak.
  • Resources: public spending is still well below the policy's goal of 6% of GDP, and teacher vacancies and training gaps persist.
  • Exam culture: high-stakes entrance tests and coaching keep learning narrow and stressful, the very injunction-style education the policy rejects.
  • Federal concerns: some States object to aspects such as the three-language formula; the plan for one umbrella regulator in place of the UGC, AICTE and NCTE (the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, introduced in December 2025 and still before a Joint Parliamentary Committee as of October 2026) has raised concerns about autonomy.

NEP 2020 treats education as a transformative tool rather than an injunction. Its promise will be realised only when funding, trained teachers, assessment reform and cooperative federalism let classrooms practise what the policy preaches: learning for life.
free.upm-2020-gs4-2a:
HatredWisdom and conscienceDehumanisationFraternity

Hatred is an intense and lasting hostility towards a person or group, unlike anger, which is a passing reaction to a particular wrong. I agree with the view. Hatred blinds wisdom, our capacity to judge truly, and silences conscience, the inner voice that tells right from wrong. When it spreads from individuals to groups, it erodes the fraternity that the Preamble names as the basis of the nation's unity and integrity.

1. Hatred destroys wisdom

  • Distorted thinking: prejudice, stereotypes and confirmation bias make a person see only what confirms his hatred and ignore facts that contradict it.
  • Emotional hijack: intense negative emotion overrides reasoning, so decisions become impulsive and self-defeating; Daniel Goleman calls this an amygdala hijack.
  • Self-harm: the Dhammapada teaches that hatred never ends through hatred, only through non-hatred; the hater suffers first, through stress, bitterness and isolation.

2. Hatred silences conscience

  • Dehumanisation: hatred turns people into enemies or vermin, so cruelty no longer feels wrong; before the Rwandan genocide (1994), radio propaganda called Tutsis cockroaches, and about 800,000 people were killed in some 100 days.
  • Moral disengagement: the psychologist Albert Bandura showed how people justify harm by blaming victims or claiming a higher cause.
  • Collective guilt: blaming a whole community for the acts of a few licenses violence against the innocent.

3. Hatred poisons a nation's spirit

  • History: the communal frenzy of Partition (1947) killed hundreds of thousands of people and left scars that still shape politics.
  • Mob violence: rumour-driven lynchings led the Supreme Court in Tehseen Poonawalla (2018) to lay down preventive, remedial and punitive measures; in the hate-speech cases (2022–23) it directed the police to register cases on their own, without waiting for complaints.
  • Lost development: riots and polarisation divert police and budgets, scare investors and harden segregated neighbourhoods.
  • Weakened democracy: citizens who hate cannot deliberate; public debate turns into tribal warfare, amplified by social media.

4. A nuance: indignation is not hatred

  • Moral anger at injustice can drive reform: public outrage after the December 2012 Delhi gang-rape led to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013. Indignation targets wrong acts; hatred targets people.
  • Opposing the wrong, not the wrongdoer: Gandhi resisted British rule without hating the British, and Nelson Mandela chose reconciliation over revenge after apartheid.

Hatred begins by harming the hater and ends by dividing the nation. Compassion, critical thinking, impartial enforcement of law and constitutional morality are its antidotes; for a civil servant, freedom from hatred is the precondition of impartiality.
free.upm-2020-gs4-2b:
Emotional intelligenceGoleman's five componentsLearnabilityNeuroplasticity

Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions and to recognise and influence the emotions of others. Peter Salovey and John Mayer defined it in 1990, and Daniel Goleman's Emotional Intelligence (1995) popularised it, arguing that it can matter as much as IQ for success at work and in life. For civil servants, who deal daily with distressed citizens, political pressure and crises, EI is a core competence.

1. Main components of EI

  • Personal and social competences: the first three components concern managing oneself (personal competence); empathy and social skills concern managing relationships (social competence), and all of them build on self-awareness.
  • The ability model: Mayer and Salovey describe four branches: perceiving emotions, using them to aid thinking, understanding them, and managing them.

2. Can EI be learned? Largely, yes

  • Neuroplasticity: the brain keeps changing with experience and practice, so emotional habits can be reshaped at any age; Goleman argues that EI competencies, unlike IQ, can be substantially developed.
  • Evidence from schools: social and emotional learning programmes, such as Delhi's Happiness Curriculum (2018) in government schools, teach mindfulness, reflection and empathy.
  • Training at work: role plays, case studies, 360-degree feedback, coaching and mentoring improve self-awareness and social skills; Mission Karmayogi courses cover behavioural competencies such as conflict resolution and leadership.
  • Personal practice: journaling, mindfulness and meditation, yoga, perspective-taking and exposure to diverse people, such as village stays during civil-service training, build empathy.

3. Limits to learning

  • Temperament: part of emotional style is inherited and shaped in early childhood, so change is gradual and uneven.
  • Practice, not lectures: knowing about EI is not the same as having it; skills need repeated real-life practice.
  • Ethical direction: EI can be used to manipulate others; it must be anchored in integrity and values.

4. Why it matters for civil servants

  • Crisis management: calm officers make better decisions during riots, disasters and epidemics.
  • Citizen interface: empathy turns rule-bound service into citizen-centric service.
  • Leadership: emotionally intelligent leaders build motivated, trusting teams.
  • Integrity under pressure: self-regulation helps an officer resist both inducements and intimidation.

EI is less a fixed gift than a set of learnable skills. Combined with integrity, it makes a civil servant calm in crisis, fair in judgement and compassionate in service.
free.upm-2020-gs4-3a:
Middle PathFour Noble TruthsKaruna and ahimsaRational inquiry

Gautama Buddha (6th–5th century BCE) attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and gave his first sermon at Sarnath. His core teaching, the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, offers a Middle Path between indulgence and self-mortification. He traced suffering to three roots: greed, hatred and delusion. Two and a half millennia later, a world troubled by conflict, consumerism, climate change, inequality and mental stress finds these teachings strikingly relevant.

1. For the individual: mind and conduct

  • Craving as the root of suffering: consumerism, debt and status anxiety show how unlimited desires breed discontent; contentment and moderation are the remedy.
  • Mindfulness (sati) and right effort: meditation reduces stress, anger and addiction; Vipassana courses held in Tihar Jail since the 1990s have helped prisoners reform.
  • Rational inquiry: in the Kalama Sutta the Buddha asked people not to accept a teaching merely because of tradition, scripture or a teacher's authority, but to test it by experience; this is the best antidote to fake news and blind faith.

2. For society: equality and compassion

  • Equality: the Sangha was open to all castes, and women were admitted as nuns; B.R. Ambedkar embraced Buddhism at Nagpur in 1956 as a faith of equality, liberty and fraternity.
  • Karuna and maitri: compassion and loving-kindness counter hate speech, polarisation and indifference to the poor.
  • Right livelihood: earning without harming others, avoiding trade in weapons, poisons and intoxicants, is a guide for business ethics.

3. For the world: peace and sustainability

  • Ahimsa and peace: amid recent wars in Europe and West Asia, his teaching that hatred is not ended by hatred shows that violence only breeds violence; Ashoka turned from conquest to Dhamma after Kalinga.
  • Interdependence (pratityasamutpada): everything arises in dependence on other things, which mirrors ecology and globalisation, where one country's emissions or epidemic affects all.
  • Middle Path and sustainability: moderate consumption is the spirit of India's Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment).

4. For governance

  • Ethical leadership: Ashoka's edicts on tolerance and welfare; the Dharma Chakra on the national flag and the Sarnath lion capital as the State Emblem.
  • Deliberation: the Sangha decided matters by discussion and consensus, an early model of participatory decision-making.
  • Public service: right speech, right action and compassion translate into honesty, courtesy and service to citizens.

The Buddha's teachings endure because they address the root causes of suffering rather than its symptoms. His Middle Path of reason, compassion and moderation guides individuals, societies and nations alike, and it remains a major source of India's soft power.
free.upm-2020-gs4-3b:
Will to powerRealismMoral dutyRules-based order

The phrase will to power comes from Friedrich Nietzsche, for whom the drive to assert and expand oneself is basic to life. In international relations, classical realists such as Hans Morgenthau (Politics Among Nations, 1948) see politics as a struggle for power among states in an anarchic world. The statement accepts this reality but holds, in the spirit of Immanuel Kant, that reason and moral duty can tame and direct it. History largely supports this view, within limits.

1. The will to power exists

  • War and conquest: colonialism, two World Wars and the Cold War arms race; the Russia–Ukraine war (since 2022) shows that force has not disappeared.
  • Arms build-up: world military spending reached US$2,887 billion in 2025, the eleventh consecutive annual rise (SIPRI, April 2026).
  • Power in institutions: the veto lets the five permanent members block Security Council action.
  • Melian logic: Thucydides' account of Athens telling the Melians that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must still describes many power relations.

2. Rationality tames it

  • Enlightened self-interest: nuclear deterrence and arms control (NPT, 1968) show that the rational fear of mutual destruction restrains even great powers.
  • Interdependence: trade, investment and supply chains raise the cost of war, and the WTO settles trade disputes by rules.
  • Institutions: the UN Charter's ban on the use of force (Article 2(4)), collective security and the International Court of Justice replace might with procedure.
  • Restraint in doctrine: India's nuclear doctrine (2003) of no first use and credible minimum deterrence is power disciplined by reason.

3. Moral duty guides it

  • Kant: his Perpetual Peace (1795) proposed a federation of free states, and his ethics demands that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means.
  • Ashoka: after the bloodshed of Kalinga he replaced conquest by war with conquest by Dhamma.
  • Humanitarian norms: the Geneva Conventions (1949), the Responsibility to Protect (2005) and climate justice through common but differentiated responsibilities.
  • India's practice: Panchsheel (1954), non-alignment, Vaccine Maitri and the G20 theme of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (2023); at Samarkand in 2022 the Prime Minister told the Russian President that this is not an era of war.

4. Limits of the taming

  • Selective morality: great powers invoke principles against rivals but not allies; critics argue that NATO's Libya operation (2011) moved from protecting civilians to regime change.
  • Weak enforcement: international law depends on the consent of states, and vetoes often paralyse the Security Council.
  • Unequal order: institutions still reflect the power balance of 1945, so their reform is itself a moral demand.

The will to power cannot be abolished, but it can be civilised. Power guided by reason produces stability; power guided also by duty produces justice. A rules-based order, reformed to be more representative, is the practical meeting point of the two.
free.upm-2020-gs4-4a:
Law and rulesDelegated legislationUltra viresInner morality of law

Laws are general, binding norms made by the legislature (Acts of Parliament or a State Legislature) and enforced by the state through the courts. Rules are a form of delegated legislation: detailed provisions framed by the executive under powers conferred by a parent Act or by the Constitution, to carry the law into effect. Article 13(3)(a) includes rules, regulations and notifications having the force of law in the meaning of law. In a wider sense, rules also include organisations' internal norms.

1. Laws and rules distinguished

  • Hierarchy: a rule cannot override or go beyond its parent Act; courts strike down rules that do so (ultra vires) or that rest on excessive delegation.
  • Legislative oversight: the Committees on Subordinate Legislation examine whether rules stay within the powers delegated.
  • Rules of conduct: the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964, framed under Article 309, show how rules shape behaviour within government.

2. Role of ethics in formulating them

  • Justice and fairness: John Rawls' veil of ignorance asks law-makers to design rules they would accept without knowing their own position in society, which protects the weakest.
  • Non-arbitrariness and proportionality: Article 14 forbids arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa, 1974), and limits on rights must be proportionate (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017); vague, sweeping provisions fail, as Section 66A of the IT Act did in Shreya Singhal (2015).
  • Participation and transparency: the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014) asks ministries to publish draft laws for at least 30 days of public comment, treating citizens as partners.
  • Inner morality of law: Lon Fuller (The Morality of Law, 1964) argued that laws must be general, public, prospective, clear, consistent, possible to obey, stable, and applied as written.
  • Responsiveness to the vulnerable: the Vishaka guidelines (1997) led to the POSH Act, 2013; the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 decriminalised 183 provisions in 42 Acts, removing fear-based rules for minor lapses.

3. Ethics in applying them

  • Spirit over letter: rules are means, not ends; officers must use discretion with compassion and record their reasons.
  • Review: rules that have outlived their purpose should be repealed rather than enforced mechanically.

Laws and rules give ethics the force of the state, while ethics gives laws their legitimacy. A law that is just in content, fair in procedure and humane in application commands willing obedience: the essence of the rule of law.
free.upm-2020-gs4-4b:
Positive attitudeResilienceSelf-efficacyStress management

An attitude is a learned tendency to think, feel and act in a particular way towards people, objects or situations. A positive attitude is not blind cheerfulness but realistic optimism: it treats problems as solvable and setbacks as temporary. Civil servants face disasters, law-and-order crises, political pressure, public scrutiny and frequent transfers; a positive attitude provides the resilience to decide calmly and keep serving under such stress.

1. Why it matters under stress

  • Clear thinking: calm officers decide better in crises; panic is contagious, and so is composure.
  • Team morale: a positive leader energises subordinates and builds trust with citizens.
  • Example: Odisha's administration worked towards a goal of zero casualties before Cyclone Phailin (2013); mass evacuation kept deaths to a few dozen, against about 10,000 in the 1999 super cyclone.

2. Personal (internal) factors

  • Values and sense of purpose: a strong motivation to serve makes hardship meaningful; the Gita's teaching of doing one's duty without attachment to its fruits reduces anxiety about outcomes.
  • Self-efficacy: Albert Bandura showed that belief in one's ability to succeed, built through mastery experiences, sustains effort under difficulty.
  • Growth mindset and optimism: Carol Dweck's research shows that people who see ability as something that can be developed treat failure as learning; Martin Seligman showed that optimism can be learned by changing how we explain setbacks to ourselves.
  • Emotional intelligence: self-awareness and self-regulation let a person manage anger, fear and frustration.
  • Physical and mental health: sleep, exercise, yoga and meditation build tolerance for stress.

3. Social and organisational factors

  • Family and upbringing: encouragement, security and role models shape early attitudes.
  • Mentors and peers: seniors who stay calm under pressure teach by example; a supportive team shares the burden.
  • Organisational culture: fair appraisal, recognition (such as the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration), protection for honest decisions and stable tenures reduce cynicism.
  • Training and support: Mission Karmayogi's behavioural modules, counselling and stress-management programmes.
  • Work–life balance: time for family, hobbies and rest prevents burnout.

4. Experience and reflection

  • Small wins: each solved problem strengthens confidence, and reflection turns setbacks into lessons.
  • Role models: Armstrong Pame built a 100-km road in Manipur (2012) largely through public contributions when funds were lacking, showing how optimism mobilises others.

A positive attitude grows from inner resources (values, self-belief, emotional balance and health) and outer support (family, mentors and a fair organisation). It can be cultivated, and it is the foundation of resilient public service.
free.upm-2020-gs4-5a:
Gender inequalityPatriarchySavitribai PhuleWomen's education

India ranked 131st of 145 in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2026, showing that constitutional equality (Articles 14, 15 and 16) has yet to become social reality. Gender inequality is rooted in patriarchy, the norms that rank men above women in the family, the economy and public life. In the nineteenth century Savitribai Phule (1831–1897), often called India's first woman teacher, challenged these norms through education and social reform.

1. Main factors responsible for gender inequality

  • Socio-cultural: son preference (a sex ratio at birth of 929 girls per 1,000 boys, NFHS-5), dowry, child marriage (23.3% of women aged 20–24 were married before 18, NFHS-5) and restrictions on women's mobility.
  • Economic: female labour force participation of only 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24); women spent about 299 minutes a day on unpaid domestic work against 97 minutes for men (Time Use Survey, 2019); few women own land or assets.
  • Educational and digital: girls drop out at the transition to secondary school, and only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5).
  • Safety: violence at home and in public spaces limits women's education, work and freedom of movement.
  • Political and institutional: only 74 women (about 14%) were elected to the Lok Sabha in 2024; the one-third reservation under the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (2023) awaits delimitation, and laws are unevenly enforced.

2. Contribution of Savitribai Phule

  • Pioneer of women's education: with her husband Jyotirao Phule she started a school for girls in Pune in 1848 and taught there herself, despite public hostility and abuse.
  • Against caste and gender together: the Phules ran schools for children of the so-called untouchable castes and opened their family water tank to them (1868).
  • Widows and unwed mothers: their home for the prevention of infanticide (Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha, 1863) sheltered pregnant widows; the couple adopted a widow's son, Yashwant, and opposed the tonsuring of widows.
  • Satyashodhak Samaj (1873): she led its work among women and promoted marriages without priests or dowry.
  • Literature and service: her poems (Kavya Phule, 1854) urged the oppressed to seek education; she died in 1897 while nursing plague patients in Pune.

3. Relevance today

  • Education as liberation: her conviction underlies the RTE Act (2009), Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015) and Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas; Pune University was renamed Savitribai Phule Pune University in 2014.
  • Intersectionality: she saw that caste and gender oppression reinforce each other, a lesson for policies on Dalit and tribal women.

Gender inequality is sustained by mindsets as much as by material gaps. Savitribai showed that education, courage and community action can break both; completing her work requires equal opportunity in work, safety, property and political voice.
free.upm-2020-gs4-5b:
Digital cultureTraditional valuesCultural lagDigital citizenship

Cheap smartphones and data have made India one of the world's largest online societies. The internet carries a distinct set of cultural values: individualism, instant gratification, openness, self-expression and global consumerism. These often clash with traditional values of family hierarchy, restraint, community, modesty and continuity. The sociologist William Ogburn called the strain that arises when technology changes faster than norms cultural lag.

1. Values the internet promotes

  • Individualism and self-expression: social media rewards personal branding, choice and visibility.
  • Instant gratification: short videos, one-click shopping and gaming train people to expect immediate rewards.
  • Questioning authority: information is open to all, so traditional sources of authority, such as elders, priests and teachers, are challenged.
  • Global and fluid identities: online communities built on shared interests cut across caste, region and nation.
  • Novelty over continuity: constant updates and trends reward the new and the viral, weakening respect for inherited customs and slow, patient learning.

2. Where they conflict with traditional values

  • Social harms: NCRB recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024; gaming addiction, pornography and deepfakes worry families and the state.
  • Consumerism: advertising-driven platforms promote a culture of wanting more, against traditions of thrift and sufficiency.

3. Not only conflict: the other side

  • Reform of unjust traditions: exposure to ideas of equality and rights has helped women and Dalits voice grievances, as in India's #MeToo movement (2018).
  • Revival of tradition: online platforms spread folk arts, classical music, yoga, regional-language content and religious services, and keep the diaspora connected to its roots.
  • Hybrid values: many young Indians combine global careers with family obligations, and online matrimonial platforms still involve families.
  • Old bonds, new media: family messaging groups, video calls with grandparents and online religious gatherings show traditional ties adapting to technology rather than vanishing.

4. Way forward

  • Digital literacy and citizenship: PMGDISHA (2017) and school lessons on safe, responsible and critical use of online content.
  • Regulation: the IT Rules, 2021 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (being phased in) protect users, especially children.
  • Family dialogue: shared screen norms rather than bans, and value education that blends rootedness with openness.

Internet values and traditional values need not be enemies. A balanced synthesis, keeping tradition's emphasis on community and restraint and the internet's emphasis on freedom and equality, is the path to a mature digital society.
free.upm-2020-gs4-6a:
Non-judgementCompassionToleranceRespect for autonomy

Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), the disciple of Sri Ramakrishna who spoke at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago (1893) and founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897), asks us to give up condemning others and to replace condemnation with help, or at least with goodwill. The quotation combines compassion, humility and respect for the freedom of others to live according to their own understanding.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Condemn none: judging others is easy and usually ill-informed, because we rarely know their circumstances, struggles or intentions; condemnation hardens divisions and helps no one.
  • Help when you can: compassion must turn into action, and a helping hand is worth more than a lecture.
  • Bless when you cannot: where we cannot help, or help is not wanted, we should wish people well and step back gracefully; folded hands signify humility, not indifference.
  • Let them go their own way: respect the autonomy of others; different paths, faiths and ways of life are legitimate, in keeping with Ramakrishna's teaching that many paths lead to the same truth.

2. Values involved

  • Compassion and tolerance: concern for others' welfare combined with acceptance of difference.
  • Humility: recognising the limits of one's knowledge, and that one may be wrong about others.
  • Dignity and autonomy: every person is entitled to choose his or her own path within the law.
  • Non-violence in thought and speech: harsh judgement is a form of violence.

3. Examples from public life

  • Vivekananda himself: he built the Ramakrishna Mission around service of the poor, seeing service of human beings as worship of God.
  • Mother Teresa: at Nirmal Hriday in Kolkata (1952) she cared for the destitute and dying without asking about their faith or past.
  • Baba Amte: at Anandwan he gave work and dignity to leprosy patients whom society shunned.
  • A contrast: online trolling and instant public shaming condemn quickly and help no one.

4. Relevance for civil servants

  • Non-judgemental service: treat people on the margins (sex workers, prisoners, drug users, migrants) with dignity and without moral prejudice.
  • Help within the law: use discretion to solve problems; where rules do not allow help, explain courteously and guide the citizen to the right forum instead of dismissing him.
  • Tolerance of dissent: respect peaceful protest and differing views, and stay impartial across faiths and communities, in the spirit of Article 51A(e).
  • Avoiding stereotypes: judging a person by caste, religion or appearance corrupts both empathy and fairness.

Vivekananda turns compassion into a practical ethic: help where possible, respect always, condemn never. For a civil servant it means empathetic and impartial service to every citizen, whatever path he or she has chosen.
free.upm-2020-gs4-6b:
Selfless serviceSelf-realisationEgo transcendencePublic service motivation

The quotation, popularly attributed to Mahatma Gandhi though not traced in his own writings, says that we discover who we truly are not by focusing on ourselves but by forgetting ourselves in serving others. Losing oneself means transcending the narrow ego and self-interest; finding oneself means discovering one's real identity, purpose and inner strength. For Gandhi, service of humanity was the path to self-realisation.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Beyond the ego: a life centred on one's own comfort and status is restless; service shifts attention to others' needs and brings inner peace.
  • Discovering capacities: in serving, we find courage, patience and skills we never knew we had.
  • Meaning and purpose: Viktor Frankl (Man's Search for Meaning, 1946) argued that people find meaning by dedicating themselves to a cause or to other people.
  • Indian tradition: the Gita's karma yoga (action without attachment to its fruits) and Vivekananda's idea of serving God in the poor (Daridra Narayana) express the same truth.

2. Values involved

  • Altruism and compassion: concern for others' welfare without expecting a return.
  • Humility: service dissolves the sense of superiority.
  • Sarvodaya and Antyodaya: the welfare of all, beginning with the last person.

3. Examples from public life

  • Gandhi's own life: from the Indian Ambulance Corps in the Boer War (1899) to nursing Parchure Shastri, a leprosy patient, at Sevagram (1939), service shaped the Mahatma; in serving the indigo cultivators of Champaran (1917) he led his first satyagraha in India.
  • Verghese Kurien: he stayed on at Anand to serve dairy farmers through Amul and Operation Flood (1970), helping make India the world's largest milk producer.
  • Kailash Satyarthi: he found his life's mission in freeing child labourers through Bachpan Bachao Andolan (1980) and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize (2014).

4. Relevance for civil servants

  • Public service motivation: officers who see their work as service, not merely a career, persist through hardship and resist corruption.
  • Field immersion: village stays and district postings show young officers what kind of administrators they can be.
  • Gandhi's talisman: recalling the face of the poorest person before taking a decision keeps policy focused on those who need it most.
  • Balance: service does not mean neglecting health or family; a burnt-out officer serves no one.

Service is not a sacrifice that diminishes us; it is self-discovery that completes us. A civil servant who loses himself in the service of the people finds his truest identity as a karmayogi.
free.upm-2020-gs4-6c:
Moral objectivismReason over emotionEthical relativismWisdom

In Plato's Phaedo, set on the day of his execution (399 BCE), Socrates argues that ordinary virtue is often a mere exchange of one feeling for another: people are brave because they fear something worse, or temperate because they want greater pleasures. True virtue, he says, rests on wisdom, the only true currency for which pleasures and fears should be exchanged. A morality based on relative emotional values, on what pleases or frightens each person or group, is therefore an illusion.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Feelings are unstable foundations: what pleases or angers us changes with mood, interest and the crowd, and a morality built on feelings shifts the same way.
  • Relativism collapses: if right were merely what each person or group feels, no one could condemn cruelty, untouchability or genocide that a group felt was justified.
  • Reason and knowledge: for Socrates virtue is knowledge; moral judgements must be examined by questioning (the Socratic method) and tested for consistency.
  • Universal principles: later thinkers built on this; Kant grounded morality in reason and duty, not inclination.

2. A balanced reading

  • Emotions still matter: compassion and indignation move us to act, and emotional intelligence is vital in public life; David Hume even held that moral judgements spring from sentiment.
  • The real target: Socrates rejects emotion cut loose from reason, not emotion itself; Aristotle's ideal is to feel the right emotion, at the right time, towards the right person and in the right way.

3. Examples from public life

  • Socrates himself: in Plato's Crito he refused to escape from prison, holding that breaking the laws of Athens would be unjust even to save his life.
  • Constitutional morality over popular morality: in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) the Supreme Court decriminalised consensual same-sex relations, holding that constitutional values, not majority sentiment, decide rights.
  • Mob lynching: outrage-driven punishment of suspects, which the Supreme Court condemned in Tehseen Poonawalla (2018), shows emotional morality at its worst.

4. Relevance for civil servants

  • Decisions on reasons, not sentiment: orders must rest on law and evidence and record their reasons, not on public outcry, media pressure or personal liking.
  • Impartiality: no favour or bias on grounds of caste, religion or personal feelings.
  • Courage: resisting popular pressure when it conflicts with law and justice.
  • Empathy with judgement: compassion should shape how a decision is delivered, while reason decides what the decision is.

Socrates reminds us that ethics must rest on reason and wisdom, with emotions as servants rather than masters. For administrators this means principled, impartial decisions that stay fair when feelings run high.
free.upm-2020-gs4-7:
Financial proprietyWelfare vs developmentFrank adviceParliamentary accountability

Rajesh Kumar must comment on a proposal to divert ₹6,000 crore from the National Housing Scheme (NHS), which has ₹8,300 crore allotted and only ₹775 crore drawn by June, to an SEZ and a gas-processing plant vital to energy security. Diverting 72% of a welfare allocation would leave just ₹1,525 crore for nine months. The case tests financial propriety, fairness to the weaker sections and a civil servant's duty to give frank and fearless advice under pressure.

Stakeholders: poor households awaiting NHS houses and the States implementing it; the Ministries of Commerce and Petroleum, the PSU and M/s XYZ Hydrocarbons; exporters and future SEZ workers; Parliament and taxpayers; the government's credibility; and Rajesh Kumar himself.

1. (a) Ethical issues in re-appropriating funds from welfare to development

  • Equity versus efficiency: development projects promise growth, but here the poor bear the cost; Rawls' difference principle and the State's duty towards the weaker sections (Article 46) favour protecting them, and the right to shelter is part of Article 21 (Chameli Singh, 1996).
  • Legality and legislative intent: Parliament voted ₹8,300 crore for NHS. Re-appropriation is allowed only between units within the same grant; if NHS and the two projects fall under different ministries' grants, as is usual, moving the money needs Parliament's approval through supplementary demands (Article 115). Doing it quietly would weaken parliamentary accountability.
  • Financial propriety: the General Financial Rules, 2017 demand the care a person of ordinary prudence takes with his own money; the poor should not pay for a failure to budget for approved projects.
  • Political neutrality: elections in four States and the scheme's publicity in rallies should neither drive nor block the decision.
  • Honouring commitments: delaying payment to an MNC chosen by global bidding would hurt energy security and India's credibility.

2. (b) Options available to Rajesh Kumar

3. Chosen course of action and why

  • Assess real needs: estimate NHS's likely spending this year from the States' readiness and past trends; release only genuine savings, and protect sanctioned instalments to the States.
  • Find lawful alternatives: where the rules allow, an advance from the Contingency Fund of India (Article 267; corpus ₹30,000 crore) for the December payment, recouped through supplementary demands in the winter session; savings from slow-moving heads; phased payment for SEZ land.
  • Record a reasoned note: set out the facts, rules, risks and options on file and discuss them with his seniors; the competent authority decides.
  • Implement the lawful decision: if overruled on a lawful policy choice, he implements it, with his advice on record; for anything unlawful, he seeks written orders and does not act against the rules.
  • Why: it serves both development and welfare, keeps Parliament informed, and combines honest advice with neutrality.

Is resigning a worthy option? Not at this stage. The proposal is a policy choice, not a crime; his duty is to advise frankly and let the elected government decide. Resigning would be an escape that leaves the poor and the process without an honest voice. It becomes a matter of conscience only if he is repeatedly pressed to act illegally and every lawful channel has failed.

Rajesh Kumar should serve both development and welfare, finding lawful money for urgent projects without silently sacrificing the poor. Courage within the system honours public trust better than walking away from it.
free.upm-2020-gs4-8:
Responsible arms tradeEnd-useSelf-relianceHuman rights

India, long one of the world's largest arms importers, is now also an exporter: its defence exports reached a record ₹38,424 crore in 2025-26 (Ministry of Defence), including BrahMos missiles to the Philippines and Akash systems to Armenia. Exports finance research, keep production lines busy and build partnerships under Atmanirbhar Bharat. But weapons are instruments of death, so an exporter carries a special moral responsibility. As Chairman of BML, my views are as follows.

Stakeholders: BML's employees and suppliers; the Indian armed forces, whose needs come first; the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of External Affairs; the buyer government, its soldiers and civilians; neighbouring countries; the international community and export-control regimes; and Indian taxpayers.

1. (a) Ethical issues in the arms trade

  • Complicity in harm: if our weapons are used for aggression, against civilians or for internal repression, we share the moral responsibility; profit cannot justify treating human lives merely as means.
  • Diversion and proliferation: weapons or their technology may be re-exported or reach terrorists and insurgents, and could one day be used against India.
  • Regional stability: exports can fuel arms races or prolong conflicts; a friendly country today may be a belligerent tomorrow.
  • National security first: export orders must not delay supplies to our own forces or leak sensitive technology.
  • Corruption and secrecy: arms deals attract middlemen and kickbacks; confidentiality must not become a cover for wrongdoing.
  • Legitimate benefits: every state has a right of self-defence (Article 51 of the UN Charter); supplying a defensive weapon such as an ATGM to a responsible government can strengthen its security and fund our own R&D and jobs.
