The real question is not whether to sell, but to whom, what and with which safeguards.
  • India's identity: a nation that champions non-violence, Panchsheel and a rules-based order must be seen as a responsible supplier, not a trader in conflict.

2. (b) Five ethical factors that should influence a decision to sell arms

3. My approach as Chairman

  • Support exports, ethically: expand capacity without compromising deliveries to the Indian Army.
  • Due diligence: seek export authorisation under the SCOMET list, which for munitions is granted by the Department of Defence Production, and rely on the MEA's assessment of the buyer; insist on end-use guarantees.
  • Technology protection: offer export versions without sensitive sub-systems where necessary.
  • Integrity: an internal export-ethics and compliance committee, no intermediaries, and full records for audit and parliamentary scrutiny.

Arms exports can strengthen self-reliance and friendships, but only when guided by responsibility: the right buyer, the right purpose and the right safeguards. India's reputation as a responsible power is itself a strategic asset that no single contract should put at risk.
free.upm-2020-gs4-9:
Child labourTribal deprivationTraffickingConvergent development

Labour contractors lure Rampura's minor tribal girls to Bt cotton farms in another State, where poor conditions damage their health; poverty and failed welfare make families consent. The practice violates Article 23 (traffic in human beings and forced labour), Article 24 (no child below 14 in hazardous employment), the right to education (Article 21A) and the State's duty to promote the interests of Scheduled Tribes (Article 46). As District Collector, I must treat both the symptom and the cause.

Stakeholders: the girls and their families; gram sabhas; contractors; cotton farmers and seed companies; NGOs; both districts' administrations; and schools, health workers, police and the Child Welfare Committee.

1. Ethical issues involved

  • Child rights versus survival: parents consent under poverty's pressure, but a child cannot meaningfully consent to harmful labour; the best interests of the child must prevail.
  • Exploitation and objectification: valuing girls for their "soft fingers" treats them as tools, not persons.
  • Gender vulnerability: girls far from home face health risks, possible abuse and lost schooling, perpetuating gender inequality.
  • Institutional failure: welfare schemes have not reached the tribal poor, and NGOs meant to protect them appear compromised.
  • Distributive justice and diffused responsibility: distant farms profit from a backward district's deprivation, while contractors, farmers and two administrations each disown the problem.

2. Steps for the minor girls

  • Rescue and rehabilitation: with the destination district's Collector and labour department, rescue the girls, bring them home safely, recover unpaid wages, give medical care and present them before the Child Welfare Committee (Juvenile Justice Act, 2015).
  • Prosecution: cases against contractors under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016), which bars children below 14 from all work except, under conditions, in family enterprises, and under the trafficking provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Section 143) where recruitment by inducement for exploitation is shown.
  • Prevention: village child protection committees, a migration register in every gram panchayat, Anti-Human Trafficking Unit checks at bus stands in the recruitment season, and awareness through gram sabhas, SHGs and Childline (1098).
  • Education and health: admission to Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas and Eklavya Model Residential Schools with bridge courses under the RTE Act; health screening and nutrition support; sponsorship under Mission Vatsalya for the most vulnerable families.
  • NGO accountability: audit and de-empanel compromised NGOs, and work with credible ones under social audit.

3. Steps to improve the district's economy

  • Work at home: wage work under the VB-G RAM G Act (125 days, which replaced MGNREGA from July 2026), planned for the lean season and paid on time.
  • Land and forest livelihoods: settle rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006; minor forest produce value chains through Van Dhan Vikas Kendras; watershed works and small irrigation for a second crop; horticulture, millets and livestock.
  • Women's enterprise: DAY-NRLM self-help groups with bank credit, aiming at Lakhpati Didi incomes.
  • Skills and safe migration: ITI and DDU-GKY training linked to jobs; adult migrants registered on e-Shram.
  • Convergence: roads, housing, water and health through the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan and, for PVTG habitations, PM-JANMAN, with gram sabha-led planning.

Child labour in Rampura is a symptom of tribal deprivation. Enforcement must be matched by livelihoods, schooling and convergence, so that no family must choose between its children's childhood and its own survival: the essence of inclusive development.
free.upm-2020-gs4-10:
IntegrityConflict of interestRule of lawMoral courage

Four labourers, two of them minors, died when a mall's roof collapsed. My preliminary enquiry has found poor-quality material, an unauthorised second basement missed in inspections, and a permission, given by my predecessor (a senior and a friend), despite encroachment on a green belt and a slip road. Colleagues want me to go slow, and the builder, a relative of a powerful minister, offers a fortune and threatens a false complaint under the POSH Act. The case tests integrity, impartiality and moral courage.

Stakeholders: the dead workers' families and the injured; other workers and future users of the mall; citizens who lose the green belt and slip road; the builder and the minister; the building inspector, the former Commissioner and other officials; the Municipal Corporation and the government; and my family and I.

1. Ethical issues involved

  • Right to life and safety: poor material and illegal construction cost lives (Article 21), and employing minors breaks the child-labour law.
  • Integrity versus inducement: offering a bribe is itself an offence under Section 8 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as amended in 2018.
  • Friendship versus duty: my friendship with the former Commissioner is a conflict of interest that must be disclosed, never allowed to bend the enquiry.
  • Esprit de corps versus accountability: colleagues' loyalty to one another cannot override loyalty to the public.
  • Rule of law: the builder's political connections must not decide the outcome.
  • Planning and environmental ethics: encroachment on a green belt and slip road harms the whole city.
  • Misuse of a protective law: threatening a false POSH complaint abuses a law meant to protect women and amounts to intimidation.

2. Options available

3. My course of action and why

  • Victims first: treatment for the injured; compensation under the Code on Social Security, 2020 and ex gratia relief; the site sealed and similar buildings audited.
  • Evidence-based enquiry: laboratory tests of materials, plans, inspection records and site measurements; responsibility fixed on the builder (criminal negligence, employing minors), the building inspector (suspension pending disciplinary proceedings) and others, without fear or favour.
  • Disclosure: inform the government in writing of my friendship with the former Commissioner and suggest that another officer assess his decision; recommend referring the nexus, with the prior approval required by Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, to the vigilance or anti-corruption bureau.
  • Bribe and threat: refuse firmly; report both in writing at once to the Chief Secretary and the anti-corruption bureau; meet the builder only in office, with a record.
  • The POSH threat: having reported it in advance, cooperate fully with any inquiry by the competent committee; the Act (Section 14) provides for action against malicious complaints, and the truth is my defence.
  • Systemic reform: review all permissions that violate the master plan, restore the green belt and slip road after due process, and introduce online plan approvals, geo-tagged inspection photographs and third-party quality audits.

Why this course: it upholds the rule of law and the dignity of those who died (duty); it prevents future tragedies (consequences); and it reflects the courage expected of an upright officer (virtue). Friendship is honoured by fairness, not by favour.

Silence would make me a partner in the next collapse. Integrity with courage, backed by a written record and transparent procedure, protects both the public interest and the honest officer.
free.upm-2020-gs4-11:
Shared valueCorporate social responsibilityComplianceInclusive development

Amria Plastic Works (APW), drawn by a 10-year tax holiday, transformed a backward village: local jobs, skilled and loyal workers, services built with company funds and care for workers during the 2020 lockdown. It reflects Gandhi's idea of trusteeship and the modern idea of creating shared value (Porter and Kramer, 2011). A critical analysis, however, also reveals compliance lapses and the risks of dependence on a single benevolent firm.

1. Critical analysis of the APW story

  • Workers as stakeholders: APW treated workers as partners, not costs; paying them through the lockdown and using idle time to plant trees showed an ethics of care when many employers laid workers off.
  • Complementing the state: buildings for a PHC and a school, and advocacy for better buses, worked with the government rather than replacing it.
  • Lapses: drawing electricity beyond the authorised load breaks supply regulations and creates a fire risk; it came to light only after an incident, suggesting that growth outpaced compliance.
  • Influence: liaising with the MLA for public transport is legitimate advocacy, provided it is transparent and seeks no private favour.

2. Ethical issues involved

  • Profit and social responsibility: how far a business should share its gains; Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates CSR spending only above certain thresholds, so much of APW's welfare is voluntary.
  • Rule of law and safety: voluntary goodness cannot substitute for statutory compliance.
  • Environmental sustainability: plastics production must meet pollution-control norms and extended producer responsibility under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.
  • Paternalism versus empowerment: welfare that depends on one owner's goodwill can create dependence rather than capability.
  • Inclusiveness: benefits, including the renovation of a place of worship, should be shared in a way that includes all communities and neighbouring villages.

3. Is APW a role model for backward areas?

Yes, with qualifications.

  • Why yes: it shows that business can bring jobs, skills and services to areas the market ignores; its cycle of local hiring, loyalty, quality and reinvestment can be replicated, and partnership with the government multiplied the gains.
  • What must be added: zero tolerance for regulatory lapses; environmental stewardship through recycling, cleaner technology and EPR; community ownership of welfare assets through panchayats and SHGs; wider inclusion of women and nearby villages; and diversification so that the village is not hostage to one firm.
  • Role of the state: better connectivity to the trunk railway line and logistics under PM Gati Shakti, reliable power, and incentives linked to local employment and compliance rather than tax holidays alone.

APW is a promising model of responsible enterprise, but a true role model must be as rigorous in compliance and environmental care as it is generous in welfare. Backed by public investment, such enterprises can make backward areas self-sustaining.
free.upm-2020-gs4-12:
Ethics of careDignity of migrantsCaring stateCivil society

When a nationwide lockdown was announced on 24 March 2020, millions of migrant workers, without wages, food or shelter, set out for their villages, many on foot. In May 2020, sixteen workers sleeping on a railway track near Aurangabad were killed by a goods train. The Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance and directed that stranded migrants be charged no fare and be given food and water. Overseeing my district's relief force, I saw that the crisis was as much ethical as logistical.

1. Ethical issues in the migrant crisis

  • Dignity and the right to life: hunger, long walks and humiliation, such as migrants being sprayed with disinfectant in Bareilly, violated the dignity protected by Article 21.
  • Justice and equity: a measure meant to protect everyone placed the heaviest burden on those least able to bear it.
  • Failure of anticipation and empathy: plans assumed a settled population; the mobile, invisible migrant was an afterthought.
  • Public health versus liberty: containment justified limits on movement, but those limits created a duty to provide food, shelter and safe transport.
  • Duties of employers and landlords: unpaid wages and evictions shifted private obligations onto the workers and the state.
  • Coordination and trust: gaps between source and destination States, and rumours, deepened panic and distrust.

2. An ethical care-giving state

  • Meaning: a state that does not wait for citizens to claim entitlements but notices vulnerability and responds with timely, respectful help. It draws on the ethics of care (Carol Gilligan, 1982), which values relationships and responsiveness alongside abstract rights; Joan Tronto (1993) breaks care into four linked elements, shown below.
  • Constitutional basis: the Preamble's promise of justice; the Directive Principles on livelihood, public assistance in unemployment, and just and humane conditions of work (Articles 38, 39, 41 and 42); and the right to live with dignity under Article 21 (Francis Coralie Mullin, 1981).
  • In practice: free foodgrains under the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (2020), Shramik Special trains from 1 May 2020, the Garib Kalyan Rojgar Abhiyaan for returnees (June 2020), and later the e-Shram portal (2021; over 30 crore registrations), One Nation One Ration Card and affordable rental housing complexes.

3. How civil society can help

  • Partnership, not substitution: civil society reaches where government cannot, but works best when the district coordinates it through one control room and shares data.
  • Rebuilding lives: skill mapping of returnees, links to local work, and help for a safe return when jobs resume.

4. Lessons from my district

  • Be prepared: a migrant help desk and database, transit camps with separate spaces for women and children, coordination with source and destination districts, and trained volunteers within the relief force.

The pandemic showed that the dignity of migrants is the true test of a humane state. A caring state, working hand in hand with an active civil society, turns rights on paper into relief on the road.
free.upm-2021-gs1-1:
Bhakti movementVernacular literatureNirguna and sagunaComposite culture

Bhakti means loving, personal devotion to God. As a movement it began with the Tamil Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva) from about the sixth century CE, and spread to Karnataka, Maharashtra, and northern and eastern India between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries. Its saints sang in the people's own languages, so Bhakti literature became the foundation of many regional literatures and a strong force for social and cultural change.

1. Nature of Bhakti literature

  • In the mother tongue: saints composed in Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, Punjabi and Telugu rather than Sanskrit, ending the priest's monopoly over religious knowledge.
  • Oral and musical: it took the form of songs meant to be sung, such as padas, dohas, abhangas, vachanas and kirtans, and spread through singing gatherings and pilgrimages.
  • Two streams: nirguna poets such as Kabir, Ravidas and Guru Nanak worshipped a formless God and rejected idols and rituals; saguna poets such as Tulsidas, Surdas and Mirabai sang of Rama and Krishna in human form.
  • Egalitarian and critical: many saints came from artisan or "low" castes (Kabir a weaver, Ravidas a leather-worker, Namdev a tailor, Chokhamela a Mahar) and attacked caste pride, ritualism and hypocrisy.
  • Women's voices: Andal, Akka Mahadevi, Lal Ded and Mirabai expressed devotion as love, often defying social norms.

2. Contribution to Indian culture

  • Growth of regional languages: the Ramcharitmanas, the Jnaneshwari, Potana's Telugu Bhagavatam and Sankaradeva's works became classics that set the literary standard of their languages.
  • Social reform: by making every devotee equal before God, Bhakti weakened caste pride and priestly ritual; Basavanna's Anubhava Mantapa brought people of all castes together for discussion.
  • Religious harmony: Kabir addressed Hindus and Muslims alike, and the Guru Granth Sahib (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) includes verses of Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and the Sufi Baba Farid, a living symbol of composite culture.
  • Music, dance and art: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda inspired Odissi dance and Pahari painting; Purandara Dasa is called the father of Carnatic music; Sankaradeva's tradition gave the Sattriya dance; Narsinh Mehta's "Vaishnava Jana To" became Gandhi's favourite bhajan.
  • Popular culture: the Ramlila based on Tulsidas, the wari pilgrimage to Pandharpur and community kirtans keep these texts alive among millions.

3. Limitations

  • Caste survived: Bhakti did not abolish the caste system; many followings later hardened into sects or castes themselves.
  • Conventional roles: saguna poetry often reinforced conventional roles of submission even as it gave women a voice.

Bhakti literature democratised religion and language: it made the vernacular a medium of high thought, valued devotion over birth, and wove Hindu, Sufi and folk traditions into India's composite culture, a legacy carried forward by later reformers and the freedom movement.
free.upm-2021-gs1-2:
Bengal RenaissanceBrahmo SamajYoung BengalRationalism

The nineteenth-century socio-religious reform movements grew out of the encounter between Indian society and colonial rule. Western education, the printing press, missionary criticism and the rediscovery of ancient texts produced an English-educated middle class that questioned sati, caste, idolatry and the denial of education and remarriage to women. Bengal led the way in the Bengal Renaissance, through the Brahmo Samaj and the radical Young Bengal group.

1. Rise of the reform movements

  • Western ideas: rationalism, humanism and liberty, spread through English education, led reformers to test customs by reason.
  • Print and press: journals such as Ram Mohan Roy's Sambad Kaumudi (1821) carried reform debates to a reading public.
  • Defensive response: missionary attacks on Indian religions pushed reformers to purify their traditions from within.
  • Orientalist scholarship: the Asiatic Society (1784) and translations of the Upanishads gave reformers a classical basis for their arguments.

2. The Brahmo Samaj

  • Ram Mohan Roy: founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), later the Brahmo Samaj. Drawing on the Upanishads, he preached monotheism and opposed idolatry and priestly ritual; his campaign led to the abolition of sati by Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 1829. He also championed English and scientific education.
  • Debendranath Tagore: his Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839) and Tattvabodhini Patrika spread rational religion in Bengali.
  • Keshab Chandra Sen: took the Samaj into social reform (inter-caste marriage, widow remarriage, women's education) and beyond Bengal. Differences split it into the Adi Brahmo Samaj and Keshab's Brahmo Samaj of India (1866); the Native Marriage Act, 1872 legalised Brahmo-style marriages; and after Keshab married his under-age daughter into the Cooch Behar royal family, the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) was formed.

3. Young Bengal

  • Derozio: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio (1809–31), a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, inspired by the French Revolution, taught his students to question everything.
  • Radical rationalism: Derozians such as Krishna Mohan Banerjee and Ram Gopal Ghosh attacked superstition, idolatry and caste, and championed women's rights, a free press, trial by jury and protection of ryots from zamindars.
  • Limitations: their open defiance of custom alienated orthodox society, they lacked a mass base, and the group faded after Derozio's dismissal and death in 1831. Yet Surendranath Banerjea later honoured them as the pioneers of modern civilisation in Bengal.

4. Growth across India

  • New organisations: Keshab's visit inspired the Prarthana Samaj (1867, Bombay; later led by M.G. Ranade), while the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873, Jyotiba Phule), Arya Samaj (1875, Dayanand Saraswati), Ramakrishna Mission (1897), the Aligarh movement and Sri Narayana Guru took reform to other regions and communities.
  • Wider social base: over time reform moved from upper-caste elites to the lower castes, and from religious doctrine to education and rights.

These movements created a modern, rational public sphere, improved the status of women and built the self-confidence that fed nationalism; their urban, elite base was their main limit.
free.upm-2021-gs1-3:
Princely statesInstrument of AccessionSardar PatelPrivy purses

At independence there were over 560 princely states, ranging from Hyderabad and Kashmir to tiny estates, together covering much of the subcontinent. The Indian Independence Act, 1947 ended British paramountcy, leaving rulers free in law to join India or Pakistan or stay independent. The States Department under Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with V.P. Menon as Secretary, integrated them through the Instrument of Accession and later mergers, but the process raised serious administrative and socio-cultural problems.

1. Administrative issues

  • Accession: by 15 August 1947 almost all states had signed Instruments of Accession (ceding defence, external affairs and communications) and Standstill Agreements; Junagadh, Hyderabad and Jammu and Kashmir held out.
  • The holdouts: Junagadh's Nawab acceded to Pakistan, but a plebiscite (February 1948) went in India's favour; Hyderabad's Nizam sought independence while the Razakars spread violence, until the police action, Operation Polo (September 1948); Kashmir's Maharaja acceded on 26 October 1947 after a tribal invasion from Pakistan. Travancore had also announced independence before acceding.
  • Merging hundreds of units: states differed enormously in size, laws, revenue systems, police and armies. Small states were merged into neighbouring provinces (as in Orissa), grouped into unions such as Saurashtra, Rajasthan, PEPSU and Travancore-Cochin, or placed under central administration.
  • Constitutional fit: the unions became Part B states headed by Rajpramukhs (1950), until the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 abolished the category.
  • Finances and privileges: state armies, debts and services had to be absorbed; rulers got tax-free privy purses (Articles 291 and 362), abolished by the 26th Amendment (1971).

2. Socio-cultural problems

  • Communal tension: a Muslim ruler over a Hindu majority (Hyderabad, Junagadh) and a Hindu ruler over a Muslim majority (Kashmir) mixed accession with the communal passions of Partition.
  • Feudal society: many states had no representative institutions, and jagirdari and forced labour were common; the Telangana peasant armed struggle (1946–51) against the Nizam's landlords showed the depth of agrarian unrest.
  • Loyalty and identity: subjects' attachment to ruling houses and the princes' loss of status bred resentment; in the North-East, Manipur's merger still evokes grievance among some groups.
  • Language and region: unions often cut across language groups; Hyderabad state was divided among Andhra Pradesh, Bombay and Mysore in 1956.
  • Unequal development: progressive states such as Mysore, Baroda and Travancore stood beside very backward ones, whose gaps had to be bridged.

3. How the challenges were met

  • Statesmanship: Patel combined persuasion, appeals to patriotism, generous privy purses and, where needed, force.
  • People's movements: the Praja Mandals and the All India States People's Conference (1927) mobilised subjects for responsible government and merger.
  • Democratisation: the 1951–52 elections and land reforms ended jagirdari power.

The integration of the princely states was a largely peaceful revolution that laid the territorial foundation of the Republic; the lingering issues of Kashmir and parts of the North-East show that emotional integration takes longer than legal accession.
free.upm-2021-gs1-4:
LandslidesTectonic activitySoil saturationSlope disturbance

A landslide is the downslope movement of rock, debris or earth under gravity. ISRO's Landslide Atlas of India (NRSC, 2023) found that about 12.6% of India's land area (excluding snow-covered areas) is landslide-prone. Of about 80,000 landslides it mapped between 1998 and 2022, the Himalaya accounted for most and the Western Ghats for about 15%. Both regions see monsoon-triggered slides, but the underlying causes differ.

1. Causes in the Himalayan region

  • Young, rising mountains: the Himalaya are still being pushed up by the northward movement of the Indian plate; their rocks are folded, faulted and fractured along thrusts such as the Main Central Thrust and the Main Boundary Thrust.
  • Earthquakes: the region is among India's most earthquake-prone; tremors loosen slopes and set off slides, as in the Sikkim earthquake of 2011.
  • Steep slopes and glacial processes: rapid river down-cutting leaves unstable valley sides; loose moraines, freeze–thaw and glacial-lake outbursts (South Lhonak, Sikkim, 2023) add to the hazard.
  • Extreme rain: cloudbursts and western disturbances meeting monsoon moisture, as at Kedarnath (2013).
  • Human pressure: road widening, tunnelling, blasting, hydropower projects and towns built on old landslide debris, as at Joshimath (subsidence, 2023). The Atlas ranks Rudraprayag and Tehri Garhwal highest in landslide density and risk exposure.

2. Causes in the Western Ghats

  • Old but steep escarpment: the Ghats are an ancient, tectonically stable block, so earthquakes matter little; the danger lies in the steep western scarp facing the monsoon.
  • Thick weathered soil over hard rock: laterite and weathered soil rest on hard basalt in the north and crystalline rock in the south. When rain saturates the soil, water collects at the soil–rock boundary, which becomes a slip surface and produces fast debris flows.
  • Intense orographic rain: the south-west monsoon dumps very heavy rain in short bursts on the windward slopes, as in Kerala in 2018 and 2019.
  • Soil piping and land-use change: underground erosion channels in Kerala's hills, quarrying, replacement of natural forest by plantations, and slope-cutting for roads and houses.
  • Examples: Malin, Pune district (2014), Pettimudi, Idukki (2020), Irshalwadi, Raigad (2023) and Wayanad (30 July 2024), which killed over 200 people.

3. Way forward

Hazard zonation and early warning by the Geological Survey of India, the nodal agency; NDMA's National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019); slope drainage and bio-engineering; and land-use control in eco-sensitive zones, as recommended by the Gadgil (2011) and Kasturirangan (2013) reports.

Landslides in both regions are natural processes made deadlier by human interference; respecting the carrying capacity of fragile slopes is the key to reducing risk.
free.upm-2021-gs1-5:
GondwanalandMineral wealthMining's share of GDPMining reforms

Gondwanaland was the southern supercontinent that included India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica. India inherited from it the Gondwana basins that hold most of its coal, while its ancient Archaean and Dharwar rocks hold iron ore, manganese, bauxite, mica and chromite. India produces about 95 minerals and is the world's second-largest coal producer, yet mining has contributed only about 2% of GDP in recent years.

1. India's mineral endowment

  • Coal: about 401 billion tonnes of resources, mainly in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh; output about 1,040 million tonnes in 2025-26.
  • Metallic minerals: iron ore of Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Goa; bauxite of the Odisha and Jharkhand plateaus; manganese and chromite.
  • Others: mica, limestone and barytes, and an inferred lithium resource found in Reasi, Jammu and Kashmir (2023).

2. Why mining's share of GDP is small

  • Quality and composition: Gondwana coal is mostly high-ash and non-coking, so steel makers import coking coal; India has little oil and few known deposits of lithium, cobalt or nickel, and is reported to be fully import-dependent for 10 of the 30 critical minerals identified in 2023.
  • Under-exploration: deep-seated and concealed deposits are poorly explored, and the old leasing regime gave private firms little reason to explore them.
  • Regulatory delays: discretionary allocation, slow clearances and litigation held mining back; the Supreme Court cancelled 214 coal block allocations (2014), and mining was halted for long periods in Bellary (Karnataka) and Goa over illegal mining.
  • Forest and tribal constraints: much mineral wealth lies under dense forests and Fifth Schedule areas; Gram Sabha rights under PESA and the Forest Rights Act, and the Samatha (1997) and Niyamgiri (2013) judgments, rightly limit unregulated mining.
  • Accounting and value addition: GDP counts only extraction as "mining"; smelting, steel and power fall under manufacturing and electricity, and raw-ore exports leave value addition abroad.
  • A services-led economy: services make up over half of GDP, so even rising mining output remains a small share.

3. Reforms to raise the contribution

  • Transparency: the 2015 amendment to the MMDR Act, 1957 made auctions compulsory and created District Mineral Foundations and the National Mineral Exploration Trust.
  • Opening up: commercial coal mining (2020); the 2023 amendment let the Centre auction 24 critical minerals and introduced exploration licences; the 2025 amendment removed the 50% cap on captive-mine sales.
  • National Critical Mineral Mission (2025): ₹16,300 crore plus investment by public-sector firms, with KABIL acquiring assets abroad.
  • Offshore minerals: auctions under the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2023.

India's Gondwana inheritance is a strategic asset rather than a large GDP sector. Sustainable mining, with exploration, transparent auctions, local benefit-sharing and mine restoration, can raise its contribution without sacrificing forests and tribal rights.
free.upm-2021-gs1-6:
Wetland reclamationUrban floodingGroundwater rechargeBlue-green infrastructure

Reclamation of water bodies means filling or draining lakes, tanks, marshes, floodplains, creeks and mangroves to create land for housing, roads, industry and IT parks. India's cities, home to 31.1% of the population in Census 2011 and growing fast, have lost many such water bodies. Lakes and wetlands act as a city's sponge, storing floodwater and recharging aquifers, so their loss has serious environmental consequences.

1. Hydrological implications

  • Urban flooding: lakes, tanks and floodplains store storm water; once built over, rain has nowhere to go. Chennai's 2015 floods were worsened by encroachment of the Pallikaranai marsh, tank beds and the Adyar floodplain; in 2022 Bengaluru flooded where lake beds and storm-water channels (rajakaluves) had been built over.
  • Groundwater depletion: paving cuts recharge. Bengaluru's water crisis of 2024, after a poor monsoon, showed how a city once served by a network of linked tanks now depends on borewells and distant rivers.
  • Blocked drainage: loss of natural channels causes waterlogging even in moderate rain.

2. Ecological implications

  • Biodiversity loss: wetlands support birds, fish, amphibians and aquatic plants; reclamation destroys feeding and breeding grounds, as urban pressure shows at Guwahati's Deepor Beel, a Ramsar site.
  • Loss of natural treatment: the East Kolkata Wetlands (Ramsar site, 2002) treat much of Kolkata's sewage naturally while producing fish and vegetables; reclamation for the city's expansion threatens this free service.
  • Mangroves and coasts: reclaiming mangroves and creeks removes buffers against storm surges and high tides; Mumbai's deluge of 26 July 2005 was worsened by the choked Mithi river and lost mangroves.

3. Pollution and climate effects

  • Shrinking lakes become sewage sinks: surviving water bodies receive untreated sewage and debris, leading to eutrophication, foam and even fires, as on Bengaluru's Bellandur lake.
  • Urban heat island: water bodies cool their surroundings; concrete in their place raises local temperatures.
  • Carbon release: drained wetlands lose stored soil carbon, adding to greenhouse emissions.
  • Land subsidence: soft reclaimed ground and heavy groundwater pumping cause sinking, as in Jakarta, whose sinking is one reason for Indonesia's planned new capital, Nusantara.

4. Way forward

  • Legal protection: the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017; the Supreme Court in Hinch Lal Tiwari v. Kamala Devi (2001) and Jagpal Singh v. State of Punjab (2011) ordered ponds and common water bodies protected and encroachments removed.
  • Restoration: Mission Amrit Sarovar (2022), water-body rejuvenation under AMRUT 2.0, and India's 103 Ramsar sites (as of October 2026).
  • Planning: mapping and notifying water bodies in master plans, "sponge city" design, permeable surfaces and buffer zones.

Water bodies are urban infrastructure, not vacant land; protecting and reviving them is far cheaper than paying for floods and water shortages.
free.upm-2021-gs1-7:
VolcanismPlate boundariesLava, ash and gasesRegional environment

Volcanic eruptions occur where magma reaches the surface, mostly along plate boundaries, namely the Pacific Ring of Fire, which holds most of the world's active volcanoes, the mid-ocean ridges and continental rifts, and over hotspots. In 2021 eruptions occurred in all these settings, from Iceland and the Canary Islands to the Caribbean, the East African Rift, Italy, Indonesia, Japan and the Pacific. Their impacts were mainly regional, not global.

1. Global occurrence in 2021

  • Divergent boundary: the Reykjanes Peninsula in Iceland erupted for the first time in about 800 years.
  • Convergent boundaries: the Ring of Fire (Semeru, Taal, Fukutoku-Okanoba, and Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai, whose eruption began in December 2021) and the Caribbean arc (La Soufrière).
  • Rift and hotspot volcanism: Nyiragongo in the East African Rift; La Palma and Kīlauea (Hawaii) over hotspots.

2. Impact on the regional environment

  • Lava and land: on La Palma, lava covered over 1,000 hectares, destroyed about 3,000 buildings and large banana plantations, and forced about 7,000 people out; flows entering the sea built new land (lava deltas). Nyiragongo's lava destroyed homes and villages on Goma's northern outskirts; dozens died, mostly while fleeing, and about 400,000 people were ordered to evacuate.
  • Ash fall: La Soufrière's ash blanketed St Vincent and drifted to Barbados, damaging crops and water supplies; about 20,000 people had been evacuated beforehand. Etna's ash disrupted flights, and Semeru's ash and pyroclastic flows buried villages and killed dozens.
  • Gases and air quality: sulphur dioxide from Taal produced volcanic smog (vog) over nearby provinces, and gas emissions on La Palma at times forced residents indoors; near Nyiragongo, scientists watched the gas-rich Lake Kivu for any dangerous release.
  • Marine environment: lava meeting seawater off La Palma released acidic plumes; pumice rafts from Fukutoku-Okanoba drifted to Okinawa, choking harbours and damaging fishing boats' engines.
  • Earthquakes and landscape change: quake swarms preceded the Reykjanes and La Palma eruptions; Fagradalsfjall's lava field became a tourist attraction.

3. Global significance

  • Little global cooling: the 2021 eruptions were too small to cool the global climate, unlike Pinatubo (1991), which lowered global temperatures by about half a degree Celsius for a year or two.
  • Value of warning: monitoring and early warning made timely evacuation possible at La Soufrière and La Palma, limiting deaths.

Volcanoes destroy, but they also build land and fertile soils. Monitoring, hazard zoning and evacuation planning, relevant even for India's active Barren Island volcano, can keep their regional impacts in check.
free.upm-2021-gs1-8:
SubcontinentPhysical isolationIndian plateUnity in diversity

A subcontinent is a large, distinct landmass that forms part of a continent but is set apart from it by physical barriers, with its own geological history, climate, drainage and culture. India, with an area of about 3.28 million sq km (about 2.4% of the world's land area), is the seventh-largest country and home to nearly 18% of humanity; with its neighbours it forms the Indian subcontinent of South Asia.

1. Physical isolation

  • Mountain walls: the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush in the north, the Purvanchal hills (Patkai, Naga and Mizo hills) in the east, and the Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges in the west separate it from the rest of Asia.
  • Seas on three sides: the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean.
  • Few gateways: contact came through passes such as the Khyber and Bolan and by sea, so India absorbed outside influences while keeping its distinctiveness.

2. Distinct geological history

  • A separate plate: the Indian plate broke away from Gondwanaland, drifted north across the Tethys Sea and collided with the Eurasian plate about 40–50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya; it is still moving north.
  • Three distinct units: the ancient, stable Peninsular plateau (a fragment of Gondwanaland), the young fold mountains of the Himalaya, and the Indo-Gangetic plain built from the sediments of the rivers between them.

3. Size and physical diversity

  • All major landforms: high mountains, vast plains, plateaus, the Thar desert, long coasts and two island groups (Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep).
  • Long boundaries: a coastline of 11,098.81 km (re-measured in 2025) and a land frontier of over 15,000 km.
  • Biodiversity: about 7–8% of the world's recorded species, and parts of four of the 36 global biodiversity hotspots.

4. Climatic and drainage unity

  • Monsoon climate: the Himalaya block cold Central Asian winds and trap the monsoon, giving the whole region a common rhythm of seasons different from the rest of Asia.
  • Own river systems: the perennial Himalayan rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra) and the seasonal peninsular rivers drain within the subcontinent into its own seas.

5. Cultural distinctiveness

  • Civilisational continuity: a shared history from the Harappan age and the ancient idea of Bharatavarsha as one land.
  • Unity in diversity: many languages (22 in the Eighth Schedule), religions and ethnic groups held together by common traditions.

India is thus a subcontinent: large, mountain-walled, geologically distinct and culturally unique, yet linked to the rest of Asia through passes and seas, which enriched rather than erased its identity.
free.upm-2021-gs1-9:
Tribal knowledgeOral traditionCommunity ownershipSustainability

Tribal knowledge systems are bodies of knowledge, practices and beliefs about nature, health, farming and social life that tribal communities have built through long observation and pass down orally. India has over 700 notified Scheduled Tribes, forming 8.6% of the population (Census 2011). Their knowledge differs from mainstream knowledge, which is formal, written, scientific and market-oriented, and from the mainstream caste-based cultural order in several unique ways.

1. Unique features of tribal knowledge

  • Holistic and eco-centric: nature is kin and sacred, not merely a resource; sacred groves such as Mawphlang in Meghalaya's Khasi Hills conserve forests through belief and taboo.
  • Oral and experiential: knowledge lives in songs, myths, rituals and practice and is learnt by doing; youth dormitories such as the ghotul of the Muria Gonds served as schools of life.
  • Collective ownership: knowledge belongs to the community, not to an individual inventor, and is shared rather than patented.
  • Local and adaptive: finely tuned to a specific ecosystem and tested over centuries, such as Apatani rice-cum-fish farming in the Ziro valley, the Zabo system of the Chakhesang Nagas and bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya.
  • Integrated: medicine, ritual, ecology and social rules are woven together, not split into disciplines.

2. Domains where it stands out

  • Ethno-medicine: the Kani tribe of Kerala shared knowledge of the arogyapacha plant, from which the Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute developed the anti-fatigue drug Jeevani; the Kanis received a share of the benefits, an early model of access and benefit-sharing.
  • Sustainable farming: mixed cropping, millets and seed-saving by communities such as the Dongria Kondh, and shifting cultivation with long fallows suited to hill ecology.
  • Disaster knowledge: during the 2004 tsunami, the Onge and Jarawa of the Andamans read the warning signs of the sea and moved to higher ground.
  • Arts and crafts: Warli, Gond and Saura paintings and Dhokra metal casting reflect nature and community.

3. Contrast with mainstream cultural systems

  • Social organisation: generally more egalitarian, without the caste hierarchy of purity and pollution; community councils decide common matters.
  • Gender: women often enjoy greater freedom, as among the matrilineal Khasi and Garo, and bride price is more common than dowry.
  • Economy: subsistence and sharing rather than accumulation.

4. Threats and safeguards

  • Threats: displacement by mines and dams, deforestation, assimilation, loss of tribal languages and biopiracy.
  • Safeguards: PESA (1996) empowers Gram Sabhas to protect customs; the Forest Rights Act (2006) recognises community forest resources; the Biological Diversity Act (2002) provides for benefit-sharing and People's Biodiversity Registers; the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (2001) blocks wrongful patents. In Niyamgiri (2013), Dongria Kondh Gram Sabhas rejected bauxite mining on their sacred hills.

Tribal knowledge is not "primitive" but a parallel science of sustainability. Drawing on it with consent and fair benefit-sharing honours the Tribal Panchsheel principle of development along the lines of the tribes' own genius.
free.upm-2021-gs1-10:
Gig economyPlatform workWomen's empowermentSocial security

The gig economy consists of short-term, task-based work outside a regular employer–employee relationship, much of it arranged through digital platforms for delivery, ride-hailing, beauty and home services, and freelancing. NITI Aayog (2022) counted 77 lakh gig workers in 2020-21 and projected 2.35 crore by 2029-30. With female labour force participation at only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24), gig work is often seen as a door to women's economic empowerment, but its record is mixed.

1. How gig work can empower women

  • Flexibility: women can choose their hours, combining paid work with the care duties that keep many out of regular jobs.
  • Low entry barriers: a smartphone and short training are enough to start in beauty services, tutoring, home cooking or freelancing.
  • Income and financial inclusion: a V.V. Giri National Labour Institute study (2025) of 355 women gig workers in Delhi-NCR found that nearly 57% earned over ₹20,000 a month; digital earnings records ease access to loans and insurance.
  • Agency and confidence: their own income strengthens women's say at home; women delivery partners and drivers challenge norms on mobility.

2. Limits and risks

  • Under-representation and segregation: women form only about 20–25% of the gig workforce (an AMCHAM–Uber estimate, 2024); in the VVGNLI sample, over three-quarters worked in beauty and wellness and under 6% in ride-hailing and delivery.
  • Safety: 76% of the women surveyed felt unsafe working at night, and fewer than 20% had access to emergency features such as panic buttons.
  • Algorithmic control: about 83% reported pressure to keep their ratings high; opaque penalties and deactivation leave them powerless.
  • No social security: no paid leave, maternity benefit or pension, and a "double burden" of paid and unpaid work.
  • Digital divide: only 54% of women have a mobile phone that they themselves use (NFHS-5), and fewer have digital skills.

3. Policy response

  • Code on Social Security, 2020 (in force since 21 November 2025): the first central law to recognise gig and platform workers; aggregators contribute 1–2% of turnover (capped at 5% of payments to such workers) to a social security fund. Under the central rules (May 2026), at least 90 days' work with one aggregator (120 days across several) in a year qualifies a worker, but benefits depend on schemes yet to be notified.
  • e-Shram: over 30 crore unorganised workers registered; the 2025-26 Budget promised identity cards and health cover under PM-JAY for platform workers.
  • State laws: Rajasthan's Platform Based Gig Workers Act, 2023 was the first State law; Karnataka and Bihar followed in 2025, Jharkhand also has one, and Telangana's Assembly passed a bill in March 2026, though implementation has been slow.

4. Way forward

Safety by design (SOS buttons, verified customers), maternity and childcare support, digital literacy, skilling beyond stereotyped work, collective voice (as SEWA shows) and gender-disaggregated data.

Gig work can empower women only if flexibility comes with security; otherwise it risks reproducing informality in a digital form.
free.upm-2021-gs1-11:
ModeratesDrain theoryConstitutional methodsPolitical education

The Moderates led the Indian National Congress from its founding in 1885 to about 1905: Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, M.G. Ranade, W.C. Bonnerjee and R.C. Dutt. Through constitutional methods, namely petitions, resolutions, speeches and memoranda (often summed up as "prayer, petition and protest"), they sought reforms within British rule. Their direct gains were modest, but they laid the ideological and organisational base of the national movement.

1. Contributions that prepared the base

  • Economic critique of colonialism: Naoroji's drain theory (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901), R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India and Ranade's writings showed that British rule impoverished India through the drain of wealth, the ruin of handicrafts and heavy land revenue. This broke the myth of a benevolent empire and became the intellectual foundation of later nationalism, including Swadeshi.
  • Political education: annual sessions in different cities, a pan-Indian platform and a nationalist press spread national consciousness and the ideas of democracy, civil liberties and representative government.
  • Constitutional demands: larger legislative councils, simultaneous ICS examinations in India and England, separation of the judiciary from the executive, lower military spending and freedom of the press; the Indian Councils Act, 1892 was a partial result.
  • Secular, all-India unity: a common platform across regions and religions; Badruddin Tyabji presided over the 1887 session.
  • Lobbying in Britain: the British Committee of the Congress (1889) and its journal India, and Naoroji's election to the House of Commons (1892).

2. Limitations

  • Narrow social base: the movement was confined to the urban, English-educated middle class; peasants and workers were not mobilised.
  • Faith in British justice: they believed the British would grant reforms once convinced, which the Extremists ridiculed as "political mendicancy".
  • Limited goals and gains: self-government within the Empire was to come only gradually, and most demands were ignored; the partition of Bengal (1905) exposed the limits of petitioning.

3. How they shaped the wider movement

  • Extremists built on their critique: Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo used the economic critique to justify Swadeshi and boycott.
  • Gandhi's mentor: Gandhi regarded Gokhale as his political guru, and the Moderates' commitment to non-violence and secular nationalism carried into the Gandhian phase.
  • Constitutional tradition: their demand for representative institutions led towards the Morley–Minto (1909) and later reforms, and their faith in parliamentary democracy, rule of law and civil liberties found a place in the Constitution.
  • Organisation: the Congress itself, the institution they built, became the vehicle of the mass movement.

The Moderates did not win freedom, but they prepared the ground: an economic critique of empire, a national platform and a liberal-democratic vision on which the Extremists and Gandhi built a mass struggle. Their contribution was foundational, though limited in method and reach.
free.upm-2021-gs1-12:
Constructive programmeKhadi and SwadeshiHarijan upliftmentNational education

Mahatma Gandhi saw the constructive programme, positive nation-building work in villages, as the other half of satyagraha. It built cadres, reached the masses and kept the movement alive between phases of struggle; he later set it out in Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place (1941). Both the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34) combined resistance to British rule with constructive work for Swaraj.

1. Constructive programmes in the Non-Cooperation Movement

  • Khadi and Swadeshi: the Congress meeting at Bezwada (1921) set targets of one crore Congress members, one crore rupees for the Tilak Swaraj Fund (which was oversubscribed) and 20 lakh charkhas; bonfires of foreign cloth went with spinning and weaving at home.
  • National education: students left government institutions for national ones such as Gujarat Vidyapith, Bihar Vidyapith, Kashi Vidyapith and Jamia Millia Islamia.
  • Hindu–Muslim unity: joint support for the Khilafat cause brought the two communities together on an unprecedented scale.
  • Social reform: removal of untouchability, temperance through picketing of liquor shops, and panchayats to settle disputes instead of British courts.
  • Turn to constructive work: after Chauri Chaura (February 1922), the Bardoli resolution suspended the movement and directed workers to khadi, national schools and anti-untouchability work.

2. Constructive programmes in the Civil Disobedience Movement

  • Salt and self-reliance: the Dandi March (12 March–6 April 1930) made salt, a basic necessity, a symbol of economic freedom.
  • Khadi and boycott: spinning, wearing khadi and boycotting foreign cloth; imports of British cloth fell sharply.
  • Prohibition: women in large numbers picketed liquor and foreign-cloth shops; prohibition was one of Gandhi's Eleven Points (January 1930).
  • Harijan upliftment: after the Poona Pact (1932) Gandhi founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932), started the weekly Harijan (1933) and toured the country (1933–34) for temple entry and against untouchability.
  • Village industries: when the movement was withdrawn, he set up the All India Village Industries Association (1934), building on the All India Spinners' Association (1925).

3. Significance

  • Struggle–truce–struggle: constructive work sustained the movement during truces and trained disciplined cadres for the next round.
  • Mass base: it carried nationalism to villages, women and the depressed classes.
  • Economic nationalism: khadi linked the poor peasant to Swaraj and hurt British textile interests.
  • Limitations: khadi cost more than mill cloth; Ambedkar criticised the Harijan campaign as paternalistic; Hindu–Muslim unity did not survive the 1920s.

The constructive programme turned the freedom struggle into a movement for social and economic regeneration; its ideals live on in Article 17, which abolished untouchability, and in Articles 43 and 47, which direct the State to promote cottage industries and prohibition.
free.upm-2021-gs1-13:
Inter-war crisisTreaty of VersaillesGreat DepressionFascism and Nazism

The First World War was fought, in Woodrow Wilson's words, to make the world "safe for democracy", and in 1919 the democratic state system seemed triumphant: new republics arose in Germany (Weimar), Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Baltic states, and the vote was widened. Yet within two decades most new democracies had fallen to dictatorships, under the strain of the Versailles settlement, the Great Depression and the appeal of fascism.

1. Causes of the challenge

  • A resented peace: the Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed a war-guilt clause, reparations and loss of territory on Germany, while Italy felt cheated of its gains (a "mutilated victory"); nationalists blamed democratic governments for these humiliations.
  • Economic crisis: German hyperinflation (1923) and the Great Depression after the Wall Street crash (1929) brought mass unemployment, about six million in Germany by 1932, and discredited liberal governments.
  • Fear of communism: after the Russian Revolution (1917), property-owners and the middle classes turned to strongmen who promised order.
  • Weak democratic roots: new states had little democratic experience; proportional representation produced unstable coalitions, and Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed rule by emergency decree.
  • Failure of collective security: the League of Nations' failure over Manchuria (1931) and Abyssinia (1935–36) emboldened aggressive regimes.

2. Nature of the challenge

  • Totalitarian ideologies: fascism and Nazism rejected parliamentary democracy, glorified the nation, the leader and war, and crushed rival parties, trade unions and the press; Stalin's USSR offered one-party communist rule as an alternative.
  • Legal routes to dictatorship: Mussolini and Hitler were appointed through constitutional means and then dismantled democracy from within, as through the Enabling Act (1933).
  • Persecution and expansion: racial laws (the Nuremberg Laws, 1935), rearmament and expansion (the Rhineland, 1936; Austria and the Sudetenland, 1938) threatened the whole international order.

3. Evaluation: serious, but not total

  • Democracy survived in Britain, France, the United States, Scandinavia, Switzerland, the Low Countries and Czechoslovakia (until Munich, 1938), and reformed itself through Roosevelt's New Deal (from 1933), Swedish social democracy and France's Popular Front (1936).
  • Democracies' own failures: appeasement at Munich (1938) and American isolationism let aggression grow.
  • A colonial contradiction: the same democracies denied self-rule to colonies such as India, weakening their moral claim.
  • Outcome: the challenge ended in the Second World War; after 1945 democracy was rebuilt in West Germany, Italy and Japan, and renewed through the UN and the welfare state.

The statement is valid: the inter-war years were the gravest crisis of liberal democracy, but its survival in key states and its renewal after 1945 show that the challenge, though serious, was not fatal.
free.upm-2021-gs1-14:
Orographic rainfallRain-shadowFöhn and chinookBarrier effect

Mountain ranges are barriers in the path of winds and air masses. Their alignment, whether across or parallel to the prevailing winds, decides where rain falls, where deserts form, how far cold or warm air can travel and which local winds blow. Air forced up a range cools and gives orographic rainfall on the windward side, while air descending the leeward side warms and dries, creating a rain-shadow.

1. Alignment of major mountain ranges

2. Impact on local weather

  • Windward rain and leeward rain-shadow: the Western Ghats intercept the south-west monsoon, so Mumbai and the Malabar coast get heavy rain while Pune and the interior Deccan receive far less; the funnel of the Khasi Hills gives Mawsynram and Sohra (Cherrapunji) some of the world's heaviest rain; Leh, behind the Himalaya, is a cold desert.
  • Barrier to cold and warm air: the Himalaya keep north India warmer in winter than places at similar latitudes. North America has no west–east barrier, so Arctic air can sweep south to Texas (as in February 2021) and moist Gulf air moves north, feeding thunderstorms and tornadoes on the Great Plains.
  • Hot, dry downslope winds: air descending the leeward slope warms by compression; the chinook ("snow-eater") of the Rockies, the föhn of the Alps and the zonda of the Argentine Andes melt snow and raise temperatures sharply within hours.
  • Deserts in the lee or alongside: the Atacama lies in the lee of the Andes and beside the cold Humboldt current; the Aravallis run parallel to the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon, so western Rajasthan stays dry.
  • Mountain and valley winds: valley breezes blow upslope by day and cold mountain breezes downslope at night; cold air settles in valleys, causing frost and fog (temperature inversion), so orchards are planted on slopes.
  • Funnelled winds: gaps between ranges channel winds, such as the cold mistral down the Rhône valley between the Alps and the Massif Central and the bora on the Adriatic coast.

3. Other effects

  • Altitude: temperature falls by about 6.5°C per km of height, so hill stations stay cool.
  • Upper-air flow: the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau split the subtropical westerly jet stream, and the plateau's summer heating aids the monsoon; western disturbances bring winter snow and rain to the western Himalaya.
  • Eastern Ghats: low and broken, they barely block the monsoon; Tamil Nadu, in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats during the south-west monsoon, gets most of its rain from the north-east monsoon (October–December).

Mountains thus act as climate dividers, creating sharp contrasts over short distances; understanding them is essential for agriculture, water management and disaster planning.
free.upm-2021-gs1-15:
Arctic amplificationSea-level riseJet streamPolar geopolitics

The two poles melt differently because they are built differently. The Arctic is an ocean ringed by land, and most of its ice is floating sea ice, apart from the Greenland ice sheet. Antarctica is a continent under an ice sheet more than 4 km thick in places, enough to raise the sea level by about 58 m. The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average; Antarctica's main threat is land ice flowing into the ocean.

1. Effects of Arctic melting on weather

  • Albedo feedback: white ice reflects sunlight while dark open water absorbs it, warming the Arctic further (Arctic amplification).
  • A wavier jet stream: a smaller temperature contrast between pole and tropics may weaken and slow the polar jet stream, a link scientists still debate; its meanders are associated with persistent heat waves, blocking patterns and cold outbreaks from a disturbed polar vortex.
  • Ocean circulation: meltwater from Greenland freshens the North Atlantic and can weaken the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), which the IPCC (AR6) says is very likely to decline this century; this could cool north-west Europe and shift tropical rain belts.
  • Permafrost thaw: releases carbon dioxide and methane, accelerating global warming.

2. Effects of Arctic melting on human activities

  • New shipping routes: the Northern Sea Route and the Northwest Passage stay open longer, shortening Europe–Asia voyages.
  • Resources and geopolitics: the Arctic is estimated to hold about 13% of the world's undiscovered oil and 30% of its undiscovered gas (USGS, 2008), sharpening rivalry; India is an Arctic Council observer (since 2013), runs the Himadri station (2008) and adopted an Arctic Policy in 2022.
  • Livelihoods and infrastructure: Inuit and other indigenous hunters lose their sea-ice platforms, thawing ground damages houses, roads and pipelines, and coasts erode.

3. Effects of Antarctic melting

  • Sea-level rise: ice loss from West Antarctica, especially the Thwaites Glacier, adds directly to the oceans. Global sea level rose 0.20 m between 1901 and 2018 and could rise 0.63–1.01 m by 2100 under very high emissions (IPCC AR6), threatening coastal cities, deltas such as the Sundarbans, and island nations such as the Maldives and Tuvalu.
  • Oceans and weather: cold, fresh meltwater can slow the sinking of dense Antarctic Bottom Water, weakening deep-ocean circulation and the Southern Ocean's uptake of heat and carbon. Antarctic sea ice fell to record lows in 2023.
  • Human activities: coastal flooding, salinisation of farmland and displacement; changes in krill stocks affect fisheries, penguins and whales. India's Maitri and Bharati stations and the Indian Antarctic Act, 2022 support research under the Antarctic Treaty (1959).

In short, Arctic melting acts mainly through weather and ocean circulation and opens new economic frontiers, while Antarctic melting acts mainly through sea-level rise; both demand deep emission cuts and coastal adaptation.
free.upm-2021-gs1-16:
Proven oil reservesOPECPetro-politicsEnergy security

Crude oil collects only where marine sediments, heat, pressure and suitable traps (anticlines, faults, salt domes) coincide, so its distribution is highly uneven. Of the world's 1,567 billion barrels of proven reserves at the end of 2024, OPEC members held 1,241 billion, or about 79% (OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin, 2025). Meanwhile, major consumers such as China, the EU, India and Japan depend heavily on imports.

1. Pattern of distribution

  • Middle East: Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and the UAE hold about half the world's proven reserves in the sedimentary basins around the Persian Gulf.
  • Americas: Venezuela has the largest proven reserves (extra-heavy oil of the Orinoco belt), Canada has vast oil sands, and the USA, through shale oil, is now the largest producer.
  • Others: Russia, Libya, Nigeria, Kazakhstan and the North Sea. India produced only about 28 million tonnes in 2024-25 and imports about 89% of its crude.

2. Economic implications

  • For producers: oil wealth funds development and sovereign funds such as Norway's, but also brings the resource curse (dependence on one export, "Dutch disease", corruption, boom-and-bust), as in Venezuela's collapse; Gulf states now seek diversification, as in Saudi Vision 2030.
  • For importers: large import bills, trade deficits, inflation and currency pressure; India's crude import bill for April–June 2026 was the highest ever for that quarter.
  • Price power: OPEC (1960) and OPEC+ manage supply, and price shocks such as the 1973 embargo, 1979, 2008, the 2020 crash and the 2022 surge ripple through the world economy.

3. Geopolitical and strategic implications

  • Conflict and intervention: oil was central to the Gulf War (1990–91) and to great-power interest in West Asia.
  • Chokepoints: about a fifth of world oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz; the 2026 West Asia crisis, which disrupted shipping there, hit India hard, as about half its crude imports use that route.
  • Sanctions as weapons: sanctions on Iran, Venezuela and Russia (including the G7 price cap of 2022) reshape trade; India stopped buying Iranian oil in 2019, and Russian crude, its largest source after 2022, was cut back after US sanctions in late 2025.

4. Social and environmental implications

  • Migration: Gulf oil economies host about 90 lakh Indians, a major source of remittances and soft power.
  • Rentier politics: oil revenue lets rulers govern without broad taxation, often delaying democracy.
  • Environment: spills (Exxon Valdez, 1989; Deepwater Horizon, 2010), gas flaring and oil-sands mining.

5. India's response

Diversified suppliers; strategic petroleum reserves of 5.33 million tonnes (Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur) with Phase II approved; overseas assets through ONGC Videsh; exploration under HELP (2016); 20% ethanol blending; electric mobility; and the National Green Hydrogen Mission.

The uneven geography of oil turns a mineral into a source of power and vulnerability; for importers such as India, diversification and the clean-energy transition are the lasting route to energy security.
free.upm-2021-gs1-17:
IT-BPM industryUrban agglomerationInequalityUrban stress

India's technology industry, led by IT-BPM services, earned about US$315 billion in 2025-26 (NASSCOM estimate), about US$246 billion of it from exports, and employs about 59.5 lakh people. It is concentrated in a few metropolitan clusters, namely Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, the National Capital Region (Gurugram, Noida) and Mumbai, helped by Software Technology Parks (from 1991), SEZs and pools of engineering talent. This agglomeration has transformed these cities' economies and societies, with both gains and costs.

1. Economic implications

  • Jobs and a new middle class: well-paid direct jobs create many more indirect jobs in transport, security, housekeeping, retail, hospitality and construction.
  • Exports and growth: software exports earn foreign exchange and raise city and State incomes; Karnataka and Telangana are among the leading IT-exporting States.
  • Start-ups and Global Capability Centres: Bengaluru and Hyderabad host start-up ecosystems and multinational R&D centres, moving the industry up the value chain.
  • Real-estate boom: demand for offices and housing raises land prices, enriching owners but pricing out lower-income residents.
  • Concentration risk: dependence on US and European clients, and the threat of automation and AI to entry-level jobs, make employment vulnerable.

2. Social implications

  • Migration and cosmopolitan culture: young professionals from across India make these cities multilingual and cosmopolitan, but also cause friction over local jobs and language, as in the debate over Karnataka's proposed local-quota bill (2024), which was put on hold.
  • Women's employment: IT is a major employer of educated women, giving many financial independence; night shifts and commutes raise safety concerns.
  • Family and lifestyle: nuclear and dual-income families, later marriages, consumerism, gated communities and work-from-home culture; long hours and stress bring burnout and lifestyle diseases.
  • Inequality and enclaves: high-income tech corridors stand beside informal workers and slums, creating "islands of prosperity" and a sharp digital and income divide.

3. Urban and environmental implications

  • Congestion: heavy traffic on corridors such as Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road and long commutes.
  • Water and lakes: lakes and drains encroached for development; Bengaluru's water crisis (2024) and the flooding of its Outer Ring Road (2022).
  • Infrastructure strain: housing, waste and power demand outpace planning, and heat islands grow.

4. Way forward

Spread IT to Tier-2 cities through STPI centres and State IT policies; invest in metro and bus transport, affordable rental housing and lake protection; reskill workers for AI under the IndiaAI Mission (2024); and widen local hiring through skilling rather than quotas.

IT industries have made Indian cities engines of globalised growth; making that growth inclusive and sustainable is the next challenge.
free.upm-2021-gs1-18:
Population educationNPEP (1980)Responsible parenthoodDemographic dividend

Population education is an educational programme that helps learners understand the population situation (size, growth, structure and distribution) and its links with resources, health and quality of life, so that they develop rational and responsible attitudes and behaviour. In India it began with the National Population Education Project (NPEP), launched by NCERT in April 1980. India is now the world's most populous country, but its fertility is already below replacement (TFR 1.9, SRS 2024).

1. Main objectives

  • Awareness of population dynamics: how births, deaths and migration shape population, and how population affects food, water, housing, jobs and the environment.
  • Responsible family life and parenthood: informed choices on age at marriage, spacing of children and family size, as a matter of rights and choice, not coercion.
  • Gender equality: countering son preference and promoting girls' education and health, given a sex ratio at birth of 918 girls per 1,000 boys (SRS 2024).
  • Adolescent health: knowledge of growing up, reproductive and sexual health, HIV/AIDS, substance abuse and life skills.
  • Sustainable development: linking population with consumption, environment and urbanisation.
  • Preparing for demographic change: reaping the demographic dividend and preparing for ageing, as the share of people aged 60+ is projected to rise from 10.5% (2022) to 20.8% by 2050 (India Ageing Report, 2023).

2. Measures to achieve them in India

  • School and teacher education: NPEP built population themes into the curriculum, textbooks and teacher training; the Adolescence Education Programme (2005), implemented by NCERT with UNFPA support, teaches life skills; NEP 2020 stresses health and well-being.
  • Health system: the Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (2014) reaches adolescents through peer educators and adolescent-friendly health clinics; Mission Parivar Vikas (2016) widens contraceptive choices in high-fertility districts; ASHAs and Anganwadi workers counsel families.
  • Legal and social measures: the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, the PCPNDT Act, 1994 against sex selection, and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015).
  • Policy framework: the National Population Policy, 2000 aimed at replacement fertility and a stable population by 2045 through voluntary choices, and set up the National Commission on Population.
  • Community and media: campaigns through mass and social media, self-help groups and panchayats, especially on World Population Day (11 July).
  • Research and data: the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai, and NFHS and SRS data guide targeting.

3. Challenges

  • Regional gaps: the TFR ranges from 2.9 in Bihar to 1.2 in Delhi.
  • Gender burden: female sterilisation (37.9% of married women) far outweighs male sterilisation (0.3%), as NFHS-5 shows.
  • Social taboos: resistance to sexuality and adolescence education in schools.
  • Weak delivery: untrained teachers and exam-driven schooling sideline these topics.

Population education has moved from "population control" to rights, choice and quality of life. Adapting it to a low-fertility, ageing India, with a focus on lagging States, men's responsibility and adolescent well-being, is the way forward.
free.upm-2021-gs1-19:
CryptocurrencyBlockchainVirtual digital assetsRegulation

A cryptocurrency is a digital asset that uses cryptography and a blockchain, a shared, tamper-resistant ledger kept by a network of computers, to record ownership and transfers without a central bank or intermediary. Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first; thousands of others, such as Ether and dollar-linked stablecoins, followed. Indian law calls them virtual digital assets (VDAs).

1. What it is: key features

  • Decentralised and peer-to-peer: there is no issuer; the network validates transactions through "proof of work" (mining) or "proof of stake".
  • Limited supply, volatile value: Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins, and prices swing sharply with speculation.
  • Pseudonymous and borderless: wallets carry addresses, not names, and transfers cross borders in minutes.
  • Not a CBDC: a central bank digital currency, such as the RBI's e-rupee (pilots from 2022), is issued and backed by the central bank.

2. Effects on global society

  • New finance: a new asset class, decentralised finance (DeFi) and cheaper cross-border remittances; spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds in the USA (2024) drew in mainstream investors.
  • Risks to savers: collapses such as Terra–Luna (May 2022) and the FTX exchange (November 2022) wiped out savings.
  • Crime: ransomware (the 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransom was paid in Bitcoin), money laundering, terror financing and dark-web trade.
  • Monetary sovereignty: El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021 but made its acceptance voluntary in January 2025 to secure an IMF loan; China banned crypto trading and mining in 2021.
  • Environment: proof-of-work mining uses huge amounts of electricity; Ethereum's shift to proof of stake (2022) cut its energy use by over 99%.
  • Regulation: the EU's MiCA regulation (fully applicable from December 2024), the US stablecoin law (GENIUS Act, 2025), FATF standards and, under India's G20 presidency (2023), an IMF–FSB global roadmap.

3. Has it affected Indian society?

  • Wide adoption: India ranked first in Chainalysis's Global Crypto Adoption Index in 2023, 2024 and 2025.
  • Legal uncertainty: the RBI's 2018 bar on banks serving crypto firms was struck down in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI (2020); as of 2026 there is still no comprehensive law, and crypto is not legal tender.
  • Tax and oversight: the Finance Act, 2022 imposed a 30% tax on VDA gains without set-off of losses and 1% TDS on transfers; VDA service providers were brought under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (2023) and must register with FIU-IND. Much trading has moved to offshore platforms.
  • Social costs: investor losses, Ponzi-style schemes, exchange hacks and crypto-funded cyber-fraud and drug trade prey on youth with low financial literacy.
  • Opportunities: blockchain jobs and uses in land records and supply chains, though many Web3 firms have moved abroad.

Cryptocurrency is neither money India recognises nor a passing fad; a clear regulatory framework with investor protection and global coordination, alongside the RBI's e-rupee, is the balanced path.
free.upm-2021-gs1-20:
Continuity and changeSanskritisationModernisation of traditionAdaptive resilience

Indian society has shown remarkable continuity over millennia, absorbing new influences without breaking with its past. Yogendra Singh (Modernization of Indian Tradition, 1973) showed how tradition and modernity coexist, while M.N. Srinivas explained change through Sanskritisation and Westernisation. Today urbanisation, education, technology and globalisation are changing family, caste, gender relations and religion, but often by adapting tradition rather than replacing it.

1. How continuity is maintained

  • Family and kinship: joint-family values persist even where households are nuclear, through regular support and shared obligations; respect for elders and arranged marriages remain strong, backed by laws such as the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007.
  • Religion, rituals and festivals: life-cycle rituals (samskaras), pilgrimages such as the Kumbh, and festivals renew community bonds across generations.
  • Caste and community networks: endogamy, caste associations and kin networks provide identity and social security.
  • Oral and artistic traditions: epics, folk arts, regional languages, cuisine and the guru–shishya tradition transmit values.
  • Adaptive mechanisms: syncretism, Sanskritisation and "compartmentalisation"; Milton Singer found industrial leaders in Madras who were modern at work and traditional at home.
  • Constitutional support: Article 29 protects the culture of minorities, and Article 51A(f) makes it a duty to value and preserve India's composite culture.

2. Changes taking place

  • Family: nuclearisation, smaller families (TFR 1.9, SRS 2024) and ageing (the 60+ share is projected to rise from 10.5% in 2022 to 20.8% by 2050) strain traditional elder care.
  • Marriage: later marriage, more self-chosen and inter-caste unions, and more divorces in cities; the Supreme Court decriminalised homosexuality (Navtej Singh Johar, 2018), though it declined to legalise same-sex marriage (2023).
  • Caste: purity-and-pollution practices have weakened in public life, but caste persists in marriage and politics; Dalit and backward-class assertion reflects new mobility.
  • Gender: girls' education, women's work and legal rights, including daughters' equal coparcenary rights (2005 amendment; Vineeta Sharma, 2020), the criminalisation of instant triple talaq (2019) and the women's reservation law (2023).
  • Values and lifestyle: a shift from ascribed to achieved status and from collectivism to individualism, consumerism, and new forms of community on social media.

3. Assessment

  • Selective and uneven: change is faster in cities and among the educated, slower in villages.
  • Mixed legacy: some continuities are valuable (family support, pluralism), others harmful (caste discrimination, dowry, son preference) and need active reform.

Indian society changes through adaptive continuity: tradition modernises and modernity is Indianised, a balance the Constitution guides through its commitment to liberty, equality and fraternity.
free.upm-2021-gs2-1:
Constitutional moralityEssential facetsJudicial reviewConstitutionalism

Constitutional morality means fidelity to the core values and spirit of the Constitution (rule of law, liberty, equality, dignity, fraternity, and checks and balances), not merely to its text. Dr B.R. Ambedkar, drawing on the historian George Grote, told the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) that it "is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." The Supreme Court has turned the idea into a doctrine for testing laws, executive action and social practices against the Constitution's essential facets.

1. Meaning and essential facets

  • Rooted in the Constitution itself: its content comes from the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and the basic structure, so it is the morality the Constitution declares, not a judge's personal view.
  • Institutional facet: every organ of the State must respect its limits, constitutional conventions and the other organs, and must not act arbitrarily.
  • Rights facet: individual dignity and liberty must be protected even against majority opinion, which makes the doctrine counter-majoritarian.
  • Transformative purpose: the Constitution seeks to change an unequal society, so inherited customs are tested against equality and dignity.

2. Judicial decisions

  • Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014): the Court said constitutional morality means bowing to the norms of the Constitution and not acting arbitrarily; it advised the Prime Minister and Chief Ministers not to choose as ministers persons charged with heinous crimes or corruption.
  • Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018): a Constitution Bench asked constitutional functionaries to work in harmony and in the spirit of the Constitution, and held that the Lieutenant Governor is ordinarily bound by the aid and advice of the elected government.
  • Navtej Singh Johar (2018): decriminalising consensual same-sex relations under Section 377 IPC, the Court held that constitutional morality must prevail over social morality.
  • Joseph Shine (2018): the offence of adultery (Section 497 IPC) was struck down because it treated a wife as her husband's property, violating dignity and equality.
