  • Indian Young Lawyers Association (Sabarimala, 2018): the majority held that excluding women aged 10–50 from the temple failed the test of constitutional morality; in 2019 wider questions of religious freedom were referred to a larger bench.

3. Criticism and limits

  • Vagueness: critics warn that an undefined standard can let judges substitute their own views for those of elected legislatures.
  • Pluralism: Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent in Sabarimala cautioned that in a pluralist society constitutional morality must also respect the freedom to practise one's faith.
  • Safeguard: the doctrine works best when applied with restraint and anchored in specific Articles and the basic structure.

Constitutional morality is the Constitution's conscience: it keeps power within limits and rights beyond the reach of passing majorities. Applied with judicial restraint and cultivated through civic education, as Ambedkar urged, it turns the text into living constitutionalism.
free.upm-2021-gs2-2:
Gender diversityHigher judiciaryCollegiumInclusive justice

Women are half of India's population, but few sit in the higher judiciary. From 1989, when Justice M. Fathima Beevi became the first woman judge of the Supreme Court, to 2021, only 11 women were appointed to it; the next, Justice V. Mohana, took oath only in June 2026, giving the Court two women judges with Justice B.V. Nagarathna. In February 2026 women held 116 of 781 sitting High Court judgeships (14.85%, Ministry of Law and Justice data).

1. Why greater representation is desirable

  • Diversity of perspective: judges' life experiences shape how they read facts and evidence; women judges add insight in cases of sexual violence, domestic abuse, custody, maintenance and workplace discrimination.
  • Equity: Articles 14 and 15(3) and India's commitments under CEDAW (ratified in 1993) call for substantive equality; an institution that guards equality should practise it.
  • Inclusiveness and public trust: a bench that mirrors society enjoys greater legitimacy, and women litigants, especially survivors of violence, may find courts more approachable.
  • Better jurisprudence: in Aparna Bhat v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2021) the Supreme Court set aside a bail condition requiring a man accused of molestation to have the complainant tie a rakhi on him, and told courts to avoid gender stereotypes; its Handbook on Combating Gender Stereotypes (2023) shows how such language can enter judgments.
  • Role models: women judges encourage women lawyers to stay in practice and seek elevation.

2. Why women remain few

  • A leaky pipeline: many women enter the district judiciary through competitive examinations, but elevation to High Courts depends heavily on senior advocates from the Bar, where women are fewer and are briefed less.
  • Opaque collegium: there are no published criteria or diversity goals, and the Memorandum of Procedure is still not finalised.
  • Age and seniority: women often become eligible late and get short tenures; Justice Nagarathna is in line to become the first woman Chief Justice of India in 2027, for about five weeks.
  • Workplace barriers: care responsibilities and few crèches or facilities in court complexes.

3. Measures

  • Diversity as a stated criterion: the collegium can consider women from both the Bar and the district judiciary and publish its criteria; former CJI N.V. Ramana (2021) backed women's demand for 50% representation.
  • Fair senior designation: transparent, points-based designation of senior advocates, as laid down in Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India (2017).
  • Support systems: crèches, flexible hours and safe infrastructure in courts.
  • Merit and diversity together: the pool of qualified women is now large, so diversity need not compromise merit.

Diversity on the bench is not tokenism but a condition of legitimacy: courts that decide questions of equality must reflect the society they serve. Progress such as four women serving at the same time as High Court Chief Justices (June 2026) and a second woman on the Supreme Court must become routine through a transparent and inclusive appointment process.
free.upm-2021-gs2-3:
14th Finance CommissionTax devolutionFiscal autonomyFiscal discipline

The 14th Finance Commission (chair: Dr Y.V. Reddy; award period 2015–20), constituted under Article 280, raised the States' share of the divisible pool of central taxes from 32% to 42%, the largest increase ever. Accepted by the Union in 2015, it shifted transfers from tied, scheme-based grants to untied devolution, letting States set their own spending priorities, and paired this with gap-filling grants and rule-based borrowing limits.

1. More, and more untied, resources

  • Vertical devolution: 42% of the divisible pool reached the States as untied money, the core of their improved fiscal position.
  • Formula-based horizontal sharing: weights for income distance, population, area and, for the first time, forest cover rewarded both need and ecological services.
  • Revenue-deficit grants: ₹1,94,821 crore for 11 States whose revenue fell short even after devolution, including ₹22,113 crore for post-bifurcation Andhra Pradesh.
  • Local bodies: ₹2,87,436 crore for duly constituted gram panchayats and municipalities, with performance grants for audited accounts and higher own revenue.

2. Fiscal discipline with flexibility

  • Borrowing limit: a fiscal deficit of 3% of GSDP, with an extra 0.25% each for States whose debt was at most 25% of GSDP and whose interest payments were at most 10% of revenue receipts, up to 3.5%, but only if they had no revenue deficit.
  • Predictability: rule-based limits rewarded prudent States and made borrowing plans stable.
  • FRBM reform: it urged eliminating the revenue deficit itself and creating an independent fiscal council.

3. How the States' fiscal position changed

  • Autonomy: a larger share of transfers came without conditions, so States could fund their own priorities instead of matching central ones.
  • Rationalised central schemes: a NITI Aayog sub-group of Chief Ministers (2015) grouped centrally sponsored schemes into core and optional ones; most core schemes moved to a 60:40 Centre–State share (90:10 for north-eastern and Himalayan States).
  • Less discretion: with the Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog (2015), discretionary plan grants ended and transfers became more formula-based.

4. Limits

  • Smaller net gain: the Union cut its share in several schemes and ended plan grants, so total transfers rose less than devolution.
  • Cesses and surcharges, which are not shared with States, grew as a share of central revenue.
  • New burdens: UDAY (2015) moved power-distribution debt onto State budgets, and GST compensation ended in 2022.
  • Later awards: the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions set the share at 41%, and the 16th (2026–31) ended revenue-deficit grants.

The 14th FC moved India from scheme-driven to trust-based fiscal federalism. Bringing cesses into the divisible pool and pairing autonomy with accountability for outcomes would consolidate its gains for cooperative federalism.
free.upm-2021-gs2-4:
Collective responsibilityParliamentary oversightCommitteesExecutive dominance

In a parliamentary system, the executive answers to the legislature every day, not only at elections. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), so it holds office only while it enjoys the House's confidence. Parliament enforces this accountability through questions, debates, motions, control of the purse and committees. How far it succeeds depends on the strength of the Opposition, the time the House sits and the majority's willingness to accept scrutiny.

1. Instruments that work

  • Questions and debates: Question Hour, Zero Hour, calling-attention notices and short-duration discussions make ministers answer in public, on the record.
  • Confidence of the House: governments have fallen on the floor of the Lok Sabha, as in 1990 and in April 1999, when the Vajpayee Government lost by one vote.
  • Control of the purse: no tax without law (Article 265) and no spending without appropriation (Article 114); the Public Accounts Committee examines the CAG's audit reports (Article 151).
  • Committees: Departmentally Related Standing Committees (since 1993), Joint Parliamentary Committees (such as those on Bofors, 1987, and 2G spectrum, 2011), and committees on government assurances and subordinate legislation.
  • Exposing irregularities: CAG reports on 2G spectrum and coal blocks were scrutinised in Parliament, and the Supreme Court later cancelled 122 licences (2012) and 214 blocks (2014).

2. Limits on accountability

  • Thin scrutiny: in the 17th Lok Sabha (2019–24), which held 274 sittings, only 16% of Bills went to committees, against 71% in the 15th; 35% passed with less than an hour of debate, and about 80% of the budget was voted without discussion in 2019–23 (PRS).
  • Disciplined majorities: the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) binds members to the party whip, so a majority government rarely loses a vote.
  • Disruptions: frequent adjournments wipe out Question Hour.
  • Bypassing Parliament: ordinances (Article 123), wide delegated legislation and the Money Bill route, as for the Aadhaar Act, 2016, reduce scrutiny.
  • A weakened Opposition: the Deputy Speaker was not elected during the entire 17th Lok Sabha, and 146 MPs of both Houses were suspended in December 2023.

3. Assessment: to what extent?

Parliament ensures accountability only partly. Its instruments are strong on paper and decisive in moments of crisis or coalition government, but under large majorities daily scrutiny weakens, and courts, the CAG, the RTI Act and the media now share much of the burden.

4. Strengthening oversight

  • Mandatory committee scrutiny of Bills, and a statutory minimum of 120 sitting days a year, as suggested by the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002).
  • Space for the Opposition: Opposition days, as in the UK House of Commons, and limiting the whip to confidence motions (Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990).

Responsible government needs a Parliament that scrutinises, not one that only ratifies. More sittings, stronger committees and a respected Opposition would restore parliamentary accountability.
free.upm-2021-gs2-5:
Pressure groupsBusiness associationsPolicy advocacyLobbying

Pressure groups are organised interests that seek to influence public policy without contesting elections. Protected by the freedom of association (Article 19(1)(c)), they carry members' views to policymakers between elections. Among the oldest and best resourced are business associations: apex chambers such as ASSOCHAM (1920), FICCI (1927) and CII (named in 1992, with roots in 1895), and sectoral bodies such as NASSCOM for IT and SIAM for automobiles. They shape policy mainly through expertise and consultation rather than agitation.

1. How business associations contribute to public policy

  • Expertise and data: pre-budget memoranda, industry surveys and sector studies give ministries information on costs, investment and jobs that government itself lacks.
  • Consultation: they take part in the Finance Minister's pre-budget consultations, the Board of Trade and stakeholder meetings, and comment on draft laws published under the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014).
  • Design of reforms: chambers supplied inputs for GST and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016), and flag problems during implementation, which leads to course corrections.
  • Voice for new sectors: NASSCOM has shaped policies for the IT industry, and start-up groups pressed for the removal of the "angel tax", which the Union Budget 2024-25 abolished.
  • Trade policy: industry concerns over cheap imports were among the reasons India stayed out of RCEP (2019).
  • Implementation partners: industry-led Sector Skill Councils set skill standards under Skill India, and chambers promote exports and CSR projects.

2. Concerns

  • Unequal voice: large firms are heard more than MSMEs, workers and consumers; as Mancur Olson argued, small, concentrated groups organise more easily than large, diffuse ones.
  • Rent-seeking: demands for tariff protection or tax breaks can raise costs for consumers and downstream industries.
  • Opaque links with politics: electoral bonds allowed anonymous corporate funding of parties until the Supreme Court struck them down in February 2024.
  • No lobbying law: unlike the US Lobbying Disclosure Act, 1995, India has no register of lobbyists or disclosure of their meetings with officials.

3. Way forward

  • Transparency: a lobbying disclosure framework and publication of the inputs received in consultations.
  • Balance: equal access for trade unions, consumer bodies and MSME associations, so that policy weighs all affected interests.
  • Independent regulators that can assess industry claims on their merits.

Business associations act as a transmission belt between markets and the State, bringing expertise, feedback and investor confidence into policymaking. With transparency and balanced consultation, their influence can serve the public interest rather than narrow gain.
free.upm-2021-gs2-6:
Primary health careWelfare StateUniversal health coverageSustainable development

Primary health care (PHC) is essential, affordable care delivered close to where people live, from immunisation and maternal care to screening for chronic diseases. The Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) and the Astana Declaration (2018) made it the foundation of "health for all". In India, Article 47 directs the State to improve public health, and the Supreme Court has read a right to health care into Article 21 (Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity, 1996).

1. A moral imperative of the Welfare State

  • Dignity and equality: illness strikes the poor hardest; when public care is weak, families borrow or sell assets, and treatment becomes a privilege of the few.
  • Low public spending: government health expenditure was only about 1.4% of GDP in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts), well below the National Health Policy, 2017 goal of 2.5%.
  • Justice for the vulnerable: rural, tribal and urban-poor households, women and the elderly depend most on public primary care.
  • An old promise: the Bhore Committee (1946) proposed a State-funded, three-tier system so that inability to pay would not deny anyone care.

2. A precondition for sustainable development

  • Human capital: 35.5% of children under five were stunted (NFHS-5); undernourished, often-ill children learn less and earn less as adults.
  • Productivity and the demographic dividend: healthy workers lose fewer days, and screening for diabetes, hypertension and cancers at the primary level prevents costly disability.
  • Cost-effectiveness: prevention and early treatment cost far less than hospital care, keeping both public and household budgets sustainable.
  • Resilience: COVID-19 showed that surveillance, vaccination and community health workers are the first line of defence; the WHO honoured India's ASHAs with a Global Health Leaders Award in 2022.
  • SDG links: PHC underpins SDG 3 and its target of universal health coverage, and advances the goals on poverty, education, gender and work.

3. India's efforts and gaps

  • Efforts: about 1.82 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs offer free drugs, diagnostics and screening for non-communicable diseases; eSanjeevani had handled over 50 crore teleconsultations by October 2026; the PM-Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (2021) builds block-level capacity.
  • Gaps: vacant posts of doctors and specialists, uneven quality across States, weak urban primary care and high out-of-pocket spending on medicines.
  • What works: Kerala's Family Health Centres and Tamil Nadu's doorstep-care scheme Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam (2021).

The statement is valid: primary health care is where ethics and economics meet. Raising public spending towards 2.5% of GDP, filling human-resource gaps and community ownership will make health for all the foundation of sustainable development.
free.upm-2021-gs2-7:
Earn while you learnVocational educationApprenticeshipSkill India

"Earn while you learn" combines study with paid, productive work through apprenticeships, stipend-based internships and work-integrated degrees. It makes vocational education affordable for poor students and gives them real workplace skills. NEP 2020 seeks to integrate vocational and academic streams, and schemes such as the PM National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (PM-NAPS) and the PM Internship Scheme apply the idea. Yet only 4.4% of youth aged 15–29 were formally skilled (PLFS 2022-23).

1. Why the approach matters

  • Removes the opportunity cost: poor youth often leave education to earn; a stipend lets them keep learning.
  • Job-ready skills: learning on the shop floor builds technical and soft skills that classrooms miss; only about half of young people are judged employable (Economic Survey 2023-24, citing the India Skills Report 2024).
  • Dignity of labour: NEP 2020 aims to give at least half of learners vocational exposure and provides a 10-day bagless period in Grades 6–8, when students intern with local craftspeople.
  • Global evidence: Germany's dual system, which combines classroom learning with paid training in firms, eases young people's transition to work.

2. Why it needs strengthening

  • Small scale: PM-NAPS had engaged about 43.47 lakh apprentices by May 2025, small relative to the number of young people entering the workforce.
  • Weak uptake: fewer than one-third of PM Internship Scheme offers had been accepted by late 2025, as low stipends, distant postings and mismatched roles deterred youth; a 2026 revamp raised the stipend and widened eligibility.
  • MSMEs stay away: small firms, which employ most workers, find apprenticeship paperwork and costs burdensome.
  • Quality and recognition: routine, low-skill tasks and weak assessment, and work-based learning rarely counts towards a degree.
  • Stigma and gender barriers: vocational routes are seen as second-best, and young women face safety and mobility constraints.

3. Making it meaningful

  • Better stipends linked to local wages, with travel and hostel support, especially for women.
  • Bring in MSMEs: simpler compliance, aggregators such as ITIs and industry bodies, and incentives for small firms in industrial clusters.
  • Credit and certification: use the National Credit Framework (2023) so that work-based learning counts towards qualifications.
  • Matching and outcomes: the Skill India Digital Hub for matching, and funding tied to completion, placement and wages.

Earning while learning turns training from a cost into an investment for poor youth. Scaled up with industry participation and quality assurance, it can make vocational education a respected route to decent jobs and help realise the demographic dividend.
free.upm-2021-gs2-8:
Self-help groupsMicrofinanceWomen's agencyMalnutrition

Gender inequality, poverty and malnutrition form a vicious cycle: women with little income or voice often eat last and least, give birth to underweight babies and raise children who grow up stunted and poor. NFHS-5 (2019-21) found 57% of women aged 15–49 anaemic and 35.5% of children under five stunted. Microfinance through women's self-help groups (SHGs), from NABARD's SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (1992) to DAY-NRLM, which has organised about 10 crore women, seeks to break this cycle.

1. How SHG microfinance can break the cycle

  • Income and assets: collateral-free group loans and savings replace moneylenders and finance dairy, poultry, tailoring and petty trade; Lakhpati Didi aims to raise 3 crore SHG members to a household income of at least ₹1 lakh a year.
  • Bargaining power: a woman who earns gains a greater say over household spending, and women tend to spend more on food, health and schooling.
  • Nutrition built in: DAY-NRLM has a food, nutrition, health and WASH component, and SHGs promote kitchen gardens and nutrition awareness.
  • Enterprise in nutrition: Kudumbashree units in Kerala make the Amrutham Nutrimix take-home ration for anganwadis, and Bihar's JEEViKA groups run Didi ki Rasoi canteens in government hospitals.
  • Voice and leadership: SHG members speak up in Gram Sabhas, work as banking correspondents and contest panchayat elections.

2. Why credit alone cannot break it

  • Over-indebtedness: aggressive lending led to the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis (2010) and the RBI's Malegam Committee; repayment stress among microfinance borrowers rose again in 2024-25.
  • Control by men: loans taken in women's names are sometimes used by male relatives.
  • Low-return activities: small loans for crowded local trades raise incomes only slightly without skills and markets.
  • Malnutrition has many causes: sanitation, safe water, care practices, health services and age at marriage matter as much as income; anaemia is common even in better-off households.
  • Uneven spread: SHG movements are stronger in the southern and eastern States, and the poorest often stay outside groups.

3. Making it work

  • Convergence: link SHGs with anganwadis under POSHAN 2.0, health centres, the Jal Jeevan Mission and the public distribution system.
  • Beyond credit: financial literacy, enterprise support such as PMFME seed capital, market access and land and housing titles for women.

The answer is yes, but only in part. Microfinance gives women the first rungs of the ladder: income, savings and voice. Breaking the cycle needs convergence of credit with nutrition, health and social change, so that SHGs become platforms of women's agency.
free.upm-2021-gs2-9:
Africa's riseSouth–South cooperationDevelopment partnershipKampala principles

Africa has the world's youngest population, with a median age under 20, and is expected to hold about a quarter of humanity by 2050 (UN). The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), trading since 2021, aims at a single market of over 1.3 billion people, and the continent holds minerals vital for clean energy, so the coming decades may well be Africa's. India's engagement, guided by the ten Kampala principles (2018), has expanded, though it remains modest beside China's.

1. Economic influence

  • Trade and investment: India is among Africa's leading trading partners and investors, trading in oil, coal, gold, medicines and vehicles, while Indian firms are active in telecom, autos and agriculture.
  • Lines of credit: over US$10 billion in concessional credit has funded railways, power, water and agro-processing projects across some 40 African countries.
  • Market access: India's duty-free tariff preference scheme for least developed countries (2008) benefits many African economies.
  • Affordable medicines: Indian generic antiretrovirals made HIV treatment affordable across Africa, and India sent COVID-19 vaccines under Vaccine Maitri.

2. Development partnership and soft power

  • Capacity building: ITEC (1964), 50,000 scholarships promised at the third India–Africa Forum Summit (2015), and tele-education and telemedicine through e-VidyaBharati and e-ArogyaBharati (2019).
  • Institutions: IIT Madras's first overseas campus, in Zanzibar (Tanzania, 2023).
  • Digital public infrastructure: NPCI International agreed with the Bank of Namibia (2024) to build an instant payment system on UPI technology.

3. Political and security influence

  • Voice of the Global South: under India's presidency, the African Union became a permanent member of the G20 (New Delhi, September 2023).
  • Presence: India decided in 2018 to open 18 new missions in Africa, and high-level visits continue, such as the Prime Minister's to Ghana and Namibia (July 2025).
  • Security: Indian peacekeepers serve in UN missions in South Sudan and the DR Congo, the Navy has run anti-piracy patrols in the Gulf of Aden since 2008, and maritime partnerships with Mauritius and Seychelles extend India's reach.

4. Limits

  • Scale: China's trade, lending and infrastructure presence are far larger.
  • Delivery: delays in projects under lines of credit dent credibility.
  • Irregular summits: the fourth India–Africa Forum Summit, due in New Delhi in May 2026, was postponed because of a public-health situation in Africa, so the forum has not met since 2015.
  • People-to-people ties: incidents of racial hostility towards African students in India have hurt goodwill.

India's influence in Africa is broad, spanning economics, development and diplomacy, but modest in scale. Faster delivery, regular summits, private investment and cooperation in AfCFTA, critical minerals and digital infrastructure can make India a lasting partner of equals in Africa's growth story.
free.upm-2021-gs2-10:
Strategic competitionGreat-power rivalryInterdependenceTechnology race

During the Cold War, the USA faced the Soviet Union, a nuclear superpower that was economically weaker and largely outside the world economy. China today combines economic size, technological ambition and rapid military modernisation while remaining deeply tied to global supply chains. The US National Security Strategy (2022) described China as the only competitor with both the intent and, increasingly, the power to reshape the international order. Hence many in Washington see it as a more complex, even existential, challenge.

1. Why China is more challenging than the Soviet Union

  • Economic weight: the Soviet economy never came close to America's, whereas China is the world's second-largest economy, its largest manufacturer and, since 2013, its largest trader in goods.
  • Interdependence as leverage: US–Soviet trade was negligible, but the US and Chinese economies are entangled through trade, supply chains and finance, so containment hurts both; China has used export curbs on gallium and germanium (2023) and rare earths (2025).
  • Technology race: the USSR led mainly in weapons and space; China competes across 5G, artificial intelligence (as DeepSeek's model showed in 2025), electric vehicles, batteries and solar power, guided by "Made in China 2025" (2015).
  • Military modernisation: the PLA Navy is the world's largest by number of ships (US Department of Defense), China is expanding its nuclear arsenal, and it rejected the 2016 arbitral award against its South China Sea claims.
  • Influence without a formal bloc: the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), the AIIB (2016) and China's global development and security initiatives build influence in the Global South, and China works within existing institutions rather than walling itself off.

2. How the USA has responded

  • Strategy: the rebalance to Asia (2011), and the 2017 National Security Strategy, which called China a revisionist power.
  • Economic tools: tariffs from 2018, which escalated sharply in 2025 before a truce; the CHIPS and Science Act and export controls on advanced chips (2022).
  • Partnerships: the Quad, AUKUS (2021) and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (2022).

3. Is the threat "existential"?

  • Not in the Cold War sense: China does not seek to overthrow the American system or export revolution, and nuclear deterrence and interdependence restrain war.
  • China's constraints: a population falling since 2022, a property-sector slump, local-government debt and few allies.
  • US strengths: alliances, the dollar, leading universities and an innovation ecosystem.
  • Shared problems: climate change, pandemics and financial stability still need cooperation.

For India, the rivalry raises its value as a trusted partner in supply chains and the Quad, but India must preserve strategic autonomy and manage its own border with China.

China is less an existential threat than a comprehensive one, economic, technological, military and normative at once, and harder to contain because it is woven into the world economy. The likely outcome is long-term managed competition rather than a new Cold War.
free.upm-2021-gs2-11:
General consentSection 6, DSPE ActPolice as a State subjectCooperative federalism

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), set up in 1963, derives its powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946. Because police and public order are State subjects (Entries 1 and 2, State List), Section 6 of the Act requires a State's consent before the CBI investigates there. Since 2018 several States, including West Bengal, Kerala, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka (2024), have withdrawn general consent, yet courts have held that this power is not absolute.

1. The legal framework

  • Union List: Entry 8 (Central Bureau of Intelligence and Investigation) and Entry 80, which allows a police force's powers to be extended to another State only with its consent.
  • DSPE Act: the Centre notifies the offences the CBI may investigate (Section 3) and extends its jurisdiction to a State (Section 5), but the State must consent (Section 6), either generally for a class of cases or case by case.

2. Why States question the CBI's jurisdiction

  • Fear of misuse: States see unilateral CBI cases as intrusion into their policing domain and allege selective, politically timed action; the Supreme Court itself called the CBI a "caged parrot" during the coal-block hearings (2013).
  • Litigation: in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (July 2024), the Supreme Court held maintainable the State's Article 131 suit against cases registered after it withdrew consent, observing that the CBI is a body established and supervised by the Union.

3. Why the States' power is not absolute

  • Constitutional courts: in State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010), a Constitution Bench held that constitutional courts can order CBI probes without State consent in exceptional cases; the Calcutta High Court did so for post-poll violence (2021) and the R.G. Kar case (2024).
  • No retrospective effect: in Kazi Lhendup Dorji v. CBI (1994), the Court held that revoking consent operates only prospectively, so pending investigations continue.
  • Central employees: in State (CBI) v. A. Satish Kumar (January 2025), the Court held that the CBI needs no State consent to register an FIR under a central law against central government employees posted in the State.
  • Yet consent matters: in Fertico Marketing (2020), the Court called the consent requirement in tune with the Constitution's federal character.

4. Reconciling federalism with the rule of law

  • Balance: policing is a State function in a "Union of States"; consent preserves that, while courts stop it from shielding wrongdoing.
  • Credible autonomy: the Director is chosen by a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India (Section 4A, added by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013); similar insulation in daily work would build trust.
  • Reform: a dedicated CBI law defining its mandate, and protocols agreed in the Inter-State Council.

Consent under Section 6 protects the States' domain, but it cannot shield corruption or serious crime from investigation. A statutory charter for the CBI and cooperative federalism in practice can reconcile State autonomy with the rule of law.
free.upm-2021-gs2-12:
Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993NHRCParis PrinciplesAccountability

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), set up on 12 October 1993, and the State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) derive from the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993, framed in line with the UN's Paris Principles. They inquire into violations, intervene in court cases, visit jails and spread rights awareness. They have achieved much, yet critics say they rarely stand up to the police, security forces and influential officials.

1. Contributions

  • Custodial justice: the NHRC requires every custodial death to be reported to it within 24 hours, and has issued guidelines on encounter killings.
  • Landmark interventions: in NHRC v. State of Arunachal Pradesh (1996), it secured protection for Chakma refugees under Article 21; it moved the Supreme Court in the 2002 Gujarat riot cases, which led to a retrial of the Best Bakery case outside the State.
  • Vulnerable groups: at the Supreme Court's request it has monitored the abolition of bonded labour and the condition of mental hospitals, and it has taken up silicosis, manual scavenging and child labour.
  • Relief: it has recommended compensation in many cases, such as the Punjab mass cremations referred by the Supreme Court.

2. Structural limitations

  • Recommendatory powers: under Section 18 the government need only report, within a month, what action it has taken or proposes on a recommendation; it is not bound to accept it.
  • Armed forces excluded: under Section 19 the NHRC can only seek a report from the Union government and cannot investigate on its own.
  • One-year bar: it cannot inquire into a violation more than a year old (Section 36(2)).
  • Executive-led selection: a committee led by the Prime Minister selects members, and the chairs are retired judges (since 2019 a former Chief Justice of India or Supreme Court judge), with few civil-society voices.
  • Borrowed investigators: police officers on deputation investigate complaints, including those against the police.

3. Practical limitations

  • Caseload: many complaints are closed on reports from the very authorities accused.
  • Weak compliance: States often delay or ignore recommendations on compensation and prosecution.
  • SHRCs: many face long vacancies, small budgets and no staff of their own.
  • International credibility: GANHRI's accreditation sub-committee deferred the NHRC's re-accreditation in 2023 and 2024, and in March 2025 recommended downgrading it from "A" to "B" status over concerns about its independence; the NHRC's challenge was rejected, and a final decision was due in November 2026.

4. Remedial measures

  • Teeth and autonomy: binding recommendations, an independent investigation wing and financial autonomy.
  • Pluralism: members from civil society, women and minorities, chosen through a transparent process in line with the Paris Principles.
  • Functional Human Rights Courts under Section 30, and filling SHRC vacancies.
  • Legal reform: ratify the UN Convention against Torture (signed in 1997) and enact an anti-torture law.

The Commissions have been the conscience-keepers of the State, but conscience without power is easily ignored. Binding powers, independence and pluralism would make them credible guardians of human rights against even the powerful.
free.upm-2021-gs2-13:
Equal protectionReasonable classificationAffirmative actionSubstantive equality

Equality is central to both Constitutions but grew from different histories. In the USA, after the Civil War, the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) barred States from denying any person "the equal protection of the laws", following the abolition of slavery (13th Amendment, 1865). India's Articles 14–18, drafted against caste and colonial discrimination, combine formal equality with a commitment to substantive equality through special provisions for disadvantaged groups.

1. Textual basis

  • USA: a brief, general guarantee; the Fourteenth Amendment binds the States, and the Supreme Court applied equal protection to the federal government through the Fifth Amendment's due process clause (Bolling v. Sharpe, 1954).
  • India: a detailed code. Article 14 combines "equality before the law" (British) and "equal protection of the laws" (American); Article 15 bars discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; Article 16 guarantees equal opportunity in public employment; Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 18 abolishes titles.

2. Judicial tests

  • USA: tiered scrutiny. Racial classifications face strict scrutiny, sex-based ones intermediate scrutiny (Craig v. Boren, 1976), and most economic laws only a rational-basis test.
  • India: reasonable classification and non-arbitrariness. A law may classify if there is an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to its object (State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952); since E.P. Royappa (1974), arbitrariness itself violates Article 14.

3. Affirmative action

  • USA: no textual basis, and courts have grown sceptical: Bakke (1978) struck down quotas but allowed race as a factor, Grutter (2003) upheld that approach, and SFFA v. Harvard (2023) ended race-conscious university admissions.
  • India: express enabling provisions in Articles 15(4), 15(5), 16(4) and 16(4A), backed by the directive in Article 46; Indra Sawhney (1992) set a 50% ceiling and the creamy-layer rule; the 103rd Amendment (2019) added an EWS quota, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022); in 2024 a seven-judge bench allowed States to sub-classify SCs and STs (Davinder Singh).

4. Private discrimination

  • USA: the equal protection clause binds only the State (Civil Rights Cases, 1883); private discrimination is tackled by statute, chiefly the Civil Rights Act, 1964.
  • India: some guarantees bind private persons directly: Article 15(2) on access to shops, public restaurants and wells, and Article 17 on untouchability, enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

5. Common ground

Both allow reasonable classification, rely on judicial review, and were shaped by social movements: the civil rights movement in America and the anti-caste struggle led by Dr Ambedkar in India.

The American model is largely colour-blind, treating equality as equal treatment of individuals, while the Indian model is transformative, treating equality as a duty to remove group disadvantage. Both continue to evolve, as each balances individual merit with social justice.
free.upm-2021-gs2-14:
Legislative CouncilArticle 169BicameralismArticle 171

Article 168 provides for a Legislative Assembly in every State and a second House in some. Under Article 169, Parliament may create or abolish a Legislative Council by law if the State Assembly passes a resolution by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting; such a law is not deemed an amendment under Article 368. As of 2026, only six States have Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

1. Constitutional provisions

  • Size and composition (Article 171): at most one-third of the Assembly's strength and at least 40 members; one-third elected by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth each by graduates and teachers, and one-sixth nominated by the Governor for literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service.
  • Continuity (Article 172(2)): a permanent House; members serve six years and one-third retire every two years.
  • Eligibility and officers: a member must be at least 30 (Article 173); the Council elects a Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Article 182).
  • Powers (Articles 197–198): the Council can delay an ordinary Bill for up to three months, and one month more if it is re-passed, and can only recommend changes to a Money Bill within 14 days; there is no joint sitting.

2. Working

  • Revising chamber: in 2020 the Andhra Pradesh Council referred two Bills on decentralisation and the CRDA to a select committee; the Assembly re-passed them, showing both its power to delay and its inability to block.
  • Expert voice: graduates', teachers' and nominated members can add knowledge to debates.
  • Route to office: Chief Ministers such as Yogi Adityanath (Uttar Pradesh, 2017–22) and Uddhav Thackeray (Maharashtra, 2020–22) sat in Councils while in office.
  • Criticism: Councils add cost, can only delay, and are sometimes used to accommodate those who lose elections.

3. Current status: a pattern of creation and abolition

  • Abolished: Punjab and West Bengal (1969) and Tamil Nadu (1986); a 2010 law to revive Tamil Nadu's Council was never brought into force; Jammu and Kashmir's ended with the 2019 reorganisation.
  • Revived and contested: Andhra Pradesh's Council was abolished in 1985, revived in 2007, nearly abolished again in 2020, and saved when the resolution was withdrawn in 2021.
  • Pending demands: Bills for Councils in Rajasthan and Assam were introduced in Parliament in 2013 but not enacted; Odisha (2018) and West Bengal (2021) Assemblies have passed resolutions seeking Councils.

4. Assessment

Councils depend on the political will of the ruling party in the Assembly, which explains their uneven spread. A national policy on when States should have a second chamber, with clear criteria and a review of functional constituencies, would end ad hoc creation and abolition.

The Legislative Council can be a useful chamber of second thought, adding expertise and deliberation to State law-making, provided it is used for bicameral scrutiny rather than political accommodation.
free.upm-2021-gs2-15:
Departmentally Related Standing CommitteesMini-ParliamentsLegislative scrutinyExecutive accountability

Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) were created in 1993 (17 committees) and expanded to 24 in 2004; 16 are serviced by the Lok Sabha and 8 by the Rajya Sabha. Each has 31 members (21 from the Lok Sabha, 10 from the Rajya Sabha), and ministers cannot be members. Often called mini-Parliaments, they examine ministries' Demands for Grants, Bills referred to them, annual reports and policy documents, extending Parliament's reach beyond the floor of the House.

1. How they keep the administration on its toes

  • Budget scrutiny: they examine each ministry's Demands for Grants before the House votes on them; since about 80% of the budget was voted without discussion in 2019–23 (PRS), committee reports are often the only detailed scrutiny.
  • Bill scrutiny: the Standing Committee on Finance examined the GST Constitution Amendment Bill (report 2013), and the Committee on Home Affairs examined the three criminal-law Bills in 2023, after which the government withdrew and reintroduced them with changes.
  • Bipartisan deliberation: meetings are in camera, the whip does not apply, and Opposition members chair several committees, so members can question officials closely.
  • Expert and public input: they invite memoranda and evidence from experts, industry and civil society.
  • Follow-up: ministries submit action-taken reports, and under Direction 73A ministers must make a statement every six months on the implementation of committee recommendations.

2. Limitations: do they inspire reverence?

  • Fewer Bills referred: referral is at the discretion of the presiding officers; only 16% of Bills went to committees in the 17th Lok Sabha, against 71% in the 15th.
  • Recommendatory only: governments can ignore reports, and reports are rarely debated in the House.
  • Short tenure and uneven attendance: committees are reconstituted every year, so members have little time to specialise.
  • Thin support: limited research staff and expertise compared with ministries.
  • Narrow remit: they do not consider day-to-day administration, and growing partisanship shows in dissent notes on contentious Bills.

3. Evaluation

DRSCs have improved the quality of many laws and exposed gaps in ministries' plans and spending, so they do keep the administration alert. But because referral is optional and reports are not binding, their influence varies with the government's majority and willingness to listen; reverence for parliamentary control is therefore partial.

4. Reforms

  • Mandatory referral of all Bills except urgent ones, and a two-year term for members.
  • Stronger support: dedicated research staff, public hearings and time in the House to debate key reports.

DRSCs are Parliament's best instrument for continuous, expert scrutiny. Making referral routine and following up their reports would turn them into a real check that sustains parliamentary control over the executive.
free.upm-2021-gs2-16:
Digital divideDigital literacyICT accessInclusive development

Digital literacy is the ability to use devices and the internet to find information, communicate and transact safely. In an economy increasingly run on Digital Public Infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, direct benefit transfers), lacking skills or access means exclusion from services, markets and jobs. Access has grown fast: by early 2025, 83.3% of rural households had internet at home (Comprehensive Modular Survey: Telecom, 2025). But use and skills lag, especially among rural women: the digital divide has shifted from access to capability.

1. Yes: how the divide has hindered development

  • Education: during the COVID-19 school closures (2020–21), children without devices or connectivity, mostly rural and poor, lost months of learning while better-off peers studied online.
  • Welfare and services: when CoWIN at first required online registration for younger adults, the Supreme Court flagged the digital divide (2021); authentication failures and online-only forms still deny some people their entitlements.
  • Livelihoods: farmers, artisans and small firms without digital skills miss market prices, e-NAM, e-commerce and online credit, and rural youth miss remote and platform jobs.
  • Safety: low-skilled users are easy targets of phishing and "digital arrest" scams.
  • Gender gap: among people aged 15 and above, only 48.4% of rural women owned a mobile phone, against 80.7% of rural men (CMS: Telecom, 2025).

2. But the picture is changing: a balanced view

  • Rapid gains among the young: 92.7% of rural people aged 15–29 had used the internet in the last three months, against 95.7% in towns (CMS 2025).
  • Assisted access: Common Service Centres, banking correspondents and SHG "Bank Sakhis" let people use services without their own skills.
  • Simpler interfaces: UPI on feature phones (UPI 123PAY, 2022), voice services and Indian-language tools such as Bhashini (2022) lower the skill barrier.
  • Many causes: weak schooling, health and infrastructure also hold development back, so digital illiteracy is one hindrance among several.

3. Why the divide persists

  • Infrastructure: BharatNet is incomplete, and coverage is patchy in hilly, forest and border areas.
  • Affordability and devices: shared phones within households leave women and the elderly dependent on others.
  • Skills and language: many users can watch videos but cannot fill forms, attach documents or transact safely; much content is still in English.
  • Social norms: restrictions on girls' and women's phone use.

4. Way forward

  • From access to skills: digital literacy in school curricula, SHGs and anganwadis, with a focus on women and the elderly.
  • No one left behind: offline and assisted alternatives, so that no entitlement depends on a smartphone.
  • Trust: stronger fraud protection and the phased roll-out of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Digital illiteracy and poor ICT access have hindered socio-economic development, most visibly in education, welfare and women's livelihoods. As access spreads, the next step is meaningful connectivity: skills, safety and services in local languages, so that Digital India becomes inclusive development.
free.upm-2021-gs2-17:
PatriarchyGender normsSocial changeSubstantive equality

Women in independent India have excelled in every field, from Indira Gandhi, the first woman Prime Minister (1966), and President Droupadi Murmu (2022) to the national team's first Women's Cricket World Cup title (2025). Yet patriarchy still shapes attitudes: India ranked 131st of 145 in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2026, and women's labour force participation was only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24). Even feminism is often dismissed as Western or anti-family. Changing this milieu needs interventions beyond education and empowerment schemes.

1. How patriarchy persists

  • In the family: son preference, dowry, unequal sharing of unpaid care work and restrictions on mobility; only 48.4% of rural women owned a mobile phone, against 80.7% of rural men (CMS: Telecom, 2025).
  • In law: the marital rape exception for adult wives continues in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Section 63).
  • In public life: women's reservation in legislatures (106th Amendment, 2023) awaits delimitation, and parties field few women.
  • In attitudes to feminism: demands for equality are framed as threats to the family rather than as constitutional rights.

2. Interventions beyond education and empowerment schemes

  • Legal reform and enforcement: effective use of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and the POSH Act, 2013 (with functioning Internal Committees); equal coparcenary rights for daughters, confirmed in Vineeta Sharma (2020); and gender-sensitive courts guided by the Supreme Court's Handbook on Combating Gender Stereotypes (2023).
  • Economic agency: land and house titles for women (PMAY-Gramin houses are registered in women's names or jointly), equal pay under the Code on Wages, crèches (required in larger establishments since 2017) and safe transport.
  • Valuing care work: the Time Use Surveys (2019, 2024) make unpaid work visible; paternity leave and public care services can share the burden.
  • Political voice: early implementation of the 106th Amendment and more party tickets for women build on the presence of women in nearly half of panchayat seats.
  • Socialisation and culture: gender-sensitive textbooks, engaging men and boys as partners, and media codes against stereotyped portrayals.
  • Institutional accountability: gender budgeting (since 2005-06), gender audits of policies and better sex-disaggregated data.

3. The role of society

Lasting change needs social movements, community leaders, faith institutions and men themselves to question discriminatory customs, as campaigns against dowry and for girls' education have done.

Patriarchy is a mindset reproduced in families, markets and institutions, so schemes alone cannot dissolve it. Combining legal reform, economic agency, political voice and changed socialisation, with men as partners, can build a gender-just society in which equality is not just permitted but expected.
free.upm-2021-gs2-18:
Civil societyAlternative service deliveryCo-productionAccountability

Civil society organisations (CSOs) and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are voluntary, non-profit bodies in the space between the State and the market, protected by the freedom of association (Article 19(1)(c)). Where government delivery is uniform, slow or distant, they offer an alternative model: community-based, flexible and innovative. The National Policy on the Voluntary Sector (2007) treats them as partners in development, not as substitutes for the State.

1. Can they offer an alternative model? Yes, in important ways

  • Innovation and reach: Akshaya Patra serves school meals under PM POSHAN; Pratham's ASER surveys and its Teaching at the Right Level method, adopted by several States, changed how learning is measured and taught.
  • Low-cost, high-quality care: Aravind Eye Care (Madurai) delivers high-volume, low-cost cataract surgery, and Jan Swasthya Sahyog provides affordable rural health care in Chhattisgarh.
  • Community ownership: SEWA organises informal women workers for savings, insurance and child care, and SHG federations run livelihood, nutrition and banking services.
  • Accountability innovations: MKSS's public hearings (jan sunwais) on village accounts led to the RTI Act, 2005, and social audits are now mandatory under MGNREGA (Section 17).
  • Crisis response: NGOs and community groups fed migrants and ran helplines during COVID-19 alongside governments.

2. More a complementary model

  • Partnerships: NGOs implement government programmes, and CSR spending (2% of average net profits for eligible companies under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013) funds many of them.
  • From pilot to policy: NGO innovations scale best when the State adopts them, as with Teaching at the Right Level and social audits.
  • Registration: NITI Aayog's NGO-DARPAN portal links NGOs with ministries.

3. Challenges of the alternative model

  • Scale and sustainability: successful pilots are hard to replicate across States, and projects end when donor funds dry up.
  • Funding regulation: the 2020 amendment to the FCRA barred sub-granting of foreign contributions, capped administrative spending at 20% and required a designated SBI account; the Supreme Court upheld it in Noel Harper (2022).
  • Accountability and transparency: some NGOs keep weak accounts or lack internal democracy, and a few have been fronts for misuse of funds, which erodes trust.
  • Capacity: low pay, high staff turnover and limited professional skills.
  • Equity and rights: NGOs cannot guarantee universal coverage or justiciable rights, and over-reliance on them risks letting the State retreat from its duties.
  • Trust deficit with government: delayed grants, suspicion of advocacy groups and an Intelligence Bureau report (2014) alleging that some foreign-funded NGOs stalled development.

Civil society can show the State what works and reach the last citizen, but it cannot replace the State's universal responsibility. A trust-based partnership, with transparency from NGOs and fair, predictable regulation from government, can turn this alternative into a powerful complement for public service delivery.
free.upm-2021-gs2-19:
Shanghai Cooperation OrganisationShanghai SpiritRATSConnect Central Asia

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) was founded in Shanghai on 15 June 2001 from the "Shanghai Five" (1996), and its Charter was signed in 2002. Guided by the "Shanghai Spirit" of mutual trust, equality, consultation and respect for diversity, it now has ten members: China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, India and Pakistan (2017), Iran (2023) and Belarus (2024). Together they hold over 40% of the world's population.

1. Aims and objectives

  • Good-neighbourliness: to strengthen mutual trust and friendly relations among members.
  • Security: to maintain peace and stability and to fight the "three evils" of terrorism, separatism and extremism, through the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS, Tashkent).
  • Broad cooperation: in politics, trade, energy, transport, science and technology, education, culture, tourism and the environment.
  • A new order: to promote what the Charter calls a democratic, fair and rational international political and economic order.

2. Critical examination

  • Achievements: confidence-building on the old Sino-Soviet border, intelligence sharing through RATS, regular summits that keep rivals talking, and steady expansion into the world's largest regional organisation by area and population.
  • Rivalries within: cross-border terrorism blocks consensus; India refused to sign the defence ministers' statement at Qingdao (June 2025) because it left out the Pahalgam attack, though the Tianjin Declaration (September 2025) condemned it.
  • China's dominance: India does not endorse the Belt and Road Initiative in SCO documents because the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
  • Weak economic integration: trade and connectivity lag far behind the security agenda.
  • Anti-Western image: the Ukraine war and Iran's conflicts tempt the SCO towards an identity that not all members share.

3. Importance for India

  • Central Asia: a platform for its Connect Central Asia policy (2012), energy and uranium ties, and connectivity through the INSTC and Chabahar, though US sanctions and the 2026 conflict involving Iran have clouded the port's future.
  • Counter-terrorism: RATS cooperation and a forum to press for zero tolerance of terrorism; the Bishkek Declaration (2026) condemned terrorism in all its forms and rejected double standards.
  • Managing China and Russia: the Prime Minister's visit to Tianjin for the 2025 summit, his first to China in seven years, helped stabilise ties, and the SCO keeps India engaged with Russia.
  • Strategic autonomy: as a member of both the SCO and the Quad, India can act as a bridge and keep the SCO from becoming an anti-Western bloc.
  • Leadership: India chaired the SCO in 2023, promotes its SECURE vision (2018), and saw English adopted as an official SCO language at Bishkek (2026).

The SCO's record is mixed: strong on dialogue, weak on delivery and divided by rivalries. For India it remains valuable for Central Asian outreach, energy and counter-terrorism, and as a stage for multi-alignment, provided it insists on respect for sovereignty and zero tolerance for terrorism.
free.upm-2021-gs2-20:
AUKUSNuclear-powered submarinesIndo-PacificMinilateralism

AUKUS, announced on 15 September 2021 by Australia, the UK and the USA, is a trilateral security partnership. Under Pillar I, Australia will acquire conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines, the first time the USA has shared naval nuclear-propulsion technology since its 1958 agreement with Britain. Pillar II covers advanced capabilities such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, hypersonics and undersea systems. It is widely seen as a response to China's naval expansion in the Indo-Pacific, though the partners do not name China.

1. Strength of AUKUS

  • A clear pathway: under the plan announced at San Diego (March 2023), US and UK submarines will rotate through Western Australia from 2027, Australia will buy at least three US Virginia-class submarines from the early 2030s, and a new SSN-AUKUS design will be built in Britain and Australia.
  • Long-term commitment: Australia has committed up to A$368 billion over three decades.
  • Political durability: a Pentagon review launched in June 2025 ended in December 2025 by endorsing the pact.
  • Wider technology cooperation: the partners began consulting Japan on Pillar II projects in 2024.
  • Deterrence: nuclear-powered submarines can stay submerged for long periods and operate far from home, extending Australia's reach.

2. Will it supersede existing partnerships?

  • Different purposes: the Quad (revived in 2017, with leaders' summits since 2021) offers public goods such as maritime domain awareness (IPMDA) and vaccines, while AUKUS is a narrow defence-technology pact; India's then Foreign Secretary said in September 2021 that AUKUS was not relevant to the Quad and would not affect its functioning.
  • A layered architecture: AUKUS sits alongside ANZUS (1951), the Five Eyes, US alliances with Japan and South Korea, and ASEAN-led forums such as the East Asia Summit, adding a layer rather than replacing any.
  • ASEAN centrality: Indonesia and Malaysia voiced concern about an arms race, so South-East Asian States still prefer ASEAN-led dialogue.
  • Repairing rifts: Australia's cancellation of a French submarine contract (2021) led France to recall its ambassadors from Washington and Canberra, but ties were later repaired.

3. Impact in the present scenario

  • Balance of power: more capable allied submarines complicate China's naval planning and strengthen deterrence.
  • Proliferation concerns: Australia will invoke a never-used IAEA provision that lets a non-nuclear-weapon State remove nuclear material for naval propulsion from safeguards; China and some others criticise this as a precedent.
  • Delivery risks: limited US shipyard capacity, rising costs and timelines stretching into the 2040s.
  • For India: a stronger allied presence in the Indian Ocean helps balance China, and India is not bound by AUKUS commitments; but it gains no direct access to its technology and must rely on its own nuclear-submarine programme and partnerships such as the Quad.

AUKUS is a capability-building complement, not a replacement, in the Indo-Pacific's lattice of overlapping partnerships. It strengthens deterrence but adds proliferation and arms-race risks, so India's interest lies in an open, rules-based Indo-Pacific anchored by the Quad, ASEAN and its own maritime strength.
free.upm-2021-gs3-1:
Base year 2011-12GVA at basic pricesGDP at market pricesMCA-21 database

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. India's national accounts are compiled by the National Statistical Office (formerly the CSO), which periodically shifts the base year to reflect the changing structure of the economy. In January 2015 the base year moved from 2004-05 to 2011-12, and the method itself changed, bringing India closer to the UN System of National Accounts (SNA) 2008.

1. What is measured: factor cost to market prices

  • Before 2015: growth was headlined as GDP at factor cost, the income earned by the factors of production (wages, rent, interest and profits); sector-wise output was also valued at factor cost.
  • After 2015: sector-wise output is measured as Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices, which adds production taxes net of production subsidies, and the headline is GDP at market prices, which also adds product taxes (such as GST) net of product subsidies.

2. Data sources and coverage

  • Corporate sector: the old series relied on the RBI's sample studies of a few thousand companies; the new one uses the MCA-21 database of annual filings of lakhs of companies with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
  • Establishment to enterprise approach: earlier, manufacturing value added was counted factory by factory from the Annual Survey of Industries and the IIP; now the whole enterprise is counted, including its head-office, marketing and other activities.
  • Financial sector: stock brokers, stock exchanges, mutual funds, pension funds and regulators such as SEBI, PFRDA and IRDAI were added, beyond banks and insurers.
  • Unorganised sector: an "effective labour input" method weights owners, hired workers and helpers by their productivity instead of treating all workers alike; local bodies and autonomous institutions are covered better.

3. Effects and debate

  • Higher growth: the new series raised growth for 2013-14 from 4.7% to 6.9%, at a time when credit, industrial output and exports were weak.
  • Criticism: experts questioned the quality of MCA-21 data (non-filing and shell companies), the use of single deflation and the gap with other indicators. In 2019 former Chief Economic Adviser Arvind Subramanian argued that growth had been overstated by about 2.5 percentage points; the Economic Advisory Council to the PM rejected this.

4. The latest revision (as of 2026)

  • Base year 2022-23 (released 27 February 2026): the new series uses double deflation for manufacturing and agriculture, supply and use tables, wider GST data, and direct estimates of the informal sector from the ASUSE and PLFS surveys. It puts nominal GDP about 3–4% lower than the old series, and growth for 2025-26 at 7.7% (provisional estimate, June 2026).

Each revision brings India's accounts closer to global standards. Regular base updates, timely surveys and transparent methods are essential for the credibility of statistics on which policy and investment depend.
free.upm-2021-gs3-2:
Annual Financial StatementRevenue budgetCapital budgetFiscal deficit

The Union Budget, called the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, must show expenditure on revenue account separately from other expenditure (Article 112(2)). It is therefore divided into a Revenue Budget, covering the government's current receipts and day-to-day spending, and a Capital Budget, covering receipts and spending that change its assets and liabilities. The distinction shows whether borrowing is used to build assets or to meet running costs.

1. Capital Budget vs Revenue Budget

  • Effect on the balance sheet: revenue items neither create assets nor reduce liabilities; capital items do, for example building a road (asset) or repaying a loan (lower liability).
  • Nature: revenue items are recurring (taxes, salaries, interest), while capital items are mostly non-recurring and lumpy (borrowings, disinvestment, a new railway line).
  • Financing: revenue spending should ideally be met from revenue receipts; capital spending can justifiably be financed by borrowing, the "golden rule" of public finance.
  • Economic impact: capital spending adds to the economy's productive capacity and has a higher multiplier, while revenue spending supports current consumption and services.

2. Components of the Revenue Budget

  • Tax revenue: direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, excise); the States' share is passed on as devolution.
  • Non-tax revenue: dividends and profits from public sector enterprises and the RBI, interest receipts, fees, fines and grants.
  • Revenue expenditure: interest payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies (food, fertiliser, fuel), grants to States and the upkeep of defence. Interest alone is budgeted at ₹14.04 lakh crore in 2026-27 (BE).
  • Grants for assets: some grants to States create capital assets but are still shown as revenue spending; hence the effective revenue deficit, which subtracts them.

3. Components of the Capital Budget

  • Debt receipts: market borrowings (dated securities), treasury bills, small savings, provident funds and external loans.
  • Non-debt receipts: recovery of loans and disinvestment of government shares.
  • Capital expenditure: roads, railways, defence equipment, loans and advances to States and PSUs, investment in shares, and repayment of debt. Capital expenditure is budgeted at ₹12.22 lakh crore in 2026-27.

4. Deficits that link the two

  • Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts: borrowing for current spending.
  • Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts: the government's total borrowing need.
  • Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.

Since the revenue deficit (1.5% of GDP) is about a third of the fiscal deficit (4.3%), most borrowing now funds capital outlay. Shrinking the revenue deficit and protecting capital expenditure improves the quality of spending and keeps public debt sustainable.
free.upm-2021-gs3-3:
Land reformsTenancy reformOperation BargaSecurity of tenure

Land reforms after Independence aimed to give "land to the tiller" through abolition of intermediaries, tenancy reform, ceilings on holdings with redistribution of surplus land, and consolidation of holdings. Zamindari abolition was largely completed by the 1960s, but tenancy and ceiling laws were weakly enforced in most States. In Kerala, West Bengal and Jammu and Kashmir, and partly Karnataka, they were implemented seriously and changed the lives of small and marginal cultivators.

1. Where land reforms worked

2. Economic gains

  • Security of tenure: recorded sharecroppers and tenant-owners could no longer be evicted at will, so they invested in wells, manure, better seeds and multiple cropping.
  • Higher productivity: small family farms use labour intensively; West Bengal's rice output grew fast in the 1980s, and a well-known study (Banerjee, Gertler and Ghatak, 2002) linked part of this rise to Operation Barga.
  • Fair share of output: legal limits on rent and crop-sharing ended rack-renting, so more of the harvest stayed with the cultivator.
  • Access to credit: a record of rights or a title (patta) let small farmers borrow from banks and cooperatives instead of moneylenders.
  • Assets for the landless: homestead plots in Kerala and redistributed ceiling-surplus land gave a house site, a kitchen garden and some security in old age.

3. Social and political gains

  • End of feudal dependence: tenants and labourers, many of them Dalits and backward castes, were freed from bonded and begar-like obligations to landlords.
  • Human development: in Kerala, land reform combined with literacy and public health produced high social indicators despite modest incomes.
  • Political voice: peasant organisations and elected panchayats (West Bengal, 1978) gave the rural poor a say in village affairs.
  • Women and the next generation: more secure household incomes supported schooling and health spending.

4. Limits even in these regions

  • Tiny holdings: redistribution and inheritance fragmented land; most beneficiaries remain marginal farmers who need off-farm income.
  • Landless labourers: in Kerala many got only house sites, not farmland.
  • Concealed tenancy elsewhere: in most States, oral leases continue, so tenants still lack credit, insurance and subsidies.

Where political will met organised peasants, land reform raised incomes and dignity. Clean digital records (DILRMP, SVAMITVA), legal leasing on the lines of NITI Aayog's Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act (2016) and farmer producer organisations can extend these gains to small farmers everywhere.
free.upm-2021-gs3-4:
Micro-irrigationPer Drop More CropWater-use efficiencyGroundwater depletion

India has about 18% of the world's population but only about 4% of its freshwater, and agriculture uses roughly 80% of the water withdrawn. NITI Aayog's Composite Water Management Index (2018) found about 60 crore people facing high to extreme water stress. Micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler systems) delivers water directly to the root zone in small, frequent doses. Promoted under PMKSY's "Per Drop More Crop", it is a key tool, but not a complete answer, to the water crisis.

1. How micro-irrigation helps

  • Saves water at the field: flood irrigation often loses half or more of the water applied to evaporation, run-off and deep percolation, while sprinklers reach about 70–80% efficiency and drip about 90%.
  • More crop per drop: even wetting, fertigation (fertiliser through the drip) and less weed growth raise yields and quality of fruit, vegetables, cotton and sugarcane.
  • Less pumping and energy: lower water needs cut diesel and electricity use; combined with solar pumps under PM-KUSUM it reduces costs further.
  • Farming in dry lands: drip has enabled orchards in rain-shadow regions such as Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh, and protects crops during dry spells.
  • Soil health: it avoids waterlogging and secondary salinity seen in canal commands.

2. Support in India

  • PMKSY (2015): subsidies for drip and sprinklers under "Per Drop More Crop", extended for 2021-26.
  • Micro Irrigation Fund (2018): a ₹5,000 crore NABARD fund that lends to States to expand coverage.
  • Potential: the Task Force on Micro Irrigation (2004) put the potential at about 69.5 million hectares, of which only a fraction is covered.

3. To what extent: the limits

  • Rebound effect: water saved on one field is often used to irrigate more land or grow thirstier crops, so total withdrawal from the aquifer may not fall unless area or extraction is capped.
  • Crop mismatch: paddy, the biggest water user, is mostly grown by flooding; without crop diversification, savings remain small.
  • Cost and scale: high initial cost, tiny fragmented plots, subsidy delays, clogging and poor maintenance limit adoption by small farmers.
  • Wrong signals: free or flat-rate farm power and MSP-led paddy procurement encourage over-pumping; Punjab extracts about 156% of its annually extractable groundwater (CGWB, 2025).
  • Wider crisis: the water crisis also involves urban supply, polluted rivers and falling recharge; micro-irrigation addresses only farm demand and may reduce return flows that recharge aquifers.

Micro-irrigation can make a large dent in farm water use, but only as part of a package: crop diversification, rational power pricing, community water budgeting under the Atal Bhujal Yojana, recharge structures and water pricing that rewards saving.
free.upm-2021-gs3-5:
S-400 TriumfLayered air defenceSudarshan ChakraCAATSA

The S-400 Triumf (NATO name SA-21 Growler), built by Russia's Almaz-Antey, is a mobile, long-range surface-to-air missile system in Russian service since 2007. India signed a deal for five squadrons in October 2018; the first arrived in December 2021, three were in service by 2023, the fourth reached India in mid-2026, and the fifth and last was still awaited in October 2026. In IAF service it is called "Sudarshan Chakra" and was used in Operation Sindoor (May 2025).

1. Technical features that make it stand out

  • Long reach: its largest missile can hit targets up to about 400 km away, letting it threaten airborne warning aircraft, tankers and fighters deep inside hostile airspace.
  • Layered defence from one system: a single battery can fire four types of missiles, with ranges of about 40, 120, 250 and 400 km, so the same unit covers short, medium and long range.
  • Powerful radars: its long-range acquisition radar can detect targets about 600 km away and scans all around (360°), while separate engagement radars track and guide missiles.
  • Wide target set: aircraft, drones, cruise missiles and short- and medium-range ballistic missiles, from very low altitude up to about 30 km.
  • Many targets at once: a battery can track and engage dozens of targets simultaneously.
  • Mobility and integration: road-mobile launchers deploy in minutes, and its command post can be linked to other air defence networks, such as the IAF's Integrated Air Command and Control System.

2. Comparison with other systems

  • Cost: India's five squadrons cost about US$5.4 billion, widely seen as cheaper than comparable Western systems.
  • Proven in use (claimed): in August 2025 the IAF chief said an S-400 had shot down a large Pakistani aircraft at about 300 km during Operation Sindoor, calling it the longest-range surface-to-air kill on record; Pakistan denies losing any aircraft.

3. A balanced view: "superior" but not invincible

  • Not best in every role: US systems such as THAAD and ship-based interceptors are better against long-range ballistic missiles above the atmosphere.
  • Physical limits: the earth's curvature limits detection of low-flying cruise missiles and drones, so shorter-range systems are still needed.
  • Vulnerabilities: stealth aircraft, electronic jamming, decoys and drone swarms can strain it, and S-400 components have reportedly been hit in the Russia-Ukraine war.
  • Strategic costs: the threat of US sanctions under CAATSA (2017), delivery delays and dependence on Russia.

The S-400 is among the most capable long-range air defence systems in the world, but India's security lies in a layered, networked shield combining it with Akash, MRSAM, QRSAM and future indigenous long-range systems, under the goal of Atmanirbhar air defence.
free.upm-2021-gs3-6:
Green Grids InitiativeOne Sun One World One GridInternational Solar AllianceTransnational grids

The Green Grids Initiative–One Sun One World One Grid (GGI-OSOWOG) was launched on 2 November 2021 at the World Leaders Summit of COP26, Glasgow, by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, together with the International Solar Alliance (ISA) and the UK COP Presidency. It combined the UK's Green Grids Initiative with India's OSOWOG idea, and its One Sun Declaration was endorsed by 80 countries.

1. Purpose of the initiative

  • Overcome intermittency: solar power is available only in daytime at any one place, but "the sun never sets" on the earth as a whole; interconnected transnational grids can carry solar power from where the sun is shining to where it is needed.
  • Cut storage needs and costs: sharing power across time zones reduces the need for costly batteries and backup coal plants, and gives buyers access to the cheapest solar electricity.
  • Speed up the energy transition: help countries move away from coal and meet their Paris Agreement goals and net-zero targets.
  • Mobilise finance and technology: bring together governments, financial institutions, power system operators and research bodies, with the World Bank as a partner, in support of the ISA's aim of about US$1 trillion of solar investment by 2030.
  • Access and equity: give developing countries, especially in Africa and small island states, reliable clean power and a share in a global green-power market.

2. When the idea was first floated

  • First Assembly of the ISA, October 2018: Prime Minister Modi first proposed connecting solar energy supply across borders, as "One World, One Sun, One Grid", at the first Assembly of the International Solar Alliance.
  • Background: the ISA itself was launched by India and France at COP21 in Paris (30 November 2015), with its headquarters at Gurugram; its membership was later opened to all UN member states.

3. Significance for India

  • Climate leadership: it complements India's COP26 Panchamrit pledges, including 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.
  • Energy diplomacy: India already trades electricity with Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh, and regional grids can deepen this.
  • Industry: large markets open up for solar modules, transmission equipment and grid services.

4. Challenges

  • Cost and technology: long undersea and overland high-voltage lines are expensive and technically demanding.
  • Sovereignty and security: countries may hesitate to depend on foreign grids, and interconnected grids are exposed to cyber attacks.
  • Regulation and geopolitics: harmonising tariffs, grid codes and power-trading rules across many nations is slow, and political tensions can disrupt supply.

GGI-OSOWOG turns the old dream of a single world grid into a practical, phased programme. Steady progress on regional interconnections, backed by finance through the ISA, can make round-the-clock clean power a global public good.
free.upm-2021-gs3-7:
WHO Air Quality Guidelines 2021PM2.5NAAQSNational Clean Air Programme

On 22 September 2021 the World Health Organization released new Global Air Quality Guidelines (AQGs), the first update since 2005. They rest on evidence that air pollution harms health at far lower levels than earlier thought; WHO estimates that it causes about 7 million premature deaths a year. The guidelines are not binding but serve as a benchmark for national standards, such as India's National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS, 2009).

1. Key points of the 2021 guidelines

  • Six classical pollutants: PM2.5, PM10, ozone, nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and carbon monoxide (CO).
  • Much stricter limits: the annual PM2.5 guideline was halved from 10 to 5 µg/m³, and the annual NO₂ guideline cut from 40 to 10 µg/m³.
  • Interim targets: stepwise targets (for annual PM2.5: 35, 25, 15 and 10 µg/m³) help highly polluted countries improve gradually.
  • Good practice statements: for pollutants without enough evidence for numerical values, such as black carbon, ultrafine particles and sand and dust storms.

2. How they differ from the 2005 update

  • Tighter values for PM2.5, PM10 and NO₂, reflecting evidence of harm even at low exposures.
  • New guidelines for 24-hour NO₂, 24-hour CO (4 mg/m³) and peak-season ozone.
  • One relaxation: the 24-hour SO₂ guideline was raised from 20 to 40 µg/m³.
  • Wider evidence: far more studies, including from low- and middle-income countries.

3. Changes needed in India's National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)

NCAP (January 2019) covers about 130 cities and aimed to cut PM10 by up to 40% by 2025-26 from 2017-18 levels. In 2025-26, 108 cities had lower PM10 than in 2017-18, but only 26 had cut it by more than 40% and only 14 met the national standard (Rajya Sabha reply, July 2026). With the target year over, its next phase needs these changes:

  • Revise the NAAQS: India's annual PM2.5 standard of 40 µg/m³ is looser than even WHO's first interim target (35); a phased path to the interim targets should be notified.
  • Target PM2.5, not just PM10: fine particles, mostly from combustion, cause most of the health damage.
