  • Airshed approach: pollution in the Indo-Gangetic plain crosses city and State boundaries; regional plans, on the model of the Commission for Air Quality Management for the NCR, are needed.
  • Legal backing and accountability: NCAP is a programme, not a law; enforceable, time-bound targets and performance-linked funding, as with Fifteenth Finance Commission grants, should continue.
  • Source-wise action and monitoring: stricter industrial and power-plant norms, clean cooking fuel, electric mobility, crop-residue and dust control, and more monitors in small towns, backed by satellite data.

The 2021 guidelines show that there is no safe level of air pollution. A phased move to WHO interim targets, with regional airshed management and accountable city plans, can turn NCAP into a health-driven clean-air mission.
free.upm-2021-gs3-8:
Seismic zonesHimalayan collisionIntraplate earthquakesEarthquake-resistant construction

About 59% of India's land is prone to moderate to severe earthquakes. The Indian Plate moves north by about 4–5 cm a year into the Eurasian Plate, building stress along the Himalaya and the North-East, while old faults inside the peninsula can also slip. The Bureau of Indian Standards divides the country into seismic Zones II to V (IS 1893); a 2025 revision added a Zone VI for the Himalaya, but it was withdrawn in March 2026.

1. Why India is vulnerable

  • Himalayan collision zone: the arc from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh lies in Zones IV and V; scientists warn of a "seismic gap" in the central Himalaya where a great earthquake is overdue.
  • North-East and the Andamans: the Shillong plateau and the Indo-Burma ranges are highly active, and the Andaman–Sumatra subduction zone can generate tsunamis.
  • Intraplate faults: even the "stable" peninsula has damaging earthquakes, as at Latur and in Kutch, and reservoir-induced seismicity has been linked to Koyna (1967).
  • Soft soils: the deep alluvium of the Indo-Gangetic plain amplifies shaking and can liquefy, endangering cities such as Delhi (Zone IV), Patna and Guwahati.
  • Human factors: non-engineered stone and brick houses, soft-storey buildings, weak enforcement of codes (IS 1893, IS 13920), dense unplanned cities and construction on steep hill slopes turn moderate quakes into disasters.
  • Cascading hazards: landslides, dam failures, fires, glacial lake bursts and tsunamis can follow strong shaking.

2. Major earthquake disasters of the last three decades

  • Latur (1993): showed that "safe" regions are not safe; the 2002 zone map merged the lowest zone into Zone II and raised the hazard level of the Latur region.
  • Bhuj (2001): the deadliest of the period; it led to the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act (2003), fed into the national Disaster Management Act, 2005, and its "build back better" reconstruction is cited as a model.
  • 2004 tsunami: a distant quake devastated India's coast and led to the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007).
  • Himalayan and North-Eastern quakes: repeatedly combined shaking with landslides, cutting off hill towns and damaging roads and power projects.
  • Common lesson: "earthquakes do not kill, buildings do"; most deaths came from the collapse of poorly built structures.

3. Reducing the risk

  • Codes and retrofitting: enforce the National Building Code (2016) and BIS codes, and retrofit schools, hospitals and lifeline buildings.
  • Planning: seismic microzonation of cities, and regulation of construction on hill slopes and soft soils.
  • Warning and response: the National Center for Seismology's network, Uttarakhand's earthquake alert app (2021), SACHET cell-broadcast alerts (2026), the NDRF and community drills under NDMA's earthquake guidelines (2007).

India cannot stop earthquakes, but it can stop them becoming catastrophes. Safe construction, informed planning and prepared communities, in line with the Sendai Framework, are the real defence.
free.upm-2021-gs3-9:
Money launderingVirtual digital assetsPMLA, 2002FATF

Money laundering is the process of disguising the proceeds of crime, such as drug trafficking, corruption, fraud or terror funding, so that they appear legitimate. It works in three stages: placement, layering and integration. UNODC estimates that 2–5% of global GDP is laundered every year. In India it is an offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, in force since 2005, and globally the standards are set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

1. How globalisation helps launderers

  • Free movement of capital: liberal capital accounts, FDI and portfolio routes allow "round-tripping" of black money through tax havens and offshore entities.
  • Trade-based laundering: in huge volumes of global trade, over- and under-invoicing of imports and exports easily hides illicit transfers.
  • Shell companies and secrecy: layered corporate structures across jurisdictions hide beneficial owners, as the Panama Papers (2016) and Pandora Papers (2021) revealed.
  • Hawala and remittances: informal value-transfer networks linked to diaspora flows move money without leaving a trail in banks.
  • Regulatory arbitrage: criminals exploit jurisdictions with weak supervision and slow cooperation.

2. How emerging technologies help launderers

  • Cryptocurrencies: pseudonymous wallets, mixers, privacy coins and decentralised exchanges move value across borders in minutes, outside banks.
  • Mule accounts and instant payments: proceeds of cyber fraud and "digital arrest" scams are split across many bank and UPI accounts and withdrawn quickly.
  • Online betting and gaming apps: illegal betting platforms, such as the Mahadev app investigated by the Enforcement Directorate, pooled and moved large sums abroad.
  • Darknet and fintech: darknet markets, e-wallets, prepaid cards and deepfakes that defeat online KYC make tracing harder.

3. Measures at the national level

  • Laws: the PMLA (upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary, 2022), the Black Money Act (2015), the amended Benami Transactions Act (2016), the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act (2018) and FEMA, 1999.
  • Covering new technology: virtual digital asset service providers were brought under the PMLA in March 2023; crypto gains are taxed at 30% with 1% TDS on transfers (2022); the Online Gaming Act, 2025 bans real-money online games.
  • Institutions: the Enforcement Directorate, FIU-IND (2004), CBDT, DRI and SFIO, with RBI's KYC norms and the Central KYC Registry.
  • Fighting fraud money: the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre's 1930 helpline freezes stolen funds, and banks use analytics to spot mule accounts.

4. Measures at the international level

  • Virtual assets: FATF's "travel rule" requires crypto platforms to share sender and receiver details; India's G20 presidency (2023) pushed a coordinated global framework for crypto-assets.
  • Beneficial ownership registers and faster mutual legal assistance and extradition.

Laundering is now borderless and digital, so the response must be too: real-time financial intelligence, regulated crypto platforms and global cooperation through the FATF and the UN, so that crime never pays.
free.upm-2021-gs3-10:
Cross-border cyber attacksCritical information infrastructureCERT-In and NCIIPCCyber deterrence

Cyberspace is now the fifth domain of conflict, after land, sea, air and space. Cross-border cyber attacks by state-backed groups, hacktivists and criminal gangs can cripple power grids, hospitals and banks without a shot being fired, and are hard to attribute. During the India–Pakistan conflict of April–May 2025 (Pahalgam and Operation Sindoor), Maharashtra Cyber, the State's nodal cyber agency, reported about 15 lakh attacks on Indian websites by Pakistan-allied hacker groups, of which only about 150 succeeded.

1. Impact on India's internal security

  • Critical infrastructure: malware was found in the administrative network of the Kudankulam nuclear plant (2019, confirmed by NPCIL), and in 2021 a US security firm reported China-linked intrusions into India's power sector.
  • Essential services: the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi (November 2022) crippled a leading hospital's digital services for days.
  • Financial system: attacks such as the ₹94 crore Cosmos Bank heist (2018) and large-scale online frauds drain money and trust; proceeds often fund organised crime.
  • Espionage: theft of defence, government and industrial data weakens national security and economic competitiveness.
  • Information warfare: fake news, deepfakes and coordinated propaganda can incite communal violence, radicalise youth and undermine trust during crises.
  • Hybrid threats: encrypted apps, crypto and the dark web help terrorists recruit, communicate and raise funds; cyber-scam compounds in South-East Asia use trafficked Indians to defraud people at home.

2. Defensive measures in place

  • Institutions: CERT-In (2004, Section 70B of the IT Act) for incident response; the NCIIPC (Section 70A) for critical information infrastructure; the National Cyber Security Coordinator; the Defence Cyber Agency (2019); and the I4C (2020) for cybercrime.
  • Rules and laws: CERT-In's directions (2022) require incidents to be reported within 6 hours; the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications Act, 2023; apps posing security risks were blocked under Section 69A in 2020; telecom equipment must come from trusted sources.
  • Citizen protection: the 1930 helpline, cybercrime.gov.in and Sanchar Saathi against fraudulent SIMs.

3. What more is needed against sophisticated attacks

  • Defence in depth: zero-trust architecture, air-gapping of critical control systems, regular audits and red-team exercises in power, banking, telecom and health.
  • Indigenous technology: trusted Indian hardware and software, quantum-safe encryption under the National Quantum Mission, and AI-based threat detection.
  • Skilled workforce: cyber cadres in police, CAPFs and ministries, and sectoral CERTs with round-the-clock monitoring.
  • Deterrence and diplomacy: better attribution, offensive cyber capability as deterrence, intelligence sharing with partners such as the Quad, and shaping global rules, including the UN Convention against Cybercrime (adopted 2024).
  • Resilience: backups, mock drills and cyber hygiene in government offices and among citizens.

Cyber attacks across borders blur the line between crime and war. A whole-of-nation approach, combining strong institutions, indigenous technology, skilled people and global partnerships, is needed for cyber resilience.
free.upm-2021-gs3-11:
V-shaped recoveryK-shaped recoveryBase effectOutput loss

A V-shaped recovery is a sharp fall in output followed by an equally quick rebound to the pre-crisis level and trend. The COVID-19 lockdown pushed India's real GDP down by nearly 24% in April–June 2020 and by 5.8% in 2020-21, the first annual contraction since 1979-80 (2011-12 series). The Economic Survey 2020-21 forecast a V-shaped recovery. The evidence suggests that the headline rebound was indeed V-shaped, but the recovery beneath it was uneven, or K-shaped.

1. Evidence that supports a V-shape

  • Quick rebound: growth turned positive by October–December 2020 and reached 9.7% in 2021-22, taking real GDP above its 2019-20 level within two years.
  • Sustained momentum: under the new series (base 2022-23), growth was 7.2% in 2023-24, 7.1% in 2024-25 and 7.7% in 2025-26, and 7.8% in April–June 2026 (NSO, 31 August 2026).
  • Policy support: free foodgrains under PMGKAY, the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme for MSMEs, a cut in the repo rate to 4% (May 2020) and a sharp rise in public capital expenditure.
  • Vaccination and reopening: over 200 crore vaccine doses had been given by July 2022, allowing services to reopen fully.
  • Other indicators: record GST collections, merchandise exports above US$400 billion for the first time in 2021-22, and a revival of bank credit.

2. Why it was not a complete "V": the K-shaped picture

  • Lost output: two years of growth were lost and output stayed below its pre-pandemic trend; the RBI's Report on Currency and Finance 2021-22 estimated that the losses might be made good only by 2034-35.
  • Uneven sectors: agriculture grew even in 2020-21 and large listed firms posted strong profits, but contact-intensive services (trade, hotels, transport) and many MSMEs recovered slowly.
  • Weak consumption and jobs: private consumption lagged, many workers returned to farms or informal work, and the second wave (April–May 2021) caused a fresh setback.
  • Unequal gains: formal firms and better-off households gained, while informal workers and small businesses lost savings and incomes.
  • Inflation: CPI inflation reached 7.8% in April 2022, eroding real wages.

3. Assessment

  • Yes, in headline numbers: the rebound in GDP was quick and sharp, helped by the low base and by policy support.
  • No, in welfare terms: the recovery was uneven across sectors, firms and households, and the gap from the pre-pandemic trend did not close quickly.
  • Since 2023: steady growth of about 7% shows the economy has moved beyond recovery to expansion, though private investment and quality jobs remain concerns.

India's recovery was V-shaped in headline GDP but K-shaped in its distribution. Sustaining growth now depends on jobs, MSME credit, private investment and human capital, so that recovery reaches every household.
free.upm-2021-gs3-12:
Infrastructure investmentMultiplier effectInclusive growthPM Gati Shakti

Infrastructure, meaning transport, power, telecom, water, housing and urban services, is the backbone of economic activity. Public investment in it has a high multiplier effect: it creates jobs during construction, lowers costs for business afterwards and "crowds in" private investment. India's Union capital expenditure is budgeted at a record ₹12.22 lakh crore in 2026-27, guided by the National Infrastructure Pipeline (2019) and PM Gati Shakti (2021).

1. How infrastructure speeds up growth: India's experience

  • Lower logistics costs: logistics costs of about 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT) hurt competitiveness; national highways expanded to about 1.46 lakh km (2024), and the Dedicated Freight Corridors and the National Logistics Policy (2022) aim to cut costs further.
  • Market integration: the Golden Quadrilateral highways linked the four metros, and studies found that manufacturing grew faster in districts along them.
  • Power and digital networks: all villages were electrified by April 2018 and about 2.8 crore households connected under Saubhagya (2017); cheap mobile data, 5G and Digital Public Infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI) created new industries and services.
  • Crowding in private capital: the public capex push since 2020-21 supported demand for steel, cement and construction and attracted private investment.
  • Air connectivity: India's airports rose from 74 in 2014 to 165 by 2026, opening up tourism and trade.

2. How infrastructure makes growth inclusive

  • Rural roads: PMGSY (2000) links villages to markets, schools and health centres, raising farm incomes and access to services.
  • Basic services: the Jal Jeevan Mission has brought tap water to about 82% of rural homes (July 2026); toilets under Swachh Bharat, LPG under Ujjwala and houses under PMAY reduce drudgery, especially for women.
  • Regional balance: UDAN regional flights (679 routes by July 2026), the Bogibeel bridge (2018) and the Sela tunnel (2024) link the North-East, hilly and remote areas.
  • Digital inclusion: BharatNet broadband and Common Service Centres take banking, direct benefit transfers, telemedicine and e-governance to villages.
  • Jobs: construction is labour-intensive and absorbs rural migrants and low-skilled workers.

3. Lessons from India's experience

  • PPP setbacks: the PPP boom of the 2000s ended in stalled projects and bank NPAs, leading to the Kelkar Committee (2015) and safer models such as the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016).
  • Execution gaps: land acquisition, clearances and cost and time overruns delay projects.
  • Financing: long-term finance is scarce; NaBFID (2021), InvITs and asset monetisation (a ₹10 lakh crore plan for 2025-30) aim to fill the gap.
  • Social and environmental costs: displacement, weak rehabilitation and heavy construction in fragile Himalayan towns such as Joshimath can make infrastructure exclusionary or unsafe.

India's experience shows that infrastructure is a necessary condition for rapid and inclusive growth, provided projects are well chosen, climate-resilient and socially fair. Integrated planning under Gati Shakti, sustainable financing and equal attention to social infrastructure can turn spending into lasting prosperity.
free.upm-2021-gs3-13:
National Food Security Act, 2013Targeted PDSNutrition securityPMGKAY

The National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013 made access to subsidised food a legal entitlement, shifting from a welfare approach to a rights-based approach. It covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population, about two-thirds of the people, a ceiling of about 81.35 crore persons based on Census 2011. It grew out of the Right to Food campaign and the Supreme Court's orders in the PUCL case (from 2001).

1. Salient features

  • Prices: grain at ₹3, ₹2 and ₹1 per kg for rice, wheat and coarse grains; since January 2023 it has been free under PMGKAY, which was extended for five years from 1 January 2024.
  • Women's empowerment: the eldest woman of the household (18 years or above) is the head of the family for issuing ration cards.
  • Accountability: District Grievance Redressal Officers, State Food Commissions, vigilance committees and social audits (Section 28), with a food security allowance if grain is not supplied.
  • PDS reforms: computerisation, Aadhaar seeding, doorstep delivery and One Nation One Ration Card for migrant workers.
  • Nutritional standards: Schedule II prescribes calories and protein for meals for children and women.

2. How it has helped reduce hunger and malnutrition

  • Assured calories: about 81 crore people receive free grain, which protected the poor during the COVID-19 lockdowns and shields them from food inflation.
  • Fewer leakages, more portability: digitised PDS and One Nation One Ration Card cut diversion and let migrants draw rations anywhere.
  • Better child growth: stunting among children under five fell from 38.4% (NFHS-4, 2015-16) to 35.5% (NFHS-5) and 29.3% in NFHS-6 (2023-24), whose fact sheets the Health Ministry released in May 2026.
  • Focus on the first 1,000 days: maternity benefits and anganwadi meals target mothers and young children.
  • Less poverty: NITI Aayog estimates that 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23; nutrition is one of its indicators.

3. Why hunger and malnutrition persist

  • Cereal-centred design: grain provides calories but not enough protein, fats and micronutrients; wasting stayed at about 19% and underweight fell only from 32.1% to 31.8% between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6, and over half of women and children were anaemic in NFHS-5.
  • Exclusion errors: coverage still rests on Census 2011 numbers, and failures of biometric authentication can deny rations.
  • Double burden: micronutrient deficiency now coexists with rising overweight and obesity.
  • Wider determinants: sanitation, safe water, women's education and care practices matter as much as food.

The NFSA has largely secured food security in terms of calories. The next step is nutrition security: fortified rice (supplied through all schemes until 2028), millets and pulses in the PDS, Poshan 2.0, better maternal care and diet diversity.
free.upm-2021-gs3-14:
Crop diversificationRice–wheat cycleDigital agricultureClimate-resilient varieties

Crop diversification means moving from a narrow, monoculture pattern to a wider mix of crops and allied activities, such as pulses, oilseeds, millets, fruits, vegetables, livestock and fisheries, suited to local soil, water and markets. The Green Revolution locked Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh into a rice–wheat cycle that now strains groundwater (Punjab extracts about 156% of its annually extractable resource, CGWB 2025), soil health and farm incomes.

1. Present challenges before crop diversification

  • Price and procurement bias: assured MSP procurement covers mainly rice and wheat; for most other crops farmers bear price risk and distress sales.
  • Skewed input subsidies: free or cheap power for pumps and low-priced urea favour water- and fertiliser-hungry crops.
  • Weak markets: perishable fruits and vegetables need cold chains, processing and assured buyers, which are scarce; tomato, onion and potato prices swing sharply.
  • Small holdings and risk aversion: most farmers are small and marginal and cannot afford a failed experiment; credit and insurance favour familiar crops.
  • Seed and yield gaps: pulses and oilseeds have low, unstable yields and limited quality seed, so India still imports much of its edible oil.
  • Climate and extension: erratic monsoons and heat waves add risk, and extension services that could guide new crops are thin.

2. How emerging technologies provide an opportunity

  • Digital agriculture: the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) is building AgriStack (farmer registry, digital crop survey) and a Krishi Decision Support System that can guide crop choice using soil, weather and market data.
  • Remote sensing and AI: satellite and AI-based crop-suitability maps and weather advisories show which crops suit each block and support crop-insurance assessment.
  • Precision farming and drones: sensors, drones (Namo Drone Didi, 15,000 drones for women's self-help groups) and micro-irrigation make high-value crops viable with less water and chemicals.
  • Better seeds: 109 high-yielding, climate-resilient and biofortified varieties of 61 crops were released in August 2024, and the genome-edited rice variety DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala, 2025) matures 15–20 days earlier, freeing time and water for another crop.
  • Market technology: e-NAM, ONDC, farmer producer organisations and solar-powered cold storage connect diversified produce to buyers and processors.
  • Protected cultivation: polyhouses and hydroponics allow vegetables and flowers near cities.

3. Policy support that technology needs

  • Incentives: the Crop Diversification Programme under RKVY (since 2013-14, in the original Green Revolution States), Haryana's Mera Pani Meri Virasat, the National Mission on Edible Oils–Oilseeds (2024), the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses and the PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (2025).
  • Crop-neutral support: assured procurement of pulses, oilseeds and millets, and per-hectare incentives rather than crop-specific price support.

Technology can make diversification profitable and less risky, but only if prices, procurement and input subsidies stop favouring rice and wheat. Aligning policy with agro-climatic zones is the key to a sustainable cropping pattern.
free.upm-2021-gs3-15:
Applied biotechnologyGenome editingAffordable healthcareBioeconomy

Applied biotechnology uses living organisms, cells and their molecules to make products for health, agriculture, industry and the environment. India's research system, led by the Department of Biotechnology (1986), ICAR, ICMR and CSIR, with start-ups supported by BIRAC, has helped its bioeconomy grow to about US$195 billion in 2025. The BioE3 policy (2024) now aims to build high-performance biomanufacturing.

1. Research and development achievements

  • Vaccines: India makes nearly 60% of the world's vaccines; indigenous products include the rotavirus vaccine Rotavac, Covaxin, ZyCoV-D (2021, the world's first DNA vaccine for humans) and the HPV vaccine CERVAVAC.
  • Advanced therapies: NexCAR19 (2023), India's own CAR-T cell therapy for blood cancers, and BIRSA 101 (2025), a CRISPR-based therapy for sickle cell disease built on CSIR-IGIB's enFnCas9.
  • Diagnostics and genomics: affordable molecular tests such as TrueNat for TB and the CRISPR-based FELUDA test for COVID-19; the Genome India project has sequenced 10,000 genomes for precision medicine.
  • Agriculture: Bt cotton (2002); marker-assisted Improved Samba Mahsuri rice, resistant to bacterial blight; the world's first genome-edited rice varieties, DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1 (May 2025); biofortified crops; and tissue-cultured planting material.
  • Industry and environment: enzymes, biofertilisers and biopesticides, second-generation ethanol, bioremediation of oil spills and polluted sites, and bio-toilets.
  • Animal health: indigenous vaccines such as Lumpi-ProVacInd (2022) against lumpy skin disease in cattle.

2. How these achievements help the poorer sections

  • Affordable healthcare: domestic vaccines reach every child free under the Universal Immunisation Programme; NexCAR19 costs a fraction of imported CAR-T therapies; and gene therapy for sickle cell disease targets an illness common among tribal communities, also addressed by the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023).
  • Higher and stable farm incomes: flood-, drought- and salt-tolerant varieties reduce crop losses for small farmers in rainfed and coastal areas; Kamala rice yields about 19% more and matures 15–20 days earlier.
  • Fighting hidden hunger: zinc- and iron-rich biofortified varieties and fortified rice in the PDS address anaemia and micronutrient deficiency.
  • Livelihoods: livestock vaccines protect the main asset of landless and women farmers, while bio-input units, biogas plants and biomanufacturing create rural jobs.
  • Cleaner surroundings: bio-toilets and bioremediation improve sanitation and water quality in poor neighbourhoods.

3. Challenges

  • Access and cost: advanced therapies remain expensive and concentrated in big hospitals.
  • Biosafety and trust: pink bollworm now resists Bt cotton, and GM mustard is on hold after the Supreme Court's split verdict (2024).
  • Research gaps: low R&D spending, weak lab-to-market translation and intellectual property barriers.

Biotechnology can be a pro-poor technology when public research, affordable pricing and strong biosafety go together. The BioE3 policy and public-private partnerships must keep equity at their centre.
free.upm-2021-gs3-16:
Blue LEDGallium nitrideWhite LED lightingEnergy efficiency

The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura "for the invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes which has enabled bright and energy-saving white light sources". Red and green LEDs had existed for decades, but without blue, white LED light was impossible. In the early 1990s they grew high-quality gallium nitride (GaN) crystals and made efficient blue LEDs, completing the colour palette.

1. Why the blue LED was a breakthrough

  • Direct conversion: an LED turns electricity straight into light, with little waste heat, unlike a hot filament or gas discharge.
  • Long life and robustness: LEDs are compact, shock-resistant and contain no mercury, unlike fluorescent tubes.
  • Full colour: red, green and blue LEDs together can produce any colour, which made LED screens possible.

2. Impact on everyday life

  • Energy saving and climate: lighting uses about a quarter of the world's electricity, and LEDs cut this sharply. India's UJALA scheme (2015) distributed over 36 crore LED bulbs, lowering household bills and peak demand, and the Street Lighting National Programme replaced street lights with LEDs.
  • Light for the off-grid poor: LED lamps run on small solar panels give cheap, safe light to people without grid power, replacing kerosene lamps that cause indoor air pollution and burns; children can study after dark.
  • Screens everywhere: LED backlights in smartphones, laptops and televisions, and giant full-colour LED displays in stadiums and streets, depend on blue LEDs.
  • Data and communication: GaN-based blue-violet lasers made high-capacity Blu-ray discs possible, and LEDs are used for Li-Fi (data sent through light).
  • Health: blue-light phototherapy treats jaundice in newborns, and ultraviolet LEDs built on the same nitride technology disinfect water and surfaces.
  • Transport and safety: LED traffic signals, vehicle lamps and lighthouses use less power and need little maintenance.
  • Farming: LED grow lights tuned to plant needs support vertical farms and polyhouses.

3. Concerns

  • Blue light at night: excessive exposure can disturb sleep and the body clock.
  • Light pollution: cheap, bright lighting harms night skies, insects and migratory birds.
  • E-waste: discarded LEDs and electronics need proper recycling.

The blue LED touches nearly every household: it lights homes cheaply, powers our screens and brings light to the off-grid poor. It shows how basic materials research can deliver energy efficiency, climate benefits and social good together.
free.upm-2021-gs3-17:
Glasgow Climate PactParis RulebookPanchamritNet zero by 2070

The 26th Conference of the Parties (COP26) to the UNFCCC was held in Glasgow from 31 October to 13 November 2021 under the UK presidency, a year late because of COVID-19. It was the first big test of the Paris Agreement's five-yearly "ratchet" of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Its main outcome, the Glasgow Climate Pact, aimed to "keep 1.5°C alive".

1. Major outcomes

  • Focus on 1.5°C: the Pact recognised that limiting warming to 1.5°C needs a 45% cut in global CO₂ emissions by 2030 from 2010 levels and net zero around mid-century, and asked countries to strengthen their 2030 targets by the end of 2022.
  • Fossil fuels named for the first time: it called for a "phasedown" of unabated coal power and a phase-out of inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies; "phase-out" of coal was changed to "phasedown" at India's suggestion.
  • Finance and adaptation: developed countries were urged to at least double adaptation finance from 2019 levels by 2025; the Pact noted with regret that the US$100 billion a year goal had not been met and began work on a new finance goal (set at COP29, 2024, at US$300 billion a year by 2035).
  • Loss and damage: a Glasgow Dialogue was set up and the Santiago Network given functions, though a fund came only at COP27 (2022).
  • Paris Rulebook completed: rules for carbon markets under Article 6 (with a 5% share of proceeds for the Adaptation Fund), the Enhanced Transparency Framework and common time frames for NDCs.
  • Voluntary pledges: over 100 countries joined the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use and the Global Methane Pledge; the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero and a Just Energy Transition Partnership with South Africa were announced.

2. India's commitments: the Panchamrit

On 1 November 2021 Prime Minister Modi announced five "nectar elements" of climate action.

  • Other initiatives: India proposed LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) as a global mass movement, launched the Green Grids Initiative–One Sun One World One Grid with the UK, and the India-led Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure launched Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRIS).
  • Climate justice: India asked developed countries to provide US$1 trillion of climate finance as soon as possible, stressed common but differentiated responsibilities, and did not join the methane and forest pledges.

3. Assessment

  • Gains: a complete rulebook, fossil fuels on the agenda, and stronger pledges, including India's net-zero year.
  • Gaps: pledges still put the world well above 1.5°C, finance remains short, and the coal language was diluted.

Glasgow moved the world from rule-making to implementation. India's Panchamrit combined ambition with climate justice, and its early achievement of 50% non-fossil capacity and NDC 3.0 (2026) show steady follow-through.
free.upm-2021-gs3-18:
LandslidesLandslide hazard zonationNLRMS 2019Slope stabilisation

A landslide is the downslope movement of rock, debris or earth under gravity. About 0.42 million sq km of India, roughly an eighth of its land area, is landslide-prone, mainly in the Himalaya, the North-East, the Western Ghats and Nilgiris and parts of the Eastern Ghats. The Geological Survey of India (GSI) is the nodal agency, and the NDMA issued a National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (NLRMS) in 2019.

1. Causes

  • Geology and slopes: steep slopes and the young, fractured and weathered rocks of the Himalaya; in the Western Ghats, thick soil over hard rock loses its grip when saturated.
  • Rainfall: most landslides are triggered by intense monsoon rain and cloudbursts, and climate change is making extreme rain more frequent.
  • Earthquakes: shaking loosens slopes in seismic zones, as in Sikkim in 2011.
  • Erosion: rivers undercutting the toe of slopes, and snowmelt.
  • Human activity: road cutting without slope protection, blasting, tunnelling, quarrying and mining; deforestation and shifting cultivation; and unplanned construction that overloads slopes and blocks natural drainage, as in Shimla and Joshimath (land subsidence, 2023).

2. Effects

  • Loss of life: the Wayanad landslides (30 July 2024) killed over 200 people; Malin (Pune, 2014) and Irshalwadi (Raigad, 2023) buried whole villages.
  • Infrastructure and economy: blocked highways and railways cut off hill towns and border areas, damage hydropower projects and hurt tourism, horticulture and trade.
  • Rivers and environment: debris can dam rivers and cause flash floods when these dams burst; soil loss, siltation of reservoirs and loss of forests and habitats follow.
  • Social: displacement, loss of homes and farmland, and trauma for mountain communities.

3. Components of the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019)

  • Landslide hazard mapping: user-friendly hazard and susceptibility maps, building on the GSI's national susceptibility mapping and ISRO's Landslide Atlas of India (2023).
  • Monitoring and early warning: instruments, rainfall thresholds and forecasting systems for vulnerable slopes and settlements.
  • Awareness programmes: for communities, local bodies, schools and tourists on warning signs and safe places.
  • Capacity building and training: for engineers, planners, officials and community volunteers in landslide investigation and mitigation.
  • Mountain zone regulations and policies: land-use zoning, building bye-laws and techno-legal rules for hilly areas.
  • Stabilisation and mitigation: drainage, retaining walls, rock bolting and bioengineering of slopes, and a Special Purpose Vehicle for landslide management.

Landslides are natural, but disasters result from where and how we build. Implementing the NLRMS through hill-specific planning, early warning and community preparedness, in line with the Sendai Framework, can shift India from relief to risk reduction.
free.upm-2021-gs3-19:
Externally aided threatsState and non-state actorsHybrid warfareWhole-of-government response

India's internal security is increasingly shaped by forces outside its borders. State actors, such as hostile governments and their intelligence agencies, and non-state actors, such as terrorist groups, insurgents, drug cartels and hacker collectives, often work together in a hybrid mix of violence, crime, propaganda and cyber attacks. Because they deny responsibility and exploit porous borders, these threats are multidimensional and hard to counter.

1. Challenges posed by external state actors

  • Proxy war through terrorism: Pakistan-based groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed have carried out attacks from 26/11 (2008) to Pulwama (2019) and Pahalgam (22 April 2025), which led to Operation Sindoor (7 May 2025).
  • Border pressure and grey-zone tactics: clashes with China, as at Galwan (June 2020), and a build-up near the Line of Actual Control.
  • Cyber and information warfare: state-linked intrusions into critical infrastructure, such as those reported in India's power sector in 2021, and disinformation during crises.
  • Economic subversion: fake currency, drug trafficking and hawala to fund militancy.

2. Challenges posed by non-state actors

  • Terror and radicalisation: online recruitment by Islamic State-inspired modules and al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent; "white-collar" modules, as in the Red Fort car explosion (November 2025).
  • Insurgents with foreign sanctuaries: some North-Eastern groups operate from camps in Myanmar, where instability after the 2021 coup has added to arms and drug smuggling.
  • Organised crime: drug syndicates of the Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle, arms smugglers and gangster networks linked to extremists abroad; drones drop arms and drugs across the Punjab border.
  • Cyber criminals and hacktivists: about 15 lakh attacks on Indian websites in April–May 2025 (Maharashtra Cyber), and scam compounds abroad that defraud Indians.
  • Extremist groups abroad: pro-Khalistan outfits seek to revive separatism through funding and propaganda.

3. Measures required

  • Secure borders and coasts: smart fencing under the Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System, anti-drone systems, the Vibrant Villages Programme (Phase I ₹4,800 crore; Phase II ₹6,839 crore to 2028-29), three-tier coastal security and fencing of the Myanmar border.
  • Intelligence and coordination: a revamped Multi-Agency Centre, NATGRID, creating the long-proposed National Counter Terrorism Centre, and better Centre–State coordination, since police is a State subject.
  • Law and investigation: the UAPA and NIA Act (both amended in 2019), the PMLA and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, with faster trials.
  • Cyber and financial defence: CERT-In, NCIIPC, the Defence Cyber Agency and the I4C; FATF standards, FIU-IND and the "No Money for Terror" agenda.
  • Deterrence and diplomacy: calibrated military responses (2016, 2019, 2025), UN listings of terrorists, adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism, and cooperation with partners.
  • Social resilience: de-radicalisation, counter-narratives, and development and jobs in border, tribal and conflict areas.

External actors exploit every gap between agencies, domains and communities. The answer is a whole-of-government, whole-of-society approach that combines strong borders, smart intelligence, the rule of law and national cohesion.
free.upm-2021-gs3-20:
TerrorismCrime–terror nexusNarco-terrorismZero tolerance

Terrorism is the use or threat of violence against civilians to create fear for political, religious or ideological ends, and India has faced it for over four decades. Its complexity lies in the many actors, motives and methods involved, and its intensity in mass-casualty attacks such as 26/11 (2008), in which 166 people were killed. There is still no agreed UN definition, as India's proposed Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (1996) remains stalled.

1. Complexity and intensity

  • Changing tactics: fidayeen and sea-borne attacks, IEDs, targeted killings, drone attacks (Jammu Air Force Station, June 2021) and attacks on tourists (Pahalgam, where 26 civilians were killed).
  • New profiles: lone actors and educated professionals radicalised online.
  • Technology: encrypted apps, social media, crypto-assets and drones make terror cheaper and harder to detect.
  • State sponsorship: support from across the border provides training, sanctuaries and deniability.

2. Causes

  • External sponsorship: use of terror as an instrument of state policy by a hostile neighbour.
  • Radical ideologies: religious extremism and global jihadist networks such as the Islamic State and al-Qaeda.
  • Grievances and alienation: perceived injustice, identity politics and unemployment among youth, which recruiters exploit.
  • Governance gaps: weak policing, slow justice, and porous borders and coasts.

3. Linkages and the obnoxious nexus

  • Narco-terror: heroin from the Golden Crescent, smuggled into Punjab and J&K, often by drones, funds militants.
  • Crime syndicates: the 1993 Mumbai blasts showed how an underworld network could carry out terror; NIA cases since 2022 target a gangster–terror nexus linked to extremists abroad.
  • Fake currency and hawala: FICN, hawala and extortion "levies" finance attacks and insurgency.
  • Politics–crime links: the N.N. Vohra Committee (1993) warned of a nexus between criminal syndicates, politicians and officials that can shelter such networks.

4. Measures to eradicate terrorism

  • Law and justice: the UAPA and NIA Act (amended 2019), Section 113 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, special courts, witness protection and quicker trials.
  • Intelligence and policing: the Multi-Agency Centre, NATGRID, NSG hubs, State anti-terror squads and forensic capacity through the National Forensic Sciences University (2020).
  • Choking finance: the NIA's terror-funding cell, the ED and FIU-IND, FATF standards (India rated "regular follow-up" in 2024) and the "No Money for Terror" initiative.
  • Counter-radicalisation and development: community policing, counter-narratives, education, jobs and surrender-cum-rehabilitation policies.
  • Global action: adoption of the CCIT, UN 1267 listings, extradition and cooperation through the Quad and the SCO's Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure.

Terrorism thrives on the nexus of ideology, money and crime. A zero-tolerance, intelligence-led and rights-respecting strategy, which breaks this nexus at home and isolates its sponsors abroad, can eradicate the menace.
free.upm-2021-gs4-1a:
Ethical performance matrixIntegrityImpartialityAccountability

A civil servant's performance cannot be judged by targets alone: how results are achieved matters as much as what is achieved. An ethical performance matrix plots an officer on a few observable traits and complements the output-focused APAR, which already asks the reporting officer to comment on integrity. The values written into the All India Services (Conduct) Rules in 2014 and the Second ARC's report on Ethics in Governance (2007) point to five such traits.

1. Five traits and why each belongs in the matrix

  • Integrity: honesty in money, decisions and words, and consistency between private belief and public action. It is the foundation: without it, every other strength, even competence, can be turned to private gain.
  • Impartiality and non-partisanship: decisions on merit and the same rules for all, whatever a person's caste, religion, wealth or political links. It gives effect to equality before the law (Article 14) and keeps citizens' trust when governments change.
  • Accountability and transparency: owning decisions, recording reasons and being open to audit, RTI and grievance review. It turns discretion into answerable power and deters misuse.
  • Empathy and compassion: sensitivity to the poor, the disabled, women and other weaker sections; the 2014 conduct rules expressly ask for responsiveness to the public, particularly the weaker sections. It makes rules humane and keeps the last person from being excluded.
  • Dedication to public service: commitment, diligence and moral courage, seen in timely delivery and in crises such as floods, elections and epidemics. It separates service from mere compliance.

2. Why a matrix rather than a single score

  • Traits balance one another: integrity without empathy becomes rigid; empathy without impartiality slides into favouritism; dedication without accountability can turn arbitrary.
  • Diagnosis, not only grading: plotting each trait separately shows where an officer needs training or mentoring, which fits Mission Karmayogi's competency-based approach (the Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies, FRAC).
  • Evidence over impression: most indicators can be drawn from records, so the assessment depends less on one superior's opinion.

3. Safeguards in using it

  • Many sources: combine the reporting officer's view with peer and citizen feedback, as in 360-degree appraisal.
  • Fairness to the officer: entries must be communicated so that the officer can represent against them, as the Supreme Court held in Dev Dutt v Union of India (2008).
  • Reward courage: the matrix must credit officers who refuse illegal orders or take honest risks, not penalise them for friction with superiors.

Plotting performance on these five traits makes ethics measurable and moves the civil service from mere rule-compliance to values-based governance, in which the way a result is achieved counts as much as the result itself.
free.upm-2021-gs4-1b:
Foundational valuesCode of ethicsProbityPrevention of misconduct

An effective public servant needs, besides competence, foundational values that guide discretion where rules are silent. The UPSC syllabus, the Second ARC's report on Ethics in Governance (2007) and the values added to the All India Services (Conduct) Rules in 2014 identify them. Non-ethical behaviour, such as corruption, favouritism, apathy and abuse of power, can be prevented only when personal values are backed by institutional safeguards.

1. Ten essential values

  • These values reinforce one another: integrity without empathy becomes harsh, and empathy without impartiality becomes favouritism.

2. Why public servants slip

  • Discretion with weak oversight: complex procedures and face-to-face dealings create opportunities for rent-seeking.
  • Pressure and culture: political or peer pressure, fear of transfer and a cynical "everyone does it" culture.
  • Low risk of punishment: long delays in inquiries and prosecution weaken deterrence.

3. Ways and means: institutional and legal

  • Clear codes: a code of ethics stating values, besides conduct rules listing prohibitions, as the Second ARC recommended; declaration of assets and conflicts of interest; rotation in sensitive posts.
  • Anti-corruption law and agencies: the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, amended in 2018 to make bribe-giving a specific offence and to require prior approval (Section 17A) before probing decisions taken in official functions; the CVC; and the Lokpal (functional since 2019) and State Lokayuktas.
  • Transparency and technology: the RTI Act, 2005; e-procurement on GeM; direct benefit transfer and faceless tax assessment (2020) reduce discretionary contact.
  • Swift, fair consequences: time-bound inquiries; protection for those who report wrongdoing under the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004); premature retirement in public interest of officers of doubtful integrity after review (FR 56(j)).

4. Ways and means: personal and cultural

  • Values-based recruitment and training: the Ethics paper in the Civil Services (Main) Examination since 2013, foundation courses and Mission Karmayogi (2020).
  • Leadership by example: the "tone at the top"; seniors who model probity and protect honest juniors.
  • Reward honesty: fair appraisals, stable tenure through Civil Services Boards (urged in T.S.R. Subramanian v UoI, 2013) and recognition such as the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration.
  • Citizen vigilance: social audits, citizens' charters, CPGRAMS and a free press make misconduct visible.

Values are the first line of defence and institutions the second. Ethical conduct lasts only when it is internalised and also enforced, combining character with compliance.
free.upm-2021-gs4-2a:
Data-driven governanceAlgorithmic biasRational decision makingHuman judgement

Rational decision making means choosing the best option on the basis of evidence, logic and foreseeable consequences. Herbert Simon showed that administrators decide with limited information, time and attention, a condition he later called bounded rationality. Digital technology (big data, real-time dashboards, geospatial imaging and artificial intelligence) promises to widen those limits. Yet data can be incomplete, biased or manipulated, and algorithms can be opaque, so its reliability as an input is genuinely debatable.

1. The case for digital inputs

  • Scale and speed: the PRAGATI platform (2015) lets the Prime Minister review stalled projects with States in real time, and the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (2021) layers data from many ministries to plan infrastructure and avoid duplication.
  • Evidence over discretion: GST network analytics and e-invoicing flag fake invoices; faceless assessment (2020) reduces scope for bias and bribery.
  • Better targeting: Aadhaar-linked direct benefit transfer weeds out duplicate and ghost beneficiaries; satellite and drone data help assess crop losses for insurance.
  • Crisis management: during COVID-19, CoWIN scheduled and certified more than 200 crore vaccine doses, giving planners real-time data on coverage.

2. Why it remains debatable

  • Garbage in, garbage out: outdated or wrong records lead to wrong decisions; biometric authentication failures in ration distribution have excluded genuine beneficiaries, especially the elderly and manual workers.
  • Bias and opacity: systems trained on past data can reproduce discrimination. Amazon scrapped an AI recruiting tool that penalised women (reported in 2018), and England withdrew its 2020 A-level grading algorithm after it lowered nearly 40% of the grades teachers had assessed.
  • Automation without accountability: Australia's Robodebt scheme (from 2016) raised false welfare debts through automated income averaging and was condemned by a Royal Commission (2023); the Dutch childcare-benefits scandal led the government to resign (January 2021).
  • Misinformation and exclusion: deepfakes and doctored data mislead decision-makers, and the digital divide leaves the poorest under-represented in the data.
  • Privacy: large databases raise the concerns recognised in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017); the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is being phased in under Rules notified in November 2025.

3. Making digital inputs reliable

  • Human in the loop: data should inform, not replace, judgement; officers must record reasons and be able to override in cases of hardship, for example through alternative authentication and audited manual entries.
  • Quality and audit: regular validation of databases, independent algorithmic audits and published methods.
  • Ethical framework: NITI Aayog's Principles for Responsible AI (2021) stress safety, equality, transparency and accountability; citizens need a right to explanation and grievance redress.
  • Inclusion: offline and assisted channels such as Common Service Centres for those left out.

Digital technology is a powerful aid to rationality, not a substitute for it. Its reliability depends on data quality, transparency and human judgement anchored in ethics: governance should be data-informed, not data-dictated.
free.upm-2021-gs4-2b:
Ethical dilemmaDomain knowledgeCreativityThird alternative

An ethical dilemma arises when two values conflict, such as rule versus compassion, development versus livelihoods, or efficiency versus equity, and every obvious option sacrifices one of them. Domain knowledge tells an official what the law, rules and technical facts permit. Innovativeness and creativity help him find a third alternative that honours both values, instead of merely choosing the lesser evil.

1. Domain knowledge: necessary but not sufficient

  • Necessary: knowledge of law, procedure and technical facts keeps solutions lawful and feasible; creativity without it can become arbitrary or reckless.
  • Not sufficient: rules are written for typical cases, while dilemmas arise in atypical ones, where literal application can cause injustice.
  • The binary trap: knowledge alone often frames choices as either/or (follow the rule or bend it), whereas many dilemmas dissolve when the problem is reframed.

2. How creativity helps resolve dilemmas

  • Reframing the problem: asking what each value really requires reveals options beyond the obvious two.
  • Mobilising new resources: community participation, partnerships, technology and convergence of schemes can meet a need without breaking rules.
  • Building in safeguards: a creative solution must still be recorded, transparent and auditable, so that flexibility does not become favouritism.
  • Moral imagination: empathy with affected people helps foresee consequences and design acceptable compromises.

3. Illustrations

  • Armstrong Pame: as a young IAS officer in Tamenglong, Manipur, he faced villages cut off for want of a road and a government that had no funds for it. Instead of choosing between rules and people, he raised donations, including his own money, and mobilised local labour to build a road of about 100 km.
  • Operation Sulaimani: the Kozhikode district administration, with the local hotel and restaurant association, gave the hungry free meal coupons without questions, reconciling dignity with accountability.
  • Land pooling (Amaravati, 2015): instead of compulsory acquisition, farmers who pooled their land were promised developed residential and commercial plots and an annual annuity, giving them a stake in the new capital; such schemes keep their promise only if the plots are delivered on time.

4. Limits and safeguards

  • Within the Constitution and law: innovation that bypasses due process ("jugaad" in rules) creates new injustice.
  • Institutional support: recognition such as the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration, and protection for honest experimentation, encourage creativity.

Domain knowledge provides the map and creativity finds the path. Combined with integrity, they let officials resolve dilemmas in ways that are lawful, humane and innovative: principled innovation rather than either rigid rule-following or rule-breaking.
free.upm-2021-gs4-3a:
PerseveranceResilienceKarma YogaLearning from failure

In these words, Swami Vivekananda reminds us that every worthwhile endeavour meets obstacles, and that success belongs to those who persist through them. The value at its heart is perseverance: steady effort in the face of failure, criticism and delay, sustained by faith in the goal. It reflects his teaching of Karma Yoga, which asks us to keep working with dedication without being shaken by immediate results.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Difficulties are normal, not signs of failure: every new idea meets resistance from habit, vested interests and scarce resources; hurdles are part of the path.
  • Setbacks carry lessons: each failure shows what to improve; persistence turns mistakes into experience.
  • "Sooner or later": results may be delayed, so patience and a long-term view are needed, in the spirit of the Gita's call to do one's duty without attachment to its fruits.
  • Not blind stubbornness: perseverance means holding on to the goal while revising methods in the light of evidence.

2. Examples from public life

  • ISRO: the first SLV-3 launch failed in 1979 and the next succeeded in 1980. Chandrayaan-2's lander crashed in 2019, yet Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023.
  • Polio eradication: despite vaccine hesitancy and difficult terrain, India's pulse polio campaigns recorded the last case in January 2011, and the WHO South-East Asia Region was certified polio-free in March 2014.
  • Arunima Sinha: she lost a leg after being pushed from a train in 2011 and climbed Mount Everest in 2013.
  • Dashrath Manjhi: the "Mountain Man" of Gaya, Bihar, spent about 22 years cutting a path through a hill with hammer and chisel so that his village could reach the nearby town.

3. Relevance for a civil servant

  • Reforms take time: GST was proposed in the mid-2000s and came into force on 1 July 2017 only after the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) and years of Centre–State negotiation.
  • Field problems are long-term: malnutrition, sanitation and land-record reform are not solved in one tenure; persistence and continuity matter.
  • Integrity under pressure: honest officers face transfers, criticism and delay; perseverance keeps them steady without turning them cynical.
  • Resilience and well-being: treating setbacks as feedback rather than personal defeat protects against burnout.

Perseverance is the bridge between vision and achievement. For a public servant committed to the public good, difficulties are tests, not verdicts; those who persevere do see the light, sooner or later.
free.upm-2021-gs4-3b:
Inner peaceEquanimityNon-violenceConflict resolution

The Dalai Lama, the Tibetan Buddhist leader and 1989 Nobel Peace laureate, holds that outer peace, harmony in families, societies and among nations, grows out of inner peace: a mind free from anger, greed, fear and hatred. Conflicts begin in the mind, and a person at war with himself spreads conflict around him. The value at its heart is equanimity joined with compassion.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • The mind is the source: the preamble to UNESCO's Constitution (1945) makes the same point: because wars begin in human minds, it is in the mind that peace must be defended.
  • Inner peace is not passivity: it is calm strength that allows clear judgement and firm, non-violent action against injustice.
  • The means: self-awareness, mindfulness, compassion and contentment; Buddhism's overcoming of greed, hatred and delusion, and the Gita's ideal of the sthitaprajna, steady in success and failure.
  • A ripple effect: a peaceful person builds a peaceful family, community and, in the end, a more peaceful world.
  • Outer measures are not enough: treaties, laws and police can contain conflict, but lasting peace needs people who have overcome prejudice and the urge for revenge.

2. Examples from public life

  • Mahatma Gandhi: satyagraha demanded inner discipline (prayer, fasting and control of anger) before resistance; he suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura (1922).
  • Nelson Mandela: after 27 years in prison, he chose reconciliation over revenge, helping South Africa's peaceful transition to democracy in 1994.
  • Emperor Ashoka: remorse after the Kalinga war turned him from conquest to dhamma, tolerance and public welfare, as his edicts record.
  • The Dalai Lama himself: he has advocated non-violence and compassion throughout his life in exile in India since 1959.

3. Relevance for a civil servant

  • Decisions under stress: riots, disasters and angry crowds demand a calm mind; an officer ruled by anger or panic escalates conflict.
  • Conflict resolution: peace committees, dialogue with protesters and mediation succeed only when the officer listens with equanimity.
  • Integrity: inner contentment weakens the pull of greed and status, the roots of corruption.
  • Well-being: long hours and constant pressure cause stress and burnout; yoga, meditation and counselling help officers stay balanced and humane.
  • Leading teams: a calm leader spreads calm, while an angry one spreads fear; inner balance helps an officer give feedback without humiliating subordinates.

Peace must be built from within. A civil servant at peace with himself judges fairly, listens patiently and becomes an instrument of social harmony.
free.upm-2021-gs4-3c:
InterdependenceCooperationSocial capitalVasudhaiva Kutumbakam

Erik Erikson (1902–1994), the psychoanalyst known for his eight stages of psychosocial development, saw human growth as a social process, from an infant's basic trust in its caregiver to an adult's care for the next generation. The quotation stresses interdependence: no individual, community or nation is self-sufficient, and the sooner we recognise our mutual need, the better for all.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Humans are social beings: life rests on families, teachers, farmers, workers and institutions; even independence is built on this web of support.
  • Erikson's own stages: the first conflict, trust versus mistrust (infancy), and the seventh, generativity versus stagnation (middle adulthood), show that healthy development needs both receiving and giving care.
  • A warning against extreme individualism: competition and self-interest without cooperation produce loneliness, inequality and conflict.
  • Interdependence, not dependence: it rests on mutual respect and reciprocity, not one-sided reliance.

2. Examples

  • COVID-19: the virus crossed every border, and the response depended on shared data, global supply chains and vaccines; India's Vaccine Maitri initiative supplied vaccines to other countries from January 2021, while community kitchens fed stranded migrants at home.
  • Climate change: emissions anywhere affect everyone; hence collective efforts such as the Paris Agreement and the International Solar Alliance (both 2015).
  • Economic interdependence: disruptions of supply chains during the pandemic and after the Russia–Ukraine war (2022) raised food, fuel and fertiliser prices far from the places where they began.
  • Community resilience: in floods and cyclones, neighbours, fishermen and volunteers are often the first responders, long before official help arrives.
  • India's ethos: the idea of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam inspired the theme of India's G20 Presidency (2023), "One Earth, One Family, One Future".

3. Relevance for a civil servant

  • Whole-of-government working: departments must coordinate rather than work in silos, as PM Gati Shakti attempts for infrastructure planning.
  • Jan Bhagidari: campaigns such as Swachh Bharat and disaster response succeed only with community participation.
  • Teamwork and humility: an officer depends on subordinates, experts and citizens; respecting their contribution improves outcomes.
  • Inclusion: a society is only as strong as its weakest members; welfare for the marginalised strengthens everyone.
  • Cooperative federalism: shared institutions such as the GST Council show that Union and States gain more by negotiating together than by acting alone.

Recognising interdependence turns competition into cooperation. For individuals, administrators and nations alike, "we need each other" is not weakness but the foundation of collective well-being.
free.upm-2021-gs4-4a:
AttitudeABC modelService orientationAttitude change

An attitude is a learned and fairly lasting tendency to evaluate people, objects and ideas favourably or unfavourably. It has three components (the ABC model): affective (feelings), behavioural (readiness to act) and cognitive (beliefs). Because attitudes decide how knowledge and skills are used, they are a key input in human development. For a public servant, the right attitude turns power into service.

1. Attitudes a public servant needs

  • Service orientation: seeing citizens as rights-holders, not supplicants, and the office as a trust, not a privilege.
  • Empathy and compassion: sensitivity to the poor, women, the disabled and other weaker sections.
  • Integrity and impartiality: a settled disposition to act honestly and treat all alike, even under pressure.
  • Openness to change: willingness to learn, accept feedback and use technology and new ideas.
  • Accountability and teamwork: owning results rather than shifting blame; respect for colleagues and subordinates.

2. How attitudes are formed

  • Socialisation: family, school, peers, religion and media shape early beliefs and feelings, which is why recruitment alone cannot guarantee the right attitude.
  • Direct experience: what one sees in the field, such as poverty, exclusion or the effect of a good scheme, changes attitudes more than lectures.
  • Observation and reinforcement: people copy role models and repeat behaviour that is rewarded.

3. Building the right attitude: the individual

  • Reflection: introspection, journalling and reading the lives of exemplary administrators help an officer examine his own biases.
  • Exposure: staying in villages, meeting tribal communities or working in slums builds empathy that classroom learning cannot.
  • Emotional intelligence: self-awareness and self-regulation turn values into consistent behaviour under stress.

4. Building the right attitude: the institution

  • Value-based selection and training: the Ethics paper in the Civil Services (Main) Examination since 2013, foundation courses and district training; Mission Karmayogi (2020) seeks to shift the civil service from "rule" to "role", with role-based learning on the iGOT platform.
  • Persuasion and dissonance: credible mentors and clear messages change beliefs; when behaviour required by the job (for example, courtesy to all applicants) conflicts with an old prejudice, the resulting cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957) tends to shift the attitude.
  • Organisational culture: leaders who model integrity, fair appraisals, recognition such as the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration, and firm action against misconduct.

Attitudes are learned, so they can be built. Through socialisation, training and example, a public servant can internalise service, empathy and integrity, so that good conduct becomes habit rather than compulsion, and governance becomes truly citizen-centric.
free.upm-2021-gs4-4b:
Crisis of conscienceEmotional intelligenceMoral courageSelf-regulation

A crisis of conscience arises when what one is asked, or tempted, to do conflicts with one's moral convictions: an order to favour a contractor, for instance, or to suppress inconvenient facts. It brings fear, guilt, anger and anxiety. Emotional intelligence (EI), popularised by Daniel Goleman (1995) with five components (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills), can help one handle these emotions without abandoning one's ethical stand. But EI is a tool; its direction must come from conscience.

1. How EI helps

  • Self-awareness: it helps one recognise fear of transfer, hope of promotion or loyalty to a superior as the forces pulling away from conscience, so they can be examined rather than obeyed.
  • Self-regulation: it replaces impulsive defiance or meek surrender with calm, giving time to gather facts and consider lawful options.
  • Motivation: an inner commitment to public service sustains one through isolation and pressure.
  • Empathy: understanding the superior's compulsions and the likely victims' suffering helps craft a response that respects people while refusing the wrong.
  • Social skills: tactful dissent, such as putting objections in writing, persuading, finding allies and escalating through proper channels, makes a principled stand effective rather than merely heroic.

2. Where EI falls short (a critical view)

  • EI is morally neutral: skilled manipulators also read and use emotions; EI can be used to rationalise a compromise ("everyone does it") or merely to soothe guilt rather than resolve its cause.
  • Conscience must lead: EI helps carry out a decision but cannot by itself tell right from wrong; that needs moral reasoning, knowledge of law and integrity.
  • Structural pressure: where honest officers are punished, EI alone cannot protect them; written instructions, stable tenure and protection for those who report wrongdoing are also needed.
  • Over-accommodation: an excessive wish to keep everyone happy can lead to avoiding a necessary confrontation.

3. Illustrations

  • An engineer told to ignore a structural defect: EI lets him control his anger, understand his superior's political pressure and propose an independent test and a faster repair plan, while refusing to certify unsafe work. Without moral courage, however, his EI would only make his surrender smoother.
  • Satyendra Dubey (2003): an engineer who exposed corruption in a national highway project and was murdered. His case shows that personal courage needs institutional protection; the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004) followed.

EI does help in a crisis of conscience: it keeps one calm, empathetic and persuasive. But it works without compromise only when guided by ethical clarity and moral courage and supported by institutions; EI is the vehicle, conscience the compass.
free.upm-2021-gs4-5a:
Non-refoulementHuman dignityOpen societyArticle 21

Non-refoulement, the principle that no one may be returned to a country where they face persecution, torture or serious human-rights violations, is the cornerstone of refugee protection. It is codified in Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention and is widely regarded as customary international law. A democracy that calls itself an open society, one that respects individual freedom and reasoned debate, professes the dignity of every human being; turning refugees back to danger contradicts its own values.

1. Ethical dimensions violated by turning refugees back

  • Human dignity and the right to life: sending a person back to likely persecution treats him as a mere means of border control, which Kant's ethics forbids.
  • Integrity of the state: a democracy that champions liberty but expels the persecuted shows a gap between professed values and conduct, and loses moral credibility.
  • Compassion and the duty to rescue: refugees, often women and children, are among the most vulnerable people; abandoning them violates care ethics.
  • Justice and non-discrimination: protecting some groups but not others on grounds of religion or ethnicity offends equality.
  • Global responsibility: refugee flows result from conflicts that no one country controls; the UN's Global Compact on Refugees (2018) calls for responsibility-sharing.

2. The other side: legitimate concerns

  • Security: states have a sovereign right to control borders, and militants may hide among refugees.
  • Resource pressures: large inflows strain jobs, land and services in poor host areas and can provoke local tensions.
  • Built-in exceptions: Article 33(2) itself excludes a refugee who is a danger to the security of the host country. These concerns justify screening and regulated stay, not blanket push-backs.

3. India's position

  • India is not a party to the 1951 Convention or its 1967 Protocol and has no refugee law; entry and stay are governed by the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 (in force since September 2025).
  • Yet it has sheltered Tibetans (1959), refugees from East Pakistan (1971) and Sri Lankan Tamils. Courts have held that Article 21 protects all persons, including foreigners (NHRC v State of Arunachal Pradesh, 1996, on the Chakmas).
  • In Mohammad Salimullah v UoI (2021), the Supreme Court declined to stop the deportation of Rohingya detained in Jammu, provided the procedure for deportation was followed, which shows the tension between sovereignty and protection.

4. Global illustrations

  • Germany admitted hundreds of thousands of Syrian and other refugees in 2015, showing compassion at scale.
  • The UK Supreme Court (November 2023) held the plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda unlawful because of the risk that they would be returned to danger; the scheme was dropped in 2024.

An open democracy may regulate entry, but returning people to persecution betrays its own values. A clear, rights-based refugee framework that balances humanity with security would honour both the Constitution's Article 21 and India's tradition of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.
free.upm-2021-gs4-5b:
ImpartialityNon-partisanshipPolitical neutralityConstitutional values

Impartiality means treating all citizens equally and deciding on merit, without fear, favour or prejudice. Non-partisanship means political neutrality: serving whichever government is lawfully elected with equal loyalty and honest advice, without allegiance to any party. Together they make a permanent civil service the steel frame that gives continuity across governments, and the All India Services (Conduct) Rules require both.

1. Why they are indispensable

  • Rule of law and equality: impartial decisions on licences, land records, police complaints and welfare give effect to Article 14; partiality turns public power into private favour.
  • Trust and legitimacy: citizens accept even unfavourable decisions when they believe the officer is neutral.
  • Continuity and stability: governments change, but a neutral service implements each government's lawful policies faithfully, preserving institutional memory.
  • Free and fair elections: officials on election duty work under the Election Commission; T.N. Seshan's firm and even-handed enforcement of the Model Code as Chief Election Commissioner (1990–96) strengthened public faith in elections.
  • Frank advice: a neutral officer can tell ministers unwelcome truths; Sardar Patel defended the All India Services in the Constituent Assembly (October 1949), arguing that officers must be free to speak their minds without fear.

2. Illustrations of the absence of these qualities

  • The Emergency: the Shah Commission (1977–78) recorded how officials carried out illegal orders, showing the cost of a pliant bureaucracy.
  • Partisan policing: biased handling of riots or complaints erodes trust; the Supreme Court's directions in Prakash Singh v UoI (2006) sought to insulate the police from political interference.

3. Necessary but not sufficient

  • Neutral, not indifferent: neutrality is towards parties, not towards constitutional values; the 1970s debate on a "committed bureaucracy" is best settled by commitment to the Constitution rather than to any party.
  • Impartiality is not mechanical equality: reservations and special measures under Articles 15(4), 16(4) and 46 are constitutional mandates, not partiality.
  • Other qualities are needed too: competence, integrity, empathy and innovation; an impartial but incompetent officer offers fair but poor service.
  • Safeguards: conduct rules that bar membership of political parties, protection under Article 311, and stable tenure through Civil Services Boards (T.S.R. Subramanian v UoI, 2013).

Impartiality and non-partisanship are indispensable, the non-negotiable foundation of a successful civil servant. Success, however, also demands competence and empathy, and above all a commitment to constitutional values that guides neutrality towards justice.
free.upm-2021-gs4-6a:
Social auditAccountabilityJudicial transparencyCitizen participation

A social audit is a process in which the people affected by a public programme, helped by independent facilitators, check its implementation against official records and discuss the findings in a public forum such as the Gram Sabha. The public hearings (jan sunwai) of the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan in Rajasthan in the 1990s pioneered it, and MGNREGA made it mandatory. It complements internal audit and the CAG by bringing the citizen's eye into governance.

1. Why it must be independent and empowered

  • Independence: an audit run by the implementing department becomes a whitewash; independent units, such as Andhra Pradesh's Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency, and facilitators drawn from the community make findings credible.
  • Empowerment: auditors need full access to records (proactive disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act), legal backing, protection from intimidation and an assured follow-up; otherwise findings gather dust.
  • Legal mandate: Meghalaya's Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017 was the first State law to extend social audit across departments and services. As of 2026, social audits remain mandatory under the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, which replaced MGNREGA from 1 July 2026, and Section 28 of the National Food Security Act provides for them.

2. How it ensures performance, accountability and ethical conduct

  • Performance: it checks whether works exist, wages are paid on time and services reach people, measuring outcomes and not just spending.
  • Accountability: public hearings fix responsibility, leading to recovery of misused funds, corrections and disciplinary action.
  • Ethical conduct: the prospect of public exposure deters corruption and builds a culture of honesty.
  • Participation: citizens become monitors rather than passive beneficiaries, deepening democracy.

3. Every sphere, including the judiciary

  • Other services: School Management Committees under the Right to Education Act, patient feedback in hospitals, citizen feedback on police stations and ward committees in cities extend the idea.
  • Judiciary: accountability must not compromise judicial independence, a basic feature of the Constitution. A social audit of courts should examine administration and access (pendency, adjournments, infrastructure, legal aid), not the merits of judgments. The National Judicial Data Grid makes pendency data public; Constitution Bench hearings have been live-streamed since 2022 following Swapnil Tripathi (2018); and, under a Full Court resolution of 1 April 2025, the Supreme Court began publishing its judges' asset declarations on its website in May 2025, with the process for judicial appointments.
  • Tools: court-user surveys, reports by bar associations and legal services authorities, and independent studies such as the India Justice Report.

4. Challenges

  • Capture by local elites, intimidation of auditors, weak follow-up and low awareness call for statutory backing, protection for facilitators and time-bound action-taken reports.

An independent, empowered social audit makes accountability run from citizens to the State, not only within government. Applied with care for judicial independence, it can make every public institution answerable to the people it serves.
free.upm-2021-gs4-6b:
IntegrityMoral authorityInner strengthTrust

Integrity, from the Latin integer ("whole"), is the consistency of values, words and actions, in public and in private, even when no one is watching. It is often seen as a restraint, but it is in fact a source of empowerment: it gives a person inner strength, freedom from fear, and the moral authority that makes others trust and follow him.

1. How integrity empowers

  • Inner strength and peace: a person of integrity has no double life to manage and no fear of exposure; a clear conscience gives the confidence to take hard decisions.
  • Freedom from pressure: one who has taken no favours cannot be blackmailed, while a corrupt officer becomes hostage to those who paid him.
  • Moral authority: people follow those who practise what they preach; leaders with integrity can ask others for sacrifice.
  • Trust and credibility: colleagues and citizens rely on one's word, which makes cooperation easier and governance cheaper.
  • Courage to dissent: integrity gives the courage to refuse illegal orders and to give frank advice.

2. Illustrations

  • Mahatma Gandhi: a life lived in the open made him the moral leader of millions; his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth, admitted his failings frankly, and this strengthened rather than weakened his authority.
  • Lal Bahadur Shastri: he resigned as Railway Minister in 1956, accepting moral responsibility for a rail accident at Ariyalur; the reputation he earned gave weight to his later appeals for sacrifice during the 1965 war and food shortage.
  • E. Sreedharan: his reputation for integrity and punctual delivery allowed him to insist on professional autonomy in building the Konkan Railway and the Delhi Metro.
  • T.N. Seshan: as Chief Election Commissioner (1990–96), his independence let him enforce the Model Code of Conduct firmly against all parties.

3. Integrity in public service today

  • Empowering the honest officer: an officer with a clean record can enforce the law against the powerful without fear of counter-allegations.
  • Institutional support: integrity pacts in procurement, asset declarations and e-governance reinforce personal honesty.
