  • The cost, and why it must be protected: honest officers may face transfers or isolation, and some, like Satyendra Dubey (2003), have paid with their lives; protecting such officers is part of making integrity empowering rather than dangerous.

Integrity is not a limit on power but its ethical foundation. It turns a person into someone whose word counts, and a public servant into a trusted leader whose authority comes from character rather than position.

Sunil faces an illegal sand-mining mafia that is protected by local functionaries and some of his own office staff, and that controls poor tribals through bribes and fear. It now threatens his life and stalks his family. Sand is a minor mineral under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and its plunder ruins rivers, revenue and tribal livelihoods. The case tests Sunil's moral courage, his prudence and his duty of care to his family.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: Sunil, his wife and mother; tribals, both victims and coerced participants; honest and compromised staff; the mafia and its patrons; police and district administration; and the river ecosystem.
  • Issues: personal safety versus public duty; rule of law versus organised crime; betrayal of trust by his own employees; exploitation of tribals, whose Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas have a say over minor minerals under PESA, 1996; environmental damage and revenue loss. The killing of IPS officer Narendra Kumar by a tractor carrying illegally mined stone in Morena (2012) shows that the threat is real.

2. (a) Options available to Sunil

  • Stop the raids and come to terms with the mafia.
  • Seek a transfer or go on leave.
  • Continue the raids alone, as aggressively as before.
  • Go to the media with the threats.
  • Continue the drive with institutional backing, protection for his family and support from the tribal community.

3. (b) Critical evaluation of the options

  • The first two options sacrifice the public interest to private safety, the third sacrifices prudence to zeal, and the fourth substitutes publicity for institutional action.

4. (c) The most appropriate course: continue, strategically and with support

  • Protect the family first: report every threat in writing to the Superintendent of Police and his superiors; register an FIR for criminal intimidation (Section 351 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita); obtain security for himself and his family, and move them temporarily to a secure place if needed.
  • Seek institutional backing: ask for a joint task force of revenue, police, mines and forest officials and the State government's support, so that the drive does not depend on one officer.
  • Clean his own office: move suspected employees out of sensitive posts, start departmental and vigilance inquiries, and share raid plans only with a small trusted team.
  • Use technology and law: e-transit passes, GPS on sand trucks, CCTV at check posts and drone surveillance of riverbeds, as the MoEFCC's Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining (2020) recommend; seize vehicles and prosecute under Section 21 of the MMDR Act and State rules, aiming at the financiers, not only the drivers.
  • Win over the tribals: hold Gram Sabha meetings, protect informants, offer livelihoods through public works and the District Mineral Foundation, and arrange a legal, transparent supply of sand so that the black market loses its customers.

Why this course: it joins courage with prudence. Duty is not abandoned, but risk is managed through the institutions that exist to protect officers. It attacks the system (insiders, financiers, illegal demand) rather than its symptoms, and treats the tribals as partners, not culprits.

Integrity in such posts needs moral courage backed by the State. By protecting his family, strengthening institutions and winning the community's trust, Sunil can uphold the rule of law without becoming its next martyr.

Academic integrityConflict of interestUndue influenceFairness

Two students, sons of the college's most influential patrons, were caught using unfair means with the help of a senior lecturer close to the management. The management wants the case "resolved" with the university's flying squad at any cost, and hints that my promotion depends on it, while students protest at the gate demanding strict action. As Vice Principal, I must weigh academic integrity and fairness against institutional image, patronage and personal gain.

1. Stakeholders

  • The two students and their families; the senior lecturer; the management; the politician and the businessman; the university and its flying squad; honest students of this and other colleges; the student union; parents and society; and myself.

2. (a) Ethical issues involved

  • Academic integrity versus institutional image: hiding malpractice to protect reputation would destroy the very credibility it seeks to protect.
  • Conflict of interest: linking my promotion to suppressing the case is an inducement that would compromise my objectivity.
  • Undue influence: affiliation and donations are being used to buy impunity; the rules must apply equally to the powerful.
  • Misconduct by a teacher: a senior lecturer aiding cheating betrays his role as a guide and model for students.
  • Fairness to honest students: cheating devalues their degrees and robs them of merit-based opportunities.
  • Obedience versus conscience: loyalty to the management against duty to the university's rules and to students.
  • Due process for the accused: the students are young and deserve a fair hearing and a proportionate penalty; the protest must not become mob justice.

3. (b) Options available and their evaluation

The option I will adopt: cooperate with the process and lead the college through the crisis

  • Cooperate fully with the flying squad: provide facts and records truthfully. The university's unfair-means committee will decide the students' case after a hearing; I will ask only for due process, not for exemption.
  • Advise the management in writing: explain that the matter cannot lawfully be "resolved" outside the university's rules, and that any attempt would invite a far bigger scandal and put the college's affiliation and reputation at risk. Politely decline the promotion-linked instruction and keep a record of it.
  • Act on the lecturer: recommend his suspension pending an inquiry and inform the university.
  • Engage the protesters: meet the student union, assure them of a fair and time-bound process, and ask them to protest peacefully; call the police only if law and order is threatened.
  • Care for the two students: inform their parents directly, respect their dignity and offer counselling.
  • Prevent recurrence: CCTV in examination halls, rotation of invigilators and an honour code.

Why this option: it upholds integrity and equal rules for all. A cover-up cannot be universalised (Kant), and in practice it would not even work, since the squad has recorded the case and students are already protesting. In the long run, an honest response protects the college's reputation better than secrecy. A promotion won through a cover-up would leave me indebted to vested interests, while the head of a college must model the honesty it teaches.

Educational institutions shape the character of future citizens. By refusing to trade fairness for promotion and handling the crisis with firmness and compassion, I can turn a scandal into a lesson in academic integrity.

As project manager, I have found a crack in a pier, possibly caused by poor material, and judge that at least three piers must be rebuilt, delaying the project by four to six months. The chief engineer orders me to ignore it to meet the Chief Minister's pre-election inauguration, mentions that the contractor is the minister's relative, and hints at my promotion. The case pits public safety and professional integrity against a political deadline and career interest.

1. Stakeholders

  • Future commuters and residents near the corridor; the State government, the minister and the Chief Minister; the chief engineer; the contractor; the inspecting team; taxpayers; the engineering profession; and myself.

2. (a) Options available

3. (b) Ethical dilemmas

  • Public safety versus political deadline: lives of future users against the inauguration date.
  • Professional judgement versus obedience: my duty as an engineer against hierarchical discipline.
  • Career versus integrity: the hinted promotion is an inducement to stay silent.
  • Public interest versus nepotism: the contractor's link to the minister creates a conflict of interest.
  • Uncertainty: the crack may truly be minor, but when lives are at stake the precautionary principle requires proof of safety, not proof of danger.

4. (c) Professional challenges and my response

  • Pressure and possible victimisation: I will put the inspecting team's findings and my assessment in writing and ask for written orders, since oral instructions should be recorded (T.S.R. Subramanian v UoI, 2013).
  • Technical disagreement with a superior: I will propose independent third-party tests (non-destructive testing, load tests and a structural audit by an IIT or NIT), so that the decision rests on evidence, not rank.
  • Delay and cost: I will keep the affected piers on hold, continue work on the unaffected spans, add shifts and use precast elements to cut the delay; recover the cost of rebuilding from the contractor under the contract's quality and defect clauses; and give the government a realistic revised date.
  • Contractor's influence: I will not certify defective work or release payment for it; if pressure continues, I will inform the Secretary and, as a last resort, the vigilance authorities.
  • Isolation: I will work closely with the inspecting team and the quality-control wing, so that the stand is institutional, not personal.

5. (d) Consequences of overlooking the observation

  • Loss of life: a weakened pier may fail under traffic loads; the collapse of an under-construction flyover in Varanasi (May 2018) killed 18 people, and the Morbi suspension-bridge collapse (October 2022) killed 135.
  • Legal liability: everyone who knowingly ignored the defect, including me, could face prosecution for causing death by negligence (Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) and departmental action.
  • Financial loss: repairing or rebuilding a finished corridor costs far more than fixing it now, besides compensation and litigation.
  • Loss of trust: in public works, in the government and in the engineering profession; contractors learn that poor work goes unpunished.

Safety is non-negotiable. A corridor inaugurated on time but unsafe would be a monument to failure; by insisting on evidence, offering solutions and resisting pressure with integrity, the project manager serves both the public and, in the end, the government itself.
free.upm-2021-gs4-10:
Duty of careDistributive justiceReciprocityTriage

During the COVID-19 surge, a hospital administrator has to send doctors, nurses and support staff into a highly infectious environment with too few beds, oxygen cylinders and protective kits. The case sets the duty of care owed to patients against the duty to protect staff, and asks how scarce resources and risks can be shared justly.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: patients and their families; clinical and non-clinical staff and their families; the hospital and the government; and the wider community.
  • Issues: duty to treat versus the right to safety; fair distribution of risk among staff; triage of scarce beds and oxygen; non-discrimination between rich and poor patients; honesty with staff and the public; and burnout among exhausted staff.

2. (a) Criteria and justification for deploying staff

  • Duty of care: health workers accept some risk as part of their calling; abandoning patients in an epidemic would violate their professional ethic and the public's trust in a public hospital.
  • Proportionality and reciprocity: the duty is not unlimited. The hospital must reduce risk and support staff: the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Package insurance scheme (2020) gave health workers fighting COVID-19 a cover of ₹50 lakh, and the Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Act, 2020 made violence against health-care workers a cognisable, non-bailable offence.
  • Fairness and transparency: duty rosters must be open and free from favouritism, with exemptions only on medical grounds.
  • Patients: beds and oxygen go by clinical need under transparent triage protocols, not by status or wealth; referrals and tele-consultation reduce overload.
  • Morale: daily briefings, mental-health support and public recognition sustain staff through long surges.

3. (b) If it were a private hospital

  • The core ethics stay the same: the duty of care, triage on clinical need and protection of staff do not depend on ownership. In Parmanand Katara v UoI (1989), the Supreme Court held that every doctor, in government or private service, must give emergency medical aid to preserve life.
  • What differs: a private hospital also owes duties to its owners, must stay solvent, and may rely on contractual staff; it does not carry the same public mandate to admit everyone.
  • But profit has limits in an emergency: under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, governments could requisition private beds and regulate charges, and several States capped COVID-19 treatment rates. Overcharging or turning away critical patients would be unethical and often unlawful.
  • My decision: the criteria for deploying staff would remain the same. In addition, I would ensure transparent billing, reserve beds for poor patients under government schemes such as PM-JAY, and never use staff shortages as an excuse to refuse emergency care. A private hospital's greater resources strengthen, rather than weaken, its duty to protect its staff.

Ownership changes the balance sheet, not the ethics. In an epidemic, both public and private hospitals must combine the duty of care with justice to patients and staff, because health workers protected today are the ones who save lives tomorrow.

Consumer safetyDouble standardsCorporate accountabilityFood Safety and Standards Act

A reputed company sold a product in India that did not match its approval and passed off rejected export consignments to domestic consumers, while claiming "almost the same quality". This violates the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, consumer rights and basic business ethics; the crisis is now one of law, health and trust.

1. Stakeholders

  • Domestic consumers, especially children and the sick; the company's owners, employees and suppliers; the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and State food safety officials; foreign buyers; and investors.

2. (a) Action by the competent authority

  • Protect consumers first: stop sales and ensure a recall (Section 28 of the FSS Act and the Food Recall Procedure Regulations, 2017); seek an emergency prohibition order (Section 34) if there is a risk to health.
  • Investigate: test all batches in accredited laboratories, trace every rejected export lot, and check whether the approval was obtained or used by misrepresentation.
  • Act on the licence: issue an improvement notice and, if the company fails to comply, suspend and then cancel its licence (Section 32).
  • Penalise and prosecute: adjudicate penalties for sub-standard and misbranded food (Sections 51 and 52); prosecute under Section 59 if the food is found unsafe; hold the officers in charge personally liable (Section 66, offences by companies). The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2026 decriminalised some minor FSS offences from 1 October 2026 but kept stringent provisions for offences that endanger health.
  • Consumer protection: the Central Consumer Protection Authority can order recall and refunds and penalise the misleading claim of "almost same quality" under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
  • Proportionality and transparency: publish the findings and target those responsible, not innocent workers and suppliers.

3. (b) Course of action for the company

  • Own up: admit the lapse publicly, apologise, recall the product voluntarily and refund consumers; cooperate fully with the regulator.
  • Fix responsibility: an independent inquiry and action against those who ordered the sale of rejected goods, with protection for employees who report wrongdoing.
  • One standard for all markets: the same specification for domestic and export products; rejected lots destroyed or reprocessed under supervision.
  • Rebuild systems: third-party audits, ISO 22000 certification, batch traceability and published test results.
  • Rebuild trust: steady, honest communication. Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol recall (1982) shows that putting consumers first can restore a brand, and Nestlé India withdrew Maggi noodles when FSSAI ordered a ban in June 2015, relaunching them in November after the Bombay High Court set the ban aside and ordered fresh laboratory tests.

4. (c) The ethical dilemmas involved

  • Profit versus consumer health: selling rejected stock saves money but endangers health.
  • Equal dignity of consumers: a double standard treats domestic buyers merely as a means of disposing of rejects, which Kant's ethics forbids.
  • Honesty versus reputation: the temptation to deny or conceal against full disclosure, which may hurt sales in the short term.
  • Shareholders versus stakeholders: duty to investors against duty to consumers and society.
  • The regulator's dilemma: strict deterrence against the jobs of workers and farmers who depend on the company; the answer is proportionate penalties on the culprits, not leniency.

Profits built on double standards are short-lived. Strict, fair enforcement and genuine corporate repentance can restore what matters most in the food business: consumer trust.

2. (b) Approach for peace in office and home

  • Self-regulation: recognise that the boss's behaviour largely reflects his own stress and does not measure Pawan's worth; practise yoga, exercise and mindfulness, in the spirit of the Gita's samatva (equanimity).

  • For Pawan: stay professional and assertive, rely on a support network, and seek professional help early.
  • For both: mediation by a respected senior officer, regular one-to-one meetings with clear expectations, and 360-degree feedback that prompts self-correction.

free.upm-2022-gs1-1:
Temple sculptureMedieval societyVisual social historyPerforming arts

Between the 8th and 16th centuries the temple was the hub of religious, economic and cultural life, and its walls were the largest canvas of the age. Built under the Chandelas, Eastern Gangas, Cholas, Hoysalas, Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara rulers, temples show gods and myths, but also kings, soldiers, dancers, merchants, couples and labourers. Read with inscriptions and travellers' accounts, these temple sculptures form a visual social history of medieval India.

1. Daily life, work and material culture

  • Occupations: friezes show herding, ploughing, carrying loads and craftsmen at work; the walls of the Sun temple at Konark (13th century) depict hunting, military processions and domestic life.
  • Dress and ornaments: the bracket figures (madanikas) of the Hoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu wear elaborate jewellery, girdles and hairstyles, a detailed record of contemporary fashion.
  • Trade and contact: the outer walls of the Hazara Rama temple at Hampi (Vijayanagara) show processions of horses, elephants and soldiers, and the nearby royal platform (Mahanavami Dibba) shows foreigners, probably Arabs or Persians, leading horses, a sign of the horse trade.

2. Women, family and leisure

  • Women's world: the surasundaris of Khajuraho (Chandela, c. 950–1050 CE) are shown applying kohl, looking into a mirror, writing a letter or removing a thorn from the foot.
  • Family and love: mother-and-child images and mithuna (loving couple) figures celebrate household life; the erotic panels reflect Tantric ideas and the belief that such images were auspicious.
  • Festivals: the dancing women and processions on the walls of the Hazara Rama temple recall the Mahanavami (Dasara) festival, which the Portuguese visitor Domingo Paes described.

3. Music, dance and the performing arts

  • Dance as worship: the gopurams of the Nataraja temple at Chidambaram carry the 108 karanas (dance poses) described in Bharata's Natyashastra.
  • Living traditions: dancing figures at the Kakatiya Ramappa temple (1213 CE, UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2021) helped Nataraja Ramakrishna revive the Perini dance in modern times.
  • Musicians: life-size female drummers and cymbal players stand on the roof of Konark's jagamohana (assembly hall).

4. Polity, war and religion

  • Kingship and war: the base friezes of Halebidu carry rows of elephants and horsemen, and other panels show kings and armies on the march.
  • Hero stones: virakals and sati stones, often set up near temples, honour warriors who died defending cattle or villages and record the practice of sati.
  • Devotion: the Chola temple at Darasuram narrates the lives of the Nayanar saints, showing the spread of Bhakti across social groups.

5. Limits of the evidence

  • Idealised images: sculpture shows courts, elites and the divine far more than peasants, labourers or the lower castes.
  • Canonical forms: many figures follow the shilpa shastras, so they must be read with inscriptions and literature.

Medieval temple sculptures are thus "history in stone": they show a hierarchical but vibrant society that worked, worshipped, fought and celebrated, and they remain a key source of social history alongside texts.
free.upm-2022-gs1-2:
Military disciplineAssured revenueDisunity of Indian powersSubsidiary alliance

From Plassey (1757) to the annexation of Punjab (1849), the English East India Company defeated nearly every major Indian power. Its armies were mostly Indian sepoys and often much smaller: at Plassey, Robert Clive had about 3,000 men against Siraj-ud-Daulah's 50,000. Victory came less from weapons than from organisation, finance and diplomacy: the Company fought as a disciplined, well-funded state against divided rulers.

1. Superior military organisation

  • Drill and discipline: sepoys were trained in European infantry drill, volley fire and formations such as the square, which could hold off the cavalry charges on which Indian armies relied.
  • Regular pay: the Company paid its standing army regularly in cash; many Indian armies, paid irregularly through chiefs, suffered desertions.
  • Unified command: a professional officer corps gave a clear chain of command; Indian armies were coalitions of contingents loyal to their own chiefs, which broke up when a leader fell.
  • Use of artillery: Indian rulers often had good guns, such as Tipu Sultan's rockets and the Sikh artillery, but rarely combined them with drilled infantry as the Company did.

2. Leadership, intelligence and diplomacy

  • Able leaders: commanders such as Clive, Eyre Coote and Arthur Wellesley chose the time and place of battle.
  • Divide and rule: the Company allied with the Nizam and the Marathas against Tipu in the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92), and used the Peshwa's weakness to sign the Treaty of Bassein (1802).
  • Subsidiary alliance (1798): Lord Wellesley made rulers such as the Nizam pay for Company troops stationed in their States and disband their own forces, so Indian money financed the Company's army and disarmed its rivals.

3. Financial and naval strength

  • Assured revenue: after the Diwani of Bengal (1765), the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa paid for a large standing army; bankers such as the Jagat Seths backed the Company in 1757.
  • Sea power: command of the sea moved troops and supplies between the Presidencies and from Britain; no Indian power had a comparable navy.
  • Staying power: the Company lost battles, as at Pollilur (1780), but could keep fighting; for an Indian ruler one defeat was often fatal.

4. Weaknesses of Indian rulers

  • Disunity: there was no common Indian cause; the Marathas, Mysore, Hyderabad and the Sikhs fought one another, and Panipat (1761) had already weakened the Marathas.
  • Treachery and intrigue: Mir Jafar's troops stood aside at Plassey, and the Sikh commanders Lal Singh and Tej Singh are widely held to have betrayed their army in 1845–46.
  • Personalised reforms: Mahadji Scindia (with de Boigne) and Ranjit Singh modernised their armies, but the reforms decayed after them.

The Company's success was therefore organisational and political more than technological: a disciplined, regularly paid army, assured revenue, sea power and diplomacy overcame larger but divided forces. The same sepoys rose in 1857 when that bond of trust broke.
free.upm-2022-gs1-3:
Colonial faminesLand revenueCommercialisation of agricultureEntitlement failure

Droughts were not new to India, but from the Bengal famine of 1770, five years after the Company acquired the Diwani, famines became more frequent and far deadlier. The Great Famine of 1876–78 killed over five million people, and the Bengal famine of 1943 an estimated two to three million. Failed monsoons were the trigger; colonial economic policy turned scarcity into famine, what Amartya Sen calls an entitlement failure.

1. Heavy land revenue and indebtedness

  • High, rigid cash demand: the Permanent Settlement (1793) and the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems fixed revenue in cash at high rates and collected it even in bad seasons.
  • Forced sales and debt: to pay the revenue, peasants sold grain cheaply at harvest and borrowed from moneylenders, so they had no reserves when the rains failed, and many lost their land.

2. Commercialisation and export of food

  • Cash crops: indigo, opium, cotton and jute expanded to meet British and world demand, sometimes at the cost of food crops and village grain stores.
  • Railways and markets: grain moved quickly to ports and towns, and prices in famine areas rose beyond the reach of labourers.
  • Exports continued: grain was exported even during famines, as in 1876–78, under a rigid belief in free trade.

3. Deindustrialisation and loss of purchasing power

  • Ruin of crafts: the decline of handicrafts pushed artisans onto the land and created a mass of landless labourers with no savings.
  • Jobs vanish first: when crops failed, farm work disappeared, so labourers and artisans starved even where food was available.

4. Neglect of irrigation and relief

  • Little investment: the government spent far more on railways than on irrigation; old tanks decayed, and large canal works were confined to a few regions such as Punjab, the Ganga–Yamuna doab and the Godavari–Krishna deltas.
  • Laissez-faire relief: Lytton's government held the Delhi Durbar (1877) in the middle of the Great Famine, and Sir Richard Temple's relief camps gave rations below subsistence.
  • Late reform: the Strachey Commission (1880) led to the Famine Codes (1883); the Lyall (1898) and MacDonnell (1901) Commissions followed the famines of 1896–97 and 1899–1900.

5. Natural and wartime triggers

  • El Niño droughts: severe monsoon failures in 1876–78 and 1896–1900 became disasters because of the weaknesses above.
  • 1943: wartime inflation, the loss of rice imports after Japan occupied Burma (1942), the "denial policy" in coastal Bengal, the cyclone of October 1942, hoarding and a slow official response caused mass deaths, although food availability had not fallen sharply.

Colonial famines thus arose from colonial political economy: drought was the trigger, not the cause. Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt linked them to the drain of wealth and over-assessment of land. After independence, buffer stocks, the public distribution system and a free press have prevented famine, as Sen argued.
free.upm-2022-gs1-4:
Igneous rocksMagma and lavaIntrusive and extrusiveRock cycle

Igneous rocks (from the Latin ignis, fire) are called primary rocks because they were the first rocks to form as the molten Earth cooled, and all other rocks are ultimately derived from them. They form when magma (molten rock below the surface) or lava (molten rock on the surface) cools and solidifies. Granite and basalt are the commonest examples; together with the metamorphic rocks derived from them, igneous rocks make up most of the Earth's crust.

1. Characteristics

  • Crystalline and hard: made of interlocking crystals of silicate minerals such as quartz, feldspar, mica, pyroxene and olivine; they are compact and resist erosion.
  • No layers or fossils: formed from a melt, they lack the strata (bedding) of sedimentary rocks, and the heat of the magma leaves no fossils.
  • Texture shows the rate of cooling: slow cooling deep in the crust gives large crystals (coarse-grained granite); quick cooling at the surface gives fine grains (basalt) or glass (obsidian); escaping gases leave holes (pumice, vesicular basalt).
  • Mostly impermeable but jointed: water moves only along joints and cracks, and weathering along joints produces tors, exfoliation domes and boulder landscapes such as Hampi.
  • Economic value: they give building stone (granite) and road metal (basalt), many metallic ores are associated with them, and their weathering forms black soil (from basalt) and red soil (from granite and gneiss).

2. Types by mode of formation

  • Intrusive or plutonic: magma cools slowly deep below the surface, forming coarse-grained granite, gabbro and diorite, later exposed by erosion.
  • Hypabyssal: magma cools at shallow depth in cracks, as dykes (vertical) and sills (horizontal), forming medium-grained rocks such as dolerite.
  • Extrusive or volcanic: lava cools quickly on the surface, forming fine-grained basalt, andesite and rhyolite, glassy obsidian, and tuff and volcanic breccia from ash and fragments.
  • Intrusive landforms: batholiths, laccoliths, lopoliths, phacoliths, sills and dykes.

3. Types by chemical composition

  • Acid (felsic): rich in silica and light minerals; light-coloured and less dense, such as granite and rhyolite; acid lava is viscous and builds steep cones.
  • Intermediate: between the two, such as diorite and andesite.
  • Basic (mafic): poor in silica and rich in iron and magnesium; dark and heavy, such as basalt and gabbro; fluid basic lava spreads widely to form plateaus such as the Deccan Traps.
  • Ultrabasic: very low in silica, such as peridotite of the upper mantle.

4. Indian examples

  • Peninsular plateau: ancient granites and granite-gneisses of the Archaean shield, as in Bundelkhand and Karnataka, cut by dolerite dykes.
  • Volcanic rocks: the basalts of the Deccan Traps, and Barren Island in the Andaman Sea, India's only active volcano.

As the parent rocks of the rock cycle, igneous rocks shape relief, soils and mineral wealth, from the black soils of the Deccan to granite building stone, which is why they are rightly called primary rocks.
free.upm-2022-gs1-5:
Colour-coded warningsFour-stage warningImpact-based forecastingCyclone preparedness

The India Meteorological Department (IMD), the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for tropical cyclones over the North Indian Ocean, issues cyclone warnings through a four-stage warning system. Since the 2006 post-monsoon season, at the request of disaster-management authorities, the later stages carry yellow, orange and red colour codes. The colours tell officials and the public at a glance how near the threat is and how urgently they must prepare.

1. The four stages and their colours

  • Pre-cyclone watch (no colour): issued 72 hours in advance by the Director General of Meteorology himself and addressed to the Cabinet Secretary and other senior officials, about a developing system and the coastal belt likely to be affected.
  • Cyclone alert (yellow): at least 48 hours before adverse weather reaches the coast; gives the storm's position, intensity and likely track, the districts at risk and advice for fishermen.
  • Cyclone warning (orange): at least 24 hours ahead, when the landfall point can be forecast; gives the landfall point and time and the expected heavy rain, gale winds and storm surge, updated every three hours.
  • Post-landfall outlook (red): at least 12 hours before landfall; forecasts the cyclone's path and the adverse weather inland after landfall.

2. IMD's general colour legend for district-wise, impact-based warnings

  • Green (no warning): no action needed.
  • Yellow (watch): be updated; the weather may turn severe.
  • Orange (alert): be prepared; severe weather is likely, with disruption of transport and power.
  • Red (warning): take action; extremely severe weather is expected, and authorities may order evacuation and stop fishing, travel and schooling.
  • Impact-based: the colour depends on both the likelihood of the event and its expected impact on people and property, not on wind speed alone.

3. What the colours mean for cyclone-prone areas

  • Administration: they trigger graded steps under State and district plans: pre-positioning of NDRF and SDRF teams, opening cyclone shelters, stocking food and medicines, and evacuating low-lying and kutcha-house areas.
  • Fishermen and ports: fishermen are told to return and not to venture out; ports hoist their own storm signals.
  • Public communication: alerts reach people through the media, sirens and SACHET (Common Alerting Protocol) SMS messages in local languages.
  • Severity: warnings are read with IMD's intensity scale.

4. Significance and gaps

  • Lives saved: the 1999 Odisha super cyclone killed about 10,000 people; Phailin (2013) and Fani (2019) killed far fewer, thanks to accurate warnings and mass evacuation.
  • Gaps: one colour for a large district may hide local differences in risk; the last mile to fishermen, migrants and the poor is uneven; frequent alerts can cause "warning fatigue". Mission Mausam (2024, ₹2,000 crore) aims at finer forecasts.

Colour codes turn scientific forecasts into actionable messages. Combined with community preparedness and the zero-casualty approach of coastal States such as Odisha, they have made cyclones far less deadly.
free.upm-2022-gs1-6:
Deccan TrapsFlood basaltRegur soilHard-rock aquifers

The Deccan Traps are among the world's largest flood basalt provinces. About 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous, fissure eruptions linked to the Réunion hotspot spread lava, layer upon layer, over west-central India ("trap" means steps, after the step-like hills). They still cover about 5 lakh sq km, mostly in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, and are over 2 km thick near the west coast.

1. Soil and agriculture

  • Regur (black cotton soil): formed by the weathering of basalt; clayey and rich in lime, iron, magnesia and potash, but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter (NCERT).
  • Moisture retention: it holds water for long and develops deep cracks in summer ("self-ploughing"), allowing rain-fed farming in a semi-arid climate.
  • Crops: cotton (Vidarbha, Saurashtra), soybean (Malwa), sugarcane, jowar and pulses, onion and grapes (Nashik) and oranges (Nagpur).
  • Industry: the cotton belt fed the textile mills of Mumbai and Ahmedabad and supports sugar and agro-processing units.

2. Minerals and stone

  • Bauxite and laterite: heavy rain on flat basalt tops leached the rock into laterite capped with bauxite, as in Kolhapur (Maharashtra), Jamnagar and Kutch (Gujarat) and the Amarkantak plateau (Madhya Pradesh).
  • Building stone: hard, durable basalt is quarried for roads, dams, railway ballast and buildings.
  • Semi-precious stones and zeolites: gas cavities in the lava are filled with agate, chalcedony, amethyst and zeolites; agates from the Rajpipla hills long supplied the bead industry of Khambhat (Cambay).
  • Limitation: the basalts are poor in metallic minerals compared with the older rocks of Chotanagpur and the Dharwar belts.

3. Water and energy

  • Groundwater: water is stored only in weathered, fractured and vesicular basalt, so these hard-rock aquifers yield little and wells fail in summer, especially in rain-shadow Marathwada.
  • Rivers and hydropower: the Godavari, Bhima and Krishna rise in the trap country of the Western Ghats, and the steep western scarp supports hydropower such as the Koyna project.
  • Wind and solar: exposed plateau ridges, as at Chalkewadi near Satara, carry wind farms, and the sunny plateaus suit solar parks.

4. Heritage, biodiversity and tourism

  • Rock-cut heritage: the caves of Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta were carved into Deccan basalt.
  • Geoheritage: Lonar Lake (Buldhana), a crater formed by a meteorite impact in basalt, is a Ramsar site (2020); the Kaas plateau near Satara is famed for its seasonal wildflowers.
  • Hill stations and forts: Mahabaleshwar, Matheran and the Sahyadri hill forts stand on flat-topped trap mesas.

5. Constraints

  • Thin soils and gully erosion on slopes, drought, scarce groundwater and sticky regur that is hard to till when wet limit the potential; the Koyna earthquake (1967) showed that large reservoirs can trigger quakes here.

The Deccan Trap's wealth lies in soil, stone and water rather than metals. Watershed development, micro-irrigation, soil-health management and geoheritage conservation can turn this potential into lasting prosperity.
free.upm-2022-gs1-7:
Wind potentialSpatial concentrationGrid integrationOffshore wind

Wind power varies with the cube of wind speed, so it pays only where winds are strong and steady. The National Institute of Wind Energy puts India's onshore potential at 1,163.9 GW at 150 m above ground (695.5 GW at 120 m). Yet installed capacity was only 59.2 GW on 30 September 2026 (MNRE), about 5% of the potential, and half of it lies in two States, although India ranks fourth in the world.

1. Potential

  • Onshore: the best resources lie in eight windy States of the west and south: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; Andhra Pradesh alone has 123.3 GW at 150 m.
  • Taller turbines: higher hubs and longer blades make moderate-wind sites viable, which is why the estimate rises sharply at 150 m.
  • Offshore: India notified a National Offshore Wind Energy Policy in 2015 and targets 30 GW by 2030; in June 2024 the Cabinet approved ₹7,453 crore of viability gap funding for the first 1 GW off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.
  • Complement to solar: wind blows strongly in the monsoon and at night, so hybrids smooth supply; the target is 100 GW of wind by 2030.

2. Present spread

  • Concentration: Gujarat (17.0 GW) and Tamil Nadu (12.3 GW) had about half of all capacity in September 2026; most of the rest is in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.
  • Large gaps: the Indo-Gangetic plains, eastern India and the North-East have almost none.

3. Reasons for the limited spatial spread

  • Physical geography: strong, steady winds occur where the monsoon is funnelled through gaps such as the Palghat gap and the Aralvaimozhi pass (Muppandal, Kanyakumari), along the Gujarat coast and over the Thar; the plains and the east have weak, variable winds.
  • Seasonality: most generation comes in the south-west monsoon months, so turbines run well below capacity for much of the year.
  • Land and ecology: turbines and access roads need large tracts; conflicts arise over common lands and orans (sacred groves) in Rajasthan, and over the habitat of the Great Indian Bustard, where the Supreme Court restricted overhead lines (2021) before revising its approach in M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024).
  • Transmission: windy sites are far from big cities; evacuation lines lag behind projects despite the Green Energy Corridors, and financially weak distribution companies delay payments or curtail wind power.
  • Auction economics: competitive bidding since 2017 rewards the windiest sites, so projects cluster, while old, low-height turbines still occupy many of the best sites.
  • Offshore costs: special vessels, port upgrades and higher tariffs have delayed offshore projects.

India's wind potential is large but geographically concentrated. Repowering, hybrids with storage, taller turbines that open up moderate-wind regions, offshore wind and stronger transmission can widen its spread and help reach the 500 GW non-fossil target by 2030.
free.upm-2022-gs1-8:
Work from homeWork–life boundaryGendered care burdenHybrid work

Work From Home (WFH) became widespread during the COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020, when offices shut and IT, finance, education and many government services moved online. Many firms have since settled on hybrid work. Because the home became the office, WFH has reshaped time, space and roles within the family, strengthening some bonds and straining others; its effect depends on gender, class and the type of family.

1. Positive effects

  • More family time: hours once lost in commuting go to children, shared meals and household decisions, and fathers are more involved in childcare.
  • Care for the elderly and sick: working children can look after ageing parents, a growing need as the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 10.5% (2022) to 20.8% by 2050 (India Ageing Report 2023).
  • Return to roots: many professionals moved back to hometowns and joint households during the pandemic, renewing ties with kin.
  • Work for women: flexible work helps some educated women, especially new mothers, stay in paid jobs; the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 allows work from home after maternity leave where the work permits.

2. Negative effects

  • Blurred boundaries: an "always on" culture, long online meetings and work at odd hours spill into family time, causing irritability and conflict.
  • Double burden on women: women already spend about 289 minutes a day on unpaid domestic work against 88 minutes for men (Time Use Survey 2024); WFH adds office work to care work, the "second shift" described by Arlie Hochschild.
  • Space and privacy: in small urban homes, parents' meetings and children's online classes compete for room, data and quiet.
  • Stress and violence: isolation and anxiety rose during the lockdowns, and the National Commission for Women reported a rise in domestic-violence complaints in 2020.

3. Evaluation

  • Class-limited: WFH is open mainly to salaried, white-collar workers; about 90% of India's workforce is informal and cannot work from home, so its effects are confined largely to the urban middle class.
  • Gender decides the outcome: where men share chores, relations improve; where they do not, WFH reinforces patriarchal roles.
  • Family form matters: nuclear families with young children face the most stress, while joint families share care but offer less privacy.
  • Hybrid work appears to balance closeness and boundaries better than full-time WFH.

4. Way forward

  • Boundaries: fixed working hours and a "right to disconnect", as in France (2017); a private member's Right to Disconnect Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in 2018.
  • Support: equal sharing of housework, workplace counselling, crèches and flexible hybrid policies.

WFH is a double-edged sword: it has brought families physically closer but not always emotionally closer. With gender-equal sharing of care and firm work–life boundaries, it can strengthen rather than strain family life.
free.upm-2022-gs1-9:
Tier-2 citiesNew middle classCulture of consumptionAspirational India

Tier-2 cities such as Indore, Surat, Coimbatore, Jaipur, Lucknow, Kochi and Bhubaneswar are among India's fastest-changing urban centres. Their growth since liberalisation, and especially since the digital spread of the 2010s, has produced a new middle class defined less by occupation or education than by lifestyle and consumption. The PRICE ICE 360° survey counted about 43 crore middle-class Indians in 2021 (household income ₹5–30 lakh a year), nearly a third of the population.

1. Why Tier-2 cities are growing

  • Spillover from metros: cheaper land, rents and wages attract IT and back-office firms, warehousing and manufacturing, as in Surat's diamond and textile trades and Coimbatore's engineering units.
  • Infrastructure and policy: the Smart Cities Mission (2015–2025), AMRUT, UDAN regional air connectivity (2016), expressways and industrial corridors.
  • Digital economy: cheap mobile data and UPI let small-town firms reach national markets; nearly half of the over 2.2 lakh DPIIT-recognised startups come from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities (DPIIT, April 2026).
  • Education and health services: coaching hubs, private colleges and hospitals draw students and patients from surrounding districts.

2. How growth creates a new middle class

  • New occupations: private-sector salaried jobs, professionals, traders, franchise owners and platform workers replace the old base of government employment.
  • Higher household incomes: dual-earner families and professionals who returned home during and after the pandemic bring metro-level incomes to smaller cities.
  • Easy credit: EMIs, credit cards and "buy now, pay later" extend purchasing power beyond current incomes.
  • Rising numbers: the same survey projects about 102 crore middle-class Indians by 2047.

3. The culture of consumption

  • Malls and brands: malls, multiplexes, branded showrooms and food chains have spread to Tier-2 cities, often through franchising.
  • E-commerce and quick commerce: online platforms give small-town buyers the same choices as metro shoppers.
  • Consumption as status: cars, smartphones, branded clothes, lavish weddings and holidays signal social mobility, what Thorstein Veblen called "conspicuous consumption" and Pierre Bourdieu "distinction".
  • Media and aspiration: television, social media and influencers spread metropolitan and global lifestyles, blended with local festivals and tastes ("glocalisation").

4. Concerns

  • Debt and insecurity: credit-driven consumption raises household debt and vulnerability to job loss.
  • Inequality: informal workers and slum dwellers are left out, and rising land prices push the poor to the periphery.
  • Environment: more vehicles, waste, water use and sprawl strain weak urban services.
  • Cultural homogenisation: local markets and crafts lose ground to chains and global brands.

The relationship is two-way: Tier-2 growth creates the new middle class, and its consumption fuels further urban growth. Planned urbanisation, financial literacy and sustainable consumption in the spirit of Mission LiFE can make this aspiration inclusive and lasting.
free.upm-2022-gs1-10:
Scheduled TribesTribal diversityArticle 342Constitutional safeguards

Census 2011 counted 705 ethnic groups notified as Scheduled Tribes under Article 342, numbering about 10.4 crore, or 8.6% of the population. They differ widely in language, region, religion, economy and level of development, from large communities such as the Bhils and Gonds to the 75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs). Yet in certain contexts the Constitution and public policy rightly treat them as one category.

1. Diversity among tribes

  • Language: speakers of Austro-Asiatic (Santhal, Munda, Ho), Dravidian (Gond, Oraon), Tibeto-Burman (Naga, Mizo, Bodo) and Indo-Aryan (Bhil) languages, besides the distinct Andamanese languages.
  • Economy: hunter-gatherers (Jarawa, Chenchu), shifting cultivators (jhum in the North-East), settled farmers (Santhal, Meena), pastoralists (Toda, Gaddi) and urban professionals.
  • Society and religion: matrilineal Khasi and Garo beside patrilineal Gonds; followers of Sarna and other indigenous faiths, Hinduism and Christianity.
  • Region and status: Sixth Schedule tribes of the North-East have autonomy, central Indian tribes live in Fifth Schedule areas, and small island groups face extinction; development levels vary sharply.

2. Contexts for treating them as a single category

  • Constitutional identity and representation: notification under Article 342, guided by the Lokur Committee's criteria (primitive traits, distinct culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact and backwardness), reservation in education and jobs (Articles 15(4), 16(4)), reserved seats in the Lok Sabha, Assemblies and local bodies (Articles 330, 332, 243D, 243T) and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A, 89th Amendment, 2003).
  • Protection from exploitation: STs share the experience of land alienation, displacement and discrimination; hence the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, land-transfer laws in Fifth Schedule areas and the Samatha judgment (1997).
  • Rights over land, forests and self-rule: PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006) give gram sabhas and forest dwellers common rights regardless of tribe.
  • Development finance and data: the Development Action Plan for STs, grants under Article 275(1), Eklavya schools and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024, ₹79,156 crore, about 63,000 villages) need one target group, and ST data (literacy 59% against 73% nationally, Census 2011) measure the overall gap.
  • Recognition and collective voice: Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 November, from 2021) honours tribal heroes, and a shared identity strengthens bargaining power.

3. Contexts that need differentiation

  • Vulnerable groups: PVTGs need special schemes such as PM-JANMAN (2023).
  • Governance and culture: Sixth Schedule councils, Article 371A (Nagaland), customary laws and education in tribal mother tongues.
  • Unequal benefits: better-off communities can capture a large share of benefits, so data must be disaggregated by community.

Tribes should be one category for rights, protection and political voice, but many categories in development design: unity of entitlement with diversity of approach, in the spirit of Nehru's Tribal Panchsheel.
free.upm-2022-gs1-11:
Reorganisation of StatesArticle 3Linguistic StatesAdministrative efficiency

India's internal map has never been fixed. From Dalhousie's annexations (1848–56) to Telangana (2014) and the division of Jammu and Kashmir (2019), provinces, princely States and Union Territories have been redrawn for conquest, administrative convenience, language, ethnicity and development. Since 1950, Article 3 lets Parliament form new States or alter boundaries by ordinary law. As of 2026, India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories.

1. Colonial phase: conquest and administrative convenience

  • Annexation: the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara 1848, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854) and the annexation of Punjab (1849) and Awadh (1856) enlarged British India.
  • Administrative units: the Central Provinces were formed in 1861, and Assam became a separate Chief Commissioner's province in 1874.
  • Political motives: Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905) was annulled in 1911, and Bihar and Orissa became a separate province in 1912.
  • Language enters: Orissa (1936) was the first province formed on a linguistic basis; Sind was separated from Bombay (1936) and Burma from India (1937).

2. Integration and linguistic States (1947–56)

  • Integration: over 550 princely States were integrated by Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon, producing the Part A, B, C and D States of 1950.
  • Caution and agitation: the Dar Commission and the JVP Committee (1948–49) advised against linguistic States, but Potti Sriramulu's death after a 58-day fast led to Andhra State (1 October 1953).
  • States Reorganisation Act, 1956: on the Fazl Ali Commission's report, India was reorganised into 14 States and 6 Union Territories.

3. After 1956: language, ethnicity, development and security

  • Language: Bombay was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960), and Punjab was reorganised to create Haryana (1966).
  • Ethnic and tribal identity: Nagaland (1963); Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura (1972); Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (1987).
  • Development and regional imbalance: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand (2000), and Telangana (2014).
  • Security and integration: in 2019 Jammu and Kashmir was split into the UTs of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The Supreme Court upheld the abrogation of Article 370 (December 2023) and asked for statehood to be restored "at the earliest"; statehood had not been restored as of October 2026, and the Assembly passed a resolution seeking it in September 2026.
  • Administrative merger: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu became one UT (2020).

4. Reorganisation within States

  • New districts: Telangana grew from 10 to 33 districts; States keep creating districts and municipal bodies to bring administration closer to people.
  • Autonomous arrangements: Sixth Schedule councils such as the Bodoland Territorial Region (2020), and statutory bodies such as the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (2012) and Ladakh's hill councils.
  • Pending demands: Vidarbha, Gorkhaland, and statehood with Sixth Schedule safeguards for Ladakh.

Reorganisation is thus a continuous process that has moved from imperial convenience to democratic aspiration; India is rightly called an "indestructible Union of destructible States". New demands should be judged by objective tests of viability and consent, perhaps through a second States Reorganisation Commission.
free.upm-2022-gs1-12:
Classical ageNagara and Dravida templesChola bronzesLocal self-government

The Gupta period (c. 320–550 CE) is often called the classical age of Indian culture: Sanskrit literature, mathematics and astronomy, Puranic Hinduism and the earliest structural temples took shape in the north. The imperial Cholas (c. 850–1279 CE) carried Dravida temple architecture, bronze sculpture, Tamil devotional literature and village self-government to their height in the south, and spread Indian culture across the seas.

1. Contributions of the Gupta period

  • Literature: Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta and Raghuvamsha; Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa; Amarasimha's Amarakosha; the Puranas took their present form, and Harisena's Prayag prashasti praised Samudragupta.
  • Science and mathematics: Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya (499 CE) used the place-value system, gave a close value of pi and explained eclipses and the Earth's rotation; Varahamihira wrote the Pancha Siddhantika and Brihat Samhita.
  • Temple architecture: the earliest structural temples, from the flat-roofed Temple 17 at Sanchi to the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh with an early shikhara and the brick temple at Bhitargaon, mark the birth of the Nagara style.
  • Sculpture and metal craft: the serene seated Buddha of Sarnath, the Varaha panel at Udayagiri, the copper Buddha of Sultanganj and the rust-resistant iron pillar at Mehrauli.
  • Religion, learning and coins: Bhagavata Vaishnavism and image worship spread; Nalanda was founded in the 5th century; gold coins show Samudragupta playing the veena.

2. Contributions of the Chola period

  • Temple architecture: the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (Rajaraja I, completed 1010 CE), Gangaikonda Cholapuram (Rajendra I) and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram (Rajaraja II) form UNESCO's "Great Living Chola Temples"; their towering vimanas made the temple the centre of the town's economic and social life.
  • Bronze sculpture: lost-wax bronzes, above all Nataraja, Shiva's cosmic dance of creation and destruction, remain a symbol of Indian art.
  • Local self-government: Parantaka I's Uttaramerur inscriptions (919 and 921 CE) describe how the village sabha chose members by lot (kudavolai) and worked through committees.
  • Literature and Bhakti: the Tamil Shaiva canon (Tirumurai) was compiled; Sekkizhar's Periya Puranam and Kamban's Ramayana belong to this age.
  • Maritime reach: Rajendra I's naval expedition against Srivijaya (1025 CE) and Tamil merchant guilds carried Indian culture to Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka.

3. Lasting legacy

  • Foundations and fusion: the Guptas set the classical canons of Indian art, literature and science; the Cholas perfected the temple as a centre of art, economy and community and blended Sanskrit and Tamil traditions.
  • Living heritage: Chola temples are still in worship, a Nataraja statue stands at CERN in Geneva, and India named its first satellite Aryabhata (1975).

The Guptas gave India its classical foundations in thought and form; the Cholas gave it its grandest temple-centred civilisation and carried it overseas. Together they show how political stability and patronage nourish lasting culture.
free.upm-2022-gs1-13:
Animal symbolismLion Capital of SarnathNandiState Emblem

Animals have carried meaning in Indian culture since the Harappan seals. The lion stands for sovereignty, courage and spiritual authority, and the bull for strength, fertility, patience and dharma. From the Ashokan Lion Capital of Sarnath, adopted as India's State Emblem, to the great Nandi facing Shiva's shrine, both figures run through mythology, art and architecture in the Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions.

1. In mythology and religion

  • Lion as power and protection: the lion is the mount (vahana) of Durga, who slays Mahishasura; Narasimha, Vishnu's man-lion avatar, protects the devotee Prahlada.
  • Lion as spiritual authority: the Buddha is called Shakyasimha (lion of the Shakyas) and his teaching the "lion's roar" (simhanada); the lion is the emblem of Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara.
  • Bull as devotion and dharma: Nandi is Shiva's mount and gatekeeper; in the Puranas, Dharma appears as a bull that stands on four legs in the Krita age and loses one in each later age.
  • Bull as strength and fertility: Rig Vedic hymns call Indra and Agni bulls (vrishabha); the bull is the emblem of Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara; farm festivals such as Pola and Mattu Pongal honour bullocks.

2. In art and sculpture

  • Harappan seals: the humped zebu bull and the one-horned "unicorn" are among the finest seal images from Mohenjo-daro.
  • Mauryan capitals: the Sarnath capital has four lions seated back to back above an abacus showing a lion, an elephant, a bull and a horse separated by wheels; the Rampurva capital (Bihar) shows a naturalistic zebu bull.
  • Later sculpture: the monolithic lion and Nandi beside the Pancha Rathas at Mamallapuram (Pallava), and the gajasimhas (lions on elephants) at the entrance of the Konark Sun temple.

3. In architecture

  • Lion: the lion-based pillars of the Pallavas (Kailasanatha temple, Kanchipuram), the rearing yalis on Vijayanagara pillars, and the simhasana (lion throne) of kings and deities.
  • Bull: Nandi mandapas face the sanctum of Shiva temples, with colossal monolithic Nandis at Thanjavur, Lepakshi and Chamundi Hills (Mysuru).
  • Modern India: the State Emblem, adopted on 26 January 1950 with Satyameva Jayate from the Mundaka Upanishad, appears on currency, passports and seals; a 6.5-m bronze emblem, unveiled in July 2022, crowns the new Parliament building, and the Ashoka Chakra on the National Flag comes from the same capital.

4. Why the two endure

  • Complementary ideals: the lion represents the ruler's power and the bull the patient strength of the farmer and the righteous order he upholds.
  • Shared across faiths: both are honoured by Hindus, Buddhists and Jains, making them unifying national symbols.

Together, the lion and the bull embody the Indian ideal of power tempered by dharma: sovereignty and courage alongside patience and service. That is why both remain living symbols, from village temples to the State Emblem of the Republic.
free.upm-2022-gs1-14:
Ocean currentsCoriolis forceUpwellingFishing grounds

Ocean currents are large, continuous movements of sea water along a definite path and direction, like rivers within the ocean. As NCERT explains, they are set in motion by primary forces and shaped by secondary forces. By moving heat, nutrients and plankton, currents decide where the world's richest fishing grounds lie: where warm and cold currents meet, and where cold water wells up along coasts.

1. Primary forces that start currents

  • Solar heating: water near the equator expands, so the sea there stands about 8 cm higher than in the middle latitudes (NCERT), creating a slight slope down which water flows.
  • Wind: planetary winds drag surface water by friction; the trade winds drive the equatorial currents, the westerlies the North Atlantic Drift, and the monsoon reverses currents in the northern Indian Ocean each season.
  • Gravity: pulls water down the slope and tends to pile it up, setting up gradient flows.
  • Coriolis force: deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, creating large circular gyres, clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south.

2. Secondary forces and modifying factors

  • Density differences: cold, salty water is denser and sinks, as in the North Atlantic, driving the deep thermohaline circulation (the "global conveyor belt"); dense Mediterranean water flows out under the Atlantic at Gibraltar.
  • Shape of coasts and sea floor: landmasses deflect or split currents, as the bulge of Brazil divides the South Equatorial Current; ridges and shelves steer deep flows.
  • Other factors: evaporation, rainfall and river inflow alter salinity, while melting ice and tides add local effects.

3. Role in the world's fishing industry

  • Meeting of warm and cold currents: mixing brings nutrients and supports plankton, the base of the food chain; the Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current over the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the Kuroshio meets the Oyashio off Japan, and the North Atlantic Drift warms the shallow banks of the North Sea.
  • Upwelling coasts: on the subtropical west coasts of continents, winds push surface water offshore and cold, nutrient-rich water rises, along the Humboldt (Peru), California, Canary (north-west Africa) and Benguela (Namibia) currents; Peru's anchoveta is among the world's largest single-species fisheries.
  • Ice-free ports and fish movement: the warm North Atlantic Drift keeps Norway's ports open in winter, and currents carry fish eggs and larvae and guide migrations.
  • India: monsoon-driven upwelling off the south-west coast supports the oil sardine and mackerel catch of Kerala and Karnataka.
  • Vulnerability: El Niño weakens Peru's upwelling and caused the anchoveta collapse of 1972–73; overfishing destroyed the Grand Banks cod stocks, forcing Canada's moratorium of 1992.

Ocean currents are the conveyor belts of marine productivity. With warming seas and overfishing threatening them, ecosystem-based fisheries management and scientific monitoring are needed to keep these grounds productive.
free.upm-2022-gs1-15:
Natural rubberEquatorial plantation cropDeforestationDeforestation-free supply chains

Natural rubber is made from the latex of Hevea brasiliensis, a tree native to the Amazon basin. It is an equatorial crop needing temperatures above 25°C, more than 200 cm of rain spread through the year and deep, well-drained soils. Seeds collected in Brazil by Henry Wickham (1876) were raised at Kew Gardens and sent to Britain's Asian colonies, which is why Asia, not South America, dominates production today.

1. Distribution of rubber-producing countries

  • Southeast Asia, the core: Thailand is the largest producer, with about a third of world output (about 33.5% of 14.9 million tonnes in 2024, Krungsri Research); Indonesia is second, and Vietnam, Cambodia, Malaysia, Laos and Myanmar also produce it. Asia produces over four-fifths of the world's natural rubber.
  • Africa, the new frontier: Côte d'Ivoire overtook Vietnam in 2023 to become the third-largest producer (ANRPC); Liberia, Nigeria, Ghana and Cameroon also grow rubber.
  • South Asia: in India, Kerala produces the bulk, followed by Tripura, with Karnataka, Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu) and other north-eastern States expanding; Sri Lanka is an older producer.
  • China: grows rubber at its climatic margin in Hainan and Yunnan (Xishuangbanna).
  • South America: Brazil, the tree's home, produces little, because South American leaf blight, a fungal disease, devastates plantations.

2. Major environmental issues

  • Deforestation: a study in Nature (2023) found that about 4 million hectares of forest in Southeast Asia have been cleared for rubber since 1993, two to three times earlier estimates; over 1 million hectares of plantations lie in areas important for biodiversity.
  • Monoculture and biodiversity loss: even-aged, single-species plantations replace multi-layered rainforest and support far fewer birds, insects and mammals; Xishuangbanna in Yunnan lost much of its tropical forest to rubber.
  • Soil erosion and water: clearing hill slopes in Kerala, Tripura and Yunnan causes erosion and landslides, and plantations can dry out soils and streams in the dry season.
  • Agrochemicals and processing waste: fertilisers, herbicides and fungicides against leaf diseases, and effluent rich in ammonia and organic matter from latex processing, pollute streams; smoke-houses add to air pollution.
  • Climate stress and disease: erratic rain, drought and fungal leaf diseases cut yields, pushing growers to clear new land.
  • Land conflicts: large concessions in Cambodia, Laos and parts of Africa have displaced forest communities.

3. Responses

  • Traceability: the EU Deforestation Regulation covers rubber; after two postponements it is due to apply from 30 December 2026, requiring proof that imports do not come from land deforested after 2020.
  • Sustainable production: the Global Platform for Sustainable Natural Rubber (2018), certification, agroforestry and intercropping, cover crops on slopes, and replanting on degraded land instead of forest.

Rubber geography is shifting from Southeast Asia's mature plantations to Africa's new frontier. Higher yields on existing land, support for smallholders and deforestation-free supply chains can meet demand without sacrificing tropical forests.
free.upm-2022-gs1-16:
Straits and isthmusesChokepointsSea lanesFreedom of navigation

A strait is a narrow sea passage joining two larger water bodies, such as Malacca or Hormuz; an isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining two landmasses and separating two seas, such as Suez or Panama, often cut by a canal. Since over 80% of world trade by volume moves by sea (UNCTAD), these narrow points act as chokepoints: they shorten routes and cut costs, but concentrate risk.

1. Significance of straits

  • Shortest routes: the Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean with the Pacific and carried about 23.2 million barrels of oil a day in the first half of 2025, 29% of maritime oil flows (US EIA); China, Japan and South Korea depend on it.
  • Energy security: Hormuz carried about 20.9 million barrels a day, about a fifth of world oil consumption, and over a fifth of global LNG trade; about half of India's crude imports pass through it, and the 2026 West Asia crisis disrupted shipping there.
  • Regional lifelines: the Bab-el-Mandeb is the gateway to the Red Sea and Suez; the Turkish Straits carry Black Sea grain and oil (the Black Sea Grain Initiative of 2022–23 depended on them); the Dover Strait is among the world's busiest shipping lanes.
  • India's neighbourhood: the Six Degree Channel south of Great Nicobar lies near the western entrance of Malacca, giving the islands strategic weight.

2. Significance of isthmuses

  • Suez Canal (1869): cut across the Isthmus of Suez, it links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and spares Europe–Asia shipping the long voyage around Africa; the grounding of the Ever Given blocked it for six days in March 2021.
  • Panama Canal (1914): across the Isthmus of Panama, it links the Atlantic and the Pacific; drought in 2023–24 forced limits on daily transits.
  • Other isthmuses: the Corinth Canal (1893) in Greece, and the Kra Isthmus in Thailand, where a canal or "land bridge" to bypass Malacca has long been proposed.
  • Land bridges: pipelines across isthmuses, such as Egypt's SUMED pipeline, move oil between seas.

3. Risks and governance

  • Vulnerability: piracy, conflict, accidents and climate shocks raise freight and insurance costs; Houthi attacks from late 2023 diverted many ships around the Cape of Good Hope.
  • Legal regime: UNCLOS (1982) guarantees "transit passage" through international straits; the Montreux Convention (1936) governs the Turkish Straits and the Constantinople Convention (1888) the Suez Canal.
  • Strategic competition: navies and port investments cluster around chokepoints (China's "Malacca dilemma"); India's Operation Sankalp (2019) escorts Indian ships in the Gulf region.
  • Alternatives: the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (2023), the International North–South Transport Corridor and the Chennai–Vladivostok maritime route.

Straits and isthmuses are the jugular veins of global trade: a single blockage raises prices worldwide. Keeping them open needs freedom of navigation under UNCLOS, maritime security cooperation, and diversified routes and energy sources.
free.upm-2022-gs1-17:
TroposphereLapse rateConvectionTropopause

The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere. Its average height is about 13 km, roughly 8 km near the poles and 18 km at the equator, where strong convection carries heat higher (NCERT). It holds about three-quarters of the atmosphere's mass and almost all its water vapour and dust, so nearly all weather, from clouds and rain to storms and winds, occurs here. It is also the layer that supports life.

1. Composition: the raw material of weather

  • Water vapour: up to about 4% of the air by volume in the humid tropics, it forms clouds, fog and precipitation and releases latent heat on condensation, the energy source of thunderstorms and cyclones.
  • Dust and aerosols: salt, smoke and dust particles act as hygroscopic nuclei around which vapour condenses; they also cause haze and smog.
  • Greenhouse gases: water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane absorb outgoing terrestrial radiation and keep the Earth's average temperature near 15°C instead of about –18°C.

2. Heating from below: lapse rate and instability

  • Heated by the ground: the troposphere is warmed mainly by terrestrial radiation, conduction and convection from the surface, so temperature falls with height, by about 6.5°C per km (1°C per 165 m).
  • Rising air cools: rising air expands and cools adiabatically; when it reaches the dew point, clouds form and rain or snow follows.
  • Instability: a steep lapse rate on hot afternoons produces cumulonimbus clouds, thunderstorms and the nor'westers (kalbaisakhi) of eastern India.
  • Inversions: on calm winter nights the ground cools fast and the lapse rate reverses, trapping fog, frost and smog, as in Delhi's winter.

3. Pressure, winds and weather systems

  • Winds: unequal heating creates pressure differences that drive planetary, seasonal (monsoon) and local winds such as the loo.
  • Air masses and storms: air masses, fronts, temperate cyclones (such as the western disturbances that bring winter rain to north-west India) and tropical cyclones all form within the troposphere.
  • Jet streams: near its top, the subtropical westerly jet steers western disturbances, and the tropical easterly jet over peninsular India is linked to the summer monsoon.
  • Water and heat transfer: evaporation, condensation and precipitation, and the transfer of heat from the tropics to the poles, take place here.

4. The tropopause: a lid on weather

  • The boundary: at the tropopause temperature stops falling, at about –80°C over the equator and –45°C over the poles.
  • A stable cap: above it the stratosphere warms with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet rays; this stable layer caps convection, so weather stays in the troposphere, and jet aircraft cruise near the tropopause to avoid turbulence.

The troposphere is the weather-making layer and the home of life. As greenhouse gases and aerosols change its composition and extreme weather intensifies, better observation, as under Mission Mausam (2024), becomes vital.
free.upm-2022-gs1-18:
SectCasteReligious denominationCross-cutting identities

A sect is a group within a religion that follows a particular teacher, doctrine or practice, such as the Lingayats, Kabirpanthis, Warkaris or Bohras. Sociologists such as Max Weber and Ernst Troeltsch contrasted the voluntary, often protest-born sect with the established church. In law, the Shirur Mutt case (1954) read a "religious denomination" under Article 26 as a group with a common faith, organisation and name. Its salience lies in how it interacts with caste, region and religion.

1. Sect and caste

  • Sect as protest against caste: Basavanna's Virashaiva movement (12th century), the Kabirpanth, the Satnamis of Guru Ghasidas (Chhattisgarh) and the Matuas of Bengal offered lower castes dignity and equality in devotion.
  • Sect turning into caste: over time many sects became endogamous and hierarchical; the Lingayats, for instance, developed internal sub-groups and act today as a powerful caste-like community.
  • Deras and Dalit identity: in Punjab, deras such as Sachkhand Ballan (Ravidassia) draw Dalit followers seeking spiritual space and status, and have become political actors.

2. Sect and region

  • Regional roots: the Warkari tradition of Pandharpur (Maharashtra), Sankardeva's Ekasarana Dharma and the satras of Majuli (Assam), the Lingayats (Karnataka), Gaudiya Vaishnavism (Bengal and Odisha) and the Bishnois (Rajasthan).
  • Shaping regional culture: their vernacular literature, such as Tukaram's abhangs, Basavanna's vachanas and Sankardeva's borgeets, helped build regional languages and identities.
  • Regional politics: mutts and sect leaders influence voting and policy in their regions.

3. Sect and religion

  • Diversity within religions: Sunni (Barelvi, Deobandi), Shia, Bohra and Ahmadiyya Muslims; Catholic, Syrian Orthodox and Pentecostal Christians; Digambara and Shvetambara Jains; Navayana Buddhists (1956); Namdhari and Nirankari Sikhs.
  • Intra-religious disputes: conflicts between sects can be as sharp as those between religions, as in the Malankara Orthodox–Jacobite church dispute, on which the Supreme Court ruled in 2017, and Shia–Sunni tensions.
  • Separate-religion claims: the Lingayat demand for minority-religion status (recommended by Karnataka in 2018) and the Sarna code demand (Jharkhand Assembly resolution, 2020) show sects seeking recognition as religions.
  • Legal questions: cases such as Sabarimala (2018) and the Dawoodi Bohra excommunication case pit denominational autonomy against individual rights.

4. Assessment

  • Secondary but cross-cutting: sect rarely replaces caste or religion, but it can soften their divisions, as when people of all castes walk together in the Warkari pilgrimage.
  • Divisive when politicised: it deepens fragmentation when it becomes a vote bank or a ground for conflict.
  • Growing salience: urban guru movements, televangelism and online religion show that sect identities are adapting rather than fading.

Indian identities are layered and overlapping: sect matters most when it coincides with caste (as for the Ravidassias) or region (as for the Lingayats). A secular State should respect denominational autonomy under Article 26 while upholding equality and individual rights.
free.upm-2022-gs1-19:
Sarva dharma sambhavaPrincipled distancePluralismConstitutional secularism

Western secularism, as in France's laïcité, keeps religion and state apart. Indian secularism means equal respect for all religions (sarva dharma sambhava) with a "principled distance" (Rajeev Bhargava) that lets the state intervene for reform and equality. "Secular" entered the Preamble through the 42nd Amendment (1976); S.R. Bommai (1994) made secularism a basic feature, and Dr Balram Singh (2024) upheld its insertion. Tolerance, assimilation and pluralism are its roots, not its whole content.

1. Tolerance: the historical root

  • Ashoka: Rock Edict XII urges restraint in speech and honour to other sects, warning that one who disparages others' sects harms his own.
  • Akbar: sulh-i-kul (peace with all), the abolition of jizya (1564) and inter-faith debates in the Ibadat Khana (1575).
  • Bhakti and Sufi saints: Kabir, Guru Nanak and Nizamuddin Auliya preached the unity of the divine across faiths.
  • Gandhi: equal regard for all religions (sarva dharma sama bhava), practised in his inter-faith prayer meetings.

2. Assimilation: synthesis, not uniformity

  • Composite culture: India absorbed Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas, Parsis, Jews, Syrian Christians, Turks and Afghans; Indo-Islamic architecture, Hindustani music, Urdu and the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb are its fruits, and Dara Shikoh's Majma-ul-Bahrain sought the meeting of Hindu and Islamic mysticism.
  • Not forced assimilation: unlike France, which banned conspicuous religious symbols in state schools (2004), India protects the distinct language, script and culture of minorities (Articles 29–30). Assimilation here means mutual borrowing, not merger into a majority culture.

3. Pluralism: the constitutional core

  • Freedoms: Articles 25–28 guarantee freedom of conscience, practice and propagation, autonomy for religious denominations, no tax to promote any religion and no religious instruction in wholly state-funded schools.
  • Group rights: minorities may establish and administer educational institutions (Article 30), and personal laws coexist, with a uniform civil code left as a directive (Article 44).
  • Judicial reading: in S.R. Bommai the Court held that the State has no religion of its own; in Aruna Roy (2002) it read secularism as sarva dharma sambhava.

4. Beyond the three: equality and reform

  • Principled distance: the State abolished untouchability (Article 17), allowed laws opening Hindu temples to all castes (Article 25(2)(b)), and instant triple talaq was struck down (Shayara Bano, 2017).
  • Equal citizenship: Articles 14–16 forbid discrimination on grounds of religion.
  • Challenges: communal violence, hate speech and the use of religion in politics show that tolerance alone, merely putting up with others, is not enough; mutual respect and fraternity are needed.

Yes, tolerance, assimilation (as synthesis) and pluralism are the civilisational foundations of Indian secularism, but the constitutional model adds equality, minority rights and reform. Strengthening fraternity, as the Preamble asks, is the best guarantee of this distinctively Indian secularism.
free.upm-2022-gs1-20:
GlobalisationTechnology diffusionResource scarcityCircular economy

Globalisation, the integration of economies through trade, capital, people and ideas, and new technology reinforce each other: containers, the internet and digital platforms made global value chains possible, and global markets spread technologies faster than ever. Both, however, operate in a world of scarce resources: water, land, energy, critical minerals and a shrinking carbon budget. India, with about 18% of the world's people but only 4% of its freshwater, feels this tension sharply.

1. Globalisation spreads technology

  • Investment and value chains: FDI and production-linked incentives brought mobile-phone assembly and semiconductor projects under the India Semiconductor Mission (2021); Indian IT firms and global capability centres plug Indian talent into global innovation.
  • Falling costs through scale: global markets made solar panels, batteries and smartphones cheap enough for mass use in India.
  • Knowledge flows: the diaspora, international research and open-source software diffuse know-how.

2. Technology spreads globalisation
