  • Digital trade: services exports, e-commerce and remote work cross borders instantly.
  • Digital public infrastructure: India's UPI has been linked with payment systems abroad, such as Singapore's PayNow (2023), and India's G20 presidency (2023) promoted digital public infrastructure as a global public good.

3. Technology as an answer to scarcity

  • Energy: India reached 50% non-fossil installed power capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its 2030 target, and had about 299 GW of renewable capacity by September 2026; the International Solar Alliance (2015) spreads solar worldwide.
  • Water and food: micro-irrigation under "Per Drop More Crop", satellite advisories, drones and India's first genome-edited rice varieties (2025) raise output per drop and per hectare.
  • Materials: extended producer responsibility for plastics, e-waste and batteries, recycling, and the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) push towards a circular economy.

4. Where scarcity strains the relationship

  • Weaponised supply chains: export curbs on critical minerals such as rare earths expose import-dependent economies; India joined the Minerals Security Partnership (2023) to diversify supplies.
  • Energy shocks: India imports about 89% of its crude oil, and the 2026 Hormuz crisis showed the risk of a globalised energy system.
  • Rebound effect (Jevons paradox): efficiency lowers costs and raises total use; data centres for artificial intelligence demand large amounts of power and water, and e-waste is rising.
  • Unequal access: green technologies and patents are concentrated in rich countries, and trade measures such as the EU's carbon border tax (CBAM, definitive phase from January 2026) can hurt developing exporters; the digital divide limits gains at home.

Globalisation and new technology are mutually reinforcing, but in a world of scarce resources they must aim at doing more with less: circular, inclusive and shared through fair technology transfer and climate finance. India's Mission LiFE, digital public infrastructure and clean-energy push show one such path.
free.upm-2022-gs2-1:
Constitutionalisation of environmentArticle 21Public interest litigationEnvironmental principles

The Constitution of 1950 said nothing explicit about the environment. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 48A (the State shall protect and improve the environment) and Article 51A(g) (a citizen's duty to protect it), but both are non-justiciable. The Supreme Court went further: by reading a healthy environment into the right to life under Article 21 and using public interest litigation (PIL), it turned environmental problems into enforceable constitutional rights. That is why many call it modern Indian law's most significant achievement.

1. How the Court constitutionalised the environment

  • Right to a healthy environment: in Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra (1985) the Court stopped limestone quarrying in the Doon valley; in Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) it held that Article 21 includes the right to pollution-free water and air.
  • Absolute liability: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas leak, 1987) made hazardous industries absolutely liable, without the exceptions of the English rule in Rylands v. Fletcher.
  • Principles made part of Indian law: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996) adopted sustainable development, the precautionary principle and polluter pays; Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) made chemical units in Bichhri, Rajasthan pay for the damage; M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) adopted the public trust doctrine.
  • Forests and climate: the T.N. Godavarman case (from 1995) protects all forests in the dictionary sense; in M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024), a case on the Great Indian Bustard, the Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.

2. Procedural innovations

  • PIL and relaxed standing: petitions by citizens such as M.C. Mehta brought the Kanpur tanneries polluting the Ganga (1987), the Taj Trapezium (1996) and Delhi's air (CNG for public transport, 1998) before the Court.
  • Continuing mandamus: the Court kept cases open for years and created expert bodies, such as the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority for Delhi (1998) and the Central Empowered Committee for forests (2002).
  • Specialised forum: the Court's call for environmental courts (A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu, 1999) and the Law Commission's 186th Report led to the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.

3. Why it is a major achievement

  • Rights where laws were weak: citizens can approach the Supreme Court directly when regulators fail.
  • A test for development: sustainable development and intergenerational equity became constitutional standards, giving future generations and wildlife a voice.

4. Limits of judicial environmentalism

  • Overreach: policy-making by courts strains the separation of powers, and judges lack technical expertise.
  • Implementation gap: after decades of orders, the Ganga and Yamuna remain polluted and Delhi's winter air is still hazardous.
  • Livelihoods: closure orders hurt workers and small units when no transition is planned.

The Supreme Court made the environment a constitutional value; strong regulators, the NGT and an executive committed to sustainable development must now carry it forward, rather than endless continuing mandamus.
free.upm-2022-gs2-2:
Article 19(1)(d) and (e)Article 19(5)Reasonable restrictionsScheduled Tribes

Article 19(1)(d) guarantees every citizen the right to move freely throughout the territory of India, and Article 19(1)(e) the right to reside and settle in any part of it. Together they express single citizenship and one national market, without internal barriers. Yet these freedoms are not absolute: under Article 19(5) the State may impose reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public or to protect the interests of any Scheduled Tribe.

1. Scope of the rights

  • Internal freedom: citizens may travel, live and work anywhere in India; about 37% of Indians were migrants by place of last residence (Census 2011).
  • Only for citizens: foreigners do not enjoy Article 19.
  • Within India only: the right to travel abroad flows from personal liberty under Article 21 (Satwant Singh Sawhney, 1967; Maneka Gandhi, 1978), not from Article 19(1)(d).
  • Linked to livelihood: these rights make the freedom of profession and trade (Article 19(1)(g)) real for migrant workers.

2. Grounds and forms of restriction

  • Interests of the general public: public order, health, morals and security. In N.B. Khare (1950) the Court upheld externment under a public safety law with safeguards, and in Kaushailiya (1964) it upheld restrictions on the movement of sex workers on grounds of public health and morals.
  • Protection of Scheduled Tribes: the Inner Line Permit under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873 (Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram and, since 2019, Manipur) and curbs on outsiders acquiring land in Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas protect tribal land and culture.
  • Public health and disasters: COVID-19 lockdowns (2020) under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897; quarantine and containment zones.
  • Public order: prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, 2023 (formerly Section 144 CrPC), curfews and externment of habitual offenders under State police laws.
  • National security: prohibited places under the Official Secrets Act, 1923, defence areas and border zones.

3. Other constitutional limits

  • Emergency: Article 358 suspends Article 19 during a national emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression (44th Amendment, 1978).
  • Special provisions: Articles 371A (Nagaland) and 371G (Mizoram) protect customary law and land ownership; Article 16(3) lets Parliament prescribe residence requirements for some public jobs.
  • Judicial review: restrictions must be reasonable and proportionate; Anuradha Bhasin (2020) required prohibitory orders to be reasoned and proportionate.

4. Assessment

  • Justified limits: most restrictions protect vulnerable tribes, public health and security, and courts can review them.
  • Real barriers lie elsewhere: hostility to migrants, "sons of the soil" politics and domicile quotas in private jobs (Haryana's 75% law, struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2023) restrict mobility more than law does.

The freedoms of movement and residence sustain fraternity and a common market. Restrictions are legitimate only when they protect the public or tribal communities and pass the test of proportionality.
free.upm-2022-gs2-3:
73rd and 74th AmendmentsDemocratic decentralisation3FsDevolution Index

The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave panchayats and municipalities constitutional status (Parts IX and IXA), with elections every five years, reserved seats for SCs, STs and women, State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions. Three decades on, decentralisation has changed who governs at the grassroots far more than how much power they hold, because the devolution of the 3Fs (funds, functions and functionaries) remains partial.

1. How the grassroots landscape has changed

  • Regular elections: periodic elections have created lakhs of elected representatives and a new generation of local leaders.
  • Social inclusion: at least one-third of seats and chairpersons' posts are reserved for women (Article 243D); 21 States and two UTs reserve 50%, and women hold nearly half of all panchayat seats. SCs and STs are represented in proportion to population.
  • Tribal self-rule: PESA (1996) gives Gram Sabhas in Fifth Schedule areas powers over minor forest produce, minor water bodies and consultation before land acquisition.
  • Planning from below: Gram Panchayat Development Plans (from 2015-16) are prepared through Gram Sabhas, strengthened by the People's Plan Campaign (2018); Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996) showed what large untied funds can do.
  • Transparency and delivery: eGramSwaraj and SVAMITVA property cards (2020), social audits of rural employment works and village water committees under the Jal Jeevan Mission bring services closer to people.

2. How far power has really been devolved

  • Devolution Index: the all-India score rose only from 39.9% (2013-14) to 43.9% (2021-22) (report for the Ministry of Panchayati Raj by IIPA, released in February 2025); Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu lead.
  • Functions: the 29 subjects of the Eleventh Schedule (18 of the Twelfth for municipalities) are transferred unevenly; parallel bodies and line departments keep real control.
  • Funds: panchayats raise only about 1% of their revenue from their own taxes; about 80% comes from Union grants and 15% from State grants. The 16th Finance Commission recommended about ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies (2026-31).
  • Functionaries: panchayats lack their own staff and depend on line-department employees.
  • Proxy power: "sarpanch-pati" practices, rotation of reserved seats every term and elite capture dilute women's and Dalits' leadership.

3. Urban local bodies lag further

  • Weak mayors: most have short, indirectly elected terms, while State-appointed commissioners hold executive power.
  • Parastatals: development authorities and water boards control key urban functions.
  • Poor finances: low property-tax collection and delayed State transfers.

4. Way forward

Activity mapping to assign clear functions, property-tax reform and own revenue, a local-government cadre, regular State Finance Commissions, capacity building under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan and action against proxy leadership.

Decentralisation has substantially changed representation and participation, moderately improved delivery, but only marginally created local self-government in Gandhi's sense of gram swaraj. Real devolution of the 3Fs is the unfinished agenda.
free.upm-2022-gs2-4:
Article 64Chairman of the Rajya SabhaCasting voteImpartiality

The Vice-President holds the second-highest constitutional office but has no executive functions of his own. Under Article 64 he is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and most of his work lies in that role. Elected by the members of both Houses (Article 66), he presides over a House of which he is not a member. C.P. Radhakrishnan became the 15th Vice-President in September 2025, after Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned in July 2025 citing health reasons.

1. Presiding officer of the House

  • Conducting business: presides over sittings, decides points of order and interprets the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States; his rulings bind the House.
  • Maintaining order: may direct a disorderly member to withdraw (Rule 255), name a member for suspension (Rule 256), and adjourn or suspend a sitting in grave disorder.
  • Casting vote: does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in case of a tie (Article 100).
  • Admitting business: decides on the admissibility of questions, motions and notices, and allots time with the Business Advisory Committee, which he chairs.

2. Guardian of the House's rights

  • Committees: constitutes committees and nominates members; the eight department-related standing committees of the Rajya Sabha work under his direction, and he can refer Bills to them.
  • Privileges: decides whether a question of privilege is in order and may refer it to the Committee of Privileges.
  • Anti-defection: decides on the disqualification of Rajya Sabha members under the Tenth Schedule; his decision is open to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).
  • Administration and representation: heads the Rajya Sabha Secretariat and speaks for the House in its dealings with the executive and other bodies.

3. Limits on the role

  • During removal proceedings: he cannot preside while a resolution for his removal is under consideration, though he may speak and take part without voting (Article 92); removal needs 14 days' notice.
  • When acting as President: he does not perform the Chairman's duties, and the Deputy Chairman presides (Article 64).
  • No role in Money Bills or joint sittings, which reflects the Lok Sabha's primacy.

4. Significance and concerns

  • Federal chamber: a fair Chairman protects the voice of the States and of smaller parties in a House where the government may lack a majority.
  • Impartiality: Chairmen come from political life; frequent disruptions and large-scale suspensions of members, as in the 2021 and 2023 sessions, have raised concern about balancing order with dissent.
  • Traditions: the first Vice-President, S. Radhakrishnan (1952–62), set standards of dignity, scholarship and consensus.

The Chairman is the custodian of the Rajya Sabha: he must let the government transact its business and the opposition voice dissent. Clear conventions on suspensions and admission of notices, and impartial conduct, keep the upper House a chamber of deliberation.
free.upm-2022-gs2-5:
102nd AmendmentArticle 338BArticle 342A105th Amendment

The National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) was first set up as a statutory body under the NCBC Act, 1993, following the Supreme Court's direction in Indra Sawhney (1992). Its mandate was narrow: to examine requests for inclusion in, or exclusion from, the Central list of backward classes. The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 repealed that Act and gave the NCBC constitutional status under Article 338B, alongside a new Article 342A on the list of socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs).

1. From a statutory to a constitutional body

  • Composition: a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other Members appointed by the President.

2. Role of the constitutional NCBC (Article 338B(5))

  • Investigate and monitor: all constitutional and legal safeguards for SEBCs, and evaluate how they work.
  • Inquire into complaints: about deprivation of rights and safeguards, with the powers of a civil court to summon persons, require documents and receive evidence.
  • Advise on development: take part in planning for the socio-economic development of SEBCs and evaluate progress under the Union and the States.
  • Report: present annual and other reports to the President with recommendations; the Government must lay them before Parliament with a memorandum on action taken.
  • Advise on the Central list: which, after the Amendment, Parliament alone can change by law (Article 342A(2)).

3. The federal question and the 105th Amendment

  • Maratha reservation case (Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil, May 2021): by 3:2, the Supreme Court read the 102nd Amendment as leaving only one Central list, taking away the States' power to identify backward classes.
  • 105th Amendment Act, 2021: restored the power of States and UTs to prepare their own lists (Article 342A(3)) and made consultation with the NCBC unnecessary for those lists, preserving federalism.

4. Significance and concerns

  • Parity and voice: the NCBC now stands alongside the NCSC and NCST, and backward classes have a dedicated grievance forum.
  • Recommendatory: its findings bind no one, and action on its reports is slow.
  • Unequal benefits: data examined by the Rohini Commission (constituted 2017, report 2023) showed about a quarter of OBC sub-castes taking about 97% of central OBC jobs and seats, while 983 communities received none.
  • Data gap: with no caste count since 1931, identification is hard; caste enumeration in Census 2027 will help.

The NCBC must grow from a list-making body into a watchdog of rights and development for backward classes. Timely reports, adequate staff and reliable caste data can make substantive equality real.
free.upm-2022-gs2-6:
PM GatiShakti National Master PlanMultimodal connectivityPublic-private partnershipLogistics efficiency

PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (NMP), launched in October 2021, is a GIS-based digital platform built by BISAG-N that puts the plans of all infrastructure agencies on one map. Its seven engines (railways, roads, ports, waterways, airports, mass transport and logistics infrastructure) are planned together to give seamless multimodal connectivity. By October 2026 it held more than 1,800 data layers covering 58 Central Ministries and Departments and all 36 States and UTs. With the National Logistics Policy (2022), it aims to cut logistics costs and delays.

1. Coordination within government

  • End of silos: roads were once dug up for pipelines and cables soon after being built; integrated planning aligns projects before work starts.
  • Institutions: an Empowered Group of Secretaries headed by the Cabinet Secretary, a Network Planning Group (NPG) of the network-planning heads of infrastructure ministries, and a Technical Support Unit; the NPG examines large projects before approval.
  • States and districts: every State and UT is on board, and the platform now supports district-level and social-sector planning, such as locating schools, health facilities and water pipelines.

2. Why the private sector is indispensable

  • Capital: the National Infrastructure Pipeline and the National Monetisation Pipeline (2021) depend on private money through PPPs, the hybrid annuity model, toll-operate-transfer and InvITs.
  • Execution and operation: private firms build most projects and run ports, terminals, warehouses and fleets; the Railways' Gati Shakti Multi-modal Cargo Terminal policy (2021) invites private investment in cargo terminals.
  • Users of public data: the PM GatiShakti Public platform (September 2025) gives private firms and citizens selected data-analytics tools for choosing sites and routes, and the Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP, 2022) shares logistics data with firms through APIs.
  • Innovation: drones, geospatial surveys and digital tracking of freight.

3. Challenges to coordination

  • Data and trust: geospatial data shared with private users must be secure, and the quality of State data layers varies.
  • Land and clearances: acquisition and forest and environmental approvals still delay projects.
  • Contract risk: disputes, delayed payments and aggressive bidding weakened PPPs in the 2010s; the Kelkar Committee (2015) urged better risk-sharing and dispute resolution.
  • Capacity: States, cities and small logistics firms lack planners and digital skills.

4. Way forward

  • Clear rules: data-sharing protocols, standard PPP contracts and quick dispute resolution.
  • States as partners: planning capacity in States and cities, and ranking through the LEADS index.
  • Outcome monitoring: track cost, time and modal shift, not just projects sanctioned.

GatiShakti's whole-of-government approach must become whole-of-nation: the government provides the plan, the data and policy certainty, and the private sector brings capital, efficiency and innovation for seamless connectivity.
free.upm-2022-gs2-7:
RPwD Act, 2016Attitudinal barriersSensitisationReasonable accommodation

The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 brings Indian law in line with the UNCRPD, which India ratified in 2007. It recognises 21 disabilities, reserves 4% of government jobs and 5% of higher-education seats for persons with benchmark disabilities, and makes accessibility a duty. Yet disability arises as much from attitudinal barriers as from physical ones. Without sensitising officials and citizens, these rights remain on paper.

1. What the Act promises

  • Equality and dignity: non-discrimination and reasonable accommodation (Section 3), inclusive education (Section 16) and accessible buildings, transport and ICT (Sections 40–46).
  • Institutions: the Chief Commissioner and State Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities, and special courts for offences.
  • A built-in duty to sensitise: Section 39 requires awareness campaigns, and Section 47 requires disability-rights training for panchayat members, legislators, administrators, police officials, judges and lawyers.

2. Why it remains largely a legal document

  • Insensitive functionaries: in Jeeja Ghosh (2016) a passenger with cerebral palsy was made to leave a flight; the Supreme Court awarded ₹10 lakh and stressed dignity.
  • Narrow reading of rights: in Vikash Kumar v. UPSC (2021) the Court had to direct that a scribe be allowed even without a benchmark disability.
  • Missed accessibility deadlines: in Rajive Raturi (November 2024) the Court found the accessibility norms of the 2017 Rules merely advisory, struck down Rule 15(1) and ordered mandatory rules.
  • Stereotypes: in Nipun Malhotra v. Sony Pictures (July 2024) the Court laid down guidelines against demeaning language and stereotyped portrayals of persons with disabilities in films and other visual media.
  • Hidden disabilities and data: autism, mental illness and learning disabilities are poorly understood in schools and offices; unfilled reserved posts and low budgets persist.

3. How sensitisation can make the Act work

  • Training functionaries: disability-rights modules in civil-service, police and judicial academies, and for teachers, doctors and frontline workers.
  • Schools: inclusive classrooms under NEP 2020, Indian Sign Language and early identification of learning disabilities.
  • Citizens: the Accessible India Campaign (2015) and the Sugamya Bharat app let citizens report barriers; media and celebrities such as Paralympians change perceptions.
  • Participation: "nothing about us without us": persons with disabilities in policy design and in accessibility audits under the social-audit duty (Section 48).
  • Data: accurate counting in Census 2027 to plan services.

The RPwD Act has the right architecture. Turning it into lived reality needs attitudinal change: officials who treat accommodation as a right, not a favour, and citizens who see ability, not disability.
free.upm-2022-gs2-8:
Direct Benefit TransferJAM trinityLeakagesExclusion errors

Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), launched on 1 January 2013, sends subsidies and benefits straight into beneficiaries' bank accounts, using the JAM trinity of Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and mobile phones. Government figures published in August 2026 (New India Samachar) put cumulative transfers at over ₹52 lakh crore through more than 900 schemes, with savings of over ₹5 lakh crore from removing fake and duplicate beneficiaries. It is a major governance reform, but it has limits.

1. Why DBT is a progressive step

  • Plugging leakages: by removing middlemen and ghost beneficiaries, it addresses the problem summed up by Rajiv Gandhi's 1985 remark that only about 15 paise of every rupee meant for the poor reached them.
  • Speed and scale: PM-KISAN (2019) pays ₹6,000 a year in three instalments to farmers, and during the 2020 lockdown cash reached women's Jan Dhan accounts within days.
  • Financial inclusion and women's agency: transfers into women's accounts, as under the PM Matru Vandana Yojana and the LPG subsidy (PAHAL), strengthen their control over money.
  • Transparency: the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) tracks funds end to end, and the DBT Bharat portal publishes scheme-wise data.
  • Choice and dignity: cash lets households decide their needs and reduces officials' discretion.

2. Limitations

  • Exclusion errors: failed Aadhaar seeding, biometric mismatches and name errors can deny benefits to the elderly, manual workers and migrants; mandatory Aadhaar-based payment of rural wages from January 2024 raised concerns about deleted job cards.
  • Last-mile access: distant branches, network failures and fees charged by some banking correspondents make withdrawal costly.
  • Cash cannot replace services: health, schooling and nutrition need functioning institutions; cash for food grains, piloted in Chandigarh and Puducherry (2015), exposed households to market prices.
  • Inflation: fixed cash amounts lose value unless they are revised.
  • Upstream targeting errors: DBT moves money efficiently but cannot correct wrong beneficiary lists based on old data such as SECC 2011.
  • Privacy and grievance: large databases need protection under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; Puttaswamy (2018) upheld Aadhaar for welfare but stressed proportionality, and grievance redress is still weak.

3. Way forward

  • Inclusive by design: alternative authentication (OTP, iris, face) and a human fallback for those whom technology fails.
  • Grievance redress: time-bound complaint handling and social audits.
  • Value protection: periodic revision of cash amounts.
  • Banking access: more and better-paid banking correspondents.
  • Cash plus services: DBT should complement, not replace, public provision.

DBT is a reform of the delivery system, not a substitute for welfare. It will be truly progressive when it is inclusive by design, combining technology with accountability and a humane fallback.
free.upm-2022-gs2-9:
Neighbourhood FirstSri Lankan economic crisisFirst responderCivilisational ties

India and Sri Lanka share civilisational bonds: Buddhism, carried by Emperor Ashoka's son Mahinda; the Ramayana tradition; language, cuisine and the Tamil people on both sides of the Palk Strait. When Sri Lanka faced its worst economic crisis in 2022, with foreign-exchange reserves exhausted, fuel and medicine shortages, suspension of foreign-debt payments in April 2022 and mass protests (the Aragalaya), India acted as its first responder under the Neighbourhood First policy.

1. India's role in the 2022 crisis

  • Financial lifeline: nearly US$4 billion in 2022: lines of credit for fuel, food, medicines and fertiliser, a US$400 million currency swap under the SAARC framework and deferral of Asian Clearing Union payments.
  • Debt restructuring: India was the first official creditor to give financing assurances to the IMF (January 2023), clearing the way for an Extended Fund Facility of about US$3 billion (March 2023), and it co-chaired the Official Creditor Committee with Japan and France.
  • Humanitarian help: rice, milk powder and medicines, including consignments from Tamil Nadu, and fertiliser for the farm season.
  • Respect for sovereignty: India supported Sri Lanka's democratic processes and economic recovery without taking sides in its domestic politics.

2. Beyond the crisis: deepening the partnership

  • Disaster relief: after Cyclone Ditwah (November 2025), India sent relief under Operation Sagar Bandhu and announced a US$450 million reconstruction package (US$350 million in concessional credit and US$100 million in grants) in December 2025.
  • Political trust: President Anura Kumara Dissanayake made India his first State visit (December 2024) and reiterated that Sri Lanka's territory would not be used against India's security.
  • Connectivity and energy: UPI services in Sri Lanka (2024), the Trincomalee energy hub and solar projects.
  • Maritime security: cooperation through the Colombo Security Conclave on maritime safety, terrorism and trafficking.

3. Strategic stakes for India

  • China factor: the 99-year lease of Hambantota port (2017) and the visit of the Chinese tracking vessel Yuan Wang 5 (August 2022) raised security concerns; India's help offered Sri Lanka an alternative to debt-heavy financing.
  • Sea lanes: Sri Lanka lies astride the main shipping routes of the Indian Ocean.
  • Credibility as a regional power: quick help without harsh conditions strengthens India's image as a responsible neighbour.

4. Irritants that test the friendship

  • Fishermen: arrests in the Palk Bay and the Katchatheevu question (1974 agreement).
  • Tamil question: full implementation of the 13th Amendment on provincial devolution.
  • Perceptions: fears in Sri Lanka of India's economic dominance, which call for transparent and people-centric projects.

India's 2022 response showed that being an age-old friend means helping quickly, at scale and without conditions. Sustaining trust needs people-centric projects, a humane solution for fishermen and respect for Sri Lanka's sovereignty, in the spirit of Neighbourhood First.
free.upm-2022-gs2-10:
BIMSTECSAARCAct East and Neighbourhood FirstBay of Bengal

SAARC (Dhaka, December 1985) brought the countries of South Asia together but has been paralysed by India–Pakistan hostility: no summit has been held since Kathmandu (2014), and the 2016 Islamabad summit was called off after the Uri attack. BIMSTEC (Bangkok Declaration, June 1997) links five South Asian and two South-East Asian countries around the Bay of Bengal. India's renewed push for BIMSTEC since 2016, when it invited BIMSTEC leaders to the BRICS outreach in Goa, has led many to see it as an alternative to SAARC.

1. Is BIMSTEC a parallel SAARC?

  • Overlap, not duplication: five countries (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka) belong to both, but BIMSTEC adds Myanmar and Thailand and excludes Pakistan, Afghanistan and the Maldives.
  • Different logic: SAARC is a South Asian identity project; BIMSTEC is a sectoral, sub-regional bridge between South and South-East Asia.
  • Complement, not replacement: SAARC has not been dissolved, and India still uses SAARC-linked tools such as the South Asian University and the SAARC currency-swap framework. BIMSTEC is a practical platform while SAARC is frozen.

2. Similarities and dissimilarities

  • Similarities: both are associations of sovereign equals that decide by consensus; both have a summit, ministerial and senior-officials structure and a permanent secretariat; both have been slow to integrate trade, with low intra-regional trade.
  • Dissimilarities: membership and geography; BIMSTEC is free of the India–Pakistan rivalry; it works through seven sectoral pillars, each led by a member, with India leading security (counter-terrorism and transnational crime, disaster management and energy security); and it has a Master Plan for Transport Connectivity (2022).

3. How BIMSTEC serves India's foreign-policy objectives

  • Neighbourhood First meets Act East: Myanmar and Thailand give India a land and sea bridge to ASEAN.
  • Connectivity for the North-East: the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project and the India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway, backed by the Transport Master Plan and the Agreement on Maritime Transport Cooperation (2025).
  • Security without a veto: counter-terrorism and disaster-management cooperation without Pakistan blocking consensus.
  • Bay of Bengal and blue economy: maritime security, fisheries, energy-grid links and a counter to China's growing presence in Myanmar, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.
  • Institution-building: the Charter (in force May 2024), the Bangkok Vision 2030, BIMSTEC's first vision document, and an Eminent Persons Group report (2025); Bangladesh now holds the chair.

4. Challenges

  • Instability: conflict in Myanmar since 2021 and political changes in member states slow cooperation.
  • Thin institutions: a small secretariat and budget, and an FTA pending for two decades.
  • Asymmetry: smaller members' fears of Indian dominance.

BIMSTEC is not a copy of SAARC but a pragmatic sub-regional platform through which India pursues connectivity, security and Act East goals. Its credibility will rest on delivering projects, a trade agreement and energy links, not on declarations.
free.upm-2022-gs2-11:
Election petitionArticle 329(b)Section 100, RPA 1951Appeal under Section 116A

Under Article 329(b), no election to Parliament or a State Legislature can be called in question except by an election petition presented to the authority provided by law. Part VI of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) makes the High Court that authority (election tribunals were abolished in 1966). In N.P. Ponnuswami (1952) the Supreme Court held that courts cannot interfere while the electoral process is under way.

1. Procedure for deciding election disputes

  • Who and when (Section 81): any candidate or elector of the constituency may file a petition within 45 days of the date of election of the returned candidate.
  • Contents (Section 83): a concise statement of material facts and full particulars of any corrupt practice alleged, verified like a pleading, with an affidavit for corrupt practices; security of ₹2,000 must be deposited (Section 117).
  • Scrutiny and trial (Sections 80A, 86, 87): a petition not complying with Sections 81, 82 or 117 is dismissed; one without material facts can be rejected at the outset (Azhar Hussain v. Rajiv Gandhi, 1986). A single judge tries it under the Code of Civil Procedure, aiming to finish within six months.
  • Decision (Sections 98, 99, 101): dismiss the petition, declare the election void, or declare another candidate duly elected, naming anyone guilty of corrupt practices.

2. Grounds on which an election may be declared void (Section 100)

  • Disqualification: the returned candidate was not qualified, or was disqualified, on the date of election.
  • Corrupt practice by the returned candidate, his election agent or anyone with their consent; Section 123 lists bribery, undue influence, appeals on religion, race, caste, community or language, promotion of enmity, booth capturing and overspending (Section 77).
  • Improper rejection of any nomination.
  • Result materially affected by other irregularities, listed in the table below.

3. Remedy against the High Court's decision

  • Appeal (Section 116A): to the Supreme Court on any question of law or fact, within 30 days of the order; the order may be stayed pending appeal (Section 116B).
  • A statutory right only: there is no common-law right to dispute an election, so the Act must be strictly followed (Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal, 1982).
  • Disqualification: a person found guilty of a corrupt practice may be disqualified for up to six years (Section 8A).

4. Important case laws

  • Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): after the Allahabad High Court voided the Prime Minister's election, the Supreme Court struck down Article 329A(4) and held free and fair elections part of the basic structure.
  • Krishnamoorthy (2015) and Lok Prahari (2018): hiding criminal antecedents, or assets and income sources, in the nomination affidavit amounts to undue influence.
  • Abhiram Singh (2017): seeking votes on the religion, caste, race, community or language of anyone, including the voter, is a corrupt practice.

Election petitions protect the purity of elections, but many outlive the House's term; dedicated election benches would make this statutory remedy meaningful.
free.upm-2022-gs2-12:
Article 213Ordinance-making powerKrishna Kumar Singh (2017)Fraud on the Constitution

The Governor is part of the State Legislature (Article 168). His legislative powers include summoning, proroguing and dissolving the Assembly (Article 174), addressing it (Article 176), dealing with Bills (Articles 200–201), nominating members to the Legislative Council (Article 171(5)) and, most significantly, promulgating ordinances under Article 213. As a rule they are exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Shamsher Singh, 1974).

1. Essential conditions for the ordinance power (Article 213)

  • Legislature not in session: the Assembly, or both Houses in a bicameral State, must not be in session.
  • Immediate necessity: the Governor must be satisfied that circumstances render immediate action necessary; since the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the finality given by the 38th Amendment, this satisfaction can be reviewed by courts.
  • Legislative competence: only on matters within the State Legislature's power; an ordinance is void wherever an equivalent Act would be void.
  • President's instructions: required where a Bill with the same provisions would need the President's previous sanction for introduction, would have been reserved for the President, or would be invalid as an Act without the President's assent.
  • Aid and advice: issued on the advice of the Council of Ministers, not in the Governor's discretion.
  • Accountability to the Legislature: it must be laid before the Legislature and ceases six weeks after reassembly, or earlier if disapproved; its maximum life is about six months and six weeks.

2. Conditions on his other legislative powers

  • Sessions: summoned and prorogued on ministerial advice, with no more than six months between sessions; Nabam Rebia (2016) held that the Governor cannot advance a session on his own.
  • Assent to Bills (Article 200): in its advisory opinion of 20 November 2025, the Supreme Court held that courts cannot fix timelines or deem assent, but prolonged, unexplained inaction invites a limited direction to decide.

3. Legality of re-promulgation without placing ordinances before the Legislature

  • D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): Bihar had kept hundreds of ordinances alive for years by re-promulgating them without placing them before the Legislature. The Court called this a "fraud on the Constitution"; re-promulgation could be justified only in exceptional cases, such as when the Legislature lacked time to pass the Bill.
  • Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017, seven judges): laying an ordinance before the Legislature is a mandatory constitutional duty; re-promulgation without doing so is a fraud on the Constitution; the Governor's satisfaction is not immune from judicial review; and a lapsed ordinance does not automatically create enduring rights.
  • Why it is illegal: it lets the executive legislate without legislative scrutiny, defeats the six-week limit and turns an emergency power into a parallel law-making route. The Union too has re-promulgated ordinances, such as the Enemy Property ordinance, promulgated five times in 2016 before Parliament passed the Act in 2017.

An ordinance is an emergency safety valve, not a parallel source of law. Regular sessions and prompt replacement Bills, with the Court's bar on re-promulgation, protect legislative supremacy and democratic accountability in the States.
free.upm-2022-gs2-13:
CentralisationState autonomyCooperative federalismCoalition politics

India's Constitution creates a "Union of States" with a strong Centre: residuary powers, Articles 249–250 and 356, and the Governor as a link. Party politics has shaped how this design works. National parties, which aim at power in New Delhi, have often favoured centralisation, while regional parties, rooted in linguistic, ethnic or regional identities, have championed State autonomy. The statement holds broadly in history, but it is too simple today.

1. Why national parties tend towards centralisation

  • One-party dominance (1950s–1980s): frequent use of Article 356, beginning with the dismissal of Kerala's elected government in 1959, central planning through the Planning Commission and discretionary grants.
  • National agenda: unity, security and uniform policies; centrally sponsored schemes in State subjects; all-India services.
  • Party organisation: central leadership often chooses Chief Ministers and State party leaders.

2. Why regional parties press for autonomy

  • Identity and language: the anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu (1965) and demands for linguistic States.
  • Autonomy documents: the Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969), the Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) and the West Bengal Memorandum (1977) sought more powers and resources for States.
  • Fiscal demands: a larger share of central taxes, inclusion of cesses and surcharges in the divisible pool and timely GST compensation.
  • Institutions: concerns about Governors' role in assent to Bills, Article 356 and the use of central agencies.

3. Why the binary is too simple

  • Positions change with power: national parties governing States demand funds and autonomy, while regional parties in Union coalitions have backed central measures.
  • Coalition era strengthened federalism (1989–2014): S.R. Bommai (1994) restricted Article 356, the Inter-State Council was set up (1990) and the Sarkaria (1988) and Punchhi (2010) Commissions recommended safeguards.
  • Consensus reforms: GST (101st Amendment, 2016) was passed with support from national and regional parties alike, creating the GST Council as a forum of shared sovereignty.
  • Decentralising steps by national governments: the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992), NITI Aayog in place of the Planning Commission (2015) and tax devolution raised from 32% to 42% by the 14th Finance Commission.
  • Centralisation within States: State governments of every kind have been reluctant to devolve power to panchayats and municipalities, so demands for autonomy often stop at the State capital.

4. Assessment

The real divide is less between national and regional parties than between those in power at the Centre and those in power in the States. Federal tensions are best handled through institutions: regular Inter-State Council meetings, consultation on Concurrent List laws, transparent transfers and neutral Governors.

Indian federalism is cooperative by design and bargaining in practice. Strong States and a strong Union are complementary, and cooperative federalism should rest on institutions rather than on which party holds power.
free.upm-2022-gs2-14:
Indirect electionSingle transferable voteTwo-round systemSemi-presidential system

India is a parliamentary democracy with a nominal head of State, so its President is indirectly elected by legislators (Articles 54–55). France's Fifth Republic (1958) is semi-presidential: the President holds real executive power and, since a 1962 referendum, has been directly elected by universal suffrage. The method of election follows from the role each President plays.

1. Election of the President of India

  • Electoral college (Article 54): elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, including Delhi and Puducherry (70th Amendment, 1992); nominated members and members of Legislative Councils do not vote.
  • Value of votes (Article 55): an MLA's vote equals the State's population divided by its elected MLAs, divided by 1,000; an MP's vote equals the total value of all MLAs' votes divided by the number of elected MPs (700 in 2022). The population base is the 1971 Census, frozen by the 84th Amendment until figures of the first Census after 2026 are published.
  • Method: proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot; the winner must reach a quota of more than half the valid votes.
  • Candidature and term: a citizen aged 35 and qualified for the Lok Sabha, with 50 proposers and 50 seconders; five-year term with re-election allowed (Article 57). Droupadi Murmu was elected the 15th President in July 2022.

2. Election of the President of France

  • Direct, two-round system: a candidate who wins an absolute majority of votes cast in the first round is elected; otherwise the top two face a run-off two weeks later.
  • Sponsorships (parrainages): each candidate needs at least 500 signatures of elected officials such as mayors and MPs, from at least 30 departments or overseas collectivities, with no more than a tenth from any one.
  • Term: cut from seven to five years by a 2000 referendum (from 2002); since the 2008 constitutional revision, no one may serve more than two consecutive terms.
  • Oversight: the Constitutional Council checks sponsorships, hears disputes and proclaims the result. Emmanuel Macron was re-elected in April 2022 and cannot stand again in 2027.

3. Critical examination

  • India's merits: indirect election fits a nominal head; the Constituent Assembly rejected direct election as costly and likely to create a rival centre of power. Including MLAs makes the President a federal symbol, and the formula balances population with Union–State parity.
  • India's limits: the result is usually predictable from party strength, citizens have no direct say, and the 1971 population base is outdated.
  • France's merits: a strong popular mandate; the run-off ensures majority support despite a fragmented field.
  • France's limits: polarisation and "voting against" in run-offs; the sponsorship rule can bar fringe candidates; and without a majority in the National Assembly, as during cohabitation (1986–88, 1993–95, 1997–2002) or after the hung Assembly of 2024, executive power is divided.

Each method suits its constitution: India's indirect election protects parliamentary supremacy and federal balance, while France's direct election gives a powerful executive a popular mandate.
free.upm-2022-gs2-15:
Model Code of ConductArticle 324Level playing fieldElection Commission of India

The Model Code of Conduct (MCC) is a set of norms for parties and candidates during elections, covering general conduct, meetings, processions, polling day, the party in power and manifestos. It has no statutory backing; its force comes from the consensus of political parties and the Election Commission of India's (ECI) powers of superintendence, direction and control under Article 324. Its evolution mirrors the ECI's growth as the guardian of a level playing field.

1. Evolution of the MCC

  • From voluntary to enforced: the code began as a self-regulatory agreement among parties; the 1979 section on the party in power shifted the focus to misuse of official machinery.
  • Seshan era (1990–96): strict enforcement, observers and countermanding of polls made the code a real constraint.
  • Timing settled: the dispute raised in the Harbans Singh Jalal case was resolved in 2001: the code applies from the date the ECI announces the schedule, ordinarily not more than three weeks before the notification.
  • Manifestos: after S. Subramaniam Balaji v. State of Tamil Nadu (2013), the ECI required manifestos to explain the rationale and financing of promises.

2. Role of the ECI in enforcing the MCC

  • Level playing field: ministers cannot combine official visits with campaigning or use official vehicles and staff, and no new schemes, grants or appointments can be announced once the code applies.
  • Action against violations: notices, censure, temporary bans on campaigning, transfer of officials and FIRs where the code overlaps with offences under criminal law and the RPA.
  • Sanction on parties: under Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, the ECI may suspend or withdraw the recognition of a party that defies the code.
  • Statutory backing for parts: a 48-hour silence period (Section 126, RPA) and a ban on exit polls during voting (Section 126A).
  • Technology and observers: cVIGIL lets citizens upload geotagged evidence, with action targeted within 100 minutes; flying squads and expenditure observers track cash and freebies.
  • New media: a voluntary code of ethics by social-media platforms (2019) and advisories on AI-generated deepfakes (2024).

3. Concerns

  • Perceived inconsistency: delayed or uneven action against prominent leaders invites criticism of the ECI.
  • Governance freeze: long, multi-phase elections keep the code in force for weeks.
  • Limited powers: the ECI cannot deregister parties except in narrow cases (Indian National Congress v. Institute of Social Welfare, 2002), and hate speech and online campaigning outpace the code.

A parliamentary standing committee recommended statutory backing in 2013, but the ECI has preferred a flexible code. The MCC shows how a convention, enforced by an independent body, can secure free and fair elections. Its future rests on swift, even-handed enforcement and on legal backing for specific areas such as deepfakes, without making it court-bound.
free.upm-2022-gs2-16:
Inflation as a regressive taxFlexible inflation targetingEmployment-rich growthReal incomes

Welfare schemes such as free foodgrains for about 81 crore people under PMGKAY, PM-KISAN and rural wage employment cushion the poor. But a poor household's well-being also depends on its real income, which inflation erodes, and on decent work, which unemployment and underemployment deny. Inflation works like a regressive tax, and joblessness keeps families dependent on transfers. Macroeconomic management is therefore as important as schemes.

1. Why inflation hurts the poor most

  • Food-heavy budgets: food and beverages carried about 46% of the weight in the CPI (2012 series), and poor households spend an even larger share on food; food inflation touched nearly 11% in October 2024.
  • No hedge: the poor hold cash rather than inflation-protected assets, and informal wages adjust slowly.
  • Erosion of welfare: fixed cash benefits and pensions lose real value.
  • Supply shocks: heatwaves, erratic monsoons and global commodity prices after 2022 drive up vegetables, pulses and edible oils. Headline CPI inflation rose again to 4.8% in August 2026.

2. Why unemployment and underemployment matter

  • Low-quality work: the usual-status unemployment rate was only 3.2% (PLFS 2023-24), but about 46% of workers remain in agriculture and most work informally, often with low productivity.
  • Youth and women: educated young people face high unemployment, and female labour force participation was only 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Jobless growth: capital- and skill-intensive sectors have grown faster than labour-intensive manufacturing.
  • Consequence: without jobs, the poor depend on welfare indefinitely and the demographic dividend is wasted.

3. Deft management: tools and recent practice

  • Monetary policy: under flexible inflation targeting (RBI Act amended in 2016), the Monetary Policy Committee aims at CPI inflation of 4% ±2%; it raised the repo rate by 250 basis points in 2022-23, cut it by 125 basis points in 2025, and raised it to 5.50% in October 2026 as inflation picked up.
  • Supply-side management: buffer stocks and open-market sales of wheat and rice, stock limits, export curbs (wheat, 2022), the Price Stabilisation Fund for pulses and onions, lower import duties on edible oils, and Bharat atta and dal at subsidised prices.
  • Fiscal prudence: a credible deficit path avoids demand-pull inflation and keeps interest rates low for investment.
  • Employment policy: labour-intensive manufacturing (textiles, food processing, leather), credit for MSMEs, PLI schemes, the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (2025) for new formal jobs, skilling under PMKVY, the Labour Codes (in force from November 2025) and 125 days of rural work under the VB-G RAM G Act from July 2026.

4. Balancing the two goals

  • Avoid over-tightening: sharp rate hikes can hurt jobs, so policy must be calibrated.
  • Index benefits: link pensions and transfers to prices.
  • Better data: monthly PLFS estimates (since 2025) allow quicker responses.

Schemes treat the symptoms of poverty; price stability and employment-rich growth treat its causes. India needs both: a welfare state that protects and an economy that employs.
free.upm-2022-gs2-17:
Donor dependenceCommunity participationAid effectivenessLocal ownership

Donor agencies include multilateral lenders such as the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, UN agencies, bilateral aid agencies and private foundations. Community participation means people's involvement in identifying needs, planning, implementing and monitoring development. The Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness (2005) recognised that aid works only with country and local ownership. Heavy donor dependence can weaken participation, but the outcome depends on how aid is designed; the view is therefore only partly true.

1. How donor dependence can weaken community participation

  • Upward accountability: NGOs and project agencies answer to donors' reporting formats, logical frameworks and timelines rather than to the people they serve.
  • Donor-driven priorities: funds follow global agendas and changing fashions, not local needs, turning communities into "beneficiaries" rather than decision-makers.
  • Parallel structures: project implementation units bypass panchayats and line departments; when funding ends, activities often collapse.
  • Token participation: meetings held to tick boxes, and user committees captured by local elites.
  • Volatility: sudden cuts halt programmes; in 2025 the USA dismantled USAID and other large donors also cut aid, disrupting health and food programmes in many countries.
  • Conditionalities: structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s and 1990s cut social spending without people's voice.

2. Why the relationship is not one-sided

  • Donors have promoted participation: World Bank-supported community-driven projects such as Swajal (1996) in the hills of Uttar Pradesh, now Uttarakhand, for demand-driven rural water supply, and the Andhra Pradesh District Poverty Initiatives Project (Velugu, 2000), which built federations of self-help groups.
  • Capacity building: donors have funded training of SHGs, community health workers and social audits.
  • The State matters more: participation depends on local institutions; Kudumbashree (Kerala, 1998), DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women in SHGs) and Gram Sabha-based planning were built mainly with domestic resources.
  • India's lower dependence: foreign aid is a tiny share of India's development spending; since 2003 India accepts bilateral aid from only a few partners, and it is itself a development partner through lines of credit and ITEC training.
  • Regulation: the 2020 amendment to the FCRA banned sub-granting of foreign funds and capped administrative costs at 20%, improving transparency but also squeezing small grassroots NGOs.

3. Justification

  • Agree where aid is supply-driven, short-term and channelled through parallel structures: dependence then erodes ownership.
  • Disagree where aid is aligned with local plans, routed through local institutions and comes with an exit strategy: it can deepen participation.
  • Localisation: the Grand Bargain (2016) committed humanitarian donors to channel 25% of funding to local and national responders, recognising this lesson.

Donor money is neither good nor bad in itself. Development lasts when communities own it, so aid should follow local priorities, strengthen panchayats and SHGs, and plan its own exit.
free.upm-2022-gs2-18:
Article 21ARTE Act, 2009Incentives and awarenessLearning outcomes

The 86th Amendment (2002) made free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a fundamental right under Article 21A, given effect by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 from 1 April 2010. The Act and allied schemes rely heavily on incentives: free schooling, textbooks, uniforms, mid-day meals and reserved seats in private schools. Incentives bring children to school, but only awareness of the value of schooling keeps them there and makes them learn.

1. The incentive architecture

  • Entitlements under the Act: a neighbourhood school, no fees or capitation, no screening tests, pupil–teacher norms and a ban on physical punishment and mental harassment (Section 17).
  • 25% seats for disadvantaged children in private unaided schools (Section 12(1)(c)), upheld in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012).
  • Schemes: PM POSHAN (mid-day meals, renamed in 2021), Samagra Shiksha (2018) for textbooks, uniforms and transport, bicycles for girls in several States, and scholarships.
  • Results: enrolment at the elementary level is close to universal, and gender gaps at entry have largely closed.

2. Why incentives alone are inadequate

  • Attendance and dropout: enrolment is not attendance; many children drop out at the transition to secondary school, especially girls, tribal children and children of seasonal migrants.
  • Learning crisis: ASER 2024 found that only 23.4% of Class 3 children in rural government schools could read a Class 2 text (16.3% in 2022), and ASER 2023 found about a quarter of 14–18-year-olds could not read a Class 2 text fluently in their regional language.
  • Low parental demand: parents of first-generation learners may value immediate earnings or sibling care over schooling.
  • Unused rights: many eligible parents do not know how to claim the 25% private-school seats, and School Management Committees, where three-fourths of members must be parents (Section 21), often exist only on paper.
  • No-detention debate: automatic promotion without remedial teaching weakened accountability; the 2019 amendment let the Union and State governments hold examinations in Classes 5 and 8, and since December 2024 central schools may hold back students who fail a re-examination after two months of extra teaching, though no child can be expelled before completing elementary education.

3. Role of awareness

  • Community mobilisation: enrolment festivals such as Gujarat's Shala Praveshotsav and campaigns by teachers and panchayats raise demand for schooling.
  • Active SMCs: trained parents can monitor teacher attendance, meals and school grants and prepare school development plans.
  • Linking school to aspirations: career guidance and vocational exposure under NEP 2020 show families the returns to education.
  • Foundational learning: NIPUN Bharat (2021) aims at foundational literacy and numeracy for every child by the end of Class 3 by 2026-27, which needs parents' engagement at home.

The RTE Act secured access; the next task is participation and learning. Awareness turns schooling from a State supply into a community demand, and that is what makes the right to education meaningful.
free.upm-2022-gs2-19:
I2U2MinilateralismWest AsiaFood and energy security

I2U2, grouping India, Israel, the UAE and the USA, was conceived at a meeting of foreign ministers in October 2021 and held its first, virtual leaders' summit on 14 July 2022. Often called the "West Asian Quad", it focuses on joint investments in six areas: water, energy, transportation, space, health and food security. Built on the Abraham Accords (2020), it reflects India's turn to minilateralism and could reshape India's place in West Asia.

1. Initiatives announced

  • Food security: the UAE committed US$2 billion to develop integrated food parks across India, with US and Israeli private-sector expertise and Indian farmland and farmers.
  • Clean energy: a hybrid renewable project in Gujarat with 300 MW of wind and solar capacity and battery storage.
  • Private capital: the grouping aims to mobilise private capital and expertise for infrastructure, low-carbon industry and public health.

2. How I2U2 can transform India's position

  • From buyer to partner: India, long an importer of Gulf oil and a source of workers, becomes a co-investor and a supplier of food to the Gulf.
  • De-hyphenation: India can work with Israel and Arab states at the same table, while keeping ties with Iran and supporting a two-state solution for Palestine.
  • Beyond the Indo-Pacific: cooperation with the USA extends from the Quad into West Asia, making India a bridge between the two regions.
  • Technology and capital: Israeli agri-tech and water management, Emirati sovereign funds and US finance support India's farm and energy transitions.
  • Connectivity: India, the UAE and the USA are also partners in the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC, 2023), planned to link India to Europe through the Gulf and Israel.
  • Economic weight: the Gulf hosts about 9 million Indians; the India–UAE CEPA (2022) and rupee–dirham settlement (2023) deepen ties.

3. Limits and challenges

  • Regional conflict: the Gaza war since October 2023 and the 2026 conflict involving Iran have slowed the grouping, and public opinion in Arab states makes visible cooperation with Israel difficult.
  • Iran factor: India's interests in Chabahar and energy mean it cannot be seen as part of an anti-Iran bloc.
  • Slow delivery: the food-park and energy projects have moved slowly, and no regular leaders' summit has followed the first.
  • Great-power competition: China's growing role in the Gulf, seen when it brokered the Saudi–Iran deal in 2023, and shifts in US policy.

4. Assessment

I2U2 will not transform India's position by itself, but it adds a new layer to India's multi-alignment: alongside the Quad, BRICS and the SCO, it shows India working with very different partners on practical goals.

If it delivers projects, I2U2 can make India a net provider of food and clean-energy solutions in West Asia and a bridge between regions; India must pursue it while preserving strategic autonomy in a volatile neighbourhood.
free.upm-2022-gs2-20:
Climate diplomacyCBDR-RCPanchamritEnergy geopolitics

India's climate policy has moved from a defensive stance, insisting that developed countries bear historical responsibility, to a proactive one that combines common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) with ambitious targets and leadership of new coalitions. Clean energy is indeed the order of the day: non-fossil sources crossed half of India's installed power capacity in June 2025, and its NDC 3.0 (2026) targets 60% by 2035. Geopolitics, from energy security to trade and great-power rivalry, has shaped this shift.

1. Phase I: equity first (1972–2008)

  • Stockholm (1972): Indira Gandhi linked poverty and the environment, arguing that development is part of the solution.
  • Rio (1992) and Kyoto (1997): India helped write CBDR into the UNFCCC; binding cuts applied only to developed (Annex I) countries, and India used the Clean Development Mechanism.
  • NAPCC (2008): eight national missions; domestic action without international obligations.

2. Phase II: voluntary commitments (2009–2015)

  • Copenhagen (2009): acting with Brazil, South Africa and China (BASIC), India announced a voluntary 20–25% cut in the emissions intensity of GDP by 2020 from 2005 levels.
  • Paris (2015): its first NDC promised a 33–35% intensity cut, 40% non-fossil power capacity and a carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes by 2030; India and France launched the International Solar Alliance at COP21.

3. Phase III: leadership and ambition (2016–2026)

  • Glasgow (2021): the Panchamrit, including 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070; India pressed for a coal "phase-down" rather than "phase-out".
  • Updated NDC (2022): a 45% intensity cut and about 50% non-fossil capacity by 2030, with Mission LiFE as a global mass movement.
  • G20 presidency (2023): the Green Development Pact, the Global Biofuels Alliance and support for tripling renewable capacity.
  • Finance diplomacy: India called the COP29 goal (2024) of US$300 billion a year by 2035 far too little; COP30 (Belém, 2025) agreed to triple adaptation finance by 2035.
  • NDC 3.0 (March 2026): a 47% intensity cut and 60% non-fossil capacity by 2035.

4. Geopolitics behind the change

  • Energy security: India imports nearly 89% of its crude oil (2025-26); the 2022 energy shock after the Russia–Ukraine war and disruption of West Asian shipping in 2026 make solar, wind and green hydrogen strategic assets.
  • Competition with China: China dominates solar modules, batteries and critical minerals; India responds with PLI schemes and the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025).
  • Trade measures: India opposes unilateral measures such as the EU's carbon border tax (CBAM, definitive phase from January 2026).
  • US retreat: the USA's second exit from the Paris Agreement took effect in January 2026, and it also announced its exit from the ISA; this widens the finance gap but opens space for India to lead the Global South through coalitions such as the ISA and CDRI.

India has turned clean energy from a burden-sharing dispute into a development and strategic opportunity. Its diplomacy now blends climate justice with climate leadership, while pressing for finance and technology on fair terms.
free.upm-2022-gs3-1:
Public-Private PartnershipInfrastructure financingStation redevelopmentAmrit Bharat Station Scheme

A Public-Private Partnership (PPP) is a long-term contract in which a private partner finances, builds or operates a public asset and bears agreed risks, in return for user charges or payments from the government. India's infrastructure needs are huge: the National Infrastructure Pipeline (2019) projected about ₹111 lakh crore of investment for 2020-25, which budgets alone cannot fund. Railway stations, sitting on valuable urban land, are natural candidates for such partnerships.

1. Why PPP is required in infrastructure

  • Resource gap: public investment competes with health, education and welfare; private capital, along with asset monetisation (National Monetisation Pipeline, 2021), widens the pool of funds.
  • Efficiency: private firms bring design skills, technology and project management, and are rewarded for finishing on time.
  • Risk sharing: construction, operation and demand risks can rest with the party best able to manage them, as in the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016) for highways.
  • Life-cycle quality and value capture: a builder who also maintains the asset has a reason to build well, and land and footfall at stations or airports can earn revenue to cross-subsidise public facilities.

2. Role of PPP in redeveloping railway stations

  • The model: the developer upgrades the station and recovers its money from long leases of surplus railway land or air space for shops, offices and hotels.
  • Rani Kamalapati (Habibganj), Bhopal: redeveloped under the PPP model and opened in November 2021, with an airport-like concourse, modern passenger amenities and commercial development on railway land.
  • Gandhinagar Capital (2021): built through a joint venture of the Railways' station development company and the Gujarat government, with a hotel above the platforms.
  • A mix of models: for the largest stations the Government chose public funding instead, approving the redevelopment of New Delhi, Ahmedabad and Mumbai CSMT (about ₹10,000 crore) in 2022, while private partners take up commercial development and services.
  • Scale-up: under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, over 1,300 stations are being upgraded in phases; 103 were dedicated in May 2025 and 75 more in July 2026, taking the number of completed stations to 261.

3. Challenges

  • Land and heritage: encroachments, unclear titles and heritage buildings complicate plans.
  • Market risk: commercial land earns well mainly in big cities, so smaller stations cannot pay for themselves.
  • Affordability and coordination: user charges may burden poorer passengers, work must go on without stopping trains, and railways, city, metro and bus agencies must plan together.

4. Way forward: hybrid designs, with public money for the core station and PPP for commercial spaces, parking, retail and maintenance; balanced risk sharing and a renegotiation framework, as the Kelkar Committee (2015) urged; and multimodal hubs with metro and bus links planned under PM Gati Shakti.

Station redevelopment shows that PPP works best as a flexible partnership: private capital where commercial returns exist, public funding where they do not, both aimed at citizen-centric stations.
free.upm-2022-gs3-2:
Inclusive growthMarket economyFinancial inclusionJAM trinity

Inclusive growth is growth that is broad-based across sectors, regions and social groups, so that the poor share in its opportunities and benefits; the Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-12) made "faster and more inclusive growth" its goal. In a market economy, prices and profits allocate resources. Markets create wealth efficiently but do not by themselves spread it fairly, so the answer lies in how markets and public policy work together.

1. Is inclusive growth possible under a market economy?

  • Yes, markets can include: after the 1991 reforms, faster growth, competition and cheaper goods and services lifted millions out of poverty; NITI Aayog estimated that multidimensional poverty fell from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21).
  • But markets alone exclude: people without assets, skills, credit or connectivity cannot take part, and growth led by capital- and skill-intensive sectors creates few jobs.
  • Market failures: private firms under-provide public goods such as health, schooling and rural roads, while information gaps and unequal bargaining power concentrate gains.
  • Hence markets plus the State: inclusion is possible when the State builds human capital, provides public goods and social protection and keeps markets competitive, as Kerala's social investments and the Nordic welfare states show.

2. Significance of financial inclusion for economic growth

The Rangarajan Committee (2008) defined financial inclusion as access to financial services and timely, adequate credit for vulnerable groups at an affordable cost.

  • Mobilises savings: PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) has over 59 crore accounts, about 56% held by women, turning idle household cash into deposits that fund investment.
  • Credit for enterprise: Mudra loans, Stand-Up India, PM SVANidhi and SHG–bank linkage finance micro-enterprises, farmers and street vendors, creating self-employment.
  • Formalisation and productivity: UPI and digital payments build credit histories, widen the tax base and cut transaction costs.
  • Efficient transfers: the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) has carried Direct Benefit Transfers of over ₹52 lakh crore through 900+ schemes, plugging leakages and freeing fiscal space.
  • Resilience and demand: insurance and pensions (PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana) protect households from shocks and sustain consumption.

3. Gaps that remain

  • Usage lags access: the RBI's Financial Inclusion Index rose to 70.0 in March 2026 from 67.0 a year earlier, but dormant accounts, low use of credit and insurance, gender gaps in usage and rising digital fraud remain.

Markets can deliver inclusive growth only when enabling public policy gives everyone the capabilities to take part. Meaningful financial inclusion, with credit, insurance and financial literacy, is one of its strongest levers.
free.upm-2022-gs3-3:
Public Distribution SystemNFSA 2013Leakages and targetingEnd-to-end computerisation

The Public Distribution System (PDS) supplies foodgrains through fair price shops: the Centre procures and allocates grain through the Food Corporation of India, and the States identify beneficiaries and distribute it. Under the National Food Security Act, 2013, it covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population, and about 81 crore people receive free grain under PMGKAY, extended for five years from January 2024.

1. Major challenges

  • Targeting errors: State-wise coverage is still based on Census 2011, so many urban poor and migrants are left out while some ineligible households hold cards; 41.41 lakh ineligible cards were deleted in 2025 alone.
  • Leakage and diversion: the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) estimated that about 46% of PDS grain leaked out before reaching households; diversion to open markets still occurs.
  • Authentication failures: biometric checks on ePoS machines fail for the elderly and manual workers, and connectivity is poor in remote and tribal areas.
  • Storage and quality: open (CAP) storage, long transport and repeated handling cause losses and poor-quality grain.
  • Nutrition gap: a cereal-heavy basket with few pulses, millets or oils does little against anaemia and hidden hunger.
  • Costs and dealers: a food subsidy bill of about ₹2 lakh crore a year, and low margins for shop dealers that encourage short weighing.

2. Making it effective

  • Better targeting: revise coverage with fresh population data, use e-KYC and data analytics to remove ineligible cards, and include the urban poor, migrants and the homeless.
  • Diversify the basket: add millets, pulses and edible oils, and link the PDS with POSHAN and school meals for nutrition security.
  • Reliable authentication: iris and OTP options, and home delivery for the elderly and disabled where biometrics fail.
  • Viable shops: higher dealer margins, permission to sell other goods, and women's SHGs and cooperatives as dealers.
  • Cash where markets work: the Shanta Kumar Committee suggested gradual cash transfers in cities; DBT for food subsidy was piloted in Chandigarh and Puducherry in 2015.

3. Making it transparent

  • End-to-end computerisation: ration-card and beneficiary data are fully digitised, almost all fair price shops use ePoS machines, 99.2% of beneficiaries are Aadhaar-seeded and 98.75% of grain is distributed with digital authentication (Rajya Sabha, March 2026).
  • Portability: One Nation One Ration Card lets migrants draw rations anywhere in the country.
  • Community oversight: social audits (Section 28) and vigilance committees (Section 29) under the NFSA, District Grievance Redressal Officers (Section 15), State Food Commissions and helplines; Chhattisgarh's reforms showed how community-run shops and computerisation cut leakage.

With technology plugging leakages, a more nutritious basket and community accountability, the PDS can grow from a grain-distribution scheme into a true nutrition safety net.
free.upm-2022-gs3-4:
Food processingValue additionPost-harvest lossesSunrise sector

Food processing turns farm, dairy, fishery and livestock produce into higher-value, longer-lasting products, from cleaning and grading to ready-to-eat foods. India is the largest producer of milk and pulses and the second-largest of fruits and vegetables, yet only a small share of its perishables is processed, and post-harvest losses are worth about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS, 2022). This makes food processing a sunrise sector linking farm and factory.

1. Scope of the food processing industry

  • Raw-material base: varied agro-climates give year-round supplies of cereals, millets, fruits, vegetables, spices, milk, eggs, meat and fish.
  • Low processing levels: the gap between production and processing leaves wide headroom for investment in perishables, dairy, meat and marine products.
  • Changing demand: urbanisation, rising incomes, working women and smaller families raise demand for packaged, ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat foods, sold through supermarkets, e-commerce and quick-commerce apps.
  • Exports: marine products, rice, spices and mango pulp already sell abroad; branded Indian foods and millet products can capture more value.
  • Allied industries: packaging, cold chains, logistics, food-testing laboratories and machinery grow alongside.

2. Significance

  • Farmers' incomes: processors offer an assured market and better prices, reducing distress sales of perishables such as tomato, onion and potato.
  • Less waste, steadier prices: processing and cold chains extend shelf life, cut losses and smooth seasonal price swings.
  • Jobs: the industry is labour-intensive and largely rural, employing many women and SHG members in micro units.
  • Nutrition: fortified foods, millet products and safe packaged food support nutrition security.
  • Exports and rural industry: value-added exports earn foreign exchange, and units near farms bring industry to villages.

3. Government support

  • Schemes: PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (2017) for cold chains and agro-processing clusters; the PLI scheme for food processing (₹10,900 crore); PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (₹10,000 crore) with One District One Product; and Operation Greens for perishables.
  • Investment: 100% FDI under the automatic route in food processing, a Food Processing Fund with NABARD and the World Food India expos.

4. Constraints

  • Bottlenecks: small, scattered farms, gaps in cold chains and power, informal units with weak access to credit and FSSAI compliance, and costly packaging hold the sector back.

Food processing can make India the food basket of the world, raising farm incomes, cutting waste and creating rural jobs, provided infrastructure, credit and quality standards keep pace.
free.upm-2022-gs3-5:
Life expectancyPopulation ageingNon-communicable diseasesGeriatric care

India's life expectancy has risen from about 32 years in 1951 to about 72 years (Human Development Report 2025), thanks to vaccines, sanitation, better nutrition and medical care. Longer lives and falling fertility are driving population ageing: the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to double from 10.5% (2022) to 20.8% by 2050 (India Ageing Report 2023). The health burden is shifting towards non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and old-age care.

1. New health challenges

  • NCD epidemic: heart disease, stroke, diabetes, hypertension, cancer and chronic lung disease now cause about two-thirds of deaths in India, and many older people live with several conditions at once.
  • Geriatric conditions: dementia, falls, frailty, arthritis and loss of vision and hearing reduce independence.
  • Mental health: loneliness, depression and elder abuse rise as families become nuclear and children migrate.
  • Long-term care: home-care services, palliative care and trained geriatricians are scarce, and the care burden falls mainly on women in families.
  • Financial insecurity: about 90% of workers are informal and lack pensions, and high out-of-pocket spending on chronic disease pushes families into poverty.
  • Unequal ageing: elderly widows, the rural poor and the disabled are most vulnerable, and digital health services can exclude them.

2. Steps taken

  • Financial protection: since October 2024 Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers everyone aged 70 and above regardless of income (Ayushman Vay Vandana card).
  • Primary care: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (health and wellness centres) screen adults for hypertension, diabetes and common cancers.
  • Geriatric services: the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (2010) supports geriatric wards and clinics, with National Centres of Ageing at AIIMS New Delhi and Madras Medical College.
