  • Rights and welfare: the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, the Elder Line helpline 14567 and the Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana for assistive devices.

3. Steps needed

  • Prevention across life: tobacco and salt control, physical activity, healthy diets and clean air, so that people reach old age in better health.
  • A care workforce: train geriatricians, nurses and community caregivers, and expand home-based, community and palliative care.
  • Financing long-term care: wider pension coverage, long-term care insurance and support for family caregivers.
  • Technology and data: telemedicine such as eSanjeevani, assistive devices, and the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) to guide policy.
  • Age-friendly cities: accessible transport, housing and public spaces, and a "silver economy" that keeps older people active.

The goal must shift from adding years to life to adding healthy years. Prevention, affordable chronic care and dignified long-term support can turn longevity into an asset rather than a burden.
free.upm-2022-gs3-6:
CelluloseDecompositionCellulasesCarbon cycle

Cellulose, a long chain of glucose units joined by β-1,4 bonds, is the most abundant organic compound on Earth and the main component of plant cell walls, where it is bound with hemicellulose and lignin as lignocellulose. Most animals cannot digest it, so its return to the air as carbon dioxide depends on micro-organisms. This decomposition closes the carbon cycle: carbon fixed by photosynthesis is released again by respiration.

1. Physical breakdown and fragmentation

  • Leaching: rain dissolves sugars and other soluble compounds from fallen leaves and wood.
  • Fragmentation by detritivores: earthworms, termites, millipedes and mites shred litter, increasing the surface area for microbes, and earthworms mix it into the soil.
  • Weathering: sunlight, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing loosen plant tissue.

2. Enzymatic breakdown by micro-organisms

  • Decomposers: fungi (such as Trichoderma and white-rot and brown-rot fungi) and bacteria (such as Cellulomonas, Clostridium and actinomycetes) secrete enzymes outside their cells.
  • Cellulase complex: endoglucanases cut the cellulose chain internally, exoglucanases release two-glucose units (cellobiose), and β-glucosidase splits cellobiose into glucose.
  • Lignin first: lignin shields cellulose; white-rot fungi break it down with peroxidases and laccases, which is why wood decays slowly.
  • Symbiotic digestion: microbes in the rumen of cattle and in the gut of termites digest cellulose for their hosts.

3. Aerobic decomposition (oxygen present)

  • Respiration: microbes oxidise glucose through glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, releasing carbon dioxide, water and energy.
  • Mineralisation: nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients in the litter are released in inorganic forms such as ammonium, nitrate and phosphate for plants.
  • Humification: resistant residues, largely from lignin, become dark, stable humus that stores carbon in the soil for decades or centuries.

4. Anaerobic decomposition (oxygen absent)

  • Fermentation: in waterlogged soils, paddy fields, wetlands, landfills and animal guts, bacteria ferment glucose into organic acids (acetic, propionic, butyric), alcohols, hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
  • Methanogenesis: methanogenic archaea turn acetate and hydrogen into methane, which is later oxidised in the air to carbon dioxide and water; this is why paddies, wetlands and cattle emit methane.
  • Incomplete decay: where it is cold, acidic or waterlogged, decay is so slow that plant matter piles up as peat, which over geological time can become coal.

Controlling factors: temperature, moisture, oxygen, pH and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the litter decide the speed; decay is fastest in the warm, humid tropics and slowest in cold or waterlogged places.

Cellulose decomposition recycles carbon and nutrients and builds soil. Managing it well, through composting, biogas and an end to crop-residue burning, turns this natural process into a tool for soil health and climate mitigation.
free.upm-2022-gs3-7:
Photochemical smogGround-level ozoneNOx and VOCsGothenburg Protocol

Photochemical smog is a brownish haze of secondary pollutants formed when nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), mainly from vehicles and industry, react in sunlight. Its main products are ground-level ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN). First explained in Los Angeles in the early 1950s, it differs from the sulphurous "London smog" of coal smoke and fog, and now affects many Indian cities in hot, sunny months.

1. Formation

  • Conditions: strong sunlight, warm temperatures, still air or a temperature inversion, and heavy traffic.
  • Ozone from NO₂: sunlight splits nitrogen dioxide into nitric oxide and an oxygen atom (NO₂ → NO + O), and the atom joins an oxygen molecule to form ozone (O + O₂ → O₃).
  • Role of VOCs: nitric oxide normally destroys this ozone again, but radicals from VOCs convert NO back to NO₂ without using up ozone, so ozone builds up through the day.
  • Other products: VOCs and NOx also form PAN, aldehydes such as formaldehyde, and fine secondary organic aerosols; levels peak in the afternoon.

2. Effects

  • Health: ozone inflames the airways, worsens asthma and reduces lung function; PAN and aldehydes irritate the eyes.
  • Crops and forests: ozone damages leaf tissue and lowers the yields of crops such as wheat and rice.
  • Materials and visibility: it cracks rubber, fades dyes and paints, and reduces visibility.
  • Climate: ozone in the lower atmosphere is also a greenhouse gas.

3. Mitigation

  • Vehicles: Bharat Stage VI norms (from April 2020), catalytic converters, CNG and electric vehicles, and better public transport.
  • VOC control: vapour recovery at fuel stations, low-solvent paints and industrial emission limits.
  • Policy: the National Clean Air Programme (2019), the Commission for Air Quality Management (set up in 2020; Act of 2021) and ozone limits in the National Ambient Air Quality Standards.

4. The 1999 Gothenburg Protocol

  • What it is: the "Protocol to Abate Acidification, Eutrophication and Ground-level Ozone", adopted in 1999 under the UNECE Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution (1979).
  • Multi-pollutant approach: the first agreement to tackle several pollutants and their effects together, it sets national emission ceilings for sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, VOCs and ammonia, the precursors of acid rain, eutrophication and smog.
  • 2012 revision: fine particulate matter (PM2.5) was added, with black carbon recognised as a component, and commitments were set for 2020 and beyond; the amended Protocol entered into force on 7 October 2019.
  • Results and relevance: the Convention's protocols have helped cut certain pollutants by 40–80%. India, outside the UNECE region, is not a party, but the regional "airshed" approach suits the Indo-Gangetic plain.

Photochemical smog is a by-product of motorisation and heat. Cutting NOx and VOCs together, as the Gothenburg Protocol does through binding ceilings, offers a template for regional air-quality cooperation in South Asia.
free.upm-2022-gs3-8:
CloudburstOrographic liftFlash floodsHimalaya

A cloudburst is an extreme, highly localised downpour. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) defines it as at least 100 mm of rain within an hour over an area of about 20–30 sq km. In the Indian subcontinent cloudbursts occur mostly over the Himalaya, and less often over the Western Ghats, during the monsoon, triggering flash floods, landslides and debris flows in narrow mountain valleys.

1. Mechanism

  • Moisture supply: monsoon winds carry huge amounts of moisture from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea to the mountains.
  • Orographic lift and convection: steep slopes force the moist air to rise rapidly, and daytime heating of the slopes adds to the uplift; as the air cools, moisture condenses into towering cumulonimbus clouds.
  • Updrafts hold the water: strong updrafts keep raindrops and ice suspended and let them grow by collision and coalescence; when the updraft weakens or collapses, the accumulated water falls almost at once.
  • Clash of weather systems: a western disturbance meeting moist monsoon winds can produce very heavy rain, as experts noted in the western Himalayan floods of August 2025.

2. Occurrence in the Indian subcontinent

  • Where: Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand are most affected, because steep, narrow valleys trap clouds and funnel water downstream.
  • When: mostly during the south-west monsoon, from June to September.
  • Why damage is high: young, loose rocks and deforested slopes turn rain into debris flows, while houses, hotels and roads sit on riverbanks.
  • Warming: air holds about 7% more moisture for each 1°C of warming, raising the risk of extreme bursts.
  • Hard to confirm: gauges and radars are sparse in the mountains, so events are often labelled cloudbursts without proof; after the Dharali flash flood in Uttarakhand (5 August 2025), IMD officials said the available data did not show a cloudburst.

3. Two recent examples

  • Kishtwar, Jammu and Kashmir (14 August 2025): a flash flood from extremely heavy rain struck Chasoti village on the Machail Mata pilgrimage route, killing at least 65 people; analysts noted that the recorded rain may not have met the formal cloudburst threshold.
  • Amarnath, Jammu and Kashmir (8 July 2022): very heavy, localised rain sent a flash flood through the pilgrims' tent camp near the holy cave, killing over a dozen people and exposing the danger of camps on stream beds.

4. Way forward

  • Observation and warning: denser Doppler radars and automatic rain gauges under Mission Mausam (2024), and nowcasting with village-level alerts.
  • Land-use discipline: no construction on floodplains and unstable slopes, regulated pilgrim camps, slope stabilisation and community preparedness, as NDMA guidelines advise.

Cloudbursts cannot be prevented, but their disaster risk can be cut through better observation, early warning and land-use discipline in the fragile Himalaya.
free.upm-2022-gs3-9:
Organised crimeCrime–terror nexusNarco-terrorismTransnational networks

Organised crime is continuing unlawful activity by a structured group that uses violence, intimidation or corruption for financial gain. The UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (Palermo Convention, 2000), which India ratified in 2011, defines an organised criminal group as three or more persons acting together to commit serious crimes for material benefit. In India, Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 now defines organised crime.

1. Types of organised crime

  • Common features: continuity, hierarchy, use of violence and corruption, profit as the motive, and operation across States and borders.
  • New forms: scam compounds abroad run online fraud and hold trafficked Indian workers, while cryptocurrency and darknet markets make crime faceless.

2. Linkages at the national level

  • Mumbai, 1993: the D-company's smuggling network landed explosives on the Raigad coast for the serial blasts, the clearest case of criminals serving terrorists.
  • Punjab: gangsters, drug smugglers and Khalistani handlers abroad share drones, weapons and couriers; the NIA has pursued gangster–terror networks since 2022.
  • Jammu and Kashmir: narcotics, hawala and fake currency fund militancy; the NIA's 2017 case traced hawala money to separatist leaders.
  • North-East: insurgent groups levy extortion "taxes" and protect drug and arms smuggling from Myanmar.
  • Left Wing Extremism: Maoists collect "levies" from contractors and businesses, and cannabis on the Andhra–Odisha border has been linked to their funding.

3. Linkages at the transnational level

  • Narco-terrorism: heroin from the Golden Crescent and methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle finance armed groups; about 3,000 kg of heroin was seized at Mundra port in 2021.
  • Fake currency: high-quality counterfeit notes are printed across the border and pushed in through Nepal, Bangladesh and the Gulf.
  • Money movement: hawala, cryptocurrency, trade-based laundering and shell companies move funds beyond regulators' reach.
  • Arms and safe havens: criminal networks abroad supply weapons and shelter fugitives, while terror groups offer protection and routes.
  • Global pattern: ISIS sold oil and antiquities and the Taliban taxed opium, showing that terror groups increasingly finance themselves through crime.

4. Response

  • Laws and agencies: the UAPA (counterfeiting high-quality currency has been a terrorist act since 2012), the PMLA, the NIA Act amendment of 2019 (adding human trafficking, arms, counterfeit currency and cyber-terrorism), the BNS, FIU-IND and NATGRID, with cooperation through the FATF, Interpol and UNODC.

Because crime and terror feed each other, India must follow the money, share intelligence across agencies and borders, and treat organised crime as a national security threat.
free.upm-2022-gs3-10:
Maritime securityCoastal securityMaritime domain awarenessPost-26/11 reforms

India has a coastline of about 11,099 km (2025 re-measurement) and an Exclusive Economic Zone of over 2 million sq km, and about 95% of its trade by volume moves by sea. Maritime security means keeping these waters, ports and coasts safe from state and non-state threats. The 26/11 Mumbai attack (2008), carried out by terrorists who came by sea, exposed gaps and led to a major overhaul of coastal security.

1. Maritime security challenges

  • Sea-borne terrorism: explosives for the 1993 Mumbai blasts were landed on the coast.
  • Smuggling: narcotics (about 3,000 kg of heroin at Mundra in 2021; about six tonnes of methamphetamine off the Andamans in November 2024), arms, gold and fake currency.
  • Piracy and attacks on shipping: Somali piracy revived in 2023–24, and a drone struck the tanker MV Chem Pluto off Gujarat (December 2023).
  • Illegal fishing and boundary issues: foreign trawlers in Indian waters and arrests of fishermen in the Palk Bay.
  • Strategic competition and gaps: Chinese research vessels in the region, lakhs of hard-to-track fishing boats, and under-equipped State marine police.

2. Organisational initiatives

  • Three-tier coastal security: the Navy is responsible for overall maritime security, the Coast Guard for coastal security in territorial waters, and State marine police for shallow waters near the shore.
  • Coordination bodies: the National Committee for Strengthening Maritime and Coastal Security, chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, and Joint Operations Centres of the Navy and Coast Guard.
  • National Maritime Security Coordinator (2022): in the National Security Council Secretariat, to bring civilian and military agencies together.
  • New units: the Navy's Sagar Prahari Bal and coastal police stations under the Coastal Security Scheme.

3. Technical initiatives

  • Coastal surveillance network: a chain of coastal radar stations with cameras and AIS receivers along the mainland and islands.
  • Information fusion: the NC3I network and the Information Management and Analysis Centre (Gurugram) build one maritime picture, and the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (2018) shares it with partners.
  • Tracking and identity: AIS on larger vessels, transponders for fishing boats, biometric identity cards for fishermen and colour coding of boats by State.
  • Platforms: the naval satellite GSAT-7 (2013), patrol aircraft, fast interceptor craft and warships such as INS Vikrant (2022).

4. Procedural initiatives

  • Exercises: Sagar Kavach drills and the national exercise Sea Vigil test how all agencies respond together.
  • Standard procedures: registration of fishing boats, SOPs for intercepting suspicious craft, and ISPS Code port security.
  • Community as "eyes and ears": fishing communities are trained to report suspicious movement.
  • Law and diplomacy: the Maritime Anti-Piracy Act, 2022, white-shipping agreements, and the SAGAR (2015) and MAHASAGAR (2025) visions for regional cooperation.

India has moved from a fragmented to a layered, networked coastal security system. A national maritime security strategy, better-equipped State marine police and full tracking of small boats can complete it.
free.upm-2022-gs3-11:
Labour productivityEmployment elasticityStructural transformationLabour-intensive manufacturing

Labour productivity is output per worker (or per hour worked). Growth can come from employing more workers or from each worker producing more; when output rises much faster than employment, growth is productivity-led and the employment elasticity of growth is low. India's recent growth fits this pattern: output has grown fast, but good jobs have not kept pace with a young, growing workforce.

1. Explaining the statement

  • The arithmetic: GDP growth roughly equals employment growth plus growth in output per worker; with modest job growth, most of India's growth has come from higher productivity.
  • Sectoral pattern: growth has been led by capital- and skill-intensive services such as IT, finance and telecom, and by capital-intensive industry, which add output with few workers; manufacturing is still only about 17% of GVA.
  • Technology and capital deepening: automation, digitalisation and better infrastructure raise output per worker in formal firms.
  • Slow reallocation: moving workers out of low-productivity farming raises average productivity, but agriculture still holds about 46% of workers (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Result: fast growth alongside underemployment, informality (about 90% of workers) and joblessness among educated youth; urban unemployment was 6.9% in September 2026 (PLFS, current weekly status).

2. Why productivity alone is not enough

  • Demographic pressure: the Economic Survey 2023-24 estimated that about 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs are needed every year until 2030.
  • Demand and equity: growth with few jobs narrows the consumer base and widens inequality.

3. A growth pattern that creates jobs without lowering productivity

  • Labour-intensive manufacturing: textiles, apparel, footwear, leather, food processing, toys and electronics assembly can absorb millions at far higher productivity than farming, riding the China-plus-one shift and new trade agreements.
  • MSMEs and clusters: easier credit, technology upgrading and cluster infrastructure help small firms grow, since they employ most non-farm workers.
  • Job-rich services: tourism, logistics, retail, health and care services, construction and housing.
  • Rural non-farm work and green jobs: agro-processing, dairy and fisheries near villages; rooftop solar installation, repair, recycling and electric mobility.
  • Skills and women: apprenticeships and Skill India raise productivity as jobs grow, while childcare, safe transport and hostels can lift women's participation.
  • Policy support: the Labour Codes (in force since November 2025) simplify compliance, and the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (₹99,446 crore, from August 2025) pays incentives to first-time employees and to employers for additional hires, aiming at over 3.5 crore jobs in two years.

India needs growth that raises productivity by moving workers into better jobs, not by doing without them. Labour-intensive manufacturing, skills and support for women's work can turn the demographic dividend into broad-based prosperity.
free.upm-2022-gs3-12:
PanchamritNon-fossil capacityCapacity vs generationEnergy subsidy reform

At COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) India's Panchamrit pledged to meet 50% of its energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030. The updated NDC (August 2022) formalised this as about 50% of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030, a goal reached in June 2025, five years early. Whether half of India's energy needs will come from renewables, however, depends on generation and total energy use, not capacity alone.

1. Yes: the capacity target is met and rising

  • Rapid growth: renewable capacity reached 299.25 GW in September 2026 (solar about 171 GW, wind about 59 GW), and non-fossil sources made up about 55% of the 554.5 GW total in August 2026.
  • Record additions: 55.3 GW of non-fossil capacity was added in 2025-26.
  • Policy push: solar parks, PM-KUSUM for farm solar, PM Surya Ghar for rooftop solar (over 50 lakh homes by August 2026), Green Energy Corridors and viability gap funding for battery storage.
  • Higher targets: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and 60% of capacity by 2035 (NDC 3.0).

2. No: half of all energy needs from renewables is unlikely by 2030

  • Capacity is not generation: non-fossil sources gave only 29.2% of electricity in 2025-26 (solar and wind about 15%), because solar works only by day and wind is seasonal; coal still produces about 70% of electricity.
  • Electricity is only part of energy: in primary energy, coal supplies over half and oil is second; transport, industry and cooking still run largely on fossil fuels.
  • Bottlenecks: storage for evening peaks, transmission delays and curtailment, land, weak discom finances, and imported cells, wafers and critical minerals.

3. How shifting subsidies from fossil fuels to renewables helps

  • The imbalance: India's energy subsidies were about ₹4.3 lakh crore (2.3% of GDP) in FY 2025, and support for fossil fuels was about three times that for clean energy (IISD, 2026).
  • Level playing field: subsidies hide the true cost of fossil energy; redirecting them makes solar, wind and storage more competitive.
  • Fund the missing pieces: savings can pay for storage, transmission, rooftop and farm solar, green hydrogen and electric mobility.
  • Smarter power subsidies: State electricity consumption subsidies (about ₹2.41 lakh crore) can be better targeted, and solarising farm feeders under PM-KUSUM cuts the cost of supplying subsidised farm power.
  • Precedent and fairness: deregulating petrol (2010) and diesel (2014) prices freed fiscal space; LPG support can stay targeted at the poor while electric cooking and biogas grow.

India has met the capacity form of the goal, but meeting half of its total energy needs from renewables will take longer. Shifting subsidies, with storage, grids and the electrification of transport and industry, can make the clean energy transition both faster and fair.
free.upm-2022-gs3-13:
Agricultural marketingUpstream and downstreamAPMC mandisFarmer's share of the consumer rupee

Agricultural marketing covers every activity from the farm gate to the consumer. It is a State subject (Entry 28, State List), regulated by each State's APMC Act. The upstream stage runs from the farm to the first point of sale (harvest, assembly, grading, storage and transport to market); the downstream stage runs from the market to processors, retailers, exporters and consumers. Bottlenecks at both ends keep the farmer's share of the consumer's rupee low.

1. Upstream bottlenecks

  • Small, scattered lots: 86% of holdings are small and marginal (Agriculture Census 2015-16), so farmers sell tiny, ungraded lots with little bargaining power.
  • Distress sales: lack of storage and the need for cash to repay loans force sales right after harvest, when prices are lowest; traders who also lend tie farmers to themselves.
  • No grading or assaying: produce is rarely cleaned, sorted or tested at the farm gate, so it fetches less and cannot be traded online with confidence.
  • Distance and transport: the National Commission on Farmers sought a regulated market within about 5 km of every farmer, but mandis are far apart and rural roads and vehicles are inadequate.
  • Losses and information gaps: post-harvest losses are worth about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS, 2022), and farmers often lack price and demand information when deciding what to sow and when to sell.
  • Weak collectives: many Farmer Producer Organisations lack capital, management skills and market links.

2. Downstream bottlenecks

  • Mandi practices: few licensed traders, cartels, commission agents, multiple fees and delayed payments lower the farmer's price.
  • Fragmented regulation: separate State laws, multiple licences and limits on inter-State trade split the national market; the 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021.
  • Long chains: produce changes hands several times before reaching consumers, adding margins and losses.
  • Weak cold chains and processing: perishables cannot be stored or processed, causing boom-and-bust cycles in tomato, onion and potato.
  • Policy uncertainty: sudden export bans and stock limits, as on wheat (2022) and onion (2023-24), disrupt trade and prices.
  • Quality and traceability: pesticide-residue limits and certification hurdles restrict exports.

3. Measures under way

  • Digital markets: e-NAM links 1,656 mandis in 23 States and 4 UTs with over 1.8 crore farmers (PIB, March 2026).
  • Upstream support: the scheme to form 10,000 FPOs (2020), the ₹1 lakh crore Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020) and the plan to upgrade rural haats into Gramin Agricultural Markets.

Fixing marketing needs work at both ends: aggregation and storage upstream, and competitive, integrated markets downstream, so that "One Nation, One Market" delivers a fair price to the farmer.
free.upm-2022-gs3-14:
Integrated Farming SystemResource recyclingSmall and marginal farmersRisk diversification

An Integrated Farming System (IFS) combines two or more interdependent enterprises, such as crops, dairy, poultry, fishery, goatery, horticulture, beekeeping, mushrooms and agroforestry, on one holding so that the waste of one becomes an input for another. Research on IFS is led by ICAR's Indian Institute of Farming Systems Research, Modipuram (Meerut). It suits India, where 86% of holdings are small and marginal (Agriculture Census 2015-16).

1. What makes IFS different

  • Synergy and recycling: crop residues feed livestock; dung goes to compost, vermicompost or a biogas plant; slurry and pond silt fertilise fields; and fish feed on farm by-products.
  • Diversification: several enterprises with different seasons and markets replace dependence on a single crop.
  • Location-specific models: rice–fish–duck systems in wet lowlands, crop–dairy–fodder systems in irrigated plains, and crop–goat–tree systems in dry regions.
  • Efficient use of land and water: a farm pond stores rainwater for fish and irrigation, and boundary trees and vertical structures use every bit of land.

2. How IFS helps small and marginal farmers

  • Higher, steadier income: milk, eggs and fish bring daily or weekly cash, and crops bring seasonal income; field studies by ICAR institutes report higher net returns than from crops alone.
  • Risk spreading: if the monsoon fails or crop prices crash, livestock and fish still earn, which matters most for rainfed farmers.
  • Lower costs and debt: farm-made manure, biogas and fodder cut spending on fertiliser, fuel and feed.
  • Year-round employment: family labour, especially women, is used through the year, reducing distress migration.
  • Nutrition at home: milk, eggs, fish, fruit and vegetables diversify the family diet.
  • Soil health and resilience: organic matter improves soil, residues are not burnt, and diverse systems withstand droughts and floods better.

3. Challenges and support

  • Challenges: initial capital for animals and ponds, skills in several enterprises, water, veterinary services, and markets for many small lots of produce.
  • Support: the Rainfed Area Development component of the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture promotes IFS, backed by RKVY, the National Livestock Mission, PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020), demonstrations by Krishi Vigyan Kendras, natural farming and FPOs for marketing.

For a farmer with one or two hectares, IFS turns a single risky crop into a self-sustaining farm enterprise that raises income, nutrition and resilience, a practical path to sustainable intensification of small farms.
free.upm-2022-gs3-15:
James Webb Space TelescopeInfrared astronomySecond Lagrange pointCosmic dawn

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), built by NASA with the European and Canadian space agencies, was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana, and began science operations in July 2022. It orbits the Sun near the second Lagrange point (L2), about 1.5 million km from Earth, and is the largest and most powerful infrared space telescope, the scientific successor to Hubble (1990) and the infrared Spitzer (2003–2020).

1. Unique features that make it superior

  • Giant mirror: a 6.5 m primary mirror of 18 hexagonal, gold-coated beryllium segments has over six times the light-collecting area of Hubble's 2.4 m mirror; it was folded for launch and unfolded in space.
  • Infrared vision: it observes from about 0.6 to 28.5 micrometres; infrared passes through dust clouds and catches light from the most distant galaxies, which cosmic expansion has stretched (redshifted) from visible into infrared.
  • Cold operation: a five-layer sunshield about the size of a tennis court keeps the instruments below about −220 °C, and a cryocooler chills the mid-infrared instrument further, so the telescope's own heat does not swamp faint signals.
  • Location at L2: unlike Hubble in low Earth orbit, it keeps the Sun, Earth and Moon behind its shield, giving a stable, cold, uninterrupted view.
  • Powerful instruments: NIRCam, NIRSpec (spectra of up to 100 objects at once), MIRI and NIRISS reveal the chemistry of galaxies, stars and planetary atmospheres.

2. Key goals of the mission

  • First light and reionisation: find the first stars and galaxies that formed after the Big Bang.
  • Assembly of galaxies: trace how galaxies and their central black holes grew and evolved.
  • Birth of stars and planetary systems: look inside the dusty clouds where stars and planets form.
  • Planets and the origins of life: study exoplanet atmospheres and objects in our own solar system.

3. Results so far

  • Record distances: MoM-z14 (2025) is seen as it was about 280 million years after the Big Bang (redshift 14.44, confirmed by spectroscopy), and early galaxies have proved brighter and more numerous than models predicted.
  • Exoplanets: it made the first clear detection of carbon dioxide in an exoplanet's atmosphere (WASP-39b, 2022).
  • Long life: a precise launch saved enough fuel for a mission of about 20 years.

4. Potential benefits for humanity

  • Answers to big questions: how the universe, galaxies, stars and planets formed, and whether life exists elsewhere.
  • Technology spin-offs: lightweight optics, infrared detectors, cryocoolers and precise mirror control have uses in medicine, industry and Earth observation.
  • Open science and inspiration: its data are shared with scientists worldwide, and its images draw young people towards science.

Webb carries Hubble's legacy into the infrared, letting humanity look back to cosmic dawn; its discoveries are already rewriting textbooks on galaxy formation and the search for life beyond Earth.
free.upm-2022-gs3-16:
VaccineActive immunityImmunological memoryVaccine platforms

A vaccine is a biological preparation that trains the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease, producing active immunity and lasting immunological memory. Since Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine (1796), vaccines have eradicated smallpox and nearly eliminated polio. India, which makes nearly 60% of the world's vaccines, developed and produced several COVID-19 vaccines on different platforms.

1. Basic principle of vaccine development

  • Mimic infection safely: present an antigen (a killed or weakened microbe, one of its proteins, or the genetic code for that protein) so that the immune system responds as it would to infection.
  • Choose the right antigen: most COVID-19 vaccines targeted the spike protein, which SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter human cells.
  • Boost the response: adjuvants such as alum strengthen and prolong immunity.
  • Prove safety and efficacy: laboratory and animal studies, then Phase I (safety), Phase II (dose and immune response) and Phase III (efficacy in large groups) trials, licensing by the regulator (CDSCO in India) and post-marketing surveillance.
  • Scale and stability: the vaccine must be mass-produced and stay stable in a cold chain, often at 2–8 °C.

2. How vaccines work

  • Antigen presentation: dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells take up the antigen and display it to helper T cells.
  • Antibodies: activated B cells produce antibodies that neutralise the virus and block its entry into cells.
  • Cell-mediated immunity: cytotoxic (killer) T cells learn to destroy infected cells.
  • Memory: memory B and T cells persist, so a later infection meets a fast, strong response that prevents severe disease.
  • Herd immunity: when enough people are immune, transmission falls and the vulnerable are protected.

3. Approaches adopted by Indian manufacturers

  • Indigenous development: Covaxin used a virus strain isolated by ICMR's National Institute of Virology, Pune; ZyCoV-D and GEMCOVAC built new DNA and mRNA platforms at home.
  • Partnerships and scale: licensing global designs (Oxford-AstraZeneca for Covishield, Novavax for Covovax, Sputnik V with Dr. Reddy's) and using India's large manufacturing base.
  • Government support: Mission COVID Suraksha (₹900 crore, 2020) through the Department of Biotechnology and BIRAC, emergency-use approvals, parallel trials and production, and the CoWIN platform; over 220 crore doses were given, and vaccines went abroad under Vaccine Maitri.

India's COVID-19 experience showed the value of multiple vaccine platforms, strong manufacturing and public research. Investing in mRNA, DNA and other new platforms now is the best preparation for the next pandemic.
free.upm-2022-gs3-17:
Global warmingGreenhouse effectKyoto ProtocolFlexible mechanisms

Global warming is the rise in Earth's average surface temperature caused by an enhanced greenhouse effect, as human emissions of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases trap more outgoing heat. The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report found the world 1.1 °C warmer in 2011-20 than in 1850-1900, and the WMO confirmed 2024 as the warmest year on record, about 1.55 °C above pre-industrial levels. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) was the first treaty with binding emission cuts.

1. Causes

  • Fossil fuels: burning coal, oil and gas for power, industry and transport is the largest source; CO₂ concentration reached 423.9 ppm in 2024 (WMO).
  • Land use: deforestation removes carbon sinks.
  • Agriculture and waste: methane from livestock, paddy and landfills; nitrous oxide from fertilisers.
  • Industrial gases: HFCs, PFCs and SF₆ have very high warming potential.

2. Effects on the global climate

  • Heat extremes: more frequent and intense heatwaves.
  • Water cycle: air holds about 7% more moisture per 1 °C, bringing heavier downpours as well as longer droughts and more erratic monsoons.
  • Cryosphere and seas: shrinking Arctic sea ice, retreating glaciers and ice sheets, and sea-level rise from melting ice and thermal expansion.
  • Oceans: warming and acidification, with mass coral bleaching (a fourth global bleaching event was declared in 2024).
  • Storms and feedbacks: more intense tropical cyclones; thawing permafrost and the loss of reflective ice amplify warming and raise the risk of tipping points.

3. Control measures in the light of the Kyoto Protocol

  • Binding targets: adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005, it required developed (Annex I) countries to cut emissions of six gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆) by 5.2% on average below 1990 levels in 2008-12; the Doha Amendment (2012) set a second period, 2013-20, and added NF₃.
  • Common but differentiated responsibilities: developing countries such as India, which ratified the Protocol in 2002, had no binding targets.
  • Domestic measures: energy efficiency, renewable energy, cleaner transport, methane recovery from landfills, and protection of forests and other sinks.
  • Flexible mechanisms: emissions trading among developed countries, Joint Implementation projects between them, and the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), which gave credits for projects in developing countries; India was among its largest hosts.
  • Adaptation Fund: financed by a share of CDM credits to help vulnerable countries adapt.

4. Limits and legacy

  • Limited reach: the USA never ratified it and Canada withdrew, while emissions grew fastest in countries without targets, so global emissions kept rising.
  • Legacy: its carbon markets shaped Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (2015) and India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023).

Kyoto showed that binding targets and carbon markets can work, but only universal participation can stabilise the climate. Deep emission cuts, finance and technology for developing countries, and adaptation must now advance together under the Paris framework.
free.upm-2022-gs3-18:
Coastal erosionLittoral driftSediment starvationIntegrated coastal zone management

Coastal erosion is the loss of land and beaches when waves, currents, tides and storms remove more sediment than rivers and longshore currents supply. The National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR) found that about 33.6% of India's mainland coastline was eroding between 1990 and 2018; among the States, West Bengal, Kerala and Tamil Nadu were the worst affected. Climate change and human interference are speeding it up.

1. Causes

  • Waves and storms: high monsoon waves on the west coast, and cyclones and storm surges on the east coast, can strip a beach within hours.
  • Sea-level rise and subsidence: the north Indian Ocean rose about 3.3 mm a year in 1993–2017, and deltas sink as sediment compacts and groundwater is pumped out.
  • Sediment starvation: dams and barrages trap the sand that rivers once carried to the coast, as in the Krishna, Godavari and Mahanadi deltas.
  • Ports, breakwaters and groynes: they block the longshore (littoral) drift of sand, so sand builds up on one side and the other side erodes.
  • Sand mining, mangrove clearing and aquaculture ponds: they remove natural buffers and weaken the shore.

2. Effects

  • Loss of land and homes: fishing hamlets, houses, roads and farmland are lost, as at Uppada in Andhra Pradesh, displacing coastal communities.
  • Livelihoods: fishers lose landing and drying space for boats and catch, and beach tourism suffers.
  • Ecosystems: turtle-nesting beaches, mangroves and dunes shrink, weakening the coast's natural defences.
  • Salinity and flooding: sea water intrudes into aquifers and fields, and storm surges reach further inland.
  • Infrastructure: ports, coastal roads and power plants need costly protection.

3. Coastal management techniques

  • Hard engineering: seawalls, revetments and tetrapods shield the land behind them; groynes trap drifting sand; offshore and submerged breakwaters reduce wave energy. They act quickly but often shift erosion to neighbouring beaches.
  • Soft engineering: beach nourishment and dune restoration; Visakhapatnam has pumped sand dredged at its port onto the city's beach since the mid-1970s, and a submerged reef with nourishment restored Puducherry's city beach.
  • Nature-based solutions: mangrove, casuarina and dune-grass belts act as bio-shields; the MISHTI programme (2023) promotes mangrove plantation.
  • Planning and regulation: the CRZ Notification, 2019, setback lines, shoreline management plans, and 526 coastal vulnerability maps at 1:25,000 scale (MoES, 2022).
  • Integrated Coastal Zone Management: managing sediment, ecosystems and development together, as in the World Bank-supported project in Gujarat, Odisha and West Bengal.

Erosion is natural, but dams, ports and sand mining have accelerated it. A shift from hard walls to working with sediment and nature, under integrated coastal zone management, is the lasting answer.
free.upm-2022-gs3-19:
Cyber securityCritical information infrastructureCERT-InNational Cyber Security Strategy

Cyber security is the protection of computers, networks, programmes and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access, preserving the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information. With over 111 crore internet subscribers (TRAI, June 2026), UPI and digital public infrastructure, India's economy and security now depend on cyberspace. Yet its overarching framework has long been the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013.

1. Elements of cyber security

  • Network security: firewalls, intrusion detection and segmentation keep intruders out of networks.
  • Application and data security: secure coding, encryption and access controls protect software and information, including personal data.
  • Endpoint and identity security: protecting devices and verifying users through strong passwords and multi-factor authentication.
  • Critical information infrastructure protection: safeguarding power grids, banking, telecom and transport, whose failure would hurt national security.
  • Operations, recovery and awareness: monitoring, incident response, backups and business continuity, and trained users, since most attacks begin with human error.

2. Challenges

  • Rising crime: NCRB recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024, mostly fraud, and ransomware crippled AIIMS Delhi in 2022.
  • State-backed attacks: espionage and attacks on critical infrastructure are hard to attribute.
  • Import dependence: reliance on foreign hardware and software creates supply-chain risks.
  • Skills gap: few trained professionals and forensic laboratories, especially with State police.
  • New technologies: AI deepfakes, insecure IoT devices and crypto-enabled crime.

3. Progress towards a comprehensive strategy

  • Laws: the IT Act, 2000 (Section 70A for critical infrastructure, Section 70B for CERT-In), the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its Rules (2025), and the Telecommunications Act, 2023 with telecom cyber security rules (2024).
  • Institutions: CERT-In's 2022 directions require incidents to be reported within 6 hours; the National Cyber Security Coordinator was given overall coordination in 2024; sectoral response teams cover power, finance and telecom.
  • Programmes: the Cyber Swachhta Kendra (2017) for cleaning botnets, Sanchar Saathi (2023) against telecom fraud, and the 1930 helpline for cybercrime victims.

4. Gaps that remain

  • No updated strategy: a draft National Cyber Security Strategy, prepared by a task force set up in 2019 under the National Cyber Security Coordinator, had not been officially released by 2025.
  • Overlapping agencies: a parliamentary committee (2023) recommended a single overarching authority, but roles still overlap.
  • Uneven capacity: States, small firms and many government departments lag in skills and cyber hygiene.
  • International cooperation: India is not a party to the Budapest Convention and relies on slow mutual legal assistance for cross-border cases.

India has built many building blocks of a strategy: laws, agencies and response systems. An updated National Cyber Security Strategy, formally adopted and regularly reviewed, with clear roles, skills, indigenous technology and public–private cooperation, would turn them into a coherent whole.
free.upm-2022-gs3-20:
Left Wing ExtremismDevelopment deficitSAMADHANMultilayered strategy

Naxalism, or Left Wing Extremism (LWE), began with the Naxalbari uprising (1967) and grew where tribal people faced land alienation, displacement, denial of forest rights and absent governance; a Planning Commission expert group (2008) examined it as a development challenge. Yet it manifests as armed violence against the State. Its reach has shrunk sharply: seven districts were affected by February 2026, and on 30 March 2026 the Home Minister told the Lok Sabha that Naxalism had been "wiped out".

1. A social, economic and developmental issue

  • Land and forests: loss of tribal land, displacement by mines and dams without fair rehabilitation, and harassment over forest produce.
  • Exclusion: poverty and poor schools, health care, roads and jobs in remote forest areas.
  • Governance deficit: absent or exploitative administration, and weak implementation of PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).
  • Exploitation by the Maoists: they used these grievances to recruit, while blowing up the schools, roads and towers that could have removed them.

2. Emerging issues

  • Residual threat: remaining cadres in the dense forests of Bastar and at inter-State tri-junctions could regroup if pressure eases.
  • Surrender and reintegration: thousands of surrendered cadres need livelihoods, safety and acceptance, or some may relapse.
  • Leadership vacuum: the killing of general secretary Basavaraju (May 2025) broke the command structure, but splinter groups may turn to extortion and crime.
  • Overground networks: front organisations and urban support networks for funds, propaganda and recruitment.
  • New grievances: mining and infrastructure in forest areas can revive conflict if gram sabha consent and benefit-sharing are ignored.
  • Rights and trust: allegations of excesses against tribals, and the legacy of Salwa Judum, which the Supreme Court ordered disbanded (2011), must be addressed to win lasting trust.

3. A multilayered strategy

  • Security layer: the National Policy and Action Plan (2015) and the SAMADHAN doctrine (2017) combine leadership, intelligence, technology and choking of finances; State forces such as the Greyhounds and the District Reserve Guard lead, with CAPF support.
  • Development layer: 1,804 bank branches and 635 post offices opened in affected areas over 12 years, along with roads and mobile towers; PM-JANMAN and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan aim to saturate tribal villages with services.
  • Rights layer: full implementation of PESA and forest rights; the Supreme Court's Niyamgiri ruling (2013) on gram sabha consent shows the way.
  • Rehabilitation layer: surrender-cum-rehabilitation policies with housing, skills and jobs.
  • Trust layer: recruitment of local youth into police and administration, quick grievance redress, accountability for excesses, and officials who stay posted in remote areas.

The near-elimination of armed Maoism shows that security plus development works. Lasting peace now depends on good governance in tribal areas: secure rights over land and forests, quality services and dignity, so that the grievances that fed Naxalism do not return.
free.upm-2022-gs4-1a:
Practical wisdomGoal displacementOutcome orientationGood governance

Wisdom, in the sense of practical wisdom (Aristotle's phronesis), is the ability to judge what really matters in a situation. An administrator absorbed in the periphery (formats, protocol, file notings, minor procedural lapses) while core issues such as delayed services, unresolved grievances and stalled projects wait, shows what Robert Merton (1940) called goal displacement: the means become ends. Such preoccupation largely defeats good governance, but a critical view shows that not all of the "periphery" is trivial.

1. Why officers get lost in the periphery

  • Defensive administration: fear of audit objections, vigilance inquiries and court cases makes officers protect themselves through procedure rather than solve problems.
  • Input-based appraisal: performance is judged by files disposed, meetings held and money spent, not by outcomes for citizens.
  • Visibility bias: ceremonies, VIP visits and reports are seen and praised; slow core work such as learning outcomes or maintenance is not.
  • Weak prioritisation: without clear goals and domain knowledge, every task looks equally urgent.

2. Why it leads to a travesty of justice (the case for agreeing)

  • Delay becomes denial: pensions, compensation and land records held up for a missing stamp or a spelling mismatch punish citizens for the system's errors.
  • Exclusion of the weakest: the poor, the elderly and the unlettered are least able to meet hyper-technical demands, so rigidity hits them hardest.
  • Misused time and resources: hours spent on trivial correspondence are taken from crises that are building up, such as disease outbreaks or stalled projects.
  • Accountability blurred: perfect files can hide failed outcomes; the officer is "compliant" while the scheme fails.

3. The critical view: the periphery is not always trivial

  • Procedure protects fairness: due process, recorded reasons and open tendering prevent arbitrariness and corruption (Article 14 and natural justice); ignoring them in the name of results breeds favouritism.
  • Small lapses can cause disasters: a skipped safety check or neglected maintenance can cost lives, so wisdom lies in knowing which detail is critical.
  • Context decides: a small error in a land record may decide a family's property; what is peripheral in one case is core in another.

4. Way forward: from rules to roles

  • Capacity building: Mission Karmayogi (2020) aims to move the civil service from rule-based to role-based functioning.
  • Outcome monitoring: PRAGATI (2015) and the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) track results rather than inputs.
  • Simplification: self-attestation of documents and the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, which decriminalised 183 provisions in 42 Acts, remove needless procedure.
  • Prioritisation tools: the Pareto (80/20) principle and the urgent–important matrix help officers focus on what matters.

Administration needs both rules and results, but rules must serve purposes. An officer with practical wisdom treats procedure as the servant of justice, not its master, and keeps the citizen's outcome at the centre: the essence of citizen-centric governance.
free.upm-2022-gs4-1b:
EmpathyCompassionEmotional intelligenceHumane administration

Intellectual competence (knowledge, analysis, judgement) tells a civil servant what is possible and lawful, and moral qualities (integrity, impartiality) tell him what is right. Empathy, the ability to understand a situation from another person's point of view, and compassion, the urge to act to relieve suffering, tell him what is humane. That is why the GS IV syllabus lists empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections among the foundational values of the civil service.

1. Meaning and place among civil-service attributes

  • Sympathy, empathy, compassion: sympathy is feeling for someone; empathy is feeling with them and seeing through their eyes; compassion adds the will to help.
  • Emotional intelligence: Daniel Goleman lists empathy as one of five components of emotional intelligence, with self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation and social skills.
  • Complement, not substitute: empathy without competence achieves little, and competence without empathy can be cold or even harmful.

2. How empathy and compassion help in crucial issues (illustrations)

  • Policies that fit real lives: understanding the life of a migrant worker produced One Nation One Ration Card, which lets families draw subsidised grain anywhere in the country.
  • Crisis management: during the COVID-19 lockdown (2020), district administrations ran shelters, community kitchens (as in Kerala) and transport for stranded migrants, decisions driven by compassion as much as by rules.
  • Winning trust: Armstrong Pame, an IAS officer in Manipur, built a road of about 100 km in Tamenglong district (2012), largely through public contributions, because villages there had no road.
  • Dignity for the needy: Kozhikode's Operation Sulaimani (2015), started by the district administration with hotel and restaurant owners, gave free meal coupons to the hungry without any questions.
  • Inclusive design: in Pragya Prasun v Union of India (April 2025) the Supreme Court held digital access to be part of the right to life and ordered KYC norms to be made accessible to acid-attack survivors and visually impaired persons; an empathetic officer can design for them without waiting for a court.

3. Critical decisions: compassion within limits

  • Fair, not partial: compassion must not become favouritism; it works through speed, dignity, guidance and lawful discretion, not by breaking eligibility rules.
  • Hard decisions made humanely: eviction, land acquisition or closure of polluting units may be necessary, but advance notice, rehabilitation and fair compensation make them just.
  • Avoiding compassion fatigue: constant exposure to suffering can numb officers; reflection, peer support and rest keep empathy alive.

Gandhi's talisman asks the decision-maker to recall the face of the poorest person he has seen and ask whether the step will help him. A civil servant who combines head and heart (competence, integrity and compassion) turns rules into humane governance.
free.upm-2022-gs4-2a:
AttitudePurposive interpretationDiscretionSpirit of the law

The rules are the same for all officers, but outcomes differ because of attitude, the settled way of thinking and feeling that shapes behaviour. Rules are general while cases are particular, so every officer exercises discretion. A positive-minded officer reads rules purposively, asking what they are meant to achieve and how the case can be solved within them; a negative-minded officer reads them literally and defensively, looking for reasons to say no.

1. Why the same rules produce different results

  • Attitude shapes interpretation: the cognitive, affective and behavioural parts of attitude decide whether a rule is seen as a tool or as a barrier.
  • Motivation and fear: public-service motivation drives problem-solving, while fear of audit and vigilance breeds file-pushing and buck-passing.
  • Spirit versus letter: most rules leave room for reasonable choices; using that room for the public good is the essence of good administration.

2. Illustrations

  • T.N. Seshan (Chief Election Commissioner, 1990–96): the Model Code of Conduct had existed for years, but he used the Election Commission's powers under Article 324 to enforce it firmly, transforming elections with the same rules.
  • Disaster response in Odisha: working within the same disaster-management framework as other States, Odisha evacuated over a million people before Cyclone Fani (2019), making "zero casualty" a working goal.
  • Citizen-friendly procedure: self-attestation of documents in place of attestation by gazetted officers (2014) showed that procedure can be read in the citizen's favour without lowering standards.
  • The negative example: rejecting a widow's pension or a student's scholarship for a spelling mismatch that the rules allow to be corrected delays justice; courts have long held that procedure is the handmaid of justice, not its mistress.

3. Caution: positive does not mean bending rules

  • Legality and fairness: a positive interpretation must stay within the law, be reasoned and be available to all similar cases; arbitrariness violates Article 14 (E.P. Royappa, 1974).
  • Prudence has a place: an officer who refuses an unlawful favour, or guards public money with the ordinary prudence the General Financial Rules demand, is responsible, not negative.
  • No favouritism: helping one applicant "creatively" while denying others is discrimination, not positivity.

4. Building a positive administrative culture

  • Protection for honest decisions: Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act (inserted in 2018) requires prior approval before investigating decisions taken in official duty, so officers need not fear bona fide choices.
  • Recognition and training: the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration (instituted 2006) and Mission Karmayogi's role-based learning reward problem-solving.
  • Outcome-based appraisal: judging officers by results for citizens encourages solution-seeking.

The rulebook is the same; the mindset makes the difference. Officers who combine legality with purposive, citizen-friendly interpretation turn rules into instruments of service rather than obstacles.
free.upm-2022-gs4-2b:
Human flourishingEthical valuesConflict resolutionConscience

Ethics is the study of right and wrong conduct and of the values that should guide human action. Organisations run smoothly when their members act ethically, because ethics creates trust, predictability and cooperation in situations that rules cannot fully foresee. Ethics seeks to promote human flourishing (Aristotle's eudaimonia), a just society and inner peace, and ethical values act as a compass when a person faces conflicting demands in daily life.

1. What ethics seeks to promote in human life

  • Dignity: every person is to be treated as an end and never merely as a means (Kant); this idea underlies human rights and Article 21.
  • Welfare and happiness: the greatest good of the greatest number (utilitarianism) and the welfare of all (Gandhi's Sarvodaya).
  • Justice and fairness: equal treatment, with special care for the least advantaged (Rawls).
  • Trust and cooperation: honesty and reliability create social capital, which makes families, markets and governments work.
  • Character and inner peace: virtues such as courage, self-control and integrity bring self-respect; the Gita's ideal of doing one's duty without attachment to its fruits frees one from anxiety.
  • Harmony with nature: compassion for living creatures and care for the natural environment, as Article 51A(g) asks, and concern for future generations.

2. Conflicts faced in day-to-day functioning

  • Personal versus professional: a relative seeks a favour in an official matter.
  • Loyalty versus honesty: a superior asks for a record to be "adjusted".
  • Compassion versus rules: a poor applicant narrowly misses an eligibility criterion.
  • Efficiency versus equity: quick results through shortcuts versus a fair process for all.
  • Confidentiality versus transparency: what to disclose, to whom and when.

3. How ethical values help resolve these conflicts

  • A hierarchy of values: the Constitution and the law come first, then the public interest, then organisational and personal interests; this ranking settles many conflicts.
  • Clear defaults: integrity makes some choices non-negotiable, such as refusing a bribe, so energy is saved for genuinely hard cases.
  • Tests of conscience: Kant's test (could everyone act this way?), the consequences test (who gains, who suffers?), the publicity test (could I defend this in public?) and Gandhi's talisman (will it help the poorest?).
  • Courage with accountability: recording reasons and seeking written instructions, as the Supreme Court advised in T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India (2013), protect both the officer and the public interest.
  • Empathy and dialogue: understanding the other side often reveals a solution that satisfies both the law and the person.

Ethics does not remove conflicts, but it gives a moral compass for resolving them consistently. An organisation whose members internalise values needs fewer rules and enjoys more trust.
free.upm-2022-gs4-3a:
Legality and moralityRights and responsibilitiesDiscretionIntegrity

Potter Stewart (1915–1985), an Associate Justice of the US Supreme Court (1958–1981), separates two things often confused: what we have the right to do, which the law permits, and what is right to do, which conscience and ethics require. Law sets the minimum standard of conduct; ethics sets a higher one. A person can act within his rights and still act wrongly, and ethical maturity lies in seeing the difference.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Legal is not always moral: exploiting a tax loophole, paying only the minimum wage while earning large profits, or spreading hurtful but lawful speech may be within one's rights, but none of them is right.
  • Rights carry responsibilities: freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) is matched by fundamental duties such as promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood (Article 51A(e)).
  • Ethics works where the law is silent: most decisions fall within discretion, and that is where character shows.
  • Self-restraint: the measure of a person is not how far he can go, but how far he chooses not to go.

2. Values involved

  • Integrity and conscience: acting on inner conviction even when no one is watching and no rule compels.
  • Responsibility: using power and freedom with concern for their effects on others.
  • Practical wisdom: judging what is fitting in a particular situation.

3. Examples from public life

  • Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned as Railway Minister after a major train accident in 1956, though no law required it, taking moral responsibility for the tragedy.
  • Responsible business: firms that recall unsafe products before any order, or refuse to cut safety costs to raise profits, show the same distinction.
  • Restraint in office: legislators and officers are entitled to perks and privileges, but using them sparingly and only for public work builds trust.

4. Relevance for civil servants

  • Discretion: many decisions (transfers, licences, relief) are within an officer's powers; ethics decides whether that power serves the public or a private interest.
  • Beyond conduct rules: the Nolan principles (1995) of selflessness, integrity and objectivity, and the Second ARC's Fourth Report, Ethics in Governance (2007), ask public servants to go beyond the letter of the law.
  • Citizen-centric choices: helping citizens through procedure rather than hiding behind it.
  • Appearance matters: what is permissible may still look improper, and in public office perception affects trust.

Stewart's distinction reminds us that legality is the floor and ethics the ceiling. A civil servant who asks not only whether an action is permitted but whether it is right earns lasting public trust.
free.upm-2022-gs4-3b:
Value inculcationFamily and schoolRole modelsCharacter building

Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (1931–2015), scientist and the 11th President of India (2002–07), saw corruption as at root a failure of character, and character is formed early, in the home and the classroom. Parents and teachers are the first agents of socialisation: children learn honesty, empathy and discipline by watching them. Laws can punish corruption, but only values instilled in childhood can prevent it and build a nation of "beautiful minds".

1. What the quotation means to me

  • Corruption begins as a value deficit: a child who sees a parent pay a bribe for a certificate learns that shortcuts are normal.
  • Learning by example: social learning theory (Albert Bandura) shows that children copy the behaviour of role models more than they follow advice.
  • Teachers shape conscience and reason: fair marking, zero tolerance of cheating and the teaching of scientific temper (Article 51A(h)) build ethical citizens.
  • Beautiful minds: minds that are honest, creative, compassionate and confident, the foundation of a developed nation.

2. Examples

  • Kalam's own life: in his autobiography Wings of Fire (1999), he credits his parents in Rameswaram and his teachers with the values and curiosity that shaped him.
  • Policy: the National Education Policy, 2020 makes ethical and constitutional values, and ethical reasoning, part of school education.
  • Everyday choices: parents who refuse to pay a bribe for a licence or an admission, and teachers who refuse to sell marks or leak papers, teach more than any sermon.

3. Limits of the idea

  • Other influences: peers, the media, social media, political leadership and the workplace also shape values; a child brought up well can still be corrupted by a corrupt system.
  • Institutions matter: laws and institutions such as the Lokpal (2013), the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018, which made bribe-giving an offence, and e-governance reduce the opportunity for corruption.
  • Consistency of role models: teacher absenteeism or parents' double standards undo any lesson.

4. Relevance for civil servants

  • Role models in society: honest officers, like parents and teachers, show citizens that integrity is possible.
  • Investing in roots: good schools, value education and teacher training are part of an anti-corruption strategy.
  • Mentoring within the service: senior officers act as teachers for juniors, and their conduct shapes the culture of an office.

Kalam's insight places the fight against corruption at its roots. Laws and institutions are necessary, but a corruption-free nation is built through value-based upbringing in every home and classroom.
free.upm-2022-gs4-3c:
Means and endsCost of successIntegritySacrifice

The 14th Dalai Lama (Tenzin Gyatso), Nobel Peace laureate (1989), asks us to measure success not only by what we gained but by what it cost. Success bought by giving up integrity, health or others' welfare is hollow; success earned by giving up comfort, ego and shortcuts is real. The thought echoes Gandhi's insistence on pure means: in Hind Swaraj (1909) he compared the means to a seed and the end to the tree that grows from it.

1. What the quotation means to me

  • The price matters as much as the prize: a victory won by cheating, exploitation or cruelty is a defeat of character.
  • Two readings: it warns against sacrificing values for success, and it honours the sacrifice of comfort and leisure that worthy success demands.
  • A broader idea of success: well-being, relationships, peace of mind and a clear conscience are part of success, not obstacles to it.
  • A long view: what is sacrificed today, such as trust or the environment, often returns as a heavier cost tomorrow.

2. Examples from public life

  • Lance Armstrong won seven Tour de France titles but was stripped of all of them in 2012 for doping; success built on dishonesty collapsed.
  • Satyam (2009): inflated accounts projected growth until the fraud was confessed and the company collapsed, hurting employees and investors.
  • Freedom fighters such as Sardar Patel and C.R. Das gave up thriving legal practices to join the national movement; their success is measured by that sacrifice.
  • Coercion to meet targets: the forced sterilisation drives of the Emergency (1975–77) met numerical targets but sacrificed consent and dignity, and made family planning suspect for years.

3. Relevance for civil servants

  • Means matter in administration: meeting targets by fudging data, coercing people or ignoring the vulnerable is failure, not success.
  • Personal sacrifice for public duty: officers who accept hard postings, or transfers rather than compromise, show what worthy success costs.
  • Balance: sacrificing one's health and family entirely is not ideal either; a sustainable life makes a better public servant.

True success is judged by what we refuse to sacrifice as much as by what we gain. For a civil servant, success that preserves integrity, the dignity of citizens and public trust is the only success worth having.
free.upm-2022-gs4-4a:
Good governancee-GovernanceDigital public infrastructureInclusion

The World Bank (1992) described governance as the manner in which power is exercised in managing a country's economic and social resources for development. Good governance is governance of high quality, marked by the eight features UNESCAP lists (shown below). India observes Good Governance Day on 25 December. The Second ARC's 11th Report (2008) saw e-governance as the route to SMART government: simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent.

1. Meaning of good governance

  • Beyond efficiency: it concerns how power is used, for whom and with what accountability, not only the speed of services.
  • Citizen at the centre: the citizen is a rights-holder, not a supplicant; services are entitlements delivered with dignity.
  • Indian framework: the Directive Principles, the RTI Act (2005), Right to Services Acts (Madhya Pradesh first, 2010) and the Good Governance Index of the Department of Administrative Reforms.

2. How e-governance has helped beneficiaries

  • Money directly to people: Direct Benefit Transfer (2013), built on Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and mobile phones (JAM), sends benefits such as PM-KISAN's ₹6,000 a year straight to bank accounts; weeding out duplicate and fake beneficiaries has saved over ₹3 lakh crore (government estimate).
  • Documents and services on the phone: DigiLocker (72 crore+ users) holds e-documents legally equal to originals, and UMANG offers about 2,575 services on one app (July 2026).
  • Portability: One Nation One Ration Card lets migrant workers draw subsidised grain anywhere in India.
  • Health at a distance: eSanjeevani had crossed 50 crore teleconsultations by October 2026, with women accounting for over 57% of its use; CoWIN recorded over 220 crore COVID-19 vaccine doses.
  • Transparency and voice: the Government e-Marketplace (2016) makes public purchases visible, CPGRAMS tracks grievances, and PRAGATI (2015) reviews stalled projects at the highest level.

3. How far: the limits

  • Digital divide: only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5); the Supreme Court flagged CoWIN's online-only registration in 2021.
  • Exclusion by technology: biometric failures hit the elderly and manual workers; a 2017 Union Food Ministry order said no one should be denied rations for lack of Aadhaar or failed authentication.
  • Privacy and fraud: NCRB recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024, about 73% of them for fraud; the DPDP Act, 2023 is still being phased in under its November 2025 Rules.
  • Digitising bad processes: putting a complex procedure online does not simplify it; process re-engineering must come first.

e-Governance has made delivery faster, cheaper and more transparent for millions, but it is a means, not an end. An assisted, "phygital" model, with Common Service Centres, Indian-language interfaces (Bhashini) and strong data protection, will turn e-governance into genuine good governance.
free.upm-2022-gs4-4b:
Digital divideTelemedicineConsent and privacyDigital inclusion

COVID-19 made online methods routine: video meetings and e-Office files in administration, online classes through DIKSHA, SWAYAM and PM eVIDYA (2020), and telemedicine under the Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (March 2020). eSanjeevani alone had crossed 50 crore teleconsultations by October 2026. In Pragya Prasun v Union of India (April 2025), the Supreme Court held digital access to be part of the right to life. Yet tools that empower the connected can exclude the vulnerable.

1. Advantages and disadvantages

  • For the system: online approvals save time and money and leave an audit trail that discourages arbitrariness.
  • For beneficiaries: eSanjeevani links over 1.42 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to doctors, so a villager can consult a specialist with a health worker beside her.

2. Ethical issues for vulnerable sections

  • Equity and justice: online-only systems exclude those without devices, connectivity or skills; only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5). Rawls's principle that arrangements must benefit the least advantaged is violated when the poor are pushed to the back of a digital queue.
  • Informed consent and autonomy: a patient with little literacy may not understand a teleconsultation or a data-sharing form, so consent becomes a formality.
  • Privacy and data protection: health records, children's learning data and identity details are sensitive; the DPDP Act, 2023, being phased in, requires verifiable parental consent for children's data.
  • Quality and accountability: the guidelines limit which medicines can be prescribed remotely, but responsibility for a missed diagnosis, or a lost school year, is blurred.
  • Dignity and the human touch: the elderly, the disabled and people in distress need empathy that a screen cannot fully give; children's mental health suffered during long online schooling.
  • Accessibility and fraud: visually impaired persons and acid-attack survivors could not complete digital KYC (the 2025 case), and OTP and "digital arrest" frauds target the elderly and new users.

3. Making online methods ethical

  • Hybrid by default: an offline or assisted option must always remain, through Common Service Centres, frontline workers and help desks.
  • Accessible design: content in Indian languages (Bhashini), screen-reader-friendly portals and simple interfaces.
  • Consent and privacy by design: minimum data, consent explained in local languages, secure platforms.
  • Digital literacy: PMGDISHA for rural households, and training for teachers, doctors and frontline staff.
  • Accountability: human review of online decisions and time-bound grievance redress.

Online methods can be a great equaliser, but only if they are designed for the last person in the queue. Digital inclusion, informed consent and accountability must accompany every online service, so that efficiency does not come at the cost of equity.
free.upm-2022-gs4-5a:
Just war theorySovereigntyInternational humanitarian lawHuman cost

The Russia–Ukraine war began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022. As of October 2026 it is in its fifth year with no general ceasefire; in late October, Russia and Ukraine said US-mediated three-way talks were planned for early November 2026. Countries have acted on national interest, but the war raises enduring ethical questions, best examined through just war theory: the ethics of going to war, of conduct in war and of ending it.

1. Ethical issues in launching the war (jus ad bellum)

  • Sovereignty: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter bars the use of force against any State; the only exceptions are self-defence against an armed attack (Article 51) and force authorised by the Security Council. The UN General Assembly deplored the invasion on 2 March 2022 (141 votes in favour; India abstained).
  • Just cause and right intention: Russia cited NATO's eastward expansion and the protection of Russian speakers; Ukraine and most UN members saw unprovoked aggression.
  • Last resort: whether diplomacy, including the Minsk agreements (2014–15), was exhausted before force was used is central to judging the decision.
  • Legitimate authority: the Security Council, meant to authorise force, was paralysed by Russia's veto (February 2022).

2. Ethical issues in its continuation (jus in bello)

  • Distinction and proportionality: attacks on civilians and on infrastructure such as power grids and hospitals violate the Geneva Conventions (1949); the UN has recorded tens of thousands of civilian casualties, and millions have fled abroad.
  • Children: the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President Putin (17 March 2023) over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.
  • Nuclear safety: fighting around Zaporizhzhia, Europe's largest nuclear power plant, has kept International Atomic Energy Agency experts on site since September 2022.
  • Global spill-over: food and fuel prices rose worldwide; the Black Sea Grain Initiative (July 2022) eased grain exports until Russia left it in July 2023.
  • Prolonging the war: maximalist positions keep soldiers and civilians dying, sanctions also hurt ordinary people, and propaganda and deepfakes corrupt public judgement.

3. National interest versus universal ethics

  • Realism and morality: States weigh energy, security and trade (Kautilya's realism) against the universal duty to oppose aggression (Kant's idea of perpetual peace).
  • India's balanced stand: India urged respect for the UN Charter and territorial integrity, and dialogue and diplomacy; its Prime Minister told President Putin at Samarkand (September 2022) that this is not an era of war. It sent humanitarian aid to Ukraine, evacuated its students through Operation Ganga (2022) and kept buying Russian oil for its energy security.
  • Ethics of neutrality: abstention is justified only if the access it preserves is actually used for peace-making.

War may serve national interests, but its human cost falls on civilians and the world's poor. Ethics demands restraint in launching war, respect for humanitarian law in fighting it, and sincere diplomacy for a just and lasting peace.
free.upm-2022-gs4-5b:
Constitutional moralityConflict of interestProbityDevotion to duty

These five ideas together form the ethical foundation of public service: loyalty to the values of the Constitution, separation of private interest from public duty, probity in conduct, responsible use of technology and devotion to duty. Each is explained below with its meaning, an example and its relevance for administrators.

1. Constitutional morality

  • Meaning: adherence to the core values of the Constitution (liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity, secularism and the rule of law) and respect for its institutions and processes, not merely its text.
  • Origin: Ambedkar, drawing on the historian George Grote, used the term in the Constituent Assembly (November 1948) and warned that it is not natural and has to be cultivated.
  • In courts and administration: the Supreme Court relied on it in Manoj Narula (2014) and Navtej Singh Johar (2018); for officers, it means upholding the Constitution even against popular or political pressure.

2. Conflict of interest

  • Meaning: a situation in which a public servant's private interest (financial, family or personal) could improperly influence an official decision; it may be actual, potential or apparent.
  • Example: an officer evaluating a tender in which a relative's firm has bid.
  • Safeguards: declaration of interests, recusal and cooling-off periods; the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, as amended in 2014, require officers to declare private interests relating to their duties.

3. Probity in public life

  • Meaning: uprightness and integrity in public conduct beyond mere legal compliance: honest use of public money, power and information.
  • Standards: the Nolan Committee (UK, 1995) set seven principles of public life: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership.
  • Indian institutions: the RTI Act (2005), the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act (2013), the Central Vigilance Commission and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (amended 2018).

4. Challenges of digitalisation

  • Digital divide: only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5), so online-only services exclude many.
  • Cybercrime and privacy: NCRB recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024; personal data must be protected under the right to privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017) and the DPDP Act, 2023.
  • Other risks: misinformation and deepfakes, algorithmic bias and the loss of human touch; the Supreme Court has held digital access to be part of Article 21 (2025).

5. Devotion to duty

  • Meaning: commitment to public service beyond the call of duty, with diligence, perseverance and selflessness, even at personal cost; the Gita's ideal of duty without attachment to its fruits.
  • Examples: Satyendra Dubey (NHAI, 2003) gave his life exposing corruption; India's ASHA workers received the WHO Director-General's Global Health Leaders Award (2022).
  • Relevance: it sustains services in disasters, remote postings and crises, when rules alone cannot.

Together, these values make a civil servant trustworthy and effective, turning the power of office into public service.
free.upm-2022-gs4-6a:
Whistle-blowerVictimisationConfidentialityPublic interest disclosure
