  • Redevelopment and beautification: slum redevelopment, mega events (the 2010 Commonwealth Games) and riverfront projects often displace the poor.

2. Yes: it marginalises them

  • Informal work: street vendors, domestic workers and construction labourers lack security and face harassment despite the Street Vendors Act, 2014.
  • Poor services: irregular water, sanitation and health care, often at higher cost.
  • Environmental risk: the poor live in flood-prone, polluted and hotter neighbourhoods.
  • Invisibility: without address proof, migrants were cut off from local welfare, as the migrant exodus during the 2020 lockdown revealed; master plans rarely provide for informal settlements.

3. But not always: the city also integrates

  • Mobility and anonymity: Ambedkar urged Dalits to leave villages for cities; urban jobs, education and anonymity loosen caste bonds and raise incomes.
  • Policy correctives: PMAY-Urban (2015) and PMAY-U 2.0 (2024, for 1 crore houses), Affordable Rental Housing Complexes (2020), PM SVANidhi (2020) for street vendors, One Nation One Ration Card, and Odisha's Jaga Mission giving land rights to slum dwellers.
  • Courts: Olga Tellis (1985) linked the right to livelihood with Article 21, and Ajay Maken v. Union of India (Delhi High Court, 2019) required surveys and rehabilitation before slum evictions.

Urbanisation in India has produced both segregation and marginalisation, but they are outcomes of policy, not inevitable. Affordable rental housing, in-situ slum upgrading, secure tenure and inclusive planning can realise the "right to the city" for the poor.
free.upm-2023-gs1-19:
JatiSanskritisationEndogamyCaste mobilisation

Caste (jati) is an ascribed, hereditary and endogamous group, traditionally tied to occupation and ritual rank. Sociologists from M.N. Srinivas to André Béteille show that it is neither frozen nor disappearing: its ritual hierarchy and links with occupation have loosened, while endogamy and caste identity have proved durable. Census 2027 will count all castes, the first such count since 1931. Caste is thus fluid in some spheres and static in others.

1. Why caste identity is fluid

  • Sanskritisation: Srinivas showed that lower castes raise their status by adopting the customs of higher castes, so groups move within the hierarchy.
  • Modernisation: education, urban jobs and migration delink caste from occupation; restaurants, trains and offices weaken rules on food and touch.
  • Political mobilisation: caste associations and parties turn castes into interest groups, as the Rudolphs observed; the "dominant caste" depends on land and numbers, not ritual rank alone.
  • Changing categories: groups seek new classification, such as demands by the Marathas, Jats and Patidars for reservation; the Supreme Court allowed sub-classification of Scheduled Castes in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024).
  • Exit and reform: Ambedkar's conversion to Buddhism (1956) and reform movements offered new identities.

2. Why caste identity is static

  • Endogamy: only about 5% of marriages are inter-caste (IHDS); matrimonial advertisements are sorted by caste, and "honour" crimes punish inter-caste couples, prompting the Supreme Court's guidelines in Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018).
  • Untouchability and atrocities: discrimination persists despite Article 17 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
  • Occupational stickiness: sanitation work and manual scavenging, banned by the 2013 Act, still fall largely on Dalits.
  • Spatial segregation: separate Dalit hamlets in villages and caste-based discrimination in urban housing.
  • Politics and policy: vote-bank politics and reservations keep caste labels alive.

3. Explaining the paradox

  • From hierarchy to identity: the ritual hierarchy of purity and pollution has weakened, but castes now act as competing communities, which Louis Dumont called the "substantialisation" of caste.
  • Public and private spheres: the market, the State and the city make caste fluid in public life, while family, marriage and community keep it static in private life.
  • Instrumental use: groups loosen caste when it is a stigma and assert it when it brings benefits.

Caste is thus fluid as hierarchy but static as identity. Inter-caste marriage, education, urban jobs and strict enforcement of anti-discrimination laws can move India towards the annihilation of caste that Ambedkar envisaged.
free.upm-2023-gs1-20:
Liberalisation 1991GlocalisationUneven developmentCommunalism

The New Economic Policy of 1991, liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, opened India to markets, foreign capital and global media. It raised growth and created a large middle class, but its uneven spread, new competition for jobs and resources, and the global flow of images and ideas also reshaped ethnic identities (based on language, tribe and region) and communalism (mobilisation of religious identity against other communities). Globalisation both homogenises culture and provokes the assertion of local identities, a process called glocalisation.

1. Impact on ethnic identity

  • Uneven development: mining and industry in resource-rich tribal regions brought displacement, as the Niyamgiri case (2013) showed, sharpening tribal assertion; uneven growth also strengthened demands for new States such as Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand (2000) and Telangana (2014).
  • Migration and nativism: migration to booming cities revived "sons of the soil" politics; Haryana's 2020 law reserving 75% of private jobs for locals was struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2023, and the State has appealed to the Supreme Court.
  • Competition for land and status: in the North-East, rivalry over land, jobs and Scheduled Tribe status fed conflicts such as the Meitei–Kuki-Zo clashes in Manipur from May 2023.
  • Revival and commodification: ethnic food, crafts, festivals (such as Nagaland's Hornbill Festival) and GI tags turn identity into a marketable asset, while the internet and diaspora networks help preserve languages.

2. Impact on communalism

  • Insecurity and competition: informal work, joblessness and competition for business and urban space can be framed in religious terms; Ashutosh Varshney's study (2002) found communal riots concentrated in towns where everyday civic ties between communities are weak.
  • Media and technology: satellite television and social media spread rumours and hate speech quickly; after mob lynchings, the Supreme Court issued guidelines in Tehseen Poonawalla v. Union of India (2018).
  • Global currents: transnational religious networks and funding, and global discourses after 2001, sharpen religious identities.
  • Changing politics: as trade unions and class politics weakened with informalisation, religious and caste identities became stronger tools of mobilisation; religious consumption, such as pilgrimage tourism and televised religion, also grew.

3. The other side

  • Integration and peace: markets, mixed workplaces and rising incomes create interdependence; the Mizo Accord (1986) and the Bodo Accord (2020) show that development with autonomy can calm ethnic conflict.
  • Multiple causes: communal tension also has roots in history, politics and local disputes, not in the economy alone.

The post-liberal economy has both sharpened and softened identity politics. Inclusive and regionally balanced growth, decent jobs, autonomy for ethnic regions, firm action against hate speech and a culture of fraternity can turn diversity into strength.
free.upm-2023-gs2-1:
Judicial independenceSeparation of powersBasic structureRule of law

Judicial independence means that judges decide cases free from pressure by the executive, the legislature, private interests or the passing public mood. The Constitution secures it through the method of appointment, security of tenure, financial autonomy and the separation of the judiciary from the executive (Article 50), and the Supreme Court has held it to be part of the basic structure (Fourth Judges case, 2015). Democracy is not mere majority rule; it is the rule of law with protected rights, which only an independent judiciary can guarantee.

1. Why independence is a prerequisite of democracy

  • Guardian of rights: Fundamental Rights are real only if courts can rule against the State. Article 32, which Dr Ambedkar called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, lets citizens move the Supreme Court directly; in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Puttaswamy (2017) the Court protected liberty and privacy against executive power.
  • Check on majorities: judicial review keeps Parliament within the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) protected the basic structure from passing majorities.
  • Integrity of elections: courts hear election petitions and have strengthened voters' rights, from candidates' disclosure of criminal records and assets (2002) to striking down electoral bonds (2024).
  • Federal umpire: the Supreme Court settles Centre–State disputes (Article 131) and, in S.R. Bommai (1994), curbed the misuse of President's Rule.
  • Equality before law: an impartial forum where the citizen and the State stand as equals is the essence of the rule of law.

2. Lessons from history

  • When independence weakened: the supersession of senior judges in appointing Chief Justices (1973, 1977) and ADM Jabalpur (1976), which denied detenus any remedy during the Emergency, showed how a pliant judiciary hollows out democracy.
  • Restoration: the Second and Third Judges cases (1993, 1998) created the collegium, Puttaswamy (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur, and in 2015 the Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (99th Amendment) 4:1, holding that executive participation in appointments threatened independence.

3. Independence must come with accountability

  • Concerns: an opaque collegium, delays because the Memorandum of Procedure is still not finalised, post-retirement posts, and allegations of misconduct, as when cash was found at Justice Yashwant Varma's residence (March 2025); after an in-house inquiry and a removal motion, he resigned in April 2026.
  • Transparency builds trust: collegium resolutions have been published since 2017, and the CJI's office is a public authority under the RTI Act (Subhash Chandra Agarwal, 2019).
  • Necessary, not sufficient: independence also needs enough judges, infrastructure and speedy justice, because delay itself erodes faith in courts.

The statement is valid: without constitutionally guaranteed independence, rights, elections and federalism would depend on the goodwill of those in power. A transparent appointment process, timely filling of vacancies and credible self-regulation will keep the judiciary independent and accountable, the true guardian of constitutional democracy.
free.upm-2023-gs2-2:
Article 39ALegal Services Authorities Act, 1987Section 12NALSA

Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), directs the State to provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities, and the Supreme Court read the right to free legal aid into Article 21 (M.H. Hoskot, 1978; Hussainara Khatoon, 1979). The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, in force from 9 November 1995 (now National Legal Services Day), set up the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and a nationwide network of legal services institutions.

1. Who is entitled to free legal aid (Section 12)

  • Vulnerable groups: members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, women and children, persons with disabilities, and victims of trafficking or begar (Article 23).
  • Victims of undeserved want: such as mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster.
  • Industrial workmen and persons in custody, including in protective and juvenile homes and psychiatric hospitals.
  • Low-income persons: those whose annual income is below a ceiling fixed by the State government, or by the Union for cases in the Supreme Court.
  • Condition: the authority must be satisfied that the applicant has a prima facie case (Section 13); under NALSA's 2010 regulations an application must be decided within seven days.

2. Role of NALSA in rendering legal aid

  • Structure: the Chief Justice of India is Patron-in-Chief and a Supreme Court judge, by practice the next senior-most, the Executive Chairman; State, District and Taluk authorities and the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee implement its policies and schemes.
  • Legal aid and advice: through panel lawyers, front offices, legal aid clinics in jails and communities, and para-legal volunteers.
  • Public defenders: the Legal Aid Defense Counsel System provides full-time defence lawyers in criminal cases, on the public-defender model.
  • Lok Adalats: National, State and Permanent Lok Adalats settle disputes by compromise; their awards are final and free of court fees.
  • Awareness and victim support: legal literacy camps, and schemes for compensation to women victims of sexual assault (2018) and legal services to acid-attack victims (2016).

3. Assessment

  • Achievements: legal aid is now a statutory right, not charity; Lok Adalats cut cost and pendency, and public defenders help undertrials.
  • Low awareness: many eligible people do not know of their entitlement, and about three-quarters of prisoners are undertrials (Prison Statistics India 2022: 75.8%), most of them poor.
  • Quality concerns: low fees for panel lawyers, weak monitoring and little continuity breed the perception that free aid is poor aid.
  • Lok Adalat limits: many settlements involve petty or pre-litigation matters, and weaker parties may feel pressed to compromise.
  • Uneven capacity: State authorities differ widely in funds and staff.

NALSA has turned Article 39A into a working system. Better-paid and monitored lawyers, legal aid from the moment of arrest and sustained legal literacy can make access to justice real for the poorest, fulfilling the promise of equal justice.
free.upm-2023-gs2-3:
74th AmendmentTwelfth ScheduleArticle 243WMunicipal finance

The 74th Amendment (1992) gave urban local bodies (ULBs) constitutional status in Part IXA (Articles 243P–243ZG), with regular elections, reservation, State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions (Article 243Y). But the crucial transfer of functions (Article 243W and the Twelfth Schedule of 18 subjects) and of taxing powers (Article 243X) was left to the discretion of State legislatures. Three decades later, a CAG compendium of performance audits in 18 States (2024) shows how sparingly that discretion has been used.

1. Functional disempowerment

  • Devolved on paper: on average 17 of the 18 Twelfth Schedule functions are devolved by law, but only 4 with full autonomy (CAG, 2024).
  • Parastatals run cities: urban planning, water supply, sewerage and transport are often handled by State development authorities, water boards and corporations answerable to the State, not to the elected council.
  • Weak city leadership: in most States the mayor is indirectly elected with a short term, while executive power lies with a State-appointed municipal commissioner.
  • Planning bodies bypassed: Metropolitan Planning Committees (Article 243ZE) are often not constituted, and ward committees (Article 243S) are weak.
  • Delayed elections: municipal polls are postponed for years and councils superseded, although Kishansing Tomar (2006) required timely elections and the Supreme Court has had to order overdue polls (Suresh Mahajan, 2022).

2. Financial disempowerment

  • Low own revenue: own sources make up only about 32% of ULBs' revenue, and resources fall 42% short of expenditure (CAG, 2024).
  • Narrow tax base: property tax is under-assessed and poorly collected, and octroi and entry taxes were subsumed in GST (2017) without a share for cities.
  • Irregular State Finance Commissions: they are set up late, their reports are delayed and their recommendations are often not implemented, so transfers remain discretionary.
  • Tied funds and thin staff: scheme grants leave little untied money; only 29% of spending goes to programme and development work, and 37% of sanctioned posts are vacant (CAG).

3. Why States hold back

  • Political rivalry: State legislators and ministers see strong mayors as competitors and value control over urban land, contracts and patronage.
  • The capacity argument: States cite weak municipal capacity, a circular argument, since capacity grows only with responsibility.
  • States' own fiscal stress after GST makes them reluctant to share revenue.

4. Signs of change

Finance Commissions have stepped in: the 15th FC linked urban grants to property-tax reform, and the 16th FC recommended about ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies for 2026–31. Kerala's devolution since the 1996 People's Plan Campaign and 50% seats for women in several States show what political will can achieve.

The statement is largely valid. Activity mapping (Second ARC, 2007), a fixed share of State revenue, a share of GST for cities, directly elected mayors with five-year terms and professional municipal cadres would turn ULBs into real city governments, the genuine third tier the 74th Amendment intended.
free.upm-2023-gs2-4:
Parliamentary sovereigntyConstitutional supremacyJudicial reviewBasic structure

Parliamentary sovereignty, as A.V. Dicey explained (1885), means that Parliament can make or unmake any law and that no court can set aside its Acts. Britain, with an uncodified constitution, still rests on this principle. India borrowed the Westminster form of parliamentary government but not British sovereignty: under a written Constitution it chose constitutional supremacy, a synthesis of British parliamentary sovereignty and American judicial supremacy.

1. The British approach

  • Legal supremacy: an Act of Parliament is the highest source of law; courts interpret but cannot invalidate it, and no Parliament can bind its successors.
  • Flexible constitution: even constitutional statutes, such as the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 that curbed the House of Lords, can be changed by an ordinary majority.
  • Practical limits: EU membership gave EU law priority (Factortame, 1990) until Brexit (exit in 2020); under the Human Rights Act, 1998 courts can only issue a "declaration of incompatibility"; devolution to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (1998) is politically entrenched.
  • Courts protect Parliament: in Miller (2019) the UK Supreme Court held the prorogation of Parliament unlawful, guarding Parliament's sovereignty against the executive.

2. The Indian approach

  • A creature of the Constitution: Parliament's laws must respect Fundamental Rights (Article 13) and the federal division of powers (Articles 245–246, Seventh Schedule).
  • Judicial review: the Supreme Court and High Courts can strike down laws (Articles 32, 226), and judicial review is itself a basic feature (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).
  • Limited amending power: Article 368 requires special majorities and, for federal provisions, ratification by half the States; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) barred destruction of the basic structure, and the NJAC amendment was struck down (2015).
  • Federal limits: Parliament can legislate on State subjects only in specified situations (Articles 249–253).

3. Points of convergence

  • Westminster institutions: both have cabinet government responsible to the lower House, which controls money matters.
  • Privileges: India's parliamentary privileges (Article 105) were modelled on those of the House of Commons, and courts cannot question proceedings for mere procedural irregularity (Article 122), though Raja Ram Pal (2007) held the exercise of privileges open to review for illegality.
  • Executive dominance: in both, a disciplined majority lets the government control the legislature, so political rather than legal sovereignty often decides outcomes.
  • Dialogue: in both, courts increasingly read laws to respect rights, and legislatures respond to judicial findings.

4. Assessment

The contrast is one of foundations. In Britain, limits on Parliament are political and conventional; in India they are legal and enforceable. Yet Indian courts too show restraint, presuming laws to be valid and striking down few of them.

India thus combines parliamentary government with a supreme Constitution: Parliament is sovereign within its sphere and the courts guard its limits. This constitutional balance, sustained by mutual restraint between the legislature and the judiciary, has served Indian democracy well.
free.upm-2023-gs2-5:
SpeakerArticle 178Tenth ScheduleImpartiality

Every State Legislative Assembly elects a Speaker and a Deputy Speaker (Article 178), and every Legislative Council a Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Article 182). As presiding officer, the Speaker is the custodian of the House's rules, dignity and privileges and of the rights of every member, especially the Opposition. The office rests on three expectations: order, impartiality and the promotion of democratic practices.

1. Maintaining order

  • Conducting business: the Speaker decides who speaks and when, admits questions and motions, and interprets the rules of procedure made under Article 208; the Speaker's rulings bind the House.
  • Discipline: the Speaker can direct a disorderly member to withdraw, name and suspend members under the rules, expunge unparliamentary words and adjourn the House in grave disorder.
  • Casting vote: the Speaker does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in case of a tie (Article 189).
  • Privileges: with the Committee of Privileges, the Speaker protects the House's privileges (Article 194), and courts cannot question its proceedings for procedural irregularity (Article 212).

2. Ensuring impartiality

  • Constitutional safeguards: removal only by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice (Article 179); the Speaker cannot preside while such a resolution is under consideration (Article 181); the salary is charged on the State's Consolidated Fund (Article 202).
  • Quasi-judicial roles: certifying Money Bills (Article 199(3)) and deciding defection petitions under Paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).
  • Concerns: petitions have been delayed for years or decided in haste. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) the Supreme Court said they should normally be decided within three months and asked Parliament to consider an independent tribunal; in Subhash Desai (2023), on the Maharashtra crisis, it asked the Speaker to decide within a reasonable time.
  • Party ties: unlike the Westminster convention, Speakers usually remain party members.

3. Facilitating best democratic practices

  • Committees: constituting financial and subject committees and referring Bills to them deepens scrutiny.
  • Voice for the Opposition: protecting Question Hour, calling attention motions and short-duration discussions, and allotting fair time to all parties.
  • Modernisation: paperless Assemblies through the National e-Vidhan Application (NeVA), following Himachal Pradesh's e-Vidhan (2014), make proceedings transparent and accessible.
  • Capacity and peer learning: orientation for new legislators, research support, and the All India Presiding Officers' Conference (first held in 1921), where presiding officers share best practices.
  • More sittings: many Assemblies meet for only a few weeks a year; Speakers can press for a minimum number of sittings so that Bills and budgets are properly debated.

The presiding officer is the conscience of the House. Resignation from party membership, an independent tribunal for defection cases, statutory time limits, a Deputy Speaker from the Opposition and a minimum number of sittings would make the Speaker a true neutral umpire and the Assembly a forum of deliberative democracy.
free.upm-2023-gs2-6:
Human Resource DevelopmentHuman capitalDemographic dividendCapability approach

Human Resource Development (HRD) is the process of improving people's health, nutrition, knowledge and skills so that they can lead productive and dignified lives, what Amartya Sen calls expanding capabilities. India's planned development favoured heavy industry and later services-led growth, while East Asian economies first built universal schooling and health care. This inadequate attention to HRD now threatens India's demographic dividend: the working-age share is expected to peak around 2041 (Economic Survey 2018-19).

1. Evidence of the inadequacy

  • Health: government health expenditure was only 1.43% of GDP, and out-of-pocket spending 43.4% of total health expenditure (National Health Accounts 2022-23).
  • Nutrition: 35.5% of children under five are stunted and 57% of women aged 15–49 are anaemic (NFHS-5).
  • Learning: enrolment is near universal, but ASER surveys show that many Class 5 children cannot read a Class 2 text; public spending on education remains below the 6% of GDP goal of the Kothari Commission and NEP 2020.
  • Skills: only 4.4% of youth aged 15–29 were formally skilled (PLFS 2022-23, cited in the Economic Survey 2023-24).
  • Women's work: female labour force participation was only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Higher education: a gross enrolment ratio of 28.4% (AISHE 2021-22), against NEP's target of 50% by 2035.

2. Why HRD was neglected

  • Growth model: the Mahalanobis strategy of the Second Plan (1956) put capital goods first, and elite institutions such as the IITs received priority over mass elementary education.
  • Fiscal squeeze: social spending, borne mostly by States, is often the first casualty of deficits.
  • Delivery failures: teacher vacancies and absenteeism, weak primary health centres and fragmented schemes reduce the return on spending.
  • Social barriers: caste, gender and regional inequalities limit who benefits.

3. Measures to address the inadequacy

  • Health and nutrition first: raise public health spending to 2.5% of GDP (National Health Policy, 2017), strengthen primary care through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, and focus POSHAN 2.0 on the first 1,000 days of life.
  • Foundational learning: NIPUN Bharat's goal of literacy and numeracy for all by Class 3, better teacher training and accountability for learning outcomes, with education spending raised towards 6% of GDP.
  • Skills linked to jobs: vocational education from school (NEP 2020), apprenticeships, industry-run ITIs and recognition of prior learning for informal workers.
  • Higher education and research: multidisciplinary universities and the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF Act, 2023).
  • Women's participation: crèches, safe transport, skilling and flexible work, building on the Labour Codes (in force from November 2025).
  • Convergence and data: outcome budgets, district-level planning and a stronger role for panchayats and municipalities in running schools and health centres.

HRD is not merely welfare spending; it is the foundation of growth. Treating health, learning and skills as national infrastructure, with sustained funding and accountability for outcomes, can turn India's young population into a true demographic dividend.
free.upm-2023-gs2-7:
Competition Act, 2002Abuse of dominanceSection 4Digital markets

The Competition Commission of India (CCI), set up under the Competition Act, 2002 on the Raghavan Committee's advice and fully functional since 2009, prevents anti-competitive agreements (Section 3), regulates mergers (Sections 5–6) and prohibits abuse of dominant position (Section 4). Being dominant is not illegal; abusing that position is. Multinational corporations (MNCs), especially digital platforms whose network effects make them gatekeepers, have been the focus of its most significant recent orders.

1. Legal tools against abuse

  • What counts as abuse (Section 4(2)): unfair or discriminatory conditions or prices, limiting production or technical development, denying market access, tying unrelated obligations to contracts, and using dominance in one market to enter another.
  • Assessing dominance (Section 19(4)): market share, resources, consumers' dependence and entry barriers in a relevant market.
  • Reach and remedies: the CCI can act against conduct abroad that harms competition in India (Section 32), issue cease-and-desist orders and impose penalties of up to 10% of turnover (Section 27).
  • 2023 amendment: penalties can be based on global turnover, settlement and commitment procedures speed up cases, and a ₹2,000 crore deal-value threshold brings digital acquisitions under review.

2. Recent decisions

  • Google Android (October 2022): a penalty of ₹1,337.76 crore for making device makers pre-install Google's apps and Search as a condition of licensing the Play Store; the NCLAT (March 2023) upheld the penalty and most directions but set aside four of them; Google and the CCI have both appealed to the Supreme Court.
  • Google Play billing (October 2022): ₹936.44 crore for forcing app developers to use Google Play's billing system. In March 2025 the NCLAT upheld the finding of abuse and the bar on anti-steering rules but cut the penalty to ₹216.69 crore; Google has appealed to the Supreme Court.
  • Meta and WhatsApp (November 2024): WhatsApp's 2021 "take it or leave it" privacy policy, forcing users to accept data-sharing with Meta, was held abusive: a ₹213.14 crore penalty and a five-year ban on such sharing for advertising. The NCLAT (November 2025) upheld the penalty and users' right to opt out but set aside the ban; in February 2026 Meta told the Supreme Court it would comply with the consent directions, its appeal pending.

3. Assessment

  • Gains: the orders opened Android and app-store markets to Indian developers and established that consent to data use must be real; the law applies equally to Indian firms, as when Coal India was penalised for abusing its dominance.
  • Limits: investigations and appeals take years while digital markets "tip"; penalties are small beside global revenues; and the CCI has too few technical experts.
  • Ex-ante rules: a draft Digital Competition Bill (2024) proposed advance obligations for systemically significant digital enterprises, like the EU's Digital Markets Act.

The CCI has shown that the dominance of MNCs is subject to Indian law. Faster procedures, technical capacity and calibrated ex-ante regulation of digital gatekeepers would make its oversight timely, while competitive neutrality, protecting competition rather than competitors, keeps India attractive for investment.
free.upm-2023-gs2-8:
e-governanceDigital divideProcess re-engineeringCyber security

e-governance is the use of information and communication technology to deliver services and run government (G2C, G2B, G2G). From the National e-Governance Plan (2006) to Digital India (2015) and digital public infrastructure such as Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker, it has made government more effective, transparent and accountable. Yet the Second ARC (11th Report, 2008) warned that e-governance is about reforming governance, not just computerising it, and several inadequacies still limit its gains.

1. What e-governance has achieved

  • Effectiveness: Direct Benefit Transfer sends money straight to bank accounts, cutting leakages; online services such as Passport Seva and e-Courts save time and travel.
  • Transparency: the Government e-Marketplace (GeM, 2016) makes public purchases visible, and the Public Financial Management System tracks the flow of funds.
  • Accountability: CPGRAMS tracks grievances, dashboards monitor schemes in real time, and e-Office leaves a trail of who decided what and when.

2. Inadequacies of access and inclusion

  • Digital divide: connectivity, devices and digital skills remain unequal between rural and urban areas, men and women, and young and old; last-mile gaps in rural broadband persist.
  • Exclusion by design: biometric failures and network outages have denied rations and wages, as with ration denials in Jharkhand (2017) linked to Aadhaar seeding.
  • Language and usability: complex forms and English-first portals deter users; Bhashini (2022), for services in Indian languages, is only a partial remedy so far.

3. Institutional and technical inadequacies

  • Translation, not transformation: paper processes are often put online unchanged, without re-engineering, so delays simply move from files to servers.
  • Silos: departments build separate databases with weak interoperability, and citizens submit the same documents again and again.
  • Capacity and vendor dependence: governments have few in-house technology experts, and vendor-designed systems sometimes fail at launch, as the new income-tax e-filing portal did (2021).
  • Cyber security and privacy: the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi's servers (November 2022) exposed vulnerabilities; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its Rules (2025) are being phased in, and critics worry about broad exemptions for the State.
  • Accountability gaps: dashboards record failures but do not fix responsibility; automated decisions are rarely explained, and grievance redress often lacks a human fallback.

4. The way forward

  • Inclusion: assisted access through Common Service Centres, offline fallbacks and accessible design for the elderly and persons with disabilities.
  • Capacity: digital skills for officials through Mission Karmayogi and in-house technology teams.
  • Trust: privacy by design, regular security audits with CERT-In and independent review of automated decisions.

e-governance has strengthened effectiveness, transparency and accountability, but technology alone cannot reform government. Bridging the digital divide, re-engineering processes and building trust, in line with the Second ARC's SMART ideal (simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent), will complete the transformation.
free.upm-2023-gs2-9:
SCOShanghai SpiritTerrorismStrategic autonomy

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), founded in 2001 from the "Shanghai Five" (1996), seeks regional security and cooperation in the "Shanghai Spirit" of mutual trust, equality, consultation and respect for diversity. It now has ten members, including India and Pakistan (2017), Iran (2023) and Belarus (2024). Its 25th-anniversary summit at Bishkek (31 August–1 September 2026) showed both its reach and the "virus of conflict" among its members.

1. The virus of conflict

  • India–Pakistan: cross-border terrorism blocks consensus; after the Pahalgam attack (22 April 2025) and Operation Sindoor (May 2025), India declined to sign the SCO defence ministers' joint statement at Qingdao (June 2025) because it left out Pahalgam.
  • India–China: the Galwan clash (2020) froze relations until the disengagement agreement of October 2024.
  • Russia and the West: the Ukraine war (since 2022) and Russia's isolation tempt the SCO towards an anti-Western identity that not all members share.
  • West and Central Asia: Iran's conflicts with Israel and the USA (2025–26) divide members; Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan clashed on their border (2021, 2022) before signing a border treaty in 2025.
  • Effects: consensus yields lowest-common-denominator texts, the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS, Tashkent) loses credibility when members shelter terror groups, and China's weight raises fears of a China-led bloc. India does not endorse the Belt and Road Initiative in SCO documents because the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

2. India's role in mitigating the problems

  • Counter-terrorism without double standards: India presses for action against terror financing, recruitment and safe havens through RATS and summit texts; the Tianjin Declaration (2025) condemned the Pahalgam attack, and the Bishkek Declaration (2026) condemned terrorism in all its forms and called double standards unacceptable.
  • Dialogue and diplomacy: India urges peaceful settlement, from the Prime Minister's "this is not an era of war" (Samarkand, 2022) to his statement at Bishkek (2026) that conflicts cannot be resolved by military means.
  • A bridge between blocs: as a member of both the SCO and the Quad, India can stop the SCO from turning into an anti-Western alliance.
  • Managing rivalry with China: the Prime Minister's visit to Tianjin for the 2025 summit, his first to China in seven years, used the SCO to help stabilise ties.
  • Connectivity that respects sovereignty: India backs projects that respect territorial integrity and offers the International North–South Transport Corridor and Chabahar to landlocked Central Asia, though US sanctions and the 2026 conflict involving Iran have clouded the port's future.
  • A positive agenda: India's SECURE vision (Qingdao, 2018) and its three pillars of Security, Connectivity and Opportunity; India-led initiatives include a Civilisation Dialogue Forum (India to host the first), a Young Scientist Forum and English, which the SCO adopted as an official language at Bishkek (2026).

The SCO remains valuable to India for Central Asian outreach, energy and counter-terrorism cooperation. By insisting on zero tolerance for terrorism, respect for sovereignty and dialogue, India can act as the balancer that keeps the Shanghai Spirit alive despite the virus of conflict.
free.upm-2023-gs2-10:
Indian diasporaRemittancesKnowledge networksSoft power

India has the world's largest diaspora: about 1.8 crore Indian-born emigrants (UN, 2020). Its Western branch, in the USA, the UK, Canada, Europe and Australia, is highly educated and prosperous and has scaled new heights in business, technology and politics. A sign of this is that the USA, which displaced the UAE as India's largest source of remittances in 2020-21, sent a 27.7% share in 2023-24 (RBI's sixth remittances survey, March 2025).

1. Rise in the West

  • Corporate leadership: Indian-origin executives head global firms such as Alphabet (Sundar Pichai) and Microsoft (Satya Nadella).
  • Political office: Rishi Sunak (UK Prime Minister, 2022–24), Kamala Harris (US Vice-President, 2021–25), Leo Varadkar (Ireland's Taoiseach, 2017–20 and 2022–24) and António Costa (Portugal's Prime Minister, and President of the European Council since December 2024).
  • Professions and academia: a large presence among doctors, engineers, scientists and university faculty.

2. Economic benefits for India

  • Remittances: India is the world's largest recipient, with record inflows of about US$135 billion in 2024-25; the share of advanced economies overtook that of the Gulf in 2023-24, reflecting skilled migration to the West.
  • Investment and start-ups: diaspora entrepreneurs and venture capitalists invest in Indian start-ups, and NRI deposits support the balance of payments.
  • Technology and services: diaspora executives helped build India's IT services industry and the Global Capability Centres that now do research and development for global firms.
  • Knowledge circulation: returnees and schemes such as VAJRA (2017) bring researchers and ideas back to Indian institutions.
  • Trade links: diaspora demand and business networks support Indian goods and trade agreements such as the India–UK CETA (signed July 2025).

3. Political benefits

  • Advocacy: Indian-American groups lobbied the US Congress for the India–US civil nuclear deal (2005–08).
  • Voice in host countries: legislators of Indian origin in the US Congress and the British and Canadian Parliaments shape debates on trade, immigration and India.
  • Soft power: yoga, cinema and festivals have gone mainstream; the UN declared 21 June the International Day of Yoga (2014), and a 2023 law made Diwali a public-school holiday in New York City.
  • Strategic goodwill: people-to-people ties are a pillar of India's partnerships with the USA, the UK and the European Union.

4. Limits

Host-country loyalties come first, and leaders of Indian origin serve their own nations. Separatist activity among a small section of the diaspora in Canada strained ties, which fell into a diplomatic crisis in 2023, and tighter immigration rules, such as a steep US fee on new H-1B visa petitions (2025), show that diaspora influence has limits.

The Western diaspora is both an economic multiplier and a strategic asset. Engaging it through OCI facilities, research partnerships and investment channels, while avoiding the export of domestic divisions, will deepen India's ties with the West.
free.upm-2023-gs2-11:
Living constitutionArticle 21Maneka Gandhi (1978)Transformative constitutionalism

A living constitution grows with society, through interpretation as much as amendment. India's Constitution, amended more than a hundred times, has also been read by its courts as a charter of transformative constitutionalism, meant to carry a hierarchical society towards liberty, equality and dignity. Nowhere is this clearer than in Article 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." These few words have become the widest source of rights in Part III.

1. From procedure to due process

  • A.K. Gopalan (1950): any procedure enacted by a legislature was enough, and Articles 19, 21 and 22 were read as separate compartments.
  • Maneka Gandhi (1978): the procedure must be "fair, just and reasonable", and Articles 14, 19 and 21 were read together (later called the "golden triangle"), bringing in due process in substance.
  • Correcting the Emergency: the 44th Amendment (1978) made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable, and Puttaswamy (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur (1976).

2. Expanding horizons of life and liberty

  • Dignity and livelihood: life includes the bare necessities of a dignified life (Francis Coralie Mullin, 1981) and the livelihood of pavement dwellers (Olga Tellis, 1985).
  • Justice for the vulnerable: speedy trial and free legal aid for undertrials (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979), humane treatment of prisoners (Sunil Batra, 1978) and safeguards on arrest (D.K. Basu, 1997).
  • Social rights drawn from the Directive Principles: education (Unni Krishnan, 1993), later Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002); emergency medical care (Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity, 1996); and food (PUCL, from 2001), later the National Food Security Act, 2013.
  • Autonomy and identity: privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), choice of partner (Shafin Jahan, 2018), sexual orientation (Navtej Singh Johar, 2018), gender identity (NALSA, 2014) and reproductive choice for unmarried women (2022).
  • New frontiers: a clean environment (Subhash Kumar, 1991) and a right against the adverse effects of climate change (M.K. Ranjitsinh, 2024); the right to die with dignity and living wills (Common Cause, 2018); and, in October 2026, the Supreme Court's recognition that children too have a fundamental right to internet access.

3. A constitution for a progressive society

  • Dialogue with Parliament: judicial readings prompted laws such as the RTE Act, 2009, the National Food Security Act, 2013 and, after Puttaswamy, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
  • Responsiveness: rights now cover technology, climate and identity, issues the framers could not foresee, without any change in the text.

4. Caveats

  • Judicial overreach: critics say courts create rights without the legislature's mandate or resources.
  • Rights on paper: long trials, crowded prisons and poor public health show that recognised rights often go unenforced.

Article 21 shows that the Constitution is a living instrument: each generation finds in "life and personal liberty" the freedoms it needs. Pairing judicial creativity with legislation and public investment will keep this dynamism in the service of a progressive society.
free.upm-2023-gs2-12:
Gender justiceArticle 15(3)Substantive equalityDignity and autonomy

Gender justice means equal rights, dignity and opportunities for all genders, together with the correction of historical disadvantage. The Constitution pursues it at three levels: formal equality through non-discrimination (Articles 14, 15(1), 16(2)), substantive equality through special provisions for women (Article 15(3)), and dignity and autonomy under Article 21. India's ratification of CEDAW (1993) and an active judiciary have turned these provisions into a living charter of women's rights.

1. Equality and non-discrimination

  • Service rules: C.B. Muthamma (1979) held discriminatory the rules that penalised women foreign-service officers for marrying; Air India v. Nergesh Meerza (1981) struck down the termination of air hostesses on their first pregnancy.
  • Against paternalism: Anuj Garg (2008) struck down a ban on women working in bars, holding that protective laws must not reinforce stereotypes.
  • Armed forces: Babita Puniya (2020) ordered permanent commission for women officers in the Army.

2. Dignity and safety

  • Workplace: Vishaka (1997), drawing on CEDAW, framed guidelines against sexual harassment, which led to the POSH Act, 2013.
  • Bodily integrity: Independent Thought (2017) held that sex with a minor wife is rape, and X v. Principal Secretary (2022) extended abortion up to 24 weeks to unmarried women.
  • Acid attacks: in Laxmi (2013) the Court regulated the sale of acid and directed compensation for survivors.

3. Autonomy within the family and personal law

  • Maintenance: Shah Bano (1985) upheld maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 CrPC, and Mohd. Abdul Samad (2024) reaffirmed that this secular remedy, now Section 144 of the BNSS, is open to her.
  • Marriage: Shayara Bano (2017) invalidated instant triple talaq, followed by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019; Joseph Shine (2018) struck down the adultery offence (Section 497 IPC) for treating a wife as her husband's property.
  • Property: Vineeta Sharma (2020) held daughters to be coparceners by birth, whether or not the father was alive in 2005.
  • Religion and equality: Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018) struck down the bar on women aged 10–50 entering Sabarimala; review petitions were referred to a larger Bench in 2019.

4. Beyond the binary, and the gaps

  • Gender identity: NALSA (2014) and Navtej Singh Johar (2018) extended gender justice to transgender and queer persons.
  • Gaps: the marital rape exception for adult wives continues in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Section 63), women's reservation in legislatures awaits delimitation, and female labour force participation is only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).

The constitutional perspective on gender justice has moved from protection to empowerment and autonomy. Turning judgments into social change through education, economic independence and political representation is the task that remains for substantive equality.
free.upm-2023-gs2-13:
Article 356S.R. Bommai (1994)Floor testCoalition politics

Article 356 allows President's Rule when the President is satisfied, on the Governor's report or otherwise, that a State's government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Dr Ambedkar hoped it would remain a "dead letter", but it was invoked over 100 times, often against governments of rival parties, as in the dismissal of nine State governments in 1977 and nine more in 1980. Since the mid-1990s its use has fallen sharply, for both legal and political reasons.

1. Legal factors

  • S.R. Bommai (1994): a nine-judge Bench made the proclamation subject to judicial review of the existence and relevance of material; majority must be tested on the floor of the House, not in Raj Bhavan; the Assembly may only be kept in suspended animation until Parliament approves; and a court can restore a dismissed government. Federalism and secularism were held to be basic features.
  • Rameshwar Prasad (2006): the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly (2005) was held unconstitutional because the Governor's report lacked relevant material.
  • Restoration in practice: in 2016 the Supreme Court restored the dismissed government of Arunachal Pradesh (Nabam Rebia) and ordered a floor test in Uttarakhand, after which President's Rule was revoked.
  • Constitutional limits: both Houses must approve a proclamation within two months, and since the 44th Amendment (1978) it can run beyond one year only during a National Emergency and with the Election Commission's certificate.
  • Floor test as the norm: courts now order early floor tests in disputes over government formation, as in Karnataka (2018) and Maharashtra (2019).

2. Political factors

  • Coalition era (1989–2014): regional parties sat in Union governments and resisted the dismissal of State governments.
  • The Rajya Sabha as a check: in 1999 President's Rule in Bihar was revoked within weeks because it could not secure the Rajya Sabha's approval.
  • Presidential scrutiny: President K.R. Narayanan returned the Union Cabinet's recommendations for Uttar Pradesh (1997) and Bihar (1998) for reconsideration.
  • Commission guidance: the Sarkaria Commission (1988) urged use only as a last resort, after a warning to the State, and the Punchhi Commission (2010) proposed localised emergencies instead.
  • Political cost: strong regional parties, an active media and voters' disapproval make toppling elected governments risky, and the courts' readiness to restore them removes any gain.

3. Use today

President's Rule is now used mainly when no government can be formed or order breaks down, as in Jammu and Kashmir (2018–19), briefly in Maharashtra (2019), in Puducherry (2021) and in Manipur (13 February 2025 to 4 February 2026). Critics note that pressure on States has shifted to other channels, such as Governors' discretion over Bills.

Judicial review, coalition politics and federal assertion have moved Article 356 close to the last resort the framers intended. Codifying the Sarkaria and Punchhi safeguards and an active Inter-State Council would make this change lasting and strengthen cooperative federalism.
free.upm-2023-gs2-14:
Civil societyWomen's representation106th AmendmentPolitical empowerment

Women are nearly half of India's voters, yet only 9% of MLAs: 390 of 4,123 members of State and UT Assemblies (ADR, March 2026), against 14% in the Lok Sabha. The 106th Amendment (2023) will reserve one-third of Assembly seats only after delimitation. Meanwhile civil society groups, from women's movements and NGOs to self-help group federations, research bodies and the media, have worked to make women's participation effective and meaningful, not merely numerical.

1. Advocacy for reservation and representation

  • Women's movements: organisations such as the National Federation of Indian Women (1954) and the All India Democratic Women's Association (1981) campaigned for one-third reservation from the 81st Amendment Bill (1996) to the 106th Amendment (2023).
  • Evidence and research: groups such as the Association for Democratic Reforms publish data on women candidates, showing that parties field few women although women win at about the same rate as men (9% against 10% in the current Assemblies).
  • Pressure on parties: non-partisan collectives such as Shakti (Political Power to Women) have urged parties to give women half their tickets and helped women ask for nominations.

2. Building a pipeline of women leaders

  • Training elected women: NGOs such as PRIA and The Hunger Project train women panchayat members in budgeting, Gram Sabha work and public speaking, creating a pool of experienced leaders for Assembly politics.
  • Self-help group federations: Kudumbashree in Kerala and SHG networks elsewhere give women organising experience, confidence and a support base for contesting elections.
  • Breaking barriers: in Nagaland, where women's groups long campaigned and went to court for women's reservation in urban local bodies, voters elected the State's first two women MLAs in 2023.

3. Making participation effective and meaningful

  • Voter mobilisation: campaigns by women's groups, alongside the Election Commission's outreach, have helped close the gender gap in turnout, making women a constituency that parties court.
  • Agenda-setting: women's charters of demands before elections push parties on safety, work, care and health.
  • Support for legislators: non-partisan research bodies such as PRS Legislative Research help legislators scrutinise Bills and budgets, and networks of women representatives encourage cross-party cooperation.
  • Countering abuse: campaigns expose online abuse and intimidation that deter women from public life.

4. Limits

  • Party gatekeeping: tickets, money and leadership remain male-dominated, and civil society cannot nominate candidates.
  • Proxy and dynastic politics: some women candidates are fielded as stand-ins for male relatives, diluting their agency.
  • Fragmented civil society: many groups are urban and divided, and curbs on foreign funding (FCRA amendment, 2020) have squeezed NGOs.

Civil society has kept women's representation on the national agenda and prepared women to lead. Early implementation of the 106th Amendment, voluntary party quotas for tickets and continued capacity building can turn presence into substantive representation.
free.upm-2023-gs2-15:
101st AmendmentGST CouncilCooperative federalismPooled sovereignty

The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) from 1 July 2017, a destination-based tax that subsumed 17 Central and State taxes and 13 cesses. It created a concurrent taxing power for the Union and the States (Article 246A) and a joint forum, the GST Council (Article 279A), making it India's boldest experiment in cooperative federalism.

1. Significance

  • A common market: input tax credit at every stage ends the cascading of taxes, and the removal of inter-State check posts speeds the movement of goods ("One Nation, One Tax").
  • Constitutional innovation: Article 246A gives Parliament and State legislatures simultaneous power to tax supplies; Article 269A provides for IGST on inter-State supplies and imports, shared between the Union and the States; Article 366(12A) defines GST.
  • Pooled sovereignty: both levels gave up independent taxes such as excise duty, service tax, VAT and entry tax for a shared base governed jointly.
  • Destination principle: revenue goes to the consuming State, helping States with large markets but little manufacturing.

2. The accommodative spirit

  • Joint decision-making: the Council includes the Union Finance Minister and the finance ministers of all States; since decisions need three-fourths of the weighted votes, neither side can impose its will alone, and most have been taken by consensus.
  • Compensation: States were guaranteed compensation for revenue loss for five years (to June 2022) at an assumed 14% annual growth; when the cess fell short during COVID-19, the Union borrowed and passed the money on to States as back-to-back loans.
  • Respect for State fields: alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside GST, petroleum products come in only on the Council's recommendation, and States keep taxes such as stamp duty and electricity duty.
  • Judicial affirmation: in Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held the Council's recommendations persuasive, not binding, because Parliament and the States hold equal power under Article 246A.
  • Shared revenue and joint reform: CGST and part of IGST reach States through the Finance Commission's divisible pool (Article 270), and "GST 2.0" moved to two main slabs, 5% and 18%, from 22 September 2025 by joint decision.

3. To what extent? The limits

  • Loss of fiscal autonomy: States gave up most of their own indirect taxes and cannot change rates on their own.
  • An effective Union veto: with one-third of the votes, the Union can block any proposal, while the States need near-unanimity to outvote it.
  • Revenue uncertainty: delayed compensation payments strained trust, and the end of compensation in June 2022 hurt manufacturing States.
  • Unfinished institutions: the dispute-settlement mechanism envisaged in Article 279A(11) has not been set up.

The 101st Amendment reflects the accommodative spirit of federalism to a large extent: it replaced unilateral taxation with pooled sovereignty and negotiation. A standing dispute-settlement mechanism, assured revenue for States and a stronger voice for them in the Council would complete the federal bargain.
free.upm-2023-gs2-16:
Parliamentary committeesPublic Accounts CommitteeEstimates CommitteeInstitutionalisation

Parliament sits for limited days but must scrutinise a vast executive, so much of its detailed work is done by committees, often called "mini-Parliaments". They are elected by the House or nominated by the presiding officer, work under the Speaker or Chairman and report to the House; their authority rests on Articles 105 and 118 and the Rules of Procedure. Among them, the three financial committees have done most to institutionalise Parliament, that is, to give it stable rules, expertise and autonomy from the executive.

1. Structure of the committee system

  • Standing and ad hoc: standing committees are permanent and reconstituted periodically; ad hoc committees are formed for a particular Bill or inquiry and dissolve after reporting.
  • Composition: members are drawn from parties roughly in proportion to their strength, and ministers do not sit on the financial committees.
  • Working: committees meet behind closed doors, take evidence from officials and experts, and present reports that, though recommendatory, carry weight with the House and the government.

2. The financial committees

  • Public Accounts Committee (1921): 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) examine the CAG's audit reports on government spending; by convention since 1967 it is chaired by a member of the Opposition.
  • Estimates Committee (1950): 30 Lok Sabha members examine the estimates and suggest economies, efficiency and alternative policies, acting as a "continuous economy committee".
  • Committee on Public Undertakings (1964): 22 members (15 + 7) examine the reports and accounts of public sector undertakings, including CAG reports on them, and their autonomy and efficiency.

3. How far they have institutionalised Parliament

  • Completing the accountability cycle: Parliament approves money (Articles 112–114), the CAG audits its use (Article 151) and the PAC examines the audit, so the executive answers for every rupee; excess spending is regularised (Article 115) only after PAC scrutiny.
  • A bipartisan culture: an Opposition chair, closed-door sittings and mostly unanimous reports let members rise above party lines.
  • Expertise and memory: permanent secretariats, the CAG's technical support and Action Taken Reports build institutional memory beyond individual MPs.
  • Norms of financial propriety: decades of reports have set standards on savings, surrenders, delays and cost overruns that ministries now follow.

4. Limits

  • Post-mortem and advisory: the PAC examines accounts years after the spending, and governments accept recommendations selectively.
  • Limited reach: the Estimates Committee examines only a few ministries each year, and many demands for grants are passed by the guillotine without discussion.
  • Declining scrutiny of Bills: the share of Bills referred to committees fell from 71% in the 15th Lok Sabha to 16% in the 17th (PRS).

The financial committees have helped make Parliament an institution that scrutinises rather than merely approves. Research staff, time-bound government replies and mandatory referral of Bills to committees would deepen parliamentary accountability and the institutionalisation of Indian democracy.
free.upm-2023-gs2-17:
Protective discriminationReasonable classificationSubstantive equalityTargeting

Welfare and development schemes for the vulnerable (Scheduled Castes and Tribes, backward classes, women, minorities, persons with disabilities and the poor) necessarily single out some people for benefits. In that sense they differentiate. But the Constitution distinguishes unfair discrimination from reasonable classification under Article 14 and from protective discrimination under Articles 15(3)–(6), 16(4) and 46, which pursue substantive equality. I therefore agree only partly: such schemes are differential by nature, but not discriminatory in the constitutional sense.

1. Why they can appear discriminatory

  • Built-in differentiation: post-matric scholarships for SC students, Stand-Up India loans for SC, ST and women entrepreneurs, and PM-JANMAN for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups exclude others by design.
  • Errors of targeting: lists based on surveys such as the SECC 2011 leave out some of the poor (exclusion errors) and include some of the better-off (inclusion errors).
  • Capture within groups: better-off families corner benefits, which is why the creamy layer applies to OBCs (Indra Sawhney, 1992) and in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) a seven-judge bench allowed States to sub-classify SCs and STs.
  • Identity versus need: poor families outside the targeted groups feel left out, a concern behind the EWS quota of the 103rd Amendment, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).
  • Barriers in delivery: documents and biometric checks can exclude the most vulnerable, and means-testing can stigmatise.

2. Why they are not discriminatory in substance

  • Reasonable classification: Article 14 permits classification founded on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus with the object of the law (Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952).
  • Equality as fairness: in N.M. Thomas (1976) the Supreme Court held that reservation is a facet of equality, not an exception to it; treating unequals equally only perpetuates inequality.
  • Constitutional mandate: Article 46 directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, and Article 38 to minimise inequalities; Dr Ambedkar saw social and economic democracy as the base of political democracy.
  • Philosophy: John Rawls's difference principle accepts inequalities that benefit the least advantaged.
  • Results: targeted programmes helped cut multidimensional poverty from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23) (NITI Aayog) and brought women and Dalits into local government.

3. Making welfare fairer

  • A universal floor with targeted top-ups: universal basic services, such as PM-JAY health cover for everyone aged 70 and above (2024), with extra support for the most deprived.
  • Better data: a dynamic social registry, periodic revision of beneficiary lists and data-based sub-classification.
  • Graduation: exit criteria such as the creamy layer, and a focus on capabilities so that beneficiaries move out of dependence.
  • Accountability: social audits and grievance redress to catch exclusion errors early.

Welfare schemes treat people differently in order to treat them as equals. The real problem is not their differential nature but poor targeting and capture; better design can make them instruments of social justice rather than division.
free.upm-2023-gs2-18:
Education–skill–employmentSkill IndiaEmployabilityNEP 2020

Education builds foundational and cognitive abilities, skills turn them into job-ready competence, and employment depends on whether the economy demands those skills. Since the National Skill Development Mission (2015) under Skill India, programmes such as PMKVY, apprenticeships and ITIs have raised the supply of trained workers to sectors such as construction, retail, logistics, health care and electronics. Yet only 4.4% of youth aged 15–29 were formally skilled (PLFS 2022-23, Economic Survey 2023-24), showing that the links in the chain remain weak.

1. How skill programmes have raised human resource supply

  • Short-term training: PMKVY (2015) and Jan Shikshan Sansthans train and certify youth, while Recognition of Prior Learning certifies workers who learnt on the job.
  • Standards: Sector Skill Councils and the National Skills Qualifications Framework align courses with industry needs, so employers can trust certificates.
  • Apprenticeships: the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (2016) shares stipend costs so that firms train apprentices on the shop floor.
  • Targeted groups: DDU-GKY (2014) for rural youth, and women's programmes such as Namo Drone Didi, build skills for new sectors.

2. Linkages between education, skill and employment

  • Education is the foundation: weak reading and arithmetic, as ASER surveys show, limit how far youth can be trained; NEP 2020 integrates vocational education from school and aimed for at least half of learners to have vocational exposure by 2025.
  • Skills bridge education and jobs: only about half of young people are judged employable (Economic Survey 2023-24, citing the India Skills Report 2024), because many degrees lack applied skills.
  • Employment builds skills: formal jobs offer on-the-job learning, but about 90% of workers are informal and receive little training.
  • Demand matters: skilling without job creation leads to underemployment; the Economic Survey 2023-24 estimated that about 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs are needed every year until 2030.
  • The educated-unemployment paradox: unemployment is higher among graduates than among those with less schooling, a sign of mismatch rather than surplus.

3. Weak links

  • Supply-driven training: courses are chosen to meet targets rather than local demand, and placement after short-term training is low.
  • Low prestige: vocational routes are seen as second-best, and ties between ITIs and industry are weak.
  • Women left out: female labour force participation of about 42% (PLFS 2023-24) wastes trained talent.
  • Fast-changing technology: automation and AI make some skills obsolete quickly, so lifelong learning is essential.

The statement holds for the supply of trained people, but supply alone does not create jobs. Aligning education, skills and employment through industry partnership, demand-led training and employment-intensive growth in manufacturing and MSMEs can turn human resources into a real demographic dividend.
free.upm-2023-gs2-19:
NATO enlargementTransatlantic partnershipStrategic autonomyMulti-alignment

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), founded in 1949 with 12 members, has grown to 32 after Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024) joined in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022). Its Madrid Strategic Concept (2022) for the first time described China's ambitions as a challenge to Allied interests, and at The Hague (June 2025) members pledged to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP by 2035. For India, which follows strategic autonomy, a stronger US–Europe partnership is a mixed blessing.

1. How it works well for India

  • Balancing China: a cohesive West attentive to Asia complements the Quad; NATO works with four Indo-Pacific partners (Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand), and the EU's Indo-Pacific Strategy (2021) supports a rules-based maritime order.
  • Technology and defence: Western cohesion eases co-production and technology transfer, from Rafale jets (France) to GE F414 engines to be made with HAL (USA), and the India–EU Trade and Technology Council.
  • Trade and supply chains: Western "de-risking" from China opens opportunities for India, backed by trade deals with the UK (CETA, signed July 2025), EFTA (in force October 2025) and the EU (announced January 2026).
  • Connectivity: the US- and EU-backed India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (2023) offers an alternative to the Belt and Road Initiative.

2. Why it may not always work for India

  • Russia pushed towards China: NATO's expansion and Western sanctions deepen Russia–China alignment, India's main strategic worry, and complicate India's defence ties with Russia.
  • Pressure on strategic autonomy: the threat of US sanctions under CAATSA (2017) over the S-400 purchase, and US sanctions in late 2025 that cut India's access to discounted Russian crude.
  • Transactional pressures: in August 2025 the USA, India's largest export market, raised tariffs on most Indian goods to 50%, including a 25% penalty for buying Russian oil. The penalty was removed in February 2026, but the episode showed how the West's confrontation with Russia can be passed on to India.
  • Eurocentric priorities: the war in Europe absorbs Western attention, raised energy and food prices for developing countries and brings pressure on India to take sides at the UN.
  • A strained partnership: since 2025, disputes over trade and burden-sharing have tested transatlantic ties themselves.

3. My view

The statement is only partly true. A strong, Asia-minded West helps India balance China and gain technology and markets, but a NATO-centred order confronting Russia pushes Moscow towards Beijing and narrows India's choices. India's interest lies in multi-alignment: deep partnerships with the USA and Europe through the Quad, trade agreements and technology councils, without joining military blocs, while keeping its ties with Russia and its voice for the Global South.

India gains most from a West that is strong but not bloc-minded; issue-based partnerships that respect its strategic autonomy, rather than alliance membership, best serve its interests.
free.upm-2023-gs2-20:
IMOMARPOL and SOLASMaritime securityGreen shipping

The oceans cover about 71% of the Earth, regulate its climate, sustain much of its biodiversity and carry around 80% of world trade by volume; the sea is thus a vital component of the cosmos that human activity must not disturb. The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a UN specialised agency based in London (convention adopted in 1948, in force from 1958), sets global shipping rules under its motto of "safe, secure and efficient shipping on clean oceans". India has been a member since 1959.

1. Protecting the marine environment

  • MARPOL (1973/78): six annexes cover oil, noxious liquids, harmful packaged goods, sewage, garbage and air pollution; the global limit on sulphur in ship fuel fell from 3.5% to 0.50% on 1 January 2020.
  • Other threats: dumping at sea (London Convention, 1972), invasive species (Ballast Water Management Convention, 2004, in force 2017) and toxic anti-fouling paints (AFS Convention, 2001).
  • Ship recycling: the Hong Kong Convention (2009) entered into force in June 2025; India, home to the Alang yard, acceded in 2019 and enacted the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019.
  • Climate: the 2023 GHG Strategy seeks net-zero emissions by or around 2050, with checkpoints for 2030 and 2040. The Net-Zero Framework, combining a global fuel standard with emissions pricing, was approved in April 2025, but its adoption was postponed in October 2025 and it had not been adopted as of October 2026.

2. Enhancing maritime safety

  • SOLAS (1974): first adopted in 1914 after the Titanic disaster, it sets standards for ship construction, fire safety, life-saving appliances and radio communication.
  • STCW (1978): minimum standards of training and certification, vital for India as a major supplier of seafarers.
  • Navigation and rescue: collision rules (COLREGs, 1972), load lines (1966), search and rescue (SAR, 1979) and the Polar Code (2017).

3. Strengthening maritime security

  • ISPS Code (2002): adopted after the 9/11 attacks, it requires security plans and officers for ships and port facilities.
  • SUA Convention (1988): with its 2005 Protocols, it criminalises unlawful acts against ships, including terrorism.
  • Piracy: the Djibouti Code of Conduct (2009) and its Jeddah Amendment (2017) helped regional states curb Somali piracy, alongside naval patrols such as India's in the Gulf of Aden since 2008.
  • New threats: guidance on cyber risks, and attacks on merchant ships in the Red Sea since late 2023.

4. Limits

  • Enforcement gap: the IMO has no enforcement power of its own; it depends on flag States, some offering "flags of convenience", and on port State control.
  • Slow consensus: the delay in adopting the Net-Zero Framework shows how divided members can stall action.
  • Capacity and equity: developing countries need finance and technology to meet stricter standards.

The IMO has made shipping one of the most closely regulated global industries. With its long coastline and large seafaring workforce, India should champion a just transition to green shipping and a secure, rules-based blue economy.
free.upm-2023-gs3-1:
Manufacturing-led growthMSMEsPLI and National Manufacturing MissionFormalisation

Manufacturing contributes only about 17% of India's GVA, well short of the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011, although it is the sector best able to absorb surplus farm labour, raise productivity and earn exports. Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), defined under the MSMED Act, 2006, are its broad base: they produce about 30% of GDP and around 45% of exports, and are the largest non-farm employers.

1. Why manufacturing and MSMEs hold the key to faster growth

  • Moving labour out of farms: about 46% of workers are still in agriculture (PLFS 2023-24); factories offer higher productivity and wages, as the East Asian economies showed.
  • Linkages and scale: manufacturing pulls up mining, logistics, finance and services through strong backward and forward linkages.
  • MSMEs spread growth: they need little capital per job, work in small towns and clusters, and supply large firms as ancillaries.
  • Trade and resilience: domestic production of electronics, drugs and components cuts import dependence and taps China-plus-one supply chains.

2. Present policies of the Government (as of 2026)

  • Formalisation: Udyam registration (2020) links units to priority-sector credit and procurement preferences.
  • Prompt payment: since 2023, Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act lets buyers deduct payments to micro and small suppliers only if paid within the MSMED Act limit (at most 45 days), backed by TReDS and the MSME Samadhaan portal.
  • New entrepreneurs: term loans up to ₹2 crore for 5 lakh first-time women, SC and ST entrepreneurs (Budget 2025-26), and PM Vishwakarma (2023) for artisans.

3. Comment: results and gaps

  • Gains: PLI had brought over ₹2.5 lakh crore of investment and about 14.5 lakh jobs by June 2026 (DPIIT data), and India is now the second-largest mobile-phone maker.
  • Stagnant share: manufacturing's share of GVA has hardly moved in decades; PLI gains are concentrated in a few, often assembly-led, sectors.
  • Missing middle: over 99% of MSMEs are micro units (NSS 73rd round) that stay small and informal, with limited access to credit, technology and markets.
  • Cost disadvantages: logistics costs of 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT), costly power and land, and skill gaps reduce competitiveness against Vietnam and Bangladesh.

The policy direction is sound; what matters now is execution: cluster infrastructure, cheaper credit, skilling and labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, footwear and food processing, so that MSMEs grow into competitive firms and manufacturing-led growth creates jobs at scale.
free.upm-2023-gs3-2:
Digital economyDigital Public InfrastructureDigital divideCyber security

Digitalisation is the use of digital technologies and data in production, payments, trade and governance. India's digital economy was 11.74% of GDP in 2022-23 (₹31.64 lakh crore) and is expected to reach nearly one-fifth of national income by 2029-30, growing almost twice as fast as the economy (MeitY report, January 2025). Its foundation is Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and open networks.

1. Status of digitalisation (as of 2026)

  • Connectivity: 111.4 crore internet subscribers (TRAI, June 2026), cheap mobile data and 5G services since 2022.
  • Payments: UPI has handled over 20 billion transactions a month since August 2025, and over 95% of banking payment transactions are digital.
  • Welfare: Direct Benefit Transfer has moved over ₹52 lakh crore through 900+ schemes; 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts and DigiLocker (72 crore+ users) support it.
  • Commerce: ONDC, GeM, GST e-invoicing and the Account Aggregator framework bring small firms into formal markets and credit.
  • Jobs and services: the digital economy employed about 1.47 crore workers (2.55% of the workforce) in 2022-23, and India hosts about 55% of the world's global capability centres (PIB, 2025).

2. Problems faced

  • Digital divide: only 33% of women against 57% of men had ever used the internet (NFHS-5); rural, elderly, poor and disabled users lag behind, and content in Indian languages is still limited.
  • Cyber fraud: phishing, "digital arrest" scams and UPI frauds erode trust; the I4C's fraud-reporting system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026, a sign of the scale of the problem.
  • Privacy and security: the DPDP Act, 2023 is being phased in under its 2025 Rules, while attacks such as the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi (2022) expose weak cyber hygiene.
  • Exclusion by design: failed biometric authentication can deny rations or pensions, and many services lack offline alternatives.
  • Uneven adoption: most MSMEs and farmers use digital tools only for payments; two apps handle most UPI traffic, a concentration risk.

3. Suggested improvements

  • Last-mile access: complete BharatNet, expand PM-WANI public Wi-Fi and make devices affordable.
  • Skills: digital literacy through Common Service Centres and schools, with Bhashini tools for services in every language.
  • Trust: enforce the DPDP Act, CERT-In's six-hour incident reporting and the 1930 fraud helpline; build fraud analytics and grievance redress into every platform.
  • Beyond payments: use account-aggregator data for cash-flow credit to MSMEs, and ONDC and e-commerce exports for small producers.
  • Future capacity: data centres, AI compute (over 45,000 GPUs under IndiaAI by June 2026) and regular official measurement of the digital economy.

India's DPI model of "public rails, private innovation" has made it a digitalisation leader; closing the gender, rural and skill divides and building digital trust will turn this reach into broad-based productivity.
free.upm-2023-gs3-3:
e-Technology in agricultureDigital Agriculture Missione-NAMPrecision farming

e-Technology in agriculture means applying ICT, mobile phones, the internet, satellites, drones, sensors, AI and digital platforms, across the farm cycle. For India's farmers, 86% of whom are small and marginal, it lowers the cost of information, inputs, credit and market access. The Digital Agriculture Mission (2024, ₹2,817 crore), which builds AgriStack, and e-NAM (2016) anchor this shift from guesswork to data-driven farming.

1. How e-Technology helps in production

  • Advisories: Kisan Call Centres (2004) answer farmers' queries in local languages, and IMD issues district-level agromet advisories that guide sowing, irrigation and harvesting.
  • Soil and inputs: Soil Health Cards (2015) give crop-wise fertiliser recommendations, cutting waste and cost; QR-coded seed traceability curbs spurious seed.
  • Precision farming: drones spray fertiliser and pesticides precisely (Namo Drone Didi provides 15,000 drones to women's self-help groups), while sensors and automated drip systems save water.
  • Crop monitoring and risk: satellites track crop health and drought; FASAL forecasts output, and YES-TECH estimates yields at gram panchayat level for faster crop-insurance claims under PMFBY.
