  • Correcting intuition: in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), the Supreme Court reasoned past popular disapproval of same-sex relations to constitutional morality and decriminalised them.
  • Strengths and weaknesses: it is consistent, impartial and justifiable, but it is slow, can turn into cold calculation, and can be misused to rationalise self-interest after the fact.

3. How the two work together

  • Intuition flags, reasoning checks: a gut feeling alerts us that something is wrong; reasoning tests whether the feeling is sound or a bias.
  • Reflective equilibrium: John Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) proposed adjusting principles and considered judgements against each other until they fit together.
  • Trained intuition: Aristotle's virtue ethics holds that good habits make right action second nature; Kohlberg showed how moral reasoning matures from conformity to principles.
  • For civil servants: in an emergency, trained intuition saves lives; in policy and quasi-judicial decisions, officers must reason and record reasons (speaking orders, natural justice).

Intuition is the moral compass and reasoning the map. Ethical maturity uses both: reasoning disciplines intuition, and intuition keeps reasoning humane.
free.upm-2023-gs4-5a:
ConscienceRule of lawInner voiceEthical decision-making

Conscience is the inner moral sense that tells a person right from wrong and responds with guilt or peace; Gandhi called it the "inner voice". Laws, rules and regulations are external, codified standards backed by the authority of the state. In ethical decision-making both guide conduct, but neither suffices alone: conscience without law can become arbitrary, and law without conscience mechanical or even unjust. Article 25 itself protects freedom of conscience.

1. Where conscience is the more reliable guide

  • Laws can be unjust: slavery, apartheid and Nazi racial laws were all legal; conscience inspired resistance, from Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience (1849) to Gandhi's satyagraha and Martin Luther King's civil rights movement.
  • Laws have gaps: they cannot foresee every situation, such as new technologies or a disaster, and conscience guides where rules are silent.
  • No hiding behind orders: the Nuremberg trials (1945–46) refused to accept superior orders as a full defence for crimes against humanity.
  • Courage against the tide: Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent in ADM Jabalpur (1976) upheld the right to life during the Emergency and cost him the office of Chief Justice; his view was vindicated when Puttaswamy (2017) overruled the majority.
  • Integrity when no one watches: laws need enforcement, but conscience regulates conduct from within, including the spirit in which rules are applied.

2. Where laws are the more reliable guide

  • Conscience is subjective: it is shaped by upbringing, religion and ideology; extremists also act "in good conscience".
  • Self-deception: people can mistake bias, anger or convenience for conscience.
  • Equality and predictability: laws apply equally to all (Article 14), so citizens know what to expect and arbitrariness is curbed.
  • Democratic legitimacy: laws reflect collective deliberation; an official's private conscience cannot override the will of the legislature.
  • Accountability: decisions based on law can be reviewed by courts and audit; decisions based only on conscience cannot be checked.

3. Reconciling conscience and law

  • Law as the floor, conscience as the ceiling: obey the law, and go beyond it in honesty, compassion and diligence.
  • An educated conscience: grounded in constitutional morality, facts and reason, and tested for impartiality, not driven by prejudice.
  • Lawful dissent: an officer whose conscience objects should record dissent, seek written orders (as T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India, 2013 advised), use grievance or whistle-blower channels, or resign, rather than defy the law covertly.
  • Law that respects conscience: in Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), the Supreme Court protected students who, for reasons of faith, stood respectfully but did not sing the national anthem.

Conscience is the source of ethical action and law its framework. Neither is reliable alone; a well-informed conscience working within the rule of law, and reforming unjust laws by lawful means, is the most dependable guide.
free.upm-2023-gs4-5b:
ProbityIntegrityPublic trustInclusive development

Probity means adherence to the highest standards of honesty, integrity and uprightness in public life. It goes beyond avoiding corruption: public office and resources must be used only for public purposes. The Second ARC's fourth report, Ethics in Governance (2007), and the UK's Nolan principles (1995) treat it as the foundation of good governance. Its absence is costly: India ranked 91st of 182 in Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index 2025.

1. Why probity is essential for effective governance

  • Trust and legitimacy: citizens obey laws, pay taxes and cooperate with officials when they believe institutions are honest.
  • Rule of law and fairness: impartial decisions in licensing, recruitment and policing ensure equal treatment (Article 14) and curb arbitrariness.
  • Value for money: honest procurement through e-tendering, the Government e-Marketplace (2016) and integrity pacts gets the best quality at the lowest cost.
  • Accountability and transparency: RTI (2005), CAG audits and the Lokpal (operational from 2019) work only when officials keep honest records.
  • Morale of the services: merit-based postings and the protection of honest officers keep talent motivated; corruption breeds cynicism and drives out the honest.

2. Why probity is essential for socio-economic development

  • Welfare reaches the poor: in 1985 Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi observed that only about 15 paise of every rupee meant for the poor reached them; Aadhaar-linked Direct Benefit Transfer has since cut leakages by removing duplicate and fake beneficiaries.
  • Investment and growth: honest, predictable regulation lowers transaction costs and attracts private investment.
  • Safety and quality: corruption in construction produces collapsing bridges and poor roads; probity in inspections saves lives.
  • Natural resources: the Supreme Court cancelled 122 telecom licences in the 2G case (2012) and 214 coal blocks (2014) because allocation lacked transparency, showing the cost of discretion without probity.
  • Social justice: corruption is a regressive tax; the poor, who depend most on public services, pay the highest share of their income in bribes.

3. Challenges and measures

  • Institutional: declaration of assets, conflict-of-interest rules, social audits and citizen's charters make probity verifiable.
  • Personal: codes and laws work only when officers internalise integrity, as the Second ARC stressed in recommending a code of ethics for civil servants.

Probity is the moral infrastructure of governance; without it, laws, schemes and budgets leak. Institutional checks combined with personal integrity turn public money into public welfare.
free.upm-2023-gs4-6a:
Guru NanakIk OnkarKirat Karni, Naam Japna, Vand ChhaknaEquality

Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the founder of Sikhism and a leading saint of the nirguna Bhakti tradition, was born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan). Through long journeys (udasis) and hymns later compiled in the Adi Granth (1604), now the Guru Granth Sahib, he preached devotion to one formless God, honest living and the equality of all human beings, rejecting caste, empty ritual and religious bigotry.

1. Major teachings

  • Ik Onkar (one God): a single, formless and all-pervading Creator, the same for all; Sikh tradition records his message that before God there is no Hindu and no Muslim, only human beings.
  • Three pillars: Naam Japna (remembering God), Kirat Karni (earning by honest labour) and Vand Chhakna (sharing with the needy).
  • Equality: he rejected caste; in the langar (community kitchen) all sit together in a row (pangat), and the sangat (congregation) is open to everyone.
  • Dignity of women: in Asa di Var he asked why woman should be called inferior when she gives birth to kings.
  • Against ritualism and hypocrisy: he valued inner purity over pilgrimages, ritual baths and outward symbols, and, according to tradition, refused the sacred thread as a boy.
  • Householder's spirituality: he taught that spiritual life is lived within family and work, not through renunciation, and himself farmed at Kartarpur in his last years.
  • Against injustice and for nature: his Babarvani verses condemned the cruelty of Babur's invasion, and the closing verse of the Japji calls air the guru, water the father and earth the great mother.

2. Relevance in the contemporary world

  • Religious polarisation: his message of oneness counters communalism, hate speech and terrorism carried out in the name of faith.
  • Inequality and discrimination: the langar, which feeds everyone free regardless of caste, creed or status, is a living model of equality and of Article 17's abolition of untouchability.
  • Ethics in economic life: honest labour and sharing are an answer to corruption, greed and consumerism; Vand Chhakna anticipates corporate social responsibility and philanthropy.
  • Gender justice: equal dignity for women supports today's agenda of women-led development.
  • Environment: reverence for air, water and earth speaks directly to falling groundwater and air pollution, including in Punjab itself.
  • Humanitarian service: gurdwara langars fed migrants, patients and stranded travellers during the COVID-19 lockdown and in many disasters.
  • For public servants: seva with humility, honest work and impartial treatment of all reflect his ideals.

Guru Nanak's synthesis of devotion, honest work and sharing offers a timeless ethic for a divided, unequal and environmentally stressed world, and points towards universal brotherhood.
free.upm-2023-gs4-6b:
Social capitalTrust and networksParticipatory governanceAccountability

Social capital refers to the networks, shared norms and trust among people that enable them to cooperate for mutual benefit. Pierre Bourdieu (1986) and James Coleman (1988) developed the idea, and Robert Putnam (Making Democracy Work, 1993) found that the regions of Italy with dense civic associations had more effective regional governments. Unlike physical capital, social capital grows with use and decays with neglect.

1. Meaning and forms

  • Bonding: close ties within a group such as a family, caste or community; it gives solidarity but can exclude outsiders.
  • Bridging: ties across groups, such as cooperatives, associations and multi-community self-help federations; it builds tolerance and wider cooperation.
  • Linking: ties between citizens and institutions of power, such as Gram Sabhas and user groups that deal with officials; it gives voice and access.
  • Elements: trust, reciprocity, shared norms, networks and civic engagement.

2. How social capital enhances good governance

  • Participation: active Gram Sabhas (Article 243A) and ward committees make planning bottom-up, as in Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996).
  • Accountability and transparency: the public hearings (jan sunwai) of the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan in Rajasthan in the 1990s fed the movement that produced the RTI Act (2005) and pioneered social audits, which MGNREGA made mandatory and which remain mandatory under VB-G RAM G, which replaced it from 1 July 2026.
  • Effective service delivery: self-help groups under Kudumbashree and DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women) run canteens, supply nutrition, and act as banking correspondents; Joint Forest Management (1990) made villagers partners in protecting forests.
  • Voluntary compliance: where people trust one another and the state, they follow rules and pay dues without coercion; villages such as Hiware Bazar and Ralegan Siddhi enforced their own water and grazing rules.
  • Resilience: during the Kerala floods of 2018 fishermen rescued thousands, and community volunteers supported the COVID-19 response.
  • Social cohesion: bridging ties and peace committees reduce communal conflict and the cost of maintaining order.

3. Limits and the way forward

  • Dark side: strong bonding without bridging can produce caste-based or khap pressures, nepotism and clientelism; elites may capture Gram Sabhas and SHGs, excluding women and Dalits.
  • Erosion: Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) traced the decline of civic life in the US; urbanisation and online polarisation pose similar risks in India.
  • Building it: civic education, inclusive SHG federations, participatory budgeting and responsive grievance systems, with the state as facilitator, not controller.

Social capital is the invisible infrastructure of good governance: it turns citizens from passive beneficiaries into co-producers of public services and guardians of accountability.
free.upm-2023-gs4-7:
Fiduciary dutyMisappropriationCompassion vs integrityDuty to report

The case sets compassion against integrity. Moved by a colleague's crisis, a bank manager secretly released ₹10 lakh from a dormant account, money held in trust for a depositor, to pay for her father's surgery. A life was saved and repayment has begun, but a depositor's money was misappropriated. Now that I know, I face a conflict between loyalty to a friend and duty to the bank and its depositors.

1. Stakeholders

  • The depositor whose money was used; my colleague and her father; the bank manager; myself; the bank, its auditors and the RBI; and depositors at large.

2. (a) Ethical issues involved

  • Breach of fiduciary duty: a bank holds deposits in trust, and using a depositor's money without consent is misappropriation whatever the motive. By a banker it is criminal breach of trust (Section 316(5), BNS, punishable with up to life imprisonment), and officers of a nationalised bank are public servants under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
  • Ends versus means: saving a life is a noble end, but the depositor was used merely as a means (Kant); good intentions do not make wrong means right.
  • Favouritism: one employee received a privilege that others in similar distress would never get.
  • Secrecy and complicity: the demand for confidentiality shows awareness of wrongdoing; it makes my colleague an accomplice and leaves her open to future pressure.
  • Weak controls: inoperative accounts (no customer-initiated transactions for two years) are a known target of fraud.
  • My own dilemma: friendship and empathy against the duty to report; silence would make me complicit too.

3. (b) Evaluation of the bank manager's behaviour

  • What was right: empathy and a wish to save a life; the outcome was good and repayment is under way.
  • What was wrong: kindness with someone else's money is misappropriation. He broke the law, the bank's rules and the depositor's rights, and exposed his colleague to prosecution.
  • Ignored lawful alternatives: a staff loan, a provident fund advance, a hospital's charity scheme, a government health scheme if the father was eligible, or help from colleagues.
  • Verdict: only a short-term utilitarian view can defend him; duty-based and virtue ethics (a virtuous banker is both compassionate and honest) condemn the act. It is serious misconduct, with the motive a mitigating factor.

4. (c) My reaction: options

  • Speak to my colleague first: with empathy, explain that the arrangement exposes her to criminal liability and that voluntary disclosure is her best protection; we report together promptly, or I will.
  • Report in writing, without waiting for repayment: to the vigilance officer or controlling office, recording her voluntary disclosure, the repayment so far and her circumstances; the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004) and the bank's whistle-blower policy protect the person reporting.
  • Restore the money at once: help her raise lawful funds so that the account is restored in full, with interest as the bank directs.
  • Accountability and reform: an inquiry into the manager's conduct and other dormant-account debits; dual authorisation and alerts for such accounts.

Why this course: it combines compassion (helping her lawfully and seeking leniency) with integrity (truth, the depositor's rights and the rule of law), and passes the test of publicity.

Compassion must work within the rules, not around them. By helping my colleague put things right and reporting honestly, I protect her, the depositor and the public trust on which banking rests.
free.upm-2023-gs4-8:
Right to lifeRule of lawEmergency medical ethicsDoctrine of necessity

As District Magistrate at a night-time landslide site about 60 km from Uttarkashi, I must choose between saving two lives, a mother bleeding in labour and her unborn child, and the legal rule that blood for transfusion must come from a licensed blood bank. With roads likely blocked, delay could be fatal. The case tests the right to life against procedure, and an officer's willingness to take responsibility.

1. Stakeholders

  • The woman, her unborn child and her husband; the doctors and volunteer donors; myself as DM and a trained physician; other landslide victims who need the team; the media; the State health department and the drug regulator.

2. (a) Ethical issues involved

  • Right to life vs rule of law: in Parmanand Katara v Union of India (1989) the Supreme Court held that every doctor must give immediate medical aid to preserve life and that procedure cannot come in the way; yet the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and its Rules allow blood collection only by licensed blood banks.
  • Patient safety (do no harm): unscreened blood can transmit HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis or malaria, and a mismatch can kill; this is the law's purpose.
  • Professional conscience: my medical training stresses saving lives, and as DM I lead disaster response under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
  • Accountability: doctors fear penalties; leadership means taking responsibility instead of passing the buck.
  • Consent and autonomy: the woman, or her husband if she cannot, must give informed consent; donors must volunteer freely.
  • Scarce resources: the medical team is also needed for other casualties.
  • Dignity and privacy: with the media present, childbirth must not become a spectacle.

3. (b) Options available to the District Magistrate

  • Waiting: legality at the cost of life is empty compliance; in Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) the Supreme Court held that failure to provide timely medical treatment violates Article 21.
  • Evacuation: the best option if feasible in time, so I would immediately request a State or IAF helicopter and SDRF and road-clearing teams, but weather and darkness may rule it out.
  • My choice, the safeguarded emergency course: the criminal law accepts necessity, an act done in good faith to prevent greater harm, as a defence (Section 19, BNS; earlier Section 81, IPC), though not as advance permission, so reasons must be recorded.
  • Clinical judgement on record: the doctors document why transfusion cannot wait.
  • Safety: grouping and cross-matching with the available kits, sterile collection bags, donors questioned about recent illness, and rapid tests if available.
  • Responsibility: I issue a written order recording the emergency and taking responsibility, so that the doctors do not bear the decision alone, and report at once to the Chief Medical Officer and the State health department, seeking regularisation.
  • Continuity: the rest of the team continues rescue work, and the media are kept away from the delivery.

Why this course: the right to life is the most basic right; the law's purpose, safe blood, is served as far as possible through screening; and responsibility is taken openly, not hidden. I would also recommend that the State frame protocols for emergency transfusion in remote disaster zones.

Laws exist to protect life. When strict compliance would defeat that purpose in a genuine emergency, a conscientious officer acts to save life, minimises risk, records reasons and accepts accountability, honouring the spirit of the law.
free.upm-2023-gs4-9:
Work–life balanceConflicting dutiesGender-sensitive workplaceOrganisational culture

Rashika, a dedicated Joint Secretary, is asked at 9:30 on a Saturday night to prepare a detailed note that will consume her Sunday, while her husband is travelling and her two small children are with a domestic helper. Having already left a sick child to attend office, she wonders whether dedication to duty must have limits. The case raises work–life balance, the double burden that working women carry, and the duty of superiors and organisations to set reasonable expectations.

1. Stakeholders

  • Rashika; her children, husband and family; her superior Mr Suresh; the Ministry and the public it serves; and women officers generally, whose careers depend on workplace culture.

2. (a) Ethical issues involved

  • Conflict of duties: duty to the public and her office against duty to her children; both are genuine moral obligations, and neither can be dismissed.
  • Limits of work ethic: punctuality, hard work and selfless service are virtues, but in excess they lead to burnout and poor decisions; Aristotle's golden mean applies to dedication too.
  • Gender roles: care work still falls largely on women; equal responsibility of the husband, and children's right to parental care, are at stake.
  • Superior's conduct: a detailed task given late on a Saturday may reflect genuine urgency, or poor planning and insensitivity; leaders owe a duty of care to their teams.
  • Self-care and dignity: rest and leisure are part of a dignified life (Article 24 of the UDHR); an exhausted officer serves the public worse.
  • Organisational culture: long hours are mistaken for commitment, and an "always on" culture drives talented women out of senior roles.

3. (b) Laws for a healthy, safe and equitable working environment for women

  • Status: the four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025.
  • For government servants: the CCS (Leave) Rules, 1972 give 180 days' maternity leave and up to 730 days' child care leave; the constitutional basis lies in Articles 15(3), 39(d) and 42.

4. (c) Suggestions to mitigate such working conditions

  • Clarify and negotiate: courteously ask Mr Suresh about the exact scope and deadline; propose a realistic timeline, and request advance notice for such tasks in future.
  • Delegate and plan: assign data collection to the Director or Deputy Secretary, and work from home on Sunday through e-Office so that she stays near the children.
  • Share care at home: discuss equal parenting with her husband and arrange family support for emergencies.
  • Personal discipline: prioritise urgent and important work, protect fixed family time and look after her health.
  • Institutional reform: no routine late-night or weekend tasking except in emergencies; back-up officers for every desk; crèches near offices; flexible hours and remote work; counselling and wellness programmes; sensitising senior officers.

Why this approach: it honours both duties instead of sacrificing one; it improves the quality of public work by preventing burnout; and it changes the system for other officers, not only for Rashika.

Dedication to duty is a cardinal civil-service value, but it should not demand the sacrifice of family and health. Reasonable limits, smarter workplaces and shared parenting make sustainable excellence possible.
free.upm-2023-gs4-10:
Political neutralityIntegrityProper channelsPoliticisation of bureaucracy

Vinod, an upright IAS officer and Managing Director of the State Road Transport Corporation, receives apparent evidence that the powerful Chairman demanded a bribe for a large order of QMR tyres. The evidence comes from an Opposition Board member who wants Vinod to expose the Chairman and promises him career rewards once his party wins. Vinod must act against corruption without becoming a political instrument, despite the risk of yet another punitive transfer. The case tests integrity, neutrality and moral courage.

1. Stakeholders

  • Vinod; the Chairman; the Board member and his party; the Chief Minister and the government; the Corporation, its employees and passengers; tyre suppliers; taxpayers; and the credibility of the civil service.

2. (a) Options available to Vinod

  • Silence: as MD he is custodian of the Corporation's money; looking away is complicity and a breach of the integrity the AIS (Conduct) Rules demand.
  • Going to the media: conduct rules bar unauthorised communication of official documents and public criticism of government policy; trial by media prejudices a fair inquiry, and the timing would serve one party before elections.
  • Accepting the offer: a promise of career growth in return for political service is an inducement; serving the Opposition destroys neutrality as surely as serving the ruling party.

Recommended course: verify and report through proper channels

  • Decline the offer: politely but firmly, and record the meeting and the documents received in a file note.
  • Verify: examine the tyre purchase file, tender process, rates and the speedy clearance of bills; order an internal audit; send the video for forensic authentication through official channels.
  • Protect public money: withhold doubtful payments and further orders where the rules allow, and move procurement to open e-tendering with an Integrity Pact.
  • Report in writing: to the Principal Secretary (Transport) and the Chief Secretary, and to the State vigilance or anti-corruption bureau or the Lokayukta, with the evidence.
  • Keep a full record: if transferred, hand over every paper so that the inquiry continues.

Why this course: it upholds the rule of law and the Nolan principles of objectivity and integrity, fights corruption without partisanship, and shows the moral courage to accept a transfer rather than compromise.

3. (b) Ethical issues arising from politicisation of the bureaucracy

  • Loss of neutrality: officers aligned with parties serve them, not the public; the all-India services were meant to give a permanent, impartial administration, which Sardar Patel saw as essential to national unity.
  • Transfers as reward and punishment: six transfers in three years show how postings are used to discipline honest officers; T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India (2013) called for fixed tenure, Civil Services Boards and written instructions.
  • Collusion and corruption: a politician–bureaucrat nexus enables rent-seeking, and officers may seek favours or post-retirement rewards.
  • Demoralisation: honest officers are sidelined, integrity becomes costly, and the service attracts and rewards conformists.
  • Partisan use of accountability: when the Opposition also tries to use officers, even genuine exposures look political and lose credibility.
  • Loss of public trust: citizens come to see the administration as partisan, and policy decisions as electoral tools.

A civil servant's loyalty is to the Constitution, not to any party. By refusing both the ruling side's pressure and the Opposition's bait, and acting through institutions, Vinod can be neutral without being passive about corruption.
free.upm-2023-gs4-11:
Workplace harassmentProfessional insecurityDignity at workEthical leadership

As Additional Director General, CPWD, I must resolve a conflict between an experienced Chief Architect, anxious about losing credit for his last major project before retirement, and Seema, a talented new Senior Architect whose ideas would improve the project and save time. His repeated public humiliation of her amounts to workplace harassment, damaging her dignity, confidence and mental health, and she may resign. The case tests ethical leadership: completing a public project while protecting an employee and correcting a senior.

1. Stakeholders

  • Seema; the Chief Architect; myself as ADG; other team members; CPWD; and the public, who pay for and use the project.

2. (a) Ethical issues involved

  • Dignity and respect at work: humiliating a colleague in public and shouting at her violate her dignity (Article 21) and the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964, which forbid conduct unbecoming of a government servant.
  • Abuse of seniority: experience and tenure are being used to intimidate a junior instead of guiding her.
  • Ego versus public interest: the wish for personal credit is blocking improvements that would add value and save time and public money.
  • Gender and inclusion: a newly joined woman professional is being undermined; even where it is not sexual harassment, such behaviour drives women out of technical careers.
  • Mental health and duty of care: her anxiety and stress are the organisation's responsibility, not only hers.
  • Merit and innovation: suppressing fresh ideas harms the organisation.
  • Empathy for the senior: his insecurity about his legacy near retirement deserves understanding, not excuse.

3. (b) Options to complete the project and retain Seema

4. (c) My response to Seema's predicament

  • Listen and reassure: meet her privately, acknowledge her record, assure her that her work is valued and that I will act, and ask her not to resign in haste.
  • Explain her options: her right to make a written complaint, with confidentiality and protection from retaliation; I will respect her choice.
  • Give her a defined role: for example, leading the design-optimisation component, reporting to a weekly project review that I chair, with access to counselling if she wishes.
  • Counsel the Chief Architect: privately and respectfully; acknowledge his experience and legacy, show that her ideas will make his project a greater success with credit shared, and state clearly that humiliation must stop or formal action will follow; record the meeting.
  • Fair process: decisions minuted in reviews, criticism given in private, and every member's contribution recorded in the project report.

Measures to prevent such occurrences

  • Respectful-workplace code: a written policy against bullying and humiliation, with a grievance committee for non-sexual harassment alongside the Internal Committee under the POSH Act, 2013.
  • Leadership training: emotional intelligence, conflict resolution and inclusive leadership through Mission Karmayogi courses.
  • Fair recognition: team awards, documented individual contributions and 360-degree feedback in appraisals of senior officers.
  • Mentoring and succession: pair retiring officers with new entrants as mentors and recognise them for it, turning insecurity into legacy.
  • Listening mechanisms: an open-door policy, staff surveys and exit interviews.

Why this approach: it balances justice and compassion, protects Seema's dignity, retains talent, completes the project and lets the Chief Architect retire with honour.

Respect at work is not a soft issue: it decides whether talent stays and public projects succeed. An ethical leader corrects behaviour early and builds a culture where credit is shared.
free.upm-2023-gs4-12:
CyberbullyingMisinformationChildren's privacyResponsible use of social media

The case shows both faces of social media. It became a tool of cyberbullying and body-shaming that pushed an 11-year-old into isolation, and then a channel for viral misinformation against a public servant's family. My counter-video, which also identifies the "likely perpetrators", who are themselves children, raises the question whether answering misuse with exposure is ethical. The case involves dignity, privacy, truth and restraint.

1. Stakeholders

  • My son; the children who bullied him and their parents; my wife and I; the school; colleagues and the public; social media platforms; and the police and cyber cell.

2. (a) Ethical issues in the use of social media

  • Cyberbullying and children's dignity: name-calling in a class WhatsApp group and caricature videos inflict lasting psychological harm; distance and group behaviour weaken empathy.
  • Age and privacy of children: 11-year-olds in messaging groups are below the minimum age of 13 that most platforms set; the DPDP Act, 2023, whose duties are being phased in under Rules notified in November 2025, requires verifiable parental consent to process children's data.
  • Misinformation and defamation: a fabricated video alleging physical bullying went viral without verification; reputation is part of the right to life (Subramanian Swamy v Union of India, 2016).
  • Trial by social media: friends and colleagues judged before knowing the facts, showing how virality replaces due process.
  • Responsibility of users and platforms: forwarding without checking spreads harm; under the IT Rules, 2021 platforms must act on complaints through grievance officers.
  • Retaliation vs restraint: answering harm with exposure keeps the cycle of hostility going.
  • Conduct of a public servant: an officer's online behaviour reflects on the service and must model restraint.

3. (b) Pros and cons of my counter-video

  • Pros explained: silence can let a lie harden into "truth"; a factual reply with evidence restores reputation, which matters for a public servant's credibility, and draws attention to a serious social problem.
  • Cons explained: the spirit of Section 74 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, which bars media disclosure of the identity of children involved in offences, argues against exposing minors online; my son asked that the matter rest; and under Rule 19 of the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964 a government servant may vindicate his private character, but must report such action to the prescribed authority (defending an official act in court or the press needs prior sanction).
  • On balance: a factual rebuttal was justified, but identifying children was not.

A better course

  • Correct my own post: remove or blur the children's faces and names, and keep only a calm, factual statement.
  • Use lawful channels: report the fake video to the platform for takedown and to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal or helpline 1930, preserving evidence; take legal advice on defamation by adults involved.
  • Involve the school: raise the bullying with the principal and the parents for restorative action, such as counselling, apology and digital-etiquette sessions.
  • Support my son: professional counselling, rebuilding his confidence in sport and class, and explaining why adults must act.
  • Inform my department as the conduct rules require.

Social media amplifies both harm and truth. Its ethical use needs verification, empathy and restraint: fight lies with facts, but never at the cost of another child's dignity. That is the essence of digital citizenship.
free.upm-2024-gs1-1:
Rig Vedic periodLater Vedic periodVarna systemAgrarian economy

The Vedic age is known mainly from the Vedic texts. In the Rig Vedic period (c. 1500–1000 BCE) the Aryans lived in the Sapta Sindhu region of the north-west as semi-nomadic, cattle-keeping tribes. In the Later Vedic period (c. 1000–600 BCE) they moved east into the Ganga–Yamuna doab, where the use of iron and Painted Grey Ware settlements mark a shift to settled farming, territorial kingdoms and a more unequal society.

1. Changes in society

  • From tribe to territory: Rig Vedic people lived in tribes (jana) under a chief (rajan), checked by assemblies such as the sabha, samiti and vidatha. In the Later Vedic period the jana settled as a janapada, the vidatha disappeared and kingship grew stronger and hereditary, backed by rituals such as the Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Ashvamedha.
  • Varna becomes rigid: Rig Vedic society was relatively fluid, and the four varnas appear only in the Purusha Sukta of the tenth (late) book. Later Vedic society was clearly divided by birth, with Brahmanas and Kshatriyas on top, Vaishyas as the main tax-payers and Shudras serving the higher varnas.
  • Decline in women's status: Rig Vedic women attended assemblies and composed hymns (Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra, Vishvavara). Later they lost the right to attend assemblies, though learned women such as Gargi and Maitreyi appear in the Upanishads.
  • New institutions: gotra (lineage) exogamy appeared, and Later Vedic texts speak of the first three ashramas (stages of life).
  • Religion: Indra and Agni lost importance to Prajapati, Rudra and Vishnu, and costly sacrifices controlled by priests became central.

2. Changes in economy

  • Pastoralism to agriculture: cattle were the chief wealth in the Rig Veda; war was called gavishti (search for cows), and barley (yava) was the main crop. In the Later Vedic period agriculture became the main occupation: texts speak of ploughs drawn by six, eight and even twenty-four oxen, and of rice (vrihi) and wheat (godhuma).
  • Iron and forest clearing: the Rig Vedic ayas probably meant copper or bronze. Iron came into use around 1000 BCE, mostly for weapons at first, but fire and iron tools helped clear the forests of the doab, as the Shatapatha Brahmana's story of Videgha Mathava suggests.
  • Crafts and trade: Later Vedic texts list many more specialised crafts than the Rig Veda, and the term shreshthin hints at merchant groups. Exchange remained largely barter, with the cow and the nishka (a gold ornament) as units of value.
  • Surplus and taxation: the voluntary gift (bali) offered to the Rig Vedic chief became a regular tax, collected by officials such as the sangrihitri (treasurer) and bhagadugha (collector of taxes).

In short, the Later Vedic age turned a pastoral, tribal and relatively egalitarian society into an agrarian, territorial and hierarchical one. These changes prepared the ground for the mahajanapadas and the second urbanisation of the sixth century BCE.
free.upm-2024-gs1-2:
Pallavas of KanchiDravida styleMamallapuramBhakti literature

The Pallavas of Kanchi, at their height from the late 6th to the 9th century CE under Simhavishnu, Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) and Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), ruled the northern Tamil country. Their reign marks the shift from rock-cut to structural temples, laying the foundations of the Dravida style, and a flowering of Sanskrit learning and Tamil devotional poetry. Kanchi, visited by Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) around 640 CE, became a great centre of learning.

1. Architecture: from caves to structural temples

  • Mahendra style (rock-cut caves): Mahendravarman I excavated pillared cave-temples (mandapas); his Mandagapattu inscription proudly says the shrine was made without brick, timber, metal or mortar.
  • Mamalla style (monoliths): Narasimhavarman I made Mamallapuram a centre of art. The five rathas, each carved from a single rock, are prototypes of later temple forms, and mandapas such as the Mahishasuramardini and Varaha caves hold fine panels.
  • Rajasimha style (structural temples): Narasimhavarman II built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi in dressed stone, with the pyramidal, tiered vimana typical of the Dravida style.
  • Later Pallava style: the Vaikuntha Perumal temple at Kanchi, of Nandivarman II's time, carries sculpted panels narrating Pallava history.

2. Sculpture and painting

  • Descent of the Ganga (Arjuna's Penance): a vast open-air relief carved on two boulders at Mamallapuram, with gods, sages and animals around a natural cleft that represents the river; its life-size elephants show remarkable naturalism.
  • Narrative panels: Durga fighting Mahishasura and Vishnu as Varaha combine movement with balance.
  • Painting: Mahendravarman I bore the title Chitrakarapuli ("tiger among painters"), and traces of murals survive in the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi and at Panamalai.

3. Literature and learning

  • Sanskrit: Mahendravarman I wrote the farce Mattavilasa Prahasana, which satirises Kapalika and Buddhist ascetics. Tradition links the poets Bharavi (Kiratarjuniya) and Dandin (Dashakumaracharita, Kavyadarsha) with the Pallava court.
  • Tamil Bhakti: Nayanars such as Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, and Alvars such as Tirumangai, sang hymns in the people's language; Appar is said to have turned Mahendravarman I from Jainism to Shaivism. Their hymns were later compiled in the Tevaram and the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
  • Court poetry: Perundevanar's Bharatavenba, a Tamil Mahabharata, and the Nandikkalambakam belong to the reign of Nandivarman III.
  • Education: the ghatika (college) at Kanchi drew students from afar; the Talagunda inscription records that Mayurasharman, founder of the Kadamba dynasty, went there to study.

4. Legacy

  • Dravida style matured: Pallava forms grew into the grand Chola temples of Thanjavur.
  • Influence beyond Tamil land: the Chalukya king Vikramaditya II, after taking Kanchi, admired the Kailasanatha, and the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal followed its model; Pallava-Grantha influenced the scripts of Southeast Asia.

The Pallavas thus gave South India its temple architecture in stone and, through the Bhakti saints, a devotional literature in Tamil. Mamallapuram, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984), remains their lasting signature.
free.upm-2024-gs1-3:
Quit India MovementCripps MissionDo or DieParallel governments

The Quit India Movement was launched when the All India Congress Committee, meeting at Gowalia Tank in Bombay, passed the Quit India resolution on 8 August 1942 and Gandhi gave the call "Do or Die". It demanded an immediate end to British rule and became the most widespread mass upsurge of the national movement during the Second World War.

1. Events that led to the movement

  • War without consent (1939): Viceroy Linlithgow declared India a party to the Second World War without consulting Indian leaders, and the Congress ministries in the provinces resigned in protest.
  • August Offer and Individual Satyagraha (1940): the offer of dominion status at an undefined future date was rejected, and Gandhi launched a limited individual satyagraha, with Vinoba Bhave as the first satyagrahi.
  • Failure of the Cripps Mission (March–April 1942): it offered dominion status after the war, a constituent assembly and the right of provinces to stay out, but no real power at once; it raised fears of partition and was rejected.
  • Japanese threat: the fall of Singapore and Rangoon in early 1942 brought the war to India's borders; Gandhi argued that the British presence invited invasion.
  • Popular discontent: rising prices, wartime shortages and the unequal treatment of Indian evacuees from Burma and Malaya deepened anger; the Working Committee endorsed a struggle at Wardha (14 July 1942).

2. Course of the movement

  • Leaderless upsurge: the top leaders were arrested early on 9 August; Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank, and students, workers and peasants carried the movement forward.
  • Underground activity: Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali led underground resistance, and Usha Mehta ran a secret Congress Radio.
  • Parallel governments: they showed that people were ready to replace British authority.

3. Results

  • Independence on the agenda: freedom became the immediate, non-negotiable demand; the British realised that India could not be ruled for long against its will.
  • Mass participation: students, women, peasants and workers joined in; Matangini Hazra was shot dead leading a procession in Tamluk.
  • Severe repression: mass arrests, firing on crowds, collective fines and even machine-gunning from the air crushed the open movement by the end of 1942; Gandhi fasted for 21 days in February 1943.
  • Limitations: the Muslim League, the Communist Party (which called the conflict a "People's War" after Germany attacked the Soviet Union in 1941), the Hindu Mahasabha and the princely states stayed away; sabotage of railways and telegraphs departed from strict non-violence.
  • Political fallout: with Congress leaders in jail, the Muslim League expanded its influence and the demand for Pakistan.

Though suppressed, Quit India was the last great mass struggle of the national movement. Together with the INA trials and the naval mutiny of 1946, it made freedom a question of when, not whether, and paved the way for the Cabinet Mission and independence in 1947.
free.upm-2024-gs1-4:
Sea surface temperatureLatent heatRapid intensificationOcean warming

Sea surface temperature (SST) is the temperature of the ocean's upper layer. Its long-term rise is a result of global warming: the ocean has absorbed about 91% of the extra heat trapped in the climate system, and the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report (2021) found the ocean surface 0.88°C warmer in 2011–2020 than in 1850–1900. Because tropical cyclones draw their energy from warm water, SST rise directly shapes their birth and strength.

1. SST rise: meaning and causes

  • Greenhouse warming: heat trapped by greenhouse gases is stored mostly in the ocean, raising both SST and the heat content of deeper layers.
  • Natural variability: El Niño years add to the trend, as in the record heat of 2023–24, and marine heatwaves have roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s (IPCC).
  • Indian Ocean: it is among the fastest-warming tropical oceans, which matters for the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.

2. Conditions for a tropical cyclone

  • Warm water: SST of about 26.5–27°C or more, extending to a depth of about 50 m.
  • Coriolis force: strong enough to spin the system, so cyclones rarely form within about 5° of the equator.
  • Weak vertical wind shear and moist mid-levels: these let a tall, organised storm column develop.
  • A pre-existing disturbance: a low-pressure area, with upper-level divergence that removes the rising air.

3. How SST rise affects tropical cyclones

  • More fuel: warmer water evaporates faster; condensation in the rising air releases latent heat, which deepens the low pressure and strengthens the winds.
  • Higher intensity: the IPCC assesses that the share of major (Category 3–5) cyclones has likely increased over the last four decades.
  • Rapid intensification: a deep, warm upper ocean lets storms strengthen sharply within a day, as Amphan (2020) did in the Bay of Bengal, leaving little time for evacuation.
  • A more active Arabian Sea: once relatively quiet, the warming Arabian Sea now produces severe storms such as Tauktae (2021) and the long-lived Biparjoy (2023).
  • Wetter storms and higher surges: air holds about 7% more moisture for every 1°C of warming, so cyclone rain is heavier; with sea-level rise, storm surges reach farther inland.
  • Shifting tracks: the latitude at which western Pacific typhoons reach peak intensity has moved poleward, exposing new coasts.

4. Limits of the link

  • Not necessarily more cyclones: the global number may stay the same or even fall, because wind shear, El Niño–La Niña and upper-air conditions also matter.
  • Self-limiting effect: a slow storm churns up cooler water from below, which can weaken it.

SST rise is turning cyclones into stronger, wetter and faster-intensifying storms. Cutting emissions, better ocean observation, the IMD's impact-based warnings, mangrove bio-shields and cyclone shelters are the way to climate-resilient coasts.
free.upm-2024-gs1-5:
Rural–urban migrationAgglomeration economiesPrimate cityExpected income

Migration in developing countries flows mainly towards large cities rather than small towns. In India, over 45 crore people (about 37%) were migrants by place of last residence (Census 2011), and urban growth is concentrated in metropolitan regions such as Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru. In many developing countries a single primate city, such as Dhaka, Lagos or Bangkok, dominates the urban system. The reasons lie in economies of scale and in the weakness of smaller towns.

1. Economic pull of large cities

  • Agglomeration economies: firms cluster where markets, suppliers and skilled labour are concentrated, so large cities create more jobs in manufacturing, construction and services.
  • Expected income: Todaro's model (1969) explains that migrants weigh the higher urban wage against the chance of finding a job; even an informal job in a metropolis pays more than farm labour.
  • A large informal sector: street vending, domestic work, construction and transport absorb unskilled newcomers quickly.
  • Diverse opportunities: a big city offers many kinds of work, so a migrant can move between jobs, while a small town often depends on one market or industry.

2. Better services and amenities

  • Health and education: specialised hospitals, colleges and coaching centres are concentrated in big cities.
  • Infrastructure: power, water, transport and digital connectivity are more reliable.
  • Urban bias: public investment has long favoured capitals and metropolitan areas, a pattern Michael Lipton called "urban bias", which widens the gap with small towns.

3. Social networks and aspirations

  • Chain migration: earlier migrants from the same village or community help with housing and jobs, lowering the cost and risk of moving.
  • Anonymity and freedom: the big city loosens caste and gender restrictions, attracting young people and women.
  • Aspirations: films, television and smartphones spread the image of the city as the place of opportunity.

4. Why small towns fail to attract

  • Weak economic base: few industries or formal jobs; many are only market or administrative centres.
  • Weak governance: urban local bodies lack funds, staff and planning capacity, so services are poor.
  • Developing-country conditions: agrarian distress, tiny holdings, landlessness and climate shocks push people to places where work is more certain, which small towns cannot promise; weak transport links also keep small towns isolated from national markets.

Consequences: the result is over-concentration: about 6.5 crore people lived in slums (Census 2011), and big cities face congestion, pollution and overstretched services, while small towns stagnate.

Balanced urbanisation needs small towns as growth centres: industrial clusters and corridors, AMRUT, the Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (2016), stronger municipal finances and counter-magnet towns, as planned for the National Capital Region. Then migration can become a choice rather than a compulsion.
free.upm-2024-gs1-6:
CloudburstOrographic liftFlash floodsWestern disturbance

A cloudburst is an extreme, highly localised downpour. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) defines it as at least 100 mm of rain within an hour over an area of about 20–30 sq km. Cloudbursts occur mostly in the Himalaya, and less often in the Western Ghats, during the monsoon, and they trigger flash floods, landslides and debris flows in narrow mountain valleys.

1. How a cloudburst forms

  • Moist air: monsoon winds carry huge amounts of moisture from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea to the mountains.
  • Orographic lift and convection: steep slopes force the air to rise rapidly, and daytime heating of the slopes adds to the lift; the air cools, moisture condenses and towering cumulonimbus clouds form.
  • Updrafts hold the water: strong updrafts keep raindrops and ice suspended and let them grow by collision and coalescence; when the updraft weakens or collapses, the accumulated water falls almost at once.
  • Clash of weather systems: experts linked the floods of August 2025 in the western Himalaya to an interaction between western disturbances and moisture-laden monsoon winds, a combination that produces very heavy rain.

2. Why the Himalaya are prone

  • Topography: steep, narrow valleys trap clouds and act as funnels that send water downstream quickly.
  • Fragile slopes: young, loose rocks and deforestation turn heavy rain into landslides and debris flows.
  • Warming: air holds about 7% more moisture for every 1°C of warming, raising the risk of extreme bursts.
  • Human factors: roads, hotels and houses built on riverbanks and floodplains increase the damage.

3. Impacts

  • Loss of life and property: sudden torrents of water and debris leave little time to escape.
  • Infrastructure: roads, bridges, hydropower projects and pilgrim routes are damaged.
  • Livelihoods: orchards, fields and tourism suffer for months.

4. Challenges in prediction

  • Small and short: a cloudburst covers a few kilometres and lasts minutes to an hour, finer than most weather models can resolve.
  • Sparse monitoring: rain gauges and automatic weather stations are few in the mountains, and ridges block Doppler radar beams; after the Dharali flash flood in Uttarakhand (5 August 2025), IMD officials said the available data did not show a cloudburst.
  • Loose use of the label: early reports often blame a cloudburst, as after Kedarnath (2013), before detailed study finds other triggers such as a glacial lake outburst or prolonged heavy rain.

Way forward: a denser network of Doppler radars and rain gauges under Mission Mausam (2024), nowcasting with village-level alerts, no construction on floodplains and unstable slopes, slope stabilisation and community preparedness as per NDMA guidelines.

Cloudbursts cannot be prevented, but their disaster risk can be reduced by better observation, early warning and land-use discipline in the fragile Himalaya.
free.upm-2024-gs1-7:
Demographic winterBelow-replacement fertilityPopulation ageingPopulation decline

A demographic winter is a long period in which fertility stays well below the replacement level of about 2.1 children per woman, so that each generation is smaller than the one before. Births fall, the population ages, the workforce shrinks and, in time, the total population declines. The UN's World Population Prospects 2024 shows that the world is moving in this direction, though at very different speeds in different regions.

1. Features of a demographic winter

  • Very low fertility: a total fertility rate (TFR) far below replacement for decades, as in East Asia and Southern Europe.
  • Ageing: the elderly come to outnumber children, and the old-age dependency ratio rises.
  • Shrinking workforce: fewer young workers and consumers slow growth and innovation.
  • Population decline: deaths exceed births.

2. Is the world moving towards it? The evidence

  • Global fertility has fallen: the global TFR is about 2.3 (2024), down from 3.3 in 1990, and more than half of all countries are now below 2.1 (UN WPP 2024).
  • Peak population in sight: the world population (8.2 billion in 2024) is projected to peak at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s and then decline slowly; 63 countries and areas, with 28% of the world's people, have already passed their peak.
  • Ageing world: people aged 65 and above are projected to outnumber children under 18 by the late 2070s.
  • East Asia already in winter: South Korea's TFR of 0.72 (2023) is the lowest of any country; Japan's births have fallen year after year, and China's population began to decline in 2022.
  • India: the TFR has fallen to 1.9 (SRS 2024), below replacement, ranging from 1.2 in Delhi to 2.9 in Bihar; the southern States are ageing fast.

3. But not a uniform winter

  • Demographic divergence: sub-Saharan Africa still has high fertility and will provide much of the world's population growth this century.
  • Population momentum: India will keep growing for decades because so many young people are entering reproductive age.
  • Migration: immigration offsets low fertility in Canada, Germany and the United States.
  • A contested term: low fertility also reflects women's education, choice and better child survival; the task is to adapt, not to panic.

4. Consequences and responses

  • Economic and fiscal: labour shortages, rising pension and health costs, and slower growth.
  • Responses abroad: childcare, parental leave and housing support, managed immigration, automation and later retirement.
  • For India: use the remaining demographic-dividend window through jobs, skills and women's employment, and prepare for ageing with pensions and geriatric care.

The world as a whole is not yet in a demographic winter but in a late demographic autumn: East Asia and much of Europe are already there, and India will follow within decades. Family-friendly policies and planning for ageing with dignity are wiser now than later.
free.upm-2024-gs1-8:
Gender equalityGender equityWomen's empowermentGender mainstreaming

Gender refers to the socially constructed roles and expectations attached to women and men. The Constitution promises equality (Articles 14 and 15) and allows special provisions for women (Article 15(3)), yet India ranked 131st of 145 countries in the World Economic Forum's Global Gender Gap Index 2026, with only about 41% parity in economic participation and opportunity. Equality, equity and empowerment are related but distinct ideas.

1. Distinguishing the three concepts

  • Gender equality: the outcome in which women and men enjoy equal rights, resources, opportunities and protection; for example, equal pay for equal work (Article 39(d), given effect by the Code on Wages, 2019).
  • Gender equity: fairness in the process. Because women start from a disadvantage, preferential treatment may be needed to reach equality, such as one-third reservation for women in panchayats (Article 243D), in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies under the 106th Amendment (2023, to take effect after the next delimitation), or 26 weeks of paid maternity leave.
  • Women's empowerment: the process by which women gain the ability to make strategic life choices; Naila Kabeer describes it through resources, agency and achievements, as when self-help groups under DAY-NRLM give women credit, voice and leadership.
  • The link: equity is the means, equality the goal, and empowerment the process by which women themselves claim it.

2. Why gender concerns matter in programme design and implementation

  • Different needs and roles: women do most unpaid care work, travel differently and face specific safety risks, so a "gender-neutral" programme is often gender-blind.
  • Avoiding exclusion: land titles are mostly in men's names, so women farmers miss credit, insurance and farm support unless schemes recognise cultivators, not only owners.
  • Better outcomes: income in women's hands is more likely to be spent on children's food, health and education, and women's participation improves targeting.
  • Avoiding harm: worksites without crèches or toilets, or programmes that add to women's workload, can make women worse off.
  • Commitments: SDG 5 and the Directive Principles require deliberate action, not neutrality.

3. Gender-responsive design in practice

  • PM Ujjwala Yojana (2016): LPG connections in women's names cut indoor smoke and drudgery.
  • PMAY-Gramin: houses in the woman's name or jointly, giving her an asset.
  • MGNREGA: at least one-third of beneficiaries are to be women, with equal wages and worksite facilities.
  • Jan Dhan: about 56% of accounts belong to women, so benefits can reach them directly.
  • Gender Budget Statement (since 2005-06): tracks allocations for women across ministries.

Programmes work best when they treat women not as passive beneficiaries but as agents of women-led development, applying gender mainstreaming at every stage, from data and design to budgeting and audit.
free.upm-2024-gs1-9:
Caste endogamyInter-caste marriageInter-religious marriageSpecial Marriage Act

Endogamy, marrying within one's own group, lies at the heart of both caste and religious community; Dr B.R. Ambedkar called it the essence of caste (Castes in India, 1916). Inter-caste marriages are still a small minority, about 5% of marriages according to the India Human Development Survey (NCAER), but they are growing, mostly between castes of similar class and status. Inter-religious marriages remain rarer and face stronger resistance.

1. Why inter-caste marriages among equals have increased

  • Education and urbanisation: co-education, urban workplaces and migration bring young people of different castes together and weaken ritual ideas of purity.
  • Class replacing caste: families increasingly seek matches of similar education, income and occupation; when socio-economic status is equal, a caste difference becomes easier to accept. Marriages across large status gaps, especially between Dalits and dominant castes, still provoke opposition and even honour killings.
  • Legal protection: in Lata Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2006) the Supreme Court protected inter-caste couples from harassment, and in Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018) it laid down guidelines against honour crimes and khap panchayats.
  • State incentives: the Dr. Ambedkar Scheme for Social Integration through Inter-Caste Marriages gives ₹2.5 lakh to couples where one partner is from a Scheduled Caste, and many States add their own incentives.
  • A shared religious frame: inter-caste couples usually share the same faith, rituals and personal law, so families adjust more easily.

2. Why inter-religious marriages remain rare

  • Religion as a community boundary: religion carries identity, rituals, food habits and personal law, so marrying across it is seen as losing a member to another community.
  • Conversion and personal law: marriage under personal law often requires conversion; the secular route, the Special Marriage Act, 1954, requires a 30-day public notice that exposes couples to family and social pressure.
  • Anti-conversion laws: several States, such as Uttar Pradesh (2021), require prior declarations before religious conversion, including conversion for marriage, adding legal scrutiny.
  • Communal polarisation: narratives that portray such marriages as conspiracies, along with residential segregation, deepen suspicion between communities.
  • Attitudes: a Pew Research Center survey (2019–20, published 2021) found that 67% of Hindus and 80% of Muslims consider it very important to stop women of their community from marrying outside the religion.

3. The constitutional position

  • Right to choose: in Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (2018, the Hadiya case) the Supreme Court held that the choice of a partner, regardless of faith, is part of liberty under Article 21.
  • Protection: courts have directed police protection and safe houses for couples facing threats.

Socio-economic parity has softened caste endogamy, but religion remains a harder boundary. Simpler notice rules under the Special Marriage Act, firm protection for couples and a culture of constitutional morality can make the right to choose a partner real.
free.upm-2024-gs1-10:
Tri-sector partnershipCorporate social responsibilityLast-mile deliveryOutcome-based finance

Poverty, malnutrition, poor learning and joblessness are too large for any one actor to solve. The government brings scale, funds and legitimacy; NGOs bring trust, community knowledge and last-mile reach; the private sector brings capital, technology and management. Since 2014, Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 has also made corporate social responsibility (CSR) spending mandatory for large companies. The most productive model is a tri-sector partnership in which each partner does what it does best.

1. What each partner brings

2. Forms of collaboration that work best

  • Government frames, partners deliver: the state sets standards and funds the programme while NGOs implement; under PM POSHAN, the Akshaya Patra Foundation runs large kitchens with public funds and corporate donations.
  • Community-centred partnerships: the SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (NABARD, 1992), built with NGOs such as MYRADA, grew into DAY-NRLM, and Kerala's Kudumbashree shows how a State mission can work through women's collectives.
  • Data-driven convergence: in the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018), NITI Aayog works with foundations and companies on health, nutrition, education and agriculture, and districts are ranked on their progress.
  • Outcome-based finance: the Educate Girls Development Impact Bond in Rajasthan (2015) paid investors only if enrolment and learning targets were met, shifting the focus from spending to results.
  • Mission-mode alliances: polio eradication combined the government's Pulse Polio campaigns with WHO, UNICEF, Rotary and others; India was certified polio-free in 2014.
  • Digital public infrastructure: Aadhaar and UPI are public platforms on which private firms build services that widen inclusion.

3. Principles for productive collaboration

  • Clear roles and shared outcomes, written into agreements with measurable targets.
  • Community participation through gram sabhas and SHGs, so that people own the programme.
  • Transparency and accountability: registration of NGOs on NITI Aayog's NGO Darpan portal, social audits and open data.
  • Long-term, well-spread funding: CSR money aligned with district plans rather than concentrated in a few industrialised States.
  • Balanced regulation: rules such as the FCRA should ensure accountability without stifling genuine civil society.

4. Risks to avoid

  • Elite capture and window-dressing: CSR used for publicity, or NGOs captured by local elites.
  • Profit over public interest: private partners may cherry-pick easy, profitable areas.
  • State withdrawal: partnerships must not become a reason for the government to give up responsibility for basic services such as health and education.

The most productive collaboration is government-led, community-centred and outcome-focused: the state stays accountable, NGOs ensure participation and the private sector adds resources and innovation, together delivering inclusive development.
free.upm-2024-gs1-11:
Imperial CholasDravida styleBrihadisvara templeChola bronzes

The Imperial Cholas (c. 850–1279 CE), whose rule began when Vijayalaya took Thanjavur and peaked under Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044), built an empire reaching Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Yet their most enduring legacy is cultural: the mature Dravida temple, the bronze Nataraja and a temple-centred civilisation. Three of their temples together form the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Great Living Chola Temples".

1. Temple architecture: the peak of the Dravida style

  • Brihadisvara (Rajarajesvaram), Thanjavur: completed by Rajaraja I around 1010 CE, its granite vimana, more than 60 m high, rises in diminishing storeys to a massive dome-shaped capstone. The towering vimana, rather than the gateway, dominates the complex, a hallmark of the Chola style.
  • Gangaikonda Cholapuram: built by Rajendra I at his new capital to celebrate his northern campaign to the Ganga; its vimana has softer, curving lines.
  • Airavatesvara, Darasuram: built under Rajaraja II, with a mandapa carved as a chariot with wheels and horses and exquisite miniature sculpture.
  • Planned complexes: enclosure walls (prakaras), pillared halls, tanks and gopurams made the temple a town in itself.

2. Sculpture and bronze casting

  • Stone sculpture: wall niches hold Dakshinamurti, Lingodbhava, Ardhanarishvara and Durga, carved with calm dignity and refined proportions.
  • Bronzes: cast by the lost-wax method, Chola images of Shiva, Parvati, Rama and the Tamil saints are treasured in museums across the world; Queen Sembiyan Mahadevi was a great patron of bronze casting.
  • Nataraja: Shiva as the cosmic dancer became the finest expression of Chola art, joining philosophy with perfect form.

3. Painting, literature and temple culture

  • Murals: frescoes in the passage around the Brihadisvara sanctum, found beneath later Nayaka paintings, show Shiva as Tripurantaka and the story of the saint Sundarar.
  • Literature: Kamban's Ramavataram, Sekkilar's Periyapuranam and Jayamkondar's Kalingattupparani belong to the Chola age.
  • Temples as institutions: inscriptions record land grants, music, dance, schools and charities, so temples were centres of economy, learning and community life.

4. Comment: art is not the only source of pride

  • Local self-government: the Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (10th century) describe village assemblies whose members were chosen by lot (kudavolai).
  • Naval power: Rajendra I's expedition against Srivijaya (1025) carried Chola power across the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia.
  • Irrigation: tanks and canals made the Kaveri delta prosperous.
  • The other side: wars and plunder of rival kingdoms, and the heavy demands of temple and state on peasants, temper the glory.

The Cholas are remembered with pride because they turned stone and bronze into lasting symbols of devotion, power and beauty, and also left a legacy of local democracy and maritime reach. Their temples are still places of worship, making Chola art a living heritage.
free.upm-2024-gs1-12:
Balance of powerAlliance systemJuly CrisisNationalism and imperialism

The balance of power is a distribution of power in which no single state or bloc can dominate the others; after the Congress of Vienna (1815) it guided European diplomacy. The First World War (1914–1918) broke out after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. The fear that one power would dominate Europe was central to the war, but it was not the only cause.

1. Arguments that it was a war for the balance of power

  • Rise of Germany: unified in 1871, Germany became Europe's strongest industrial and military power, and Britain, France and Russia drew together to contain it.
  • Rival blocs: the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, 1882) faced the Triple Entente, built through the Franco-Russian alliance (1894), the Entente Cordiale (1904) and the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907).
  • Britain's entry: Britain declared war on 4 August 1914 after Germany invaded Belgium, whose neutrality it had guaranteed in 1839; its deeper aim was to prevent German domination of the continent and the Channel coast.
  • Naval race: Germany's challenge to British naval supremacy after HMS Dreadnought (1906) threatened Britain's position.
  • The Balkans: the decline of the Ottoman Empire left a vacuum that Austria-Hungary and Russia competed to fill, as in the Bosnian crisis (1908) and the Balkan Wars (1912–13).

2. Other causes that were equally important

  • Nationalism: Serbian and Pan-Slav nationalism, Pan-Germanism and France's wish to recover Alsace-Lorraine, lost in 1871.
  • Imperialism: rivalry for colonies, markets and raw materials, seen in the Moroccan crises (1905, 1911).
  • Militarism: arms races and rigid war plans, such as Germany's Schlieffen Plan, turned mobilisation into war.
  • German ambition: the historian Fritz Fischer (1961) argued that Germany sought expansion and world power, going beyond mere balance.
  • Diplomatic failure: Germany's "blank cheque" to Austria-Hungary and Austria's harsh ultimatum to Serbia turned a local crisis into a general war.

3. War aims went beyond balance

  • Territorial gains: Italy joined the Allies in 1915 on promises of territory, and the Sykes–Picot Agreement (1916) divided Ottoman lands.
  • Ideology: the United States entered in 1917 after unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram, with Wilson speaking of making the world "safe for democracy".
  • Peace settlement: the Treaty of Versailles (1919) punished Germany rather than restoring a balance, and the League of Nations sought to replace the balance of power with collective security.

It is therefore correct only in part to say the war was fought for the balance of power. Strategic fear explains why the great powers joined in, while nationalism, imperialism and militarism explain why the conflict became so total. The failure to build a stable order in 1919 helped sow the seeds of the Second World War.
free.upm-2024-gs1-13:
DeindustrialisationIndustrial RevolutionOne-way free tradeLoss of patronage

Before 1750 India was among the world's leading producers of cotton textiles: Bengal muslins, Coromandel chintzes and Gujarat calicoes were sold across Asia and Europe. The Industrial Revolution in England from the late 18th century, with the spinning jenny, water frame, mule, power loom and steam engine, made machine-made cloth far cheaper. Indian handicrafts declined sharply in the 19th century, a process called deindustrialisation. The Industrial Revolution was the main force, but colonial policy decided how hard it hit.

1. Role of the Industrial Revolution

  • Cheap machine goods: Lancashire mills produced cloth at a fraction of the cost of hand-made textiles, so Indian goods lost first their foreign and then their home markets; by the 1880s, two-thirds of the cotton clothes worn by Indians were made of British cloth (NCERT).
  • Demand for raw materials: British industry needed raw cotton, indigo and jute, so India became an exporter of raw materials and an importer of manufactures.
  • Steam transport: steamships and, from 1853, railways carried British goods deep into the interior, ending the protection that distance had given village artisans.
  • Spinning hit hardest: cheap mill yarn ended hand-spinning, often done by women, as a source of income.

2. Colonial policies that magnified the impact

  • One-way free trade: the Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's monopoly of trade with India and let British goods in at low duties, while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain.
  • Coercion of weavers: after Plassey (1757), Company agents (gomasthas) forced Bengal's weavers to sell at low prices, ruining many even before the machines arrived.
  • No protection or support: the colonial state neither protected Indian industry nor spread new technology, unlike the governments of Germany, Japan or the United States.

3. Other causes

  • Loss of patronage: the decline of the Mughal and regional courts and their nobility removed the main buyers of luxury crafts.
  • Changing tastes: a new Western-educated class preferred imported goods.
  • Decline of old towns: centres such as Dhaka, Murshidabad and Surat lost their markets.

4. Extent and debate

  • Ruralisation: displaced artisans crowded into agriculture; Amiya Kumar Bagchi estimated that the share of people dependent on industry in Gangetic Bihar fell from 18.6% (1809–13) to 8.5% (1901).
  • Uneven decline: historians such as Morris D. Morris and Tirthankar Roy note that hand-weaving survived by using cheap mill yarn and serving local tastes, and some crafts adapted.
  • Modern industry: Indian cotton mills arose from 1854 in Bombay, but they were too few to absorb the displaced artisans.

The Industrial Revolution was the primary cause, but colonial rule made its effect devastating by opening India's markets while denying it protection; countries that faced the same machines with their own governments industrialised instead. That is why Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt saw the ruin of crafts as part of the colonial drain.
free.upm-2024-gs1-14:
Groundwater depletionIndo-Gangetic plainFood securityArsenic contamination

The deep alluvial aquifers of the Indo-Gangetic plain are among the most productive in the world. They made the plain India's food bowl after the Green Revolution, and the Indo-Gangetic basin alone accounts for about a quarter of all groundwater withdrawn worldwide. The Central Ground Water Board's 2025 assessment puts national extraction at about 61% of the annually extractable resource, but parts of the plain draw far more than they recharge.

1. The decline: nature and causes

  • Over-extraction: the rice–wheat system, free or flat-rate power for pumps and cheap tubewells encourage heavy pumping; Punjab (156%) and Haryana (137%) draw far more than is replenished each year, and Delhi (92%) is close to the limit.
  • Hotspots: a study of the basin (MacDonald and others, Nature Geoscience, 2016) found water levels falling across about 30% of it, particularly near major cities, while canal seepage kept them stable or rising elsewhere; CGWB data put the plain's worst over-extraction in Punjab and Haryana.
  • Quality crisis: the same study found that over 60% of the groundwater down to 200 m was unsafe for drinking or irrigation because of salinity or arsenic; arsenic is widespread in Bihar, West Bengal and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
  • Less recharge: paved cities, filled ponds and erratic monsoon rain reduce recharge.

2. Effects on food security

  • Availability: the plain grows much of India's wheat and rice: Uttar Pradesh is the largest wheat producer, and Punjab and Haryana are among the biggest suppliers to the central pool; falling water tables shrink the irrigated area and yields, especially of water-hungry paddy.
  • Access and affordability: deeper borewells and bigger pumps raise costs, pushing small and marginal farmers into debt or out of farming and raising food prices.
  • Utilisation (nutrition and health): arsenic passes from irrigation water into rice and vegetables, and from wells into drinking water, causing skin lesions and cancers.
  • Stability: groundwater is India's buffer against drought; as it runs down, harvests become more vulnerable to failed monsoons and heatwaves under climate change.
  • Ecological feedback: dry-season river flow depends partly on groundwater, so its decline also hurts fisheries.

3. Way forward

  • Manage demand: diversify from paddy to pulses, maize and millets with assured procurement; promote direct-seeded rice and micro-irrigation under PMKSY ("Per Drop More Crop"), and incentives such as Haryana's Mera Pani Meri Virasat.
  • Price power sensibly: metered or solar power for pumps (PM-KUSUM) and separate farm feeders to curb waste.
  • Recharge and govern aquifers: Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) for community water budgeting, Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain, Mission Amrit Sarovar (2022) and aquifer mapping under NAQUIM.
  • Ensure safe water: arsenic-free piped supply under the Jal Jeevan Mission and testing of irrigation water.

Groundwater is the hidden foundation of India's food security. Unless the Gangetic plain moves from unchecked extraction to sustainable aquifer management, the food bowl of the past could become the water-stressed zone of the future.
free.upm-2024-gs1-15:
Aurora borealisAurora australisSolar windMagnetosphere

Auroras are natural displays of coloured light in the night sky of high latitudes. The aurora borealis (northern lights) appears around the North Pole and is seen from Alaska, Canada, Iceland and Scandinavia; the aurora australis (southern lights) appears around the South Pole and is seen from Antarctica, Tasmania and New Zealand. Both usually occur in an oval band around the geomagnetic poles, at about 60–75° latitude and roughly 100–300 km above the ground.

1. What auroras are

  • Forms: shimmering curtains, arcs, rays and diffuse glows that shift and ripple across the sky.
  • Colours: set by the gas that glows and its height; green light from oxygen is the most common.
  • Twin displays: the northern and southern auroras occur at the same time, at the two ends of the same magnetic field lines.
  • Location: the thermosphere and ionosphere, far above weather clouds.

2. How auroras are triggered

  • Solar wind: the Sun constantly sends out charged particles, mainly electrons and protons, carrying its magnetic field.
  • Solar storms: solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and fast streams from coronal holes deliver stronger bursts of particles and energy.
  • Magnetosphere: Earth's magnetic field shields the planet, but when the field carried by the solar wind points southward, opposite to Earth's, the two connect (magnetic reconnection) and energy is stored in the long magnetic tail on the night side.
