  • Particles rain down near the poles: further reconnection in the tail releases this energy and accelerates electrons along field lines that converge near the magnetic poles.
  • Collision and glow: the electrons strike oxygen and nitrogen in the upper atmosphere and excite them; as these return to their normal state, they release light.

3. Why near the poles, and sometimes farther

  • Field geometry: Earth's field lines dip into the atmosphere near the magnetic poles, so particles enter there.
  • Storms widen the oval: the extreme (G5) geomagnetic storm of 10–11 May 2024, driven by several CMEs from sunspot region AR 13664 and the strongest since the "Halloween" storms of 2003, pushed auroras far south, across Europe and much of the United States.
  • Solar cycle: auroras are most frequent near the maximum of the 11-year sunspot cycle, which Solar Cycle 25 reached around 2024–25.

4. Significance

  • Space-weather risks: strong storms disturb satellites, GPS, radio links and power grids; Quebec's power grid collapsed in a storm in March 1989.
  • Science: India's Aditya-L1, stationed at the L1 point, studies the Sun, and its data showed that two colliding CMEs in the May 2024 storm set off magnetic reconnection across about 1.3 million km (ISRO, 2025).
  • Tourism: aurora viewing supports the economies of Nordic countries.

Auroras are a vivid sign of the Sun–Earth connection. The same solar storms that light up polar skies can damage satellites and grids, which is why space-weather monitoring by missions such as Aditya-L1 matters.
free.upm-2024-gs1-16:
TornadoSupercellWind shearTornado Alley

A twister, or tornado, is a violently rotating column of air that reaches from the base of a thunderstorm (cumulonimbus) cloud to the ground, often visible as a funnel of condensation and debris. It is small, usually tens to a few hundred metres wide, and short-lived, yet its winds can exceed 300 km/h, making it the most violent storm on Earth. The United States records the most tornadoes in the world, about 1,200 a year, most of them in the Great Plains and the southern states near the Gulf of Mexico.

1. How a twister forms

  • Instability: warm, moist air near the ground lies beneath cooler, drier air, so rising air parcels build towering thunderclouds.
  • Wind shear: winds that change speed and direction with height set up a horizontal rolling motion in the lower atmosphere.
  • Mesocyclone: a strong updraft tilts this roll upright, creating a rotating updraft inside a supercell thunderstorm.
  • Touchdown: downdrafts on the storm's rear flank tighten the rotation and bring it down to the ground.
  • Rating: tornadoes are graded on the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, from EF0 to EF5, by the damage they cause.

2. Why most twisters occur around the Gulf of Mexico

  • Warm, moist Gulf air: southerly winds carry warm, humid air from the Gulf of Mexico northwards over the plains, supplying heat and moisture.
  • Clashing air masses: cold, dry polar air from Canada and hot, dry air from the south-western deserts and the Mexican plateau meet this moist air, creating sharp fronts and a "dry line".
  • No east–west mountain barrier: the Rockies and the Appalachians run north–south, so these air masses meet freely over the flat Great Plains.
  • Jet stream and shear: in spring the jet stream lies overhead, giving the strong wind shear needed for supercells.
  • Seasons and regions: "Tornado Alley" in the southern and central Plains peaks in spring and early summer; in "Dixie Alley" (Gulf states such as Mississippi and Alabama) tornadoes also strike in late autumn and winter, and hurricanes that make landfall from the Gulf spawn many more.

3. Twisters elsewhere

  • Bangladesh and eastern India: the pre-monsoon nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi) produce tornadoes; the Daulatpur–Saturia tornado in Bangladesh (1989) is regarded as the deadliest on record.
  • Other regions: Argentina's Pampas and parts of Europe see tornadoes, and waterspouts form over warm seas.

4. Reducing the risk

  • Detection: Doppler radars reveal rotation inside storms, and the US National Weather Service issues tornado watches and warnings.
  • Preparedness: storm shelters, building codes and drills save lives; eastern and north-eastern India need better radar coverage for nor'westers.

Twisters need a rare combination of moisture, instability, wind shear and lift. Warm Gulf air colliding with cold, dry continental air over open plains makes North America the world's tornado capital.
free.upm-2024-gs1-17:
Regional disparityDiversityBalanced regional developmentConvergence

Regional disparity is the unequal distribution of income, infrastructure, human development and opportunities across regions: between States, within States and between rural and urban areas. India's disparities are stark: a working paper of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM, September 2024) found that Bihar's per capita income was only about 33% of the national average in 2023-24, while Delhi's was two and a half times it.

1. Forms of regional disparity

  • Inter-State: the southern and western States have pulled ahead; the five southern States together produced 30.6% of India's GDP in 2023-24.
  • Intra-State: Vidarbha and Marathwada in Maharashtra, Bundelkhand in Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, and north Karnataka lag far behind the better-off parts of their States.
  • Rural–urban and core–periphery: metropolitan regions attract investment, while tribal, hill and forest areas remain poor.

2. How regional disparity differs from diversity

  • Different questions: diversity asks how to respect differences; disparity asks how to reduce inequality.
  • Where they overlap: diversity becomes divisive when it coincides with disparity, as in tribal and north-eastern regions where cultural difference and underdevelopment reinforce each other.

3. How serious is regional disparity in India?

  • Wide income gaps: Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are far above the average, while Uttar Pradesh is at about half and Bihar at a third; West Bengal's share of national GDP fell from 10.5% (1960-61) to 5.6% (2023-24).
  • Human development gaps: in NITI Aayog's SDG India Index 2023-24, Kerala and Uttarakhand scored 79 against a national 71, while Bihar was at the bottom; multidimensional poverty is highest in Bihar.
  • Migration and friction: workers from the poorer north and east migrate to the south and west, sometimes provoking "sons of the soil" tensions.
  • Political and federal strain: demands for special category status and new States, Left-wing extremism in neglected tribal districts, and disputes between richer and poorer States over Finance Commission devolution.
  • Signs of hope: the Aspirational Districts Programme shows that focused effort can improve health, nutrition and schooling in the poorest districts.

4. Measures

  • Fiscal equalisation: the income-distance criterion (42.5% weight under the 16th Finance Commission) sends more resources to poorer States.
  • Targeted programmes: Aspirational Districts (2018, 112 districts), Aspirational Blocks (2023, 500 blocks) and PM-DevINE for the North-East.
  • Investment in lagging regions: infrastructure, industrial corridors and skilling in the eastern States.

Diversity is India's strength; regional disparity is its weakness. Narrowing the gaps through human capital, infrastructure and fair fiscal transfers is essential for balanced regional development and national unity.
free.upm-2024-gs1-18:
Affirmative actionSubstantive equalityCreamy layerSub-classification

The Constitution aims at substantive equality: Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4) allow special provisions and reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward classes; Article 46 directs the State to promote their educational and economic interests; Articles 330 and 332 reserve seats in legislatures; and Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Seven decades of affirmative action have produced real gains, yet its benefits have not reached many of the most deprived.

1. Achievements

  • Political voice: 84 SC and 47 ST seats in the Lok Sabha, and reservation in panchayats and municipalities, have produced leaders from these communities.
  • Education and jobs: reserved seats in colleges and public employment have created a Dalit and tribal middle class.
  • Legal protection: the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 strengthened safeguards against caste violence.

2. Why the benefits do not reach fully

  • Concentration within groups: a few better-off communities corner most benefits; data examined by the Rohini Commission (2018) showed that about a quarter of OBC sub-castes received about 97% of central OBC jobs and seats, while 983 communities, over a third of the total, received none.
  • Shrinking public sector: reservation applies to government jobs and institutions, a small and shrinking share of employment, while contract jobs and the private sector lie outside it.
  • Unfilled posts: backlog vacancies and the "not found suitable" label in faculty and senior posts leave reserved positions empty.
  • Weak foundations: poor schooling, dropouts, learning gaps and delayed scholarships mean many cannot compete even for reserved seats.
  • Persistent discrimination: untouchability, atrocities, manual scavenging despite the 2013 Act, and residential segregation continue.
  • Land and livelihoods: most Dalit households remain landless, tribals have been displaced by dams and mines, and many forest-rights claims have been rejected.
  • Invisible groups: PVTGs, denotified and nomadic tribes, Dalit women and persons with disabilities often fall through the cracks.

3. Recent responses

  • Sub-classification: in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (August 2024), a seven-judge bench allowed States to sub-classify SCs and STs so that the most backward get a fair share.
  • Creamy layer: it applies to OBCs since Indra Sawhney (1992); in Davinder Singh four judges favoured extending it to SCs and STs, but this remains under debate.
  • Better data: caste enumeration in Census 2027 will help target benefits.
  • Beyond quotas: Stand-Up India, PM-AJAY and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan focus on assets, skills and livelihoods.

Affirmative action has opened doors but not yet levelled the field. Moving from quotas to capabilities, through good schools, land, credit and skills, data-based sub-classification and firm enforcement of anti-discrimination laws, will carry social justice to the last person.
free.upm-2024-gs1-19:
Feminisation of migrationPersonal autonomyPatriarchal bargainRenegotiated family ties

Globalisation after the 1991 reforms created new jobs in IT and IT-enabled services, banking, retail, hospitality, healthcare, aviation and export manufacturing. These drew skilled, young, unmarried women from small towns and from different classes and castes to cities such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and Gurugram. This feminisation of migration, for work rather than marriage, is reshaping women's personal freedom and their relationships with their families.

1. Drivers of the trend

  • Demand for educated workers: service industries value communication and technical skills and recruit women in large numbers.
  • Investment in daughters: smaller families invest in daughters' higher education and increasingly see a daughter's job as an asset.
  • Support systems: hostels, paying-guest homes, company transport and smartphones make living away from home possible.

2. Impact on personal freedom

  • Economic independence: an own income and bank account give women control over spending, saving and lifestyle.
  • Autonomy and mobility: the anonymity of the city frees them from neighbourhood surveillance; they choose their clothes, friends, leisure and careers.
  • Choice in marriage: marriage is delayed, and women have a greater say in when and whom they marry, including partners from other castes; the Supreme Court has held that adults living together is not an offence (S. Khushboo, 2010).
  • New identities: a professional identity builds confidence.

3. Limits to this freedom

  • Safety: harassment at work and in public spaces and the risks of night travel persist; the POSH Act, 2013 and the SHe-Box portal offer redress, but enforcement is uneven.
  • New forms of control: hostel curfews, landlords' rules for single women and constant phone checks by families.
  • Precarity and double burden: long hours, contract jobs and, after marriage, the burden of housework and care.
  • Class differences: in low-end jobs globalisation can reproduce patriarchy, as in the Sumangali scheme in Tamil Nadu's textile mills, where young unmarried women worked for years for a lump sum meant for their dowry.

4. Relationship with the family

  • From dependence to interdependence: daughters send money home, pay for siblings' education and support parents, gaining a stronger voice in family decisions.
  • Intergenerational tension: conflicts arise over the timing of marriage, choice of partner and lifestyle; many women strike a "patriarchal bargain", accepting some family control in return for the freedom to work.
  • Ties at a distance: phones and video calls keep daily contact, but distance strains the expectation that daughters care for ageing parents.
  • A changing marriage market: working women are increasingly preferred as brides, though dowry and expectations of a career break after marriage persist.

The trend has widened women's personal freedom and turned daughters into earners whose voice counts, but that freedom remains conditional. Safe housing such as Sakhi Niwas under Mission Shakti, safe transport, crèches and strict enforcement of the POSH Act can make it a lasting social transformation.
free.upm-2024-gs1-20:
Cultural diversitySocio-economic marginalityIntersectionalityStructural exclusion

India's cultural diversity is vast: 705 Scheduled Tribes, 121 languages, all the major religions and thousands of castes (Census 2011). Socio-economic marginality means exclusion from resources, opportunities and power. Many groups defined by culture, such as tribes, Dalits and some religious minorities, are also among the poorest, which suggests a high correlation. A critical look shows that the link is real but neither uniform nor caused by diversity itself.

1. Evidence of a strong correlation

  • Scheduled Tribes (8.6% of the population): with distinct languages and cultures, their literacy was about 59% against 73% nationally (Census 2011); they bear the brunt of displacement by dams and mines, and the 75 PVTGs are the most deprived.
  • Scheduled Castes (16.6%): ritual exclusion translated into landlessness, dependence on manual and casual labour, and continuing discrimination.
  • Religious minorities: the Sachar Committee (2006) found that Muslims lagged in education, credit and public employment, forming only about 3% of IAS officers.
  • Linguistic and regional groups: remote hill and border communities, including parts of the North-East, face poor connectivity and markets, and children taught in a language other than their mother tongue fall behind.
  • Intersectionality: tribal and Dalit women face several layers of disadvantage at once.

2. Why the proposition is only partly true

  • Prosperous minorities: Parsis, Jains and Sikhs are culturally distinct yet relatively well off, and trading communities such as Marwaris and Chettiars prosper.
  • Diversity within groups: some SC, ST and OBC families form a creamy layer; the Mizos, a tribal people, have very high literacy (Mizoram about 91%, Census 2011).
  • Region matters: Dalits and Muslims in Kerala or Tamil Nadu are generally better off than those in Bihar or Uttar Pradesh, and poor households exist among dominant castes too, the rationale of the EWS quota.
  • Correlation is not causation: marginality was produced by history and structure (untouchability, colonial forest laws, land alienation, unequal public investment), not by cultural difference as such.

3. Consequences of the overlap

  • Grievance and conflict: where cultural difference and deprivation coincide, identity can turn into grievance, feeding autonomy movements, unrest in tribal belts and communal mobilisation.
  • Policy blind spots: treating a group as homogeneous lets its better-off members capture benefits meant for the poorest.

4. Way forward

  • Enforce safeguards: Articles 15(4), 16(4), 29, 30 and 46, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).
  • Target the poorest: schemes such as PM-JANMAN (2023) for PVTGs and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan, guided by disaggregated data.

The link between diversity and marginality is significant but shaped by history, region and class. Policy must remove structural exclusion while respecting identity, so that India's diversity becomes a source of inclusive strength rather than inequality.
free.upm-2024-gs2-1:
Electoral reformsOne Nation, One ElectionKovind Committee129th Amendment Bill

Free and fair elections are part of the basic structure of the Constitution (Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975). Yet money power, criminalisation and near-continuous polling have prompted a series of committees, from the Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) to the Law Commission. The most ambitious recent proposal is "One Nation, One Election" (ONOE): holding Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections together, as India did from 1951–52 to 1967, recommended by the Ram Nath Kovind High-Level Committee (2024).

1. Why electoral reforms are needed

  • Money power: candidates face spending limits but parties do not; in ADR v. Union of India (February 2024) the Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme for its opacity.
  • Criminalisation: the Vohra Committee (1993) exposed the criminal–political nexus; Lily Thomas (2013) ended the protection that let convicted sitting legislators keep their seats.
  • Independence of the referee: after Anoop Baranwal (2023), the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 created a selection committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and a Union Minister, which critics say leans towards the executive.
  • Perpetual campaigning: since the premature dissolution of several Assemblies (1968–69) and the Lok Sabha (1970) broke the common cycle, some State goes to the polls almost every year, and the Model Code of Conduct repeatedly freezes new decisions.

2. Reforms suggested by committees

The common thread is to curb money and muscle power, protect the Election Commission's independence and cut the cost and frequency of elections.

3. ONOE: proposal and status

  • Kovind Committee: constituted in September 2023, it reported in March 2024, proposing that Lok Sabha and Assembly elections be synchronised first and municipal and panchayat elections follow within 100 days, with a single electoral roll. The Union Cabinet accepted it in September 2024.
  • Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024: introduced on 17 December 2024, it inserts Article 82A and amends Articles 83, 172 and 327; a companion Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill covers Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Status (October 2026): both Bills are with a Joint Parliamentary Committee chaired by P.P. Chaudhary, whose term was extended in July 2026 to the Winter Session of 2026.

4. Merits and concerns

  • Merits: lower costs for the exchequer and parties, one deployment of security forces and staff, fewer interruptions by the Model Code and more time for governance.
  • Federal concerns: cutting an Assembly's term to match the Lok Sabha may dilute federalism, a basic feature (S.R. Bommai, 1994), and national issues may overshadow State issues.
  • Accountability: a House elected only for a short unexpired term weakens the mandate, and frequent elections are themselves a check on governments.
  • Logistics: many more EVMs, VVPATs and staff would be needed at once.

ONOE addresses the frequency of elections, not their integrity. It should advance through broad consensus with the States, alongside long-pending reforms: transparent party funding, decriminalisation and inner-party democracy.
free.upm-2024-gs2-2:
Lok AdalatArbitral tribunalAlternative dispute resolutionCompoundable offences

Article 39A (42nd Amendment, 1976) directs the State to secure equal justice and free legal aid. With huge arrears in courts, alternative dispute resolution (ADR) offers quicker and cheaper justice; Section 89 of the Civil Procedure Code lists arbitration, conciliation, mediation and judicial settlement, including settlement through Lok Adalats. Lok Adalats and arbitral tribunals are both ADR forums, but they differ in their source of authority, their method and the cases they can take up.

1. Lok Adalats

  • Origin and law: these "people's courts" began in Gujarat in 1982 and gained statutory status under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; NALSA and the State, district and taluk legal services authorities organise them.
  • Method: a bench of a judicial officer with lawyers or social workers helps the parties reach a compromise in pending or pre-litigation disputes. It cannot adjudicate; if there is no settlement, the case returns to the court (State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh, 2008).
  • Award: deemed to be a decree of a civil court, final and binding, with no appeal (Section 21); court fees already paid are refunded.
  • Permanent Lok Adalats (2002 amendment): for public utility services such as transport, power, water and hospitals; unlike ordinary Lok Adalats, they may decide a dispute on merits if conciliation fails.

2. Arbitral tribunals

  • Law: the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law (1985).
  • Consent-based: jurisdiction flows from an arbitration agreement; parties choose one or more arbitrators (an odd number), or the court appoints them.
  • Adjudication: the tribunal decides on merits; the award is enforced like a decree (Section 36) and can be set aside only on limited grounds, such as conflict with public policy (Section 34).
  • Speed: amendments of 2015 and 2019 set time limits for awards (Section 29A), and the India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019 promotes institutional arbitration.

3. Do they hear civil and criminal cases?

  • Lok Adalats: civil and some criminal. They settle civil disputes such as money recovery, bank loans, motor accident claims, labour, land acquisition compensation, utility bills and family disputes (except divorce), and compoundable offences; they have no jurisdiction over offences that are not compoundable (Section 19(5)).
  • Arbitral tribunals: civil only. Only disputes over private rights, mostly commercial, are arbitrable. In Booz Allen and Hamilton (2011) the Supreme Court held criminal offences, matrimonial disputes, guardianship, insolvency, testamentary matters and certain tenancy disputes non-arbitrable; Vidya Drolia (2020) laid down a test of arbitrability.
  • Reason: a crime is a wrong against society, prosecuted by the State, so it cannot be settled by private agreement, except compoundable offences that the law allows the victim to compromise.

Both forums ease the burden on courts: Lok Adalats deliver free, consensual justice to ordinary litigants, while arbitration gives commercial certainty. Together with the Mediation Act, 2023, they can make ADR the first resort rather than the last.
free.upm-2024-gs2-3:
Parliamentary supremacyCabinet dominanceCollective responsibilityLegislative scrutiny

India adopted the Westminster model: the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), so in theory Parliament controls the executive. In practice, a cabinet backed by a disciplined majority controls Parliament: it sets the agenda, drafts nearly all laws and steers the budget, which Ramsay Muir called the "dictatorship of the cabinet". Bound by the Constitution and judicial review, India's Parliament was never sovereign like Britain's; cabinet dominance has narrowed its role further.

1. How the cabinet has come to dominate

  • Majority and the whip: the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule, 1985) disqualifies members who defy the party whip, so a majority cabinet's Bills almost always pass.
  • Control of time and agenda: government business takes precedence; only 14 private members' Bills have ever become law, the last in 1970.
  • Thin scrutiny: in the 17th Lok Sabha (2019–24), which held 274 sittings, only 16% of Bills went to committees and 35% passed with less than an hour of debate; about 80% of the budget was voted without discussion in 2019–23 (PRS).
  • Law-making by the executive: ordinances (Article 123), sometimes re-promulgated, which Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) called a fraud on the Constitution, and wide delegated legislation.
  • Bypassing the second chamber: certifying Bills such as the Aadhaar Act, 2016 as Money Bills kept them beyond the Rajya Sabha's power to amend.

2. Signs of weakening parliamentary control

  • Opposition sidelined: for the first time, the Deputy Speaker was not elected during the entire 17th Lok Sabha, and 146 MPs of both Houses were suspended in December 2023.
  • Fewer sittings: the Lok Sabha sits far less than in the 1950s, below the minimum of 120 days a year suggested by the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002).
  • Prime ministerial dominance: power concentrated in the Prime Minister's Office can reduce even the cabinet to a secondary role.

3. Why parliamentary control is not wholly lost

  • Confidence of the House: governments have fallen on the floor of the Lok Sabha, as in 1990 and in April 1999, when the Vajpayee Government lost by one vote.
  • Coalitions and the Rajya Sabha: coalition governments (1989–2014) had to negotiate, and a government without a Rajya Sabha majority must bargain; the land acquisition ordinance was allowed to lapse in 2015.
  • Committees and questions: Departmentally Related Standing Committees (since 1993), the Public Accounts Committee and Joint Parliamentary Committees scrutinise the executive; Question Hour keeps ministers answerable.

4. Restoring the balance

  • Mandatory committee scrutiny of Bills, a statutory minimum number of sittings and Opposition days, as in the UK House of Commons.
  • Limit the whip to confidence and no-confidence motions (Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990), and frame transparent rules for certifying Money Bills.

Cabinet leadership is the essence of responsible government, but leadership must not become control. Stronger committees, more sittings and space for the Opposition would restore parliamentary accountability.
free.upm-2024-gs2-4:
Comptroller and Auditor GeneralRegularity auditPropriety auditPerformance audit

Under Article 149 and the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) (Article 148) audits the accounts of the Union, the States and bodies they fund. Dr B.R. Ambedkar described the office as probably the most important under the Constitution. Its mandate has grown from checking whether money was spent legally to asking whether it was spent wisely, the essence of propriety audit.

1. Legality: regularity audit

  • Mandatory: the CAG checks that spending was covered by a grant voted by the legislature, incurred by a competent authority under the rules and properly accounted for.
  • Appropriation and finance accounts: compare actual spending with grants, exposing excess or unauthorised expenditure.
  • Reports: submitted to the President or the Governor (Article 151) and laid before the legislature, where the Public Accounts Committee, chaired by an Opposition member, examines them.

2. Propriety: beyond the letter of the law

  • Meaning: an expenditure may be legal yet wasteful, extravagant or unfair. Propriety audit tests it against canons of financial propriety, such as the General Financial Rules, 2017 standard that an official should spend public money with the vigilance a person of ordinary prudence would use with his own.
  • Discretionary: unlike regularity audit, propriety audit is left to the CAG's judgement.
  • Performance audit: an extension of propriety that asks about economy, efficiency and effectiveness, as in the 2023 audits of the Bharatmala Pariyojana (cost escalation) and of the beneficiary database of Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY.

3. Why propriety matters: examples

  • 2G spectrum (2010): the CAG estimated a presumptive loss of up to ₹1.76 lakh crore from allotting spectrum on a first-come, first-served basis instead of by auction; the Supreme Court cancelled 122 licences in 2012.
  • Coal blocks (2012): the CAG estimated a windfall gain of ₹1.86 lakh crore to private allottees; the Supreme Court cancelled 214 allocations in 2014.
  • Commonwealth Games (2011 report): questioned costs, delays and procurement.
  • Impact: such audits pushed the shift to auctions of natural resources and to transparent procurement.

4. Limits and criticism

  • Hindsight and policy: critics argue that presumptive-loss estimates second-guess policy choices and make officials risk-averse.
  • Advisory reports: the CAG cannot enforce its findings; follow-up depends on the PAC and on ministries' action-taken notes, which are often delayed.
  • Gaps: for secret-service expenditure the CAG must accept a certificate from the competent authority, and the CAG is appointed by the executive without any selection panel.

Legality is the floor of accountability; propriety is its spirit. Timely audits, prompt follow-up by the PAC and restraint in avoiding policy judgements together make the CAG a true guardian of the public purse.
free.upm-2024-gs2-5:
73rd and 74th AmendmentsSubsidiarityRural–urban continuumGood governance

The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) made panchayats and municipalities "institutions of self-government" (Articles 243G and 243W), with 29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule and 18 in the Twelfth. Built on the principle of subsidiarity, they bring decisions close to citizens. As towns spread into villages, States increasingly merge peri-urban panchayats into municipalities, raising the question of how to govern the rural–urban continuum.

1. Role of local bodies in good governance

  • Participation: the Gram Sabha (Article 243A) approves plans and selects beneficiaries; Gram Panchayat Development Plans (since 2015) make planning bottom-up; municipalities of over three lakh people must have ward committees (Article 243S).
  • Inclusion: seats are reserved for SCs and STs, and at least one-third for women (Articles 243D, 243T); women now hold nearly half of all panchayat seats.
  • Accountability and service delivery: social audits in Gram Sabhas and public display of works; local water and sanitation committees under the Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat show local ownership of services.
  • Resources: State Finance Commissions (Articles 243I, 243Y) and Finance Commission grants; the 16th Finance Commission recommended about ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies.
  • Limits: weak devolution of funds, functions and functionaries, parallel parastatals, delayed municipal elections and proxy rule by relatives of women representatives dilute these gains.

2. Merging rural with urban local bodies: the context

Census 2011 counted 3,892 census towns, urban in character but governed as villages. Article 243Q lets the Governor declare a "transitional area" a Nagar Panchayat, and large cities such as Greater Hyderabad (2007) were formed by merging surrounding local bodies.

3. Pros of merger

  • Integrated planning: one authority can plan growth corridors, check unauthorised layouts and work with the Metropolitan Planning Committee (Article 243ZE).
  • Economies of scale: water supply, sewerage and solid-waste management that small panchayats cannot provide.
  • Fiscal strength: a wider property-tax base and eligibility for urban missions such as AMRUT.

4. Cons of merger

  • Democratic deficit: a village becomes a small part of a distant corporation, with fewer representatives per person.
  • Livelihood and welfare loss: farmers and labourers may lose rural employment and housing schemes and face higher taxes before urban services arrive.
  • Overstretched corporations: many already struggle with their existing areas.
  • Consent: mergers are often decided by State governments without the Gram Sabha's consent, provoking local protests.

Merger should follow objective criteria (population, density, non-farm work) under Article 243Q, with phased taxes, protected entitlements and ward-level participation. The Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (2016) shows that urban amenities can reach villages without dissolving their self-government.
free.upm-2024-gs2-6:
Public charitable trustCharitable purposePhilanthropyInclusive development

A public charitable trust dedicates property to a purpose that benefits the public or a section of it, unlike a private trust for named beneficiaries governed by the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. Public trusts are regulated by State laws such as the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950 and by income-tax law, which exempts income applied to a "charitable purpose" such as relief of the poor, education, medical relief or other objects of general public utility.

1. Potential for inclusive development

  • Education and research: J.N. Tata's endowment led to the Indian Institute of Science (1909), and the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust founded the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (1936) and the Tata Memorial Hospital (1941); the Azim Premji Foundation (2001) works with government schools.
  • Health: trust hospitals offer subsidised care; Maharashtra's law requires charitable hospitals to reserve beds for indigent and weaker-section patients.
  • Nutrition and welfare: the Akshaya Patra Foundation serves school meals under PM POSHAN, and temple, gurdwara and waqf institutions run free kitchens, schools and hospitals.
  • Relief: trusts mobilise quickly in disasters; the PM CARES Fund (2020) is itself a public charitable trust.
  • CSR channel: Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires qualifying companies to spend 2% of average net profits on CSR, much of it through trusts and foundations.

2. Why trusts suit vital public issues

  • Last-mile reach: community roots let them serve tribal, disabled or very poor groups that schemes miss.
  • Innovation: flexible funds allow pilots that governments can later scale.
  • Long horizons: endowments sustain institutions for decades, beyond electoral cycles.

3. Constraints

  • Fragmented regulation: there is no uniform central law, and Charity Commissioners exist only in a few States, such as Maharashtra and Gujarat.
  • Misuse: some trusts are used for tax avoidance or profiteering; capitation fees in trust-run colleges were barred in T.M.A. Pai (2002).
  • Opaque governance: family control and weak disclosure of accounts and outcomes.
  • Concentration: philanthropy clusters in a few cities and sectors, leaving poorer regions underserved.
  • Compliance burden: tighter tax registration and FCRA rules (2020) weigh on small and foreign-funded trusts.

4. Way forward

  • Transparency: a model law with a national registry and online disclosure of accounts and outcomes, building on NITI Aayog's NGO Darpan portal.
  • Partnership: outcome-based partnerships with government in health, education and nutrition, and new funding channels such as SEBI's Social Stock Exchange framework (2022).
  • Smart regulation: tax incentives for giving in underserved regions, with risk-based rather than blanket controls.

Public charitable trusts carry India's tradition of daan and seva into modern development. With transparency and partnership, they can become genuine partners in inclusive growth, complementing rather than replacing the State.
free.upm-2024-gs2-7:
Vicious cycleHuman capitalFirst 1,000 daysNutrition security

Poverty limits food, clean water, health care and schooling; the resulting malnutrition weakens learning, health and earning capacity, which perpetuates poverty, often across generations. NFHS-5 (2019-21) found 35.5% of children under five stunted, 32.1% underweight and 57% of women anaemic. This erodes human capital: the World Bank's Human Capital Index put India at 0.49 in 2020, meaning a child born then would be only about half as productive as with full health and education.

1. How the cycle damages human capital

  • Irreversible early damage: stunting in the first 1,000 days, from conception to age two, impairs brain development and later school performance.
  • Disease burden: 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months were anaemic (NFHS-5); malnutrition and infections such as diarrhoea feed on each other.
  • Lower productivity: stunted, anaemic adults earn less and lose more working days.
  • Inter-generational transmission: undernourished adolescent girls, especially those married early (23.3% of women aged 20–24 married before 18, NFHS-5), give birth to low-birth-weight babies.
  • Unequal burden: stunting is highest among SC and ST children and in the poorest households.

2. Progress so far

  • Falling poverty: multidimensional poverty fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23), with 24.82 crore people moving out (NITI Aayog); the World Bank estimates that extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011-12) to 5.3% (2022-23).
  • Large safety net: the National Food Security Act, 2013 and free grain for about 81 crore people, ICDS, PM POSHAN, Mission POSHAN 2.0 and Anaemia Mukt Bharat. Yet stunting fell only from 38.4% (NFHS-4) to 35.5%.

3. Steps to break the cycle

  • Focus on the first 1,000 days: maternity benefits (PMMVY), counselling on breastfeeding and complementary feeding, quality take-home rations and growth monitoring through the Poshan Tracker.
  • Diverse diets: add pulses, eggs, millets and fortified foods to the PDS and school meals; promote kitchen gardens and biofortified crops.
  • Water, sanitation and health: the Jal Jeevan Mission, Swachh Bharat, deworming, full immunisation and "test, treat and talk" camps for anaemia.
  • Women's agency: keep girls in school, end child marriage and expand self-help groups (about 10 crore women under DAY-NRLM), since women's education and income improve child nutrition most.
  • Income security: rural wage employment (125 days under the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025), skilling, and health cover such as PM-JAY so that illness does not push families back into poverty.
  • Convergence: joint village plans by anganwadi workers, ASHAs and ANMs, better pay and training for frontline workers, and community-based management of acute malnutrition.

Breaking the cycle needs a shift from food security to nutrition security, centred on the first 1,000 days and on women. Nutrition is one of the most cost-effective investments a country can make in its human capital and growth.
free.upm-2024-gs2-8:
Democratic governancePublic trustIntegrityCommitment to public service

In a democracy sovereignty rests with the people, and civil servants, though unelected, exercise power on their behalf as trustees. Democratic governance therefore needs more than legal compliance; it needs legitimacy, which rests on public trust. Lord Hewart's dictum that justice "should manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done" (1924) applies equally to administration: integrity, one of the seven principles of public life set out by the Nolan Committee (1995), and commitment must both be visible.

1. Why public perception matters

  • Legitimacy of unelected power: citizens accept decisions on land, licences or benefits when they believe officials are fair and honest.
  • Cooperation and compliance: trust improves tax compliance, participation in campaigns such as immunisation, and use of grievance systems.
  • Neutrality across governments: a civil service seen as impartial provides continuity; one seen as partisan loses credibility with much of the public.
  • Development: perceived corruption and arbitrariness deter investment and hurt the poor most.
  • Morale and recruitment: a respected service attracts talent. Sardar Patel, addressing administrative service probationers at Metcalfe House on 21 April 1947 (now Civil Services Day), urged them to treat the common people as their own and to serve in a spirit of service.

2. What erodes the perception

  • Corruption and collusion: the Vohra Committee (1993) described a nexus of criminals, politicians and bureaucrats.
  • Politicisation: transfers and postings by patronage; in T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) the Supreme Court asked for fixed tenures and Civil Services Boards.
  • Colonial mindset: red tape, delay and insensitivity towards ordinary citizens.
  • Lapses at entry: recruitment paper leaks and the UPSC's cancellation (2024) of a probationer's candidature for misrepresentation dented faith in merit.

3. Building a positive perception

  • Values and codes: the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968 require integrity and political neutrality; the Second ARC's report on Ethics in Governance (2007) recommended a code of ethics for civil servants.
  • Transparency: the RTI Act, 2005, proactive disclosure, e-office, annual property returns and digital service delivery reduce discretion.
  • Accountability: the Lokpal (first appointed in 2019), CVC oversight, appraisal with multi-source feedback and premature retirement of officers of doubtful integrity under FR 56(j).
  • Responsiveness: citizens' charters, Right to Services laws, CPGRAMS and social audits show commitment in daily service.
  • Capacity and protection: Mission Karmayogi (2020) for competency-based training, and Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act (2018) to shield bona fide decisions from frivolous probes.

4. Role models

T.N. Seshan's enforcement of the Model Code, E. Sreedharan's time-bound delivery of the Konkan Railway and the Delhi Metro, and Armstrong Pame's people-funded road in Manipur (2012) show how individual conduct builds public trust in the whole service.

In a democracy perception is part of reality: a civil servant must be honest and be seen to be honest. Institutionalising ethics, transparency and responsiveness turns individual integrity into lasting public trust.
free.upm-2024-gs2-9:
China plus oneDe-riskingTrusted supply chainsStrategic autonomy

COVID-19 disruptions, the US–China rivalry and China's use of trade as leverage have pushed Western countries to diversify supply chains, through strategies described as "China plus one", de-risking (European Commission, 2023) and friend-shoring. With a large market, a skilled workforce, democratic institutions and a central place in the Indo-Pacific, India is being fostered as a trusted alternative and as a partner to balance China's political and economic weight.

1. India as an alternative supply-chain hub

  • Electronics: Apple's contract manufacturers have expanded iPhone assembly in India; in April–June 2025 India's share of US smartphone imports rose to 44%, while the share of US smartphone shipments assembled in China fell to 25% (Canalys).
  • Semiconductors: Micron's assembly and test plant at Sanand, Gujarat (announced in 2023), alongside the India Semiconductor Mission (2021).
  • Critical minerals: India joined the US-led Minerals Security Partnership (2023) to diversify supplies of lithium, cobalt and rare earths.
  • Resilience frameworks: the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative with Japan and Australia (2021), the IPEF Supply Chain Agreement and the India–EU Trade and Technology Council.
  • Trade agreements: the India–EFTA TEPA (2024) and the India–UK CETA (2025), backed by Production Linked Incentive schemes.

2. India as a strategic partner to balance China

  • Quad: India, the US, Japan and Australia cooperate on maritime domain awareness (IPMDA, 2022), critical technologies and health security.
  • Defence and technology: India is a US Major Defence Partner (2016) and has signed the foundational agreements LEMOA, COMCASA and BECA (2016–20); GE F414 engines are to be co-produced with HAL (2023 MoU), MQ-9B drones were bought in 2024, and iCET (2023) became TRUST (2025).
  • Europe: France has supplied Rafale jets and Scorpène submarine technology, and the EU treats India as a key Indo-Pacific partner.
  • Alternatives to the BRI: the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (2023) and Western support for India's Global South leadership, as when the African Union joined the G20 under India's presidency (2023).

3. Limits of the partnership

  • India's own dependence on China: Indian factories still import electronic components, solar cells and pharmaceutical ingredients from China, so assembly shifts faster than value addition.
  • A transactional West: US tariffs on most Indian goods rose to 50% in August 2025, including a 25% Russian-oil penalty. The penalty was removed in February 2026, with a framework for an interim trade deal, and the reciprocal tariffs lapsed after a US Supreme Court ruling; but a new 10% duty has covered about half of India's exports since July 2026, and the deal was unsigned in October 2026.
  • Strategic autonomy: India is a partner, not an ally; it buys Russian defence equipment, belongs to BRICS and the SCO, and stayed out of RCEP.
  • Domestic bottlenecks: logistics costs, land and regulatory delays and skill gaps slow the shift.

The West's interest gives India a historic opening, but it must turn assembly into deep manufacturing and preserve its strategic autonomy, partnering with the West on its own terms while managing its relations with China.
free.upm-2024-gs2-10:
Extended neighbourhoodConnect Central AsiaConnectivityGreat-power competition

The five Central Asian Republics (CARs), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, form part of India's extended neighbourhood, linked to it by the Silk Road, Buddhism and the Mughals' Central Asian roots. Rich in energy and minerals, and lying between Russia, China, Iran and Afghanistan, they have regained importance. India's Connect Central Asia policy (2012) and the first India–Central Asia Summit (virtual, January 2022) mark deeper engagement, though geography still limits it.

1. Diplomatic relations

  • Summit and ministerial formats: the India–Central Asia Dialogue of foreign ministers (first in Samarkand, 2019; fourth in New Delhi, June 2025) and the 2022 Summit; the Prime Minister visited all five republics in 2015.
  • Multilateral platforms: India became a full member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2017 and chaired it in 2023.
  • Shared security concerns: a stable Afghanistan, terrorism and drug trafficking; the June 2025 Dialogue unequivocally condemned the Pahalgam terror attack.
  • Soft power: ITEC training, scholarships, Indian films and yoga, and many Indian medical students in the region.

2. Economic relations

  • Energy and minerals: Kazakhstan is a key uranium supplier for India's reactors; the Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India (TAPI) gas pipeline remains stalled; an India–Central Asia Rare Earth Forum works on critical minerals.
  • Connectivity: the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the Ashgabat Agreement (joined in 2018), with Iran's Chabahar port as the gateway; India Ports Global signed a 10-year contract for its Shahid Beheshti terminal in 2024.
  • Constraints: trade stays modest because Pakistan denies transit; the US reimposed sanctions on Chabahar in September 2025; a conditional waiver expired in April 2026 without renewal, and the 2026 conflict involving Iran has left India's role there uncertain.

3. Strategic relations

  • Defence ties: joint exercises such as KAZIND (Kazakhstan), Dustlik (Uzbekistan) and Khanjar (Kyrgyzstan), and training of officers.
  • A crowded field: Russia remains the security guarantor through the CSTO; China leads in trade and investment through the BRI and its own China–Central Asia summits (2023, 2025); the US, EU, Japan and Turkey also court the region. India offers itself as a non-threatening partner.

4. Growing significance in regional and global geopolitics

  • A new "Great Game": Russia's preoccupation with Ukraine has opened space for China, the West and middle powers.
  • Resources for the energy transition: uranium, rare earths and gas.
  • Alternative corridors: the Middle Corridor across the Caspian bypasses Russia, while the INSTC links India to Russia and Europe.
  • Afghanistan: stability next door shapes terrorism and narcotics flows.

India's engagement is warm but thin: no direct access, slow projects and limited investment leave it behind China. Operationalising Chabahar and the INSTC, air-freight corridors, digital payments, pharmaceuticals and education can turn goodwill into strategic depth in this extended neighbourhood.
free.upm-2024-gs2-11:
Paper leaksPublic Examinations Act, 2024Organised crimeFederal scope

Repeated paper leaks in recruitment and entrance examinations have hurt millions of aspirants and eroded faith in merit. The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, enacted in February 2024 and in force from 21 June 2024, is the first central law aimed specifically at unfair means in public examinations. The 2026 Amendment Act (passed in July 2026; assent on 31 July 2026) made its penalties harsher and its trials faster.

1. Aims and objects

  • Credibility of examinations: bring transparency, fairness and credibility to public examinations and assure young people that sincere effort will be rewarded.
  • Target organised networks: deter paper-leak gangs, insiders, service providers and institutions that collude for money.
  • Fill a legal gap: such offences were earlier handled only under general criminal law.
  • A model for States: States may adopt or adapt it for their own examinations.

2. Main provisions of the 2024 Act

  • Coverage: examinations of the UPSC, the SSC, the Railway Recruitment Boards, IBPS, the National Testing Agency (NTA), and Union ministries and their attached offices for recruitment, plus any authority the Centre notifies.
  • Unfair means: leaking question papers or answer keys, assisting candidates, tampering with computer systems or with documents used for merit lists, and conducting fake examinations or issuing fake admit cards or offer letters.
  • Duties of service providers: they must report wrongdoing and cannot shift examination centres without permission; their managers are personally liable.
  • Procedure: offences are cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable; an officer not below Deputy Superintendent of Police investigates, and the Centre may transfer a case to a central agency.

3. The 2026 amendment: speed and deterrence

  • Investigation: a special task force may be set up, and investigations must be completed within two months.
  • Special Fast Track Courts: a Court of Session in every State and Union Territory, with special public prosecutors; trials to finish within three months of the chargesheet.
  • Appeals: to a two-judge bench of the High Court, filed within 30 days.

4. Are university and State Board examinations covered?

  • No. The Act applies only to "public examinations" held by the central recruitment and testing bodies in its Schedule or by authorities the Centre notifies, and the 2026 amendment did not widen this. Class X and XII board examinations, universities' own semester examinations and State Public Service Commission examinations are not in the Schedule.
  • Partial exception: entrance tests run by the NTA, such as NEET-UG, JEE (Main), CUET and UGC-NET, are covered, so admission to universities is protected even though university examinations are not.
  • Constitutional reason: State public services (Entry 41) and universities (Entry 32) are in the State List, and education is in the Concurrent List. States must legislate for their own examinations, as Rajasthan, Gujarat, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand have done.

Harsher punishment is necessary but not sufficient. Secure computer-based testing, encrypted logistics, accountable service providers and the NTA reforms suggested by the K. Radhakrishnan Committee (2024) must accompany the law to restore trust in examinations.
free.upm-2024-gs2-12:
Right to privacyArticle 21Presumption of legitimacyBodily autonomy

In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) a nine-judge Bench unanimously held that privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and to the freedoms of Part III, overruling M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to that extent. Privacy is a natural right inherent in human dignity, which the Constitution recognises rather than creates. It is not absolute, but any limit must pass a test of proportionality.

1. Why privacy is intrinsic to life and liberty

  • Dignity and autonomy: a dignified life requires control over one's body, mind, information and intimate choices.
  • Bodily privacy: in Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests were held to violate Articles 20(3) and 21.
  • Decisional privacy: Suchita Srivastava (2009) recognised a woman's reproductive choice as part of personal liberty.

2. Law on DNA tests for paternity

  • Presumption of legitimacy: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, now Section 116 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, makes birth during a valid marriage, or within 280 days of its dissolution while the mother remains unmarried, conclusive proof of legitimacy unless non-access is shown.
  • No roving inquiry: Goutam Kundu (1993) held that blood or DNA tests cannot be ordered as a matter of course and that no one can be compelled to give a sample.
  • Adverse inference: Sharda v. Dharmpal (2003) allowed courts to order medical tests in matrimonial cases and to draw an adverse inference from refusal.
  • Eminent need: later cases allow a test only where paternity cannot otherwise be settled, weighing privacy and the child's dignity against the interest in knowing parentage.

3. DNA testing of a child in the womb

  • No specific law: no statute provides for a court-ordered prenatal paternity test, and the presumption of legitimacy concerns a child already born.
  • The mother's bodily integrity: a foetal sample must come from the pregnant woman (blood, amniotic fluid or placental tissue). After Puttaswamy, Selvi and Suchita Srivastava she cannot be forced; at most a court may draw an adverse inference from refusal.
  • Risk to the foetus: invasive sampling risks miscarriage, so ordering it in a civil dispute would rarely be proportionate.
  • PCPNDT Act, 1994: prenatal diagnostic procedures are permitted only to detect specified abnormalities, and disclosing the sex of the foetus is banned. As paternity is not a permitted purpose, prenatal paternity testing arguably fits poorly within the Act (no court has settled this) and could be misused for sex selection.
  • Foetal tissue after the pregnancy has ended: in Ms X v. Mr Z (Delhi High Court, 2001) the court allowed DNA testing of foetal tissue preserved by AIIMS after a terminated pregnancy: privacy is not absolute and the discharged foetus was no longer part of her body, though she herself could not be compelled to give a sample.

The mother's bodily autonomy and the future child's dignity make prenatal paternity testing an exceptional measure at most. Courts should prefer post-birth testing on strict necessity; a DNA law with privacy safeguards would bring clarity.
free.upm-2024-gs2-13:
Cooperative federalismFiscal federalismGovernor's roleInter-State Council

India is a "Union of States" (Article 1) with a strong Centre, yet federalism is part of the basic structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994). Over the past decade the Union has reshaped Centre–State relations through fiscal, institutional and legislative changes. Some have deepened cooperative federalism; others have left several States feeling that power is being centralised.

1. Recent changes

  • Fiscal: GST (101st Amendment, 2016) pooled indirect taxes in the GST Council; compensation to States ended in 2022, and "GST 2.0" moved to two main slabs from September 2025. The 16th Finance Commission (2026–31) kept the States' share at 41% but ended revenue-deficit grants.
  • Borrowing and transfers: off-budget borrowings now count against State limits (Kerala's challenge was referred to a Constitution Bench in 2024); cesses and surcharges outside the divisible pool have grown; 50-year interest-free loans support State capital spending, partly tied to reforms.
  • Institutions: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission (2015), and Centrally Sponsored Schemes were rationalised.
  • Territory and legislation: Article 370 was abrogated and Jammu and Kashmir reorganised into two Union Territories (2019); the GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023 restored the Lieutenant Governor's final say over Delhi's services after a Constitution Bench ruling (May 2023).
  • Security: the BSF's jurisdiction was extended to 50 km from the border in Punjab, West Bengal and Assam (2021), and several States withdrew general consent to the CBI.
  • Governors: delays in assent led to State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (April 2025); the Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025) held that courts cannot fix timelines or deem assent.

2. Sources of the trust deficit

  • Fiscal: a shrinking effective share of tax revenue and conditional transfers.
  • Political: Governors seen as agents of the Centre, and disputes over central agencies.
  • Legislative: Concurrent List laws framed without adequate consultation, such as the farm laws (2020, repealed in 2021).
  • Representation: fears that population-based delimitation will penalise States that controlled population growth.

3. Measures to build trust

  • Institutional dialogue: regular meetings of the Inter-State Council (Article 263), as the Punchhi Commission (2010) urged, and active Zonal Councils and NITI Aayog's Governing Council.
  • Fiscal fairness: bring cesses and surcharges into sharing or cap them, set up the GST dispute-settlement mechanism under Article 279A(11), and keep transfers predictable.
  • Governors: appoint after consulting the Chief Minister (Sarkaria Commission, 1988), decide on Bills within a reasonable period as the Punchhi Commission urged, and use discretion sparingly.
  • Consultation: consult States before legislating on Concurrent List subjects, as Sarkaria recommended, and design schemes with flexible funds.
  • Consensus: settle delimitation by agreement and agree protocols for central agencies that respect the States' domain over police and public order.

Federalism works best as "Team India": a strong Centre and confident States. Institutionalised dialogue, fair finances and constitutional morality in the use of central powers can rebuild trust between them.
free.upm-2024-gs2-14:
Public interest litigationLocus standiJudicial activismBasic structure

Public interest litigation (PIL) lets any public-spirited person or group approach the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court (Article 226) on behalf of those who cannot do so themselves. Pioneered by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer in the late 1970s and settled in S.P. Gupta (1981), which relaxed locus standi, PIL turned the Supreme Court into a forum for the poor and a powerful policy actor.

1. Reasons for the growth of PIL

  • Post-Emergency legitimacy: after ADM Jabalpur (1976), the Court sought to regain public trust by opening its doors to the disadvantaged.
  • Failures of the State: undertrials languishing in jail (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979), bonded labour (Bandhua Mukti Morcha, 1984) and pavement dwellers (Olga Tellis, 1985) showed rights left unenforced.
  • Expansive Article 21: after Maneka Gandhi (1978), life came to include livelihood, a clean environment, food, education and dignity.
  • Procedural innovation: letters treated as petitions (epistolary jurisdiction, as in Sunil Batra), fact-finding commissions, amicus curiae and continuing mandamus (Vineet Narain, 1997; the T.N. Godavarman forest case since 1995).
  • Active civil society and media brought issues such as pollution, custodial violence and corruption to court.

2. What PIL achieved

  • Judicial guidelines: Vishaka (1997) on sexual harassment, in force until the 2013 Act; D.K. Basu (1997) on arrest; Prakash Singh (2006) on police reform.
  • Policy outcomes: CNG buses in Delhi (M.C. Mehta), cooked mid-day meals (PUCL, 2001) and disclosure of candidates' criminal records and assets (2002).
  • Accountability: the electoral bonds scheme was struck down in 2024.

3. Is it the world's most powerful judiciary?

  • Arguments for: it can strike down constitutional amendments under the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; NJAC case, 2015); judges are appointed through a judiciary-led collegium; Article 142 allows orders for "complete justice"; and it has original, appellate, advisory (Article 143) and writ jurisdiction with very liberal standing.
  • Comparisons: the US Supreme Court reviews laws but not constitutional amendments and requires a concrete "case or controversy"; the UK Supreme Court cannot strike down Acts of Parliament; Germany's Federal Constitutional Court can test amendments against the Basic Law's eternity clause, so India is not unique in every respect.
  • Arguments against: power on paper is limited by implementation, as with the partial compliance with Prakash Singh; pendency and a heavy special-leave docket strain the Court; and charges of overreach invite resistance.
  • Self-restraint: in Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) the Court laid down guidelines against frivolous "publicity interest litigation".

PIL has made the Supreme Court arguably among the most powerful courts in the world in reach and remedies, though weaker in enforcement. Its legitimacy rests on using that power with judicial restraint, as a last resort when other branches fail.
free.upm-2024-gs2-15:
SecularismPrincipled distanceEstablishment ClauseWall of separation

India is a secular State: it has no State religion and treats all faiths equally. The word "secular" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), but the idea was built into Articles 14–16 and 25–30 from the start; S.R. Bommai (1994) held secularism a basic feature, and in Dr Balram Singh (2024) the Supreme Court upheld its insertion. The US instead follows a "wall of separation" under the First Amendment (1791).

1. India as a secular State

  • Freedom of religion: Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health; Article 26 lets denominations manage their affairs.
  • No State religion: no tax to promote a religion (Article 27) and no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions (Article 28).
  • Equality: no discrimination on grounds of religion (Articles 15, 16) and a single electoral roll (Article 325); appeals on grounds of religion are a corrupt practice (Abhiram Singh, 2017).
  • Principled distance: the State may regulate secular activities linked to religion and reform practices, such as throwing open Hindu temples to all (Article 25(2)(b)), abolishing untouchability (Article 17) and ending instant triple talaq (Shayara Bano, 2017).
  • Group rights: minorities may run their own educational institutions (Article 30); personal laws continue, while a uniform civil code is a Directive Principle (Article 44), now in force in Uttarakhand (2025).

2. Secularism in the US Constitution

  • Establishment Clause: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion; Jefferson's "wall of separation" (1802) was applied to the States in Everson v. Board of Education (1947).
  • Free Exercise Clause: protects religious practice; the State cannot interfere in a church's internal matters such as choosing ministers (Hosanna-Tabor, 2012).
  • No religious test for public office (Article VI).
  • Limits on State support: school-sponsored prayer was struck down in Engel v. Vitale (1962); the Lemon test (1971) gave way in Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022) to a test of history and tradition; and States may not exclude religious schools from neutral aid programmes (Carson v. Makin, 2022).

3. Comparison and assessment

  • Different histories: the American founders sought to keep government away from religion and avoid an established church; India had to manage deep religious diversity, Partition and caste hierarchy, so it chose engagement over separation.
  • Strengths: the Indian model allows social reform and protects minorities; the US model avoids State entanglement but leaves reform to society.
  • Challenges: in India, charges of selective intervention, courts deciding what is "essential" to a religion and communal polarisation; in the US, continuing disputes over religion in schools and public life.

Indian secularism is not anti-religion but sarva dharma sambhava with principled distance. Its strength lies in even-handedness: equal distance and equal respect in practice, not only in law.
free.upm-2024-gs2-16:
Citizens' CharterSevottamRight to ServicesCitizen-centric administration

A Citizens' Charter is a public commitment by a service-providing organisation on its services, standards, timelines, grievance redress and citizens' obligations. Launched in the UK in 1991, it came to India after the Conference of Chief Ministers (1997), with the DARPG as nodal agency. It marked a shift from a "ruler" to a "servant" mindset, treating citizens as stakeholders rather than supplicants.

1. A landmark initiative

  • Spread: charters were adopted by Union ministries, States, banks, railways, hospitals and municipal bodies.
  • Sevottam (2006): the DARPG's model linked charters with grievance redress and service-delivery capability, with the BIS standard IS 15700:2005.
  • Second ARC, 12th Report (2009): "Citizen Centric Administration" called for specific, consultative charters backed by redress.
  • From charter to right: Right to Services Acts, starting with Madhya Pradesh (2010), made time-bound delivery enforceable, and CPGRAMS handles grievances online.

2. Factors hindering its promise

  • Top-down drafting: charters were prepared without consulting users or front-line staff, so standards were vague or unrealistic.
  • No legal teeth: a charter is a declaration, not a right; there is rarely compensation for failure, and the Citizens' Right to Grievance Redress Bill, 2011 lapsed in 2014.
  • Low awareness: few citizens know of charters, which are often only in English or on websites.
  • Unchanged work culture: untrained, under-resourced staff and no link between charter compliance and performance appraisal.
  • One-time exercise: many charters copy a standard format, are not updated and lack independent monitoring.
  • Weak redress: grievances are often closed without resolution and without escalation.

3. Measures to realise its potential

  • Statutory backing: a national law on time-bound services and grievance redress, with penalties on officials and compensation to citizens, as in State Right to Services Acts.
  • The Second ARC's seven-step model: define services, set standards, build capability, perform, monitor, evaluate independently and improve continuously.
  • Participation: draft charters with citizens' groups, and use citizen report cards, pioneered by Bengaluru's Public Affairs Centre, and social audits.
  • Office-specific charters: separate, measurable charters for each field office rather than one for a whole ministry.
  • Technology: online applications with tracking, dashboards and automatic escalation through CPGRAMS and State portals, with assisted access at Common Service Centres.
  • Incentives: recognise offices that meet their standards and link charter performance to appraisal.

The charter will realise its promise only when it moves from declaration to entitlement: backed by law, owned by staff and monitored by citizens, making citizen-centric administration a daily reality.
free.upm-2024-gs2-17:
Universal health coverageOut-of-pocket expenditurePrimary health careRegulation of private care

Health is a State subject (Entry 6, State List), and Article 47 directs the State to improve public health; the Supreme Court has read a right to health care into Article 21 (Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity, 1996). Yet care in India is largely marketised: government health expenditure was only 1.43% of GDP and out-of-pocket spending 43.4% of total health expenditure (National Health Accounts 2022-23), against the National Health Policy, 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP.

1. Why the State must check marketisation

  • Market failure: patients cannot judge their own needs or the quality of care (information asymmetry, as Kenneth Arrow showed in 1963), which invites over-treatment and unnecessary procedures.
  • Impoverishment: medical bills push families into debt; PM-JAY covers hospitalisation but not most outpatient care and medicines.
  • Urban bias: private hospitals cluster in cities, leaving rural and tribal areas underserved.
  • Public goods: disease surveillance, immunisation and prevention bring no profit, and COVID-19 showed the value of a strong public system.

2. Containing marketisation through regulation

  • Standards and prices: the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 for registration and standards; price caps on cardiac stents and knee implants (2017); generic medicines through Jan Aushadhi Kendras.
  • Strategic purchasing: PM-JAY (₹5 lakh per family a year, extended in 2024 to everyone aged 70 and above) buys care at fixed package rates.
  • Rights-based law: Rajasthan's Right to Health Act, 2023.

3. Extending public health care to the grassroots

  • Comprehensive primary care: about 1.82 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs offering maternal and child care, screening for non-communicable diseases, free drugs and diagnostics, and teleconsultation through eSanjeevani.
  • Human resources: fill vacant posts of doctors and specialists, place community health officers at every centre, pay and train ASHAs and ANMs better, and use incentives and bonds for rural service.
  • Infrastructure: the PM-Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (2021) for critical-care blocks, block public health units and public health laboratories.
  • Financing: raise public spending towards 2.5% of GDP, with States spending more than 8% of their budgets on health (NHP 2017), and cut out-of-pocket costs through free medicines.
  • Community ownership: village health, sanitation and nutrition committees, Jan Arogya Samitis and panchayats monitor services; Tamil Nadu's doorstep-care scheme Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam (2021) and Kerala's Family Health Centres show what works.
  • Regulated partnerships: services such as dialysis under the Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (2016) through public–private partnerships with clear standards.

A strong public health system is the best regulator of the private market: when good public care is available nearby, private providers must compete on quality and price. Investing in primary care and health workers is the surest path to universal health coverage.
free.upm-2024-gs2-18:
e-governanceInteractive Service ModelTransparencyAccountability

e-governance is the use of ICT to transform how government works and how it relates to citizens, businesses and its own employees (G2C, G2B, G2E, G2G). The Second ARC's 11th Report (2008) stressed that it is about reforming governance, not just digitising forms. Of the commonly cited models of digital governance (broadcasting, critical flow, comparative analysis, e-advocacy and interactive service), the Interactive Service Model is the most advanced, enabling two-way interaction between citizens and government.

1. More than routine service delivery

  • Transparency: proactive disclosure (Section 4 of the RTI Act), open data (National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy, 2012) and digital audit trails reduce discretion.
  • Accountability: dashboards, application tracking and grievance metrics make officials answerable.
  • Participation: citizens become co-producers of policy, not just recipients of services.

2. Features of the Interactive Service Model

  • Two-way channels: citizens apply, track, complain and give feedback online; government responds and reports back.
  • Direct participation: consultations, polls and crowd-sourcing bring citizens into decision-making.
  • Integration: it combines the other models, so information, comparison and mobilisation feed into services and policy.
  • No middlemen: fewer face-to-face contacts reduce discretion and rent-seeking.

3. Evaluation: what it has achieved

  • Participation: MyGov (2014) hosts consultations and crowd-sources ideas, and the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014) asks ministries to publish draft laws for at least 30 days.
  • Grievance redress: CPGRAMS lets citizens lodge and track complaints against any ministry and rate the outcome.
  • Top-level monitoring: PRAGATI (2015) lets the Prime Minister review projects and grievances with Union Secretaries and Chief Secretaries by video link.
  • Traceable transactions: the Government e-Marketplace (2016), the RTI online portal and UMANG leave a digital trail.

4. Limits

  • Digital divide: only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5); language, disability and age add barriers.
  • Tokenism: consultations seldom report how inputs were used, and the 2014 policy is not binding and is often bypassed.
  • Closure without resolution: grievances are marked "disposed" without satisfying citizens.
  • Privacy and security: large databases raise risks of surveillance and breaches, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is still being phased in.

The Interactive Service Model turns e-delivery into e-democracy. Assisted access through Common Service Centres, Indian-language interfaces such as Bhashini, feedback that is acted upon and strong data protection will make it a genuine tool of transparency and accountability.
free.upm-2024-gs2-19:
Counter-Terrorism CommitteeResolution 1373CTEDSanctions regime

Terrorism has become transnational: networks such as Al-Qaida and ISIL, foreign terrorist fighters, online radicalisation and cross-border financing threaten global peace. After 9/11 the UN Security Council, acting under Chapter VII, adopted Resolution 1373 (2001), binding on all member States, and set up the Counter-Terrorism Committee (CTC) of all 15 Council members to monitor it. The Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate (CTED), created by Resolution 1535 (2004), supports it.

1. The CTC and its associated bodies

  • Duties under 1373: criminalise terror financing, freeze terrorist assets, deny safe haven, tighten border controls and share information.
  • Expanding mandate: Resolutions 1624 (2005) on incitement, 2178 (2014) on foreign terrorist fighters and 2462 (2019) on terror financing.

2. Effectiveness: achievements

  • Global norms: most States have enacted counter-terrorism and terror-financing laws and set up financial intelligence units, often after CTED assessments.
  • Capacity building: country visits and technical assistance with UNOCT and partners such as the FATF.
  • New threats: India, chairing the CTC in 2022, hosted its special meeting in Mumbai and New Delhi, which adopted the Delhi Declaration on countering terrorist use of new technologies such as drones, social media and online payments.
  • Sanctions listings: Jaish-e-Mohammed chief Masood Azhar (2019) and Lashkar-e-Taiba's Abdul Rehman Makki (2023) were listed, though only after long delays.

3. Limitations

  • No agreed definition of terrorism: India's proposed Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (1996) remains stuck.
  • Great-power politics: sanctions committees work by consensus, so one member can block listings through "technical holds", as China did for years on Masood Azhar and in 2022 on Sajid Mir.
  • No enforcement teeth: the CTC relies on States' reports and cannot penalise non-compliance or name State sponsors.
  • Opacity: CTED's assessments are mostly confidential, and reasons for holds are not disclosed.
  • Rights concerns: overbroad national laws adopted in the name of Resolution 1373 have been criticised for curbing civil liberties.
  • Technology gap: encrypted apps, crypto-assets and drones evolve faster than UN norms.

4. Way forward

  • Legal clarity: adopt the CCIT and a common definition of terrorism.
  • Fair listing: make holds time-bound and reasoned, and publish summaries of CTED assessments.
  • Coordination: align the CTC's work with the FATF and regulate the terrorist use of new technologies.

The CTC has built a global legal framework against terrorism, but its effectiveness depends on the political will of the P5. Without consensus on definitions and listings, zero tolerance for terrorism remains more slogan than practice.
free.upm-2024-gs2-20:
Sea lanes of communicationNeighbourhood FirstMaritime securityStrategic competition

The Maldives, a chain of about 1,190 coral islands in 26 atolls, lies about 70 nautical miles from India's Minicoy island and astride the main east–west sea lanes of communication of the Indian Ocean. Small in size but large in location, it is central to India's Neighbourhood First policy and to its maritime vision of MAHASAGAR (2025), which widened SAGAR (2015).

1. Geopolitical and geostrategic importance

  • Shipping channels: the Eight Degree Channel between Minicoy and the Maldives, and the channels through the archipelago, carry shipping between the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Aden in the west and the Strait of Malacca in the east.
  • Trade and energy flows: much of India's oil and gas imports from the Gulf and its trade with Europe and East Asia pass nearby, as do the energy imports of China and Japan.
  • Proximity: a hostile presence here could watch India's western naval movements and its island territories.
  • Arena of competition: China built the China–Maldives Friendship Bridge (2018) and lends for infrastructure, and the US signed a defence framework with the Maldives (2020).
  • Climate frontline: as a low-lying small island State, it is a partner in India's climate diplomacy.

2. The India–Maldives relationship

  • First responder: Operation Cactus foiled a coup (1988); India sent relief after the 2004 tsunami, water during Malé's crisis (Operation Neer, 2014) and early COVID-19 vaccines (2021).
  • Development partner: the Greater Malé Connectivity Project, India's largest in the Maldives, and the Hanimaadhoo airport runway (inaugurated in October 2024).
  • Economic lifeline: in October 2024 the two sides signed a US$400 million and ₹3,000 crore currency swap and adopted a vision for a Comprehensive Economic and Maritime Security Partnership; during the Prime Minister's July 2025 visit India extended a ₹4,850 crore line of credit, and talks on a free trade agreement began.
  • A strained phase: an "India Out" campaign preceded President Muizzu's election (2023), and Indian military personnel operating aircraft there were replaced by civilians in 2024.

3. Impact on maritime security and regional stability

  • Maritime domain awareness: coastal radars and the Information Fusion Centre–Indian Ocean Region (Gurugram) help track piracy, smuggling and illegal fishing.
  • Security cooperation: exercises such as Ekuverin (armies) and Dosti (coast guards, with Sri Lanka), and the Colombo Security Conclave, whose members include India, the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Mauritius.
