  • Strategic competition: Chinese loans, infrastructure and visits by research vessels in the region could shift the balance near India's coast.
  • Regional stability: India's financial support helps the Maldives avoid debt distress, preventing a crisis that rivals could exploit.

The Maldives' value lies in its location, but India's influence rests on trust. Respect for Maldivian sovereignty, quick delivery of people-centred projects and steady economic support will keep it a partner in a secure and stable Indian Ocean.
free.upm-2024-gs3-1:
Social sector expenditureInclusive growthRights-based welfareHuman capital

Social services cover education, health, water and sanitation, housing, nutrition, social security and the welfare of weaker sections. After the 1991 reforms, growth accelerated, and the Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-12) made inclusive growth (growth that reduces poverty and widens opportunity for all) its central goal. Public social spending, shared by the Union and the States, is the main tool for turning growth into human capital and social protection.

1. Pattern of public expenditure on social services

  • States carry most of the load: health, school education and water are State or Concurrent subjects, so States spend most of the money; the Union shapes priorities through Centrally Sponsored Schemes and Finance Commission transfers.
  • Education and health dominate: education is the largest head, followed by health, with rising shares for rural employment, food subsidy, housing and drinking water.
  • Revenue-heavy: most spending goes on salaries, subsidies and transfers; capital spending on hospitals, schools and laboratories remains small.
  • From services to entitlements: spending shifted from supply-side programmes to legal rights (work, education, food) and to Direct Benefit Transfer through the JAM trinity.

2. Trend in recent years

  • Rising amounts and share: combined Union and State spending on social services rose from ₹14.8 lakh crore (2020-21) to ₹25.7 lakh crore (2024-25 BE), about 15% a year, and its share in total government expenditure rose from 23.3% to 26.2% (Economic Survey 2024-25).
  • Health gained most: health spending grew about 18% a year and education about 12%; the government's share of total health expenditure rose from 29% (2014-15) to 48% (2021-22).

3. Consonance with inclusive growth: the gains

  • Poverty reduction: NITI Aayog estimates that 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23.
  • Wider access: near-universal elementary enrolment, institutional deliveries, toilets, tap water and pucca houses for the poor.
  • Protection from shocks: MGNREGS and free foodgrains cushioned the poor during COVID-19, and out-of-pocket health spending fell to 39.4% of total health expenditure (2021-22), though it rose to 43.4% in 2022-23.

4. Limits: why the consonance is only partial

  • Below benchmarks: government health spending was only 1.43% of GDP (2022-23) against the 2.5% target of the National Health Policy, 2017; education spending remains below the 6% of GDP goal of the Kothari Commission and NEP 2020.
  • Quality deficit: weak learning outcomes and vacant posts in schools and hospitals; most informal workers still lack social security.
  • Regional gaps: poorer States with the greatest needs spend the least per person.
  • Short-term bias: cash transfers and subsidies have grown faster than long-term investment in human capital.

Post-reform social spending has made growth inclusive in access but not yet in quality and outcomes. Raising health and education spending towards national targets, with a sharper focus on outcomes and lagging States, is the next step.
free.upm-2024-gs3-2:
Food inflationSupply shocksFlexible inflation targetingPolicy coordination

Food carries the largest weight in India's Consumer Price Index: about 46% for food and beverages in the CPI (base 2012). Food inflation stayed high through 2023-24 and 2024-25, touching nearly 11% in October 2024 even as core inflation eased, and headline CPI inflation rose again to 4.8% in August 2026. This tests the RBI's flexible inflation targeting regime, which aims at CPI inflation of 4% ±2%.

1. Causes of persistent food inflation

  • Weather shocks: heatwaves (2022), an El Niño year (2023), erratic monsoons and unseasonal rain hit wheat, pulses and vegetables; climate change makes such shocks more frequent.
  • Perishables: tomato, onion and potato prices swing sharply because they cannot be stored long and cold chains are thin.
  • Structural mismatch: rising incomes shift diets towards pulses, milk, eggs, meat and fruits, where supply grows slowly; India imports over half of its edible oil and part of its pulses, so world prices feed in.
  • Supply-chain weaknesses: small holdings, many intermediaries, post-harvest losses and weak storage widen the gap between farm-gate and retail prices.
  • Cost-push and policy: costlier diesel, fertiliser and labour, MSP increases, hoarding, and stop-go export bans and stock limits.

2. How the RBI responds

  • Framework: under Section 45ZA of the RBI Act (amended 2016), the six-member Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate to keep CPI inflation at 4% ±2%; the Government has retained this target for 2026-31.
  • Looking through, then acting: the RBI usually "looks through" a one-off food shock but tightens when it spreads to expectations and core prices.
  • Record: it raised the repo rate by 250 bps in 2022-23, held it at 6.5% through the food-price spike of 2023-24, cut it by 125 bps in 2025 as food prices eased, and raised it to 5.50% in October 2026, shifting its stance to "calibrated tightening" as inflation picked up.

3. Effectiveness against food inflation

  • Limited direct effect: interest rates cannot raise crop output or build cold chains, and demand for food barely responds to rates.
  • Useful indirect effect: a credible policy anchors expectations and checks second-round effects; inflation has been lower and more stable than in 2009–13, when it often exceeded 9%.
  • Costs: tightening against supply shocks slows growth and investment, while transmission is weak in the informal and rural economy.
  • Debate: the Economic Survey 2023-24 suggested exploring a target that excludes food, but the headline CPI target has been retained.

4. Better tools for food prices

  • Coordination: monetary policy must work alongside the Government's supply-side measures: storage, crop diversification, climate-resilient seeds and a stable trade policy.

Monetary policy is a necessary anchor for expectations but not a cure for food inflation. Lasting price stability needs supply-side reforms that make food production and markets resilient to climate shocks.
free.upm-2024-gs3-3:
Land reformsLand to the tillerPolitical willPeasant mobilisation

Land reforms after Independence had four parts: abolition of intermediaries such as zamindars, tenancy reform, ceilings on landholdings with redistribution of surplus land, and consolidation of holdings. Zamindari abolition was largely completed by the 1960s, but tenancy and ceiling laws mostly failed because of benami transfers and concealed tenancies. Jammu and Kashmir, Kerala and West Bengal, and partly Karnataka, were the exceptions where the tiller really gained.

1. Where land reforms succeeded

2. Factors behind success

  • Political will and ideology: committed governments made reform a core programme: Sheikh Abdullah's "Naya Kashmir" manifesto in J&K, the Communist ministry of 1957 and later governments in Kerala, and the Left Front in West Bengal after 1977.
  • Peasant mobilisation: earlier struggles such as the Tebhaga movement in Bengal (1946-47), the Punnapra-Vayalar revolt in Travancore (1946) and the work of the Kisan Sabhas created organised tenants who could resist eviction and press for implementation.
  • Administrative innovation: Operation Barga recorded sharecroppers through village camps run by officials with peasant organisations; Kerala and Karnataka used land tribunals that took quick, local decisions.
  • Local institutions: elected panchayats (West Bengal, 1978) and peasant unions backed tenants against landlords.
  • Social awakening and literacy: in Kerala, social reform movements such as that of Sree Narayana Guru and high literacy made tenants aware of their rights.
  • Simple, self-executing laws: Kerala vested ownership in tenants by law and J&K paid no compensation, leaving fewer loopholes; the First Amendment (1951) and the Ninth Schedule shielded such laws from court challenges.

3. Why reforms failed elsewhere

  • Landed elites: landlords dominated legislatures and local administration in States such as Bihar.
  • Loopholes: benami and fictitious transfers, generous exemptions and ceilings fixed per individual rather than per family.
  • Poor land records and oral tenancies: tenants could not prove their status and were evicted through so-called "voluntary surrenders".
  • Weak organisation of the poor and long court battles that delayed redistribution.

4. Lessons for today

  • Updated records: digitised land records under DILRMP and SVAMITVA property cards make rights provable.
  • Legal leasing: NITI Aayog's Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act (2016) would secure tenants while keeping land markets active.

Land reform succeeded where political will met organised peasants and simple, local administration. Clean records, legal leasing and land for the landless can complete this unfinished agenda of social justice.
free.upm-2024-gs3-4:
Shree AnnaNutri-cerealsHidden hungerClimate-resilient crops

Millets are small-seeded, hardy grasses: major millets such as jowar (sorghum), bajra (pearl millet) and ragi (finger millet), and minor millets such as kodo, kutki, foxtail, proso and barnyard. India, the world's largest producer, notified them as Nutri-Cereals (2018), led the UN's International Year of Millets (2023) and branded them Shree Anna in the Union Budget 2023-24. They can fight both hidden hunger and lifestyle diseases.

1. Nutritional value

2. Role in health security

  • Anaemia and micronutrient deficiency: NFHS-5 (2019-21) found 57% of women aged 15–49 and 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months anaemic; iron- and zinc-rich millets add these nutrients at low cost.
  • Child undernutrition: with 35.5% of children under five stunted (NFHS-5), millets in mid-day meals (PM POSHAN) and anganwadi food add protein, calcium and energy.
  • Lifestyle diseases: about 10.1 crore Indians have diabetes (ICMR-INDIAB, 2023); the fibre and low glycaemic index of millets slow the release of sugar and help control weight.
  • Dietary diversity: they correct the rice-wheat monotony that the Green Revolution and the PDS created.

3. Role in nutritional security

  • Availability under climate stress: millets grow on poor, dry soils with little water and few inputs, so they keep producing food in drought years.
  • Access and affordability: they are grown by small rain-fed farmers; the NFSA allows coarse grains to be supplied through the PDS, and States such as Karnataka and Odisha (Odisha Millets Mission, 2017) supply them through ration shops and schools.
  • Sustainability: less fertiliser, pesticide and groundwater; crop residues make good fodder.
  • Livelihoods: value addition (flour, ready-to-eat foods), a PLI scheme for millet-based products and ICAR-IIMR Hyderabad as a Global Centre of Excellence raise the incomes of tribal and dryland farmers.

4. Challenges

  • Cereal bias: procurement and the PDS have long favoured rice and wheat, so the area under millets has shrunk since the 1960s.
  • Processing and shelf life: minor millets are hard to dehull, pearl millet flour turns rancid quickly, and anti-nutrients such as phytates need soaking or malting.
  • Low yields and perception: weak seed and extension support, and the image of a "poor man's food".

Millets join nutrition, climate resilience and farmers' incomes. Steady procurement, processing hubs, local supply through the PDS and behaviour-change campaigns can make Shree Anna a pillar of India's nutritional security.
free.upm-2024-gs3-5:
Patenting life formsTRIPS Article 27.3(b)Section 3(j)Lab-to-market gap

"Life materials" are living organisms and their parts, such as micro-organisms, genes, cells and plant varieties. Since Diamond v Chakrabarty (1980), when the US Supreme Court upheld a patent on an oil-eating bacterium engineered by Ananda Chakrabarty, intellectual property over life has expanded, but within limits set by the WTO's TRIPS Agreement (1995), ethics and biodiversity law. India files more patents than ever, yet few reach the market.

1. Present world scenario of IPR on life materials

  • TRIPS minimum standard (Article 27.3(b)): members may exclude plants, animals and essentially biological processes from patents, but must patent micro-organisms and microbiological processes and protect plant varieties by patents or a sui generis system.
  • Broad protection in the USA: genetically modified organisms, the Harvard "oncomouse" and engineered cells are patentable; but in Myriad Genetics (2013) the Supreme Court held that naturally occurring DNA cannot be patented, while synthetic cDNA can.
  • Ethical limits in Europe: the EU Biotech Directive (1998) bars patents on plant and animal varieties, human cloning, germ-line modification and commercial use of human embryos.
  • Plant breeders' rights: the UPOV Convention protects new varieties; India chose its own PPV&FR Act, 2001, which also protects farmers' rights.
  • Benefit-sharing: the CBD (1992), the Nagoya Protocol (2010) and the WIPO Treaty on Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (2024), which requires patent applicants to disclose the origin of genetic resources, aim to stop biopiracy.

2. India's patent surge

  • Rapid growth: 1,10,375 applications were filed in 2024-25, 62% of them by Indian residents, and Indians received 32% of patents granted, against 15% in 2013-14. India is now among the world's leading filers: WIPO ranks its patent office sixth by filings (2025).

3. Reasons for low commercialisation

  • Patents as a metric: institutions are ranked and faculty rewarded for filing patents, not for licensing them, so many are filed with no market in view.
  • Weak technology transfer: few professional technology-transfer offices, little licensing expertise and thin industry–academia links.
  • Low R&D spending: gross R&D spending is only 0.84% of GDP (2023-24), against over 2% in most developed countries.
  • Valley of death: scarce risk capital, pilot plants and manufacturing support to turn prototypes into products.
  • Defensive patents: many patents, including those of foreign firms, protect markets rather than products made in India; Form 27 working statements show many unworked patents.
  • Delays and costs: examination delays, renewal fees and litigation risk lead many patents to lapse.

4. Way forward

  • Funding for translation: the National IPR Policy (2016) makes commercialisation an objective; the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (2023) and the ₹1 lakh crore RDI scheme (2025) fund industry-linked research.
  • Right incentives: reward licences and royalties rather than filings, and build regional technology-transfer hubs.

The world is moving towards regulated ownership of life, balanced by benefit-sharing. India must convert its patent surge into products through industry links, risk capital and a culture that values licensing over counting.
free.upm-2024-gs3-6:
FASTag (RFID)National Electronic Toll CollectionMulti-Lane Free FlowGNSS-based tolling

India collects user fees on national highways under the National Highways Fee Rules, 2008. Electronic toll collection uses FASTag, a passive Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) sticker on the windscreen, linked to a bank account or wallet, under NPCI's National Electronic Toll Collection (NETC) programme. FASTag became mandatory in February 2021; over 98% of highway user fees are now collected through it, and there were 6.23 crore active FASTag users in mid-2026.

1. The technology

  • RFID reading: a reader at the toll lane reads the tag's unique ID; the NETC system checks it with the issuing bank, debits the toll and the barrier lifts.
  • Interoperability: any bank's FASTag works at any plaza; users top up through UPI or net banking and get an SMS for each deduction.
  • Add-ons: an annual pass for private cars (August 2025, over 77 lakh issued by June 2026); vehicles without a valid tag pay a higher fee.

2. Advantages and limitations

  • Advantages: shorter queues, less idling, fuel and emissions; transparent digital records that curb revenue leakage and cash handling; traffic data for planning.
  • Still stop-and-go: barriers remain, and misreads, damaged or blacklisted tags and low balances cause queues.
  • Misuse and errors: loose tags moved between vehicles, wrong vehicle class, wrongful or double deductions and slow refunds.
  • Plaza-based charging: users pay a fixed fee at each plaza, whatever the distance actually travelled.

3. Proposed changes for seamless tolling

  • Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF): overhead gantries with Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras and FASTag readers charge vehicles at highway speed without barriers. The first phase covers 17 plazas; six were live by August 2026 (Choryasi in Gujarat, Mundka in Delhi, Gharaunda in Haryana, and Manoharpura, Daulatpura and Shahjahanpur in Rajasthan), and bids were invited for 104 more.
  • GNSS-based tolling: amended NH Fee Rules (2024) allow distance-based tolls through on-board units using satellite positioning, with 20 km each way a day free; pilots ran on the Bengaluru–Mysuru and Panipat–Hisar highways. In July 2026 the Government said no final decision had been taken, as expert committees raised security and privacy concerns.

4. Potential hazards of the transition

  • Privacy and surveillance: continuous location data and number-plate cameras create detailed records of movement, which need safeguards under the DPDP Act, 2023.
  • Cyber risks: hacking of toll systems, cloned tags, and GPS jamming or spoofing.
  • Enforcement gaps: without barriers, collection depends on readable High Security Registration Plates and on recovering dues from defaulters; wrong charges may multiply disputes.
  • Exclusion and cost: fitting on-board units, and users without bank accounts or smartphones.

The shift from barriers to free flow can save time and fuel, but it should be phased in with strong data protection, cyber security and quick grievance redress to keep public trust.
free.upm-2024-gs3-7:
Industrial effluentsZero Liquid DischargePolluter paysNamami Gange

Rivers receive industrial effluents from tanneries, textile dyeing, distilleries, pulp and paper, sugar, pharmaceutical and chemical units. Sewage is larger in volume, but industrial waste is more toxic, carrying heavy metals such as chromium, dyes and persistent chemicals. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) counts 296 polluted river stretches (down from 311); hotspots include Kanpur's tanneries on the Ganga, Ludhiana's dyeing units on the Buddha Nallah and Tiruppur's units on the Noyyal.

1. Why the problem persists

  • Clusters of small units: MSMEs cannot afford their own treatment plants, and common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) often run below capacity or standard.
  • Weak enforcement: State Pollution Control Boards are short of staff and laboratories, penalties are low, and untreated effluent is discharged at night or injected into the ground.
  • Cheap water: low prices for fresh water give industry little reason to recycle.

2. Mitigation measures

  • Cleaner production at source: process changes such as chrome recovery in tanneries, enzymes instead of harsh chemicals, and in-plant water recycling cut the pollution load.
  • Treatment: effluent treatment plants in large units and CETPs for clusters, with primary, secondary and tertiary treatment and safe sludge disposal.
  • Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD): reverse osmosis and evaporators recycle all water; Tiruppur's dyeing units moved to ZLD after court-ordered closures in 2011.
  • Real-time monitoring: Online Continuous Effluent Monitoring Systems (OCEMS), required by the CPCB since 2014 for 17 categories of highly polluting industries, send data directly to regulators.
  • Economic tools: the polluter-pays principle, environmental compensation, pollution charges and tradable effluent permits.
  • Nature-based solutions: constructed wetlands, bioremediation and riverside buffers polish treated water.

3. Government initiatives

  • Laws: the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 requires consent to establish and operate; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 sets effluent standards; the Water (Amendment) Act, 2024 replaced jail for many violations with penalties of ₹10,000 to ₹15 lakh.
  • Namami Gange (2014): ₹20,000 crore to 2021, extended to March 2026 with ₹22,500 crore; it inspects grossly polluting industries in the Ganga basin and funds CETPs, such as one for Kanpur's Jajmau tannery cluster.
  • Regulatory tools: CPCB's Red, Orange, Green and White categories of industries (2016), OCEMS and the National Water Quality Monitoring Programme.
  • Courts and NGT: M.C. Mehta (1987) closed Kanpur tanneries that lacked treatment plants; Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996) applied polluter-pays and precaution to tanneries polluting the Palar; the NGT levies environmental compensation.

4. Way forward

  • Stronger, well-staffed pollution control boards; cluster CETPs with ZLD; public disclosure of OCEMS data; realistic pricing of industrial water; and basin-level planning that treats each river as one system.

Clean rivers need prevention at source more than cure at the outfall. Strict enforcement of the polluter-pays principle, backed by technology and transparency, can make industrial growth compatible with living rivers.
free.upm-2024-gs3-8:
Environmental Impact AssessmentPublic hearingEnvironmental activismJudicial review

Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) predicts a project's environmental and social effects before it is approved. Made mandatory in 1994 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and now governed by the EIA Notification, 2006, it has four stages: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal. The public hearing, appeals to the National Green Tribunal (2010) and public interest litigation give NGOs and activists their main entry points.

1. Role of NGOs and activists

  • Watchdogs on EIA quality: they expose copied or one-season baseline data, hidden forests and wildlife, and under-counted displacement.
  • Voice of affected people: they translate technical reports, mobilise villagers for public hearings and record objections.
  • Litigation: petitions before the NGT, High Courts and the Supreme Court can suspend clearances or force fresh studies.
  • Expert alternatives and advocacy: independent studies by groups such as the Centre for Science and Environment, and campaigns against dilution, such as the opposition to the 2020 draft EIA Notification.
  • Monitoring after clearance: they check compliance with clearance conditions and report violations.

2. Four examples

  • Silent Valley: the dam on the Kunthipuzha would have drowned one of the last tracts of undisturbed tropical evergreen forest in the Western Ghats; one of India's first great environmental campaigns, backed by scientists, showed that ecological value could outweigh a power project.
  • Narmada: the dam was built, but the movement made resettlement and environmental safeguards conditions of approval, and the controversy led to the World Bank's Inspection Panel (1993).
  • Niyamgiri: bauxite from the hills sacred to the Dongria Kondh was meant for Vedanta's alumina refinery at Lanjigarh; activism, the N.C. Saxena Committee's findings on violations of the Forest Rights Act and the Supreme Court made gram sabha consent decisive.
  • Vanashakti: one NGO's petition reshaped EIA law for all projects by ruling out routine post-facto approval.

3. Assessment

  • Positive: better scrutiny of projects, protection of tribal rights and biodiversity, and a stronger rule of law in environmental governance.
  • Concerns: delays and cost overruns; an Intelligence Bureau report (2014) alleged that some foreign-funded NGOs were stalling development; tighter FCRA rules (2020) now limit foreign funding.
  • Limits of influence: most projects still receive clearance, as Kudankulam did despite prolonged protests, and hearings are often a formality.

NGOs and activists act as the conscience of EIA, filling gaps left by weak regulators. Making EIA independent and participatory from the start would turn confrontation into constructive engagement.
free.upm-2024-gs3-9:
Narco-terrorismGolden Crescent and Golden TriangleNDPS Act, 1985Drug–terror nexus

Narco-terrorism is the nexus in which drug trafficking finances terrorism and insurgency, terrorist groups use and protect smuggling routes, and drug abuse weakens society from within. India lies between the world's two largest illicit opium regions, the Golden Crescent (Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan) to the west and the Golden Triangle (Myanmar, Laos, Thailand) to the east, which makes it both a transit route and a growing market.

1. How narco-terrorism has spread across the country

  • Punjab and Jammu and Kashmir: heroin from the Golden Crescent is pushed across the border, increasingly by drones that also drop weapons; the NIA has investigated narco-terror modules run by handlers in Pakistan.
  • Sea routes: about 3,000 kg of Afghan heroin was seized at Gujarat's Mundra port in 2021, and a record haul of about six tonnes of methamphetamine was seized at sea off the Andaman Islands (November 2024).
  • North-East: heroin and methamphetamine tablets from Myanmar enter through Manipur and Mizoram; armed groups tax the trade, and illicit poppy is grown in some hill areas.
  • Left Wing Extremism: cannabis grown in the forests of the Andhra–Odisha border has been linked to Maoist funding; Andhra Pradesh destroyed about 7,500 acres of it under Operation Parivarthana (2021-22).
  • New tools: darknet markets, cryptocurrency, courier parcels and hawala make the trade faceless.
  • Social cost: a 2019 national survey (AIIMS for the Social Justice Ministry) estimated about 2.3 crore opioid users; addicted youth become easy recruits and couriers.

2. Why it is a serious threat

  • Self-financing terror: drugs give terror groups money without visible state sponsorship.
  • Crime–terror convergence: gangsters, smugglers and terrorists share routes, safe houses and weapons.
  • Corruption: traffickers buy influence among officials in border areas.
  • Many fronts: threats come from the western and eastern land borders and from the sea at once.

3. Measures to counter narco-terrorism

  • Intelligence-led enforcement: pool NCB, NIA, BSF, Coast Guard and State police data through the Multi-Agency Centre and NATGRID, and target kingpins rather than couriers.
  • Technology: counter-drone grids along the Punjab–Jammu border, AI-based container scanning, and darknet and crypto forensics.
  • Follow the money: attach drug assets under the NDPS Act and PMLA, and regulate crypto exchanges.
  • Alternative livelihoods: help poppy and cannabis growers shift to other crops.
  • Demand reduction: campaigns in schools and communities, treatment instead of stigma, and speedy trials.
  • Regional cooperation: joint operations and intelligence sharing with Myanmar, Bangladesh and the Gulf countries.

Narco-terrorism joins crime, terror and public health, so it needs a whole-of-government and whole-of-society response: secure borders, a hunt for the money trail and a drug-free youth, the goal of Nasha Mukt Bharat.
free.upm-2024-gs3-10:
Right to privacyData Principal and Data FiduciaryConsent-based processingData Protection Board

In K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017), a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held privacy, including informational privacy, to be a fundamental right under Article 21 and urged a data protection law. After the Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2018) report and a Bill withdrawn in 2022, Parliament passed the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 (assent 11 August 2023), India's first comprehensive law on personal data.

1. Context

  • Data-driven economy: Aadhaar, UPI, e-commerce and social media generate vast personal data, while data breaches and cyber fraud are rising.
  • Weak earlier law: Section 43A of the IT Act and the 2011 rules on sensitive personal data covered only companies and offered little remedy.
  • Global standards: the EU's GDPR (2018) set a benchmark, and Indian firms need trusted rules for cross-border data flows.
  • Constitutional mandate: Puttaswamy requires any intrusion on privacy to meet the tests of legality, necessity and proportionality.

2. Salient features

  • Scope: digital personal data processed in India, and processing abroad linked to offering goods or services to people in India; personal or domestic use and data made public by the person are excluded.
  • Lawful grounds: processing needs consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given after a clear notice (in English or any Eighth Schedule language) and open to withdrawal; or certain legitimate uses such as state subsidies, medical emergencies, disasters and employment.
  • Duties of Data Fiduciaries: keep data accurate, adopt reasonable security safeguards, report breaches to the Board and to affected persons, erase data once the purpose is served, and redress grievances. Significant Data Fiduciaries must also appoint a Data Protection Officer in India and an independent data auditor and carry out periodic impact assessments.
  • Rights of Data Principals: information, correction, erasure, grievance redress and nomination, with a duty not to file false complaints.
  • Children: verifiable parental consent for users under 18, and no tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising aimed at them.
  • Cross-border transfer: allowed except to countries the Centre restricts by notification.
  • Exemptions: the Centre may exempt its agencies for sovereignty, security and public order, and allow exemptions for research and start-ups.
  • Enforcement: a Data Protection Board of India working digitally, appeals to the TDSAT, and penalties up to ₹250 crore per breach. The Act also widened the RTI Act's personal-information exemption (Section 8(1)(j)).

3. Implementation and concerns

  • Phased roll-out: under the Rules, Board provisions applied at once, consent managers come in from November 2026 and most duties of firms from May 2027.
  • Concerns: wide exemptions for the state, a Board appointed by the Centre, dilution of the RTI Act, and no compensation for affected individuals.

The Act turns the right to privacy into enforceable duties. Its success will depend on an independent Board, narrow use of exemptions and a culture of privacy by design.
free.upm-2024-gs3-11:
Labour CodesLabour market flexibilitySocial security for gig workersFlexicurity

Labour is in the Concurrent List, and India had 29 central labour laws besides State laws, with overlapping definitions and heavy compliance. On the lines suggested by the Second National Commission on Labour (2002), Parliament merged the 29 laws into four Codes: the Code on Wages, 2019, and the Industrial Relations, Social Security and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Codes, 2020. They came into force on 21 November 2025.

1. Merits

  • Simplification: one registration, one licence and one return, common definitions and web-based inspections reduce compliance costs and "inspector raj".
  • Flexibility for growth: the higher threshold of 300 workers for layoffs and standing orders, and fixed-term employment, may encourage firms to grow and hire formally instead of staying small.
  • Universal wage floor: minimum wages now cover all workers, not only listed employments, with timely payment.
  • Wider social security: gig and platform workers are recognised for the first time, ESIC coverage widens, and fixed-term workers get gratuity after one year.
  • Gender and safety: equal remuneration, night work for women with safeguards, mandatory appointment letters and annual health check-ups.

2. Demerits

  • Weaker job security: easier layoffs, fixed-term contracts and a higher contract-labour threshold may encourage "hire and fire" and casualisation.
  • Curbs on collective action: notice requirements for strikes in all establishments and new rules on union recognition weaken bargaining power.
  • Gaps in coverage: higher factory and contract-labour thresholds leave many small units out; benefits for gig workers depend on schemes yet to be framed, not on enforceable entitlements.
  • Enforcement concerns: "inspector-cum-facilitators" and self-certification may dilute enforcement when most workers are informal.
  • Limited consensus: central trade unions opposed the Codes and have held nationwide strikes against them.

3. Progress so far

  • Codes in force: from 21 November 2025, after years of delay while rules were drafted.
  • Central rules: final central rules were notified on 8 May 2026 for establishments where the Centre is the appropriate government.
  • State rules: since labour is a concurrent subject, each State must frame rules; by October 2026 only a handful, such as Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Gujarat, had final rules under all four Codes, while most large States were still finalising theirs.
  • Social security: the e-Shram portal (2021) has registered over 30 crore unorganised workers; the Central Rules set out how gig and platform workers register and qualify (at least 90 days' work with one aggregator in a year), but actual benefits depend on schemes to be notified under the Code.

The Codes aim at flexicurity: flexibility for enterprises with security for workers. Timely State rules, funded social security for gig workers and genuine tripartite dialogue will decide whether they deliver both jobs and decent work.

Regional air connectivityUDAN-RCSViability Gap FundingModified UDAN

India is the world's third-largest domestic aviation market, yet for long, flying remained confined to a few metros. The National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016 led to the Regional Connectivity Scheme UDAN ("Ude Desh ka Aam Naagrik"), launched on 21 October 2016 to make flying affordable and revive unserved airports; the first UDAN flight (Shimla–Delhi) took off in April 2017. Operational airports rose from 74 in 2014 to 165 in 2026.

1. Need for regional air connectivity

  • Geography: hill States, the North-East, Ladakh and the islands have slow, landslide-prone surface links; air travel is often the only quick link.
  • Economic growth: Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities need connectivity to attract investment, tourism and trade; Krishi UDAN (2020) helps move perishables from remote areas.
  • Social access: quick access to referral hospitals, universities and jobs; helicopters serve medical emergencies.
  • Strategic and disaster needs: border regions and relief operations depend on airstrips and helipads.
  • Balanced development: it eases pressure on metro airports and spreads the benefits of aviation.

2. The UDAN scheme

  • Market-based design: airlines bid for unserved and under-served routes, and the bidder seeking the least Viability Gap Funding (VGF) wins.
  • Affordable fares: about half the seats on UDAN flights carry capped fares (about ₹2,500 for an hour's flight).
  • Shared support: the Centre funds VGF through a levy on flights on major routes, and States pay 20% (10% in the North-East); States also cut VAT on aviation fuel and provide land, power and security.
  • Variants: helicopter and seaplane routes (using water aerodromes) and Krishi UDAN for farm produce.

3. Achievements

  • New destinations: small towns in the North-East, the Himalayan States and central India came onto the air map for the first time.
  • Ecosystem: growth of regional airlines and helicopter services, with jobs in tourism and hospitality.

4. Shortcomings

  • Sustainability: many routes closed once VGF ended; a CAG audit (2023) found that many awarded routes never started and several revived airports lay unused.
  • Weak regional airlines: small carriers with few aircraft collapsed, and aircraft and pilots are scarce.
  • Infrastructure and costs: lack of night-landing facilities, weather disruptions in hilly regions, and high taxes on aviation fuel.

5. The next phase

  • Modified UDAN (launched 4 July 2026) provides ₹28,840 crore for 2026-27 to 2035-36 to develop 100 new airports and 200 helipads, support operations at about 441 aerodromes, and extend VGF to up to five years, tapering from the third year.

UDAN has made flying more democratic and brought many small towns onto the national air map. Its next phase must focus on viable routes, reliable regional airlines and airports that stay in use after subsidies end.
free.upm-2024-gs3-13:
Irrigation efficiencyGroundwater over-exploitationPMKSYCommand area development

Irrigation is the backbone of India's food security, and agriculture uses the bulk of the country's fresh water. Yet only about half of the gross cropped area is irrigated; the rest depends on the monsoon. India is the world's largest user of groundwater, which now irrigates more than half of the irrigated area. Recent years have exposed a crisis of water-use efficiency, ageing canals and climate variability.

1. Major challenges

  • Groundwater over-exploitation: the CGWB's 2025 assessment found about 11% of assessment units (730 of 6,762) over-exploited; Punjab extracts 156% of its annual recharge.
  • Inefficient canal irrigation: unlined canals lose water to seepage, flood irrigation wastes it, and tail-end farmers get little; much of the irrigation potential created is never utilised.
  • Incomplete projects: long delays and cost overruns from land acquisition, funding gaps and inter-State disputes (Cauvery, Krishna, Mahadayi).
  • Ageing and silting: reservoirs lose storage to silt, traditional tanks are encroached, and many dams are decades old.
  • Perverse incentives: free or flat-rate power and very low water charges encourage paddy and sugarcane in water-scarce regions.
  • Climate change: erratic monsoons, more frequent droughts and floods, and changing glacier melt.
  • Water quality: waterlogging and salinity in canal commands, and arsenic, fluoride and nitrate in groundwater.

2. Measures taken by the government

  • PMKSY (2015): an umbrella for "Har Khet Ko Pani" and "Per Drop More Crop", covering faster completion of major projects (AIBP), command area development, repair and restoration of water bodies, micro-irrigation and watershed development; extended for 2021-26 with ₹93,068 crore.
  • Completing projects: 99 priority AIBP projects funded through NABARD's Long Term Irrigation Fund (2016).
  • Micro-irrigation: subsidies for drip and sprinkler systems and NABARD's ₹5,000 crore Micro Irrigation Fund (2018).
  • Modern command areas: the Modernisation of Command Area Development and Water Management sub-scheme (2025) pilots piped, pressurised irrigation managed by water user societies.
  • Groundwater: the Atal Bhujal Yojana (₹6,000 crore, seven States), CGWA extraction guidelines (2020), aquifer mapping, Jal Shakti Abhiyan "Catch the Rain" and Mission Amrit Sarovar.
  • Power and dam safety: solar pumps under PM-KUSUM, separate farm feeders, the Dam Safety Act, 2021 and the DRIP programme for old dams.
  • New sources: river-linking, beginning with the Ken–Betwa project (foundation stone, December 2024).

3. Remaining gaps

  • Low adoption: micro-irrigation still covers a small share of the irrigable area.
  • Institutions: water user associations are weak, and water and power remain under-priced.

India must shift from creating irrigation potential to using every drop efficiently: "more crop per drop", participatory irrigation management, rational power pricing and crop diversification are the way forward.

Buffer stockPrice stabilisationFoodgrain storageOpen Market Sale Scheme

A buffer stock is the reserve of foodgrains, mainly wheat and rice, that the Food Corporation of India (FCI, 1965) and State agencies hold beyond immediate needs. It serves the National Food Security Act, 2013, under which about 81 crore people now receive free foodgrains, helps stabilise prices, and meets emergencies such as droughts. Buffer norms are fixed for each quarter and are highest on 1 July, after wheat procurement.

1. Importance for stabilising agricultural prices

  • Floor for farmers: procurement at the Minimum Support Price prevents distress sales when bumper harvests depress market prices.
  • Ceiling for consumers: releases through the Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) and the PDS cool prices in lean seasons; record OMSS wheat sales in 2023-24 and the launch of Bharat Atta (2023) and Bharat Rice (2024) checked cereal inflation.
  • Smoothing shocks: stocks carried over from good years cover drought years and global price spikes.
  • Pulses and onions: the Price Stabilisation Fund (2014-15) builds buffers of pulses and onions that are released when prices spike.
  • Trade and expectations: comfortable stocks allow calibrated export policy and discourage hoarding.

2. Challenges in storing buffer stocks

  • Stocks above norms: in many years stocks far exceed the buffer norms, raising carrying costs and the food subsidy bill of about ₹2 lakh crore a year.
  • Open storage: part of the grain is kept under "covered and plinth" (CAP) storage, exposed to rain, pests and rodents; in the PUCL case (2010) the Supreme Court remarked that grain rotting in godowns should rather be given to the poor.
  • Regional mismatch: procurement is concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and a few rice States, so godowns there are choked while grain must be moved long distances to deficit States.
  • Old technology: most grain is stored in bags in conventional godowns; mechanised silos are few, and quality falls with long storage and repeated fumigation.
  • Leakages and costs: pilferage, high handling and transport costs, and a high economic cost per quintal.
  • Market distortions: large public stocks crowd out private trade, reinforce the rice-wheat bias and draw scrutiny under WTO rules on public stockholding.
  • Perishables: onion buffers suffer heavy losses because of weak cold storage.

3. Way forward

  • Reform the system: the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) recommended restructuring the FCI, leaving procurement to capable States and moving towards cash transfers where markets work well.
  • Modernise storage: silos, private godowns under the Private Entrepreneurs Guarantee scheme, the cooperative-sector storage plan through PACS, and negotiable warehouse receipts regulated by the WDRA.

Buffer stocks are India's shock absorber for food prices, but they work best when they are lean, modern and well located, with stocks matched to norms and losses cut through scientific storage.
free.upm-2024-gs3-15:
Freshwater scarcityDesalinationWastewater reuseAtmospheric water generation

About 97% of the Earth's water is saline; of the roughly 2.5% that is fresh, most is locked in ice caps and deep aquifers, leaving less than 1% easily usable. Population growth, urbanisation, pollution and climate change have made water stress acute: India has about 18% of the world's people but only 4% of its freshwater, and Chennai's reservoirs ran dry in 2019. Alternative technologies can create "new water", but each has costs.

1. The range of alternatives

  • Supply from new sources: desalination of seawater and brackish water, recycling of wastewater, and harvesting moisture from the air.
  • Low-cost options: rainwater harvesting, solar stills, fog nets and advanced membranes such as graphene-based filters.

2. Desalination

  • How it works: reverse osmosis (RO) forces seawater through semi-permeable membranes at high pressure; thermal plants distil it; NIOT's low-temperature thermal desalination plants in Lakshadweep use the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water.
  • Merits: a practically unlimited source, independent of rainfall, for coastal cities and islands; Chennai's Minjur and Nemmeli plants supply part of its drinking water, and Gulf countries depend heavily on it.
  • Demerits: high energy use (about 3–4 kWh per cubic metre for seawater RO) and cost; each litre of fresh water leaves roughly 1.5 litres of salty brine that harms marine life; viable mainly near coasts.

3. Recycling of wastewater

  • How it works: sewage passes through biological treatment, ultrafiltration, RO and ultraviolet disinfection to reach industrial or even drinking quality.
  • Merits: a reliable source that grows with the city, cheaper than desalination, and it cuts river pollution; Singapore's NEWater can meet up to 40% of its water demand; India's National Framework on Safe Reuse of Treated Water (2022) promotes reuse, and thermal power plants near cities must use treated sewage.
  • Demerits: the public "yuck factor", health risks from emerging contaminants such as drug residues, and the need for sewerage networks and strict monitoring.

4. Atmospheric water generation (AWG)

  • How it works: machines cool humid air below its dew point so that water condenses, or use desiccants and new materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs, recognised by the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), which can capture moisture even from dry air.
  • Merits: decentralised supply without any river or aquifer, useful for islands, border posts, disaster relief and remote villages.
  • Demerits: high energy use per litre, small output, dependence on humidity and temperature, and high cost.

These technologies are supplements, not substitutes, for saving water: pricing, efficient irrigation, rainwater harvesting and protecting water bodies come first. Powering desalination and AWG with renewables, and building public trust in reuse, can make water security sustainable.
free.upm-2024-gs3-16:
Near-Earth asteroidsPotentially hazardous asteroidsPlanetary defenceKinetic impactor

Asteroids are rocky or metallic bodies left over from the formation of the solar system about 4.6 billion years ago. Most orbit the Sun in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter, where Jupiter's gravity prevented them from forming a planet. Those whose orbits come close to Earth's are near-Earth objects (NEOs); asteroids larger than about 140 m that come within about 7.5 million km of Earth's orbit are classed as potentially hazardous.

1. What asteroids are

  • Composition: carbon-rich (C-type, the most common), stony (S-type) and metallic (M-type).
  • Groups: main-belt asteroids, Trojans that share Jupiter's orbit, and near-Earth asteroids.
  • Size: from a few metres to about 940 km (Ceres, now classed as a dwarf planet).

2. How real is the threat of extinction?

  • It has happened before: an asteroid about 10 km wide struck Chicxulub (Mexico) about 66 million years ago, triggering the extinction of about three-quarters of species, including the non-avian dinosaurs.
  • Smaller impacts are far more common: the Tunguska airburst (Siberia, 1908) flattened about 2,000 sq km of forest, and the Chelyabinsk meteor (Russia, 2013) injured about 1,500 people, mostly through shattered glass.
  • Low probability, high impact: extinction-level impacts are separated by tens of millions of years, and none of the known near-Earth asteroids larger than 1 km (most have been found) threatens Earth for at least a century; many 140 m-class "city-killers" remain undiscovered.
  • Recent scares: 2024 YR4 briefly had an impact probability of about 3% for 2032 (February 2025) before further observations ruled it out; Apophis (about 340 m) will pass within about 32,000 km of Earth on 13 April 2029 without hitting it.

3. Strategies to prevent a catastrophe

  • Find and track: sky surveys such as Pan-STARRS and ATLAS, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile (first images, 2025) and NASA's planned space telescope NEO Surveyor; NASA and ESA compute impact probabilities, rated on the Torino scale (0–10).
  • Kinetic impactor: NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately struck the moonlet Dimorphos on 26 September 2022 and shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 32 minutes, the first proof that humans can deflect an asteroid; ESA's Hera (launched October 2024) will survey the result in 2026–27.
  • Other deflection methods: a gravity tractor (a spacecraft's gravity slowly tugs the asteroid off course), laser ablation, and, for large or late-detected objects, a nuclear stand-off explosion, which raises legal questions under the Outer Space Treaty (1967).
  • Global coordination: the International Asteroid Warning Network and the Space Mission Planning Advisory Group, endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 2013, and NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office (2016).
  • Civil defence: if warning time is short, evacuation of the impact zone; India's ISRO tracks space objects through its NETRA programme.

The risk of extinction in our lifetime is tiny, but smaller impacts are a real, low-probability, high-impact risk. Better surveys, tested deflection and international cooperation turn an act of fate into a manageable hazard.
free.upm-2024-gs3-17:
Disaster resilienceVulnerability and capacitySendai Framework 2015–2030Build Back Better

The UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction defines resilience as the ability of a system, community or society exposed to hazards to resist, absorb, accommodate, adapt to, transform and recover from their effects in a timely and efficient manner, preserving its essential structures and functions. It shifts the focus from relief to risk reduction, the spirit of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), adopted at Sendai, Japan, in March 2015.

1. What disaster resilience means

  • Absorb and bounce back: a resilient city keeps hospitals, power and water running during a flood and restores services quickly.
  • Bounce forward: recovery should leave people safer than before ("Build Back Better"), as Odisha did with cyclone shelters and warnings after the 1999 super cyclone.
  • Many dimensions: physical, social, economic, institutional and environmental resilience reinforce one another.

2. How resilience is determined

  • Risk equation: disaster risk depends on hazard, exposure and vulnerability, reduced by capacity; resilience rises as vulnerability falls and capacity grows.
  • Determinants: quality of buildings and infrastructure, incomes and savings, insurance, health and education, social networks, early-warning systems, governance, and healthy ecosystems such as mangroves and wetlands.
  • Measurement: indicators of robustness, redundancy, resourcefulness and rapidity; tools such as UNDRR's Disaster Resilience Scorecard for Cities (based on its "Ten Essentials") and hazard maps such as BMTPC's Vulnerability Atlas of India.

3. Elements of a resilience framework

  • Understanding risk: hazard mapping, vulnerability assessment and disaster databases.
  • Governance: laws and institutions such as the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (NDMA, SDMAs, DDMAs), amended in 2025 to add urban disaster management authorities and national and State disaster databases.
  • Investment in risk reduction: mitigation funds at national and State level, building codes, and resilient infrastructure promoted by the India-led Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019).
  • Preparedness and early warning: IMD and INCOIS forecasts, SACHET alerts, drills and trained volunteers such as Aapda Mitra.
  • Response, recovery and risk transfer: NDRF and SDRFs, insurance (including crop insurance), and reconstruction that builds back better.
  • Inclusion: women, persons with disabilities and the poor at the centre of planning.

4. Global targets of the Sendai Framework

The Framework sets four priorities (understanding risk; strengthening risk governance; investing in risk reduction for resilience; and enhancing preparedness and building back better) and seven global targets to be achieved by 2030:

India's first National Disaster Management Plan (2016) is aligned with Sendai. Building resilience into every development decision, so that each new road, school and house is safer than the last, is the essence of risk-informed development.
free.upm-2024-gs3-18:
Urban floodingEncroachment of drainageExtreme rainfallSponge cities

Urban flooding is the inundation of built-up areas when rainfall exceeds the capacity of drains and natural sinks. Unlike rural floods, it rises within hours, because concrete surfaces send most rain straight into drains, and losses are concentrated where people, assets and services cluster. With climate change bringing more intense short spells of rain, the NDMA treats it as a distinct disaster, with separate Guidelines on Management of Urban Flooding (2010).

1. Causes

  • Extreme rainfall: a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so very heavy spells and cloudbursts are becoming more frequent.
  • Loss of natural sponges: lakes, wetlands, mangroves and floodplains have been built over, such as Bengaluru's lakes and storm-water channels and Chennai's Pallikaranai marsh.
  • Inadequate drainage: old drains designed for low rainfall intensity (Mumbai's for about 25 mm an hour), clogged by silt, plastic and solid waste.
  • Impervious surfaces: concrete and asphalt cut infiltration and speed up runoff.
  • Blocked outfalls: high tides in coastal cities and sudden releases from reservoirs add to or trap floodwaters.
  • Governance gaps: many agencies but no single owner of drainage, weak land-use enforcement and poor local early warning.

2. Two major urban floods

  • Common lessons: both floods were made worse by building on drainage paths and by poor coordination of tides, reservoirs and warnings.
  • A national problem: floods in Hyderabad (2020), Bengaluru (2022) and Delhi (2023, when the Yamuna reached a record level) show that no large city is immune.

3. Policies and frameworks

  • Law and institutions: the Disaster Management Act, 2005; its 2025 amendment provides for Urban Disaster Management Authorities for State capitals and municipal-corporation cities.
  • NDMA Guidelines (2010): a flood-warning network for cities, ward-level hazard mapping, drains designed for higher rainfall, rainwater harvesting and removal of encroachments; the National Disaster Management Plan (2016) also covers urban floods.
  • Urban Flood Risk Mitigation Programme: funded from the National Disaster Mitigation Fund, with ₹3,075.65 crore for seven large cities (Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Pune) and ₹2,444.42 crore for 11 more cities in a second phase.
  • Urban missions: storm-water drains and revival of water bodies under AMRUT and the Smart Cities Mission; CPHEEO's Manual on Storm Water Drainage Systems (2019).
  • Early warning: an integrated flood-warning system for Mumbai (IFLOWS-Mumbai, 2020), IMD nowcasts and SACHET alerts.
  • Ecological protection: the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 and Coastal Regulation Zone norms.

Urban floods are as much a planning failure as a natural hazard. Moving from grey to blue-green infrastructure (sponge cities, restored lakes, permeable surfaces and risk-sensitive land-use plans) is the lasting answer.
