India shares about 3,488 km of border with China, along an undefined Line of Actual Control (LAC), and 3,323 km with Pakistan, where the international border in the plains gives way to the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir. Both run through high mountains, deserts and marshes, and both carry the legacy of wars (1947-48, 1962, 1965, 1971, 1999), unresolved claims and a growing China–Pakistan nexus.

1. Conflicting issues

2. Security challenges

  • Military build-up and grey-zone tactics: China's roads, airfields, dual-use border villages and a mega dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo (construction began in 2025) widen the infrastructure gap and raise water-security concerns.
  • Cross-border terrorism: infiltration across the LoC, tunnels, and drones dropping weapons in Jammu and Punjab.
  • Smuggling: narcotics, arms and fake currency from Pakistan feed a narco-terror nexus.
  • Two-front threat: coordinated pressure from China and Pakistan.
  • Terrain and depopulation: extreme weather, stretches where fencing is impossible, and out-migration from remote Himalayan villages, which weakens the "eyes and ears" on the border.

3. Border Area Development Programme (BADP)

  • Aim: launched in 1986-87 on the western border, and now run by the MHA, to meet the special needs of people in remote villages near the international border, so that a settled population acts as the first line of vigilance.
  • Coverage: villages within 10 km of the first habitation from the international border, in 111 districts of 16 States and 2 UTs, with roads, schools, health centres, drinking water, power and livelihood works chosen through State annual action plans.
  • Progress: over 39,000 works have been sanctioned since 2004-05, and the Government now describes BADP as being in its "sunset phase" (PIB, September 2026).
  • Vibrant Villages: since 2023 the Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP-I, ₹4,800 crore, northern border with China) and VVP-II (2025, ₹6,839 crore to 2028-29, other land borders including Pakistan) have taken over much of this role, with connectivity, livelihoods and tourism to stop out-migration.

4. Border Infrastructure and Management (BIM) Scheme

  • Nature: a central sector umbrella scheme of the MHA's Department of Border Management, with ₹13,020 crore for 2021-22 to 2025-26; its continuation for the 16th Finance Commission period is under way.
  • Components: border fencing, floodlighting, border roads, border outposts, helipads and foot tracks, plus technological solutions (the Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System, or "smart fence") where fencing is not feasible.
  • Pakistan border: fencing and floodlighting of most of the international border in Punjab, Rajasthan and Gujarat, smart-fence pilots in Jammu (2018), and anti-tunnel and anti-drone measures.
  • China border: outposts and roads for the ITBP, complemented by the BRO's strategic roads and tunnels such as Atal (2020) and Sela (2024).

Secure borders need both guards and settled communities. Combining fencing and technology with thriving border villages, in a whole-of-government approach, turns India's frontiers from zones of tension into lines of strength.
free.upm-2024-gs3-20:
Social media and encryptionEnd-to-end encryptionIT Rules, 2021Lawful access with privacy

Social media platforms and end-to-end encrypted (E2EE) messaging services, in which only the sender and receiver can read messages, have transformed communication for hundreds of millions of Indians. The same speed, scale, anonymity and encryption let hostile actors spread propaganda, recruit, coordinate and defraud while hiding from law enforcement, the so-called "going dark" problem. India must protect security without undermining privacy, a fundamental right (Puttaswamy, 2017).

1. The security challenge

  • Radicalisation and recruitment: terror groups such as the Islamic State recruit online and shift to encrypted apps for planning.
  • Disinformation and hybrid warfare: WhatsApp rumours led to lynchings (2018); hostile accounts spread fabricated claims during Operation Sindoor (2025); deepfakes erode trust.
  • Coordination of crime: handlers can guide attackers in real time, as in 26/11 (2008, over internet phone calls), while drug, arms and child-abuse networks hide behind encryption.
  • Cyber fraud: "digital arrest" scams, phishing and fake investment apps run through messaging platforms.
  • Jurisdiction: data sits on foreign servers, so evidence needs slow mutual legal assistance; VPNs and fake accounts defeat tracing.

2. Measures adopted at various levels

  • Traceability dispute: WhatsApp challenged the first-originator rule in the Delhi High Court (2021), arguing that it would break end-to-end encryption for all users.
  • Blocking in emergencies: thousands of accounts spreading hostile propaganda were blocked under Section 69A during Operation Sindoor.
  • Fighting fraud: the I4C's citizen financial fraud reporting system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026, and the Sanchar Saathi portal helps block fraudulent mobile connections used by scamsters.

3. Other remedies

  • Targeted lawful access, not weaker encryption: warrant-based access to devices, analysis of metadata and court-supervised orders, rather than "backdoors" that endanger every user.
  • Independent oversight: judicial or parliamentary review of interception and blocking orders, so that they meet the proportionality test.
  • Capacity building: cyber forensic laboratories, trained police in every district, AI tools to detect deepfakes and bot networks, and a specialised cyber cadre.
  • Platform accountability: risk audits, algorithmic transparency and quick responses to lawful requests, as under the EU's Digital Services Act (2022).
  • Faster cross-border evidence: data-access agreements with the countries that host major platforms.
  • Digital literacy: media literacy in schools and counter-narratives from trusted community voices.

Security and privacy are not opposites. A calibrated, rights-respecting approach that combines targeted access, platform responsibility, institutional capacity and digital literacy can keep India's cyberspace both safe and free.
free.upm-2024-gs4-1a:
Bounded rationalityAlgorithmic accountabilityHuman oversightFairness

Herbert Simon (Administrative Behavior, 1947) showed that administrators decide with limited information, time and attention, a condition he later called bounded rationality. Artificial Intelligence (AI) promises to widen these limits by analysing vast data quickly and consistently, and governments now use it in tax scrutiny, welfare targeting and legal research. Whether it can be a dependable input for rational decision-making is, however, as much an ethical question as a technical one.

1. The ethical case for AI as an input

  • Consistency and objectivity: an algorithm applies the same criteria to every file, reducing whim, fatigue and favouritism; faceless income-tax assessment (2020) cut personal interface and discretion.
  • Evidence-based decisions: analysis of large datasets improves the targeting of welfare and the detection of fraud and leakages, serving the utilitarian goal of the greatest good.
  • Efficiency and access: translation tools such as Bhashini bring services to citizens in their own language; the Supreme Court's SUPACE portal (2021) assists judges with research without deciding cases.
  • Less corruption: fewer human touchpoints mean fewer opportunities for rent-seeking.

2. Why it remains debatable: ethical concerns

  • Bias at scale: AI learns from past records; if they reflect caste, gender or regional bias, the machine reproduces it for millions, offending equality under Article 14.
  • Opacity: "black-box" models cannot always explain their outputs, but administrative law requires reasoned orders and a fair hearing (natural justice).
  • Accountability gap: when an algorithm errs, responsibility is blurred among the officer, the vendor and the programmer.
  • Automation bias: officials tend to defer to the machine even when their own judgement is better.
  • Privacy and compassion: data-hungry systems must meet the Puttaswamy (2017) tests of legality, necessity and proportionality; and equity, mercy and context cannot be fully coded, so a rule applied rigidly to an exceptional case can be cruel.

3. Making AI dependable: an ethical framework

  • Human in the loop: AI should advise and officers decide, recording their own reasons, especially where rights, liberty or livelihood are at stake.
  • Explainability and appeal: citizens should know when AI is used and have a right to human review.
  • Bias audits and data quality: independent testing before deployment and at intervals.
  • Clear accountability: the India AI Governance Guidelines (MeitY, November 2025) rest on principles such as people first, fairness and equity, accountability and being understandable by design.
  • Capacity: training officers in data literacy and AI ethics under Mission Karmayogi.

AI can widen the bounds of rationality, but it cannot carry moral responsibility. Used as a decision-support tool under human judgement, transparency and accountability, it can make administration both more rational and more just; used as a substitute for judgement, it risks automated injustice.
free.upm-2024-gs4-1b:
Dimensions of ethicsMoral responsibilityProfessional ethicsEthical decision-making

Ethics (from the Greek "ethos", character) is the study of right conduct. Morally responsible behaviour does not flow from a single source: it draws on several dimensions, namely the individual's character, the duties and consequences attached to an action, relationships with others, the legal and institutional framework, and responsibility to nature. In professional life these dimensions work together as the basis of ethical decision-making, especially where rules are silent.

1. Key dimensions of ethics that influence human action

  • Personal (character): virtues such as honesty, courage and self-control (Aristotle's virtue ethics; the Indian idea of dharma as right conduct) make behaviour consistent even when no one is watching.
  • Normative (duty and consequences): Kant's duty-based ethics asks whether an act respects persons and could be a universal rule; utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill) weighs outcomes for all affected. The Gita's call to do one's duty without attachment to its fruits joins duty with selflessness.
  • Relational and social: fairness, care and respect for others, including Rawls's priority for the least advantaged. Social and cultural norms shape what people think is right, sometimes wrongly (caste or gender bias), so they must be tested against constitutional morality.
  • Legal and institutional: laws, codes and organisational rules set the minimum standard and make conduct enforceable.
  • Environmental and global: responsibility to other species and to future generations (intergenerational equity).

2. How these dimensions shape professional decision-making

  • Resolving dilemmas: professionals face clashes between duties, such as loyalty to an employer versus public safety. An engineer who finds a structural flaw must put the safety of users first, even at a cost to the firm.
  • Conflicts of interest: the personal dimension (integrity) and the legal one (codes) combine in disclosure and recusal, for instance when a relative bids for a contract.
  • Stakeholder thinking: the consequential and relational dimensions make firms weigh the effect of decisions on employees, customers and communities, as in corporate social responsibility under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Accountability and transparency: recording reasons and opening decisions to scrutiny (the RTI Act in public service) keep discretion honest.
  • Organisational culture: leaders' example decides whether ethics is mere compliance with rules or shared, internalised values.

3. An integrated approach

Professionals rarely apply one theory alone; good decisions test options against all dimensions in turn.

The dimensions are complementary: law sets the floor, principles give direction, character sustains conduct under pressure, and care humanises it. A professional who integrates them shows ethical competence: doing the right thing, for the right reason, in the right way.
free.upm-2024-gs4-2a:
Military-industrial complexResponsibility of great powersJust warPeace-building

The statement holds that peace demands conviction and action, not rhetoric. Yet world military spending reached a record US$2,887 billion in 2025, the eleventh consecutive annual rise (SIPRI, April 2026). In his farewell address of 1961, US President Eisenhower warned against the unwarranted influence of the "military-industrial complex". When profits from arms sales shape foreign policy, powerful nations face a sharp ethical test of their professed commitment to peace.

1. The ethical problem

  • Profit from suffering: treating wars as markets uses human lives as a means to commercial ends, contrary to Kant's principle of respect for persons.
  • Conflict of interest: the largest arms exporters include permanent members of the UN Security Council, the body given primary responsibility for international peace and security (Article 24 of the UN Charter).
  • Prolonged wars: a steady flow of weapons to warring parties lengthens conflicts and multiplies civilian suffering: displacement, famine and the destruction of schools and hospitals.
  • Double standards: preaching peace while selling weapons erodes the credibility of the rules-based order.

2. Ethical considerations for powerful nations

  • Power as trusteeship: greater power means greater responsibility for global welfare, not licence for national gain.
  • Restraint in the arms trade: honour the Arms Trade Treaty (in force 2014), which bars transfers where arms would be used for genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes, and report transfers to the UN Register of Conventional Arms.
  • Humanitarian law: uphold the Geneva Conventions (1949): protect civilians and allow humanitarian aid.
  • Just war principles: force only as a last resort, proportionate, and discriminating between combatants and civilians; self-defence is lawful (Article 51), profiteering from others' wars is not.
  • Disarmament and diplomacy: Article 26 of the UN Charter asks the Security Council to plan the regulation of armaments with the least diversion of the world's resources; mediation, ceasefires and peacekeeping must come before deterrence.
  • Root causes: development aid, climate finance and post-conflict reconstruction build lasting peace.

3. India's perspective

  • Civilisational values: non-violence and Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family) shape India's call for dialogue and diplomacy, expressed in its stand that the present era is not one of war (Samarkand, 2022).
  • Practice: India is one of the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping and supports humanitarian aid in conflict zones.
  • Balance: India itself was the fifth-largest military spender in 2025 (US$92.1 billion, SIPRI), which shows that legitimate defence needs differ from the commercial promotion of wars.

The gap between talking about peace and acting for it is the gap between interest and ethics. Powerful nations must match their power with responsibility, restraining the arms trade, upholding humanitarian law and investing in diplomacy, so that peace becomes a practice, not a slogan.
free.upm-2024-gs4-2b:
Greed vs needIntergenerational equityClimate justiceSustainable development

Global warming is a moral failure as much as a scientific problem. Unchecked consumption, extraction for profit and the use of the atmosphere as a free dump reflect greed rather than need. The World Meteorological Organization found 2024 to be the first calendar year about 1.55°C above pre-industrial levels, and about a million species face extinction (IPBES, 2019). Restoring equilibrium requires change in values, institutions and technology, guided by intergenerational equity.

1. Ethical roots of the crisis

  • Anthropocentrism: nature is valued only for its use to humans, not for its own sake.
  • Consumerism: success is measured by GDP and possessions; the richest emit far more per head than the poor, who suffer most.
  • Tragedy of the commons: the atmosphere, oceans and forests are used by all but protected by none (Garrett Hardin, 1968).
  • Injustice: historical emitters grew rich, while small island states, farmers and future generations, who have no voice today, bear the cost.

2. Changing values: from greed to need

  • Indian ethos: the Atharvaveda's Bhumi Sukta treats the Earth as a mother and humans as her children; Jain aparigraha (non-possession) and Gandhian simplicity and trusteeship teach limited wants.
  • Mission LiFE (2022): asks citizens to move from mindless consumption to mindful use: saving energy and water, cutting waste and single-use plastic.
  • Deep ecology and education: recognising the intrinsic value of all life; environmental education from school onwards.

3. Institutions and policy

  • Constitution and courts: Article 48A and Article 51A(g); the polluter-pays and precautionary principles (Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996); in M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024) the Supreme Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.
  • Clean energy: the Panchamrit pledges at COP26 (2021), including 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070; non-fossil sources already make up about 55% of installed capacity (CEA, August 2026).
  • Market and disclosure tools: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023), the Green Credit Programme (2023) and SEBI's BRSR disclosures make firms pay for and report their footprint.
  • Nature-based solutions: the Green India Mission and MISHTI mangroves (2023).

4. Global equilibrium through climate justice

  • Common but differentiated responsibilities: under the UNFCCC (1992) and the Paris Agreement (2015), developed nations must lead and provide finance and technology; COP29 (2024) set a goal of US$300 billion a year by 2035.
  • Law and solidarity: the ICJ advisory opinion (July 2025) set out states' obligations on climate change; the loss and damage fund (COP27, 2022) and the International Solar Alliance (2015) support vulnerable nations.

The answer is not to abandon development but to redefine it as sustainable development: meeting today's needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs (Brundtland Report, 1987). When restraint becomes a value and nature a partner, society and environment can return to balance.
free.upm-2024-gs4-3a:
Assimilation without imitationDiscernmentCultural self-confidenceAuthenticity

Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), who presented Vedanta to the world at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago (1893), combined deep pride in India's heritage with openness to the West's science, organisation and work ethic. The quotation advises open-minded learning joined to discerning assimilation: take what is good from everyone, but digest it so that it becomes part of one's own nature, without losing one's identity. Its core value is authenticity.

1. What the quotation conveys

  • Openness and humility: no person or culture has a monopoly on wisdom; a learner must be willing to learn from anyone.
  • Discernment (viveka): absorb only what is good and suitable; reject blind imitation of fashions or foreign models.
  • Assimilation, not imitation: as food is digested into the body, ideas must be adapted to one's own context, values and needs before they nourish.
  • Self-respect: imitation breeds a sense of inferiority; Vivekananda criticised both the blind rejection and the blind copying of the West.

2. Examples from history and public life

  • The Indian Constitution: it took the parliamentary system from Britain, fundamental rights from the USA and Directive Principles from Ireland, but adapted them, for instance into a federation with a strong Centre suited to India's diversity.
  • Gandhi: he drew on Tolstoy, Ruskin and Thoreau, yet satyagraha was rooted in the Indian ideals of truth and ahimsa.
  • Science and technology: ISRO learnt through international cooperation but built frugal, indigenous capability (Chandrayaan-3, 2023); UPI, a home-grown digital public infrastructure, is now offered to other countries.
  • Development models: the large-scale self-help group models of Andhra Pradesh and Kerala (Kudumbashree) shaped the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (2011), and each State adapts them to its own conditions.

3. Relevance in the present context

  • Globalisation and social media: young people are exposed to global trends every day; the challenge is to learn skills and ideas without consumerist imitation or loss of cultural roots.
  • Policy-making: practices from abroad work only when tailored to Indian federalism, diversity and capacity; transplanted models fail without such adaptation.
  • Education: NEP 2020 combines global standards with Indian languages and knowledge systems.
  • For civil servants: learning from other districts, States and countries, and adapting innovations to local needs rather than copying them, is the essence of good administration; an officer may learn from others' styles, but must develop a moral compass of his own.

Vivekananda's advice is a formula for confident openness: be a learner, not a copier. For individuals and for a nation aspiring to be developed, absorbing the best of the world while staying rooted in its own values is the path to authentic progress.
free.upm-2024-gs4-3b:
Faith and strengthConviction and capabilityMoral courageNation-building

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (1875–1950), India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, combined faith, a firm conviction in a cause, in values and in the people, with strength: organisational ability, resolve and the will to act. The quotation holds that conviction without capacity is wishful thinking, while strength without faith lacks direction and can turn into coercion. Great work needs both: values to guide and capability to deliver.

1. What the quotation conveys

  • Faith: belief in an ideal and in oneself; it gives purpose, hope and perseverance in adversity.
  • Strength: physical, moral, organisational and institutional; the ability to turn belief into results.
  • Interdependence: faith alone becomes passivity; strength alone can become arrogance or misuse of power.
  • Moral strength: the courage to stand firm under pressure is itself the essence of integrity.

2. Examples from Patel's life and public life

  • Bardoli Satyagraha (1928): Patel organised peasants against an enhanced land-revenue assessment; faith in non-violence, joined to disciplined organisation, won the struggle and earned him the title "Sardar".
  • Integration of the princely states (1947–49): with V.P. Menon, he brought more than 550 princely states into the Union through persuasion and the Instrument of Accession, and through firmness where needed, as in Junagadh and Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948).
  • The All India Services: his faith in a neutral, competent civil service and his determination in defending it in the Constituent Assembly gave India an enduring administrative framework.
  • Modern examples: after Chandrayaan-2's lander failed, ISRO's faith in its scientists and its technical strength produced Chandrayaan-3's landing (2023); the COVID-19 vaccination drive combined public trust with logistical strength (CoWIN).

3. Relevance in the present context

  • Nation-building: the goal of Viksit Bharat by 2047 requires both aspiration and capacity: skills, infrastructure and strong institutions.
  • Unity: amid divisive forces, faith in constitutional values must be matched by strong institutions; National Unity Day (31 October, since 2014) honours Patel's legacy.
  • For civil servants: faith means commitment to constitutional values and public service; strength means competence, decisiveness in crises and the courage to resist pressure. Odisha's cyclone preparedness, built after the 1999 super cyclone, shows how resolve and capacity together save lives.
  • For individuals: students and professionals succeed when self-belief is matched by sustained effort and skill.

Patel's life shows that conviction must be matched by capability. For a nation and its public servants, faith provides direction and strength provides delivery; together they make great work, and national unity, possible.
free.upm-2024-gs4-3c:
Legality vs moralityIntentionGood willConscience

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) distinguished legality, the outward conformity of actions with law, from morality, the inner motive behind them. Law regulates external acts that violate the rights of others; ethics judges the intention itself. For Kant, the only thing good without qualification is a good will, so a person who merely plans to harm another is already morally at fault, even if he never acts.

1. What the quotation conveys

  • Law needs an act: criminal liability generally requires a guilty act (actus reus) with a guilty mind (mens rea); mere thoughts are not punished. Even offences such as criminal conspiracy and attempt require some outward step.
  • Ethics looks within: moral guilt begins in thought and motive; Indian traditions too stress purity of mind, and the Dhammapada opens with the idea that the mind shapes all actions.
  • A higher standard: law is the minimum; ethics is the higher standard. A person can obey every law and still be unethical.
  • Self-regulation: ethics depends on conscience, not fear of punishment.

2. Present context

  • Corruption: an official who avoids bribes only from fear of vigilance has legal, not ethical, integrity; when oversight weakens, he may fall. Lasting probity needs internalised values.
  • Loopholes: aggressive tax avoidance or hateful speech that stops just short of illegality may be lawful, yet it violates the spirit of the law and harms others.
  • Technology: law lags behind AI, data and social media; where rules are silent, ethical intention must guide designers and users.
  • Limits of the state: the state must not punish thoughts, since that would destroy liberty of thought and invite the "thoughtcrime" of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four. Shaping intentions is the task of family, education and self-discipline, not of the police.

3. Relevance for civil servants

  • Conflict of interest: even contemplating private gain from an official decision breaches the spirit of public service; disclosure and recusal must come before temptation becomes action.
  • Impartiality: fair decisions need a mind free from prejudice, since biased intentions show up as unequal treatment.
  • Integrity beyond compliance: the Nolan principles of selflessness and integrity, and values-based training under Mission Karmayogi, aim at the motive, not just the act.
  • Self-audit: daily reflection on one's motives is the first line of vigilance.

Law guards the boundary; ethics guards the mind. A society governed only by law needs ever more policing, while one guided by conscience needs less. For public servants, purity of intention is the first safeguard of integrity.
free.upm-2024-gs4-4a:
Contextual justiceLiving ConstitutionConstitutional moralityMiscarriage of justice

Justice means giving each person their due. Yet what a society regards as just evolves with knowledge, values and circumstances: practices once accepted, such as untouchability or criminalising consensual same-sex relations, are now recognised as unjust. Courts treat the Constitution as a living document, read through transformative constitutionalism. Continuous scrutiny of laws and practices is therefore essential to prevent a miscarriage of justice, though some core values must remain constant.

1. Why justice is contextual: examples

  • Changing social understanding: Section 377 was upheld in Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013); five years later Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations as understanding of dignity and identity grew.
  • Gender equality: the adultery law, which treated a wife as her husband's property, was struck down in Joseph Shine (2018); women officers won permanent commission in the Army in Babita Puniya (2020).
  • Technology: Section 66A of the IT Act, framed before the age of social media, was struck down for vagueness in Shreya Singhal (2015).
  • Colonial laws: sedition, used against freedom fighters, was kept in abeyance in S.G. Vombatkere (2022) amid concerns of misuse, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 dropped the offence by that name.
  • Development and rights: land taken for a "public purpose" under the 1894 Act was once seen as just; the 2013 land acquisition law added consent, social impact assessment and fair compensation.

2. Why constant scrutiny is necessary

  • Prevent injustice to individuals: outdated laws punish the innocent; years after Section 66A was struck down, people were still being booked under it, and the Supreme Court had to intervene again.
  • Include the unheard: recognition of transgender persons (NALSA, 2014) and the rights-based RPwD Act, 2016 came when earlier frameworks ignored them.
  • Institutional review: judicial review (Article 13), Law Commission reports, repeal of obsolete laws, and sunset or review clauses in policies keep law in step with society.
  • Administrative practice: rules on documents, eligibility or service delivery must be revisited when technology or social conditions change.

3. A caution: not everything is relative

  • Core values endure: dignity, equality, liberty and non-violence do not change; context changes how they are applied, not their worth. The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) protects this core from passing majorities.
  • Guard against relativism: "changing context" must not become a cover for majoritarian whims or for diluting rights; change should come through reasoned, constitutional processes.
  • Certainty of law: too frequent change erodes the rule of law; the aim is considered evolution, not constant flux.

Justice is a moving target anchored to fixed stars. Laws and practices must be scrutinised continuously by courts, legislatures and public deliberation, while constitutional morality keeps the core of dignity and equality intact, so that yesterday's justice does not become today's injustice.
free.upm-2024-gs4-4b:
Form vs substanceSpirit of lawReasoned discretionCitizen-centric administration

Rules exist to serve purposes. When officials apply them mechanically, insisting on form (procedures, formats, technicalities) while ignoring substance (the purpose behind them), the result can be injustice: the eligible are denied and the honest are harassed. The statement calls for a perceptive civil servant who reads the spirit of law and uses discretion to achieve its true intent, while staying within the bounds of legality.

1. How mindless literalness causes injustice

  • Exclusion from welfare: denying rations to a poor family because a fingerprint fails to authenticate defeats the purpose of food security; in October 2017 the Department of Food and Public Distribution directed that no one be denied rations for lack of Aadhaar or failed biometrics.
  • Red tape: files returned for minor format errors; pensions held up over a spelling mismatch in documents.
  • Rules as a shield: officials hide behind rules to avoid responsibility; Robert Merton called this goal displacement, where obeying the rule becomes an end in itself.
  • Ignoring context: demanding documents from flood or fire victims who have lost everything treats unequal situations as equal.

2. Illustrations of a purposive approach

  • Self-attestation (2014): trusting citizens to attest their own documents replaced a costly formality.
  • Courts: procedure is treated as a handmaid of justice; the Supreme Court has accepted letters and postcards as writ petitions (epistolary jurisdiction), and Article 142 lets it do complete justice.
  • Armstrong Pame (2012): when regular procedures could not deliver, he mobilised public contributions to build about 100 km of road in Manipur's Tamenglong district.
  • Disaster relief: collectors who release relief after on-the-spot verification, regularising documentation later, honour the purpose of relief codes.

3. Limits: substance is not a licence for arbitrariness

  • Rule of law: procedure often protects rights; Maneka Gandhi (1978) requires procedure to be fair, just and reasonable, not merely followed.
  • Non-arbitrariness: in E.P. Royappa (1974) the Supreme Court held that arbitrariness is opposed to equality under Article 14; deviations must be reasoned, recorded and in good faith.
  • Accountability: a perceptive officer seeks approval where needed and reports genuine hardship so that rules are corrected; the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, which decriminalised 183 provisions in 42 Acts, shows such simplification.

Rules are means, not ends. A perceptive civil servant is neither a slave to form nor a law unto himself: he upholds the spirit of law through reasoned discretion, so that procedure serves justice instead of defeating it.
free.upm-2024-gs4-5a:
Code of ethicsCode of conductIntegrity and probityEthics infrastructure

A code of conduct lists enforceable dos and don'ts, as in the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964 and the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968. A code of ethics states the values that should guide judgement where rules are silent. The Second ARC's 4th Report, Ethics in Governance (2007), recommended codes of ethics for ministers, legislators and civil servants; a 2014 amendment added a list of values to the AIS Conduct Rules, but a comprehensive, standalone code is still absent.

1. Why a code of ethics is needed

  • Grey areas: conduct rules cannot foresee every dilemma: political pressure, social media, AI and data use, or conflicts of interest.
  • From compliance to commitment: internalised values work even when no one is watching, whereas rules alone breed box-ticking.
  • Public trust: a published code tells citizens what they can expect of their officials.

2. A suggested model: a three-tier code

  • Tier 1, core values: allegiance to the Constitution, integrity, impartiality and political neutrality, objectivity, accountability, transparency, empathy for weaker sections and dedication to service. These echo the Nolan principles (UK, 1995): selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership.
  • Tier 2, standards for practice: disclosure of conflicts of interest and recusal; gifts and hospitality; use of official information; conduct on social media; fair procurement; respectful workplaces (POSH Act, 2013); and ethical use of AI and personal data.
  • Tier 3, guidance: illustrative dilemmas with suggested approaches, and a confidential ethics helpline for advice before acting.
  • Drafting: short, simple and participatory, involving officials of all levels and citizens; anchored in a law on public service values, as the Second ARC proposed. A draft Public Services Bill listing such values was circulated in the mid-2000s but never enacted.

3. Making it work: institutional support

  • Ethics advisers: an ethics officer in each department, with an independent body to review compliance alongside the CVC and Lokpal.
  • Training and appraisal: ethics modules under Mission Karmayogi; integrity and behaviour assessed in APARs and 360-degree feedback.
  • Transparency: proactive disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act, asset declarations and social audits.
  • Protection: safe channels for whistle-blowers under the PIDPI Resolution (2004) and the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.
  • Review: periodic ethics audits and updates as new risks emerge. Comparable models include the UK Civil Service Code (integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality), Canada's Values and Ethics Code for the Public Sector (2012) and the OECD Recommendation on Public Integrity (2017).

The code of conduct sets the floor; the code of ethics sets the direction. A short, participatory, value-based code, backed by an ethics infrastructure, would move governance from fear of rules to ownership of values, strengthening integrity, probity and transparency.
free.upm-2024-gs4-5b:
Bharatiya Nyaya SanhitaNyaya over dandaReformative justiceVictim-centric justice

On 1 July 2024, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860, alongside the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. The Government presented the change as a shift from danda (punishment) to nyaya (justice): from a colonial code designed to control subjects to a citizen-centric law, with 358 sections against the IPC's 511, rooted in the Indian idea of justice as fairness, equality and impartiality.

1. Justice, equality and impartiality in the BNS

  • Indian ethos: in Kautilya's thought, danda existed to prevent matsya nyaya, the law of the fish in which the strong devour the weak; justice means protecting the vulnerable.
  • Justice for the vulnerable: offences against women and children come first (Chapter V); sexual intercourse by deceitful means, including a false promise of marriage, is a separate offence (Section 69).
  • Equality: mob lynching, murder by five or more persons on grounds such as caste, community, sex, language or belief, is punishable with death or life imprisonment (Section 103(2)); the definition of "gender" includes transgender persons.
  • Impartiality: sedition is dropped by name; Section 152 punishes acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, aiming at acts against the nation rather than criticism of government. Organised crime and terrorist acts are now defined in the general criminal law (Sections 111 and 113).

2. The shift from punishment to justice

  • Community service: for the first time, Section 4(f) adds community service as a punishment, for six minor offences, including first-time theft of property worth under ₹5,000 when it is returned, defamation and public misconduct while drunk. It reforms offenders and eases jail overcrowding.
  • Victim-centric procedure (BNSS): Zero FIR and e-FIR, and victims to be informed of the progress of investigation within 90 days.
  • Relief for undertrials: a first-time undertrial who has served one-third of the maximum sentence is to be released on bail.
  • Speed and science: time limits for investigation and judgment; forensic investigation mandatory for offences punishable with seven years or more; videography of search and seizure.

3. A critical view

  • Continuity: much of the IPC is retained, including the death penalty and the marital rape exception.
  • Concerns of misuse: the broad words of Section 152, and the BNSS provision allowing 15 days of police custody to be taken in parts within the first 40 or 60 days, need restraint and judicial oversight.
  • Gaps in detail: community service is defined only briefly in the BNSS, without guidelines on the kind of work, supervision or duration.
  • Implementation: justice depends on police reform, forensic capacity and filled judicial vacancies, not on new text alone.

The BNS marks a symbolic and substantive turn from danda to nyaya. Its spirit of justice, equality and impartiality will be realised only if police, prosecutors and courts internalise reformative and victim-centric justice and apply strong powers with restraint.
free.upm-2024-gs4-6a:
Gender equalityGlass ceilingWork-life balanceGender-sensitive workplace

The Constitution guarantees equal opportunity in public employment (Articles 14, 15 and 16), and NALSA (2014) extended equality to transgender persons. Women's presence in public service has grown since the first women IAS (1951) and IPS (1972) officers, but it thins at higher levels: of about 2.4 lakh women in police, 90% serve in the constabulary (India Justice Report, 2025). Female public servants face challenges that stem not from ability but from working conditions and attitudes.

1. Gender-specific challenges

  • Stereotypes and the glass ceiling: women are often given "soft" postings such as welfare or education and less often finance, home or field-intensive roles; their authority may be questioned by subordinates and the public.
  • Work-life balance: a disproportionate share of care work at home, long hours, night duties and frequent transfers strain families.
  • Sexual harassment and safety: in offices, on field visits and at night; Internal Committees under the POSH Act, 2013 are often missing or ineffective, and in Aureliano Fernandes (2023) the Supreme Court directed that they be constituted in all departments.
  • Infrastructure gaps: separate toilets, rest rooms, crèches and safe transport are lacking, especially in police stations and remote postings.
  • Pressure and scrutiny: isolation in male-dominated networks, gendered trolling and character attacks when they act firmly; transgender employees also face stigma and a lack of facilities.

2. Measures to increase efficiency

  • Supportive leave and care policies: central government women employees get 180 days' maternity leave and up to 730 days of Child Care Leave in their career; these should be matched by crèches, flexible hours where possible and spouse-posting norms.
  • Equal opportunity in postings: assign women to core ministries and field roles on merit; avoid tokenism.
  • Capacity and leadership: mentoring, leadership programmes and gender-sensitisation of all staff under Mission Karmayogi.
  • Safety and representation: gender audits of offices and police stations; meeting the 33% target urged by the Union Home Ministry's advisories for women in police; gender budgeting (since 2005-06) to fund facilities.

3. Maintaining high standards of probity

  • Institutional backing: honest officers must be protected from punitive transfers and smear campaigns; written orders and supportive seniors reduce pressure.
  • Transparent systems: e-office, online processes and clear delegation reduce discretionary pressure on all officers.
  • No stereotypes: probity depends on values and systems, not gender; but diverse teams improve decisions and make it easier for women citizens to approach police and welfare offices.
  • Role models and peer networks: the example of women officers who resisted pressure sustains integrity among younger officers.

Equality in law must become equality at work. Gender-sensitive policies, safe workplaces and fair postings will let women public servants work to their full potential, and diversity with integrity will make administration more empathetic and effective.
free.upm-2024-gs4-6b:
Mission KarmayogiRule to roleCompetency-based learningCitizen-centric service

Mission Karmayogi, the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (NPCSCB), was approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2020 to make civil servants creative, proactive, professional, transparent and technology-enabled. Its core idea is a shift from "rule-based" to "role-based" management: each official is trained for the competencies that the role demands. The name evokes the ideal of the karmayogi, one who works with dedication and without selfish motive.

1. Architecture of the Mission

  • Institutions: the Prime Minister's Public HR Council at the apex, the Capacity Building Commission (2021), and Karmayogi Bharat, a non-profit company that runs the iGOT Karmayogi digital platform.
  • Competency framework: a Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies (FRACs) covering domain, functional and behavioural competencies; every ministry prepares an annual capacity building plan.
  • Scale (as of 2026): more than 1.7 crore registered users and over 5,600 courses in 23 languages on iGOT (Lok Sabha reply, August 2026).
  • Accountability for learning: from the 2025-26 reporting year, Central Government employees and All India Services officers must complete prescribed iGOT courses each year, and completion is captured in their APARs.

2. Empowering civil servants for productive efficiency

  • Right skills for the right role: a procurement officer learns e-procurement and contract management, a district officer learns data-based monitoring; mismatch between person and post falls.
  • Learning anytime, anywhere: short, mobile-friendly courses replace one-time training at entry, allowing continuous upgrading.
  • Behavioural competencies: modules on ethics, empathy, teamwork and communication address the conduct and behaviour the Mission emphasises, alongside technical skills.
  • Performance culture: competency data can inform postings and appraisals, rewarding learning rather than seniority alone.
  • Breaking silos: a common platform for Central and State officials spreads good practices; the National Learning Week (October 2024) encouraged collective learning.

3. Better delivery at the grassroots

  • Frontline staff: most citizens meet government through junior and field staff; role-based training for them improves courtesy, speed and accuracy in services such as land records, health and welfare schemes.
  • Local languages: courses in Indian languages make learning accessible to State and district employees.
  • Karmayogi Prarambh (2022): an online orientation module for new recruits builds a citizen-first attitude from the first day.
  • Digital service delivery: training in DBT, e-office and grievance portals reduces delays and discretion.
  • Self-development: officials gain confidence and career mobility, linking personal growth with public service.

4. Challenges

  • Box-ticking: course completion does not guarantee behaviour change; outcomes in service delivery must be measured.
  • Incentives: postings and promotions must reward competence; frequent transfers waste training.
  • Access: the digital divide and workload of field staff need offline and blended options.

Mission Karmayogi can turn civil servants from rule-followers into problem-solvers. Its success will depend on linking learning to roles, rewards and real citizen outcomes, so that capacity building also becomes character building for a citizen-first administration.

Sustainable innovationCorporate responsibilityNet zeroIntergenerational equity

The case mirrors a global trend: data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, about 1.5% of world demand, and the IEA (Energy and AI, 2025) expects this to more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030, driven mainly by AI. As CEO and majority shareholder of ABC, whose emissions have risen 48% since 2019, I must reconcile innovation, profitability and sustainability while keeping the promise of net zero by 2030.

1. Stakeholders

  • Shareholders and employees; customers; communities sharing power and water with data centres; regulators and activists; the host country; competitors; and future generations.

2. (a) Immediate response

  • Own the problem: acknowledge the rise publicly and reaffirm the 2030 goal with a time-bound plan; no greenwashing.
  • Independent audit: measure Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions and each data centre's energy and water use; set annual interim targets.
  • Governance: a board sustainability committee; executive pay, including mine, linked to climate targets.
  • Quick wins: shift flexible computing to hours and sites with surplus renewable power, improve cooling, and pause low-value, energy-hungry AI projects.

3. (b) Ethical issues

  • Innovation versus sustainability: short-term market share against planetary limits.
  • Intergenerational equity: today's profits paid for by tomorrow's climate.
  • Honesty: a net-zero pledge without action misleads investors and the public.
  • Conflict of interest: as majority shareholder, my own wealth depends on short-term value, against my duty to society.
  • Climate justice: a Third World firm needs room to grow, yet its emissions harm the vulnerable everywhere, and data centres compete with households for power and water.

4. (c) Arguments on the necessity of the penalty

I would accept the penalty, explain its necessity to the board, shareholders and staff, and ask the authority only that it be fair; it rests on the polluter-pays principle.

  • Logical: emissions are a cost dumped on others; a penalty prices it, makes clean power the cheaper choice, and costs less than future carbon prices, lost customers or stranded assets.
  • Ethical: our emissions have left our own net-zero path; accepting the penalty is accountability towards the communities and future generations who bear the harm.
  • Credibility: willing acceptance proves that the 2030 pledge is real, protects long-term reputation and forestalls harsher regulation.
  • Fairness, to the authority: rules should apply to all firms on transparent metrics, not single out a developing-country challenger; part of the penalty could fund binding green investment, since AI also helps optimise grids.

5. (d) Measures to balance AI innovation and the footprint

  • Clean power: long-term purchase agreements for solar, wind and storage, and round-the-clock carbon-free supply.
  • Green AI: smaller, specialised models, efficient chips and code, energy use reported per model, and priority for high-value uses.
  • Efficient data centres: liquid cooling, waste-heat reuse, water recycling and siting in renewable-rich regions.
  • Transparency and circularity: independently assured disclosures; offsets only for residual emissions; longer server life and responsible e-waste recycling.

Why this course: it treats future generations as ends, not means (Kant), maximises long-run welfare, and reflects Gandhian trusteeship, apt for a majority owner.

A technology leader is measured not only by the power of its models but by the cleanliness of the power that runs them. Sustainable innovation is not a cost to business but the condition of its licence to operate.

RadicalisationRule of lawCounter-narrativeIntelligence-led policing

The case concerns online radicalisation: a global terror group exploiting graduate unemployment, long screen hours and communal networks to recruit youth, especially from one community. As DGP, Raman must act swiftly but within the rule of law, separating criminal incitement from lawful dissent and avoiding the profiling of a whole community, which would only feed the terrorists' narrative.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: the youth and their families; the targeted community; the public; police and intelligence agencies; social media platforms; the State government.
  • Issues: security versus liberty (Articles 19 and 21); equality versus profiling (Articles 14 and 15); privacy in social media monitoring (Puttaswamy, 2017); reform versus punishment of misled youth. Criticism of government policy is lawful; speech becomes punishable when it incites violence or public disorder (Kedar Nath Singh, 1962; Shreya Singhal, 2015).

2. (a) Options available to Raman

  • Handlers and recruiters: register cases under the UAPA, 1967 and the BNS where evidence exists; coordinate with the NIA and the Intelligence Bureau; trace funding.
  • Online content: have unlawful content removed through platforms and, where necessary, blocking orders under Section 69A of the IT Act, following due process.
  • Sympathisers: separate those who only forwarded messages from active members; counsel them with families, teachers and respected community leaders instead of criminalising them.
  • Opportunity: with the State government, link youth to skilling, apprenticeships, job fairs and sports.

3. (b) Strengthening the existing set-up

  • Specialised unit: a counter-radicalisation wing in the State Anti-Terrorism Squad, with psychologists and social workers; special prosecutors for speedy trials.
  • Cyber capacity: trained staff and digital forensic labs in the Cyber Cell, linked to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C, 2020) and CERT-In.
  • Counter-narratives: credible voices such as youth icons, scholars and victims' families, online and in colleges, in local languages; digital literacy to recognise propaganda.
  • Community policing: beat constables, peace committees, college liaison officers and helplines for worried parents, treating the community as partners, not suspects.
  • Safeguards: written SOPs for social media monitoring with tests of necessity and proportionality, limits on data retention and review by senior officers.

4. (c) Action plan for intelligence gathering

  • Human intelligence: revive the beat system and community contacts; trusted residents give the earliest warning.
  • Technical and open-source intelligence: social media analytics with human verification; interception only with legal authorisation under the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the IT Act.
  • Fusion: the State Multi-Agency Centre linked to the IB's Multi-Agency Centre, NATGRID and CCTNS; joint task forces with neighbouring States.
  • Financial intelligence: with FIU-IND, track hawala, crypto-assets and front organisations.
  • Capacity and accountability: training in cyber forensics, languages and analysis; audit trails to prevent misuse against dissenters or a community.

Why this approach: it prevents violence (the greatest good), respects the dignity and equality of every citizen (Kant; Article 14), and preserves the state's moral legitimacy, itself a weapon against terror.

Terrorism is defeated when the state is firm with recruiters, fair to communities and humane with misled youth. Intelligence-led, rights-respecting policing wins both the security battle and the trust of the people.

Rule of law vs protection of lifeMinimum forceMoral courageGender-sensitive policing

Left Wing Extremism has been sharply reduced: on 30 March 2026 the Home Minister told the Lok Sabha that Naxalism had been "wiped out" from the country. Residual pockets like Rohit's district show why consolidation matters. Rohit has captured ten armed Naxalites, two of them top leaders involved in an ambush, but over 500 agitated tribal women are advancing. Cut off from his superior, he must reconcile the rule of law with the protection of life.

1. Stakeholders

  • Rohit and his team; the captured Naxalites, who are accused persons with legal rights; the tribal women and villagers; the security personnel attacked in the ambush and their families; the IG and the State; and the people of the district, whose trust in development work is at stake.

2. (a) Options available to Rohit

3. (b) Ethical dilemmas

  • Rule of law versus right to life: releasing wanted insurgents betrays justice; firing on civilians betrays the duty to protect.
  • Justice for colleagues attacked in the ambush versus compassion for misled villagers.
  • Ends versus means: a lawful goal (custody) pursued by disproportionate means loses its legitimacy.
  • Responsibility without guidance: with no contact with his superior, Rohit must decide alone and answer for it.
  • Short-term order versus long-term trust: bloodshed would undo years of development work and hand the Naxalites a propaganda victory.

4. (c) The most appropriate course: hold firm, de-escalate, secure the detainees

  • No release under pressure: the apprehended face grave charges; yielding would reward coercion and endanger future operations.
  • No firing on unarmed women: force only as a last resort, graduated and minimal.
  • Secure and separate: a small team moves the detainees, especially the two leaders, to a protected position or out by an alternative route; the rest form a cordon without provoking the crowd.
  • Dialogue: through women personnel and trusted local figures such as elders, panchayat members or teachers, explain that the detainees will be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (Article 22(2)), will get a fair trial and that families may meet them lawfully.
  • Communication and record: relay a message to the nearest post for reinforcements, including women police; log every decision with reasons.

Why: it upholds both law and life (proportionality); refuses to sacrifice innocent civilians as a means (Kant); avoids the worst outcomes (consequentialism); and combines courage with prudence.

5. (d) Precautions with women protesters

  • Women police should handle women protesters; a woman may be searched only by a woman and, except in exceptional cases with a magistrate's prior permission, not arrested between sunset and sunrise (BNSS, as earlier the CrPC).
  • Non-lethal methods: barricades and warnings in the local language; no lathi charge or firing on women.
  • Dignity and care: no abusive language; medical aid for the injured; special care for elderly and pregnant women and children.
  • Video-record the operation for accountability and to counter false narratives.
  • Stay alert: armed cadres may use the crowd as a shield, but not every woman should be treated as hostile.
  • Follow-up: dialogue through women's self-help groups and anganwadi workers to address grievances.

Rohit's test is to be firm on law, gentle with people. Holding the insurgents without shedding civilian blood upholds both justice and humanity; the moral ascendancy the police seek is won by restraint, not by firing.
free.upm-2024-gs4-10:
Conflict of interestFiduciary dutyImpartialityPatient welfare

Sneha heads procurement for a new super-speciality centre, and her brother, a reputed supplier in financial difficulty, has bid. The hospital is private and trusts her fully, but the situation is a clear conflict of interest: affection for her brother against her fiduciary duty to the hospital, other bidders and, above all, patients. Trust placed in her raises, not lowers, her responsibility, since equipment chosen today decides patient safety for years.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: Sneha; her brother and his employees; the hospital's management and owners; other bidders; doctors and staff; patients and their families; regulators and the public.
  • Issues: conflict of interest and possible nepotism; fairness to other bidders; transparency; the temptation to misuse trust; compassion for family against impartiality; and quality and cost of care.

2. (a) Sneha's course of action

  • Disclose in writing her relationship with the bidder to management at once.
  • Recuse herself from evaluating the bids and from the final decision; another senior official should chair the committee for this procurement.
  • Objective process: pre-announced specifications; certification and regulatory compliance of devices; separate technical and financial evaluation; biomedical engineers and clinicians on the committee; reasons recorded for every choice.
  • Let the best bid win, even if it is her brother's; a contract won through a clean process is legitimate.
  • Help her brother, if at all, personally, never through her employer's contracts.

3. (b) How she would justify her choice

  • Integrity and impartiality: decisions must rest on merit; the Nolan principles of integrity and objectivity, framed for public life, apply equally to positions of private trust.
  • Fiduciary duty: as the hospital's agent she must serve its interests, not her family's. If every manager favoured relatives (Kant's universalisability test), institutions would collapse.
  • Fairness: every bidder deserves an equal chance (justice as fairness).
  • Consequences: the best equipment at a fair price serves patients and the hospital's long-term reputation.
  • Protection for all: recusal shields her brother from allegations, her own reputation from suspicion, and management's trust from betrayal.

4. (c) How vested interest compromises medical ethics

  • Non-maleficence: substandard or unsuitable equipment can cause misdiagnosis, treatment failure or injury; the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 exist precisely to protect patients.
  • Beneficence: patients are denied the best available technology when choices serve someone's private interest.
  • Justice and affordability: inflated procurement costs are passed on to patients, raising out-of-pocket spending and pricing out the poor.
  • Trust: patients cannot judge equipment; they rely on the institution's integrity, and conflicts of interest betray that reliance. India's medical ethics codes bar doctors from taking gifts or commissions from the health-care industry for the same reason.

Integrity is tested most when no one is watching and everyone trusts us. By disclosure and recusal, Sneha can be fair to her brother, the hospital and the bidders, and keep the patient's welfare at the centre of every decision.
free.upm-2024-gs4-11:
Water justiceCompeting needsImpartialitySustainable groundwater use

In a severe summer, the District Collector must protect drinking water, which the National Water Policy (2012) places first, while balancing farmers' livelihoods, industrial jobs and allegations of corruption. Clean water is part of the right to life under Article 21 (Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar, 1991). The core ethical test is fairness: restrictions must fall on all users and be seen to do so, not only on the weakest.

1. Stakeholders

  • Farmers; industries and their workers; households, especially poor families and the women who fetch water; vigilance teams and district officials; the State government and groundwater regulators; panchayats; and the river and aquifers themselves, on which future generations depend.

2. (a) Options available to the District Magistrate

  • Legal tools: prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS where needed; powers as chair of the District Disaster Management Authority (Disaster Management Act, 2005) if a drought is declared; enforcement of the Central Ground Water Authority's 2020 guidelines and State groundwater law, which require permission for extraction by industry.

3. (b) Actions that serve mutually compatible interests

  • Clear priorities: drinking water first, then life-saving irrigation for standing crops, then industry with mandatory cuts, announced publicly.
  • Verify the farmers' complaint: inspect industrial borewells, meters and permissions; seal illegal borewells; levy environmental compensation; require water recycling and reuse of treated sewage.
  • Shared sacrifice: pro-rata cuts for all bulk users; industries fund tanker supply and recharge structures in nearby villages through CSR, so jobs continue while burdens are shared.
  • Relief for farmers: advisories on less water-intensive crops, micro-irrigation under PMKSY's Per Drop More Crop, crop insurance and drought relief where eligible, and wage work on tank desilting and recharge.
  • Transparency: a joint monitoring committee of farmers, industry and officials; publication of the district's water budget and inspection reports; a grievance cell.
  • Long term: community water budgeting on the lines of the Atal Bhujal Yojana, "Catch the Rain" recharge, and industrial water audits.

4. (c) Administrative and ethical dilemmas

  • Administrative: drinking water versus livelihoods; limits on the Collector's powers over industries regulated by the CGWA and pollution control boards; weak enforcement capacity; and the law-and-order risk of a prolonged protest.
  • Ethical: equity versus efficiency; jobs versus water justice; firmness of law versus compassion for distressed farmers; and present use versus the needs of future generations.
  • Integrity: the allegation of bribery must be inquired into, not dismissed; if officials have colluded with industry, disciplinary and criminal action must follow, since perceived bias destroys the authority needed to enforce cuts.

Why this course: it applies the public trust doctrine (M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath, 1997), under which the state holds natural resources as trustee for all; it protects the least advantaged first (Rawls); and it maximises welfare by saving both water and jobs.

In scarcity, fairness is the first resource. Transparent, shared rationing with drinking water first can save both the district's water and the people's trust in administration.
free.upm-2024-gs4-12:
Research integrityInformed consentData ethicsIntellectual property

In an epidemic, speed saves lives, but a drug approved on manipulated data can cost many more. Dr Srinivasan is being pressed to hide negative outcomes, skip informed consent and use a rival's patented compound. Each shortcut violates research integrity, the law (the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 and the Patents Act, 1970) and the first principle of medicine, do no harm.

1. Stakeholders and ethical issues

  • Stakeholders: trial participants and future patients; the public facing the epidemic; the company and its shareholders; Dr Srinivasan and his team; the rival firm; regulators (CDSCO and ethics committees); doctors and the scientific community.
  • Issues: falsification and selective reporting of data (scientific fraud); violation of autonomy and dignity by skipping consent; infringement of intellectual property; profit and first-mover advantage against patient safety; and loyalty to the employer against professional integrity.

2. (a) What I would do

  • Refuse all three shortcuts firmly and record my objection in writing.
  • Accelerate lawfully: adaptive and seamless trial designs, more trial sites, digital data capture, early meetings with CDSCO, and the accelerated approval route the 2019 Rules provide for serious diseases, unmet needs and emergencies.
  • Respect intellectual property: seek a licence or collaboration with the rival firm, or develop our own compound; in a national emergency, compulsory licensing under the Patents Act is the government's lawful route.
  • Brief management candidly: fraud invites rejection, recalls, lawsuits and criminal liability. Ranbaxy's 2013 guilty plea in the US over adulterated drugs and false statements to regulators, with a US$500 million settlement, shows the cost.
  • Escalate if pressed: to the ethics committee and compliance, and as a last resort to the regulator; reset targets honestly.

3. (b) Options and consequences

  • Duty ethics (Kant): honesty and consent are duties that cannot be traded for speed; participants are never mere means.
  • Consequences: short-term gains are far outweighed by long-term harm; thalidomide's birth defects and the withdrawal of Vioxx (2004) show how hidden risks become tragedies.
  • Virtue: courage and honesty, with the prudence to find lawful ways to go faster; pure ends require pure means, as Gandhi taught.

4. (c) How data ethics and drug ethics protect humanity

  • Trustworthy evidence: registering trials in advance (the Clinical Trials Registry-India, since 2007) and reporting negative results stop harmful drugs from reaching millions.
  • Protection of participants: consent and ethics review under the Nuremberg Code (1947), the Declaration of Helsinki (1964) and the ICMR guidelines (2017) sustain public willingness to join trials, which is vital in pandemics.
  • Safety after launch: the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (2010) tracks adverse effects.
  • Privacy: participants' health data must be kept confidential, as ethics guidelines and the DPDP Act, 2023 (being phased in) require.
  • Equitable access: fair pricing, licensing and sharing, the spirit of the WHO Pandemic Agreement (2025), ensure that breakthroughs reach everyone.

Speed and ethics are not enemies. Science without integrity endangers the very humanity it seeks to save; Dr Srinivasan must choose the honest path and make it as fast as possible, because public trust is the most precious medicine in an epidemic.
free.upm-2025-gs1-1:
Harappan town planningCitadel and lower townBurnt bricksCovered drains

The Harappan Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) built South Asia's first planned cities. Excavations at Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R.D. Banerji, 1922), Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi reveal an architecture that was utilitarian rather than monumental: standard bricks, planned streets, covered drains and large public structures, but no clearly identified palace or temple.

1. Town planning

  • Grid layout: main streets ran north–south and east–west and crossed at right angles, dividing the town into rectangular blocks; narrow lanes led into the residential quarters.
  • Citadel and lower town: a raised, walled citadel on the west held public buildings, while a larger lower town to the east housed the people. Dholavira had a three-fold division into citadel, middle town and lower town.
  • Walls and platforms: settlements were fortified, and buildings stood on raised mud-brick platforms, partly as protection against floods.

2. Materials and houses

  • Standardised bricks: burnt bricks in the uniform ratio 1:2:4 were used over a vast area, showing common standards of measurement; Kalibangan used mud bricks and Dholavira mainly stone.
  • Courtyard houses: one or two storeys built around an open courtyard, with wells, bathrooms and kitchens; doors opened into side lanes rather than main streets, ensuring privacy.
  • Social differences: houses ranged from small two-room dwellings to large mansions, and rows of small single-room units near the Harappa granaries are often read as workers' quarters.
  • Plain style: walls were plain, with little ornament; the true arch was unknown, and corbelling was used to span drains and openings.

3. Public architecture

  • Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro: a tank of about 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m, made watertight with a layer of bitumen, with steps at both ends and rooms around it, probably for ritual bathing.
  • Granaries: large structures at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, possibly for storing grain, though their function is debated.
  • Lothal "dockyard": a brick basin linked to a channel, interpreted as a dock (some see it as a water tank); Kalibangan and Lothal also had fire altars.
  • Dholavira: a chain of rock-cut reservoirs and a large open ground, showing skill in water management in arid Kutch.

4. Sanitation and water supply

  • Covered drainage: house drains joined brick-lined street drains with manholes and soak pits, among the most advanced systems of the Bronze Age world.
  • Water supply: Mohenjo-daro had several hundred wells; Dholavira stored rain and stream water in reservoirs.
  • Civic discipline: regular cleaning of drains points to some form of municipal authority.

The plan was not uniform everywhere, and in the late phase houses encroached on streets. Still, Harappan architecture combined standardisation, sanitation and civic order on a scale unmatched in its age; Dholavira's inscription as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021) shows its lasting value for urban planning.
free.upm-2025-gs1-2:
Sulh-i-kulIbadat KhanaDin-i-IlahiComposite culture

Akbar (r. 1556–1605) moved from orthodox Sunni practice to a policy of sulh-i-kul ("peace with all"), described by his court historian Abul Fazl in the Akbarnama and the Ain-i-Akbari. His syncretism was both a personal search for truth and a strategy for ruling an empire in which Muslims were a minority. It blended Islamic, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, Christian and Sufi ideas in policy, court ritual and culture.

1. Political and administrative aspects

  • Ending discrimination: Akbar abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and the jizya on non-Muslims (1564), treating all subjects alike.
  • Rajput partnership: his marriage to the Kachhwaha princess of Amber (1562) began alliances that brought Rajputs such as Raja Man Singh into the highest ranks of the nobility, while non-Rajput Hindus such as Raja Todar Mal (a Khatri) headed the revenue administration.
  • Mahzar (1579): a declaration signed by leading ulema that allowed Akbar, as a just ruler, to decide between conflicting interpretations of Islamic law, reducing the hold of orthodox clerics.
  • Theory of kingship: Abul Fazl presented the emperor as receiving divine light (farr-i-izadi), a ruler above sectarian divisions and responsible for the welfare of all.

2. Dialogue among faiths

  • Ibadat Khana (1575): the House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri, first for Sunni scholars, was opened from 1578 to Shias, Brahmins, Jains, Zoroastrians and Christians.
  • Wide contacts: Jesuit missions came from Goa (the first in 1580); the Jain monk Hiravijaya Suri and the Parsi priest Dastur Meherji Rana were honoured at court.
  • Translation bureau (Maktab Khana): the Mahabharata was rendered into Persian as the Razmnama, and the Ramayana and other Sanskrit works were translated, to make Indian traditions known to the Persian-reading elite.

3. Din-i-Ilahi and court culture

  • Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi, 1582): a discipleship order of nobles who pledged loyalty to the emperor, not a new religion; it had very few members, Birbal among them.
  • Ilahi era (1584): a solar calendar counted from his accession was adopted for official records.
  • Art and architecture: Fatehpur Sikri mixed Persian arches with Hindu brackets, chhajjas and chhatris; the Hamzanama paintings fused Persian and Indian styles.

4. Limitations

  • Orthodox opposition: Badauni criticised these policies in his Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh, and religious grievances fed the revolts in Bihar and Bengal (1580–81).
  • Elite and personal: the experiment stayed within the court and did not survive Akbar; Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679.
  • Political motive: historians debate how far it was conviction and how far a strategy to strengthen imperial authority.

Akbar's syncretism turned tolerance into a principle of governance. Though personal and short-lived, sulh-i-kul shaped a composite culture that anticipates the modern Indian idea of equal respect for all faiths.
free.upm-2025-gs1-3:
KhajurahoNagara styleSurasundariBreadth of life

The Chandelas of Bundelkhand built the temples of Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) mainly between about 950 and 1050 CE. Of the many temples they raised, only about 20 survive, in Hindu and Jain groups, and they were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. Built of fine sandstone in the Nagara style, their walls carry thousands of sculptures that pulse with energy and portray almost every aspect of human life, sacred and secular.

1. Resilient vigour: energy in form and movement

  • Dynamic postures: figures stand in tribhanga (three bends), twist their torsos and raise their arms, so the stone seems to move.
  • High relief and deep carving: figures project boldly from the wall and play with light and shade; full, rounded bodies with sharp features mark the central Indian style.
  • Power and energy: rearing vyalas or shardulas (leonine mythical beasts) overpowering warriors symbolise vitality and the control of energy.
  • A rising architecture: the shikhara rises in clustered miniature spires (urushringas), like a mountain range, so that the whole temple appears to surge upward; the Kandariya Mahadeva is the finest example.

2. Breadth of life: the whole range of experience

  • Divine world: Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars (the colossal monolithic boar in the Varaha shrine), Devi, the dikpalas, and Jain tirthankaras in the eastern group.
  • Daily life: women writing letters, applying kohl, removing a thorn from the foot, playing with a ball, dancing and making music; teachers with pupils, masons and potters at work.
  • Court and war: processions of soldiers, horses and elephants, hunting scenes and royal assemblies, notably in the friezes of the Lakshmana temple.
  • Love and desire: the mithuna (amorous couple) figures form only a small fraction of the sculpture; they are read as auspicious symbols, tantric imagery or a celebration of kama as one of the four goals of life (purusharthas).

3. Sculpture fused with architecture

  • Organised bands: figures run in horizontal registers on the walls and balconies, so that sculpture and structure form one design.
  • Surasundaris: graceful celestial maidens on the projections and recesses are the soul of the decoration.
  • Material: fine-grained sandstone allowed delicate detail in ornaments, hair and drapery.

4. Significance

  • Harmony of faiths: Shaiva, Vaishnava and Jain shrines stand side by side under the same patrons.
  • A social record: dress, ornaments, instruments, weapons and occupations of the period are preserved in stone.
  • A balanced view of life: dharma, artha, kama and moksha appear together, presenting the temple as a model of the cosmos.

In Khajuraho the Chandela sculptors turned stone into a living world: vigorous in movement and all-embracing in theme, it marks a high point of medieval Indian art.
free.upm-2025-gs1-4:
Sea-level riseSmall island statesClimate displacementContinuity of statehood

Global mean sea level rose by about 0.20 m between 1901 and 2018, and the rate accelerated to about 3.7 mm a year in 2006–2018 (IPCC Sixth Assessment Report). For low-lying Small Island Developing States (SIDS) such as Tuvalu, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands and the Maldives, most of whose land lies within a metre or two of the sea, rising seas threaten not just economies but their very existence as inhabited nations.

1. How climate change endangers islands

  • Rising seas: thermal expansion of warming oceans and melting glaciers and ice sheets raise sea level; by 2100 it may rise a further 0.28–0.55 m under very low emissions and 0.63–1.01 m under very high emissions (IPCC AR6, relative to 1995–2014).
  • Flooding and erosion: high "king tides" and storm surges wash over atolls, eroding beaches, homes and airstrips.
  • Salt in fresh water: seawater intrudes into the thin freshwater lens beneath atolls, spoiling drinking water and pulaka (giant taro) pits.
  • Dying reefs: warming and acidification bleach corals, weakening the reefs that protect and build atolls and that sustain fisheries.
  • Stronger cyclones: Cyclone Pam (2015) devastated Vanuatu and Winston (2016) battered Fiji.

2. Examples

3. Why their "very existence" is at stake

  • Statehood: if territory disappears, can a state survive? The Falepili Union treaty recognises that Tuvalu's statehood will continue despite sea-level rise, and the ICJ advisory opinion (July 2025) observed that the disappearance of one element of a state "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood".
  • Maritime zones: shrinking coastlines could shift baselines and exclusive economic zones, on which tuna revenues of Kiribati and Tuvalu depend; Pacific Islands Forum leaders resolved in 2021 to preserve their maritime zones, and the ICJ opinion held that UNCLOS does not oblige states to update duly established baselines and outer limits as the sea rises.
  • People and culture: relocation threatens language and land-based identity; under the Falepili mobility pathway, up to 280 Tuvaluans a year may settle in Australia. "Climate refugees" are not protected by the 1951 Refugee Convention, though the UN Human Rights Committee (Teitiota v. New Zealand, 2020) said climate harm could bar deportation in future.
  • Economy: tourism (Maldives), fisheries and infrastructure face rising losses and debt.

4. Way forward

  • Mitigation: the 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement, championed by the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS).
  • Adaptation and finance: seawalls, raised land and mangroves, funded through the loss and damage fund (agreed at COP27, 2022).
  • Partnerships: India supports island states through the Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRIS) initiative of the CDRI (COP26, 2021); India's own Lakshadweep and Sundarbans islands face similar risks.
