For island nations, climate change is an existential threat, not a distant one; deep emission cuts, adaptation finance and legal guarantees of statehood are needed so that they survive as nations with dignity.
free.upm-2025-gs1-5:
Primary activitiesMining and fishingPhysiographic divisionsResource geography

Primary activities directly extract resources from nature. Besides farming (cultivation), they include non-farm primary activities: gathering of forest produce, forestry and lumbering, pastoralism (animal rearing on natural pastures), fishing, and mining and quarrying. Because each depends on what the rocks, relief, climate and water of a place offer, their distribution in India closely follows its physiographic divisions: the Himalaya, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the desert, the coasts and the islands.

1. Types of non-farm primary activities

  • Gathering: collection of minor forest produce such as tendu leaves, mahua flowers, sal seeds, lac and honey, mainly by tribal communities.
  • Forestry and lumbering: timber, bamboo, resin and fuelwood from natural and planted forests.
  • Pastoralism: rearing sheep, goats, camels and cattle on natural pastures, often by seasonal migration (transhumance).
  • Fishing: marine and inland capture fisheries and aquaculture; India is the world's second-largest fish producer, most of it from inland waters.
  • Mining and quarrying: extraction of coal, metallic ores, oil and gas, building stone and salt.

2. Relation to physiographic features

  • Geology decides minerals: the old crystalline and Gondwana rocks of the Peninsula hold almost all of India's coal, iron ore, bauxite and mica, so mining belts lie in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka.
  • Relief and climate decide forests and pastures: the Himalayan slopes and alpine meadows (bugyals and margs) support summer grazing, while the dry Thar favours hardy camels, sheep and goats.
  • Coastline and rivers decide fishing: a long coastline, continental shelf and large river systems support marine fishing on both coasts and inland fisheries in the plains and deltas.
  • Sedimentary basins decide oil: Assam, the Cambay basin, Mumbai High and the Krishna–Godavari basin lie in sedimentary rocks.

3. Issues

  • Ecological stress: illegal mining in the Aravallis, sand mining in rivers, overfishing and loss of mangroves.
  • Social costs: displacement of tribal people from mineral-rich plateaus; the National Green Tribunal banned rat-hole coal mining in Meghalaya (2014).
  • Low value addition: ores and fish are often exported raw.

4. Way forward

The District Mineral Foundations (MMDR Amendment, 2015), PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020) and joint forest management can make these activities sustainable and share their benefits with local communities.

In short, India's physiographic diversity explains why mining clusters on the Peninsular plateau, pastoralism in the Himalaya and the Thar, and fishing along the coasts; planning must respect these natural limits.
free.upm-2025-gs1-6:
Solar energyEnergy transitionClean airGreen jobs

India receives about 4–7 kWh of solar energy per square metre per day on roughly 300 sunny days, a potential of about 748 GWp (National Institute of Solar Energy). Installed solar capacity reached about 171 GW by 30 September 2026 (MNRE), the largest part of India's renewable capacity, and non-fossil sources crossed half of installed power capacity in June 2025. Solar power is central to the target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.

1. Ecological benefits

  • Low-carbon power: solar plants emit no carbon dioxide while operating, so every unit replaces coal-based power and supports India's climate pledges and net-zero goal for 2070.
  • Cleaner air: no sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides or particulates, which matters in polluted regions such as the Indo-Gangetic plain; solar pumps under PM-KUSUM (about 25 lakh pumps) replace diesel pumps.
  • Water saving: photovoltaic plants need water only for cleaning panels, unlike thermal plants that use large volumes for cooling; floating solar, as at Omkareshwar on the Narmada, also reduces evaporation from reservoirs.
  • Smart land use: rooftops, canal tops (Gujarat) and floating plants avoid new land, while large parks use arid, unproductive land in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
  • Less pressure on forests: solar lighting and cooking in remote villages reduce kerosene and fuelwood use.

2. Economic benefits

  • Energy security: sunlight is domestic and free, cutting dependence on imported coal, oil and gas and protecting the economy from fuel-price shocks.
  • Cheap power: solar is among the cheapest sources of new electricity, which lowers costs for distribution companies and industry.
  • Manufacturing and jobs: module manufacturing capacity grew from 2.3 GW (2014) to about 172 GW (March 2026), helped by the PLI scheme and domestic-content rules; installation and maintenance create local jobs.
  • Farmers' incomes: under PM-KUSUM farmers run solar pumps and small plants and can sell surplus power; at Pavagada (Karnataka) farmers lease drought-prone land to the park for a steady rent.
  • Household savings: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) offers rooftop solar with up to 300 free units a month; over 50 lakh homes had joined by August 2026.

3. Examples

4. Limits to manage

  • Intermittency: solar works only by day, so storage is needed; the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana (2026) supports 5,000 MW of floating solar with storage.
  • Generation lags capacity: non-fossil sources still produced only about 29% of electricity in 2025-26.
  • Dependence and waste: imported polysilicon and wafers, and a coming wave of panel waste, need domestic manufacturing and recycling.

Solar energy thus combines climate protection with economic gains for farmers, households and industry; with storage, grids and recycling, it can be the backbone of India's energy transition.
free.upm-2025-gs1-7:
TsunamiSubduction zoneRing of FireEarly warning

A tsunami (Japanese for "harbour wave") is a series of very long ocean waves caused by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water, usually by an undersea earthquake. Unlike wind waves, which stir only the surface, a tsunami moves the whole water column. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed about 2.3 lakh people in 14 countries, more than 10,000 of them in India, showing its destructive power.

1. How tsunamis are formed

  • Undersea earthquakes: at subduction zones the overriding plate is locked and bent; when it suddenly slips back, the sea floor jerks upward and lifts the water above it. Large (usually above magnitude 7), shallow-focus quakes with vertical movement are the main cause.
  • Submarine landslides: slumps on continental slopes, as off Papua New Guinea in 1998, displace water.
  • Volcanic eruptions: the collapse of Krakatoa (1883) and the eruption of Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai (2022) produced tsunamis.
  • Rarely, meteorite impacts.
  • Physics: in the deep ocean the waves are hundreds of kilometres long but often less than a metre high, so ships barely notice them; their speed equals the square root of gravity times depth, so they slow near the coast, where their height grows sharply.

2. Where tsunamis occur

  • Pacific Ring of Fire: most tsunamis occur around the Pacific subduction zones: Chile (1960, magnitude 9.5, the largest recorded earthquake), Alaska (1964), Japan (Tohoku, 2011) and Kamchatka (magnitude 8.8, July 2025), which triggered Pacific-wide warnings and evacuations in Japan and Hawaii.
  • Indian Ocean: the Sunda Trench off Sumatra–Andaman (2004) and the Makran subduction zone off Pakistan and Iran, whose 1945 tsunami struck the Arabian Sea coasts.
  • Mediterranean and Atlantic: Lisbon (1755) and Messina (1908).
  • India's exposure: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie near the Sunda Trench; the east coast faces Sumatra, and the west coast the Makran zone.

3. Consequences

  • Natural defences matter: villages behind dense mangroves, as at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu, suffered less damage in 2004.

4. Preparedness

  • Early warning: the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007) watches seismic stations and ocean sensors and also serves other Indian Ocean countries.
  • Community readiness: Venkatraipur and Noliasahi in Odisha were the first Indian villages recognised as "Tsunami Ready" by UNESCO's IOC (2020).
  • Planning: coastal zoning, shelters, evacuation drills and mangrove bio-shields under NDMA guidelines; World Tsunami Awareness Day is observed on 5 November.

Tsunamis cannot be prevented, but deaths can: the Kamchatka warnings of 2025 showed that early warning, education and evacuation turn a hazard into a manageable event. India must keep building coastal resilience.
free.upm-2025-gs1-8:
Smart Cities MissionUrban povertyDistributive justiceInclusive cities

The Smart Cities Mission (SCM), launched on 25 June 2015, chose 100 cities through a challenge to provide core infrastructure and a decent quality of life through "smart solutions": area-based development of a part of each city plus pan-city digital services. It closed on 31 March 2025 with over 90% of about 8,000 projects completed. Whether it reduced urban poverty and advanced distributive justice, a fair sharing of the benefits and burdens of development, is a mixed story.

1. How smart cities address urban poverty

  • Basic services: water supply with SCADA metering, sewerage and solid-waste projects improved services in many neighbourhoods, in convergence with AMRUT, Swachh Bharat and PMAY-Urban.
  • Safety and emergency response: Integrated Command and Control Centres, now in all 100 cities, run CCTV, emergency helplines and traffic control; they also worked as war rooms during COVID-19.
  • Human development: smart classrooms in municipal schools, upgraded health centres and e-governance kiosks reached poorer users in several cities.
  • Mobility and public space: footpaths, cycle tracks, public bicycles and parks benefit those who walk, cycle or cannot afford private space.
  • Livelihoods: vending zones and digital payments, with convergence of PM SVANidhi loans for street vendors.

2. Distributive justice: the yardstick

  • Constitutional mandate: Article 38(2) directs the State to minimise inequalities of income, status and opportunity; Article 39(b) and (c) seek a fair distribution of resources.
  • Local mandate: the 74th Amendment's Twelfth Schedule lists urban poverty alleviation, slum improvement and safeguarding the interests of weaker sections as municipal functions.
  • Rawls' difference principle: inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged.

3. Where the mission fell short

  • "Islands of excellence": area-based development covered only a small part of each city, often already better-off central areas.
  • Evictions and gentrification: redevelopment and beautification sometimes displaced street vendors and slum dwellers, and rising land values pushed the poor to the periphery.
  • Technocratic governance: company-style Special Purpose Vehicles bypassed elected urban local bodies, weakening accountability to poor voters.
  • Missing priorities: affordable housing, public transport and flood control, which matter most to the poor, were largely outside the mission; the digital divide limits use of e-services.

4. Way forward

  • Pro-poor design: in-situ slum upgrading and rental housing, protected vending zones under the Street Vendors Act (2014), and universal basic services.
  • Participation: participatory budgeting (pioneered by Pune) and ward committees.
  • Livelihood security: urban employment schemes such as Kerala's Ayyankali scheme (2010), and use of the ₹1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund (Budget 2025-26) for inclusive projects.

The smart city improved services and urban management but often stopped short of inclusion; a city is truly smart only when its gains reach the slum and the street vendor, in the spirit of distributive justice.
free.upm-2025-gs1-9:
Steel frameProfessionalismConstitutional patriotismNation-building

After independence, India's civil services were reoriented from colonial control to serving a democratic, developmental nation. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, who addressed the first batch of probationers at Metcalfe House on 21 April 1947 (now Civil Services Day), told the Constituent Assembly in October 1949 that without a good all-India service with the independence to speak its mind, India would not remain united. Its ethos joins professionalism with a nationalistic consciousness rooted in the Constitution.

1. Professionalism

  • Merit: open, competitive recruitment by the Union Public Service Commission (Articles 315–320) and rigorous training.
  • Neutrality and integrity: the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968 require political neutrality and integrity, while Article 311 protects officers from arbitrary dismissal so that they can give frank advice.
  • Expertise and rule of law: decisions based on evidence, law and procedure, applied impartially to all citizens.
  • Continuous learning: Mission Karmayogi (2020) shifts training from rules to roles and competencies.

2. Nationalistic consciousness

  • Unity and integrity: the All India Services (Article 312) serve both the Union and the States, and officers often work far from their home States, building a national outlook.
  • Nation-building record: civil servant V.P. Menon worked with Patel to integrate the princely states; officers run elections, the census and food security.
  • Service in hard areas: border districts, Left-wing extremism–affected areas and the North-East need commitment beyond routine.
  • Constitutional patriotism: loyalty is to the Constitution and its goals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, not to a party or a narrow identity.

3. How the two combine in practice

  • Balance: professionalism without national purpose becomes mere technocracy, and national zeal without professionalism becomes partisanship; the ethos needs both.

4. Challenges to the ethos

  • Politicisation: frequent transfers and pressure; the Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) called for fixed tenure and civil services boards.
  • Committed bureaucracy: the 1970s debate showed the risk of commitment to a ruling party instead of to constitutional goals.
  • Red tape and corruption: status-quo attitudes erode trust; the Second ARC (Tenth Report) urged performance management and accountability.
  • Generalist versus specialist: complex sectors need domain expertise, prompting debates on lateral entry.

The ideal Indian civil servant is a professional patriot: competent, neutral and honest, and committed to the unity and constitutional values of the nation. Reforms in tenure, training and accountability will keep this steel frame relevant.
free.upm-2025-gs1-10:
GlobalisationConsumer cultureGlocalisationCultural hybridisation

Globalisation is the intensifying flow of goods, capital, people, technology and ideas across borders; in India it accelerated after the 1991 reforms. Critics, following sociologists such as George Ritzer ("McDonaldization"), argue that it mainly spreads an aggressive consumer culture of brands, credit and conspicuous consumption. The evidence shows that this effect is real but is only one of several outcomes.

1. Yes: globalisation has fuelled consumerism

  • Markets everywhere: malls, e-commerce, quick-commerce apps and "buy now, pay later" credit encourage impulse buying, even in small towns.
  • Advertising and identity: global brands, influencers and social media link status and self-worth to what one owns, a modern form of Veblen's "conspicuous consumption".
  • Lifestyle diseases: fast food and sedentary habits have spread; about 24% of women and 23% of men aged 15–49 are overweight or obese (NFHS-5).
  • Ecological footprint: fast fashion, e-waste and plastic packaging grow with consumption.
  • Manipulation: the Central Consumer Protection Authority had to issue guidelines against "dark patterns" in online selling (2023).

2. No: it has done much more

  • Jobs and incomes: IT services, global capability centres and export industries created millions of jobs; Indians abroad sent home about US$135 billion in 2024-25.
  • Knowledge and technology: the internet, smartphones and open knowledge spread education and innovation; India's digital public infrastructure is now shared with other countries.
  • Rights and social change: global ideas of human rights, gender equality and environmentalism strengthened Indian movements, such as the #MeToo campaign (2018).
  • Cultural hybridisation: global brands adapt to India (vegetarian menus, small sachets), while yoga (International Day of Yoga since 2015), Indian food and cinema travel the world.
  • Counter-trends: organic food, millets, minimalism and "vocal for local" show that global flows also spread ideas of sustainable consumption, as in Mission LiFE (2022).

3. Why outcomes differ

  • Local filters: Indian values of thrift, joint families and festival-based spending moderate consumerism.
  • Inequality: the rich consume global brands, while many poor people experience globalisation as insecure work rather than shopping.
  • Policy: consumer protection (Consumer Protection Act, 2019), regulation of advertising and digital literacy shape how far consumerism goes.

Globalisation is therefore not only an aggressive consumer culture; it is a double-edged process of opportunity and risk. With informed citizens and sensible regulation, India can take its gains while promoting sustainable lifestyles.
free.upm-2025-gs1-11:
Satyashodhak SamajGulamgiriShudra–AtishudraSubaltern emancipation

Jotirao Phule (1827–1890), born in a Mali (gardener) family of Pune, was the pioneer of anti-caste reform in western India. Through writings such as Gulamgiri (1873) and Shetkaryacha Asud (1883), and through the Satyashodhak Samaj (founded on 24 September 1873), he spoke for the subaltern classes: the Shudras and Atishudras, women, peasants and workers, whom both caste society and colonial rule had marginalised. He was honoured with the title "Mahatma" in 1888.

1. Shudras and Atishudras (lower castes and "untouchables")

  • Gulamgiri (Slavery): argued that caste was a system of slavery imposed through Brahminical texts; he retold myths, presenting King Bali as the just ruler of the original inhabitants, and dedicated the book to the people of the United States who fought against slavery.
  • Direct action: he opened schools for "untouchable" children in the early 1850s and threw open his family's water tank to them in 1868.
  • Satyashodhak Samaj: rejected priestly mediation, conducted marriages without Brahmin priests and was open to all castes and religions.

2. Women

  • Education: with his wife Savitribai Phule, he started a school for girls in Pune in 1848, one of the first run by Indians.
  • Widows: his home for the prevention of infanticide (Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha, 1863) sheltered pregnant widows; he adopted a widow's son and supported widow remarriage.
  • Patriarchy: he opposed child marriage and the tonsuring of widows, and defended Tarabai Shinde's Stri Purush Tulana (1882), a sharp critique of male domination.

3. Peasants and workers

  • Shetkaryacha Asud (The Cultivator's Whipcord): exposed how the Kunbi peasant was exploited by moneylenders, priests, Brahmin village officials and colonial revenue and forest policies, and proposed irrigation, agricultural education and modern methods.
  • Labour: his Satyashodhak associate Narayan Meghaji Lokhande organised Bombay's mill workers from the 1880s, among the earliest labour organising in India.
  • Colonial state: he criticised costly government that taxed the poor to educate the elite.

4. Education for all

  • Hunter Commission (1882): Phule demanded free and compulsory primary education, teachers from the lower castes, scholarships and practical schooling, and criticised spending that favoured higher education for upper castes.
  • Literature and theatre: his play Tritiya Ratna (1855) and his ballads spread his message in simple Marathi.

5. Limits of the claim "almost all"

  • Some groups less central: Adivasis, artisans and the Muslim poor received less attention.
  • Regional reach: his movement was strongest in Maharashtra, and later non-Brahmin politics came to be dominated by the landed Maratha–Kunbi castes.
  • Colonial rule: he saw British rule as a relative opening for the lower castes, a view nationalists criticised.

Phule linked caste, gender and class oppression long before these were studied together. B.R. Ambedkar counted him among his three gurus, and his vision of social democracy still guides the struggle for equality.
free.upm-2025-gs1-12:
Nation-buildingIntegration of princely statesPlanned economyNon-alignment

At independence India faced the trauma of Partition, millions of refugees, over 560 princely states, mass poverty and illiteracy, and the Cold War. In the first phase of independence, roughly 1947 to the mid-1960s, leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel and B.R. Ambedkar consolidated the new nation in its polity, economy, education and foreign relations, a process historians such as Bipan Chandra call nation-building.

1. Polity: unity and democracy

  • Integration of princely states: Patel and V.P. Menon used the Instrument of Accession and standstill agreements; Junagadh joined after a plebiscite (1948), Hyderabad after police action (September 1948), and Jammu and Kashmir acceded in October 1947.
  • Constitution (26 January 1950): universal adult franchise, fundamental rights, a strong federal Union and independent institutions such as the Election Commission, the UPSC and the judiciary.
  • First general elections (1951–52): about 17.3 crore voters, most of them unlettered, voted freely, establishing democracy's legitimacy.
  • Linguistic reorganisation: Andhra State (1953), the States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55) and the Act of 1956 accommodated diversity; French Pondicherry (1954) and Portuguese Goa (1961) were integrated.

2. Economy: planning for self-reliance

  • Planning Commission (1950): the First Plan (1951–56) stressed agriculture and irrigation; the Second (1956–61), based on the Mahalanobis model, built heavy industry.
  • Mixed economy: Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956 gave the public sector the commanding heights; steel plants came up at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur.
  • Agrarian change: abolition of zamindari, tenancy reforms and the Community Development Programme (2 October 1952).
  • Infrastructure: multipurpose projects such as Bhakra–Nangal, Hirakud and the Damodar Valley Corporation.

3. Education and science

  • Commissions: the University Education Commission (1948–49, S. Radhakrishnan) led to the University Grants Commission (1953, statutory in 1956); the Secondary Education Commission (1952–53, A.L. Mudaliar) reformed schools.
  • Constitutional goal: Article 45 aimed at free and compulsory education for children up to 14.
  • Science and technology: the Atomic Energy Commission (1948), CSIR laboratories, IIT Kharagpur (1951) and AIIMS (1956) laid a base for self-reliance.
  • Kothari Commission (1964–66): led to the National Policy on Education (1968).

4. International relations

  • Non-alignment: independence of judgement in the Cold War, through the Asian Relations Conference (1947), Bandung (1955) and the first NAM summit at Belgrade (1961).
  • Panchsheel (1954): five principles of peaceful coexistence agreed with China.
  • Commonwealth (1949): India stayed a member as a republic, keeping useful ties.
  • Peace-building: India chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission in Korea (1953) and joined UN peacekeeping in Gaza and the Congo.

The early decades thus gave India a democratic, united and self-reliant foundation. Setbacks such as the 1962 war and food shortages showed the limits, but the institutions built then still sustain the Republic.
free.upm-2025-gs1-13:
Liberty, equality, fraternityPopular sovereigntyRights of ManNationalism

The French Revolution (1789–1799) overthrew absolute monarchy and the privileged order of the Ancien Régime. Its Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August 1789) proclaimed that men are born free and equal in rights and that sovereignty rests with the nation. Its slogan "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity", and its warnings about revolutionary excess, still shape politics more than two centuries later.

1. Democracy and rights

  • Popular sovereignty: the ideas of Rousseau (the "general will"), Montesquieu (separation of powers) and Voltaire replaced divine-right monarchy with government by consent.
  • Rights-based constitutions: the 1789 Declaration inspired later bills of rights, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and fundamental rights in modern constitutions, including India's Part III.
  • Rule of law and citizenship: the idea that all citizens are equal before one law underlies today's democracies.

2. Equality and fraternity

  • End of privilege: the National Assembly abolished feudal privileges on 4 August 1789; the Napoleonic Code (1804) gave France one uniform civil law, later carried across much of Europe.
  • Indian echo: the Preamble promises liberty, equality and fraternity; Ambedkar, however, said he drew these ideals from the teachings of the Buddha rather than from the Revolution, which shows their universal appeal.
  • Unfinished equality: Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791), yet French women won the vote only in 1944; slavery was abolished in 1794, restored by Napoleon in 1802 and ended only in 1848. Rights expand through continued struggle, as today's movements for gender and racial justice show.

3. Nationalism and the modern state

  • The nation of citizens: the tricolour, the Marseillaise, the metric system and a centralised administration made France a nation-state; mass conscription (1793) created the citizen army.
  • Spread of ideas: Napoleon's conquests carried these ideas across Europe and stirred Italian and German nationalism; in India, Tipu Sultan and Raja Rammohan Roy responded to ideas from revolutionary France.
  • Secular state: church lands were nationalised and the clergy placed under the state, a step towards French laïcité.
  • Political vocabulary: "left" and "right" come from the seating of the 1789 Assembly.

4. Warnings that remain relevant

  • Terror: the Reign of Terror (1793–94) under Robespierre showed how revolutionary virtue can justify mass executions; "the revolution devours its children".
  • From revolution to dictatorship: Napoleon's rise shows that without institutions, popular movements can end in authoritarian rule, a lesson seen again after the Arab Spring (2011).
  • Populism and emergency powers: appeals to the "will of the people" against minorities and the suspension of rights remain dangers for democracies.

The French Revolution remains relevant because its promises of liberty, equality and fraternity are still being fulfilled, and its excesses still warn us. Its lasting lesson is that rights need strong institutions to survive.
free.upm-2025-gs1-14:
Continental shelfSedimentary basinsPetroleum systemDeepwater oil

Petroleum forms from tiny marine organisms (plankton) buried in fine sediments and slowly "cooked" by heat and pressure, mostly at about 60–120°C (the oil window). Oil accumulates only where four elements coincide in a petroleum system: a source rock, a porous reservoir rock, an impermeable cap rock and a trap. Off-shore reserves lie beneath the sea floor of continental shelves, slopes and, increasingly, deep waters, and their distribution follows the geography of thick marine sediments.

1. Geographical explanation of off-shore distribution

  • Passive continental margins: where continents rifted apart, thick wedges of sediment piled up on the new margins: the Gulf of Mexico, Brazil's Campos and Santos basins (with "pre-salt" fields below thick salt), West Africa (Angola, Nigeria) and Guyana, where major finds were made from 2015.
  • Deltas of great rivers: rivers supply huge volumes of organic-rich sediment: the Niger, the Mississippi and India's Krishna–Godavari (KG-D6).
  • Shallow seas and rift basins: the North Sea (UK and Norway) lies over ancient rift basins; the Persian Gulf, a shallow sea over one of the world's richest basins, holds Safaniya (Saudi Arabia), the largest off-shore oil field; the Caspian has Kashagan (Kazakhstan).
  • India: Mumbai High (discovered 1974), the KG and Cauvery basins and prospects in the Andaman Sea.
  • Where oil is absent: the deep ocean floor of basalt with thin sediments, and the ancient crystalline shields.

2. On-shore occurrences of oil

  • Fold belts and forelands: anticlines along mountain fronts, as in the Zagros of Iran and Iraq and Assam's Digboi (oil struck in 1889).
  • Interior and rift basins: Ghawar in Saudi Arabia (the largest conventional oil field), West Siberia, the Permian Basin (USA), and in India the Cambay basin (Ankleshwar) and Barmer (Mangala, Rajasthan).
  • Unconventional oil: oil sands of Alberta, extra-heavy oil of the Orinoco belt (Venezuela) and shale or tight oil (Bakken and Permian, USA), extracted by fracking.

3. Differences between off-shore and on-shore oil

  • Technology frontier: off-shore output has moved from shallow shelves to deep and ultra-deep water, which needs advanced seismic imaging and floating production.
  • Gas: many off-shore basins, such as the KG basin, are richer in natural gas.

4. Significance for India

  • Energy security: India imports most of its crude oil, so off-shore exploration of its sedimentary basins under the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (2016) and the Open Acreage Licensing Policy is a priority.
  • Environmental care: oil-spill contingency plans and protection of coral and mangrove coasts must accompany exploration.

Off-shore oil follows the geography of thick marine sediments on continental margins and deltas, while on-shore oil follows fold belts and interior basins; together they shape the geopolitics of energy.
free.upm-2025-gs1-15:
Geospatial planningGIS and remote sensingDrones and AILocational and areal planning

Locational planning decides where a facility should go, such as a school, hospital, warehouse or solar park; areal planning organises land use over an area, such as a city master plan, a watershed or a district. Remote sensing (RS) supplies satellite imagery, and the Geographic Information System (GIS) overlays and analyses layers of spatial data. Drones add very high-resolution images on demand, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) turns these huge data streams into maps, predictions and decisions.

1. What each technology adds

  • Remote sensing: satellites such as Resourcesat and Cartosat, and the radar mission NISAR (2025), which sees through clouds, map land use, crops, floods and urban growth.
  • Drones: fly below clouds and give orthophotos at a few centimetres' resolution, and LiDAR for 3D terrain, over villages, corridors and mines.
  • GIS: overlays layers (slope, soils, population, roads, hazards) for site-suitability analysis, network analysis and land-use zoning.
  • AI: machine learning extracts buildings, roads and water bodies from imagery, detects encroachment and change, and predicts demand and urban sprawl.

2. Locational planning

  • Social infrastructure: schools, health centres and ration shops can be placed by mapping population and travel time, so that no habitation is left out.
  • Infrastructure corridors: the PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (2021) is a GIS platform that brings the data layers of many ministries together to align roads, railways and pipelines and avoid forests and settlements.
  • Energy and industry: solar and wind parks are sited using irradiance, wind speed, slope and land-use layers; AI optimises warehouse and EV-charging locations.
  • Disaster-safe siting: flood, landslide and cyclone hazard maps keep new settlements out of danger zones.

3. Areal planning

  • Rural land records: under SVAMITVA (launched 2020), drones have mapped the inhabited areas of about 3.3 lakh villages and over 3 crore property cards have been prepared (July 2026), which helps credit and gram panchayat development plans.
  • Urban planning: GIS-based master plans for AMRUT cities, and the NAKSHA pilot (February 2025) for aerial and drone survey of land records in 152 urban local bodies.
  • Agriculture and watersheds: the digital crop survey, watershed plans on ISRO's Bhuvan portal and drone-based crop assessment.

4. Making their use effective

  • Enabling rules: the Drone Rules, 2021 (Digital Sky, green zones up to 400 ft), the liberalised geospatial guidelines (2021) and the National Geospatial Policy (2022).
  • Data and standards: shared, interoperable datasets and open APIs instead of departmental silos.
  • Capacity and ground truth: trained staff in districts and towns, and field verification by gram sabhas, as under SVAMITVA.
  • Safeguards: privacy under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023), checks on algorithmic bias, and human judgement in final decisions.

Combining AI and drones with GIS and RS turns planning into evidence-based spatial decisions; with good data governance and local participation, it can make Indian cities and villages better planned and more resilient.
free.upm-2025-gs1-16:
Plate tectonicsSea-floor spreadingSubductionWilson cycle

The Earth's rigid outer shell, the lithosphere, is broken into seven major and several minor plates that move a few centimetres a year over the softer asthenosphere. Alfred Wegener (1912) proposed that the continents were once joined in a supercontinent, Pangaea; Harry Hess's sea-floor spreading (early 1960s) and the theory of plate tectonics (late 1960s) explained how. The interaction of plates at their boundaries constantly changes the shape and size of continents and ocean basins.

1. Why plates move

  • Driving forces: mantle convection (suggested by Arthur Holmes in the 1930s), the push of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and, most importantly, the pull of sinking slabs at subduction zones.
  • Evidence: matching coastlines and Glossopteris fossils across the southern continents; symmetric magnetic stripes on either side of ridges; and an ocean floor no older than about 200 million years.

2. Divergent boundaries: oceans open and continents split

  • Continental rifting: a continent stretches and cracks, forming a rift valley, as in the East African Rift today.
  • Young oceans: the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden are narrow new oceans where Arabia is moving away from Africa.
  • Sea-floor spreading: at mid-ocean ridges magma creates new oceanic crust; the Atlantic widens by a few centimetres a year along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which surfaces in Iceland.

3. Convergent boundaries: oceans shrink and continents grow

  • Subduction: dense oceanic plates sink into the mantle at trenches such as the Mariana Trench; the Pacific basin is slowly shrinking, ringed by the volcanoes and earthquakes of the "Ring of Fire".
  • Continental growth: subduction builds mountain arcs such as the Andes, and island arcs and crustal fragments (terranes) get welded onto continents.
  • Collision: after breaking away from Gondwana, the Indian plate moved north, closed the Tethys Ocean and collided with Eurasia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau; India still pushes north by a few centimetres a year.

4. Transform boundaries: sliding without creation or destruction

  • Lateral movement: plates slide past each other along faults such as the San Andreas (California), shifting pieces of continents sideways.
  • Ridge offsets: transform faults cut mid-ocean ridges into segments, giving them a zigzag shape.

5. The long-term pattern: the Wilson cycle

  • Opening and closing of oceans: J. Tuzo Wilson showed that ocean basins open, mature, shrink and close over hundreds of millions of years.
  • Supercontinent cycle: Rodinia (about a billion years ago) broke up; Pangaea assembled and then split from about 200 million years ago; geologists expect a new supercontinent to form within the next few hundred million years.

The map of the world is therefore not fixed: tectonic movements continually open and close oceans and break and weld continents, which also explains the location of mountains, earthquakes and volcanoes; plate tectonics is the unifying theory of physical geography.
free.upm-2025-gs1-17:
Ganga BasinPopulation densityAlluvial soilsWater resources

The Ganga Basin covers about 26% of India's land area (about 8.61 lakh sq km in India) across ten States and Delhi, and supports about 43% of India's population (2001 Census; MoEF status paper). Its average density, about 520 persons per sq km in 2001, far above the national average, makes it one of the most crowded river basins in the world. Yet the distribution is uneven and closely mirrors its land, soil and water resources.

1. Distribution and density

  • West to east gradient: density rises from the Upper Ganga plain to the Middle and Lower plains, where rainfall is higher and rice supports more people per hectare; Bihar is the most densely populated major State.
  • North and south margins: density falls towards the Himalaya in the north and the plateaus of Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand, Malwa and Chotanagpur in the south.
  • Urban clusters: Delhi–NCR, Kanpur, Lucknow, Patna and Kolkata form dense nodes along rivers and transport lines.

2. Land: relief shapes settlement

  • Flat alluvial plains: level land, easy to plough, irrigate and connect, supports continuous chains of villages and towns.
  • Himalayan sector: steep slopes and cold climate keep Uttarakhand and Himachal sparsely populated, except in valleys (duns) such as Dehradun and in pilgrimage towns.
  • Bhabar and Terai: the porous, pebbly bhabar is thinly settled; the marshy, once malarial Terai was cleared and settled after the 1950s and is now densely farmed.
  • Southern uplands and delta fringe: the Chambal ravines and rugged plateaus are thinly peopled except around mining towns such as Dhanbad; the mangrove core of the Sundarbans is protected forest.

3. Soils: fertility supports numbers

  • Khadar and bhangar: the new floodplain alluvium (khadar) is renewed by floods, and the older alluvium (bhangar) is fertile when irrigated.
  • Rice and multiple cropping: fertile loams and clays of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal support two or three crops a year and very high rural densities.
  • Problem soils: saline–alkaline (usar) patches and the thin red and black soils of the southern uplands support fewer people.

4. Water: perennial rivers and aquifers

  • Perennial rivers: the snow-fed Ganga, Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak and Kosi, with monsoon rain, assure water all year.
  • Irrigation: canals such as the Upper Ganga Canal (1854) and dense tube wells drove the Green Revolution in western Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.
  • Groundwater: a vast alluvial aquifer, depleted in the west and contaminated with arsenic in Bihar and West Bengal.
  • Floods: the Kosi and the Damodar, the "sorrows" of Bihar and Bengal, bring fertile silt but also recurrent losses.

The Ganga Basin shows how fertile land, rich soils and assured water sustain dense populations. But tiny holdings, out-migration from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, falling water tables and a polluted river (the target of Namami Gange) show that these limits now call for river-basin management.
free.upm-2025-gs1-18:
Fast foodNutrition transitionUltra-processed foodsObesity

Fast food, ready-to-eat food served quickly, ranges from global chains' burgers and pizzas to Indian street food such as vada pav and momos, and is spreading from metros to small towns. It grows despite rising health concerns: about 24% of women and 23% of men aged 15–49 are overweight or obese (NFHS-5, 2019–21), and an estimated 10.1 crore Indians have diabetes (ICMR-INDIAB, 2023). The paradox lies in the forces of the nutrition transition.

1. Economic and demographic drivers

  • Urbanisation and incomes: a growing urban middle class has more money to spend, and eating out has become a form of leisure.
  • Young population: students, young workers and migrants living alone are the main customers, drawn by price, taste and brand image.
  • Time poverty: dual-income nuclear families, long commutes and more women in paid work leave less time for cooking.

2. Technology and business models

  • Food-delivery apps, cloud kitchens and quick-commerce bring food to the door in minutes, with discounts that encourage frequent orders.
  • Franchising has carried chains into tier-2 and tier-3 cities, with value meals priced for local budgets.
  • Glocalisation: vegetarian menus, paneer and aloo-based items and Indian spices have adapted global formats to Indian tastes.
  • Marketing: celebrity endorsements, combo offers and advertising aimed at children build habits early.

3. Social and psychological factors

  • Engineered taste: high salt, sugar and fat make processed food tasty and cheap per calorie.
  • Social symbolism: chain outlets are places for friends, dates and children's birthdays, and social-media food trends add glamour.
  • Distant risk: the harm is delayed and invisible, so convenience today outweighs disease tomorrow; low nutrition literacy and unclear labels add to this.
  • Continuity with tradition: street snacks such as chaat and vada pav are old habits, so fast food fits in easily.

4. The health cost and the response

  • Rising non-communicable diseases: NCDs now cause about two-thirds of deaths in India, and childhood obesity is increasing alongside undernutrition, the "double burden of malnutrition".
  • Regulation: FSSAI capped industrial trans fats at 2% of oils and fats from January 2022, and its 2020 school regulations bar the sale and advertising of foods high in fat, sugar and salt in and near schools.
  • Labelling: under pressure from the Supreme Court in a public-interest case, FSSAI proposed, in an affidavit, red front-of-pack warnings such as "HIGH SUGAR", "HIGH SALT" and "HIGH FAT" for packaged food (August 2026).
  • Awareness: the Eat Right India movement (2018), the Fit India Movement (2019) and the promotion of millets during the International Year of Millets (2023).

India's experience shows that awareness alone does not change diets when convenience, price and marketing push the other way. Clear warning labels, healthy school food, reformulation and affordable traditional options can make the fast-food boom compatible with public health.
free.upm-2025-gs1-19:
Sustainable developmentEnvironmentalism of the poorJust transitionLivelihood security

Sustainable development, defined by the Brundtland Report (1987) as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own, requires growth with environmental protection. In India, where millions depend directly on forests, land, coal and cheap fuels, green rules can impose real costs on the poor. At the Stockholm Conference (1972), Indira Gandhi argued that poverty and need are the greatest polluters; yet the poor are also the first victims of environmental damage.

1. Where the conflict is real

  • Forests and protected areas: relocation from tiger reserves and limits on grazing, fuelwood and forest produce hurt forest dwellers; in 2019 the Supreme Court ordered the eviction of forest dwellers whose claims were rejected, and then stayed its own order after protests (Wildlife First v. Union of India).
  • Coal transition: coal-dependent districts of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh rely on mining jobs and royalties, so a phase-down threatens livelihoods.
  • Pollution controls: construction bans under Delhi's Graded Response Action Plan halt daily-wage work; closing polluting brick kilns and tanneries costs jobs; stubble-burning bans burden small farmers.
  • Green projects themselves: large solar parks, hydropower and compensatory afforestation can take common lands used by the poor.
  • Cost of clean options: LPG and electric vehicles cost more than firewood and old vehicles.

2. Why the conflict is not inevitable

  • The poor suffer most from degradation: air pollution caused about 1.67 million deaths in India in 2019 (Lancet Planetary Health, 2020); droughts, floods and heatwaves hit farmers and outdoor workers hardest.
  • Environmentalism of the poor: Chipko (1973), Appiko (1983) and the Niyamgiri gram sabhas (2013) show poor communities defending the ecosystems that sustain them.
  • Rights together: Article 21 covers both livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985) and a clean environment (Subhash Kumar, 1991); in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024) the Supreme Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change.
  • Green livelihoods: watershed works under MGNREGA, rooftop solar and solar pumps, and forest-produce enterprises create jobs while protecting nature.

3. Reconciling growth, ecology and the poor

  • Principles: polluter pays and precaution (Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996); consultation of gram sabhas under PESA and their consent before forest land is diverted under the Forest Rights Act framework (as in Niyamgiri).
  • Global equity: common but differentiated responsibilities, so that India's poor do not pay for emissions they did not cause.

4. Comment

The conflict is real in the short run and at the local level, especially where livelihoods depend on extraction. In the long run, however, environmental protection is pro-poor, because the poor depend most on healthy ecosystems.

Sustainable growth in India must be inclusive green growth: protection designed with the poor, compensation for those who lose, and green jobs, so that the transition is a just transition.
free.upm-2025-gs1-20:
Tribal developmentDevelopment-induced displacementRehabilitationSelf-governance

India's Scheduled Tribes number about 10.4 crore, 8.6% of the population (Census 2011), and live mostly in the forested, mineral-rich hills of central and eastern India and the North-East. Since independence, dams, mines, industries and protected areas have displaced them in disproportionate numbers, so much of tribal policy has revolved around displacement and rehabilitation. Yet tribal development under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules is wider than these two axes.

1. Why displacement and rehabilitation look central

  • Scale: by widely cited estimates of the scholar Walter Fernandes, tribals make up about 40% of the people displaced by development projects since 1947, though they are less than a tenth of the population.
  • Geography of resources: coal, iron ore and bauxite belts and dam sites overlap tribal homelands: Hirakud, Sardar Sarovar (the Narmada Bachao Andolan), Polavaram, and mines in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh; tiger reserves have also relocated villages.
  • Poor rehabilitation: cash in place of land, loss of forests and community, landlessness and migration; a Planning Commission expert group (2008) linked such alienation to Left-wing extremism.

2. Legal shift from rehabilitation to rights

  • Samatha judgment (1997): the Supreme Court held that tribal land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to private mining companies.
  • LARR Act, 2013: social impact assessment, consent of affected families for private and PPP projects, land for land and extra benefits for Scheduled Tribes, and gram sabha consent in Scheduled Areas.
  • Niyamgiri (2013): the Supreme Court let gram sabhas decide whether bauxite mining affected their religious and cultural rights; they rejected it.

3. Other axes of tribal development

  • Rights over land and forests: the Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights, and forbids eviction until claims are settled.
  • Self-governance and identity: PESA (1996) empowers gram sabhas over land, minor forest produce and minor minerals; Nehru's Tribal Panchsheel asked for development "along the lines of their own genius".
  • Human development: literacy among STs was about 59% against 73% nationally (Census 2011); Eklavya Model Residential Schools and the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) address gaps.
  • Livelihoods and infrastructure: Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (2018); PM-JANMAN (2023) for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups; the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (approved September 2024, ₹79,156 crore) covering about 63,000 villages and over 5 crore tribal people through 17 ministries.

4. My opinion

Displacement and rehabilitation are the most visible and contested axes, especially in mineral-rich central India, but they do not define all of tribal development: North-Eastern tribes under the Sixth Schedule, for example, are more concerned with autonomy, land and identity. Reducing tribal policy to rehabilitation treats tribals as victims of development rather than its agents.

The way forward is to avoid displacement where possible, ensure prior informed consent and benefit-sharing, and pursue rights-based, self-governed development that respects tribal culture.
free.upm-2025-gs2-1:
Corrupt practicesSection 123Undue influenceLok Prahari (2018)

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 lists corrupt practices in Section 123: acts by a candidate, his election agent or another person with their consent that destroy the voter's free choice. Proved in an election petition, they void the election (Section 100(1)(b)) and can lead to disqualification. In Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018) the Supreme Court linked legislators' unexplained wealth to this framework.

1. Corrupt practices under Section 123

  • Bribery (Section 123(1)): any gift, offer or promise of gratification to make a person stand or not stand, withdraw, vote or refrain from voting.
  • Undue influence (Section 123(2)): any direct or indirect interference with the free exercise of an electoral right, such as threats of injury or social ostracism, or of divine displeasure.
  • Communal appeals (Section 123(3), (3A)): seeking votes on grounds of religion, race, caste, community or language, or promoting enmity; Abhiram Singh (2017) extended the bar to appeals to the voter's religion or caste.
  • Others: glorifying sati, false statements about a rival, free conveyance of voters, overspending, help from government servants and booth capturing.

2. Disproportionate assets: the Lok Prahari case

  • Non-disclosure is undue influence: on 16 February 2018 Justices J. Chelameswar and S. Abdul Nazeer held that hiding the assets and income sources of candidates and their associates is an attempt to "suppress, misguide and keep people in the dark", amounting to undue influence.
  • Unexplained wealth: where assets grow without relation to known income, "the only logical inference" is some abuse of the legislator's constitutional office, inconsistent with the rule of law.
  • Directions: nomination affidavits (Form 26) must disclose the income sources of the candidate, spouse and dependants; the Union never set up the asset-monitoring mechanism the Court sought, and the Court later found no contempt.

3. Analysis: is the wealth itself undue influence?

  • Not by itself: Section 123(2) targets interference with a voter's choice in an election; growth of assets during a term does not, on its own, interfere with any voter, and corrupt practices are quasi-criminal charges needing strict proof.
  • Concealment crosses the line: hiding or falsifying the wealth in Form 26 deceives voters, which Lok Prahari treats as undue influence; using such money to buy votes is bribery.
  • The right forum: a disproportionate rise is illicit enrichment under Section 13(1)(b) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as legislators are public servants (P.V. Narasimha Rao, 1998); a conviction disqualifies under Section 8 of the RP Act.
  • False affidavits: Section 125A punishes them with up to six months' imprisonment but does not disqualify, a gap the Law Commission (244th Report, 2014) proposed to close.

Unexplained wealth is a symptom of corruption rather than, by itself, undue influence; its concealment is what vitiates an election. A statutory asset-monitoring mechanism and time-bound trial of election petitions would give the 2018 judgment real teeth.
free.upm-2025-gs2-2:
Articles 323A and 323BTribunalisationTribunals Reforms Act 2021National Tribunals Commission

Tribunals are specialised quasi-judicial bodies that decide disputes in fields such as service matters, tax, company law and the environment. The 42nd Amendment (1976), following the Swaran Singh Committee, inserted Articles 323A and 323B to let legislatures create them. The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 rationalised them but met repeated judicial objections, leading to a new law in 2026.

1. Why tribunals are needed alongside courts

  • Expertise: benches of judicial and technical members suit technical disputes, as in the National Green Tribunal (2010) or the NCLT and NCLAT under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
  • Speed and flexibility: they are not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or strict rules of evidence, follow natural justice and can work to statutory time limits.
  • Relief to courts: moving service disputes to the Central Administrative Tribunal (1985) and tax appeals to the ITAT eases the load on High Courts.
  • Access and cost: less formal procedures and benches in many cities help litigants.
  • Supplements, not substitutes: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) made judicial review under Articles 226, 227 and 32 part of the basic structure, so tribunal orders can be challenged before a High Court.

2. Problems that prompted reform

  • Executive control: parent ministries fund, staff and appoint tribunals while also litigating before them.
  • Vacancies, short tenures and overlapping bodies delayed justice.
  • Earlier attempt: the Finance Act, 2017 merged tribunals (26 to 19), but Rojer Mathew (2019) struck down the rules framed under it.

3. The 2021 rationalisation and its impact

  • Abolition: bodies such as the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Airport Appellate Tribunal were dissolved, and their work moved to High Courts and civil or commercial courts.
  • Uniform conditions: a four-year term, a minimum age of 50, and search-cum-selection committees chaired by the CJI or his nominee, with two Union Secretaries.
  • Burden shifted: High Courts received specialised cases without new judges; the Delhi High Court created an Intellectual Property Division (2021).
  • Clash over independence: the Act re-enacted provisions the Court had struck down in July 2021. In Madras Bar Association (19 November 2025) the Court struck down its appointment and tenure provisions and ordered a National Tribunals Commission within four months.
  • Response: the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 (assent 13 August, in force from 25 August 2026) set up a five-member National Tribunals Commission to oversee appointments, review performance, handle complaints against members and maintain a National Tribunals Data Grid for 16 tribunals; members get five-year terms (chairpersons up to 70, members up to 67).

Rationalisation has made the system leaner, but its impact depends on independence: an autonomous Commission, judicial primacy in selection and adequate staff would let tribunals deliver speedy, expert justice without diluting judicial review.
free.upm-2025-gs2-3:
Article 72Article II, Section 2Judicial reviewPre-emptive pardon

The pardoning power is an act of executive grace that corrects judicial errors and tempers justice with mercy. In India it rests in Article 72 (President) and Article 161 (Governor); in the USA in Article II, Section 2, which lets the President "grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offences against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment". The two differ in who really decides, how far courts can review it and when it can be used.

1. Similarities

  • Executive power: in both countries it belongs to the head of the executive and is outside legislative control.
  • Wide range: both cover full pardons and lesser clemency, including for military offences.
  • Purpose: mercy, correction of miscarriages of justice and public interest.

2. Differences

  • Real authority: India's President is bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74; Maru Ram, 1980), whereas the US President acts personally; the Justice Department's Pardon Attorney only advises.
  • Federal reach: the US President cannot pardon State crimes, while India's President can pardon any death sentence, even under a State law.

3. Limits in both countries

  • India: Kehar Singh (1989) denied a right to an oral hearing but kept the power reviewable; Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allows review for mala fides, non-application of mind, irrelevant or political considerations and arbitrariness; in Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) unexplained delay in deciding mercy petitions became a ground for commutation, and 15 death sentences were commuted.
  • USA: no State offences, no impeachment and no relief from civil liability; in Burdick (1915) the Court held that a pardon may be refused because accepting it implies guilt. Checks are mainly political, and whether a President can pardon himself is untested.

4. What are pre-emptive pardons?

  • Meaning: a pardon granted before any charge or conviction, covering offences that may have been committed, so that future prosecution is barred.
  • USA: valid since Ex parte Garland (1866); Gerald Ford pardoned Richard Nixon (1974) for offences he "has committed or may have committed"; Joe Biden pardoned his son for any offences since 2014 (December 2024) and, on 20 January 2025, General Mark Milley, Dr Anthony Fauci and members and staff of the House January 6 Committee. Critics say such pardons place allies above the law.
  • India: Article 72 speaks of a person "convicted of any offence", which is generally read to rule out pre-emptive pardons; the nearest tools are withdrawal from prosecution with the court's consent and a magistrate's tender of pardon to an accomplice who turns approver.

India treats pardon as a constitutional duty exercised on advice and open to review, while the USA treats it as a near-absolute personal prerogative. Time limits for mercy petitions in India and norms against self-serving pardons in the USA would keep the power about mercy, not impunity.
free.upm-2025-gs2-4:
J&K Reorganisation Act 2019UT with legislatureArticle 239ALieutenant Governor

The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, in force from 31 October 2019, ended the State's special status under Article 370 and split it into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, with a legislature, and Ladakh, without one. The Supreme Court upheld the change in In re Article 370 (December 2023), ordering elections by 30 September 2024 and statehood "at the earliest". The UT's first Assembly was elected in September–October 2024.

1. Nature of the Assembly

  • A UT legislature on the Puducherry model: Section 13 extends Article 239A to J&K, so the Assembly exists under an Act of Parliament and is subordinate to it, unlike a State legislature with its own constitutional sphere.
  • Unicameral, five-year term: the Legislative Council was abolished, and the term fell from six years under the former J&K Constitution to five.
  • Composition: 114 seats, of which 24 for Pakistan-occupied Kashmir stay vacant; the 2022 delimitation fixed 90 elected seats (Jammu 43, Kashmir 47), with 7 reserved for SCs and, for the first time, 9 for STs.
  • Nominated members: the LG may nominate two women and, since a 2023 amendment, two Kashmiri migrants (one a woman) and one person displaced from PoK.
  • Transitional status: statehood had not been restored as of October 2026, and the Assembly passed a resolution seeking it in September 2026.

2. Powers and functions of the Assembly

  • Legislative (Section 32): it may make laws on State List matters except "public order" and "police", and on Concurrent List matters as far as they apply to UTs; Parliament can legislate on any matter for the UT, and its law prevails in a conflict.
  • Financial: it votes the budget and demands for grants, but Money and financial Bills need the LG's recommendation.
  • Executive accountability: the Council of Ministers, led by the Chief Minister and capped at 10% of the Assembly's strength, is collectively responsible to it; questions, motions and committees enforce this.
  • Assent: Bills go to the LG, who may assent, withhold assent or reserve them for the President.
  • Electoral: its elected members choose the UT's four Rajya Sabha members.

3. Limits: the Lieutenant Governor

  • Discretion: the LG acts on ministers' advice except in matters outside the Assembly's powers and those relating to All India Services and the Anti-Corruption Bureau; differences of opinion go to the President.
  • Business Rules: amendments in July 2024 route proposals on police, public order, All India Services, the Anti-Corruption Bureau and the Advocate General's appointment to the LG through the Chief Secretary.
  • Effect: a dual power structure, closer to Delhi than to a State, with friction over control of officials.

The Assembly restores representative government, but within a subordinate framework. Early restoration of statehood, as the Supreme Court directed, and cooperative working between the LG and the elected government would complete the democratic transition.
free.upm-2025-gs2-5:
Article 76Attorney GeneralArticle 88Legal counsel

The Attorney General (AG) for India, appointed by the President under Article 76, is the Union's highest law officer and chief legal adviser. He must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge, holds office during the pleasure of the President and receives remuneration fixed by the President. Assisted by the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General (non-constitutional posts), he is both the government's counsel and an officer of the Constitution.

1. Responsibilities

  • Legal advice: to advise the Government of India on legal matters referred by the President (Article 76(2)), keeping policy within constitutional limits.
  • Assigned duties: under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987, to appear for the Union in all its Supreme Court cases, to represent it in Presidential References under Article 143, such as the 2025 Reference on assent to State Bills, and to appear in any High Court when required.
  • Statutory functions: for example, his or the Solicitor General's consent is needed before a private person can move the Supreme Court for criminal contempt (Contempt of Courts Act, 1971).

2. Rights

  • Audience: a right of audience in all courts in the territory of India (Article 76(3)).
  • Parliament: the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses, their joint sittings and any committee of which he is named a member, but without a vote (Article 88).
  • Privileges: the privileges and immunities of a Member of Parliament (Article 105(4)).
  • Private practice: he is not a full-time government servant and may take private briefs, subject to restrictions.

3. Limitations

  • Conflict of interest: he should not advise or hold a brief against the Government of India, or in cases in which he is called upon to advise it.
  • Prior permission: he should not defend accused persons in criminal prosecutions, or accept a directorship in any company, without the government's permission.
  • No security of tenure: the Constitution fixes neither a term nor grounds of removal; by convention he resigns when the government changes.
  • Advisory status: he is not a member of the Cabinet, and his opinion does not bind the government.

4. Sound governance: the tension in the role

  • Dual loyalty: as the government's counsel he defends its policies; as an officer of the Court he owes candour to the Constitution. In ADM Jabalpur (1976) Attorney General Niren De argued that during the Emergency a detenu had no remedy even against unlawful deprivation of life, a reminder of what is at stake.
  • Preventing litigation: the government is the biggest litigant (National Litigation Policy, 2010), so frank advice before decisions saves public money.

The AG's value lies in independent legal counsel: telling the government what the law permits, not merely what it wants. A fixed tenure and a published code of conduct would strengthen the office as a guardian of constitutional governance.

Social capitalSelf-help groupsWomen's agencyGender equity

Social capital is the networks, norms of reciprocity and trust that enable people to act together, a concept developed by Pierre Bourdieu, James Coleman and Robert Putnam. Women build it through self-help groups (SHGs), cooperatives, unions and community networks. It complements economic capital (income, assets) and human capital (education, health) by turning schemes and rights into real agency, the core of empowerment and gender equity (SDG 5).

1. Forms of women's social capital

2. How it advances empowerment

  • Economic: group savings and credit replace collateral; the SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (NABARD, 1992) and DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women) turned thrift groups into enterprise platforms, and Lakhpati Didi aims to raise 3 crore SHG members to a household income of at least ₹1 lakh a year.
  • Collective bargaining: SEWA (1972) organised informal women workers; Kudumbashree (Kerala, 1998) links women's groups with local governments.
  • Social change: collectives challenge harmful norms; rural women in Nellore district, Andhra Pradesh, led the anti-arrack movement (1992), and the women of Reni village saved their forest in the Chipko movement (1974).
  • Political voice: SHG membership builds confidence to speak in Gram Sabhas, and women now hold nearly half of panchayat seats.
  • Information and services: peer networks spread knowledge on health, nutrition and digital finance, through Bank Sakhis and Namo Drone Didis.

3. Why it complements, but cannot replace, other capitals

  • Structural barriers remain: women's labour force participation is only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24), and few own land or houses; networks cannot substitute for assets, education and jobs.
  • Exclusion and elite capture: bonding groups may mirror caste and class hierarchies and leave out the poorest, Dalit and migrant women.
  • Burden and debt: group work adds to unpaid care work, and aggressive microfinance led to the Andhra Pradesh crisis of 2010.
  • Instrumental use: women are sometimes treated as delivery agents of schemes rather than decision-makers.

4. Strengthening it

  • Rights and assets: daughters' coparcenary rights (Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005) and joint titles for houses and land.
  • Planning voice: women's federations in Gram Panchayat Development Plans and Mahila Sabhas.
  • Support services: crèches, legal and digital literacy, and gender budgeting.

Women's social capital is the multiplier that makes money, skills and rights work for women; combined with assets and public services, it can move India from women's development to women-led development.

e-governanceBack-end integrationUser-centric designDigital divide

e-governance uses ICT to deliver services and integrate government (G2C, G2B, G2G). India's journey from the National e-Governance Plan (2006) to Digital India (2015) and digital public infrastructure has built powerful back-ends for identity, payments and databases. Yet the Second ARC (11th Report, 2008) warned that e-governance is about reforming governance, not just technology, and many projects still digitise processes for the government's convenience rather than designing around the citizen.

1. Evidence of a technology and back-end bias

  • Integration first: projects stress databases, seeding, dashboards and interoperability, as in the India Enterprise Architecture framework (2018); success is counted in transactions, not citizen satisfaction.
  • Authentication over access: biometric checks for rations and Aadhaar-based wage payments under MGNREGA (mandatory from January 2024) excluded people when fingerprints failed or networks dropped; ration denials in Jharkhand (2017) linked to Aadhaar seeding drew wide concern.
  • Digital-only channels: CoWIN at first required online registration for younger adults, a digital divide the Supreme Court flagged (2021); only 33% of women, against 57% of men, had ever used the internet (NFHS-5).
  • Poor usability: complex forms, English-first interfaces and portals that fail at launch, such as the new income-tax e-filing portal (2021).
  • Weak feedback: grievance redress is often online-only, with no human fallback.

2. Why the bias arises

  • Vendor-led procurement pays for systems, not service outcomes.
  • Translation, not transformation: old paper procedures, documents and approvals are often put online unchanged, without re-engineering them around the citizen.
  • Departmental silos: each ministry builds its own platform for its own data needs.
  • Monitoring as the goal: real-time data on beneficiaries and staff takes priority over ease of use.
  • Little design capacity: few user researchers, and little testing with rural, elderly or disabled citizens.

3. Not the whole picture

  • UPI (2016): simple, interoperable and mobile-first, it shows that strong back-ends serve users when design is citizen-centric.
  • Assisted access: Common Service Centres and Kerala's Akshaya centres (2002) help those who cannot use apps.
  • Simplification: DigiLocker, UMANG (one app for many services), Passport Seva and Bhashini (2022) for Indian languages.
  • Principles exist: e-Kranti (2015) promised "transformation, not translation", mobile-first services and language localisation.

The bias is real but not inevitable. The Second ARC's SMART ideal (simple, moral, accountable, responsive, transparent), design for the last user, offline fallbacks and privacy by design under the DPDP Act, 2023 would make e-governance truly citizen-centric.
free.upm-2025-gs2-8:
Civil societyNon-State actorsDissentPartnership

Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) are voluntary, non-profit associations in the space between the family, the market and the State: NGOs, trade unions, cooperatives, self-help groups, faith-based bodies and social movements. As non-State actors they are independent of government and protected by Article 19(1)(c). Because their watchdog role often brings them into conflict with governments, some see them as anti-State, but the evidence is mixed.

1. Why the perception arises

  • Opposition to projects: campaigns against large dams, mines and power plants, such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan, have delayed projects; an Intelligence Bureau report (2014) alleged that some foreign-funded NGOs were stalling development.
  • Foreign funding: concern over external influence led to the FCRA, 2010 and its 2020 amendment, which barred sub-granting, capped administrative spending at 20% and required a designated SBI account; the Supreme Court upheld it in Noel Harper (2022).
  • Litigation and protest: PILs and agitations can stall policies, and a few groups have been accused of links with extremist or separatist agendas.
  • Accountability deficit: weak financial transparency and internal democracy in some NGOs erode trust.

2. Why they are better seen as non-State, not anti-State

  • Partners in delivery: Akshaya Patra serves school meals under PM POSHAN, Pratham's ASER surveys inform education policy, and SHGs implement livelihood missions.
  • Co-authors of law: the MKSS-led campaign produced the RTI Act, 2005; the Right to Food campaign shaped the NFSA, 2013; ADR's petition led to disclosure of candidates' criminal records and assets (2002).
  • Crisis responders: NGOs and community groups fed migrants and ran helplines during COVID-19 alongside governments.
  • Recognition: Article 43B (97th Amendment, 2011) promotes cooperatives, and the National Policy on the Voluntary Sector (2007) treats NGOs as partners.
  • Dissent is democratic: criticising a government is not opposing the State; in Shreya Singhal (2015) the Supreme Court protected discussion and advocacy short of incitement.

3. Verdict

I agree only partly. Confrontational episodes and opaque funding explain the perception, but most CSOs complement the State, and even critical ones strengthen democracy by voicing the excluded and improving policy.

The way forward is a trust-based framework: audits and disclosure by CSOs, and consultation (as under the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy, 2014) and proportionate regulation by the State, so that civil society remains a partner and conscience of democracy.
free.upm-2025-gs2-9:
Digital public infrastructureKampala principlesCo-developmentCapacity building

India's Africa policy rests on the ten Kampala principles set out by the Prime Minister in Uganda's Parliament (July 2018), which promise a partnership guided by African priorities and pledge India's digital experience to Africa's development. India's digital public infrastructure (DPI), open and interoperable systems such as Aadhaar and UPI, and decades of capacity building give this partnership a demand-driven character.

1. Mutual respect

  • Demand-driven: grants, lines of credit and training follow partners' priorities, without political conditions.
  • Equal voice: under India's presidency the African Union became a permanent member of the G20 (New Delhi, September 2023), and the G20 endorsed a framework for DPI.
  • Data sovereignty: systems built with Indian help are owned and run by African institutions.
  • Political engagement: the third India–Africa Forum Summit (2015) brought together all 54 African countries.

2. Co-development

  • Open-source identity: MOSIP, the Modular Open Source Identity Platform developed at IIIT Bangalore, is used mostly by African countries, such as Ethiopia for its Fayda digital ID; countries adapt it rather than buy a proprietary product.
  • Payments: NPCI International agreed with the Bank of Namibia (2024) to build a central-bank-led instant payment system on UPI technology, the first such arrangement in Africa; UPI and RuPay were launched in Mauritius (2024), and India agreed to share its UPI experience with Ghana (2025).
  • Global public goods: India shares DPI components through the G20 Global DPI Repository (2023).

3. Long-term institutional partnerships

  • Tele-education and telemedicine: the Pan-African e-Network (2009), succeeded by e-VidyaBharati and e-ArogyaBharati (e-VBAB, 2019), links African students and hospitals to Indian institutions.
  • Training: the ITEC programme (1964) and 50,000 scholarships promised at the 2015 Summit build skills.
  • Institutions: the first IIT campus abroad, IIT Madras in Zanzibar (Tanzania, 2023), and the Kofi Annan Centre of Excellence in ICT in Accra (2003), built with Indian support.

4. Challenges

  • Scale: China's Digital Silk Road brings larger finance for networks and data centres.
  • Gaps on the ground: uneven electricity and broadband limit DPI adoption.
  • Delivery and safeguards: slow implementation, and the need for data protection and cyber security in partner countries.

India's digital partnership treats Africa as a co-creator, not a market. Linking payment systems across borders, co-developing AI for African languages and regular summit-level reviews would turn goodwill into a durable South–South compact.
free.upm-2025-gs2-10:
DeglobalisationSovereign nationalismEconomic securityMultipolarity

After the Cold War, globalisation seemed irreversible: the WTO (1995), China's entry into it (2001) and Francis Fukuyama's "End of History" thesis assumed that open markets and liberal democracy would erode borders. Since the 2008 financial crisis, however, trade integration has slowed ("slowbalisation"), and sovereign nationalism, the assertion of national control over trade, borders, technology and identity, has become a defining feature of world politics.

1. The globalisation phase (1991–2008)

  • Open markets: tariff cuts, global value chains and capital flows; India's 1991 reforms tied it to world markets.
  • Rules-based multilateralism: a WTO with binding dispute settlement, and expansion of the EU and NATO.

2. Signs of sovereign nationalism

  • Economic nationalism: US tariffs on steel and aluminium (2018) and sweeping "reciprocal" tariffs (2025), reaching 50% on many Indian goods from August 2025 before most of them were lifted in February 2026 (new, smaller US duties followed later in 2026); the WTO Appellate Body has not functioned since December 2019.
  • Industrial policy: the US CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act (2022), China's self-reliance drive and the EU's carbon border mechanism put security and jobs ahead of efficiency.
  • Borders and identity: Brexit (2016 referendum, exit in 2020), anti-immigration movements and sovereignty-first parties in many democracies.
  • Weaponised interdependence: sanctions on Russia after 2022, exclusion of banks from SWIFT, export controls on chips and "friend-shoring" of supply chains.
  • Retreat from multilateralism: vaccine nationalism during COVID-19, and the US exit from the Paris Agreement and the WHO (announced in January 2025, effective January 2026).

3. Why it has happened

  • Uneven gains: job losses and inequality in Western industrial regions fuelled a backlash.
  • Power shift: China's rise turned interdependence into a security concern.
  • Shocks: the 2008 crisis, the pandemic and wars exposed fragile supply chains.
  • Technology: control of data, chips and AI is now treated as sovereignty.

4. Limits of the thesis

  • Re-globalisation, not deglobalisation: trade remains near record levels, and services and digital trade keep growing.
  • New trade deals: India signed agreements with the UAE (2022), Australia (2022), EFTA (2024) and the UK (2025).
  • Shared risks: climate change, pandemics and AI still need cooperation, now often through minilaterals such as the Quad.

India's response combines both trends: Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and production-linked incentives alongside new trade agreements, strategic autonomy and a call for reformed multilateralism.

The world is not returning to autarky; it is moving towards a managed, security-conscious globalisation in which nations seek sovereignty and interdependence at once.
free.upm-2025-gs2-11:
Constitutional moralityJudicial independenceJudicial accountabilityIn-house procedure

Constitutional morality means fidelity to the core values and spirit of the Constitution (rule of law, liberty, equality, dignity, and checks and balances), beyond its bare text. Dr B.R. Ambedkar, quoting the historian George Grote in the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948), warned that it "is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." The Supreme Court calls it the fulcrum that restrains high functionaries and citizens alike, and it binds judges, the Constitution's guardians, most of all.

1. The concept

  • Restraint in power: in Manoj Narula (2014) the Court said it means to "bow down to the norms of the Constitution" and not act arbitrarily.
  • Values over popular morality: in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) and Joseph Shine (2018) constitutional morality prevailed over social or majoritarian morality.
  • Institutional harmony: in Government of NCT of Delhi (2018) the Court asked constitutional functionaries to work in the spirit of the Constitution.
