  • Criticism: the idea is open-ended and can widen judicial discretion, so it must be applied with restraint.

2. A shield for judicial independence

  • Basic structure: judicial independence is a basic feature; the Fourth Judges case (2015) struck down the NJAC to protect it.
  • Safeguards: removal only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 124(4)), salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, a bar on discussing judges' conduct in legislatures (Articles 121, 211) and contempt powers (Articles 129, 215).
  • Duty of other organs: governments must not delay appointments or transfer judges punitively.

3. A demand for judicial accountability

  • Self-regulation: the Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997) and the in-house procedure (1999) set standards of conduct.
  • Transparency: the CJI's office is a public authority under the RTI Act (Subhash Chandra Agarwal, 2019), and collegium resolutions have been published since 2017.
  • Criminal law: judges are public servants under the Prevention of Corruption Act, but prosecution needs the CJI's consent (K. Veeraswami, 1991).
  • Discipline: in C.S. Karnan (2017) a sitting High Court judge was jailed for contempt. After cash was found at Justice Yashwant Varma's residence (March 2025), an in-house inquiry was followed by a removal motion and a statutory inquiry; he resigned in April 2026.

4. Striking the balance

  • Independence is not immunity, and accountability must not become executive control.
  • Impeachment is rare: no judge has been removed; the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami failed (1993), and Justice Soumitra Sen resigned (2011) after the Rajya Sabha voted for removal.
  • Reforms: a judiciary-led statutory complaints body (the Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010 lapsed), a finalised Memorandum of Procedure, cooling-off periods before post-retirement posts and routine asset disclosure.

Constitutional morality asks judges to be independent of power yet answerable to the Constitution. Transparent and credible self-regulation is the best guarantee of public trust, the ultimate source of judicial legitimacy.
free.upm-2025-gs2-12:
Article 368Special majorityFederal ratificationBasic structure

Unlike the USA, where amendments need ratification by three-fourths of the States, India entrusts amendment to its ordinary legislative institutions: Parliament and, for federal matters, the State Legislatures. Under Article 368 an amendment needs a special majority and, in some cases, ratification by half the States, making the Constitution "partly rigid, partly flexible". The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) adds substantive limits.

1. Procedural limitations

  • Initiation: only by a Bill in either House of Parliament, moved by a minister or a private member; State Legislatures cannot initiate amendments.
  • Each House separately: there is no joint sitting to resolve a deadlock.
  • Federal ratification: entrenched provisions need resolutions of half the State Legislatures, though no time limit is prescribed.
  • Assent: the President must give assent (24th Amendment, 1971).
  • Courts enforce procedure: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) struck down Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule for want of ratification, and Rajendra N. Shah (2021) struck down Part IXB on cooperatives insofar as it covered State cooperatives, for the same reason.
  • A real hurdle: the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was defeated in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026, getting 298 votes to 230, short of the 352 required.

2. Substantive limitations

  • The debate: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) allowed Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights; Golak Nath (1967) denied it; the 24th Amendment restored the power.
  • Basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973): Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic features.
  • Applications: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) struck down the 39th Amendment's clause on the Prime Minister's election; Minerva Mills (1980) invalidated Article 368(4) and (5), holding limited amending power itself basic; the NJAC case (2015) struck down the 99th Amendment.
  • Ninth Schedule: I.R. Coelho (2007) held laws placed there after 24 April 1973 open to basic-structure review.
  • Restraint too: Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the 103rd Amendment (EWS quota), showing that the doctrine strikes only at the core.

3. Assessment

  • Flexible by design: a simple procedure has allowed more than a hundred amendments, adapting the Constitution to new needs.
  • Checked by courts: the basic structure protects democracy, federalism, secularism and judicial review from passing majorities, though critics see it as judicial supremacy.

India's amending process balances flexibility and stability: open to change through democratic institutions, yet anchored by a judicially guarded basic structure.
free.upm-2025-gs2-13:
CollegiumJudges casesNJACSenate confirmation

Article 124(2) provides that the President appoints Supreme Court judges after "consultation" with the Chief Justice of India and such judges as he deems necessary. Through the Judges cases the Supreme Court read "consultation" to give the judiciary primacy, creating the collegium, a body not mentioned in the text. The USA follows a political model: presidential nomination and Senate confirmation (Article II, Section 2).

1. Evolution of the collegium

  • Executive phase: the supersessions of senior judges in appointing Chief Justices in 1973 and 1977 raised fears for independence.
  • First Judges case (S.P. Gupta, 1981): "consultation" did not mean concurrence, so the executive had primacy.
  • Second Judges case (1993): primacy for the CJI's opinion, formed with the two senior-most judges; a reiterated recommendation binds the government.
  • Third Judges case (1998, a Presidential Reference): a collegium of the CJI and the four senior-most judges for the Supreme Court.
  • NJAC and after: the 99th Amendment (2014) created a National Judicial Appointments Commission, but the Fourth Judges case (2015) struck it down 4:1; resolutions have been published online since 2017, and in 2023 the collegium published even the government's objections to names it reiterated.

2. India's collegium

  • Advantages: it insulates appointments from political pressure, protects independence, draws on judges' close knowledge of candidates' work, and the seniority convention for the CJI has ended supersession.
  • Disadvantages: opacity and no written criteria; "judges appointing judges" without external accountability; charges of nepotism and poor diversity (few women, SC, ST and OBC judges); and, with the Memorandum of Procedure still not finalised, delays and friction as the government holds back names.

3. The US system

  • Advantages: democratic legitimacy through an elected President and Senate; public hearings by the Senate Judiciary Committee bring scrutiny; life tenure "during good behaviour" protects independence after appointment.
  • Disadvantages: openly ideological, partisan appointments; Merrick Garland (2016) was denied a hearing; since 2017 justices are confirmed by a simple majority after the filibuster was removed; and life tenure makes the Court's balance depend on deaths and strategic retirements.

4. Critical assessment

Neither model is ideal: India guards independence at some cost to transparency, while the USA secures democratic accountability at some cost to neutrality.

India needs a transparent collegium: a finalised Memorandum of Procedure with objective criteria, a permanent secretariat, time limits for both the collegium and the government, and attention to diversity, so that judicial independence commands public confidence.
free.upm-2025-gs2-14:
Fiscal federalismPlanning CommissionFinance CommissionGST Council

The Seventh Schedule divides taxing powers, and Part XII (Articles 264–293) distributes revenues and provides for formula-based transfers through the Finance Commission (Article 280). But from 1950 a second channel, the Planning Commission, an executive body, shaped Centre–State finances through plan assistance and Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS). The move to NITI Aayog (2015), GST (2017) and recent Finance Commissions has redrawn India's fiscal federalism.

1. Planning era (1951–2014): centralised development

  • Dual channel: the Finance Commission covered tax shares and grants (Articles 270, 275), while plan transfers flowed as discretionary grants under Article 282.
  • Plan formula: the Gadgil formula (1969) and the Gadgil–Mukherjee formula (1991) allocated central plan assistance among States.
  • Growth of CSS: tied, centrally designed schemes multiplied, so the Union shaped States' spending priorities.
  • Criticism: the Rajamannar Committee (1969) and the Sarkaria Commission (1988) criticised central dominance and discretionary transfers.
  • Reforms: the 80th Amendment (2000) placed all central taxes in the divisible pool, and fiscal responsibility laws (FRBM Act, 2003, and State laws) imposed discipline.

2. Recent reforms

  • More untied money: the 14th FC raised the States' share from 32% to 42% (2015–20); the 15th and 16th FCs fixed 41%.
  • End of planning: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015 without power to allocate funds; the plan and non-plan distinction ended in 2017-18, and CSS were rationalised in 2016.
  • GST (101st Amendment, 2016): taxing powers were pooled in the GST Council (Article 279A); compensation ended in June 2022, and "GST 2.0" moved to two main slabs (5% and 18%) from September 2025.
  • 16th FC (2026–31): a new "contribution to GDP" criterion (10%), larger local-body grants (₹7.91 lakh crore) and an end to revenue-deficit grants.
  • Capital support: 50-year interest-free loans to States for capital investment (since 2020-21), partly tied to reforms.

3. Impact on fiscal federalism: how far?

  • Positive: a larger untied share, rule-based transfers, a common market and the GST Council as a forum of cooperative federalism.
  • Shrinking pool: cesses and surcharges lie outside the divisible pool and reduce the States' effective share.
  • Lost autonomy: States gave up most indirect taxes to GST, though Mohit Minerals (2022) held the Council's recommendations persuasive, not binding.
  • Borrowing curbs: off-budget borrowings now count against State limits under Article 293(3); Kerala's challenge was referred to a Constitution Bench (2024).
  • Conditional transfers: CSS conditions and the end of revenue-deficit grants strain weaker States.

Fiscal federalism has moved from plan-based centralism to rule-based, negotiated federalism. Folding cesses into the divisible pool and a stronger Inter-State Council would deepen cooperative fiscal federalism.
free.upm-2025-gs2-15:
Pressure groupsEnvironmental movementsPublic interest litigationAdvocacy

Pressure groups are organised groups that seek to influence public policy without contesting elections or seeking power. Environmental pressure groups include research and advocacy NGOs, grassroots movements, legal activists and global networks. In India they range from the Bombay Natural History Society (1883) and the Chipko movement (1973) to the Centre for Science and Environment (1980).

1. Raising awareness

  • Mass mobilisation: Chipko women hugged trees to stop commercial felling; the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad's campaign helped save Silent Valley, declared a national park in 1984.
  • Evidence-based reports: CSE's State of India's Environment (first in 1982) and its studies on air pollution and pesticide residues in soft drinks (2003) brought science to the public.
  • Citizen science: bird counts and biodiversity surveys by BNHS and others build public interest.

2. Influencing policies

  • Laws: Chipko led to a 15-year ban on green felling in the Himalayan forests of present-day Uttarakhand (1980); after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), pressure for stronger law produced the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • Rights of forest dwellers: the Campaign for Survival and Dignity pressed for the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Participation: public hearings in environmental clearances (mandatory since 1997) give groups a formal voice, and the draft EIA Notification, 2020 drew wide objections.
  • Institutions: advocacy, together with the Supreme Court and the Law Commission, led to the National Green Tribunal (2010).

3. Advocating protection through courts

  • M.C. Mehta cases: absolute liability for hazardous industries (oleum gas leak, 1986), protection of the Taj (1996) and CNG for Delhi's public transport.
  • Principles: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996) adopted the precautionary and polluter-pays principles.
  • Forests and communities: the T.N. Godavarman case (from 1995) protected all forests in the dictionary sense; in Niyamgiri (2013) Gram Sabhas rejected bauxite mining.
  • Climate: in M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024), a case on the Great Indian Bustard, the Supreme Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.

4. Limitations

  • "Anti-development" label: campaigns against dams and mines are seen as costly delays, and foreign-funded groups face FCRA action, as when Greenpeace India's registration was cancelled (2015).
  • Elite and urban bias: some campaigns protect urban amenities more than the livelihoods of the poor.
  • Courts over legislatures: reliance on litigation can produce orders that are hard to implement.

Environmental pressure groups are the conscience keepers of India's development. Genuine public hearings, open data and consultation, with accountability on their side, can reconcile growth with sustainable development.
free.upm-2025-gs2-16:
Paradox of povertyAsset inequalityResource curseInclusive growth

The paradox of poverty is the persistence of deprivation amid abundance: fast growth, surplus food stocks and rich natural resources. The World Bank estimates that India's extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011-12) to 5.3% (2022-23) at US$3 a day, yet the richest 1% hold over 40% of national wealth (World Inequality Lab, 2024). A central reason why growth does not reach everyone is unequal ownership of land, capital, minerals and human capital.

1. The paradox in India

  • Rich lands, poor people: Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh hold much of India's coal and iron ore, yet their tribal districts are among the poorest; Jharkhand is one of the most multidimensionally poor States (NITI Aayog MPI, 2023).
  • Full granaries, hungry people: the PUCL right-to-food case (2001) began when grain rotted in godowns during a drought, and 35.5% of children under five are still stunted (NFHS-5).
  • Equal consumption, unequal wealth: a consumption Gini of 25.5 (2022-23) places India among the world's most equal societies (World Bank), while wealth is highly concentrated.
  • Growth without enough good jobs: most workers remain in low-productivity farming and informal work.

2. How unequal ownership causes poverty

  • Land: small and marginal farmers hold about 86% of holdings but operate only about 47% of the area (Agricultural Census 2015-16); landless labourers depend on uncertain wage work.
  • Capital and credit: without collateral the poor borrow from moneylenders at high rates, and debt forces distress sales of assets.
  • Human capital: unequal access to good schools and health care limits earnings; out-of-pocket spending (43.4% of health expenditure, 2022-23) pushes families into poverty.
  • Natural resources: mines and dams have displaced tribal communities while profits flow elsewhere, a local "resource curse" documented by the Xaxa Committee (2014).
  • Social barriers: caste and gender restrict ownership; women and Dalits own a small share of land.

3. A balanced view

  • Other causes matter: low productivity, regional disparities, weak governance and climate shocks also explain poverty.
  • Public action works: multidimensional poverty fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23), about 24.82 crore people (NITI Aayog, 2024), helped by housing, sanitation, cooking gas, bank accounts and food security.

Poverty amid plenty is less a shortage of resources than a problem of their distribution. Secure land rights, community shares in mineral wealth, women's ownership and universal quality education and health can turn growth into inclusive prosperity.
free.upm-2025-gs2-17:
SubsidiarityLocal knowledgeDecentralisation73rd and 74th Amendments

The statement reflects the principle of subsidiarity: decisions should be taken at the lowest level able to take them, where information about needs and conditions lies. Friedrich Hayek (The Use of Knowledge in Society, 1945) showed that much knowledge is local and dispersed, and James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State (1998) explained why top-down schemes that ignore it fail. India's 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) sought to bring decisions closer to people, but development planning remains largely centralised.

1. Where the statement holds

  • Uniform schemes: centrally designed schemes with uniform norms, unit costs and targets ignore differences of terrain, culture and need, so assets are built but not used, such as toilets without water.
  • Hollow devolution: States have transferred few of the 29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule (and 18 in the Twelfth) with matching funds, functions and functionaries; State Finance Commissions are irregular, and parallel bodies bypass panchayats.
  • Information up, decisions down: frontline workers such as ANMs, anganwadi workers and teachers know the problems but have little discretion, while dashboards reward reporting over results.
  • Urban gap: city governments rarely control planning, water or transport, which lie with State parastatals, so local problems such as flooding persist.

2. Evidence that proximity works

  • Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996): devolving about 35–40% of plan funds to local bodies improved local services.
  • Gram Panchayat Development Plans (since 2015): with the "Sabki Yojana Sabka Vikas" campaign (2018), Gram Sabhas set their own priorities.
  • Aspirational Districts (2018) and Blocks (2023): local data, convergence and competition improved health, nutrition and education indicators.
  • Community management: watershed work at Hiware Bazar (Maharashtra) and Joint Forest Management echo Elinor Ostrom's Nobel-winning (2009) work on local management of commons.

3. Critical evaluation

  • Some decisions need scale: vaccination drives (Pulse Polio, COVID-19), direct benefit transfers, highways and macroeconomic policy gain from central design.
  • Local capture: dominant castes and elites can capture local bodies, and proxy representation ("sarpanch-pati") and weak capacity limit gains.
  • Externalities: air pollution and river basins cross boundaries and need higher-level coordination.
  • Technology helps: real-time data and geospatial platforms now carry local information upward, though data cannot replace local judgement.

The statement is largely valid but not absolute. Multi-level governance, built on activity mapping (Second ARC, 6th Report, 2007), untied funds such as the 16th FC's ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies and strong local capacity, can place each decision where knowledge and accountability meet.
free.upm-2025-gs2-18:
NCPCROnline child safetyPOCSO and IT ActDPDP Act 2023

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), a statutory body under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, monitors safeguards for child rights, inquires into violations and monitors the POCSO Act, 2012, the RTE Act, 2009 and the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015. In the digital era, children face online risks that these laws were not designed for.

1. Challenges children face online

  • Sexual exploitation: grooming, sextortion and the spread of child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM).
  • Harmful content and conduct: cyberbullying, violent or self-harm content and deepfakes.
  • Addiction and gambling: excessive screen time, gaming and betting apps.
  • Data exploitation: profiling, tracking and targeted advertising.
  • Divides: many poor children, especially girls, lacked devices for online schooling during COVID-19; cyber crime overall rose 17.9% in 2024 to over one lakh cases (NCRB).

2. Existing policies

  • NCPCR's own tools: the POCSO e-Box (2016) and the e-Baal Nidan portal for complaints, and it has backed stronger age verification of children online.
  • Courts: in Just Rights for Children Alliance (2024) the Supreme Court held that storing or viewing CSEAM is an offence under POCSO; on 15 October 2026 it held that children too have a fundamental right to internet access, called a complete ban inappropriate, suggested parental guidance and "child modes", and asked the Union to consider guidelines and SOPs.

3. Gaps

  • Fragmentation: child safety is spread across laws, ministries and portals, without a single online-safety code.
  • Enforcement: platforms based abroad, encryption and slow takedowns weaken action.
  • Age checks vs privacy: document-based verification risks excessive data collection.
  • Limited teeth: NCPCR's recommendations are not binding, and it lacks technical staff and data on online harm.

4. Measures the Commission can initiate

  • Child online safety code: with MeitY, recommend age-appropriate design, privacy by default, a "child mode" and quick grievance redress, drawing on the UK's Age Appropriate Design Code.
  • Inquiries and audits: use its civil court powers (Section 14) for suo motu inquiries into platforms, and publish compliance reports.
  • Monitoring POCSO online: track CSEAM reports with NCRB, I4C and State Commissions, and press for time-bound takedowns and fast-track trials.
  • Digital literacy: cyber-safety modules with NCERT and CBSE, awareness for parents and teachers, and links to counselling such as Tele-MANAS (14416).
  • Children's voice: an annual report on children online, prepared in consultation with children.

Protecting children online means safety without exclusion. As the child-rights watchdog, NCPCR can bridge laws, platforms and families so that the internet becomes a space for learning and play, not exploitation.
free.upm-2025-gs2-19:
Energy securityWest AsiaDiversificationClean energy diplomacy

Energy security, meaning energy that is available, affordable, reliably delivered and sustainable, is a core national interest for India, which imports about 89% of its crude oil (2025-26) and nearly half its gas. West Asia supplies a large part of it, is a major source of remittances, and the Gulf countries alone host about 90 lakh (9 million) Indians. The 2026 West Asia crisis, which disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, showed how closely energy, diaspora and diplomacy are tied.

1. Energy at the heart of India's West Asia policy

  • Supply: Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the UAE are among the top crude suppliers, and Qatar and the UAE supply LNG under long-term contracts.
  • Investment both ways: an ONGC Videsh-led consortium holds 10% of the Lower Zakum field (UAE, 2018), and ADNOC stores crude in India's Mangaluru strategic reserve.
  • Strategic partnerships: the India–UAE CEPA (2022), the India–Saudi Strategic Partnership Council (2019), I2U2 (2022) and the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC, 2023).
  • Sea lanes: the Navy's Operation Sankalp (2019) escorted Indian ships in the Gulf.
  • More than "influence": India's leverage comes from being the third-largest oil consumer and a balancer that engages Saudi Arabia, Iran, Israel and the UAE at once; ties also rest on diaspora, trade, food security and counter-terrorism.

2. Vulnerabilities exposed

  • Chokepoint risk: about half of crude imports and most LPG and LNG imports pass through Hormuz, which the 2026 Iran–US–Israel conflict disrupted.
  • Sanctions: India stopped buying Iranian oil in 2019, and Russian crude, its largest source after 2022, was cut back after US sanctions in late 2025.
  • Thin buffers: strategic reserves of 5.33 million tonnes cover only about 9.5 days of need.
  • New dependencies: solar modules, batteries and critical minerals depend on Chinese supply chains.

3. Integrating energy security with foreign policy

  • Multi-alignment: buy from all sources while keeping strategic autonomy, as with Russian crude after 2022.
  • From buyer to partner: turn energy trade into joint refining, storage, petrochemical and green hydrogen projects with Gulf states, settled partly in rupees (with the UAE since 2023).
  • Transition as security: non-fossil sources already make up over half of installed power capacity, and the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) and the 500 GW non-fossil target for 2030 cut import exposure.
  • Crisis diplomacy: evacuation capacity, naval escorts and engagement with all sides protect both energy flows and the diaspora.

Energy security will remain a driver, though not the only kingpin, of India's foreign policy. Balancing West Asian partners, diversifying suppliers and leading the clean energy transition will turn dependence into strategic interdependence.
free.upm-2025-gs2-20:
UNSC reformVetoGreat-power rivalryReformed multilateralism

The United Nations (1945) reflects the power balance of the Second World War: five permanent members (P5) with a veto dominate the Security Council, which has been enlarged only once, from 11 to 15 members in 1965. Reform needs a Charter amendment under Article 108, ratified by two-thirds of members including all the P5. The Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN), under way since 2009, have yet to produce a negotiating text; in September 2026 the G4 voiced concern at the lack of concrete progress.

1. The East–West confrontation

  • Veto as a weapon: Russia vetoed a resolution on its invasion of Ukraine (2022); Russia and China vetoed tougher sanctions on North Korea (2022) and several resolutions on Syria; the USA vetoed several Gaza ceasefire resolutions (2023–25). Since 2022 the General Assembly must debate every veto.
  • Rival visions: the West upholds a liberal, rules-based order; Russia and China, with their "no limits" partnership (2022), push a multipolar order built on sovereignty and non-interference.
  • Reform through a bloc lens: China resists a permanent seat for Japan and has not endorsed India's bid; Russia backs India and Brazil but sees Germany and Japan as strengthening the Western camp; the USA supports modest expansion but opposes extending the veto.
  • Defence of privilege: the France–Mexico initiative (2015) to restrain the veto in mass atrocities has not been joined by the USA, Russia or China.
  • Spillover: funding cuts and US withdrawals, such as from the WHO (effective January 2026), have deepened the UN's financial crisis.

2. Critical evaluation: more than an East–West problem

  • North–South divide: Africa's Ezulwini Consensus (2005) seeks two permanent seats with veto and five non-permanent seats; the L.69 group and the G4 seek expansion in both categories.
  • Regional rivalries: the Uniting for Consensus group (Italy, Pakistan, Argentina, South Korea and others) opposes new permanent members, mirroring rivalries with Germany, India, Brazil and Japan.
  • Procedure as a veto: the IGN works by consensus and without a text, so any group can stall it.
  • Some convergence: the Pact for the Future (2024) committed members to reform the Council and redress the historical injustice against Africa, and all P5 accept some expansion in principle.

3. India's stand

India, a non-permanent member eight times (most recently 2021–22), works through the G4 and L.69 for text-based negotiations within a fixed time frame and argues for reformed multilateralism that reflects today's world.

The East–West rivalry makes reform harder, but the deeper obstacle is that every veto player, great power or regional rival, prefers the status quo to a loss of relative position. Only a coalition that bridges East and West, and North and South, can make the Council representative and effective.
free.upm-2025-gs3-1:
Human Development IndexInequality-adjusted HDILoss due to inequalityInclusive growth

The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UNDP since 1990 and built on the ideas of Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, measures a country's average achievement in health, knowledge and standard of living. The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), introduced in the 2010 Human Development Report, discounts each of these averages for how unequally it is shared. The gap between the two, the "loss due to inequality", shows how far progress has failed to reach everyone.

1. HDI and IHDI distinguished

  • What HDI measures: it is the geometric mean of three indices: life expectancy at birth; mean and expected years of schooling; and gross national income per capita (PPP, log-scaled). It describes the "average" person.
  • What IHDI adds: it reduces each dimension's average by the inequality in its distribution across people, so it shows the human development of the "actual" person.
  • Relation between them: IHDI equals HDI only under perfect equality; otherwise it is lower, and the percentage gap is the loss due to inequality.

2. India's position

  • Steady progress: India's HDI reached 0.685 in HDR 2025 (rank 130 of 193), in the "medium" group and close to the 0.700 threshold of "high" human development; life expectancy rose to 72 years.
  • Large inequality loss: the IHDI of 0.475 means about 30.7% of India's human development is lost to inequality, one of the highest losses in the region (UNDP).
  • Where the gap lies: unequal incomes, uneven quality of schooling and health care across States, castes and rural–urban areas, and gender gaps; HDR 2025 notes that women's labour force participation and political representation lag behind.

3. Why the IHDI is a better indicator of inclusive growth

  • Distribution, not averages: inclusive growth means broad-based gains; IHDI falls when gains are concentrated among a few, even if GDP and HDI rise.
  • Pinpoints the weak dimension: it reports inequality separately for health, education and income, guiding targeted policy, for example on learning outcomes or out-of-pocket health spending.
  • "Leave no one behind": it matches SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) and Sen's capability approach, judging progress by what the actual person can do and be.
  • Tracks policy impact: a shrinking loss over time shows whether welfare programmes are spreading gains.

4. Limits of the IHDI

  • It does not show overlapping deprivations in the same household, which the Multidimensional Poverty Index captures; it does not separate caste, gender or regional gaps; and it relies on household surveys that lag.

The HDI tells us how far India has come; the IHDI tells us how many have come along. Narrowing the inequality loss through quality schooling, health care and decent jobs, especially for women, is the real test of inclusive growth on the road to Viksit Bharat 2047.
free.upm-2025-gs3-2:
ProtectionismBilateralismWTO crisisExport diversification

After decades of multilateral liberalisation under the WTO (1995), the world economy is turning to tariffs, industrial subsidies and one-to-one deals. The WTO's Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since December 2019, and in August 2025 the USA, India's largest export market, raised tariffs on most Indian goods to 50%. For India, which needs export-led manufacturing to become a developed nation by 2047, this shift brings serious challenges.

1. Challenges for the Indian economy

  • Tariff shocks: the 2025 US tariffs hit labour-intensive exports such as textiles, gems and jewellery and shrimp. The extra 25% "Russian oil" tariff was removed on 7 February 2026 and the reciprocal tariffs lapsed after the US Supreme Court ruling of 20 February 2026; a temporary 10% tariff on all countries followed, and in July 2026 the USA announced new 10% duties on about half of India's exports to it.
  • A weakened WTO: with no working Appellate Body and no agreement on agriculture at MC14 (Yaoundé, March 2026), India's food-stockholding programme and its right to fair dispute settlement are less secure.
  • Green and standards protectionism: the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (definitive phase from January 2026) taxes the carbon in steel, aluminium and cement exports; due-diligence rules raise compliance costs for MSMEs.
  • Trade diversion: goods shut out of Western markets, especially Chinese steel, chemicals and solar products, are dumped in India, hurting domestic producers.
  • Technology and services barriers: chip export controls and a steep US fee on new H-1B visa petitions (2025).
  • Unequal bargaining: in bilateral deals larger economies press for access to agriculture, dairy and data, sensitive areas for a country of small farmers.

2. How the challenges can be met

  • Smart bilateralism: a wider network of trade deals: the UAE CEPA and Australia ECTA (2022), the EFTA TEPA (in force October 2025), the UK CETA (signed July 2025), the Oman CEPA (signed December 2025), FTAs with New Zealand and the EU (announced December 2025 and January 2026), and a framework for an interim deal with the USA (February 2026), its first tranche still in legal drafting in October 2026.
  • Diversify markets and products: Africa, Latin America and ASEAN; electronics, pharmaceuticals, defence goods, and services through Global Capability Centres.
  • Competitiveness at home: PLI schemes, PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy (2022) to cut logistics costs; lower tariffs on inputs; simpler compliance for exporters.
  • Trade defence and standards: anti-dumping and safeguard duties through the DGTR, and quality standards against substandard imports.
  • Financial resilience: trade settlement in rupees (RBI, July 2022) and ample forex reserves.
  • Reform multilateralism: work with developing countries to restore the Appellate Body and secure a permanent solution on public stockholding, and use the G20 and BRICS to oppose unilateral tariffs.

India should neither retreat into protectionism nor depend on any one market. Strategic openness, combining competitive manufacturing, diversified FTAs and a strong voice for a rules-based WTO, can turn disruption into a larger share of global value chains.
free.upm-2025-gs3-3:
High-value cropsCrop diversificationMarket accessRisk-bearing capacity

High-value crops (HVCs) such as fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation and medicinal crops earn far more per hectare than cereals. Rising incomes, urbanisation and exports have increased demand for them; India is the world's second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables, and horticulture output now exceeds foodgrain output. Yet a farmer's decision to shift away from cereals depends on agro-climatic, economic, institutional and personal factors, with risk at the centre.

1. Agro-climatic and resource factors

  • Climate and soil: apples need temperate hills (Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir), grapes and pomegranates the dry Deccan (Nashik, Solapur), and spices the humid Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka).
  • Assured water: most vegetables and flowers need frequent watering; drip and sprinkler irrigation, supported under PMKSY's "Per Drop More Crop", has enabled orchards in dry regions.
  • Land and gestation: small holdings suit labour-intensive vegetables, while orchards take several years to bear fruit and suit farmers who can wait for returns.

2. Economic and market factors

  • Profitability and demand: higher net returns per hectare and demand from cities, processors and exporters (grapes and mangoes to Europe and the Gulf) pull farmers towards HVCs.
  • Price risk: most HVCs have no MSP, and gluts cause crashes in tomato and onion prices; assured MSP and procurement keep paddy and wheat attractive.
  • Perishability and market access: HVCs need nearby markets, good roads, cold storage and pack-houses, so peri-urban farmers shift first.
  • Costs and credit: planting material, inputs, labour and protected cultivation (polyhouses) need capital, so access to credit matters.

3. Institutional and policy factors

  • Schemes: the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (2014-15), Operation Greens for perishables and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020) for pack-houses and cold storage.
  • Collective action: Farmer Producer Organisations (10,000 FPO scheme, 2020) and cooperatives such as Mahagrapes help small farmers aggregate, grade and bargain; contract farming offers assured buyers.
  • Insurance: under PMFBY farmers pay a higher premium (5%) for annual commercial and horticultural crops than for food crops (2% kharif, 1.5% rabi), and many fruit and vegetable risks remain uninsured.
  • Information: Krishi Vigyan Kendras, e-NAM price data and mobile advisories reduce uncertainty.

4. Farmer-specific factors

  • Risk-bearing capacity: marginal farmers often grow cereals first for household food security.
  • Education and experience: better-informed and younger farmers adopt new crops faster.
  • Labour: HVCs need more labour; family labour, including women, makes them viable.

Diversification towards high-value crops can raise incomes, improve nutrition and save water, but farmers move only when risk is shared. Price stabilisation, cold chains, insurance and FPO-led markets can make high-value agriculture the next growth engine for small farmers.
free.upm-2025-gs3-4:
Agricultural supply chainPost-harvest lossesCold chainFarm-to-fork

Agricultural supply chain management (SCM) is the coordinated management of the flow of produce, information and money from inputs and the farm gate through aggregation, storage, processing and transport to the final consumer. India is a top producer of milk, pulses, cereals, fruits and vegetables, but fragmented chains cause post-harvest losses of about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS study for the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, 2022) and leave farmers with a small share of the consumer's price.

1. Scope of supply chain management

  • Upstream: quality seed, fertiliser, credit and advisories planned around market demand, as in buy-back and contract arrangements.
  • Aggregation at the farm gate: FPOs, cooperatives and primary agricultural credit societies (PACS) collect, clean, grade and sort produce from many small farms.
  • Storage and logistics: warehouses, silos, cold stores, reefer trucks, Kisan Rail and air cargo for perishables; electronic negotiable warehouse receipts from WDRA-registered warehouses let farmers borrow against stored produce.
  • Processing and packaging: milling, pulping, freezing and packaging add value and extend shelf life.
  • Marketing: APMC mandis, e-NAM, organised retail, e-commerce, ONDC and exports with traceability systems run by APEDA.

2. Significance

  • Lower losses: the NABCONS study found losses of up to about 15% for fruits and 12% for vegetables, far above those for cereals; cold chains and quick transport cut this waste.
  • Better prices for farmers: fewer intermediaries and direct links to buyers raise the farmer's share, as dairy cooperatives on the Amul model show.
  • Stable consumer prices: storage and buffer stocks smooth the seasonal swings in tomato, onion and potato prices.
  • Food and nutrition security: efficient procurement, scientific storage and distribution under the National Food Security Act, 2013 reduce grain spoilage and leakage.
  • Exports and jobs: standard-compliant, traceable chains open global markets and create rural jobs in grading, packing, logistics and processing.
  • Sustainability: less food waste means less water, fertiliser and emissions wasted with it.

3. Government initiatives along the chain

4. Challenges

  • Fragmentation: small, scattered holdings make uniform, bulk supply difficult.
  • Infrastructure gaps: cold storage is concentrated in a few States and used mostly for potatoes; pack-houses and reefer vans are scarce near farms.
  • Market rules: multiple intermediaries, mandi fees and stocking limits deter private investment.
  • Quality and standards: weak grading, residue testing and certification limit premium and export markets.

An integrated, farm-to-fork supply chain led by FPOs, digital platforms and private investment in cold chains can raise farmers' incomes, cut waste and stabilise prices, making Indian agriculture market-led and resilient.
free.upm-2025-gs3-5:
Nuclear fusionITERTokamakClean baseload energy

Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei, deuterium and tritium, into helium and releases enormous energy, as in the Sun. It needs a plasma hotter than 100 million °C, held by powerful magnets in a doughnut-shaped tokamak. ITER, being built at Cadarache in France by seven partners, aims to produce ten times the heating power fed into its plasma. India joined ITER in 2005 and has built its own fusion programme alongside.

1. Evolution of India's fusion programme

  • Institutional base: plasma research that began at the Physical Research Laboratory, Ahmedabad, led to the Institute for Plasma Research (IPR), Gandhinagar (1986), now under the Department of Atomic Energy.
  • ADITYA (1989): India's first indigenous tokamak, later upgraded as ADITYA-U to study plasma behaviour and control.
  • SST-1: a steady-state superconducting tokamak (first plasma in 2013) that gave experience in superconducting magnets, cryogenics and long-pulse operation.
  • ITER-India: IPR hosts India's domestic agency for ITER, which has trained Indian industry to make large, precise fusion components.
  • Legal readiness: the draft rules under the SHANTI Act (August 2026) provide for a composite licence that also covers fusion reactors.

2. India's contributions to ITER

  • Partnership: India is one of seven members (EU, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA). The EU, as host, bears about 45% of the cost and each other member about 9%, mostly in kind, as components made at home.
  • The cryostat: the world's largest stainless-steel vacuum chamber, about 29 m across and 29 m tall and weighing about 3,850 tonnes, fabricated by Larsen & Toubro in sections at Hazira (Gujarat) and assembled at the ITER site; it encloses the tokamak and its magnets.
  • Other systems: shielding, cooling, cryogenic, heating and diagnostic packages (table); Indian engineers at the site gain first-hand know-how.

3. Implications of ITER's success for global energy

  • Near-limitless fuel: deuterium comes from seawater and tritium can be bred from lithium; a few grams of fuel release as much energy as tonnes of coal.
  • Climate: no carbon dioxide is emitted during operation, and fusion would give steady baseload power to complement solar and wind on the way to net zero.
  • Safety and waste: no chain reaction, so no meltdown risk; no long-lived high-level waste, only activated materials; little proliferation risk.
  • Energy geopolitics: abundant fuel would reduce dependence on oil and gas exporters and chokepoints, a major gain for import-dependent India.
  • Realistic timeline: ITER is an experiment, not a power plant; research operations are planned for the mid-2030s and power-producing successors (DEMO) only around mid-century, so fusion cannot replace near-term renewables and fission.

By sharing in ITER for a small part of its cost, India has become a co-owner of fusion know-how. If ITER succeeds, fusion could be the ultimate clean energy of the second half of the century, while renewables and fission carry the nearer transition.
free.upm-2025-gs3-6:
Energy independence 2047Clean technologyBiotechnologyCircular bioeconomy

On Independence Day 2021 the Prime Minister set the goal of making India energy independent by 2047. Today India imports about 89% of its crude oil and close to half of its gas, and the 2026 West Asia (Hormuz) crisis showed how exposed this makes the economy. Clean technologies that turn domestic sunlight, wind, biomass and waste into energy are the route to independence, and biotechnology can turn India's farm and urban waste into fuel.

1. Clean technology pathway to 2047

  • Renewables with storage: the target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030; non-fossil sources already make up about 55% of installed capacity (CEA, August 2026). Batteries, pumped storage and green energy corridors must handle the evening peak.
  • Green hydrogen: the National Green Hydrogen Mission (January 2023, ₹19,744 crore) aims at 5 million tonnes a year by 2030, replacing grey hydrogen and imported ammonia in refineries and fertiliser plants.
  • Electric mobility: electric two- and three-wheelers and buses, backed by PM E-DRIVE and battery PLI, cut oil use in transport.
  • Nuclear power: a target of 100 GW by 2047, the SHANTI Act, 2025 that opens the sector to private Indian firms, and small modular reactors.
  • Domestic supply chains: PLI for solar modules and the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025), so that freedom from oil does not become dependence on imported panels and lithium.
  • Efficiency first: PAT, UJALA and star labels reduce demand itself.

2. The crucial role of biotechnology

  • Ethanol: better yeasts and enzymes raise fermentation yields; India reached E20 (20% ethanol in petrol) in 2025, and the ministry says blending since 2014 has saved about ₹1.4 lakh crore of foreign exchange.
  • Second-generation ethanol: cellulase enzymes and engineered microbes break down rice straw, cotton stalks and bamboo; PM JI-VAN plants such as Panipat (rice straw, 2022) also reduce stubble burning.
  • Compressed biogas (CBG): anaerobic microbes turn cattle dung, press mud and municipal waste into CBG under SATAT and GOBARdhan; city gas networks must blend CBG, rising to 5% by 2028-29.
  • Advanced fuels: algae-based (third-generation) biofuels, biohydrogen from microbial fermentation, and sustainable aviation fuel, with a 1% blending target for international flights by 2027.
  • Policy push: the BioE3 Policy (August 2024) funds biomanufacturing hubs and biofoundries, including microbial carbon capture; the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 (amended 2022) sets the framework.

3. Challenges

  • Food versus fuel: grain and cane ethanol competes with food and uses much water.
  • Cost and scale: 2G ethanol, green hydrogen and algal fuels remain costly.
  • Intermittency and minerals: solar and wind need storage, and batteries need imported critical minerals.

Energy independence is best read as energy self-reliance: a mix of renewables, storage, green hydrogen, nuclear and bioenergy built on domestic manufacturing. By turning waste into wealth, biotechnology can make the circular bioeconomy a pillar of a secure and green Viksit Bharat 2047.
free.upm-2025-gs3-7:
Carbon Capture, Utilisation and StorageHard-to-abate sectorsNegative emissionsNet zero 2070

Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) is a set of technologies that capture carbon dioxide from large point sources such as power plants, steel, cement and refineries, or directly from the air, and then either use it to make products or store it permanently deep underground. The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report treats carbon dioxide removal as unavoidable for balancing residual emissions at net zero. India committed ₹20,000 crore over five years to CCUS in the Union Budget 2026-27.

1. What CCUS involves

  • Capture: post-combustion capture with solvents such as amines that absorb CO₂ from flue gas; pre-combustion capture after gasification; oxy-fuel combustion; and direct air capture.
  • Transport: compressed CO₂ moves by pipeline or ship to a user or a storage site.
  • Utilisation: urea, methanol (with green hydrogen), soda ash, polymers, carbonated building materials, food-grade CO₂, and enhanced oil recovery (EOR).
  • Storage: injection about a kilometre or more underground into saline aquifers, depleted oil and gas fields or basalts, where it is trapped or turns into rock; Norway's Sleipner project has stored CO₂ under the North Sea since 1996.

2. Potential role in tackling climate change

  • Hard-to-abate sectors: most of cement's CO₂ comes from heating limestone, not from fuel, so clean power alone cannot remove it; steel, fertilisers and refineries likewise need capture.
  • Coal transition: coal still produces about 70% of India's electricity; capture on newer plants could limit emissions locked in over their long lives.
  • Negative emissions: bioenergy with carbon capture and direct air capture remove CO₂ already emitted, offsetting residual emissions on the path to net zero by 2070.
  • Circular carbon economy: CO₂ becomes a raw material for methanol, urea and building products.
  • Carbon markets: verified captured and stored tonnes could earn credits under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

3. India's efforts

  • Policy: NITI Aayog's CCUS policy framework (2022); the DST's CCUS R&D roadmap (December 2025), in three phases from pilots (2025-30) to commercial deployment (2035-45); and the Budget 2026-27 outlay for power, steel, cement, refineries and chemicals.
  • Pilots: projects in steel, power and oil fields (table) already turn CO₂ into methanol and food-grade gas or inject it into old wells.

4. Limitations

  • High cost and energy penalty: capture is expensive (IEEFA puts average full-chain costs in Europe at about US$198 per tonne) and consumes part of a plant's own energy.
  • Small scale so far: global capture is a tiny fraction of emissions; storage needs mapped geology and long-term leak monitoring.
  • Moral hazard: it can become an excuse to prolong fossil-fuel use.
  • Rules: India still needs a clear framework for storage rights, liability and monitoring.

CCUS is no substitute for renewables and efficiency, but a complement for emissions that nothing else can remove. Clear storage rules, carbon pricing and shared CO₂ hubs in industrial clusters can make it a vital bridge to net zero 2070.
free.upm-2025-gs3-8:
Seawater intrusionCoastal aquifersOver-extractionManaged aquifer recharge

Seawater intrusion is the landward movement of saline water into fresh coastal aquifers. Fresh groundwater flowing towards the sea normally holds back the denser seawater; by the Ghyben–Herzberg relation, every metre of fresh water above sea level keeps the fresh–salt boundary about 40 metres below sea level. Over-pumping lets this saline wedge advance inland. With a coastline of about 11,099 km (2025 re-measurement), India faces the problem from Gujarat to West Bengal and in its islands.

1. Causes of seawater intrusion

  • Over-extraction: heavy pumping for irrigation, industry and cities creates cones of depression that draw seawater in, as along the Saurashtra coast of Gujarat and in the Minjur aquifer north of Chennai.
  • Reduced recharge: paved urban surfaces, filled-up tanks and wetlands, and dams that cut river flows to the coast reduce fresh water reaching aquifers.
  • River sand mining and dredging: lowered riverbeds and deepened creeks let tidal water travel further upstream and seep into aquifers.
  • Sea-level rise and storm surges: a slowly rising sea pushes the boundary inland, and cyclone surges flood land with seawater that percolates down, as in the Sundarbans.
  • Coastal land use: brackish-water aquaculture ponds and salt pans salinise nearby wells; loss of mangroves and dunes removes natural barriers; on small islands such as Lakshadweep, fresh water floats as a thin lens that over-pumping easily spoils.

2. Impacts

  • Drinking water: coastal towns and villages lose their wells and must depend on tankers or costly desalination.
  • Agriculture: saline irrigation water and soils cut yields of paddy, coconut and vegetables and can force farmers to abandon land.
  • Long recovery: a salinised aquifer can take decades to recover even after pumping stops.

3. Remedial measures

  • Manage demand: permission for groundwater use under the Central Ground Water Authority's guidelines (2020), metering, micro-irrigation, salt-tolerant crop varieties, and no heavy pumping close to the shore.
  • Increase recharge: check dams, percolation tanks, recharge wells and rooftop rainwater harvesting, mandatory in Tamil Nadu since 2003; Jal Shakti Abhiyan's "Catch the Rain" and Amrit Sarovar ponds.
  • Physical barriers: tidal regulators and bandharas across creeks and estuaries, as in Gujarat's salinity-ingress prevention works on the Saurashtra coast, and underground cut-off walls.
  • Hydraulic barriers: a line of injection wells creates a ridge of fresh water that pushes the salt wedge back, used in coastal California.
  • Alternative supplies: desalination (Chennai's Minjur and Nemmeli plants) and treated wastewater reduce pressure on aquifers.
  • Protect natural buffers and monitor: mangrove restoration under MISHTI (2023), CRZ rules, regulation of aquaculture and sand mining, and CGWB aquifer mapping (NAQUIM) with coastal monitoring wells.

Seawater intrusion is slow but nearly irreversible. Integrated coastal aquifer management that balances pumping with recharge, protects mangroves and plans for sea-level rise must be part of India's water security strategy.
free.upm-2025-gs3-9:
TerrorismCross-border terrorismUAPA and NIAZero tolerance

Terrorism is the use or threat of violence against civilians to spread fear for political, religious or ideological ends. It is a global scourge, from al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks to the Islamic State, and India has been among its worst-hit victims for four decades. There is still no agreed UN definition, as India's proposed Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (1996) remains stalled; at home, the UAPA, 1967 and Section 113 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 define a "terrorist act".

1. How terrorism has manifested in India

  • Cross-border terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir: Pakistan-based groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed carried out the Pulwama attack (February 2019, 40 CRPF personnel killed) and the Pahalgam attack (22 April 2025), in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists, were killed.
  • Urban and sea-borne attacks: the Mumbai serial blasts (1993), the Parliament attack (2001) and 26/11 in Mumbai (2008), whose attackers came by sea.
  • Home-grown and online radicalisation: Islamic State-inspired modules recruit online; investigators linked the car explosion near Delhi's Red Fort (10 November 2025), now probed by the NIA, to a "white-collar" module of doctors and other professionals with alleged links to Jaish-e-Mohammed.
  • Insurgency and Left Wing Extremism: Maoist violence in central India and armed groups in the North-East, both now sharply reduced.
  • New tools: drone drops of arms and drugs across the Punjab border, the drone attack on the Jammu Air Force Station (June 2021), narco-terror and crypto-financing.

2. Counter-measures adopted by the State

  • Legal: the UAPA, amended in 2019 to designate individuals as terrorists; the NIA Act, amended in 2019 to let the NIA probe offences against Indians abroad; the PMLA against terror finance; and the new criminal laws of 2023.
  • Institutional: the National Investigation Agency (2009), NSG regional hubs set up after 26/11, a revamped Multi-Agency Centre for real-time intelligence sharing, NATGRID linking databases, and CCTNS connecting police stations.
  • Borders and coasts: smart fencing under the Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System, three-tier coastal security after 26/11, and anti-drone systems.
  • Financial: the NIA's terror-funding and fake currency cell, FATF compliance (India rated "regular follow-up" in 2024) and the "No Money for Terror" conference (New Delhi, 2022).
  • Military doctrine: surgical strikes (2016), the Balakot strike (2019) and Operation Sindoor (7 May 2025), which hit nine terrorist-linked sites, signalling that terror attacks will be met with force.
  • Diplomacy and society: UN 1267 listings, the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance (April 2025), and de-radicalisation and surrender programmes at home.

3. Remaining gaps

  • Coordination: police is a State subject, and a national counter-terrorism centre has not been created.
  • Justice and rights: slow trials and low conviction rates under special laws weaken deterrence and raise concerns of misuse.

India's response has moved from reaction to a zero-tolerance, whole-of-government doctrine. Intelligence-led policing, speedy trials, de-radicalisation and global cooperation, including adoption of the CCIT, are needed to defeat a threat that respects no borders.
free.upm-2025-gs3-10:
Left Wing ExtremismRed CorridorSAMADHANSecurity and development

Left Wing Extremism (LWE), or Naxalism, is an armed movement inspired by Maoist ideology that seeks to overthrow the State through "protracted people's war". It began with the Naxalbari uprising (1967) and was consolidated as the CPI (Maoist) in 2004. The Government set 31 March 2026 as the deadline to end it; on 30 March 2026 the Home Minister told the Lok Sabha that Naxalism had been "wiped out" from the country.

1. Understanding LWE

  • Ideology and method: it rejects parliamentary democracy and wages guerrilla war from forest bases; the CPI (Maoist), formed by the merger of the People's War Group and the Maoist Communist Centre, was banned under the UAPA in 2009.
  • The Red Corridor: at its height it spread across forested, mineral-rich tribal areas of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal; affected districts were cut from 126 to 90 in 2018, and to seven by February 2026, of which three (Bijapur, Sukma and Narayanpur, all in Chhattisgarh's Bastar region) were "most affected".
  • Roots: land alienation, displacement by mines and dams, denial of forest rights and weak administration in remote tribal areas.

2. How people are affected

  • Violence against civilians: villagers branded "police informers" were killed after kangaroo courts ("jan adalats"); landmines and IEDs maimed many. The Home Minister put the toll over the decades at about 20,000 lives.
  • Development blocked: schools, roads and mobile towers were destroyed, and contractors paid extortion "levies".
  • Tribals caught in the crossfire: displacement, forced recruitment, including of children, and fear; State-backed vigilantism (Salwa Judum) also hurt them, and the Supreme Court ordered it disbanded in Nandini Sundar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2011).
  • Security forces: heavy losses, as in the Dantewada ambush (April 2010, 76 killed).

3. Measures to eliminate LWE

  • Policy framework: the National Policy and Action Plan (2015) combines security, development and rights; the SAMADHAN strategy (2017) stresses smart leadership, actionable intelligence, technology and choking finances.
  • Security operations: CAPF and State forces such as the Greyhounds and the District Reserve Guard, fortified police stations and forward camps in core areas, and operations such as Operation Black Forest (2025) on the Chhattisgarh–Telangana border; CPI (Maoist) general secretary Basavaraju was killed in May 2025.
  • Results: in the last three years 706 Maoists were neutralised, 2,218 arrested and 4,839 surrendered (Home Minister, March 2026).
  • Development and connectivity: roads, mobile towers, 1,804 bank branches and 635 post offices over 12 years, Eklavya schools and ITIs, and the Special Central Assistance and Security Related Expenditure schemes.
  • Rights and rehabilitation: forest rights titles, PESA, PM-JANMAN and Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan, and surrender-and-rehabilitation policies.

The near-elimination of armed Maoism shows the success of a calibrated security-plus-development approach. Preventing a relapse now depends on good governance in tribal areas: secure land and forest rights, PESA, quality services and dignity for Adivasis.
free.upm-2025-gs3-11:
Fiscal Health IndexNITI AayogFiscal prudenceDebt sustainability

States carry most public spending on health, education, police and agriculture, and hold about a third of India's government debt, so national fiscal stability depends on them. NITI Aayog's Fiscal Health Index (FHI), first released in January 2025, ranks States on the soundness of their finances. Its second edition (March 2026) uses CAG-verified data for FY 2023-24 and ranks 18 major States, with 10 North-Eastern and Himalayan States ranked separately.

1. Design of the index

  • Five sub-indices: Quality of Expenditure, Revenue Mobilisation, Fiscal Prudence, Debt Index and Debt Sustainability, each built from simple ratios (table).
  • Composite score and categories: States get a score out of 100 and are grouped as Achievers, Front Runners, Performers or Aspirational.
  • Results of FHI 2026: Odisha leads (73.1), followed by Goa and Jharkhand; Kerala, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Punjab (12.4) are "Aspirational".

2. FHI as a tool for assessing fiscal performance

  • Beyond one number: it looks past the single 3%-of-GSDP deficit target of FRBM laws to judge the quality of spending, the strength of own revenues and the burden of debt.
  • Objective and comparable: CAG-verified accounts make scores comparable across States and, edition by edition, over time, revealing trends, not just one year's snapshot.
  • Diagnostic: sub-index scores show each State's weak spot. Achievers combine strong own revenue, high capital outlay, contained deficits and moderate debt, while Aspirational States carry high debt and heavy committed spending on salaries, pensions and interest.
  • Early warning: a low or falling score flags debt stress, as in Punjab, before it becomes a crisis.

3. How it encourages prudent and sustainable fiscal policies

  • Competitive federalism: public rankings create peer pressure and reputational incentives, as NITI's SDG India Index has done for development outcomes.
  • Market discipline: lenders and rating agencies can price State government bonds by fiscal strength, rewarding prudent States with cheaper borrowing.
  • Better quality of spending: by rewarding capital outlay and development spending, it nudges States away from untargeted subsidies and populist giveaways.
  • Revenue effort: scoring own revenue pushes States to widen tax bases, revise user charges and collect non-tax revenue such as mining royalties.
  • Policy linkage: the scores can inform Finance Commission grants, borrowing limits and the Centre's interest-free capital loans to States, and guide each State's medium-term fiscal plan.

4. Limitations

  • Hidden liabilities: off-budget borrowings, guarantees and losses of power distribution companies are not fully captured.
  • Time lag and context: data are two years old, and special-category States with weak tax bases need separate yardsticks, as the index partly recognises.
  • Relative scores: a better rank need not mean absolute improvement.

The FHI turns fiscal data into a report card that States cannot ignore. Linking it to incentives and adding off-budget debt and guarantees can make competitive and cooperative fiscal federalism work together for sustainable public finances.
free.upm-2025-gs3-12:
Production Linked IncentiveAtmanirbhar BharatDomestic value additionGlobal value chains

The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme pays eligible firms a percentage of their incremental sales of goods made in India over a base year, for about five years. Launched in 2020 for mobile phones, bulk drugs and medical devices, it was extended to 14 sectors with an outlay of nearly ₹2 lakh crore, making it the centrepiece of Atmanirbhar Bharat in manufacturing.

1. Rationale

  • Stagnant manufacturing: its share of GDP has hovered around 15–17% for decades, too low to employ India's young workforce.
  • Cost disadvantages: Indian firms face higher costs of capital, power, logistics and compliance than rivals in China and Vietnam; an output-linked incentive offsets this disability while firms build scale.
  • Import dependence: electronics, bulk drugs (APIs) and solar modules came largely from China, a strategic risk exposed during COVID-19.
  • China-plus-one: firms diversifying supply chains could be drawn to India.
  • Performance-based design: money is paid only after output is achieved, and it is not tied to exports, unlike earlier export subsidies such as MEIS that a WTO panel ruled against in 2019.

2. Achievements

  • Overall: by June 2026, about ₹2.59 lakh crore of actual investment, production and sales of ₹23.79 lakh crore and over 14.5 lakh direct and indirect jobs; incentives of ₹36,754 crore had been paid (DPIIT data).
  • Mobile phones: 99.2% of mobile phones used in India are now made in India (MeitY), and India has become a major exporter of smartphones.
  • Pharmaceuticals and devices: cumulative sales of about ₹4 lakh crore under the pharmaceuticals scheme by June 2026 (PIB), domestic production of critical bulk drugs, and manufacture of CT scanners, MRI systems and cath labs.
  • Other sectors: solar modules drew the most investment; the white-goods scheme is building domestic capacity for air-conditioner compressors and other components.

3. Shortcomings

  • Uneven uptake: large-scale electronics received over half of all incentives paid (about ₹19,091 crore), while nothing had been paid under advanced chemistry cell batteries and little under textiles, IT hardware and steel.
  • Shallow value addition: much electronics output is assembly of imports.
  • Slow disbursal: only about a fifth of the outlay had been paid in six years, since payment depends on meeting output targets and several schemes started late.

4. Improving functioning and outcomes

  • Deepen value chains: shift support to components and sub-assemblies, as the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (2025) and the India Semiconductor Mission do.
  • Reward what matters: link incentives to domestic value addition, R&D and jobs, not sales alone.
  • Faster, transparent payments: online claims, time-bound verification and independent evaluation of each scheme.
  • Fix the fundamentals: lower input tariffs, cheaper logistics, reliable power and easier land and labour rules, so firms stay competitive after incentives end.
  • Redesign laggards: revise or close schemes with poor uptake, and bring in MSME suppliers.

PLI has shown, most clearly in mobile phones, that performance-linked support can make India a manufacturing base. Its lasting success will be judged by domestic value addition, jobs and the ability of firms to compete without subsidies.
free.upm-2025-gs3-13:
Groundwater depletionOver-exploitationAtal Bhujal YojanaAquifer management

India is the world's largest user of groundwater, which supplies most of its irrigation and drinking water. The Central Ground Water Board's 2025 assessment put extraction at about 61% of the annually extractable resource nationally, but about 11% of assessment units (730 of 6,762) are over-exploited. Punjab (156%), Rajasthan (147%) and Haryana (137%) extract far more than they recharge, and falling water tables threaten food and water security.

1. Factors responsible for depletion

  • Power and price policies: free or flat-rate electricity for farm pumps, as in Punjab, makes pumping almost costless, so farmers have no reason to save water.
  • Cropping pattern: assured MSP and procurement make water-hungry paddy and sugarcane profitable even in semi-arid Punjab, Haryana and Maharashtra.
  • Tube-well revolution: cheap pumps and borewells have replaced canals and tanks; groundwater now irrigates more than half of India's irrigated area.
  • Legal vacuum: under the Indian Easements Act, 1882, groundwater is treated as attached to land, so landowners may pump without limit.
  • Urbanisation and industry: cities such as Bengaluru, Chennai and Delhi rely on borewells, while concrete surfaces cut recharge.
  • Less recharge and more stress: encroached tanks and wetlands, deforestation and short, intense monsoon spells increase runoff; arsenic, fluoride, nitrate and salinity make part of the resource unusable.

2. Steps taken by the government

  • Regulation: the Central Ground Water Authority (1997, under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986) issued guidelines in 2020 requiring permission for groundwater extraction by industry, infrastructure and bulk users; model groundwater bills have helped States enact their own laws.
  • Community management: the Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019, ₹6,000 crore) in seven States rewards gram panchayats for water budgeting and demand-side measures.
  • Aquifer mapping: the National Aquifer Mapping and Management Programme (NAQUIM) of the CGWB maps aquifers to guide local plans.
  • Recharge: Jal Shakti Abhiyan "Catch the Rain", Mission Amrit Sarovar (2022, 75 ponds in each district), watershed works and MGNREGA water conservation assets.
  • Water-saving farming: micro-irrigation under PMKSY "Per Drop More Crop"; crop diversification incentives such as Haryana's "Mera Pani Meri Virasat"; Punjab's Preservation of Subsoil Water Act, 2009, which bars early paddy sowing and transplanting so that it moves closer to the monsoon.
  • Power reforms: separate feeders for farm power, pioneered by Gujarat's Jyotigram Yojana (2003), and solar pumps under PM-KUSUM that let farmers sell surplus power instead of overusing water.

3. Gaps

  • Weak enforcement: farm pumping, the largest user, is largely unregulated.
  • Perverse incentives: free power and paddy procurement continue to reward overuse.
  • Data: too few real-time monitoring wells to manage aquifers locally.

Groundwater is India's invisible lifeline. Moving from unchecked extraction to aquifer stewardship, through rational power pricing, crop diversification, recharge and community regulation, is essential for long-term water security.
free.upm-2025-gs3-14:
Food processingValue additionEmployment generationPMFME and PLISFPI

Food processing turns farm, dairy, fishery and livestock produce into higher-value, longer-lasting products. India has a strong raw-material base: it is the largest producer of milk and pulses and the second-largest of fruits and vegetables. Yet only a small share of its perishable output is processed, and post-harvest losses are worth about ₹1.53 lakh crore a year (NABCONS, 2022). The sector links farm and factory, cuts waste and is among the largest employers in organised manufacturing.

1. Scope of food processing industries

  • Abundant, diverse raw material: varied agro-climates give year-round supplies of fruits, vegetables, millets, spices, milk, fish and shrimp.
  • Low processing levels: the large gap between production and processing means wide headroom for value addition and loss reduction.
  • Growing demand: urbanisation, rising incomes, smaller families and more working women increase demand for packaged, ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat foods, sold through supermarkets, e-commerce and quick-commerce apps.
  • Exports: marine products, rice, spices and mango pulp already sell abroad; branded Indian foods can capture more value.
  • Labour-intensive and rural: micro and small units in villages and towns employ many people, including women in self-help groups, and create demand for packaging, logistics and cold chains.

2. Measures taken by the government to generate employment

  • PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (2017): integrated cold chains, food processing units, agro-processing clusters, backward and forward linkages, and Operation Greens for perishables, mostly in rural areas.
  • PLI Scheme for Food Processing Industries (₹10,900 crore, 2021-22 to 2026-27): incentives for ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat foods, processed fruits and vegetables, marine products, mozzarella cheese and millet-based products, and support for branding Indian foods abroad.
  • PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME, 2020, ₹10,000 crore): a 35% credit-linked subsidy of up to ₹10 lakh for micro units, seed capital for SHG members and common facilities under One District One Product.
  • Investment and credit: 100% FDI under the automatic route in food processing; 100% FDI (government route) in retail trade, including e-commerce, of food made in India; a ₹2,000 crore Food Processing Fund with NABARD; priority-sector lending; and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for post-harvest units.
  • Skills and markets: NIFTEM institutes, the sector skill council for food industries, and the World Food India expos that connect processors with investors and buyers.

3. Challenges

  • Supply side: small, scattered farms make steady, uniform supply difficult.
  • Infrastructure: gaps in cold chains, reliable power and testing labs raise costs.
  • Informality: most units are tiny and unregistered, with weak access to credit, technology and FSSAI compliance.

With the right infrastructure and policy push, food processing can be the bridge between farm and factory, a jobs engine for rural India and women, and a pillar of India's ambition to be the food basket of the world.
free.upm-2025-gs3-15:
NanotechnologyNano-fertilisersPrecision agricultureFarmers' incomes

Nanotechnology is the control of matter at 1–100 nanometres (a nanometre is a billionth of a metre), where particles have a very high surface-area-to-volume ratio and new properties. In agriculture this allows nutrients and pesticides to be delivered in smaller, targeted doses and crops to be monitored in real time. India's Nano Mission (2007) and IFFCO's Nano Urea (liquid, 2021) and Nano DAP (2023) have taken it from the laboratory to the field.

1. Advancements in agriculture

  • Nano-fertilisers: nano urea and nano DAP are sprayed on leaves, which absorb nitrogen and phosphorus more efficiently than from soil-applied granules, reducing losses through leaching and volatilisation; nano forms of zinc and other micronutrients are also being developed.
  • Nano-pesticides: nano-encapsulation releases the active ingredient slowly at the target, lowering doses, residues and runoff into water bodies.
  • Nano-sensors and precision farming: sensors detect soil moisture, nutrients, pathogens and pesticide residues, and link to IoT devices and drones for real-time decisions.
  • Seeds and soil: nano-coatings can improve germination, while nano-clays and hydrogels help sandy soils hold water in dry spells.
  • Post-harvest and food safety: nano-silver and nano-clay packaging films extend shelf life; nano-based kits give quick diagnosis of plant and animal diseases.
  • Water: nano-filters such as IIT Madras's AMRIT remove arsenic and iron from water.

2. Uplifting the socio-economic status of farmers

  • Lower input and transport costs: IFFCO says a 500 ml bottle of nano urea can replace a bag of granular urea, which is far easier for a small farmer to carry and store.
  • Higher net incomes: precise inputs, healthier crops, fewer post-harvest losses and residue-free produce fetch better prices, including in export markets.
  • New rural jobs: drone spraying of nano-fertilisers creates work; the Namo Drone Didi scheme provides drones to women's self-help groups to offer spraying services.
  • Soil, water and health: smaller chemical loads protect soil health, groundwater and farmers' own health, lowering long-term costs.
  • Fiscal gains for welfare: lower use of subsidised, largely imported fertilisers would ease the subsidy bill and free funds for farmers.
  • Climate resilience: hydrogels and sensors help farmers cope with dry spells and erratic rain.

3. Caution needed

  • Evidence: some independent field studies have questioned the yield claims made for nano urea, so long-term, independent trials by ICAR and agricultural universities must guide advice to farmers.
  • Safety: nanoparticles may build up in soil and food chains; India has no nano-specific law, so testing, labelling and liability rules need strengthening.
  • Access: small farmers need demonstrations, extension and credit to avoid a "nano-divide".

Nanotechnology can make Indian farming precise, resource-efficient and profitable, but only if it is backed by independent evidence, a risk-based regulator and extension that reaches the smallest farmer.
free.upm-2025-gs3-16:
Semiconductor manufacturingIndia Semiconductor MissionFabs and OSATSupply-chain resilience

Semiconductors are the foundation of phones, computers, cars, telecom, defence systems and AI. Their production is concentrated in a few places, notably Taiwan for advanced chips, so the 2021 chip shortage and US–China export controls exposed import-dependent India. The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM, December 2021, ₹76,000 crore) and ISM 2.0 (₹1,27,500 crore, approved July 2026) aim to make India a manufacturing hub.

1. Challenges for the semiconductor industry in India

  • Capital intensity and long gestation: a single fab costs billions of dollars, takes years to build and needs constant upgrading as technology moves on.
  • Technology access: process know-how, intellectual property and equipment such as lithography machines are held by a few foreign firms, so India depends on partners such as PSMC (Taiwan) and Micron (USA).
  • Infrastructure: fabs need uninterrupted, high-quality power, huge volumes of ultra-pure water, specialty gases and chemicals, and dust-free clean rooms.
  • Thin supply chain: there is almost no domestic base for wafers, equipment, materials or gases.
  • Talent: India is strong in chip design, but short of fab process engineers and technicians.
  • Global competition and geopolitics: large subsidies in the USA, EU, Japan and China, export controls and tension around Taiwan; earlier Indian fab proposals did not take off.

2. Salient features of the India Semiconductor Mission

  • Institution: a specialised, independent business division within the Digital India Corporation under MeitY, led by industry experts, runs the schemes.
  • Fiscal support: up to 50% of project cost for silicon and display fabs, and up to 50% of capital expenditure for compound semiconductor, sensor and ATMP/OSAT units, with additional support from States.
  • Design Linked Incentive (DLI): financial support for Indian chip-design start-ups and MSMEs; the Chips to Startup programme builds design skills.
  • Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL), Mohali: modernisation of the government's own fab.
  • Progress: by May 2026, 12 projects worth about ₹1.64 lakh crore were approved in six States, including Tata Electronics–PSMC's fab at Dholera (India's first commercial fab), Micron, CG Power–Renesas and Kaynes units at Sanand, a Tata unit in Assam and units in Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh. Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi had begun commercial production by September 2026.
  • Milestones: the first made-in-India chips, including ISRO-SCL's Vikram 3201 space processor, were presented at SEMICON India 2025; C-DAC launched the DHRUV64 microprocessor.
  • ISM 2.0 (Cabinet, 15 July 2026): extends support to equipment, materials, gases and Indian chip IP, and targets meeting 70–75% of domestic chip demand by 2029.

3. Way forward

  • Ecosystem first: plug-and-play semiconductor parks with assured water, power and gas supply.
  • People: specialised courses and industry-linked training for fab technicians and engineers.
  • Partnerships and demand: trusted technology partners and assured demand from electronics, automotive and defence buyers.

India has moved from ambition to first production. Sustained policy support, reliable utilities and a skilled workforce can make it a trusted node in global semiconductor supply chains.
free.upm-2025-gs3-17:
MiningEnvironmental hazardsSustainable miningMine closure
