Minerals such as coal, iron ore, bauxite and limestone are the base of India's energy, steel and cement, and critical minerals such as lithium are vital for the clean-energy transition, for which India launched the National Critical Mineral Mission in 2025. But mining, especially open-cast mining, which yielded about 96% of India's coal in 2023-24, strips away forests, soil and rock, making it one of the most environmentally hazardous economic activities.

1. Why mining is an environmental hazard

  • Land and forests: clearing forests and dumping overburden destroy habitats and wildlife corridors, as feared in Chhattisgarh's Hasdeo Arand, and leave land barren.
  • Water: deep pits cut through aquifers and lower water tables; acid mine drainage and heavy metals from tailings pollute streams; silt chokes rivers.
  • Air and health: dust from blasting, crushing and trucks causes respiratory disease and silicosis; coal-seam fires at Jharia have burned for over a century, releasing toxic gases and causing land subsidence.
  • Soil and slope instability: topsoil is lost, erosion rises, unstable dumps slide, and underground workings can cause subsidence and even minor earthquakes.
  • Illegal and sand mining: riverbed sand mining lowers water tables and weakens bridges; illegal iron-ore mining led the Supreme Court to halt mining in Bellary (2011) and Goa (2012).
  • Social costs: Adivasi communities in Fifth Schedule areas lose land, forests and livelihoods.

2. Remedial measures required

  • Before mining: environmental impact assessment with public hearing (EIA Notification, 2006), forest clearance with compensatory afforestation (CAMPA Act, 2016), Gram Sabha consent under PESA and the Forest Rights Act, and no-go areas for dense forests and corridors.
  • During mining: water sprinklers and mist cannons, covered conveyors and rail transport in place of trucks, controlled blasting, garland drains and settling ponds, reuse of treated mine water by nearby villages, and green belts.
  • Monitoring and enforcement: the Indian Bureau of Mines' satellite-based Mining Surveillance System and drones against illegal mining; star rating of mines for sustainable practices; sand-mining guidelines (2016, 2020); and stiff penalties, as in Common Cause v. Union of India (2017), where the Supreme Court ordered recovery of the full value of illegally mined ore in Odisha.
  • Benefit sharing: District Mineral Foundations under the MMDR Amendment Act, 2015 fund health, water and livelihoods for mining-affected people through PMKKKY.
  • After mining: mandatory progressive and final mine-closure plans with financial assurance; backfilling, topsoil replacement and native plantation; pit lakes as water bodies; eco-parks and solar farms on reclaimed land.
  • Less fresh mining: recycling of metals and recovery of critical minerals from waste and tailings support a circular economy.

Mining is indispensable, but sustainability must run from exploration to closure. "Mine, restore and return", backed by strict enforcement, community benefit-sharing and recycling, can reconcile mineral security with environmental justice.
free.upm-2025-gs3-18:
Paris AgreementNationally Determined ContributionsPanchamritNet zero 2070

The Paris Agreement (2015) under the UNFCCC aims to hold warming "well below 2 °C" and to pursue 1.5 °C. Each country sets its own Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and must update it every five years with higher ambition. India, the third-largest emitter in total but low per capita, guided by common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR-RC), submitted its intended NDC in October 2015, announced the Panchamrit at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) and updated its NDC in August 2022.

1. India's commitments under the Paris Agreement (2015)

  • Emissions intensity: reduce the emissions intensity of GDP by 33–35% by 2030 from the 2005 level.
  • Clean power: about 40% of cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030, with technology transfer and low-cost finance, including from the Green Climate Fund.
  • Carbon sink: an additional sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent through more forest and tree cover by 2030.
  • Other goals: sustainable lifestyles, a cleaner development path, adaptation in agriculture, water, coasts and health, finance mobilisation and capacity building.

2. Review of performance

  • Ahead of schedule: the 40% non-fossil capacity goal was met in 2021, nine years early, and 50% was reached in June 2025; emissions intensity fell 36% between 2005 and 2020 (fourth Biennial Update Report, December 2024).
  • Institutions: the National Action Plan on Climate Change (8 missions), State action plans, the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019).
  • Gaps: coal still produces about 70% of electricity; adaptation needs are under-funded, and the developed countries' US$100 billion a year goal was met only in 2022.

3. Strengthening at COP26: the Panchamrit (2021)

  • Five nectar elements: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030; one billion tonnes less projected carbon emissions by 2030; a 45% cut in the carbon intensity of the economy by 2030; and net zero by 2070.
  • LiFE: India also proposed "Lifestyle for Environment" as a global mass movement.

4. Updating the first NDC in 2022

  • Approved by the Cabinet on 3 August 2022 and communicated to the UNFCCC, covering 2021–2030.
  • Higher ambition: the intensity target rose from 33–35% to 45% by 2030, and the non-fossil capacity target from 40% to about 50% of installed capacity by 2030.
  • New element: a mass movement for LiFE became part of the NDC.
  • Unchanged: the 2.5–3 billion tonne sink target; the other Panchamrit pledges stay as domestic goals, and net zero by 2070 was set out in the long-term strategy submitted at COP27 (November 2022).
  • Since then: NDC 3.0 (March 2026) raises the targets to a 47% intensity cut and 60% non-fossil capacity by 2035.

India has under-promised and over-delivered: the 2022 update turned Glasgow's political pledges into formal NDC targets. Meeting net zero by 2070 will need climate finance, technology transfer and a just transition from coal, guided by CBDR-RC and LiFE.
free.upm-2025-gs3-19:
Insurgency in the North-EastEthnic conflictPeace accordsAct East

The North-East, eight States joined to the rest of India by the narrow Siliguri Corridor and sharing about 98% of their boundaries with Bhutan, China, Myanmar, Bangladesh and Nepal, faces security challenges rooted in ethnic diversity, identity politics, difficult terrain and porous borders. Since 2014 the Government has signed a series of peace accords, and the Home Ministry reports that insurgency incidents in 2025 were 82% lower than in 2014, the lowest in two and a half decades.

1. Major challenges to internal security and the peace process

  • Unfinished insurgencies: Naga talks under the 2015 Framework Agreement with NSCN(IM) remain stuck on a separate flag and constitution; holdout groups such as ULFA(I) and some NSCN factions operate from camps in Myanmar.
  • Ethnic conflict in Manipur: Meitei–Kuki-Zo violence since 3 May 2023 has killed hundreds and displaced about 60,000 people; President's Rule, imposed on 13 February 2025, was revoked on 4 February 2026 to make way for a popular government led by Y. Khemchand Singh.
  • Porous Myanmar border: the 1,643 km border, the Free Movement Regime and the 2021 coup in Myanmar have eased arms and drug trafficking from the Golden Triangle and refugee inflows; the Centre decided in 2024 to fence the border and curb the regime.
  • Identity, land and boundaries: fears of demographic change from migration, overlapping territorial claims of tribes, and inter-State boundary disputes, such as the Assam–Mizoram clash of July 2021.
  • Trust deficit: incidents such as the killing of civilians at Oting, Nagaland (December 2021), extortion by armed groups and debates over AFSPA.

2. Peace accords and agreements of the past decade

  • Insurgency settlements: the Bodo (2020), Karbi (2021), Adivasi (2022), DNLA and ULFA (2023) accords in Assam, and the NLFT(SD) (2019) and NLFT–ATTF (2024) accords in Tripura together brought over 10,000 cadres into the mainstream.
  • Manipur: the UNLF agreement (November 2023), a cessation of operations with the ZUF (2022), and revised suspension-of-operations ground rules with Kuki-Zo groups UPF and KNO (September 2025).
  • Autonomy and identity: the Bodoland Territorial Region (2020), the TIPRA agreement on indigenous issues in Tripura (March 2024) and the Frontier Nagaland Territorial Authority (February 2026).
  • Boundary settlements: the Assam–Meghalaya MoU (March 2022) resolving six of twelve disputed areas, and the Assam–Arunachal MoU (April 2023) covering 123 villages.
  • Peace dividend: AFSPA has been withdrawn completely from Tripura (2015) and Meghalaya (2018) and from most of Assam; civilian deaths are down 97% since 2014 (MHA).

3. Way forward

  • Complete the unfinished: a final Naga settlement, reconciliation, rehabilitation of the displaced and recovery of looted arms in Manipur.
  • Deliver on accords: time-bound funds and institutions promised in each accord.
  • Develop and connect: PM-DevINE, Act East connectivity, and border fencing with safeguards for cross-border communities.

The accords have moved the North-East from insurgency to integration. Implementing them in letter and spirit, and healing Manipur, can make the region India's gateway to Act East.
free.upm-2025-gs3-20:
Maritime securitySea lines of communicationCoastal securityMAHASAGAR

About 95% of India's trade by volume and 70% by value moves by sea, and most of its crude oil arrives by tanker. With a coastline of about 11,099 km (2025 re-measurement), an Exclusive Economic Zone of over 2 million sq km, and major ports that handled a record 915 million tonnes in 2025-26, maritime security, meaning safe sea lanes, ports and coasts, is vital to India's economy, energy and sovereignty.

1. Why maritime security is vital for India's sea trade

  • Energy lifelines: the Strait of Hormuz carries about half of India's crude imports and most of its LPG and LNG; the 2026 West Asia crisis showed how quickly disruption raises costs.
  • Freight, insurance and competitiveness: insecurity raises insurance premiums and forces long detours, as when Red Sea attacks in 2023–24 sent ships around the Cape of Good Hope.
  • Blue economy and infrastructure: fisheries, offshore oil and gas, ports and undersea data cables depend on secure waters.
  • Strategic role: India seeks to be the first responder and a net security provider in the Indian Ocean.

2. Maritime and coastal security challenges

  • Piracy: Somali piracy revived in 2023–24; the Indian Navy rescued the hijacked MV Ruen in March 2024 under Operation Sankalp.
  • Attacks on shipping: missile and drone attacks by the Houthis in the Red Sea, and the drone strike on the tanker MV Chem Pluto off the Gujarat coast (December 2023).
  • Sea-borne terrorism: the 1993 Mumbai blasts used explosives landed on the Raigad coast, and the 26/11 attackers (2008) arrived by boat.
  • Smuggling: narcotics (about 3,000 kg of heroin seized at Mundra port in 2021), arms, gold and fake currency.
  • Fishing and boundary issues: illegal fishing by foreign trawlers and the arrest of fishermen in the Palk Bay.
  • Strategic competition: Chinese research and survey vessels and dual-use ports in the region, such as Gwadar and Hambantota.
  • Weak coordination: many agencies, under-equipped State marine police and lakhs of small fishing boats that are hard to track.

3. Way forward

  • Coordination: strengthen the National Maritime Security Coordinator (2022) in the National Security Council Secretariat, and adopt a national maritime security strategy.
  • Surveillance: a coastal radar chain, AIS transponders on fishing boats, the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (Gurugram, 2018) and the NC3I network to share the maritime picture.
  • Capability: a stronger Navy and Coast Guard, indigenous warships such as INS Vikrant (2022), better-equipped State marine police, and coastal communities as "eyes and ears".
  • Law: the Maritime Anti-Piracy Act, 2022 allows prosecution of pirates caught on the high seas.
  • Partnerships: SAGAR (2015), expanded as MAHASAGAR (2025), the Quad, the Indian Ocean Rim Association, the Colombo Security Conclave and white-shipping agreements.
  • Economic resilience: diversified energy routes, strategic reserves and more Indian-flagged ships.

India's prosperity rides on the sea. A whole-of-government maritime strategy combining surveillance, capable forces, coordinated agencies and regional partnerships under MAHASAGAR can secure trade and make India the Indian Ocean's preferred security partner.
free.upm-2025-gs4-1a:
Digital ethicsFree speech vs harmPrivacyAlgorithmic accountability

Social media has turned every user into a publisher and created a borderless digital public sphere. It has amplified unheard voices, helped in disasters and widened democratic debate. But the same features that make it powerful (speed, anonymity, virality and data-driven design) also create ethical dilemmas: situations in which two legitimate values, such as freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) and protection from harm, pull in opposite directions.

1. Free expression vs harm to others

  • Speech vs hate and rumour: rumours of child-lifters spread on messaging apps led to mob lynchings in 2018; in Tehseen Poonawalla v UoI (2018) the Supreme Court asked governments to curb content that incites such violence. Yet over-zealous blocking chills legitimate dissent.
  • Who decides what is true? If platforms or governments remove content, they risk becoming censors; if they do nothing, falsehood outruns correction. In Shreya Singhal v UoI (2015) the Court struck down the vague Section 66A of the IT Act: limits on speech must be narrow and lawful.
  • Trial by social media: viral outrage can destroy reputations before facts are known, undermining the presumption of innocence.

2. Connectivity vs privacy

  • "Free" services paid for with data: platforms profit by profiling users for targeted advertising; the Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018) showed how harvested data can be used to influence voters.
  • Consent as a formality: long, opaque terms reduce consent to a click, although privacy is a fundamental right (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017). The DPDP Act, 2023, whose duties are being phased in under the DPDP Rules notified in November 2025, requires informed consent, but tension with state access to data remains.

3. Engagement vs well-being

  • Addictive design: infinite scroll, likes and autoplay are built to maximise screen time, raising concerns about anxiety, sleep loss and poor attention among adolescents.
  • Children: the DPDP Act requires verifiable parental consent for users under 18 and bars tracking and targeted advertising aimed at them; Australia has set a minimum age of 16 for social media accounts (from December 2025). The dilemma is protection versus autonomy and access to information.
  • Cyberbullying and trolling, especially of women and minorities, push people out of public debate.

4. Authenticity vs manipulation

  • Anonymity: it protects whistle-blowers and dissenters but also shields trolls, bots and fake accounts; tracing originators, in turn, threatens encryption and privacy.
  • Deepfakes: generative AI blurs truth and fiction; the IT Amendment Rules, 2026 (in force from 20 February 2026) require AI-generated ("synthetic") content to be labelled prominently, and complaints about non-consensual intimate or morphed images to be acted on within two hours.
  • Influencer ethics: paid promotions passed off as personal opinion deceive followers; the Department of Consumer Affairs' guidelines (January 2023) require influencers to disclose them.

The answer lies not in sacrificing one value for another but in balancing them through ethics by design, transparent algorithms, proportionate regulation and digital literacy, so that every user becomes a responsible digital citizen.
free.upm-2025-gs4-1b:
Constitutional moralityRule of lawGood governanceAccountability

Constitutional morality means respect for the core norms of the Constitution, not merely its text: the rule of law, liberty, equality and dignity. Introducing the Draft Constitution on 4 November 1948, Dr B.R. Ambedkar took the idea from the historian George Grote ("a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution") and added, in his own words, that it "is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." The statement adds how: through civic education and adherence to the rule of law.

1. Meaning: why it must be cultivated

  • Beyond legality: an act may be legal yet violate the Constitution's spirit; constitutional morality guides where the text is silent.
  • Judicial articulation: in Manoj Narula v UoI (2014) the Supreme Court described it as bowing to the norms of the Constitution and not acting arbitrarily; in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) it held that constitutional morality prevails over majoritarian social morality.
  • How it is cultivated: civic education (Fundamental Duties under Article 51A), training of officials, and daily practice in which institutions keep within their limits.

2. Significance for the public servant

  • Loyalty to the Constitution, not to persons: the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, as amended in 2014, require officers to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution and democratic values, and to act with political neutrality.
  • Compass for discretion: non-arbitrariness is part of equality (E.P. Royappa, 1974); constitutional morality guides choices where rules leave room for judgement.
  • Protection of the vulnerable: it obliges officials to protect individual rights even against popular pressure, as in Shakti Vahini v UoI (2018), where the Court directed the police and district officials to protect couples threatened with "honour" crimes.
  • Moral courage: it helps the officer refuse illegal orders and give frank advice.

3. Role in promoting good governance

  • Rule of law and predictability: decisions follow law and due process, not whim; in its November 2024 judgment on demolitions, the Supreme Court held that the executive cannot act as judge and punish the accused by demolishing homes.
  • Equity and inclusion: the Directive Principles and Article 14 push administration towards the last citizen, not the most influential one.
  • Transparency and participation: proactive disclosure under the RTI Act, 2005, consultation and reasoned orders make governance open.

4. Role in ensuring accountability

  • Answerability to law and citizens: constitutional morality treats power as a trust; officials must explain their decisions to courts, the legislature (through the CAG and committees) and the public.
  • Natural justice: fair procedure (Maneka Gandhi, 1978) and speaking orders make decisions reviewable.
  • Limits on coercive power: safeguards on arrest and custody (D.K. Basu, 1997) show that even the state's strongest powers remain answerable.

Constitutional morality turns the Constitution from a legal document into a living ethic of administration. Cultivated through civic education, training and example, it makes the civil servant the guardian of a just and accountable state.
free.upm-2025-gs4-2a:
ClausewitzWar and politicsJust warDiplomacy first

The Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz, in On War (published 1832), argued that war is not an end in itself but the pursuit of political purpose by other means; the statement in the question expresses this idea. War and diplomacy are thus two instruments of the same statecraft: force is used when talks fail, and talks resume when force has achieved, or failed to achieve, its aim. Contemporary conflicts both confirm and challenge this view.

1. Where the statement holds today

  • Wars still serve political aims: in the Russia–Ukraine war (since February 2022) the fighting is tied to disputes over security, NATO expansion and sovereignty, and ceasefire diplomacy has run alongside the battlefield.
  • Force as signalling: limited, calibrated strikes are used to deter rather than to conquer, as in India's responses to cross-border terrorist attacks in 2016, 2019 and 2025, which it presented as limited action against terrorist targets, not a wider war.
  • Negotiating while fighting: in the Gaza war that followed the attack of 7 October 2023, hostage and ceasefire negotiations through mediators ran alongside the military campaign.
  • Coercive diplomacy: threats, military exercises and naval deployments strengthen a negotiating hand.

2. Where it falls short

  • Means overtake ends: once begun, wars escape political control; Clausewitz himself warned of the "fog" and "friction" of war. Mass civilian deaths, displacement and famine conditions outlast any political gain.
  • The nuclear age: between nuclear powers, total war would destroy the very political purpose it serves; deterrence, not war, becomes the instrument.
  • Non-state actors: terrorist groups and militias, such as those attacking Red Sea shipping since late 2023, wage war for ideology or identity, not for negotiable state policy.
  • Grey-zone and hybrid conflict: cyber-attacks, disinformation, sanctions and the weaponisation of trade, energy and supply chains blur the line between war and peace.
  • Law and ethics: the UN Charter (Article 2(4)) bans the use of force except in self-defence (Article 51) or with Security Council authorisation, and the Geneva Conventions (1949) bind conduct in war; war is no longer an ordinary tool of policy.

3. An ethical perspective

  • Just war theory: force is justified only for a just cause, as a last resort and with proportionality (jus ad bellum), and must spare civilians (jus in bello).
  • Indian thought: Kautilya placed danda (force) after sama, dana and bheda; Krishna's peace mission preceded the Mahabharata war; Ashoka turned from conquest to dhamma after Kalinga; Gandhi showed the power of non-violent struggle.
  • India's position: at Samarkand in September 2022, India's Prime Minister told the Russian President that today's era is not an era of war, stressing dialogue and diplomacy.

Clausewitz rightly saw that war is always political, but in an interdependent, nuclear world it is the costliest and least certain instrument of politics. Ethics demands that diplomacy be the first resort, force the last and proportionate, and lasting peace the purpose.
free.upm-2025-gs4-2b:
National security vs ecologyEnvironmental clearanceHimalayan fragilitySustainable security

India's land frontiers in the Himalaya, from Ladakh to Arunachal Pradesh, and island frontiers such as Great Nicobar, are also among its most ecologically sensitive areas. The build-up of roads, airfields and dams across the Line of Actual Control has pushed India to fast-track strategic infrastructure, often with relaxed environmental clearance. This creates a genuine dilemma, because national security and ecological security both protect the nation and its people.

1. Context: controversies over clearances

  • Exemptions by law: the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 exempts forest land within 100 km of international borders, the LoC or the LAC from prior clearance for strategic linear projects of national importance.
  • Char Dham roads: in Ministry of Defence v Citizens for Green Doon (December 2021) the Supreme Court allowed wider roads on three strategic feeder roads, saying it could not second-guess the armed forces' needs, but set up an oversight committee under Justice A.K. Sikri.
  • Great Nicobar project: a port, airport and township near the Malacca Strait, with strategic value but large forest diversion and concerns for coral reefs, turtle nesting and the Shompen, a PVTG.
  • Siang Upper Multipurpose Project: the proposed 11,200 MW dam in Arunachal Pradesh, a water-security buffer against China's project on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo, is still at the pre-feasibility stage, its site not yet fixed, amid protests by sections of the Adi community over the loss of ancestral land and livelihoods (as of October 2026).

2. The ethical dilemmas

  • Security vs sustainability: the state's first duty is to defend its territory, but Articles 48A and 51A(g) and intergenerational equity demand protection of fragile ecosystems. Joshimath's subsidence (2023) and the South Lhonak glacial-lake burst that destroyed the Teesta-III dam (October 2023) show that ecological damage also endangers strategic assets.
  • Secrecy vs transparency: strategic projects need confidentiality, but secrecy weakens scrutiny, and "national security" can become a blanket shield.
  • Speed vs due diligence: splitting the Char Dham project into segments under 100 km avoided a full Environmental Impact Assessment, ignoring cumulative impacts.
  • National interest vs local rights: border communities hold rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and customary laws, and are the eyes and ears of the frontier; alienating them weakens security itself.
  • Utilitarian vs rights-based reasoning: the security of the many is weighed against irreversible losses borne by a few.

3. Towards sustainable security

  • Cumulative assessment: study the carrying capacity of whole valleys, even when individual projects are exempt.
  • Independent expert oversight: confidential expert review, as by the Char Dham committee, reconciles secrecy with scrutiny.
  • Better engineering: tunnels, scientific muck disposal and drainage make roads safer and more durable.
  • Community partnership: consultation, fair compensation and local jobs, as the Vibrant Villages Programme intends, keep border people invested in security.

Security and ecology are not rivals: a landslide that cuts a border road is as much a threat as an adversary. The ethical path is sustainable security: build what is strategically necessary, in the least damaging way, with transparency to experts and respect for border communities.
free.upm-2025-gs4-3a:
ResilienceEquanimityTirukkuralCrisis leadership

The couplet comes from the Tirukkural of Thiruvalluvar, in its chapter on not losing heart in adversity. It means that those who stay calm and undisturbed in trouble end up defeating trouble itself: the problem, not the person, is "troubled". It celebrates equanimity (the sthitaprajna of the Bhagavad Gita) and resilience, the capacity to face setbacks with composure and keep acting.

1. What the couplet conveys

  • Response shapes outcome: suffering depends partly on how we respond; panic multiplies problems, while a steady mind finds solutions.
  • Equanimity, not indifference: to be "untroubled" is to remain composed and purposeful, not passive or careless; calm allows clear thinking and decisive action.
  • A shared insight: the Gita's ideal of one who is undisturbed in sorrow, the Buddhist virtue of upekkha, and the Stoic idea that our judgements, more than events, disturb us express the same truth.
  • Emotional intelligence: in modern terms, it is self-regulation, which lets a person manage stress and lead others in a crisis.

2. Examples from public life

  • ISRO's resilience: after the SLV-3 failure of 1979, Satish Dhawan took responsibility and the team, led by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, succeeded in 1980; after the Chandrayaan-2 lander was lost in 2019, Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023.
  • Odisha's disaster management: after the 1999 super cyclone, calm and systematic preparation enabled the evacuation of around a million people before Phailin (2013) and Fani (2019), keeping deaths low.
  • Arunima Sinha: a national-level volleyball player who lost a leg after being pushed from a train in 2011, she climbed Mount Everest in 2013.
  • Gandhi: the humiliation at Pietermaritzburg (1893) became the starting point of satyagraha rather than a cause of despair.

3. Relevance in the present context

  • For civil servants: disasters, pandemics, law-and-order crises and political pressure demand a calm leader; composure prevents panic among staff and citizens, as district control rooms showed during COVID-19.
  • For young people: in an age of exam pressure, job insecurity and social-media comparison, the couplet teaches that failure is an event, not an identity.
  • For institutions: organisations that treat crises as learning opportunities build resilience, through standard operating procedures, drills and after-action reviews.
  • A caution: equanimity must not become complacency; being prepared is part of being untroubled.

In an age of crises and constant noise, Thiruvalluvar teaches that inner stability is the first defence against adversity. A civil servant who stays calm, prepared and purposeful can turn trouble into an opportunity for service.
free.upm-2025-gs4-3b:
AttitudeSelf-transformationGrowth mindsetCitizen-centric administration

The statement, popularly attributed to the American psychologist and philosopher William James (1842–1910) though not traced in his own writings, holds that our lives are shaped less by circumstances than by our attitudes: the settled ways in which we think, feel and act towards people, events and ourselves. Since attitudes are learnt, they can be changed; and when attitudes change, behaviour and outcomes follow. This is the essence of self-transformation.

1. What the quotation conveys

  • Attitude has three parts: a cognitive part (beliefs), an affective part (feelings) and a behavioural part (actions); changing a belief changes feelings and conduct.
  • Internal locus of control: people who believe they can shape their lives take ownership instead of blaming fate or others.
  • Support from psychology: cognitive behavioural therapy treats distress by changing thought patterns, and the idea of a growth mindset shows that ability can be developed through effort.
  • A realistic reading: poverty and discrimination are real constraints; a changed attitude is necessary but not sufficient, and must be matched by opportunity and support.

2. Examples

  • Gandhi: the insult at Pietermaritzburg (1893) changed his attitude to injustice and turned a hesitant lawyer into the leader of satyagraha.
  • Ashoka: after the Kalinga war, a change of heart turned a conqueror into a ruler devoted to dhamma, tolerance and public welfare, as his edicts record.
  • Social change: Swachh Bharat relied on changing attitudes to sanitation, not only on building toilets; women's self-help groups such as Kerala's Kudumbashree turned dependence into enterprise and confidence.

3. Relevance in the present context

  • For individuals: resilience, mental health and lifelong learning depend on treating failure as feedback; a positive attitude helps people adapt to rapid technological change.
  • For society: deep problems such as gender bias, caste prejudice, wasteful consumption and indifference to rules are attitudinal; Mission LiFE (2022) seeks to change consumption habits to address climate change.
  • For civil servants: the move from a "ruler" to a "servant" attitude is the core of administrative reform. Mission Karmayogi (2020) seeks to shift the civil service from "rule" to "role", and empathy towards citizens changes how every scheme is delivered.

Laws and institutions succeed only when attitudes change. For individuals and for the nation, shifting from cynicism to hope and from entitlement to service is the most powerful lever of transformation.
free.upm-2025-gs4-3c:
Social moralityRule of lawCharacter buildingVoluntary compliance

Swami Vivekananda believed that a nation is built by character, not merely by institutions. Laws set the minimum standard of behaviour and punish deviation, but they work only when citizens have internalised values such as honesty, compassion and respect for others. The quotation contrasts external compulsion (law) with inner conviction (morality), and places a society's real strength in the latter.

1. What the quotation conveys

  • Laws are necessary but not sufficient: law is the floor and ethics the ceiling; no law can foresee every situation or reach every private act.
  • Enforcement depends on consent: the state cannot post a policeman at every corner; societies function because most people obey rules voluntarily.
  • Morality makes laws work and makes good laws: the abolition of sati (1829) rested on the reform movement led by Raja Ram Mohan Roy; reform of attitudes gave the law its force.
  • Character-building: Vivekananda stressed "man-making" education, building inner strength and selflessness, as the base of national regeneration.

2. The present context: the gap between law and morality

  • Laws that society evades: dowry has been illegal since 1961 and child marriage is barred by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, yet both persist; manual scavenging was outlawed in 1993 and again in 2013 but continues.
  • Corruption and rule-breaking: strict anti-corruption and traffic laws have limited effect where bribes and rule-breaking are socially tolerated.
  • Technology outpacing law: deepfakes, online fraud and data misuse spread faster than rules can be written; ethical users are the first line of defence.
  • Moral energy at work: Swachh Bharat became a people's movement, and fishermen and volunteers rescued thousands in the Kerala floods of 2018, showing that citizens' values can achieve what laws alone cannot.

3. Relevance for governance and civil servants

  • Ethical leadership: officers who act with integrity even where rules are silent, for instance declining favours that are technically permissible, set the tone for society.
  • Behavioural approaches: the Economic Survey 2018-19 urged the use of "nudges" in policy, shaping social norms rather than relying only on penalties.
  • Value education: NEP 2020 emphasises ethical and constitutional values, and Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) remind citizens of their obligations.
  • A caution: popular morality can be prejudiced; it must be guided by constitutional morality, as the Supreme Court held in Navtej Singh Johar (2018).

Laws and morality are complementary: laws set the floor, morality raises the ceiling. A society of moral citizens needs fewer laws and obeys them better, so character-building through family, education and example is the surest foundation of national strength.
free.upm-2025-gs4-4a:
Social re-engineeringCritical thinkingEthical frameworkEvidence-based policy

Social re-engineering means deliberately reshaping social structures and behaviour (on gender, caste, health, sanitation or nutrition) through public policy, and welfare schemes are its main tools. A civil servant implementing them needs reason (logic, data and evidence), critical thinking (questioning assumptions and anticipating side-effects) and an ethical framework (justice, dignity, compassion and constitutional values). Reason without ethics can be cruel; ethics without reason can be ineffective.

1. Why reason and critical thinking are needed

  • Correct diagnosis: the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) ranks 112 districts on 49 indicators across health, education, agriculture, financial inclusion and infrastructure, so effort goes where the gaps are.
  • Better targeting: linking Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and mobile numbers for direct benefit transfer removed duplicate and fake beneficiaries and cut out middlemen.
  • Questioning assumptions: Ujjwala showed that a gas connection alone did not ensure use; low refill rates revealed that affordability was the barrier, so a targeted subsidy per refill was added from 2022.
  • Seeing the real obstacle: Bihar's bicycle scheme for schoolgirls (2006) recognised that distance, not only attitude, kept girls out of secondary school, and girls' enrolment rose.

2. Why an ethical framework is needed

  • Reason alone can dehumanise: the target-driven sterilisation drive of the Emergency (1975–77) pursued a "rational" population goal through coercion; it violated dignity and set back family planning for years.
  • Technology must serve justice: when failed biometric authentication denied rations to genuine beneficiaries, the Centre directed in October 2017 that no one be denied food for lack of Aadhaar or failed authentication.
  • Dignity in behaviour change: sanitation campaigns that publicly shamed people for open defecation in some places were rightly criticised; change must be persuaded, not humiliated, into being.
  • Priority to the weakest: Rawls's idea that inequalities must benefit the least advantaged, and Gandhi's talisman of recalling the poorest person, keep schemes focused on those most in need.

3. Reason and ethics together: examples

  • Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015): data on the falling child sex ratio (918 in Census 2011) identified the worst districts, while community campaigns worked to change how families value daughters.
  • Social audits: under MGNREGA, the evidence of muster rolls and worksite checks is placed before the Gram Sabha, combining verification with participation and accountability.
  • Exception handling: good administrators design fall-back options, such as manual verification or doorstep delivery, so that a rule meant for efficiency does not exclude the old, disabled or remote.
  • Learning from evaluation: NITI Aayog's Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office studies outcomes so that schemes are redesigned on evidence, not assumption.

Social re-engineering touches lives deeply, so a civil servant must combine head and heart: evidence-led and value-anchored. Reason ensures that schemes work; ethics ensures that they are just. Together they deliver inclusive transformation.
free.upm-2025-gs4-4b:
AhimsaAnekantavadaAparigrahaTriratna

Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism and a contemporary of the Buddha, was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali. After twelve years of austerity he attained kaivalya (supreme knowledge), and he attained nirvana at Pavapuri. Preaching in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, the people's language, he offered liberation through ethical conduct rather than ritual. His core teachings of ahimsa, anekantavada and aparigraha speak directly to today's world.

1. Major teachings

  • Triratna (three jewels): right faith (samyak darshan), right knowledge (samyak jnana) and right conduct (samyak charitra) together lead to liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
  • Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha came from Parshvanatha; Mahavira added brahmacharya. Monks follow them strictly as mahavratas, while lay followers practise them as milder anuvratas.
  • Ahimsa: every living being, even plants and water, has a soul (jiva); non-violence must be practised in thought, word and deed.
  • Anekantavada and syadvada: reality has many aspects, so any statement is true only from a particular standpoint; this teaches intellectual humility and tolerance.
  • Self-effort and equality: liberation depends on one's own conduct, not on a creator god or on rituals; Mahavira questioned the claims of birth-based superiority and admitted women into the sangha.

2. Relevance in the contemporary world

  • Violence and war: amid wars and terrorism, ahimsa offers a basis for dialogue; through his Jain mentor Shrimad Rajchandra, it shaped Gandhi's satyagraha.
  • Climate and ecology: aparigraha and reverence for all life favour limited wants and minimal waste, the spirit of Mission LiFE (2022); respect for even the smallest life forms supports the protection of biodiversity.
  • Polarisation and post-truth: anekantavada encourages listening to opposing views, reducing hate and echo chambers on social media and supporting diplomacy based on dialogue.
  • Consumerism and corruption: aparigraha checks greed, which drives both over-consumption and corruption; a public servant who limits wants is less open to temptation.
  • Personal well-being: self-discipline, fasting and the practice of seeking and granting forgiveness (kshamavani during Paryushana) promote mental peace and better relationships.

3. Contemporary recognition and limits

  • Recognition: India marked the 2,550th Nirvana Mahotsav of Mahavira in 2024, and Prakrit, the language of the Jain Agamas, was granted classical language status in October 2024.
  • Limits: extreme asceticism cannot be practised by all; what matters is the essence: non-violence, restraint and openness.

In a world of conflict, greed and ecological crisis, Mahavira's message of non-violence, non-possession and many-sidedness offers a timeless code for individuals, societies and states: live and let live, and want less, harm less.
free.upm-2025-gs4-5a:
SvadharmaSense of responsibilityNishkama karmaPersonal fulfilment

The statement echoes the Bhagavad Gita (18.45): a person attains perfection by being devoted to his own duty (svadharma); the Gita also asks that duty be done without attachment to its fruits (nishkama karma). For a civil servant, duty means service to the Constitution and the people. When it is done with full commitment, it builds a deep sense of responsibility and becomes the source of lasting personal fulfilment.

1. Devotion to duty and the sense of responsibility

  • Ownership beyond compliance: a devoted officer owns outcomes, not just files. Armstrong Pame, an IAS officer, built a 100 km road through crowd-funding in Manipur's Tamenglong district in 2012, linking villages that had waited decades for road access.
  • Firmness under pressure: T.N. Seshan, as Chief Election Commissioner (1990–96), enforced the Model Code of Conduct strictly, restoring the credibility of elections.
  • Duty even at personal cost: Satyendra Dubey, an engineer with the NHAI, exposed corruption in the Golden Quadrilateral project and was killed in 2003; his case led to the 2004 whistle-blower resolution and later the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.
  • Kant's insight: an act has moral worth when it is done from a sense of duty, not for reward or out of fear.

2. Devotion to duty and personal fulfilment

  • Intrinsic motivation: seeing a school run, a road built or a grievance resolved gives a satisfaction that no posting or praise can match; Maslow called this self-actualisation.
  • Flourishing through virtue: Aristotle's eudaimonia holds that a fulfilled life lies in doing one's work excellently and virtuously.
  • Detachment protects: nishkama karma lets the officer give his best regardless of transfers, criticism or recognition, reducing frustration over outcomes beyond his control.
  • Visible legacy: E. Sreedharan, a railway engineer and civil servant, found fulfilment in building the Konkan Railway and the Delhi Metro with speed and integrity.

3. Critical analysis: devotion with discernment

  • Duty is not blind obedience: the Nuremberg trials rejected "following orders" as a defence, and Hannah Arendt's account of Eichmann warned of the banality of evil; a civil servant's duty is to the Constitution and to conscience.
  • Conflicts of duty: duties to family, health and office can clash; balance and prudence, not self-destruction, sustain long careers of service.
  • Burnout: devotion must be supported by fair workloads, mental-health support and recognition, such as the PM's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration.
  • Compassion with rules: rigid duty without empathy can fail the very citizens it is meant to serve.

Devotion to duty, guided by constitutional values and conscience, makes a civil servant both responsible and fulfilled: the reward lies in the work itself. The Gita calls yoga skill in action (yoga karmasu kaushalam): work done with excellence and detachment is itself the path to perfection.

Facilitative governanceEase of livingCitizen-centric administrationHolistic development

Holistic development combines economic growth with social inclusion, human development and environmental sustainability, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals. A "command and control" bureaucracy cannot deliver it alone. The civil servant must move from regulator (licensing, inspecting, penalising) to enabler and facilitator: removing barriers, building capacities and partnering with citizens, businesses and civil society. Regulation remains, but light, smart and trust-based.

1. Ease of doing business and ease of living

  • Simplify and decriminalise: the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 decriminalised 183 provisions in 42 central Acts; at district level, redundant permissions and forms should be weeded out.
  • Time-bound services: the National Single Window System (2021) and State public-service guarantee laws, pioneered by Madhya Pradesh in 2010, fix deadlines and penalise delay.
  • Trust by default: self-attestation of documents (2014), faceless tax assessment and deemed approvals reduce contact with officials and the scope for rent-seeking.
  • Local economic ecosystems: support One District One Product clusters, farmer producer organisations (10,000 FPOs scheme, 2020), start-ups and easy credit.

2. Human development and inclusion

  • Saturation and convergence: the Aspirational Districts (2018) and Aspirational Blocks (2023) programmes show how data, convergence and friendly competition lift the most backward areas.
  • Empowering women: self-help groups, bank linkage and the Lakhpati Didi initiative turn beneficiaries into entrepreneurs.
  • Last-mile access: camps, Common Service Centres, DigiLocker and doorstep delivery bring services to the elderly, disabled and remote.

3. Participation and sustainability

  • People's planning: Gram Panchayat Development Plans and Gram Sabhas let communities set priorities.
  • Partnerships: CSR funds, NGOs and public–private partnerships add resources and ideas; Jal Shakti Abhiyan's "Catch the Rain" campaign (2021) relies on community effort.
  • Green growth: facilitate rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar (2024), natural farming and waste-to-wealth enterprises.

4. Capacity and mindset of the civil servant

  • Competence: Mission Karmayogi (2020) shifts training from "rule" to "role"; officers need skills in data, negotiation and project management.
  • Integrated planning: PM Gati Shakti (2021) and dashboards help coordinate departments instead of working in silos.
  • Empathy and accessibility: open office hours, responsive grievance redress (CPGRAMS) and feedback loops.
  • Outcome accountability: key performance indicators, social audits and rewards for innovation, alongside firm action against misuse.

A facilitator does not abandon regulation but makes it smart, minimal and fair. By trusting citizens, removing friction and building capacity, the civil servant becomes a catalyst of inclusive and sustainable development.
free.upm-2025-gs4-6a:
Code of ethicsCompliance-based cultureValue-based cultureEthical leadership

A code of ethics states the values an organisation stands for, such as integrity, impartiality and service, while a code of conduct lists specific do's and don'ts. Lynn Sharp Paine (Harvard Business Review, 1994) distinguished a compliance-based strategy, which uses rules, monitoring and penalties to prevent misconduct, from an integrity- or value-based strategy that builds shared values and self-governance. An ethical work culture needs both: rules as the floor, values as the driving force.

1. Putting a code of ethics in place

  • Participatory drafting: involve staff at all levels so that the code addresses real dilemmas in the workplace: procurement, gifts, conflicts of interest, harassment and data use.
  • Anchor it in law and good practice: build on the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964 or the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968, the Second ARC's report on Ethics in Governance (2007), which recommended a code of ethics for civil servants, and the Nolan principles.
  • Keep it simple and visible: short, with examples, displayed in offices and signed by every employee on joining.

2. Compliance-based measures

  • Reduce discretion: clear delegation of powers, e-office files, e-procurement and the Government e-Marketplace (GeM), and Integrity Pacts in large contracts, as the CVC advises.
  • Preventive vigilance: rotation on sensitive posts, internal audit, asset declarations and random checks.
  • Safe reporting channels: an Internal Committee under the POSH Act, 2013, protection under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, and a confidential complaints box.
  • Fair and consistent enforcement: time-bound inquiries with natural justice; no one is above the code.

3. Value-based measures

  • Tone at the top: I would follow the code first, declining gifts, recording reasons for decisions and admitting mistakes, because staff copy what leaders do, not what they say.
  • Ethics training: induction and refresher sessions built on real case studies and dilemmas, through platforms such as Mission Karmayogi's iGOT.
  • Recognise integrity: reward honest and helpful conduct in appraisals and public appreciation, not only output.
  • Psychological safety: an open-door policy so that staff can raise concerns or ask for advice without fear; an ethics officer to counsel on grey areas.
  • Fairness to staff: transparent postings, reasonable workloads and timely grievance redress reduce the excuses people use to justify misconduct.

4. Monitoring and renewal

  • Ethics audit: periodic staff and citizen surveys and reviews of complaints to find weak spots.
  • Update the code as new risks such as AI tools and data privacy emerge.

Rules without values breed box-ticking; values without rules lack teeth. By combining a clear compliance framework with value-based leadership, I would make integrity the normal way of working, not an exception.
free.upm-2025-gs4-6b:
Fiscal accountabilityLeakagesOutcome budgetingValue for money

The IMF's April 2025 World Economic Outlook projected India to become the fourth-largest economy in 2025, just ahead of Japan; after the rupee's fall and a new GDP series (base year 2022-23), its April 2026 Outlook placed India sixth. Dollar rankings swing with exchange rates; what lifts India sustainably is how well each rupee is spent. Yet funds in several sectors remain under-utilised or misutilised, and plugging these leakages needs accountability for both money and results.

1. Why funds are under-utilised or misutilised

  • Under-utilisation: poor planning, late releases, weak implementing capacity, procedural delays and the "March rush" leave funds unspent or parked in bank accounts, as with welfare cesses and some dedicated funds.
  • Misutilisation: diversion to other purposes, inflated bills, ghost beneficiaries and collusion between officials and contractors.
  • Weak follow-up: audit findings and utilisation certificates are not acted upon in time, so no one is held responsible.

2. Measures for financial accountability

  • Just-in-time release: the Single Nodal Agency system and SNA-SPARSH release central funds for schemes only when they are needed, ending the parking of idle balances.
  • End-to-end tracking: the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) follows money from the treasury to the beneficiary; DBT removes middlemen.
  • Transparent procurement: e-procurement, GeM and Integrity Pacts reduce collusion and inflated prices.
  • Outcome budgeting: link allocations to measurable results through the Output–Outcome Monitoring Framework, so that spending is judged by results, not just by money spent.

3. Measures for institutional accountability

  • Act on audit: the CAG's performance audits and the Public Accounts Committee's recommendations should be followed by time-bound action-taken reports.
  • Local monitoring: DISHA committees (2016), chaired by MPs, review central schemes in each district; dashboards make progress public.
  • Social audit and transparency: social audits of rural employment and food schemes, proactive disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act, and citizen report cards let beneficiaries check spending.
  • Deterrence: prompt vigilance inquiries, the Lokpal (operational since 2019) and recovery of misused funds, with responsibility fixed on individuals.

4. Capacity and ethics

  • Strengthen implementing capacity: trained staff, engineers and accountants in States and local bodies, with flexible funds for local needs.
  • Cooperative federalism: timely central releases and States' matching shares avoid stop-start spending.
  • Ethic of trusteeship: the General Financial Rules, 2017 expect officers to guard public money as a prudent person guards his own; integrity, frugality and recognition of good performers build this culture.

Rankings depend partly on exchange rates, but value for money depends on governance. Treating every rupee as a public trust, linking spending to outcomes and enforcing answerability will speed India's journey to the third-largest economy and, more importantly, improve citizens' lives.
free.upm-2025-gs4-7:
Personal vs professional dutyDisaster leadershipFilial obligationEmotional intelligence

Vijay, as Deputy Commissioner, heads the District Disaster Management Authority under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. With over 200 dead, about 5,000 injured, roads and telecommunications cut and heavy rain resuming, the rescue phase is far from over. At the same moment, as his mother's only child in India, he faces the sacred duty of performing her last rites. It is a classic conflict between personal and professional duty.

1. Stakeholders

  • Vijay; his sister in the USA and relatives in Kerala; the injured, homeless and stranded people; district staff, rescue forces and volunteers; the State government; and public trust in the administration.

2. (a) Options available to Vijay

  • Option 1: leave for Kerala at once, handing over charge informally.
  • Option 2: stay on duty; relatives keep the body in a mortuary briefly or perform the rites, with Vijay joining by video and completing later rituals himself.
  • Option 3: inform the State, request a senior officer to take charge, and make a short visit after a proper handover.
  • Option 4: ask his sister to fly from the USA to perform the rites.

3. (b) Ethical dilemmas

  • Public duty vs filial duty: his oath binds him to the people; culture and conscience bind him to his mother.
  • Grief vs composure: a grieving leader must still think clearly, which calls for emotional intelligence.
  • Consequences vs obligations: many survivors' lives weigh against a deeply felt duty to a parent.
  • Leadership vs self-care: his absence may demoralise staff, yet denying himself any chance to mourn is also harmful.
  • Public resources: using a rescue helicopter for personal travel would misuse resources meant for the sick and old.

4. (c) Critical evaluation of the options

5. (d) The most appropriate course

A combination of Options 2 and 3:

  • Inform the State at once: report his bereavement and the worsening situation to the Chief Secretary and request a senior officer to take charge.
  • Strengthen the second line: make the Additional Deputy Commissioner the Incident Commander under the Incident Response System, delegate sectors to SDMs and coordinate with the NDRF, SDRF and Army.
  • Honour his mother: ask relatives to keep the body in a mortuary for a short time or, if delay is unavoidable, a relative or family elder (or his sister, if she can come) performs the rites while he joins by video.
  • Go after the handover: once the relief officer takes charge and rescue is under control, take a few days' leave by regular transport and return for rehabilitation.

Why this course:

  • Lives that can be saved come first: his mother is beyond help, but the injured are not; the rites can wait briefly or be performed by others.
  • Role morality: he accepted a role whose core duty is protecting people in a crisis, the svadharma of a district head.
  • Universalisability: if every officer left mid-disaster, no response could work.
  • Compassion is not denied: he still honours his mother, only with a change in timing, and the State should grant his leave promptly.

Vijay's choice is not between his mother and his duty but about timing and arrangements. Staying at the helm through the acute crisis while honouring his mother reflects duty with compassion.
free.upm-2025-gs4-8:
Right to shelterEnvironmental justiceSustainable developmentIntergenerational equity

The case pits two constitutional commitments against each other: the state's duty to provide shelter, which the Supreme Court read into Article 21 in Chameli Singh v State of UP (1996), and its duty to protect forests under Article 48A and Article 51A(g). Clearing an ecologically sensitive forest that sustains tribal livelihoods in order to house the poor risks solving one injustice by creating another. The test is sustainable development: meeting today's needs without compromising tomorrow's.

1. Stakeholders

  • Homeless and economically weaker families; tribal and nomadic communities who depend on the forest; wildlife; nearby residents who rely on its water, soil and climate services; the forest, revenue, housing and police departments; and future generations.

2. (a) Can deforestation be ethically justified?

  • Consequences: the short-term benefit to some is outweighed by long-term losses to many: rainfall, groundwater, soil and biodiversity that cannot be restored quickly.
  • Duties and rights: a good end does not justify violating the rights of forest communities, whose rights must be settled and whose Gram Sabhas must have their say before forest land is diverted, as the Supreme Court's Niyamgiri judgment (2013) underlined.
  • Justice: the least advantaged include tribal families, not only the homeless; the precautionary principle (Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996) and the public trust doctrine (M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath, 1997) weigh against irreversible loss.
  • Verdict: deforestation of a sensitive zone is not justified while alternatives exist; at most, minimal use of forest land can be a last resort, with legal clearance, community consent and compensation.

3. (b) Challenges in balancing conservation and development

  • Socio-economic: scarce, costly urban land; loss of livelihoods from forest produce and grazing; higher future costs from floods, erosion and water scarcity; and a remote forest site may lack jobs, schools and transport for the new residents.
  • Administrative: overlapping laws (the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, Forest Rights Act and Wildlife Act); coordination between departments; unclear land records; housing targets that clash with long clearance processes; and compensatory afforestation often on poor land.
  • Ethical: competing rights of two vulnerable groups; the voiceless (wildlife and future generations); genuine consent; and the risk that "welfare" becomes a cover for diverting land.

4. (c) Alternatives and policy interventions

  • Find other land: map government, vacant and brownfield land; use land pooling and land banks.
  • Build denser and smarter: multi-storey affordable housing, in-situ slum redevelopment and rental housing under the Affordable Rental Housing Complexes scheme (2020) and PMAY-Urban 2.0 (2024).
  • Protect forest communities: recognise individual and community forest rights; add value to forest produce through Van Dhan Vikas Kendras.
  • Reduce human–wildlife conflict: restore corridors, install early-warning systems and solar fences, and pay compensation quickly.
  • Improve law and order directly: patrols, lighting and community policing.
  • If any forest land is unavoidable: use the smallest area outside the sensitive core, with Gram Sabha consent, forest clearance, native-species compensatory afforestation and green building norms.

Housing the homeless and protecting forests both serve human dignity. The administration should pursue housing without deforestation: alternative land, denser design and rights-based forest governance, so that welfare today does not become disaster tomorrow.
free.upm-2025-gs4-9:
Conflict of interestConfidentialityNepotism and undue influenceIntegrity

Subash, Secretary PWD, faces pressure from two directions on the same project. His son wants confidential information about the road's location to buy land cheaply, and the Minister wants his nephew's company favoured and the project rushed for political gain. Both demands would turn public office into private advantage. The case tests Subash's integrity, impartiality and moral courage against affection for his son and loyalty to a Minister who trusts him.

1. Stakeholders

  • Subash; his son Vikas; the Minister and his nephew's company; landowners along the likely route; other contractors; the State exchequer; road users and taxpayers; and the civil service's credibility.

2. (a) Ethical issues involved

  • Conflict of interest: his son deals in land near the likely project. The All India Services (Conduct) Rules, as amended in 2014, require officers to declare private interests relating to their duties and resolve conflicts in the public interest.
  • Misuse of confidential information: sharing an unannounced decision for private profit is like insider trading; it breaches conduct rules on unauthorised communication of official information and could attract the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
  • Nepotism and favouritism: steering the contract to the Minister's nephew would deny equal opportunity (Article 14) and violate the General Financial Rules' requirement of transparent, competitive procurement.
  • Exploitation of farmers: landowners who sell cheaply to insiders before the announcement would lose the gains that are rightfully theirs.
  • Political pressure vs neutrality: rushing a project for the Minister's image can compromise due diligence on design, environment and land acquisition.

3. (b) Options available to Subash

4. (c) The most appropriate course: refuse both, tactfully and transparently

  • With his son: explain firmly that sharing the information is illegal and would cheat farmers, without hinting at the location; warn him that any land deal that looks like insider dealing would expose them both; declare the potential conflict of interest in writing; keep project files away from home.
  • With the Minister: explain politely that the nephew's company is welcome to compete in open e-tendering on equal terms, and that any favour would invite audit, vigilance and litigation that would harm the Minister himself. Seek written confirmation of any oral instruction, as the Supreme Court urged in T.S.R. Subramanian v UoI (2013).
  • Fast but sound: offer a realistic timeline with a detailed project report, environmental assessment and land planning, so that an early announcement does not compromise quality.
  • Close the information gap: announce the alignment publicly once finalised; a preliminary notification under Section 11 of the RFCTLARR (land acquisition) Act, 2013 bars land transactions in the notified area without the Collector's approval, curbing speculation.
  • Escalate if pressure continues: brief the Chief Secretary; recusal only as a last resort.

Why this course: it upholds the rule of law and the Nolan principles of selflessness, integrity and objectivity; it treats office as a trust, not a means to private ends (Kant); it protects the farmers, the weakest party; and it even shields the son and the Minister from legal trouble while preserving a working relationship.

Integrity is tested most when pressure comes from those we love or trust. By saying no with tact and reasons and making the process transparent, Subash protects the project, the public and even his own family, showing that public office is a public trust.

Financial proprietySplitting of ordersIntegrity vs careerMoral courage

Rajesh's reporting officer wants computer stationery bought "on priority" from a particular vendor. The estimate of ₹35 lakh exceeds Rajesh's delegated power of ₹30 lakh, and the office's "common practice" is to split the order so that the boss's sanction is not needed, a practice the General Financial Rules expressly forbid and Audit would object to. With his promotion resting on the same officer's ACR, Rajesh must choose between career interest and financial propriety.

1. Stakeholders

  • Rajesh; his reporting officer; the named and other vendors; office staff; the PSU, its shareholders and taxpayers; Audit and the Chief Vigilance Officer.

2. (a) Options available to Rajesh

3. (b) Ethical issues involved

  • Integrity vs self-interest: the fear of a poor ACR tempts Rajesh to bend rules for career gain.
  • Financial propriety and rule of law: splitting a demand to avoid a higher sanction defeats the delegation of financial powers, which exists to ensure scrutiny of large spending.
  • Favouritism: a boss naming one vendor for a ₹35 lakh purchase raises questions of fairness and possible conflict of interest; public procurement must be open and competitive, as CVC guidelines require.
  • Normalisation of deviance: a "common practice" does not make a wrong right; conformity and groupthink erode institutional integrity.
  • Power asymmetry: the ACR can become a tool of pressure; equally, the reporting officer has a duty to appraise fairly.
  • Accountability: Rajesh, not his boss, would sign the split orders and face the audit and vigilance consequences.

4. (c) The most appropriate option

Submit the full demand for sanction, through a transparent procurement process, while handling the boss with tact.

  • Verify and aggregate: confirm the genuine requirement and quantities, and treat the whole demand as one purchase.
  • Follow due procedure: obtain competitive prices through the Government e-Marketplace or a tender, as the rules applicable to the PSU require; if the named vendor offers the best value, it may win fairly.
  • Show initiative within the rules: prepare the file quickly, with a clear note explaining why the boss's sanction is needed and proposing a fast-track timeline to meet the urgency.
  • Speak to the boss personally: present the step as protecting him and the organisation from audit objections; most superiors respect a subordinate who saves them from trouble.
  • If pressure continues: ask for written instructions, record his view on file and, only if the irregularity persists, inform the next higher authority or the CVO.
  • Fix the system: suggest annual rate contracts and demand aggregation, ending the need to "split".

Why this option:

  • Integrity is non-negotiable: a promotion earned by breaking rules is a liability that audit or vigilance may expose later.
  • Universalisability: if every officer split orders, delegation of powers would become meaningless.
  • The ACR system offers protection: entries must be communicated so that an officer can represent against unfair grading (Dev Dutt v UoI, 2008).
  • Means matter: Gandhi's insistence on pure means applies to small purchases as much as to great causes; courage and prudence, the virtues of a good officer, are both served.

A career built on integrity outlasts any single appraisal. By processing the purchase lawfully and tactfully, Rajesh shows that initiative within rules is the true mark of an efficient and trustworthy officer.
free.upm-2025-gs4-11:
Social auditAccountabilityLeakagesRight to work

MGNREGA (enacted 2005, in force from 2006) gave every rural household a legal guarantee of up to 100 days of wage employment a year, giving effect to the right to work in Article 41. The irregularities left by my predecessor (ghost workers, fake muster rolls, works that never existed and siphoned funds) are not mere mismanagement; they are corruption that robs the poorest of a legal entitlement.

Note (as of 2026): the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 replaced MGNREGA from 1 July 2026, with 125 days of work and mandatory social audits; the remedies below apply equally.

1. Stakeholders

  • Genuine job-seekers and their households; the Gram Panchayat, sarpanch and scheme staff; my predecessor and any complicit officials; the State and Union rural development departments; the social audit unit; and taxpayers.

2. (a) My reaction and restoring the programme

  • Reaction: serious concern but no panic or pre-judgement; the first priority is the workers who were cheated, the second is fixing the system, and the third is fixing responsibility through due process. I would inform my superiors at once.
  • Immediate steps: secure all records (muster rolls, measurement books, job-card registers, bank statements); freeze suspicious payments; stop technical sanction for new works in this Panchayat until verification, while keeping genuine works open so that no one who demands work is denied it.
  • Restore normal working: hold a special Gram Sabha, re-verify job cards, register demand with dated receipts, open works from the approved shelf and pay pending wages to genuine workers, with compensation for delay.

3. (b) Actions on each irregularity

4. (c) How I would deal with the situation as a whole

  • Fix responsibility fairly: a time-bound inquiry, with natural justice for all, including my predecessor, whose case I would report to the State government with evidence; criminal cases where fraud is proved.
  • Transparency: a special social audit by the Gram Sabha with the independent social audit unit; wall paintings and information boards showing works, wages and payments; proactive disclosure under the RTI Act.
  • Grievance redress: a helpline, the Ombudsperson and quick resolution of complaints, with protection for those who report wrongdoing.
  • Prevention: training of scheme staff, rotation on sensitive posts, monthly reconciliation of MIS and bank data, and community monitoring by self-help groups.
  • Withstand pressure: local interests that benefited from the fraud may resist; I would act firmly, document every step and keep superiors informed.

Why this approach: it puts the rights of the poor first (Gandhi's talisman); it combines firmness with fairness, so that action is credible and lawful; and it repairs the system so that the fraud does not recur under another officer.

The promise of rural employment is dignity through work. Prompt correction, firm but fair action and community-led transparency can restore that promise and rebuild trust in local governance.
free.upm-2025-gs4-12:
Humanitarian dutyNon-refoulementBorder securityRule of law

At night, Ashok learns that 200–250 people, mostly women and children, some bleeding, are fleeing a civil war in the neighbouring country, with about ten armed soldiers in uniform among them. He cannot reach the Home Secretary. He must weigh humanitarian duty against national security and immigration law, on his own judgement and within minutes.

1. Stakeholders and legal position

  • Stakeholders: the fleeing civilians and soldiers; local residents; border police and central forces; the State government, MHA and MEA; the neighbouring regime and rebels; and Ashok himself.
  • Law: India is not party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and has no refugee law; entry is governed by the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 (in force since September 2025). But Article 21 protects every person (NHRC v State of Arunachal Pradesh, 1996), and non-refoulement (not returning people to danger) is widely regarded as customary international law.

2. (a) Options available to Ashok

3. (b) Ethical and legal dilemmas

  • Compassion vs security: saving lives against the risk that militants or weapons slip in.
  • Law vs conscience: no refugee law versus the right to life and India's humanitarian tradition (Tibetans in 1959, East Pakistan refugees in 1971, Sri Lankan Tamils).
  • Discretion vs hierarchy: acting without orders risks overstepping authority; waiting risks lives.
  • Status of the soldiers: deserters seeking asylum or combatants? Returning them may expose them to punishment; keeping them may anger one side.
  • Diplomacy vs human rights: ties with the neighbouring regime and local resource pressures versus protection of people in distress.

4. (c) The most appropriate option

Admit the civilians on humanitarian grounds, and the soldiers only after disarmament, under strict control.

  • Immediate relief: a guarded holding area near the border; doctors for the injured; food, water and shelter; women police for women and children.
  • Screening: search for weapons; record names, photographs and biometrics; prevent dispersal inland.
  • Communication: reach the State and the MHA by police wireless, satellite phone or the central forces' network; record every decision with reasons.
  • No push-back or deportation without the Central Government's decision.

Why: the right to life cannot wait; controlled, temporary entry balances humanity with security; it reflects Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and Article 51(c); and recorded, good-faith action keeps Ashok within the rule of law.

5. (d) Extra precautions with soldiers in uniform

  • Disarm at the border line: take custody of weapons, ammunition and explosives, list and seal them, and search each soldier.
  • Keep them apart: separate from civilians, whom they could intimidate, and under armed guard.
  • Verify identity: deserters, regular troops or disguised rebels? Joint questioning with intelligence agencies and central forces.
  • Humane treatment: medical care and food; disarmed, they are out of combat and entitled to dignity under the spirit of the Geneva Conventions; by analogy with the rule for neutral states (Hague Convention V, 1907), intern them away from the conflict zone.
  • No unilateral return: repatriation or asylum only by decision of the MHA and MEA, as when Myanmar soldiers who fled into Mizoram in 2023–24 took refuge with the Assam Rifles and were flown back home through official channels.
  • Discipline: minimum force; no media access or contact with local armed groups.

Ashok's guide should be humanity with vigilance: open doors for the suffering, closed doors for arms, upholding both the right to life and national security.
free.upm-2026-gs1-1:
Ashokan edictsDhammaBrahmi scriptEpigraphic sources

The inscriptions of Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest deciphered written records of Indian history. Engraved on rocks, polished pillars and cave walls from Afghanistan to Karnataka, most are in Prakrit written in the Brahmi script, which James Prinsep deciphered in 1837. Because they speak in the emperor's own voice ("Devanampiya Piyadasi"), they are a first-hand source on the Mauryas.

1. Political history and extent of the empire

  • Find-spots mark the frontiers: edicts at Shahbazgarhi (Pakistan), Kandahar (Afghanistan), Kalsi, Girnar, Dhauli, Erragudi (Andhra Pradesh) and Brahmagiri (Karnataka) outline an empire from the Hindu Kush to the Deccan.
  • Kalinga war: Rock Edict XIII records the conquest of Kalinga eight years after Ashoka's consecration, with 1,50,000 people deported and 1,00,000 killed, and his remorse; Rock Edict IV says the sound of the war drum gave way to the sound of Dhamma.
  • Neighbours and diplomacy: Rock Edicts II and XIII name the southern kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras), Sri Lanka and five Greek kings such as Antiochus II and Ptolemy II, whose known dates help fix Mauryan chronology.
  • Identity of the king: the Maski edict (found in 1915) first gave the name "Asoka", linking the Piyadasi of the edicts with the Ashoka of the chronicles.

2. Administration and the policy of Dhamma

  • Officials: rajukas, pradesikas and yuktas toured every five years (Rock Edict III); Dhamma Mahamattas were appointed in the thirteenth regnal year (Rock Edict V).
  • Paternal kingship: the Separate Kalinga Edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada declare that "all men are my children".
  • Justice and welfare: Pillar Edict IV gave condemned prisoners a three-day respite; other edicts mention medical care for humans and animals, wells and roadside trees.
  • Ethics of Dhamma: tolerance of all sects (Rock Edict XII), respect for elders, kindness to slaves and servants, and a ban on animal sacrifice (Rock Edict I).

3. Religion, economy, society and culture

  • Buddhism: the Bairat (Bhabru) edict names Buddhist texts; the Schism Edict warns monks against splitting the Sangha.
  • Rare economic data: the Rummindei pillar records Ashoka's visit to Lumbini, which he exempted from bali and whose share of produce (bhaga) he cut to one-eighth.
  • Patronage of all sects: the Barabar caves were gifted to the Ajivikas.
  • A multilingual empire and its art: Kharosthi in the north-west and Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar show adaptation to local scripts; the Sarnath lion capital is India's national emblem.

4. Limitations

  • Royal voice: the edicts state the king's ideals, not how far they were enforced.
  • Silences: little on his predecessors, trade or the empire's decline; dates are given only in regnal years.
  • Need for corroboration: they must be read with the Arthashastra, the Indica, the Buddhist chronicles and archaeology.

In sum, the inscriptions turn Mauryan history from legend into documented history, revealing an empire's extent and administration and an early experiment in ethical governance.
