Macaulay's Minute (1835)Anglicist–Orientalist debateDownward filtrationEnglish education

Thomas Babington Macaulay, the Law Member of the Governor-General's Council, wrote his Minute on Indian Education on 2 February 1835. It settled the Anglicist–Orientalist controversy over how to spend the one lakh rupees a year set aside for education by the Charter Act of 1813, arguing for English and Western science instead of Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning. Lord William Bentinck's resolution of 7 March 1835 accepted it.

1. What the Minute proposed

  • English as the medium: government funds were to support English schools and colleges, not oriental printing and stipends.
  • Contempt for Indian learning: Macaulay claimed that "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia".
  • A class of interpreters: he wanted "a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect" to stand between the rulers and the ruled.
  • Downward filtration: educating a small upper class, it was assumed, would spread knowledge to the masses through the vernaculars.

2. Impact on colonial administration

  • Language of power: after 1837 English replaced Persian in higher administration and courts, with vernaculars in the lower courts.
  • A cheap subordinate bureaucracy: Hardinge's resolution (1844) made English the passport to government jobs, producing clerks, translators and lawyers who ran the Raj at low cost.
  • Uniform, codified rule: the same Anglicist outlook shaped Macaulay's draft of the Indian Penal Code (enacted 1860) and his 1854 report on a competitive ICS examination, held in London in English, which kept Indians at a disadvantage.

3. Impact on education

  • Western knowledge: English schools and colleges spread science, history and political thought; Wood's Despatch and the universities of 1857 built on this base.
  • Neglect of mass education: filtration did not reach the masses, and literacy was only about 18% even in 1951.
  • Decline of indigenous learning: pathshalas, madrasas and tols lost patronage, and Sanskrit and Persian scholarship shrank.
  • Elite–mass gap and rote learning: an English-knowing elite drifted away from the people, and education became exam-oriented and job-centred.

4. Unintended consequences

  • A modern middle class: English-educated Indians led social reform and founded the Indian National Congress (1885).
  • Weapons against the Raj: ideas of liberty, democracy and nationalism were turned against colonial rule.
  • A link language: English connected an all-India intelligentsia and press, even as Indian-language literature also flourished.

Macaulay's Minute thus left a dual legacy: it served colonial administration but also created the class that challenged it. The NEP 2020 emphasis on teaching in the mother tongue wherever possible, at least up to Class 5 and preferably till Class 8, seeks to balance English with Indian languages.

SatyagrahaMass mobilisationConstructive programmeStruggle–truce–struggle

Before 1917, nationalist politics, from the Moderates' petitions to the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, was largely confined to the educated middle classes and a few regions. Gandhi's satyagraha, non-violent resistance rooted in truth, carried the movement to villages, factories and homes and turned the Indian National Congress into a mass party. Historian Bipan Chandra described the national movement as one of the biggest mass movements of modern times.

1. Early experiments: local grievances, national lessons

  • Champaran (1917): indigo cultivators bound by the tinkathia system (indigo on 3/20 of their land) won relief through the Champaran Agrarian Act (1918).
  • Kheda (1918): peasants refused land revenue after crop failure; Vallabhbhai Patel joined the struggle.
  • Ahmedabad (1918): mill workers won a 35% wage increase after Gandhi's first hunger strike.
  • Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919): the first all-India hartal reached towns across the country.

2. Who was mobilised

  • Peasants: no-revenue campaigns, the Bardoli satyagraha (1928) which made Patel "Sardar", and forest satyagrahas during Civil Disobedience.
  • Women: they made salt, picketed liquor and foreign-cloth shops; Sarojini Naidu led the Dharasana salt raid (1930), and Usha Mehta ran the underground Congress Radio in 1942.
  • Communities and regions: the Khilafat alliance brought in Muslims in large numbers; Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars joined from the NWFP; in the Naga hills the young Rani Gaidinliu responded to the call during Civil Disobedience.
  • Students, traders and the depressed classes: students left government colleges, merchants refused to sell foreign cloth, and the Vaikom satyagraha (1924–25) and the anti-untouchability campaign after the Poona Pact (1932) reached the lowest castes.

3. Tools of mass mobilisation

  • Simple symbols: salt, the charkha, khadi and the Gandhi cap were understood by everyone.
  • Non-violence: it made participation safe for women, children and the old, and gave the movement moral superiority.
  • Organisation: the Nagpur Congress (1920) introduced a four-anna membership, linguistic provincial committees and village-level units.
  • Constructive programme: khadi, communal unity, basic education and the removal of untouchability kept workers active between struggles.

4. Significance and limits

  • Significance: mass participation destroyed the moral authority of the Raj, built a political culture that prepared India for universal adult franchise (1950), and produced an inclusive nationalism.
  • Limits: control from the top, as in the withdrawal after Chauri Chaura (1922); restraint on peasants' class demands against zamindars; falling Muslim participation after the Khilafat phase; and Ambedkar's criticism that Dalit interests were subordinated.

Thus the true significance of the Gandhian movements lay in turning subjects into citizens: by drawing millions into politics, they made independence a people's achievement and laid the base of Indian democracy.

Fujiwhara effectBinary interactionCyclone trackMerger

The Fujiwhara effect, or binary interaction, is the mutual rotation of two nearby cyclonic vortices around a common centre. It is named after the Japanese meteorologist Sakuhei Fujiwhara, who described it in 1921 from water-tank experiments. For tropical cyclones, the interaction becomes noticeable within about 1,400 km, speeds up within about 650 km, and can end in merger or the shearing out of one storm within about 300 km.

1. How the interaction works

  • Mutual steering: each cyclone's circulation pushes the other, so the pair rotates around a point between them, anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
  • Unequal partners: the centre of rotation lies nearer the larger, stronger storm; the smaller one orbits it.
  • Equal partners: two storms of similar size "dance" around a midpoint and may deflect each other.
  • Where it occurs: most often in the busy Western Pacific, but also in the Atlantic, the Eastern Pacific and the south-eastern Indian Ocean near Australia (Seroja and Odette, 2021).

2. Impact on movement (track)

  • Erratic and looping tracks: Typhoon Parma (2009) stalled and looped near Luzon in the Philippines while interacting with Typhoon Melor, prolonging heavy rain.
  • Sudden changes of direction and speed: a storm may swing towards or away from land, or speed up once the pair separates.
  • Forecast uncertainty: track models diverge, so warnings must cover a wider area and landfall timing becomes harder to predict.

3. Impact on intensity

  • Absorption and merger: a larger storm can absorb a smaller one and grow; in the Eastern Pacific (2017), Hurricane Hilary strengthened while the weaker Irwin was deflected north-westward, weakened and dissipated.
  • Shear on the weaker storm: the outflow of the dominant cyclone creates vertical wind shear over its partner, disrupting its structure and weakening it.
  • Stalling and upwelling: a slow or stalled storm churns up cooler water and may weaken, but it also dumps rain over the same area for longer.
  • Bigger wind field: a merged system can be larger and longer-lived, widening the zone of wind and storm surge.

4. Significance for disaster management

  • Better prediction: ensemble models and close tracking of simultaneous systems by agencies such as the IMD's Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre, New Delhi.
  • Flexible preparedness: evacuation plans must allow for sudden track changes and prolonged rainfall.

In short, the Fujiwhara effect makes cyclone tracks and intensity less predictable; recognising it early helps forecasters and disaster managers widen warnings and plan for uncertainty.
free.upm-2026-gs1-5:
TundraPermafrostArctic resourcesFragile ecosystem

Tundra is the treeless biome of the high latitudes beyond the tree line (northern Russia, Canada, Alaska, Greenland and Scandinavia) and of high mountains above it (alpine tundra, as in Ladakh). Long, severe winters, a growing season of only about 50–60 days and permanently frozen subsoil, or permafrost, allow only mosses, lichens, sedges and dwarf shrubs. Yet the region holds vast hydrocarbons, minerals and new sea routes, so its fragility and its value pull in opposite directions.

1. Why the tundra is ecologically fragile

  • Low-energy system: cold, little precipitation and slow growth and decomposition mean low biodiversity and short food chains (lichen–caribou–wolf), so the loss of one species ripples through.
  • Permafrost: its thaw makes the ground sink (thermokarst), damages buildings and pipelines, and releases carbon dioxide and methane; permafrost stores about twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
  • Slow recovery: vehicle tracks and oil spills persist for decades because the cold slows natural breakdown.
  • Amplified warming: the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average since 1979 (Rantanen et al., 2022), shrinking sea ice and pushing shrubs northwards.

2. Why it is economically important

  • Hydrocarbons: the US Geological Survey (2008) estimated that the Arctic holds about 13% of the world's undiscovered oil and 30% of its undiscovered gas; Prudhoe Bay (Alaska) and Yamal LNG (Russia) already produce.
  • Minerals: nickel, palladium and copper at Norilsk (Russia), diamonds in Canada's Northwest Territories, and rare earths and uranium in Greenland.
  • Shipping: the Northern Sea Route and the Northwest Passage can shorten voyages between Asia and Europe or North America as sea ice retreats.
  • Livelihoods and science: reindeer herding (Sami, Nenets), fisheries and tourism; research stations such as India's Himadri (Svalbard, 2008); India's Arctic Policy (2022) and observer status in the Arctic Council (2013).
  • Alpine tundra: in Ladakh's Changthang, Changpa herders rear pashmina goats.

3. Critical examination: where the two collide

  • Development damages the base: in May 2020 about 21,000 tonnes of diesel leaked at Norilsk when a storage tank failed, a failure linked to thawing permafrost under its supports.
  • Climate paradox: melting ice opens resources and routes, but burning them adds emissions that speed up the thaw.
  • Limits of the "boom": high costs, harsh conditions and investor caution (Shell abandoned Alaskan Arctic drilling in 2015) mean much of the potential remains speculative.
  • Rights and geopolitics: Indigenous peoples are often bypassed, and since 2022 geopolitical rivalry has strained Arctic Council cooperation.

The tundra is valuable precisely because it is cold and remote; its wealth can be used only through sustainable development with strict environmental standards, Indigenous consent and global emission cuts, or its fragility will erase its economic importance.

Aeolian processesDeflationDune encroachmentDesertification

Aeolian processes (named after Aeolus, the Greek god of winds) are the erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind. Desertification, as defined by the UNCCD (1994), is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variations and human activities. ISRO's atlas (2021) found 97.85 million ha (29.7%) of India's land degraded in 2018-19; in the Thar, wind is the main agent.

1. Aeolian processes at work

  • Deflation: wind lifts and removes loose silt, clay and organic matter, leaving hollows (blowouts) and a stony surface (desert pavement or reg).
  • Abrasion: sand-laden wind blasts surfaces close to the ground, shaping mushroom rocks, yardangs and ventifacts.
  • Transport: most sand moves by saltation (bouncing grains); fine dust travels in suspension for hundreds or thousands of kilometres; coarse grains creep along the surface.
  • Deposition: sand forms barchans, seif dunes and sand sheets; fine dust settles as loess.

2. How wind drives desertification and land degradation

  • Loss of topsoil fertility: deflation strips the finest, nutrient- and humus-rich layer, cutting water-holding capacity and yields.
  • Sand encroachment: moving dunes and sand sheets bury farmland, villages, roads, railway lines and canals, such as stretches of the Indira Gandhi Canal in western Rajasthan.
  • Damage to plants: saltating sand cuts seedlings and buries crops, so re-vegetation fails.
  • Dust storms: pre-monsoon dust storms over north-west India damage crops, reduce visibility and harm health.
  • Feedback loop: less vegetation exposes more soil to wind; Jule Charney (1975) argued that bare, brighter land in the Sahel could itself reduce rainfall.

3. Human factors that intensify wind action

  • Overgrazing and fuelwood collection remove the protective cover of grasses and shrubs in the Thar.
  • Ploughing of marginal sandy land: the US Dust Bowl of the 1930s followed the ploughing of the Great Plains during a drought.
  • Water mismanagement: the shrinking Aral Sea has left an exposed seabed that now feeds salt and dust storms.
  • Mining and quarrying: gaps created in the Aravallis are believed to let sand and dust move eastward.
  • Climate change: hotter, drier spells and erratic rain make soils more erodible.

4. Way forward

  • Shelterbelts and dune stabilisation: CAZRI (Jodhpur, 1959) techniques using grasses such as sewan, shrubs and micro-windbreaks.
  • Programmes: the Desert Development Programme (1977-78), watershed schemes, the Aravalli Green Wall Project (2023) and India's target to restore 26 million ha of degraded land by 2030.
  • Global models: Africa's Great Green Wall and China's Three-North Shelterbelt.

Wind is the sculptor of drylands, but human misuse turns it into an agent of desertification; protecting vegetation cover is the key to land degradation neutrality.

Transboundary riversHydro-diplomacyIndus Waters TreatyWater security

South Asia's great river systems, the Indus and the Ganga–Brahmaputra–Meghna, rise in the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau, the "Third Pole", and cross national borders. They sustain irrigation, hydropower, fisheries and navigation for hundreds of millions of people. But because the sources lie upstream (China, India, Nepal) and demand keeps rising, the same rivers are also a recurring source of transboundary and internal disputes.

1. Water as an asset

  • Food security: the canal-irrigated Indus plains of Indian and Pakistani Punjab and the Ganga plains are the region's granaries.
  • Hydropower and energy trade: Bhutan's Chukha, Tala and Mangdechhu projects export power to India, and Nepal's hydropower is a growing export.
  • Navigation and connectivity: the India–Bangladesh Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade (1972) links National Waterway 1 on the Ganga with Bangladesh's rivers.
  • Cooperation frameworks: the Indus Waters Treaty (1960, brokered by the World Bank) survived wars; the Ganga Waters Treaty (1996) shares Farakka's lean-season flows; the Kosi (1954), Gandak (1959) and Mahakali (1996) agreements link India and Nepal.
  • Ecology and livelihoods: the Sundarbans delta, inland fisheries and groundwater recharge.

2. Water as a source of conflict

  • India–Pakistan: India placed the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance in April 2025 after the Pahalgam terror attack. On 31 August 2026 a Court of Arbitration at The Hague held that the treaty remains in force; India rejects the court as illegally constituted and says the treaty stays in abeyance until Pakistan ends support for cross-border terrorism.
  • India–Bangladesh: the Teesta agreement has remained unsigned since 2011, and the 30-year Ganga treaty expires in December 2026; Bangladesh has sought talks on its renewal.
  • China and the lower riparians: China's mega hydropower project on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) near Medog raises fears in India and Bangladesh about flows, sediment, seismic risk and data sharing.
  • India–Nepal: recurring Kosi floods (the 2008 Kusaha breach) and slow progress on Pancheshwar breed mistrust over "unequal" treaties.
  • Within countries: India's Cauvery, Krishna and Mahadayi disputes, and Pakistan's Sindh–Punjab quarrels.

3. Why the asset turns into conflict

  • Upstream–downstream asymmetry: the upper riparian controls flows, while the lower one fears scarcity and floods.
  • Climate stress: retreating glaciers, erratic monsoons and falling groundwater sharpen competition.
  • Securitisation: rivers get tied to terrorism, territorial disputes and nationalism, as in India–Pakistan ties.
  • Weak institutions: bilateral treaties and no basin-wide body or binding data-sharing mechanism.

4. Way forward

  • Basin-level cooperation: joint flood forecasting, real-time data sharing and joint hydropower in the GBM basin.
  • Benefit sharing: trading power, navigation and flood control rather than dividing water volumes.
  • Demand management: efficient irrigation and groundwater regulation.

South Asia's rivers can be either a bridge or a battleground; turning shared water into shared prosperity needs trust, data and hydro-diplomacy that treats basins as wholes.
free.upm-2026-gs1-8:
Unity in diversityComposite cultureCommunalismRegionalism

India is home to all the major world religions, 121 languages (22 of them in the Eighth Schedule) and 705 Scheduled Tribes (Census 2011), besides thousands of castes and many regional cultures. Unity in diversity means a shared civilisational and constitutional identity that accommodates these differences instead of erasing them. Communalism (the use of religious identity against other groups) and regionalism (placing regional above national interest) have repeatedly tested this unity but have not broken it.

1. Bonds that hold the diversity together

  • Constitutional framework: secularism (part of the basic structure, S.R. Bommai, 1994), fundamental rights, minority rights under Articles 29–30, single citizenship, and the duty to promote harmony (Article 51A(e)).
  • Federal accommodation: linguistic States (1956), the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and the special provisions of Article 371 accommodate identity instead of suppressing it.
  • Shared culture: pilgrimage networks (Char Dham, Kumbh), the Bhakti–Sufi traditions, common festivals and the inclusive nationalism of the freedom struggle.
  • Modern unifiers: the world's largest elections, a single market under GST, the Railways, cinema, cricket and the armed forces.

2. The challenge of communalism

  • Episodes of violence: Partition (1947), the anti-Sikh riots (1984), Mumbai (1992–93), Gujarat (2002), Muzaffarnagar (2013) and north-east Delhi (2020).
  • New forms: misinformation and hate speech on social media, polarisation during elections, and residential ghettoisation in cities.
  • Costs: loss of life and trust, economic disruption and a damaged international image.

3. The challenge of regionalism

  • Forms: "sons of the soil" campaigns against migrants, demands for separate States (Telangana, created in 2014), inter-State water disputes such as the Cauvery, and language rows such as the anti-Hindi agitation of 1965 in Tamil Nadu.
  • Insurgency: separatist movements in parts of the North-East and Punjab in the past.
  • Positive regionalism: pride in regional identity and competition for development need not be divisive; they can enrich the nation.

4. Why unity endures (assessment)

  • Cross-cutting identities: a person may be Tamil, Muslim, a farmer and an Indian at once, so no single fault line splits the nation.
  • Democratic channels: grievances are voiced through elections, courts and federal bargaining; the Mizo Accord (1986) and the Bodo Accord (2020) turned insurgents into stakeholders.
  • Everyday coexistence: shared festivals, mixed workplaces and neighbours protecting each other during riots.
  • Caution: unity is not automatic; communal polarisation and regional economic inequality can erode it if ignored.

Unity in diversity thus remains India's defining feature because it rests on accommodation, not assimilation; strengthening constitutional morality, fraternity and balanced regional development will keep it so.

Social model of disabilityRPwD Act, 2016AccessibilityInclusion

Disability is not merely an impairment of the body or mind; it arises when a long-term impairment meets barriers (physical, attitudinal, communicational and institutional) that prevent full and equal participation. This rights-based understanding underlies the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD, 2006), which India ratified in 2007, and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016. Census 2011 counted 2.68 crore persons with disabilities (2.21% of the population).

1. Understanding disability: from charity to rights

  • Medical model: a defect in the individual to be cured; the person is treated as a patient.
  • Charity model: an object of pity, cared for in segregated institutions.
  • Social model: society disables people through barriers; the problem is the staircase, not the wheelchair.
  • Rights-based model: dignity, autonomy, non-discrimination and participation; "nothing about us without us".
  • Intersectionality: women, the rural poor and those with invisible disabilities face multiple disadvantages.

2. India's framework

  • Constitution: Article 41 (public assistance in cases of disablement), Entry 9 of the State List, and Articles 14, 15 and 21.
  • RPwD Act, 2016: 21 specified disabilities (up from 7 under the 1995 Act), including acid-attack survivors, autism and specific learning disabilities; 4% reservation in government jobs and 5% of seats in higher education for persons with benchmark disabilities (40% or more).
  • Schemes: the Accessible India Campaign (2015), the UDID card and assistance for aids and appliances (ADIP).
  • Courts: Vikash Kumar v. UPSC (2021) extended reasonable accommodation (a scribe) beyond benchmark disability; in Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (November 2024) the Supreme Court struck down Rule 15(1) of the 2017 Rules and ordered mandatory accessibility rules.

3. Why an inclusive policy framework is needed

  • Persistent exclusion: only about 55% of persons with disabilities were literate (Census 2011), and most remain outside formal jobs.
  • Accessibility gap: buildings, transport and websites remain largely inaccessible; the Raturi judgment showed that voluntary guidelines had failed.
  • Weak data: different definitions and an ageing population mean the true numbers are higher; Census 2027 must count them properly.
  • Implementation gaps: unfilled reserved posts, low budgets and weak State commissions.
  • Economic case: an ILO study (2009) of ten low- and middle-income countries estimated that excluding persons with disabilities from work costs 3–7% of GDP.

4. Elements of an inclusive framework

  • Universal design: enforceable standards for buildings, transport and digital services.
  • Inclusive education and skills: NEP 2020, Indian Sign Language and assistive technology.
  • Work and social protection: incentives for private hiring, reasonable accommodation, disability pensions and health cover.
  • Participation: persons with disabilities in decision-making, and accessible polling with the Election Commission's postal-ballot option for voters with benchmark disabilities.

India's growing success at the Paralympics shows what ability can achieve when barriers fall; moving from charity to rights and inclusion is both a constitutional duty and a development necessity.

Digital empowermentDigital Public InfrastructureDigital divideInclusion

Social empowerment means enabling people, especially the marginalised, to gain voice, access, choice and dignity. Digital technology (mobile phones, the internet and Digital Public Infrastructure such as Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker) lowers the cost of reaching information, money, services and markets. With 111.4 crore internet subscribers (TRAI, June 2026), India is testing this at scale. The evidence suggests that it does empower, but only when access, skills and safeguards go with it.

1. Yes: how digital technology empowers

  • Financial inclusion: 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts, 56% held by women (August 2026); UPI, with over 20 billion transactions a month since August 2025, lets street vendors accept payments and build a credit record.
  • Leak-proof welfare: Direct Benefit Transfer has moved over ₹52 lakh crore through 900+ schemes, cutting out middlemen and fake beneficiaries.
  • Identity and documents: DigiLocker (72 crore+ users) and Aadhaar give migrants and the poor portable proof of identity and entitlement.
  • Women and livelihoods: digital bookkeeping in self-help groups, women drone pilots under Namo Drone Didi, and online markets (ONDC, GeM) for small sellers.
  • Education and health: DIKSHA, SWAYAM and e-Sanjeevani telemedicine reach remote areas; Bhashini tools help people use services in their own languages.
  • Voice and accountability: RTI Online, CPGRAMS and social-media campaigns let citizens raise grievances and expose injustice.

2. But: limits and new forms of disempowerment

  • Digital divide: only 33% of women against 57% of men had ever used the internet (NFHS-5); rural, elderly, poor and disabled people lag behind.
  • Exclusion by design: failed biometric authentication can deny rations or pensions to manual workers and the elderly.
  • Harm online: cyber fraud, deepfakes, online harassment of women, and misinformation that can fuel hatred.
  • Privacy and surveillance: large databases need strong protection; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) and its Rules (2025) are a start.
  • Precarious platform work: gig jobs give income but little security; the Code on Social Security, in force since November 2025, recognises gig workers.

3. Conditions for real empowerment

  • Access: BharatNet, PM-WANI public Wi-Fi and affordable devices.
  • Skills: PMGDISHA and Common Service Centres as assisted access points.
  • Safeguards: offline alternatives, grievance redress and data protection.

Digital technology is a powerful enabler, not an automatic empowerer: it empowers when it reaches the last citizen with skills and safeguards, so inclusive design must accompany digital expansion.

Vijayanagara styleRaya gopuramKalyana mandapaIndo-Islamic synthesis

The Vijayanagara Empire (founded 1336; capital at Hampi until the defeat of 1565) created an imperial architecture whose ruins at Hampi are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986). Its builders inherited the Dravida temple tradition of the Cholas and Pandyas and the ornate Chalukya–Hoysala traditions of the Deccan, and combined them with the Indo-Islamic forms of the contemporary Deccan Sultanates, producing a distinct and eclectic style.

1. Continuity with past traditions

  • Dravida temple plan: the sanctum with its vimana, pillared mandapas and enclosure walls (prakaras) continued the Chola–Pandya pattern.
  • Older Deccan forms: the early temples on Hemakuta hill at Hampi follow older Deccan styles with stepped pyramidal roofs.
  • Carving tradition: richly sculpted pillars and brackets carried forward Chalukya–Hoysala ornamentation, now in hard local granite.
  • Growth of old shrines: the Virupaksha temple grew around an older shrine of the local deity; Krishnadevaraya added the hall in front of the main shrine to mark his accession and is credited with its eastern gopuram.
  • Narrative relief: the Ramayana panels of the Hazara Rama temple continue the old tradition of epic friezes.

2. Contemporary innovations in temples

  • Raya gopurams: towering gateways that dwarfed the central tower and announced royal authority from a distance.
  • Kalyana mandapas and Amman shrines: halls for the divine marriage festival and separate shrines for the consort goddess became standard.
  • Composite pillars: pillars carved with rearing horses and yalis; the Vitthala temple has musical pillars and a stone chariot (a Garuda shrine).
  • Temple towns: chariot streets and pillared bazaars, as at the Vitthala temple, made temples centres of trade.
  • Monolithic sculpture: the giant Ugra Narasimha and the Badavilinga at Hampi.

3. Contemporary practices: Indo-Islamic synthesis in secular buildings

  • Lotus Mahal: cusped Islamic arches combined with tiered, pyramidal Hindu roofs.
  • Elephant Stables: a row of domed chambers with arched entrances.
  • Queen's Bath: an arched corridor around a pool, with balconies.
  • Court culture: rulers styled themselves "Hindu Suratrana" (Sultan among Hindu kings), and court dress and buildings borrowed freely from the Sultanates.

4. Urban planning and hydraulic engineering

  • Royal and sacred centres: the Mahanavami Dibba, a great platform with reliefs of processions, hunting, dancers and foreign visitors, overlooked the royal enclosure.
  • Water management: the Hiriya canal drew water from the Tungabhadra; aqueducts, the Kamalapura tank and stepped tanks served palaces and fields.
  • Fortification: Abdur Razzaq (1440s) described seven lines of fortification enclosing fields and settlements.

5. Legacy

  • Successors: the Nayakas of Madurai and Thanjavur carried the gopuram and pillared-hall style further; within the empire itself, the 16th-century Lepakshi temple (Andhra Pradesh) is known for its murals and hanging pillar.

Vijayanagara architecture was thus a confident synthesis, rooted in Dravida and Deccan tradition yet open to Indo-Islamic forms; conserving Hampi preserves this shared heritage.

Linguistic reorganisationPotti SriramuluStates Reorganisation CommissionPopular movements

The demand for language-based provinces grew within the national movement itself: in 1920 (Nagpur session) the Congress organised its provincial committees on linguistic lines, and Orissa (1936) became the first province formed on a linguistic basis. After independence, however, the leadership, haunted by Partition, hesitated. It was popular agitations, above all Potti Sriramulu's fast unto death for Andhra, that forced the issue and led to the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

1. Reluctance at the top

  • Dar Commission (1948): preferred administrative convenience and rejected language as the sole basis.
  • JVP Committee (1948–49): Nehru, Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya advised postponement, putting unity, security and integration of the princely States first.
  • Fear of fragmentation: leaders worried that linguistic loyalties would weaken the new nation.

2. Pressure from below

  • Andhra: Potti Sriramulu fasted for 58 days and died on 15 December 1952; the violent protests that followed made Nehru announce Andhra State on 19 December, and it was formed on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as capital.
  • Samyukta Maharashtra and Mahagujarat: the plan to keep Bombay a bilingual State provoked mass agitation; more than a hundred people were killed in police firing (commemorated at Hutatma Chowk, Mumbai), and the State was split into Maharashtra and Gujarat on 1 May 1960.
  • Punjabi Suba: the movement led by Master Tara Singh and Sant Fateh Singh ended in the creation of Punjab and Haryana on 1 November 1966.
  • Aikya Kerala and Samyukta Karnataka: movements of writers, students and the regional press led to Kerala and an enlarged Mysore State in 1956 (renamed Karnataka in 1973).

3. The Centre's response

  • States Reorganisation Commission: Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru (report 1955) accepted language as an important but not the only criterion and rejected "one language, one State".
  • 1956 Act and the 7th Amendment: 14 States and 6 Union Territories from 1 November 1956, with safeguards for linguistic minorities (Articles 350A and 350B).
  • Later concessions: Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960) and Punjab–Haryana (1966) came only after renewed agitation.

4. Comment: only from below?

  • Largely yes: the leadership's stated policy was postponement, and every major change followed mass agitation, fasts and violence.
  • But the idea came from above too: the Congress itself had endorsed linguistic provinces (1920, Nehru Report 1928).
  • Regional elites and parties: middle classes seeking jobs and education in their language, and parties such as the CPI (Visalandhra, Aikya Kerala) and the Akali Dal, organised the pressure.
  • The Centre shaped the outcome: it delayed Punjab until 1966, kept Bombay bilingual until 1960, and built in minority safeguards.
  • Result: contrary to fears, accommodating languages strengthened national unity and deepened democracy by bringing administration closer to the people.

Linguistic reorganisation was thus a bottom-up demand met by negotiated accommodation from the top; it shows how Indian federalism absorbs popular pressure without breaking the Union.

Regional imbalanceFive-Year PlansColonial legacyBalanced regional development

Colonial rule left India with a lopsided economy: modern industry, finance and infrastructure clustered around the port cities of Bombay, Calcutta and Madras and in plantation and mining enclaves, while the interior was deindustrialised and agrarian. After independence India adopted planned development through the Planning Commission (1950) and Five-Year Plans. Reducing regional disparities was one stated aim, alongside growth, self-reliance and social justice, but not the only or the main one.

1. Colonial roots of regional imbalance

  • Port-centred economy: railways linked hinterland raw materials to the ports, and industry grew mainly in the presidency towns.
  • Land systems: the Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal and Bihar discouraged investment in land, while Punjab's canal colonies received irrigation.
  • Deindustrialisation: old handicraft centres such as Dhaka and Murshidabad declined, leaving no industrial base in large parts of the interior.

2. How planning tried to correct it

  • Public sector in backward areas: the Second Plan (1956–61) set up steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur in mineral-rich but backward regions; Bokaro followed.
  • Industrial Policy Resolution (1956): explicitly sought to reduce disparities in development between regions; industrial licensing was meant to consider location.
  • River-valley projects: the Damodar Valley Corporation (1948), Hirakud and Bhakra–Nangal brought irrigation and power.
  • Transfers: the Gadgil formula (1969) for plan assistance gave weight to backward and special-category States; Finance Commissions added fiscal equalisation.
  • Area programmes: the Drought Prone Areas Programme (1973), the Desert Development Programme (1977-78), hill-area and tribal sub-plans, and the Backward Regions Grant Fund (2006-07).

3. Results: imbalances persisted

  • Green Revolution: concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, it widened the gap with eastern India.
  • Freight equalisation (1952–1993): equal prices for minerals everywhere removed the locational advantage of Bihar, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh.
  • Enclave development: steel townships had weak links with the surrounding tribal economy and caused displacement.
  • Concentration continued: licensing could not stop investment from flowing to Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; after 1991, private capital favoured States with better infrastructure and skills.

4. Comment

  • Partly true: planning did aim at balance and built an industrial and infrastructure base in backward regions.
  • But growth came first: the Mahalanobis strategy prioritised heavy industry and national growth; regional balance was a secondary objective, often traded off.
  • New approach: NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission, and the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018, 112 districts) and Aspirational Blocks Programme (2023, 500 blocks) target backward areas through data and competition.

Planning softened but did not erase the colonial imprint; balanced development today needs infrastructure, human capital and cooperative federalism that lets lagging States catch up.

Local windsLooFoehn effectAdiabatic warming

Local winds are small-scale winds produced by local differences in temperature, pressure and relief. The Loo of the north Indian plains is a hot, dry continental wind created by intense summer heating, whereas the Chinook of North America and the Foehn of the Alps are warm, dry winds that descend the leeward slopes of mountains and warm by adiabatic compression. They therefore differ in origin, season and impact.

1. Regions of prevalence

  • Loo: the plains of north and north-west India and Pakistan: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
  • Chinook: the eastern (leeward) slopes of the Rocky Mountains, from Alberta in Canada to Montana and Colorado in the USA.
  • Foehn: the northern (leeward) valleys of the Alps in Switzerland, Austria and southern Germany.

2. Nature and mechanism

  • Loo: a strong, gusty, hot and dry westerly wind blowing from the Thar over intensely heated plains, with temperatures of 45–50°C; it is a product of the summer heat low over north-west India, not of relief.
  • Foehn mechanism: moist air forced up the windward slope cools and loses moisture as rain or snow; after crossing the crest it descends and warms at the faster dry adiabatic rate (about 10°C per km), arriving much warmer and drier.
  • Chinook: the same föhn-type process east of the Rockies; at Spearfish, South Dakota (1943), a chinook raised the temperature by about 27°C in two minutes.
  • Foehn: the original Alpine wind that gave the process its name; similar winds include the Zonda of Argentina.

3. Climatic impacts

  • Loo: heat waves, heatstroke and dehydration; high evaporation, wilting crops and drying ponds; peak power demand and fire risk. It often ends with pre-monsoon dust storms and thunderstorms.
  • Chinook: melts and evaporates snow rapidly, exposing pasture for cattle in winter and reducing heating needs; but it also causes rapid snowmelt, wild temperature swings and grassland fire risk.
  • Foehn: melts snow early, lengthens the growing season and helps ripen grapes and maize; it also raises avalanche and forest-fire risk.

4. Similarities and differences

  • Similar: all three are warm, dry, gusty winds that sharply lower humidity.
  • Different origin: Chinook and Foehn are orographic, produced by mountains; the Loo is thermal, produced by surface heating.
  • Different value: Chinook and Foehn are often welcome in cold seasons, whereas the Loo is largely harmful in an already hot season.

With climate change making heat waves more intense, the Loo calls for heat action plans such as Ahmedabad's (2013, the first in South Asia), while chinook and foehn regions must manage avalanche and fire risks.

Climate-smart agricultureRemote sensingFASALFood security

Climate-smart agriculture (CSA), a concept promoted by the FAO (2010), has three pillars: sustainably raising productivity, adapting to climate change, and reducing emissions where possible. Indian farming, largely rainfed and dominated by small holdings (average 1.08 ha, Agriculture Census 2015-16, the latest published), is highly exposed to droughts, floods and heat. Satellites for Earth observation (IRS, EOS-04, NISAR), weather (INSAT-3D, 3DR, 3DS) and navigation supply timely, large-area data that farmers and planners otherwise lack.

1. Productivity: informed and precise farming

  • Crop forecasting: FASAL produces pre-harvest forecasts for rice, wheat, cotton, jute, sugarcane, pulses and oilseeds through the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre; CHAMAN does the same for horticulture.
  • Krishi-DSS: a cloud-based geospatial platform that combines satellite images, weather, soil health and water availability for decisions.
  • Precision inputs: vegetation indices from satellites show crop stress, and satellite-guided drones (as under Namo Drone Didi) spray inputs precisely.
  • Resource maps: groundwater-prospect maps, command-area monitoring and the Bhuvan geoportal guide water and land use.

2. Adaptation and resilience

  • Weather and agromet advisories: IMD uses INSAT data for forecasts and district-level agromet advisories that guide sowing, irrigation and harvesting.
  • Drought monitoring: a geoportal built with ISRO's Space Applications Centre combines rainfall, soil moisture, crop condition and reservoir storage.
  • Crop insurance: YES-TECH under PMFBY estimates yields at gram panchayat level using technology, for paddy and wheat from Kharif 2023 and soybean from Kharif 2024, for quicker, more transparent claims.
  • All-weather eyes: radar satellites such as EOS-04 and NISAR (2025) see through monsoon clouds to map floods, crop damage and soil moisture.

3. Mitigation

  • Stubble burning: satellite fire counts from IARI's CREAMS laboratory track crop-residue burning in Punjab and Haryana and guide enforcement.
  • Efficient inputs: targeted water and fertiliser use reduces energy use and nitrous oxide emissions; rice-area mapping helps target methane-saving practices.
  • Carbon: mapping of agroforestry and soil carbon supports future carbon markets.

4. Contribution to food security

  • Availability: early production estimates guide procurement, buffer stocks and trade decisions.
  • Stability: early warning of drought, floods and pests reduces shocks to supply and prices.
  • Access: faster insurance claims and targeted relief protect farm incomes.
  • Data foundation: the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024, ₹2,817 crore) builds AgriStack, with farmer IDs and a digital crop survey, on which satellite services can draw.

5. Challenges

  • Small, mixed plots that test satellite resolution, and cloud cover during kharif.
  • Last-mile gap: advisories must reach farmers in their language, with trust and the means to act.
  • Capacity and data issues: ground-truthing, State capacity, data privacy and links with private agri-tech firms.

Satellites have turned Indian agriculture from guesswork towards evidence-based farming; integrating them with AgriStack, extension services and insurance can make farms climate-resilient and food supplies secure.

Indo-PacificGeo-economicsGlobal value chainsMaritime trade

For about four centuries after the voyages of Columbus and Vasco da Gama, the Atlantic was the hub of world trade, linking Europe with the Americas and, after 1945, anchoring the US-led Bretton Woods order. Since the 1960s the rise of Japan, the East Asian Tigers, China, ASEAN and India has pulled the centre of gravity towards the Indo-Pacific, which India sees as stretching from the shores of Africa to those of the Americas (Shangri-La Dialogue, 2018).

1. Evidence of the shift

  • Factory Asia: China has been the world's largest trader in goods since 2013, and production networks link Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, ASEAN and, increasingly, India.
  • Mega trade blocs: RCEP (in force since 2022) is the world's largest trade bloc, covering about 30% of world GDP and population; the UK's accession to the CPTPP (signed 2023, in force December 2024) shows its pull beyond the region.
  • Ports and sea lanes: most of the world's ten busiest container ports, led by Shanghai and Singapore, are in Asia; trade worth an estimated US$3.4 trillion passed through the South China Sea in 2016 (CSIS).
  • Growth momentum: the WTO (October 2026) projects Asia's merchandise exports to grow 9.9% in 2026, the fastest of any region, while Europe's contract marginally.

2. Drivers

  • Demography and markets: Asia has nearly 60% of the world's population and the fastest-growing middle classes.
  • Value chains and technology: cost competitiveness, FDI, and semiconductor and electronics hubs in Taiwan, South Korea and China.
  • Energy flows: the largest importers of oil and gas (China, India, Japan, South Korea) draw tankers across the Indian Ocean.
  • Connectivity and diversification: the Belt and Road Initiative, the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (2023), and "China plus one" strategies benefiting Vietnam and India.

3. Why the shift is only gradual

  • Atlantic strengths endure: the US and EU remain the biggest consumer markets, financial centres (dollar and euro) and technology leaders; the US–EU relationship is the world's largest in trade and investment.
  • Indo-Pacific risks: disputes in the South China Sea, tension over the Taiwan Strait, attacks on Red Sea shipping since late 2023, and vulnerable chokepoints.
  • Fragmentation: US–China tariff wars and "de-risking" are reshaping supply chains; Asian trade depends heavily on China; India stays out of RCEP.

4. Implications for India

  • Opportunity: Act East (2014), the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (2019), the Quad, IPEF (2022) and SAGAR (2015) position India at the centre of Indian Ocean trade.
  • Infrastructure: Sagarmala, the new Vizhinjam deep-water transshipment port and the planned Great Nicobar port can capture transshipment now handled at Colombo and Singapore.
  • Challenge: India must raise manufacturing competitiveness to join value chains.

The statement is largely valid: the world is moving towards a multipolar trading system in which the Indo-Pacific is the main engine while the Atlantic retains financial and technological weight, and India's maritime strategy will decide how much it gains.

Land-use changeUrbanisationDeforestationLand degradation

Land-use and land-cover change is the conversion of land from one use or cover to another: forest to farmland, farmland to built-up area, wetland to aquaculture. India has about 2.4% of the world's land but about 18% of its people, so competition for land is intense and human drivers now outweigh natural ones. ISRO's atlas found 29.7% of India's land degraded in 2018-19, while forest cover is 21.76% (ISFR 2023).

1. Major drivers

  • Agricultural expansion and intensification: Green Revolution irrigation and rice–wheat monocropping in the north-west; conversion of grasslands and wetlands; shorter jhum cycles in the North-East.
  • Urbanisation: urban sprawl swallows farmland, lakes and floodplains, as in Bengaluru's lakes and Chennai's Pallikaranai marsh.
  • Infrastructure and industry: highways, industrial corridors, airports and special economic zones fragment land.
  • Mining and energy: coal in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, iron ore in Bellary, large dams such as Sardar Sarovar and Tehri, and large solar parks such as Bhadla in Rajasthan.
  • Forest diversion and coastal conversion: diversion under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023), monoculture plantations, and shrimp farms replacing mangroves.
  • Tourism and settlement in the hills: unplanned construction in Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh.

2. Physical (geographical) consequences

  • Land degradation: soil erosion, and salinity and waterlogging in canal commands such as parts of Punjab and the Indira Gandhi Canal area.
  • Hydrological change: rice–wheat cropping has depleted groundwater in Punjab and Haryana; paving and lost wetlands cause urban floods, as in Chennai (2015) and Bengaluru (2022).
  • Slope instability: road-cutting and construction in the Himalaya trigger landslides and subsidence, as at Joshimath (2023).
  • Micro-climate: urban heat islands and reduced evapotranspiration change local temperatures.
  • Coastal change: loss of mangroves increases erosion, storm-surge damage and saline intrusion.

3. Ecological and human consequences

  • Biodiversity: habitat loss and broken corridors increase human–wildlife conflict, especially with elephants; loss of grasslands and collisions with power lines have pushed the Great Indian Bustard to the brink.
  • Carbon: forest loss releases carbon, though tree plantations add some sinks.
  • Displacement and conflict: dams and mines displace tribal communities, as the Niyamgiri case (2013), in which gram sabhas rejected bauxite mining, showed.
  • Food security: fertile farmland near cities is lost to construction.

4. Way forward

  • Planning: scientific land-use planning, zoning and protection of wetlands (Wetlands Rules, 2017) and floodplains.
  • Monitoring: satellite land-use maps from NRSC and Bhuvan to track change.
  • Restoration: India's target to restore 26 million ha of degraded land by 2030, and green-cover and watershed programmes.

Land-use change is unavoidable in a developing country, but unplanned change converts development into disaster risk; integrating land-use planning with ecology is the key to sustainable development.

Urban casteEndogamyCastelessnessCaste associations

Classical theories of modernisation expected industrialisation and urbanisation to dissolve caste: anonymity, occupational mobility, education and the market would replace ascribed status with achievement. Seven decades on, urban India shows transformation rather than disappearance. Ritual hierarchy and purity–pollution practices have weakened in public life, but caste survives in endogamy, social networks, housing and politics, often in less visible forms.

1. Signs that caste is weakening in cities

  • Public spaces: restaurants, buses, the metro and offices mix people of all castes; untouchability is abolished (Article 17) and openly practised far less in urban public life.
  • Occupational mobility: jobs in IT, services and start-ups are filled on credentials, and hereditary occupations are declining.
  • A new middle class: education and reservations have created an SC and ST middle class; Dalit entrepreneurs organised the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (2005).
  • Marriage choices: love and inter-caste marriages are more visible in metros.
  • Class and lifestyle: profession, income and consumption increasingly define urban status.

2. Signs that caste persists

  • Endogamy: only about 5% of Indian marriages are inter-caste (India Human Development Survey, NCAER); matrimonial websites and newspaper advertisements are sorted by caste.
  • Residential segregation: studies of large Indian cities find neighbourhoods divided by caste, and landlords screen tenants by surname or diet.
  • Caste-linked work: sanitation and sewer cleaning are still done mostly by Dalits, despite the 2013 Act prohibiting manual scavenging.
  • Discrimination in campuses and offices: the deaths of Rohith Vemula (2016) and Payal Tadvi (2019) drew attention to campus discrimination; Seattle became the first US city to ban caste discrimination (2023), showing that caste travels with migrants.
  • Hidden privilege: sociologist Satish Deshpande argues that upper castes convert inherited caste advantages into education, networks and jobs, and then present themselves as "casteless".

3. Caste reinvented in the city

  • From hierarchy to identity: caste associations act as interest groups, as the Rudolphs showed in "The Modernity of Tradition" (1967).
  • Politics: caste mobilisation in urban wards, and reservation demands from dominant groups such as the Marathas, Jats and Patidars.
  • Data and policy: the Bihar caste survey (2023) and the decision (April 2025) to enumerate caste in Census 2027, the first full caste count since 1931.
  • Online: caste pride pages and community groups on social media.

4. Assessment and way forward

  • Not disappearing: caste is fading from public ritual but persists in private life, opportunities and politics.
  • Remedies: enforcement of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, equity cells in campuses, fair-housing norms, mechanisation of sanitation work, and incentives for inter-caste marriage (the Dr. Ambedkar Scheme, 2013, offers ₹2.5 lakh).

Urban India has made caste less visible but not irrelevant; real change needs what Ambedkar called the "annihilation of caste" (1936): equal opportunity, inter-caste social life and constitutional morality in private as well as public life.

Demographic transitionBelow-replacement fertilityPopulation ageingDemographic dividend

The demographic transition is the shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a society develops. India is in its late phase: the total fertility rate (TFR) has fallen to 1.9 (SRS 2024), below the replacement level of 2.1; the birth rate is 18.3 and the death rate 6.4 per 1,000. The transition opens a window for a demographic dividend but brings serious challenges.

1. An uneven transition across regions

  • North–south divide: Bihar's TFR is 2.9 and Delhi's 1.2 (SRS 2024); Kerala and Tamil Nadu are ageing, while Bihar and Uttar Pradesh remain young.
  • Federal tensions: the freeze on Lok Sabha seats until the first Census after 2026 (84th Amendment, 2001) is due to end, and southern States fear losing seats for controlling population; the 16th Finance Commission gives 10% weight to demographic performance.
  • Migration: young workers move from the north and east to the south and west, raising issues of portability of benefits, housing and social friction.

2. Ageing and its burdens

  • Rapid ageing: the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to double from 10.5% (2022) to 20.8% by 2050, and to exceed the share of children by 2046 (India Ageing Report 2023, UNFPA–IIPS).
  • Old-age insecurity: about 90% of workers are informal, so few have pensions; ageing is feminised, with many elderly widows.
  • Health burden: non-communicable diseases now cause about two-thirds of deaths, demanding geriatric and long-term care.
  • Weaker family support: nuclear families and migration reduce care at home.

3. Turning the dividend into reality

  • Jobs: the Economic Survey 2023-24 estimated that about 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs are needed every year until 2030.
  • Human capital: 35.5% of children under five are stunted (NFHS-5), and learning gaps persist.
  • Women's work: female labour force participation was only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • A closing window: the working-age share is expected to peak around 2041 (Economic Survey 2018-19); India risks growing old before it grows rich.

4. Social and gender challenges

  • Son preference: the sex ratio at birth is 918 girls per 1,000 boys (SRS 2024).
  • Low-fertility trap: experience in East Asia shows that very low fertility is hard to reverse.
  • Critical view: falling fertility also brings gains: healthier mothers, more investment per child and higher per-capita income; the challenges are manageable with timely policy.

Policy responses: NEP 2020 and Skill India for human capital, Mission Parivar Vikas (2016) for high-fertility districts, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY for everyone aged 70 and above (2024), and social security under the Labour Codes (2025).

India's transition is a success with consequences: the task now is to convert a shrinking window of opportunity into lasting prosperity through human capital, jobs, health and dignified ageing.
free.upm-2026-gs1-20:
GlobalisationYouthGlocalisationAspirations

Globalisation, the growing integration of economies, societies and cultures through trade, capital, technology and migration, accelerated in India after the 1991 reforms and the internet revolution. Its deepest effects are felt by youth (aged 15–29 under the National Youth Policy, 2014), who form about a quarter of India's population and are its most connected, mobile and aspirational section. The impact is mixed across the social, political, economic and cultural spheres.

1. Economic sphere

  • New opportunities: IT and business services, global capability centres, start-ups and export industries have created well-paid jobs; Indians abroad sent home record remittances (about US$135 billion in 2024-25).
  • Gig and platform economy: NITI Aayog (2022) counted 77 lakh gig workers in 2020-21 and projected 2.35 crore by 2029-30; the work is flexible but insecure.
  • Challenges: skill mismatch, educated unemployment, informality, automation and AI, and brain drain of trained talent.

2. Social sphere

  • Individual choice: delayed marriage, partner choice, nuclear families and more inter-caste relationships, often backed by courts.
  • Gender: young women's aspirations for education and careers have risen, though online harassment and backlash persist.
  • Consumerism and lifestyle: branded consumption and fast food bring lifestyle diseases; social-media pressure adds to anxiety and loneliness; drug abuse is a growing concern.
  • Inequality: rural, poor and female youth gain less, widening the digital and opportunity divide.

3. Political sphere

  • Awareness and activism: global ideas of rights, transparency and environmentalism shape youth politics; the India Against Corruption movement (2011) and protests after the Delhi gang-rape (2012) spread through social media.
  • Participation: young voters and volunteers engage through digital campaigns and platforms such as MY Bharat (2023).
  • Risks: misinformation, echo chambers, polarisation and online radicalisation; "clicktivism" can replace sustained engagement.

4. Cultural sphere

  • Hybridisation (glocalisation): fusion music, Indian content on global streaming platforms, and fandoms of K-pop and anime.
  • Global reach of Indian culture: International Day of Yoga (since 2015), Indian cuisine and cinema; "Naatu Naatu" won the Oscar for Best Original Song (2023).
  • Concerns: homogenisation, the pull of English over Indian languages, and conflicts between global values and local traditions, which sometimes provoke identity assertion.

Globalisation has made Indian youth more aspirational and globally confident, but its benefits are uneven; skills, decent jobs, digital literacy and rootedness in Indian values can help youth become global citizens with local roots.

In NALSA v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a "third gender" and held that the right to self-identify one's gender flows from dignity and personal liberty under Article 21. K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy, including bodily and decisional autonomy, a fundamental right. The 2019 Act gave a "right to self-perceived gender identity" (Section 4(2)); the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 (assented to on 30 March 2026) replaces self-identification with medical verification.

1. What the 2026 amendment changes

  • Narrower definition: a transgender person now means persons with socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta, persons with intersex variations, and persons compelled by force or deceit to assume a transgender identity; persons with different sexual orientations and self-perceived identities are expressly excluded.
  • Self-identification removed: Section 4(2) is deleted, so trans men, trans women and genderqueer persons outside these groups lose recognition under the Act.
  • Medical gatekeeping: the District Magistrate issues a certificate of identity only after examining the recommendation of a medical board (the "authority") headed by the Chief Medical Officer, and hospitals must report gender-affirming surgery to the District Magistrate and the board.
  • Harsher penalties: the 2019 offences (such as denying access to public places or forcing a person out of home) keep six months to two years; new offences carry 10 years to life for kidnapping and grievous hurt to force a transgender identity on an adult (life if a child), and 5 to 10 years for compelling such a person into begging or servitude.

2. Effect on privacy and self-identity

  • Departure from NALSA: NALSA treated gender identity as a deeply felt internal experience, not a biological test; making a medical board the judge reverses this.
  • Bodily privacy: a compulsory examination intrudes on bodily integrity and decisional autonomy protected in Puttaswamy, and exposes intimate data to officials.
  • Equality and welfare: persons left out of the definition may lose access to the National Portal for Transgender Persons, the SMILE scheme and Garima Greh shelters, raising concerns under Articles 14, 15 and 19(1)(a) (expression of gender).
  • Retrospective doubt: the words "nor shall ever have been so included" may unsettle certificates already issued.
  • Chilling effect: broad criminal clauses may deter doctors from offering gender-affirming care.

3. The government's rationale and the proportionality test

  • Preventing misuse: verification is meant to ensure that welfare and affirmative action reach genuine beneficiaries.
  • Protection: harsher penalties target forced castration, trafficking and forced begging, which are real harms.
  • Proportionality: under the Puttaswamy test the aim is legitimate, but a less intrusive tool, such as a sworn self-declaration with penalties for fraud, may achieve it.

In May 2026 the Supreme Court issued notice on petitions challenging the amendment but did not stay it. Keeping self-determination at the core, with light-touch safeguards against fraud, would honour both dignity and the State's legitimate interest.

Article 15(3)73rd and 74th Amendments106th AmendmentSubstantive equality

Women are neither a numerical minority nor a caste-based backward class, so their claim to reservation rests not on Articles 15(4) and 16(4) but on Article 15(3), which permits special provisions for women, and on the idea of substantive equality. That is why women's quotas are horizontal: they cut across SC, ST, OBC and general categories. Their journey has run from panchayats (1992) to Parliament (2023), though no legislative seat has yet been reserved.

1. Why reservation became necessary

  • Under-representation: women were under 5% of the first Lok Sabha and are only about 14% of the 18th Lok Sabha (2024).
  • Structural barriers: patriarchy, care burdens, costly elections and party gatekeeping keep women off candidate lists.
  • Early reluctance: women members of the Constituent Assembly such as Renuka Ray opposed reserved seats, trusting adult franchise and equal citizenship.
  • Towards Equality (1974): the Committee on the Status of Women in India exposed women's political marginalisation and proposed statutory women's panchayats, though its majority did not favour reserved seats in legislatures.

2. Local bodies: from experiment to constitutional mandate

  • State initiatives: Karnataka's 1983 panchayat law reserved 25% of seats for women, and the National Perspective Plan for Women (1988) proposed 30% in local bodies.
  • 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992): at least one-third of seats and of panchayat chairpersons' posts (Article 243D), and one-third of municipal seats (Article 243T), including one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs.
  • Beyond one-third: Bihar became the first State to reserve 50% of panchayat seats (2006); 21 States and two UTs now do so, and women hold nearly half of all panchayat seats.
  • Limits: proxy rule by husbands ("sarpanch-pati"), rotation of seats every term and weak devolution dilute real power.

3. Parliament and Assemblies: a long wait

  • Failed attempts: the 81st Amendment Bill (1996), examined by the Geeta Mukherjee Committee, and later versions lapsed; the 108th Amendment Bill passed the Rajya Sabha in 2010 but lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha in 2014.
  • 106th Amendment (2023), the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam: reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly (Articles 330A, 332A, 239AA), including within SC and ST seats, for 15 years, with rotation after each delimitation.
  • Conditional start (Article 334A): it takes effect only after a delimitation based on the first Census taken after the Act's commencement. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which sought earlier implementation through a delimitation based on the 2011 Census, with the Lok Sabha enlarged to up to 850 seats, was defeated in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026: it got 298 votes to 230, short of the 352 (two-thirds of members present and voting) required.
  • Gaps: there is no OBC sub-quota and no reservation in the Rajya Sabha or the Legislative Councils.

Women's leadership in local bodies has created a pool of experienced women politicians; implementing legislative reservation through political consensus on delimitation would turn formal equality into substantive representation.

Speaker's neutralityTenth ScheduleKihoto HollohanIndependent tribunal

The Speaker (Article 93) is the presiding officer and impartial custodian of the Lok Sabha's rights. The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) made the Speaker the final authority on disqualification for defection (Paragraph 6), and Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld this, subject to judicial review. Because the Speaker is elected by the ruling majority and usually remains a party member, this adjudicatory role has drawn the office into partisan controversy.

1. Why the office has become vulnerable

  • Judicial review of disqualification orders (Kihoto Hollohan) corrects perverse decisions.

  • Conventions: several Speakers have given up party posts and ruled against their own parties.

  • Independent adjudicator: give defection cases to the President or Governor acting on the Election Commission's advice (Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990) or to a tribunal of retired judges, as suggested in Keisham.
  • Statutory timeline: write a three-month limit into the Tenth Schedule, with automatic transfer to the tribunal if it is missed.
  • Narrower whip: confine disqualification to voluntarily giving up party membership and to votes on confidence and no-confidence motions, as the Goswami Committee proposed, restoring MPs' freedom on ordinary Bills.
  • Westminster conventions: the Speaker should resign party membership on election, parties should not contest the Speaker's seat, and a Deputy Speaker should be elected promptly, by convention from the Opposition.

  • Mortality and morbidity: undernutrition weakens immunity and underlies a large share of child deaths from diarrhoea and pneumonia.

  • Caste and class: stunting is highest among ST and SC children and in the poorest households, about twice the level in the richest.

  • Social determinants: sanitation, safe water and mothers' education strongly shape child nutrition.

  • Rights and goals: the right to food is part of Article 21 (PUCL v. Union of India, from 2001), Article 47 makes raising nutrition a primary duty of the State, and SDG 2 seeks to end malnutrition by 2030.

India's higher bureaucracy, led by the IAS, follows the generalist model inherited from the ICS and the Macaulay Report (1854): officers recruited young through a common examination rotate across sectors, from district administration to finance and trade. Sardar Patel defended the All India Services as the steel frame of a united India.   • Holistic view: generalists see links across sectors, which suits coordination roles such as the District Collector and the Cabinet Secretariat.
  • Field knowledge: early postings as Sub-Divisional Magistrate and Collector give a grassroots understanding of how policy lands, valuable in elections, disasters and pandemics.
  • National integration: the All India Services (Article 312; All India Services Act, 1951), with officers serving outside their home States, keep a common administrative standard across the federation.
  • Neutrality and continuity: permanent, politically neutral officers provide institutional memory across changing governments.
  • Adaptability: officers trained to learn quickly can lead multidisciplinary teams and draw on specialists for technical advice.

2. Limitations in contemporary governance

  • Shallow expertise: complex areas such as financial regulation, cyber security, health systems and climate need depth that frequent rotation does not build.
  • Short tenures: frequent transfers break continuity; in T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) the Supreme Court called for minimum tenures and Civil Services Boards.
  • Generalist–specialist friction: generalist control over technical services (engineers, doctors, scientists) affects morale and the quality of decisions.
  • Process over outcomes: a rule-bound, risk-averse culture and seniority-based promotion weaken accountability for results.
  • Closed system: entry mainly at a young age, with little lateral movement, limits fresh skills and outside perspectives.

3. Reforms to combine the two

  • Domain specialisation: the Hota Committee (2004) and the Second ARC (10th Report, 2008) recommended assigning officers to domains in mid-career.
  • Lateral entry: begun in 2018, it has brought specialists in at Joint Secretary, Director and Deputy Secretary levels; an August 2024 advertisement was withdrawn over reservation concerns, showing the need for a transparent framework.
  • Capacity building: Mission Karmayogi (2020) shifts training from "rule to role" through competency frameworks and the iGOT Karmayogi platform, supported by the Capacity Building Commission.
  • Performance: multi-source appraisal, stable tenures and review of non-performers under FR 56(j).

The answer is not to abandon the generalist but to build "generalists with specialisation": field-rooted officers with domain depth, working alongside lateral talent in a performance-oriented service.

The Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA), launched at the Quad Leaders' Summit in Tokyo (May 2022), gives partner countries near-real-time data on "dark" shipping.   • A shared public good: IPMDA tracks vessels that switch off their transponders, illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, smuggling and disasters, threats that SAGAR treats as common to all littorals.

  • Non-military framing: focusing on fisheries, disaster relief and climate rather than naval confrontation reassures small States and fits SAGAR's development-first ethos.
  • Complementary capacity: India's coastal radar chains in Mauritius, Seychelles, Maldives and Sri Lanka, patrol vessels and hydrographic surveys give partners the means to use the data.

  • Different geographies: IPMDA began with the Pacific islands and South-East Asia, whereas SAGAR centres on the Indian Ocean.
  • Different philosophies: SAGAR is inclusive and India-led; the Quad is a minilateral of four democracies that China and some littorals view as containment.
  • Data without capacity: many small island States lack ships and aircraft to act on what they see.
  • Dependence and continuity: reliance on US-funded commercial vendors and the uneven rhythm of Quad summits make long-term sustainability uncertain.
  • Sovereignty sensitivities: some partners hesitate to be seen relying on Quad data, and Chinese research and fishing fleets show that competition at sea continues.

The statement is broadly valid: IPMDA supplies the "awareness" layer that SAGAR lacked and gives the Quad a constructive, non-military face. But it is a partial bridge, because trust and presence still come from India's own instruments, such as the Colombo Security Conclave, white-shipping agreements and bilateral capacity building.

  • Checks in the USA: a presidential veto that two-thirds of each House can override, Senate confirmation of appointments, judicial review (Marbury v. Madison, 1803) and impeachment.

2. Actual authority: Indian Prime Minister vs US President

  • Where the PM is stronger: with a Lok Sabha majority, the PM controls both the executive and the legislative agenda; party discipline under the anti-defection law ensures that Bills and budgets pass; senior appointments need no legislative confirmation; and the PM can advise early dissolution.
  • Where the President is stronger: a fixed term independent of Congress, a personal national mandate, real command as Commander-in-Chief, executive orders and a qualified veto.
  • Limits on the PM: coalition compulsions (as in 1989–2014), a Rajya Sabha without a majority, collective responsibility, assertive States, an active judiciary and the President's role when no party has a majority.
  • Limits on the President: Congress controls the purse; divided government can stall his agenda; the Senate must approve treaties and key appointments; courts strike down executive actions; and the 22nd Amendment limits him to two terms.

3. Assessment

India practises a functional separation within a fused political executive, while the USA practises structural separation. A majority Prime Minister can therefore be more powerful at home than a US President facing a hostile Congress, though a coalition Prime Minister is much weaker.

In both systems, the real safeguard lies in institutional independence: a vigilant legislature, an independent judiciary and free elections.

Pluralist democracy holds that power is shared among many competing groups rather than monopolised by the State or one class, Robert Dahl's "polyarchy". In India, pressure groups (trade unions, farmers' bodies, professional associations), social movements (Chipko, the Narmada Bachao Andolan, the right-to-information movement) and corporate lobbies (FICCI, CII, NASSCOM) use the freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c) to influence policy between elections.

1. How they deepen pluralism by voicing excluded interests

  • Rights-based laws: the MKSS-led campaign produced the RTI Act, 2005; the Right to Food campaign, backed by the PUCL case (2001), shaped the NFSA, 2013; the Campaign for Survival and Dignity pressed for the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Marginalised identities: disability groups helped secure the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; transgender and LGBTQ activism led to NALSA (2014) and Navtej Singh Johar (2018).
  • Women and the environment: the Vishaka case (1997) was brought by women's groups; Chipko and the Narmada movement made ecology and resettlement political issues.
  • Farmers: the 2020–21 movement led to the repeal of the three farm laws in 2021.
  • Corporate associations: supply expertise for reforms such as GST and the insolvency code and represent new sectors such as IT and start-ups.

2. To what extent: the limits

  • Unequal voice: organised, urban and resource-rich groups are heard more, while informal workers, Adivasis and migrants remain weakly organised; as Mancur Olson argued, small, concentrated groups outmobilise large, diffuse ones.
  • Sectional pressure: some groups use bandhs and blockades, or defend narrow privileges.
  • Shrinking civic space: the 2020 amendment to the FCRA barred sub-granting of foreign contributions and capped administrative spending at 20%, constraining many NGOs.
  • No lobbying law: unlike the US Lobbying Disclosure Act, 1995, India has no register of lobbyists.

3. Corporate wealth and political power: a threat to institutional autonomy?

  • Opaque political finance: electoral bonds (2018), with the cap on corporate donations removed, allowed unlimited anonymous funding; in ADR v. Union of India (February 2024) the Supreme Court struck down the scheme as violating voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a), and also the removal of the cap.
  • Capture and cronyism: concentrated ownership in infrastructure, telecom and media, revolving doors between regulators and firms, and tailored policies can erode the autonomy of legislatures, regulators and the press.
  • Costly elections: candidates' spending is capped (₹95 lakh for a Lok Sabha seat in larger States), but party spending is not.
  • Institutional pushback: the Supreme Court's cancellation of 122 2G licences (2012) and 214 coal blocks (2014), and the electoral-bonds verdict, show that institutions can resist capture.

Group politics has broadened Indian pluralism, but the convergence of money and power is a real risk. A lobbying disclosure law, transparent party finance (including partial state funding, as the Indrajit Gupta Committee suggested in 1998) and independent regulators can keep democracy plural rather than plutocratic.

Transparency means that information on how decisions are made is openly available; accountability means that those in authority must answer for their decisions and face consequences. Long seen mainly as tools against corruption (Santhanam Committee, 1964), they serve a wider purpose: building the trust of citizens, investors and civil society in the policy process. The Second ARC's first report (2006) called the right to information the "master key to good governance".

1. Why trust, not only anti-corruption, is the goal

  • Legitimacy and compliance: citizens pay taxes, follow public-health advice and accept reforms when they trust the process, not merely the honesty of officials.
  • Policy acceptance: the three farm laws of 2020, passed with little consultation, were repealed in 2021 after prolonged protests, showing how a trust deficit can stall reform.
  • Investor confidence: retrospective taxation (2012) damaged India's image until the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 withdrew such demands.
  • Social capital: high-trust societies need less coercion and have lower transaction costs.

2. Rule of Law as the foundation of trust

  • Non-arbitrariness: Article 14 forbids arbitrary action (E.P. Royappa, 1974); reasoned orders and natural justice (Maneka Gandhi, 1978) make decisions predictable and fair.
  • Independent institutions: the CAG (Article 148), the Election Commission, Information Commissions, the Lokpal and the courts check power impartially.
  • Stable, clear laws: predictable regulation and timely justice matter as much to a farmer as to an investor.
  • Openness by default: Section 4 of the RTI Act requires proactive disclosure, though critics fear that the DPDP Act, 2023 widened the personal-information exemption in Section 8(1)(j).

3. Participatory governance as the engine of trust

  • Consultation: the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014) requires draft Bills to be placed in the public domain for at least 30 days.
  • Grassroots voice: Gram Sabhas, social audits (pioneered by the MKSS and made mandatory under MGNREGA) and participatory budgeting give citizens ownership of decisions.
  • Feedback loops: citizen report cards (pioneered by Bengaluru's Public Affairs Centre), CPGRAMS grievance redress, MyGov and citizens' charters make services responsive.

4. A caveat: corruption control still matters

  • False choice: corruption itself destroys trust, so the Prevention of Corruption Act, the Lokpal and Direct Benefit Transfer, which removes intermediaries, remain indispensable.
  • Floor and ceiling: controlling corruption is the floor of good governance; stakeholder trust is its ceiling.

Transparency and accountability are means; legitimacy is the end. Governance rooted in the rule of law and genuine participation turns citizens from subjects into stakeholders, the essence of good governance.
