The rights-based approach turns welfare from discretionary charity into legal entitlements that citizens can claim and courts can enforce. Its constitutional mandate lies in the expanded Article 21 (food, livelihood, health, dignity), Article 21A (education) and the Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39, 41, 42, 47). But rights on paper depend on integrated delivery and adequate public money.

1. The mandate and its legal instruments

2. Non-integrated governance weakens rights

  • Departmental silos: nutrition depends on the ministries of women and child development, health, food and Jal Shakti, yet planning, budgets and data remain separate.
  • Centre–State fragmentation: uniform Centrally Sponsored Schemes, delayed fund releases and frequent redesign leave States little flexibility.
  • Weak local government: panchayats and municipalities, closest to citizens, still lack funds, functions and functionaries despite the 73rd and 74th Amendments.
  • Exclusion errors: fragmented databases, authentication failures and the digital divide deny entitlements to the poorest, and grievance redress is weak.

3. Minimal public investment hollows them out

  • Health: government health expenditure was only 1.43% of GDP and out-of-pocket spending 43.4% of total health expenditure (National Health Accounts 2022-23), against the National Health Policy, 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP by 2025.
  • Education: public spending remains well below the 6% of GDP goal set by the Kothari Commission and NEP 2020, and teacher vacancies dilute RTE norms.
  • Frontline workforce: anganwadi workers and ASHAs, the backbone of delivery, are honorary, overburdened and underpaid.
  • Fiscal choices: committed expenditure and short-term cash transfers crowd out investment in the services that make rights real.

4. Can the mandate still be realised?

  • Yes, conditionally: Kerala and Tamil Nadu show that sustained investment and integrated public services deliver results; Chhattisgarh's PDS reforms and One Nation One Ration Card improved access; DBT has reduced leakages.
  • Courts as catalysts: the PUCL right-to-food orders turned mid-day meals into an entitlement, and Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) made emergency care part of Article 21.
  • The path: convergent district plans, a unified social registry, outcome budgets, devolution to local bodies, statutory grievance redress (district grievance officers and State Food Commissions under the NFSA) and raising health and education spending to target levels.

Rights without resources and coordination remain paper promises. A whole-of-government approach backed by adequate public investment is what converts the constitutional mandate into lived entitlement.

Education is both a fundamental right, under Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) and the RTE Act, 2009, and the foundation of the human capital that drives productivity and innovation. The NEP 2020 aims to make India a "global knowledge superpower". The debate is whether the State should treat education mainly as a welfare duty towards the disadvantaged or as a strategic investment in national competitiveness.

1. The case for a welfare obligation

  • Constitutional duty: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) recognised a right to education; Article 21A and the RTE Act made schooling free and compulsory for children aged 6–14, and the 25% private-school quota was upheld (Society for Unaided Private Schools, 2012).
  • Equity: education is the main ladder of mobility for SCs, STs, girls and the poor; PM POSHAN meals, scholarships and residential schools target them.
  • Social returns: educated mothers have healthier children and smaller families, and education strengthens citizenship and democracy.
  • Market failure: poor families cannot pay, and private providers neglect remote areas, so the State must provide.

2. The case for a strategic investment

  • Knowledge economy: IT services, Global Capability Centres, semiconductors and AI need advanced skills; human capital explains much of East Asia's rise.
  • Thin research base: India's gross expenditure on R&D is only 0.84% of GDP (2023-24), against China's 2.58%; the ANRF Act, 2023 and the ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation scheme (2025) aim to change this.
  • Higher education gap: a gross enrolment ratio of 28.4% (AISHE 2021-22) against NEP's target of 50% by 2035, and few Indian universities among the world's best.
  • Global links: UGC regulations (2023) allow foreign universities to open campuses in India, and a skilled diaspora builds knowledge networks.

3. Critical evaluation: a false binary

  • Welfare alone falls short: near-universal enrolment has not ensured learning; ASER surveys show many Class 5 children cannot read a Class 2 text.
  • Strategy alone excludes: a focus on elite institutions and STEM can neglect foundational learning, humanities and the poor, and rising fees can commercialise education.
  • Foundational learning is both: NIPUN Bharat's goal of literacy and numeracy for all by Class 3 is welfare and strategy at once.
  • East Asian lesson: South Korea and China built universal, good-quality basic education before world-class research, showing that equity is the base of excellence.
  • Funding gap: public spending remains below the 6% of GDP goal set by the Kothari Commission and NEP 2020.

Education should be treated as a welfare foundation with a strategic direction: universal quality schooling as a right, and research universities and skills as national investment, together building a knowledge-driven and inclusive nation.
free.upm-2026-gs2-19:
Indian diasporaLiving bridgeRemittancesSoft power

India has the world's largest diaspora: about 1.8 crore Indian-born emigrants (UN, 2020), and over 3 crore Non-Resident Indians and Persons of Indian Origin by the Ministry of External Affairs' estimate. Often called a living bridge between India and the world, it carries culture, capital and knowledge across borders. Whether this translates into geopolitical influence and strategic leverage deserves a critical look.

1. A cultural bridge and source of soft power

  • Heritage abroad: yoga, Indian cuisine, cinema and festivals have global reach; the UN declared 21 June International Day of Yoga (2014), and a 2023 law made Diwali a public-school holiday in New York City.
  • Institutional links: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (since 2003), the Overseas Citizen of India scheme (2005) and the Know India Programme keep later generations connected.
  • Girmitiya ties: descendants of indentured workers in Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad and Tobago and Guyana anchor India's goodwill in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

2. An economic factor

  • Remittances: India is the world's largest recipient, with record inflows of about US$135 billion in 2024-25, which cushion the current account deficit and support households in Kerala, Punjab and other States.
  • Investment and trade: diaspora entrepreneurs invest in India and connect Indian firms to global markets.

3. A knowledge network

  • Technology leadership: Indian-origin leaders head firms such as Alphabet and Microsoft, and diaspora engineers helped build India's IT services industry and its Global Capability Centres.
  • Brain circulation: schemes such as VAJRA (2017) bring overseas researchers to Indian institutions, and returnees seed start-ups.

4. Geopolitical influence and strategic leverage

  • Political voice: Indian-origin leaders have reached the highest offices, such as Rishi Sunak (UK Prime Minister, 2022–24), Kamala Harris (US Vice-President, 2021–25) and Tharman Shanmugaratnam (Singapore President, 2023).
  • Advocacy: Indian-American groups lobbied Congress for the India–US civil nuclear deal (2005–08).
  • Security of nationals: large evacuations such as Operation Ganga (Ukraine, 2022), Kaveri (Sudan, 2023) and Ajay (Israel, 2023) show both responsibility and reach.

5. Critical view: limits of the bridge

  • Loyalty lies with host countries: Indian-origin politicians serve their own nations, and their policies are not necessarily pro-India.
  • Divisive fringes: separatist activity among a small section of the diaspora in Canada has long strained ties, which fell into a diplomatic crisis in 2023.
  • Vulnerable workers: millions in the Gulf face restrictive labour systems, wage theft and sudden crises.
  • Host-country curbs: tighter visa and immigration rules show that diaspora influence cannot override host-country interests.
  • Brain drain: skilled emigration means lost talent and public investment.

The diaspora is a genuine strategic asset, but its leverage is indirect and conditional. Protecting workers, engaging all segments and avoiding the export of domestic divisions will turn this living bridge into lasting soft power.

Belt and Road InitiativeCPECStrategic encirclementNeighbourhood First

The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, finances ports, roads, railways and power projects across Asia, Africa and Europe. In South Asia, its flagship is the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC, 2015), and every South Asian neighbour of India except Bhutan has signed up in some form. India has stayed out, objecting that CPEC passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and violates its sovereignty. The BRI has made South Asia an arena of great power competition.

1. How the BRI has changed South Asia

  • From regional to global contest: Chinese finance has drawn the US, Japan and the EU into South Asia, through the US Millennium Challenge Corporation compact with Nepal, Japan's projects in Bangladesh and the Indo-Pacific frameworks of the Quad.
  • New dependencies: large, opaque loans contributed to debt distress; Sri Lanka's 2022 default led to India's assistance of about US$4 billion.

2. Strategic implications for India's security

  • Encirclement fears: ports at Gwadar, Hambantota and Kyaukphyu could support Chinese naval logistics (the "string of pearls"); a Chinese submarine docked in Colombo in 2014 and the tracking ship Yuan Wang 5 called at Hambantota in 2022.
  • Two-front pressure: CPEC deepens China–Pakistan collusion along the western front, while Chinese infrastructure in Tibet and the Doklam stand-off (2017) near the Siliguri Corridor show pressure in the east; the Galwan clash (2020) highlighted the risk.
  • Digital and economic security: Chinese telecom networks, surveillance technology and control of critical infrastructure in neighbours raise data and supply-chain risks.

3. Implications for India's regional influence

  • Loss of primacy: neighbours play China against India to gain bargaining power, weakening India's traditional leadership.
  • Competition in development finance: China offers speed and scale that India's lines of credit cannot match, though India's aid, mostly grants and concessional credit, creates less debt.
  • Opportunity: BRI's debt problems and the backlash against them have revived interest in India as a reliable first responder, as in Sri Lanka in 2022.

4. India's response

  • Neighbourhood First (2014) and SAGAR (2015): connectivity, capacity building and crisis assistance.
  • Alternative corridors: Chabahar port, the Kaladan multimodal project, BBIN connectivity and the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (2023).
  • Maritime security: the IFC-IOR, the Colombo Security Conclave and the Quad.
  • Partnerships: joint projects with Japan and support for transparent, sustainable financing standards.

The BRI has made South Asia contested, but not lost. India's advantage lies in geography, culture and trust; delivering projects quickly and on fair terms will keep it the preferred partner of its neighbours.

Digital Rupee (e₹)Central Bank Digital CurrencyTwo-tier distributionProgrammable money

The Digital Rupee (e₹) is India's Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC): legal tender issued by the Reserve Bank of India in digital form. Like a currency note, it is a direct liability of the RBI and is exchangeable one-to-one with cash, so it carries no credit risk. The RBI Act, 1934 was amended through the Finance Act, 2022 to allow it, and the RBI's Concept Note (October 2022) set out its design.

1. What the Digital Rupee is

  • Sovereign money, not bank money: a UPI payment moves a bank deposit, whereas e₹ moves the RBI's own money from wallet to wallet; settlement is final.
  • Two variants: wholesale e₹-W for settling large inter-bank transactions (pilot from 1 November 2022) and retail e₹-R for people and merchants (pilot from 1 December 2022).
  • Not a cryptocurrency: it has a central issuer and a stable value, unlike private crypto assets, which India taxes but does not treat as legal tender.

2. Working of India's CBDC

  • Two-tier model: the RBI creates and issues e₹; authorised banks distribute it to customers' digital wallets and handle KYC, so the RBI does not deal with the public directly.
  • Token-based retail e₹: each token behaves like a note or coin; a user loads the wallet from a bank account and pays persons or merchants by scanning a QR code, including UPI QR codes.
  • Account-based wholesale e₹: banks settle large-value transactions; their balances are redeemed into current accounts at the end of the day.
  • New features: programmability (money usable only for a set purpose), offline payments for areas with weak connectivity, and a sandbox for fintech firms to test products.

3. Progress so far

  • Scale: over 80 lakh users and more than 12 crore retail transactions worth over ₹28,000 crore (RBI Deputy Governor, December 2025).
  • Circulation: retail e₹ in circulation fell about 24% to ₹771.7 crore at end-March 2026 from ₹1,016.5 crore a year earlier (RBI Annual Report 2025-26), a sign that UPI already meets most needs.
  • Programmable welfare: food subsidy was paid as programmable CBDC to PDS beneficiaries in Gujarat, Puducherry and Chandigarh, redeemable only for eligible goods at fair price shops.
  • Wholesale and tokenisation: tokenised certificates of deposit are being piloted with wholesale CBDC settlement.
  • Cross-border: an MoU with Singapore's central bank and BIS projects (Rialto, Mandala); cross-border pilots are planned for 2026-27.

4. Challenges

  • Low adoption: free, instant UPI leaves users little reason to switch.
  • Privacy: fears of transaction tracking call for strong safeguards under the DPDP Act, 2023.
  • Bank disintermediation: a large shift of deposits into e₹ could hurt bank lending; hence it pays no interest.

The e₹ is a calibrated, pilot-led reform. Its future lies less in competing with UPI than in programmable welfare, offline payments and cheaper cross-border settlement.

Financial inclusionInclusive growthJAM trinityFI-Index

The Rangarajan Committee (2008) defined financial inclusion as access to financial services, and timely and adequate credit, for vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups at an affordable cost. Where most workers are informal, exclusion from finance traps households in moneylender debt, so inclusion is a building block of inclusive growth, not merely a banking goal.

1. An integral part of economic inclusion

  • Credit for livelihoods: Mudra loans (2015), Stand-Up India, PM SVANidhi (2020) and SHG–bank linkage give small borrowers working capital and reduce dependence on moneylenders.
  • Savings and assets: PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) has over 59 crore accounts with about ₹3.17 lakh crore in deposits (August 2026).
  • Risk protection: PMJJBY, PMSBY and the Atal Pension Yojana (2015) protect families from falling back into poverty after a death, accident or old age.
  • Formalisation: digital payments build credit histories that enable collateral-free loans to MSMEs and street vendors.

2. An integral part of social inclusion

  • Women's agency: about 56% of Jan Dhan accounts belong to women, and SHGs under DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women) give them savings, credit and a voice.
  • Direct Benefit Transfer: the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) delivers scholarships, pensions and PM-KISAN directly, cutting out middlemen who exploit the poor.
  • Reach: 78% of Jan Dhan accounts are in rural or semi-urban areas; business correspondents and the India Post Payments Bank (2018) serve remote, tribal and hill villages.
  • Necessary but not sufficient: dormant accounts, low use of credit and insurance, and digital fraud show that access alone is not inclusion; the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis (2010) showed that credit without safeguards can deepen distress.

3. RBI's Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index)

  • Design: launched in August 2021 and published annually, it scores inclusion from 0 (complete exclusion) to 100 (full inclusion) using 97 indicators across banking, investments, insurance, postal and pension services.
  • Three sub-indices: Access (35%), Usage (45%) and Quality (20%); quality covers financial literacy, consumer protection and deficiencies in services.
  • Trend: the index rose to 70.0 in March 2026 from 67.0 a year earlier, driven mainly by higher usage (RBI, July 2026).

4. Usefulness of the index

  • Measures depth, not just accounts: the heavy weight on usage and quality shifts attention from opening accounts to using them well.
  • Single, comparable measure: it combines banking, insurance, pension, postal and securities services and tracks progress year by year.
  • Guides policy: it shows which dimension lags, helping targets under the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion.
  • Limits: a single national figure does not show which States, social groups or genders are left out, and it relies mostly on supply-side data from institutions.

Financial inclusion is the gateway to social and economic citizenship. The next step is meaningful inclusion: State-level and gender-wise indices, financial literacy and strong protection against digital fraud.

In 1986 the government launched Technology Missions to solve national problems in a time-bound mission mode, covering drinking water, literacy, immunisation, telecommunications, dairy and oilseeds. In agriculture they began with the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (TMO, 1986), which brought the Yellow Revolution. The model, which joins research, extension, inputs, prices and markets under one plan, was later extended to pulses, maize, cotton, horticulture and jute.

1. Major Technology Missions in agriculture

  • TMO: improved seeds, plant protection and crop practices, with assured MSP and market support through NAFED and import controls on edible oils.
  • Cotton mission (2000): four mini-missions covered research (ICAR), transfer of technology, market yards, and modernisation of ginning and pressing factories; the Union Budget 2025-26 announced a five-year Mission for Cotton Productivity.
  • Horticulture mission for the North-East and Himalayan States: planting material, post-harvest handling and markets; it later merged into the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (2014-15).
  • New-generation missions: the National Mission on Edible Oils (oil palm, 2021; oilseeds, 2024) and the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (2025) revive the TMO approach to cut imports.

2. Role in food security

  • Availability: oilseed output more than doubled between the mid-1980s and the mid-1990s, and India came close to self-sufficiency in edible oils in the early 1990s.
  • Nutritional security: oilseeds and pulses supply fats and proteins, and horticulture supplies vitamins and minerals; India is now the second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables.
  • Economic access: higher yields and assured prices raised the incomes of dryland farmers, who grow most oilseeds and pulses, improving their ability to buy food.
  • Stability: hardy crops such as groundnut, mustard and pulses diversify rain-fed farming and reduce risk in drought years.
  • Import substitution: saving foreign exchange on edible oils and pulses protects food security against world price shocks.

3. Limitations

  • Gains not sustained: after import duties on edible oils were cut in the late 1990s, cheap palm and soybean oil flooded in; India now imports over half of its edible oil.
  • Cereal bias: MSP and procurement still favour rice and wheat, so farmers find oilseeds and pulses riskier.
  • Rain-fed constraints: low seed replacement, little irrigation and climate shocks keep yields below world levels.
  • Fragmented delivery: frequent restructuring and weak convergence among departments diluted focus.

Technology Missions show that the mission mode works when technology, prices and markets move together. The new oilseed, pulse and cotton missions can secure nutrition security if they learn from the TMO's early success and later slide.

Agricultural marketingAPMC regulationIntermediariese-NAM and e-commerce

Agricultural marketing covers everything from the farm gate to the consumer: assembly, grading, storage, transport and sale. It is a State subject (Entry 28, State List, "markets and fairs") and is regulated by each State's APMC Act. Because the chain is long and fragmented, farmers, especially growers of perishables, get a small share of the consumer's rupee.

1. Factors responsible for inefficiency

  • Too few, distant markets: the National Commission on Farmers (Swaminathan) sought a regulated market within about 5 km of every farmer; many farmers instead sell to village traders at low prices.
  • Long chain of intermediaries: commission agents, wholesalers and retailers each take a margin; market fees, cartels among licensed traders and delayed payments add to the farmer's loss.
  • Weak infrastructure: few assaying labs, grading facilities, cold stores and warehouses, and poor rural roads, so produce is sold ungraded and post-harvest losses are high, especially in fruits and vegetables.
  • Small, scattered lots: 86% of holdings are small and marginal, so farmers lack bargaining power and must sell immediately after harvest (distress sale) to repay loans.
  • Fragmented regulation: separate State APMC laws, multiple licences and restrictions on inter-State trade split India into many markets; the 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021, so reform rests with the States.
  • Information gaps: farmers often do not know prices in other markets or future demand, which fuels boom-and-bust cycles in tomato, onion and potato.

2. How e-commerce reduces these inefficiencies

  • e-NAM (14 April 2016): links APMC mandis on one electronic platform with online bidding, assaying and payment into farmers' bank accounts; it covers 1,656 mandis in 23 States and 4 UTs, over 1.8 crore farmers and 4,724 FPOs, with trade of about ₹4.84 lakh crore since 2016 (PIB, March 2026).
  • More buyers, better price discovery: traders from other mandis and States can bid on the same lot, which weakens local cartels.
  • Fewer intermediaries: the open network ONDC, agri-tech platforms and buyer apps let FPOs sell directly to retailers, processors and exporters, often buying at the farm gate.
  • Warehouse-based trading: electronic negotiable warehouse receipts (regulated by the WDRA) let farmers store produce, take a loan against it and sell when prices improve.
  • Transparency: real-time prices on apps help farmers decide when and where to sell, and give the government data to manage volatility.

3. Limits of e-commerce

  • Physical gaps: without assaying, grading and cold chains, distant buyers hesitate to bid for produce they cannot see.
  • Digital divide: low digital literacy and patchy internet exclude many small farmers.
  • Little inter-State trade: most e-NAM trades are still local auctions, and several States have not fully adopted unified licences.

E-commerce is a force multiplier, not a substitute for physical infrastructure. Combined with FPO aggregation, farm-gate assaying, cold chains and State-led APMC reform, it can make "One Nation, One Market" a reality.

Fruits, vegetables and flowers are perishable: ripening enzymes soften them, microbes rot them, and a glut at harvest crashes prices. India is the world's second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables, yet only a small share is processed. Biotechnology, the use of living cells, microbes and their enzymes, helps farmers slow spoilage and turn surplus produce into stable, value-added products.

1. How biotechnology helps in processing perishables

  • Less spoilage: natural compounds and harmless microbes slow ripening and rotting, so farmers can stagger sales instead of selling in distress.
  • More value: enzymes and microbial fermentation convert produce into pulp, juice, wine, vinegar and pickles that keep for months.
  • Better raw material: tissue culture supplies uniform, disease-free planting material, such as banana plantlets and seed potatoes for ICAR-CPRI's low-sugar "Kufri Chipsona" processing varieties used for chips.
  • Safety and exports: biotech diagnostics (ELISA, PCR) detect pathogens and toxins quickly, helping produce meet export standards.

2. Example 1: Mango – enzymes and a bio-based freshness spray

  • Enzyme-assisted pulping: India's mango pulp industry, centred on Totapuri mangoes in Chittoor (Andhra Pradesh) and Krishnagiri (Tamil Nadu), uses pectin-degrading enzymes to lower pulp viscosity, raise juice yield and clarify juice. Aseptically packed pulp keeps for months and is exported, giving growers an assured outlet in glut years.
  • Hexanal formulation: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, with Canada's University of Guelph, developed formulations based on hexanal, a natural plant compound that inhibits phospholipase D, the enzyme that breaks down cell membranes during ripening. Sprayed on trees before harvest, or used as dips and stickers after it, it kept mangoes fresh for up to about three weeks longer in trials, letting farmers hold fruit for better prices.

3. Example 2: Grapes – fermentation into wine

  • Microbial fermentation: selected yeasts (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) convert grape sugars into wine, a product that lasts for years, unlike table grapes that spoil in days.

Nuclear reactors are classed by the speed of the neutrons that keep fission going. Thermal reactors, such as India's PHWRs and the Kudankulam VVERs, slow neutrons down with a moderator. A Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) uses fast neutrons and breeds more fissile fuel than it burns. The 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, designed by IGCAR and built by BHAVINI with over 200 Indian firms, attained first criticality on 6 April 2026.

1. FBR vs thermal reactor

  • Breeding: a blanket of uranium-238 around the core absorbs fast neutrons and turns into plutonium-239; later, a thorium blanket can make uranium-233.
  • Why sodium: liquid sodium carries heat well without slowing neutrons and works at near-atmospheric pressure, but it burns in air and reacts violently with water, so it needs special safety systems.
  • Fuel efficiency: thermal reactors use only a small part of uranium's energy, while FBRs with fuel recycling can extract many times more from the same uranium.

2. Criticality explained

  • Meaning: a reactor is critical when each fission causes, on average, exactly one more fission, so the chain reaction sustains itself at a steady rate. Below this it is subcritical and dies out; above it, it is supercritical and power rises.
  • First criticality: the first time a new reactor's chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, at very low power. It is a controlled, safe milestone, not an emergency.
  • Control: operators reach and hold criticality by slowly withdrawing neutron-absorbing control rods.
  • What follows: low-power physics tests, step-by-step power raising, grid connection and commercial operation.

3. Implications for India's clean energy future

  • Stage II of Bhabha's programme: the PFBR multiplies India's modest uranium by producing plutonium and, later, uranium-233 for stage III thorium reactors, using one of the world's largest thorium reserves.
  • Low-carbon baseload: nuclear power gives round-the-clock electricity to balance solar and wind; non-fossil sources are about 55% of capacity, but coal still produces about 70% of electricity.
  • Net zero and 100 GW: fast reactors support the goal of 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047 and net zero by 2070; two more 500 MWe FBRs are at the pre-project stage at Kalpakkam.
  • Closed fuel cycle: reprocessing and recycling reduce long-lived waste.
  • Technology leadership: India will be the second country after Russia with a commercial fast breeder; the SHANTI Act, 2025 now allows private Indian companies into nuclear power, though reprocessing stays with the Centre.

4. Concerns

  • Delays and cost: construction began in 2004, and criticality came over 15 years late.
  • Safety: sodium handling and plutonium security need strict regulation by an independent AERB.

The PFBR's criticality turns Bhabha's vision into reality. Timely commercial operation and fleet-mode FBRs can make nuclear power a pillar of clean energy security.

India's ecologically-sensitive areas, such as the young and fragile Himalaya, the Western Ghats, coasts and islands, need roads, tunnels, hydropower and tourism facilities for connectivity, defence and livelihoods. Poorly planned projects, however, cut slopes, block drains and crowd floodplains, turning natural hazards into disasters. The Sendai Framework (2015–30) and the India-led CDRI (2019) call for risk-informed development: the answer is to build differently, not to stop building.

1. The contradiction: lessons from recent disasters

  • Kedarnath (2013): a cloudburst and glacial-lake outburst swept away settlements and roads built along the Mandakini river.
  • Joshimath (January 2023): land subsidence cracked hundreds of houses in a town built on old landslide debris, with poor drainage, unregulated construction and nearby hydro and road works.
  • Silkyara tunnel (November 2023): a collapse in a Char Dham road tunnel trapped 41 workers for 17 days.
  • Sikkim (October 2023): the South Lhonak glacial lake burst and destroyed the Teesta-III dam at Chungthang.
  • Wayanad (30 July 2024): landslides in the Western Ghats killed over 200 people in an area flagged as ecologically sensitive by the Gadgil panel (2011).

2. Why development raises risk

  • Ignoring geology: roads and buildings on unstable slopes or old debris, and vertical slope cuts without retaining structures.
  • Piecemeal clearances: large projects split into small parts escape a full Environmental Impact Assessment; the Char Dham road project was divided into segments under 100 km, and cumulative impacts of many dams on one river are rarely studied.
  • Exceeding carrying capacity: unregulated hotels and traffic in hill towns load fragile slopes and drainage.
  • Climate change: heavier rain, cloudbursts and glacier retreat raise hazards faster than designs assume.

3. Managing the contradiction

  • Risk-informed planning: landslide and hazard zonation (GSI is the nodal agency), carrying-capacity studies for hill towns, and building bylaws that keep construction off floodplains and debris slopes.
  • Better assessment: strategic and cumulative EIA for river basins and corridors, no splitting of projects, and expert monitoring, as the Supreme Court's high-powered committee did for Char Dham.
  • Engineering for resilience: geotechnical surveys, slope stabilisation, scientific muck disposal, drainage, and escape passages and safety audits in tunnels.
  • Nature-based solutions: forests, wetlands and mangroves (MISHTI, 2023) act as natural buffers; eco-sensitive zones protect critical slopes.
  • Institutions and people: glacial-lake monitoring and early warning, local disaster plans under the DM (Amendment) Act, 2025, and community participation in project decisions.

Development and safety need not be rivals. Building resilience into every project, guided by Sendai's "Build Back Better" and the principle of risk-informed development, will let the Himalaya and the Western Ghats gain infrastructure without paying for it in lives.

Fake news is false or misleading content presented as news; disinformation is falsehood spread deliberately to deceive. With hundreds of millions of social-media users, encrypted messaging and cheap AI tools that create deepfakes, a rumour can reach millions within hours in India. Hostile states and extremists use it as a tool of hybrid warfare, making it a threat to internal security and to public order (a State subject, Entry 1 of the State List).

1. How fake news threatens internal security and public order

  • Communal violence: a doctored video helped inflame the Muzaffarnagar riots (2013).
  • Mob lynching: WhatsApp rumours about child-lifters led to lynchings in 2018, after which WhatsApp limited message forwarding in India.

2. Salient features of the amendments to the IT Rules, 2021

The IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, made under the IT Act, 2000, require platforms to remove unlawful content and appoint grievance and compliance officers.

  • 2022: Grievance Appellate Committees hear users' appeals against platforms' decisions, and platforms must respect users' constitutional rights.
  • 2023: a Central Government fact-check unit could flag "fake" content about government business; the Supreme Court stayed it (March 2024) and the Bombay High Court struck it down (September 2024) under Articles 14 and 19.
  • 2025 (in force 15 November 2025): takedown intimations under Rule 3(1)(d) only from senior officers (Joint Secretary rank, or DIG rank for the police), stating the legal basis and the exact content, with a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer.
  • 2026 (notified 10 February, in force 20 February): defines "synthetically generated information" (AI-made or altered audio-visual content that looks real); platforms must label it prominently and, where technically feasible, embed permanent metadata that cannot be removed; large platforms must obtain and verify users' declarations; AI tools must block unlawful synthetic content such as child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images.
  • Faster action (2026): takedown on government or court orders cut from 36 hours to 3 hours; complaints about intimate or morphed images to be acted on within 2 hours (earlier 24); grievances resolved in 7 days (earlier 15). 3. Concerns

  • Free speech: tight deadlines may push platforms to over-remove lawful content, against the spirit of Shreya Singhal (2015).
  • Executive discretion and feasibility: takedowns lack independent review, and reliable deepfake detection is still hard.

The answer lies in calibrated co-regulation: transparent takedowns, independent oversight, quick fact-checks and mass digital literacy, balancing public order with free speech.

Energy security is the uninterrupted availability of energy at an affordable price (IEA). India is the world's third-largest energy consumer and third-largest oil consumer; its peak power demand hit a record 270.8 GW on 21 May 2026. With crude-oil import dependence of about 89%, the 2026 West Asia (Hormuz) crisis exposed how fragile this security is.

1. Key challenges

  • Heavy import dependence: crude imports met 88.7% of needs in 2025-26 (89.1% in April–June 2026), as domestic output fell from 34.2 million tonnes (2018-19) to 28.4 million tonnes (2024-25); about 47% of gas is imported as LNG, and steel makers import coking coal.
  • Chokepoints and geopolitics: the Strait of Hormuz carries about half of India's crude imports and most LPG and LNG imports; the Iran–US–Israel conflict of 2026 raised the import bill, while sanctions in late 2025 cut access to discounted Russian crude.
  • Thin buffers: Strategic Petroleum Reserves of 5.33 million tonnes (Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur) cover only about 9.5 days of crude needs, far below the IEA norm of 90 days of net imports.
  • Coal lock-in and intermittency: non-fossil sources are about 55% of capacity but coal still produces about 70% of electricity; solar fades just as evening demand peaks.
  • New dependencies: polysilicon, wafers and cells largely from China, and lithium, cobalt, nickel and rare earths for batteries.
  • Affordability: loss-making discoms and low per-capita electricity use (1,460 kWh in 2024-25).

2. Measures for security with growth and sustainability

  • Diversify and buffer: buy crude from Russia, the USA, West Africa and Latin America; sign long-term LNG contracts; build SPR Phase II (Chandikhol 4 and Padur-II 2.5 million tonnes), moving towards 90 days of cover.
  • Raise domestic supply: open-acreage exploration under HELP, deep-water fields in the KG basin, commercial coal mining, and coal gasification (100 million tonnes by 2030) to cut imports of LNG, ammonia and methanol.
  • Clean energy with storage: reach 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 with battery and pumped storage and green energy corridors; the National Green Hydrogen Mission (5 million tonnes a year by 2030); E20 ethanol blending (achieved 2025) and compressed biogas.
  • Nuclear power: 100 GW by 2047, the ₹20,000 crore small modular reactor mission, the PFBR's criticality (April 2026) and the SHANTI Act, 2025 that admits private Indian firms.
  • Efficiency first: PAT, UJALA, star labels, the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and electric mobility.
  • Secure supply chains: the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025), overseas mineral assets through KABIL, PLI for solar modules and batteries, ALMM rules for domestic cells, and energy diplomacy through the International Solar Alliance and the Global Biofuels Alliance (2023).

India must manage the energy trilemma of security, affordability and sustainability together. Diversified supplies, larger reserves and a storage-backed clean transition can carry it towards the goal of energy independence by 2047.

At Independence India was food-deficit: foodgrain output was only about 50.8 million tonnes in 1950-51, and the droughts of 1965–67 left the country dependent on PL-480 wheat from the USA, a "ship-to-mouth" existence. Today output exceeds 350 million tonnes (2024-25), free grain reaches about 81 crore people under PMGKAY, and India is a leading rice exporter. Technology, prices and institutions together made this possible; the new task is diversification.

1. How scarcity turned into surplus

  • Institutional base (1950s): abolition of zamindari, multipurpose dams such as Bhakra-Nangal, fertiliser plants and agricultural universities.
  • Green Revolution (from 1966-67): high-yielding dwarf wheat from Norman Borlaug's programme and new rice varieties, led in India by M.S. Swaminathan and Minister C. Subramaniam, with irrigation, fertilisers and credit; wheat output more than doubled between 1965-66 and 1971-72.
  • Price and procurement: the Agricultural Prices Commission (now CACP) and the Food Corporation of India (both 1965) gave assured MSP, procurement, buffer stocks and the PDS.
  • Spread and consolidation: research by ICAR, Kisan Credit Cards (1998), the National Food Security Mission (2007), RKVY (2007) and Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India (2010-11).
  • Rights-based food security: the National Food Security Act, 2013 turned surplus into a legal entitlement.

2. Why diversification is now needed

  • Cereal bias: MSP and assured procurement favour rice and wheat, while pulses and edible oils are imported.
  • Ecological stress: paddy–wheat in Punjab and Haryana has depleted groundwater and degraded soils.
  • Nutrition: 35.5% of children under five are stunted (NFHS-5), so diets need pulses, fruits, vegetables, milk and fish.
  • Incomes and climate: high-value and hardy crops raise incomes and spread risk.

3. Policies for diversification

  • Price signals: the government sets relatively higher MSPs for pulses, oilseeds and millets to encourage a shift, with procurement under PM-AASHA; Haryana's "Mera Pani Meri Virasat" (2020) pays farmers to shift from paddy.
  • Markets and processing: e-NAM, 10,000 FPOs, PM Kisan SAMPADA and "One District One Product" link new crops to buyers.
  • Water and inputs: micro-irrigation under PMKSY, natural farming and seed missions support less water-hungry crops.
  • Result and gaps: horticulture output now exceeds foodgrains, and India leads in milk; but the pull of paddy procurement, weak markets for pulses and oilseeds, and small holdings slow the shift.

India has moved from food security to nutrition security as its goal. Remunerative prices, assured markets and water-smart policies can make diversification the "Evergreen Revolution" that M.S. Swaminathan envisioned.

Mission Drishti is the first satellite of GalaxEye Space, a Bengaluru start-up founded in 2021 by IIT Madras alumni. Launched on 3 May 2026 on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg, California, the 190 kg satellite was billed as the world's first OptoSAR satellite: it carried an optical camera and a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) on one platform, designed to fuse their images. It was described as the largest Earth-observation satellite built by India's private sector.

1. Salient features of Mission Drishti

  • Orbit and size: about 190 kg, in a sun-synchronous orbit of about 500 km.
  • Dual payload: an optical (electro-optical) imager and a SAR with a deployable 3.5 m antenna, imaging the same area together, at a combined resolution of about 1.2–3.6 m.
  • Onboard intelligence: an NVIDIA Jetson Orin edge-computing chip to process and fuse data in orbit, and electric propulsion for orbit control.
  • NewSpace milestone: a product of the 2020 reforms that opened space to private firms.
  • Intended uses: defence surveillance, crop monitoring, disasters and maritime watch.
  • Status: in July 2026 GalaxEye reported that a geomagnetic (solar) storm had damaged a critical component; contact was lost and recovery looked unlikely. Its onboard computing and communication had worked in the first weeks, but it never completed its early-orbit phase; the company plans two larger (300 kg) satellites.

2. Imaging techniques used

  • Optical imaging (passive): records sunlight reflected from the surface, giving photo-like images that are easy to interpret; in multispectral form it also shows crop health. It fails at night and under cloud, smoke or haze.
  • Synthetic Aperture Radar (active): the satellite sends microwave pulses and records their echoes; its motion along the orbit is used to "synthesise" a very long antenna, sharpening resolution. Microwaves pass through cloud and work day and night, revealing floods, ships and ground movement, but images are grainy.
  • OptoSAR fusion: by design, both sensors image a spot at the same moment from the same platform, and onboard software aligns (co-registers) and merges them with AI, combining optical clarity with radar's all-weather reliability. GalaxEye claimed about three times more information than conventional satellites.

3. Why it was called the world's first of its kind

  • Separate satellites until now: optical (Sentinel-2, Cartosat) and radar (Sentinel-1, RISAT, NISAR) missions fly separately, so their images are taken at different times and angles and must be matched on the ground.
  • Matching errors: in the gap ships move and floods spread, so combined products lose accuracy and arrive late.
  • One platform, one moment: GalaxEye says Drishti was the first satellite built to carry both sensors together, capture simultaneously and fuse onboard, hence "OptoSAR".
  • Value for India: monsoon cloud hides much of India for months, so fused all-weather data aids defence and disaster response.

Even though the satellite was lost, Mission Drishti proved that Indian start-ups can attempt frontier space technology. Lessons on space-weather resilience can help GalaxEye's planned constellation deliver all-weather sovereign Earth observation.

Human approval for high-stakes actions, permission limits, audit trails and skilling can make agentic AI a safe force multiplier for Viksit Bharat.

  • Weak municipal capacity: low user fees, few trained staff and poor data.
  • Technology mismatch: wet, low-calorie waste burns poorly in waste-to-energy plants, which risk emitting dioxins.
  • Informal sector and behaviour: waste-pickers recover recyclables without social protection, and littering and local opposition to facilities persist.

  • Extended Producer Responsibility: producers must ensure collection and recycling of plastic packaging, e-waste and batteries; the C&D Waste Rules, 2025 (from April 2026) set recycling targets for large construction projects.

  • Slow biomining: clearing legacy waste has missed deadlines set by the NGT, and the Supreme Court (2024) criticised the large quantity of waste left untreated every day.

4. Indore: a success story

  • Cleanest city in Swachh Survekshan seven years running (2017–2023) and part of the Super Swachh League (2024-25).
  • Segregation at source: door-to-door collection of segregated waste (up to six streams) by GPS-tracked vehicles, bin-free streets, user charges and spot fines.
  • Processing, not dumping: a 550-tonne-a-day bio-CNG plant (2022) under GOBARdhan fuels city buses; about 100 acres were reclaimed at the Devguradia dumpsite after legacy waste was cleared.
  • People and leadership: citizen ownership, NGOs and continuity in municipal leadership.

In any disaster, the community is the first responder: in the first hours, most survivors are pulled out by neighbours long before official teams arrive. The Sendai Framework (2015–30) calls for an "all-of-society" approach, and India's Disaster Management Act, 2005, the National Disaster Management Plan and the Prime Minister's Ten-Point Agenda (2016) stress community-based disaster risk management (CBDRM). 1. Why community participation is the cornerstone

  • Local knowledge: people know local hazards, safe routes and who is most vulnerable; in the 2004 tsunami, indigenous tribes of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands moved to higher ground using traditional knowledge.
  • The golden hour: local volunteers act within minutes, when rescue saves the most lives.
  • Ownership: plans, drills and shelters built with people are actually used and maintained.
  • Social capital: self-help groups and panchayats rebuild livelihoods faster than distant agencies.

  • Odisha's cyclone model: after the 1999 super cyclone killed about 10,000 people, community-managed cyclone shelters, trained village volunteers and drills helped evacuate around a million people before Phailin (2013) and over a million before Fani (2019), cutting deaths sharply.

  • Gujarat earthquake (2001): owner-driven reconstruction, with money and technical help for families rebuilding their homes, became a global model.

  • Institutionalise it: village and ward disaster committees linked to panchayat and municipal plans; the DM (Amendment) Act, 2025 adds urban disaster management authorities and disaster databases.
  • Train and equip volunteers: expand Aapda Mitra, NCC, NSS, civil defence and home guards, with insurance cover, kits and regular drills.
  • Inclusive planning: follow NDMA's guidelines on disability-inclusive DRR (2019); involve women's SHGs as first responders.
  • Last-mile warnings: SACHET alerts in local languages, cell broadcast, sirens and community radio.
  • Awareness: school safety programmes, mock drills and traditional knowledge.

Communities are the first and last responders. Empowering, funding and training them turns disaster management from relief into resilience, the true spirit of a whole-of-society approach.

In India, Fake Indian Currency Notes (FICN) and money laundering through hawala, front companies and misused charities have funded militancy in Jammu and Kashmir, insurgency in the North-East and Left Wing Extremism.   • Economic terrorism: Indian agencies have traced high-quality FICN to printing networks across the border, smuggled through Nepal, Bangladesh and the Gulf; the West Bengal border (Malda) has been a major route.
  • Dual purpose: fake notes fund terror modules and weaken trust in the rupee.
  • Law: since a 2012 amendment, producing or circulating high-quality counterfeit currency is a "terrorist act" under Section 15 of the UAPA; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 also punishes counterfeiting.
  • Response: the NIA's Terror Funding and Fake Currency cell, the MHA's FICN Coordination Group, an India–Bangladesh MoU on FICN (2015) and new note security features after demonetisation (2016).

2. Money laundering and terror funding

  • Channels: hawala, false trade invoicing, shell companies, cash couriers, misused non-profits, crypto assets and illegal betting apps.
  • Narco-terror: drugs from the Golden Crescent, sometimes dropped by drones across the Punjab border, fund militant networks.
  • Examples: NIA's 2017 case against separatist leaders in J&K traced hawala money; extortion "levies" fund Maoists.
  • Response: the ED enforces the PMLA, upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (2022); FIU-IND analyses suspicious transaction reports; virtual-asset service providers were brought under the PMLA in 2023; the FCRA was tightened in 2020.

  • India's rating: India's mutual evaluation (adopted June 2024) placed it in "regular follow-up", the best category, shared with only a few G20 countries.

Defeating terror finance needs a whole-of-government approach at home and diplomacy that makes the FATF and the UN hold state sponsors to account, so that "No Money for Terror" becomes a global norm.

A Ph.D. evaluation is a position of public trust: the examiner certifies, under his own signature, that a thesis is original and worthy of a doctorate. Getting generative AI to write the report and submitting it with a few changes hands the judgement to a machine while the signature stays human. 1. Accountability: answerability for the verdict

  • Non-delegable duty: the university appointed the professor for his expert judgement. Tools may assist, but the assessment of originality, method and contribution cannot be outsourced; he remains answerable for every line he signs.
  • Risk of error: AI tools can misread data, invent references or give generic praise. A wrong verdict may fail a deserving scholar or pass a weak thesis, and the blame cannot be shifted to software.
  • Confidentiality: uploading an unpublished thesis to a public AI tool may breach the candidate's intellectual property and the university's confidentiality norms; many journals bar reviewers from feeding manuscripts into generative AI for this reason.
  • Answerability to stakeholders: the candidate, the university, the regulator and employers all rely on the report; a degree is only as credible as its evaluation.

  • Misrepresentation: presenting machine-written text as one's own considered opinion is intellectual dishonesty, the very fault examiners must detect under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018.
  • Double standard: a professor who would penalise a student for undisclosed AI use cannot use it himself; integrity means consistency between what one demands and what one does.
  • Fairness to the scholar: years of research deserve a careful reading; a shortcut violates the duty of care owed to the candidate.
  • Role model: teachers shape the ethical culture of academia; such conduct normalises shortcuts among future researchers.

3. The right course

  • Honest refusal over dishonest acceptance: heavy workload justifies asking for more time or declining the assignment, not cutting corners.
  • Disclosure: if AI is used for limited support, the university should be told.
  • Institutional policy: universities should frame clear rules for examiners on AI use, in line with the India AI Governance Guidelines (MeitY, November 2025), whose principles include accountability and a people-first approach with human oversight.

AI can assist, but it cannot replace professional judgement: whoever signs a report owns it. Accountability and intellectual honesty require the professor either to evaluate the thesis himself or to decline openly.

As the district's administrative officer, I am expected to facilitate investment, yet I am also the statutory guardian of their rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA), PESA, 1996 and, in Scheduled Areas, the Fifth Schedule. This dual role creates several ethical challenges.

  • Legal duty under pressure: under Section 4(5) of the FRA, no forest dweller can be evicted until the recognition and verification of rights is complete. Pressure from the company, and sometimes from above, to speed up clearances will test my integrity.
  • Consent, not mere consultation: in the Niyamgiri case (Orissa Mining Corporation v MoEF, 2013), the Supreme Court left it to the gram sabhas to decide whether bauxite mining would affect their religious and cultural rights, and they rejected it.   • Information asymmetry: project documents are often technical and in English; honesty requires translation, open public hearings and time to deliberate.

  • Avoiding conflict of interest: gifts, hospitality or CSR offers from the business house must not influence official decisions.

  • The most vulnerable: women, the elderly, PVTGs and families without land records risk being left off compensation lists.

  • Empathy with neutrality: sympathy for the community must not turn into bias against legitimate development; I must be fair to both sides.
  • Loyalty versus conscience: if superiors push for shortcuts, I must give frank advice on file rather than silently comply.

The DM faces a clash between the urge to help a suffering endangered tribe quickly and the duty to do no harm. The university study only suggests a possible remedy; without clinical trials, the supplement's safety, dose and effectiveness are unknown, and distributing it would make the tribe subjects of an unregulated experiment. The answer is therefore no: the DM should not apply the research directly, but should help it become a lawful trial while providing proven care now.

1. Medical ethics perspective

  • Non-maleficence: minerals can be toxic in excess (excess fluoride, for example, itself causes skeletal fluorosis); an untested dose could worsen the deformity or harm children and pregnant women.
  • Informed consent: the Nuremberg Code (1947) and the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) make voluntary, informed consent essential. Language barriers, low literacy and dependence on officials make genuine consent from an isolated tribe very difficult.
  • Regulatory route: the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 and the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017) require ethics-committee approval, trial registration, compensation for injury and added protection for vulnerable groups.
  • Justice: a vulnerable community should share in the benefits of research, not merely bear its risks.

2. Administrative ethics perspective

  • Rule of law and competence: a DM has no authority to approve or prescribe an untested remedy; doing so exceeds his mandate and exposes the state to liability.

  • Trust: a failed experiment could destroy the tribe's trust in health services for years.
  • Protective duty: Article 46 obliges the state to protect Scheduled Tribes from exploitation, and Article 21 includes the right to health; for an endangered tribe, the state is a trustee, not an experimenter.

  • Diagnose first: a medical team from the state health department, ICMR or a medical college should study the causes (nutrition, water quality, genetics), since proven measures may already exist.
  • Fast-track, do not skip, the trial: facilitate an approved trial with independent monitoring and community consultation.
  • Care now: nutrition support, physiotherapy, orthopaedic aids and disability certification under the RPwD Act, 2016.

National security, the protection of sovereignty, territorial integrity and citizens' lives, is a precondition for enjoying rights. Yet powers used in its name, such as preventive detention, surveillance and special laws, can erode the fundamental rights of Part III and India's commitments under the ICCPR. The ethical task is not to choose one over the other but to reconcile them through proportionality and the rule of law.

1. Why the two are interdependent

  • Security protects rights: terrorism, insurgency and cyber-attacks threaten the right to life itself; protecting citizens is the state's first duty.
  • Rights strengthen security: abuses alienate communities and feed insurgency; legitimacy and public trust are the best counter-insurgency tools.
  • Constitutional design: Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India and the security of the State, while Article 22 allows preventive detention only with safeguards.

2. Where the tension arises

  • Special laws: UAPA, AFSPA and preventive detention laws give wide powers; in Union of India v K.A. Najeeb (2021), the Supreme Court upheld bail despite UAPA's strict bail clause because prolonged pre-trial detention violated Article 21.
  • Surveillance and privacy: Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy a fundamental right; in the Pegasus matter (Manohar Lal Sharma v UoI, 2021), the Court held that invoking national security does not place the state beyond judicial review and appointed an expert committee.
  • Internet shutdowns: in Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Court held that suspensions must be necessary, proportionate, temporary and subject to review.
  • Armed forces in disturbed areas: in Extra Judicial Execution Victim Families Association v UoI (2016), it held that there is no absolute immunity for excessive force, even under AFSPA.

3. How to strike the balance

  • Targeted and time-bound measures: sunset clauses and periodic review prevent emergency powers from becoming permanent.
  • Independent oversight: prior authorisation and review of surveillance, as in the safeguards on phone-tapping laid down in PUCL v UoI (1997); speedy trials and compensation for wrongful detention.
  • A non-derogable core: after the 44th Amendment (1978), Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency; Article 4 of the ICCPR likewise bars derogation from the right to life and the ban on torture.
  • Reform of special laws: the Jeevan Reddy Committee (2005) and the Second ARC's report on Public Order (2007) recommended repealing AFSPA and placing necessary powers in a more humane legal framework.
  • Ethical training of forces: human-rights modules, body cameras and community policing build professionalism and trust.

Security without rights slides into authoritarianism; rights without security remain fragile. A rule-of-law approach, in which every security measure is lawful, necessary, proportionate and accountable, keeps India both secure and free.

In his closing speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949, Dr B.R. Ambedkar urged Indians to abandon civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha once constitutional methods were open, calling them the "grammar of anarchy". Yet history also shows that peaceful, conscientious law-breaking, or civil disobedience, has advanced social justice. Modern democracies must therefore balance constitutional order with the claims of conscience.

1. The ethical dilemma

  • Ambedkar's logic: where courts, elections, a free press and legislatures exist, bypassing them weakens the rule of law; if every group disobeys laws it dislikes, democracy degenerates into rule by the street.
  • Context matters: Ambedkar himself led the Mahad Satyagraha (1927) and the Kalaram Temple entry movement (1930) when constitutional routes were closed to Dalits; his caution concerned a democracy in which those routes are open.
  • The case for disobedience: Thoreau, Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr held that there is a moral duty to resist unjust laws, openly and non-violently, while accepting the penalty.
  • Genuine concerns on both sides: a policy may pursue a legitimate aim such as security or development while hurting a group's rights; majority will and minority rights both carry moral weight.

2. How democracies should respond

  • Protect peaceful protest as a right: Article 19(1)(a) and (b) guarantee free speech and peaceful assembly; in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v UoI (2018), the Supreme Court balanced protesters' rights with residents' rights at Jantar Mantar and Boat Club.
  • Set reasonable limits: in Amit Sahni v Commissioner of Police (2020), the Shaheen Bagh case, the Court held that public ways cannot be occupied indefinitely; dissent must not trample others' rights.
  • Answer with dialogue, not repression: the repeal of the three farm laws in 2021 after a year-long protest shows the value of consultation; the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014) should be followed for contentious laws.
  • Keep constitutional channels effective: prompt courts, parliamentary committees, RTI and grievance systems make disobedience less necessary.
  • Respond proportionately: minimum force, no blanket bans, and preventive detention only as a last resort.

3. Ethical principles to guide

  • Constitutional morality: Ambedkar's own ideal, which binds both rulers and citizens to respect constitutional limits.
  • Rawls's conditions: in A Theory of Justice (1971), civil disobedience is justified only against clear and substantial injustice, after normal appeals fail, and in a public, non-violent form.
  • Gandhian satyagraha: truth, non-violence and self-suffering, which seek to convert the opponent rather than coerce him.

Ambedkar's warning and Gandhi's method are reconciled when dissent is non-violent, public and a last resort, and when the state is responsive. A mature democracy keeps its channels so open that conscience rarely needs to break the law.

  • Public trust doctrine: in M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997), the Supreme Court held that the state is a trustee of natural resources such as rivers, forests and the seashore.   • Frugality: the General Financial Rules, 2017 expect every officer to guard public money as carefully as a prudent person guards his own.
  • Intergenerational equity: District Mineral Foundations, created by the MMDR Amendment Act, 2015, return part of mining wealth to affected communities, while forest and water protection preserves the trust for future generations.

3. Fairness to the weakest

  • Gandhi's talisman: before a decision, recall the poorest person you have seen and ask whether the step will help him; this is a practical test of fairness in targeting.
  • Inclusive delivery: priority to PVTGs, persons with disabilities and the landless; camps in remote areas so that entitlements reach those who cannot reach the office.
  • Persuading private trustees: channelling CSR funds (Section 135, Companies Act, 2013) and local philanthropy into district priorities such as schools and nutrition is a modern form of trusteeship.

  • Trusteeship relies on persuasion and conscience; it must be backed by law, audit and rule-based discretion, so that "trust" does not become an excuse for paternalism.

Trusteeship turns authority into service. When officers see themselves as custodians rather than masters of power and resources, governance becomes fair, frugal and inclusive.
